docs.title: Everpure Tech Atlas
docs.text:
A strategy-level knowledge base on storage, AI storage and the competitive landscape around Everpure (formerly Pure Storage; NYSE: P, formerly PSTG).

It is written for a corporate-development / strategy professional with a semiconductor-M&A background who needs to hold credible, efficient conversations with Everpure product managers, engineering leaders and the Office of the CTO. The atlas explains how things work, why the trade-offs exist, and what they mean strategically. The default depth is L2 (mechanism): enough to whiteboard a design and say why it wins for a workload, without implementation detail.

Read it as a website: the same content is published as an MkDocs site via GitHub Pages (see Building the site). On github.com, every chapter renders natively, including Mermaid diagrams.

简体中文参考译本 / Simplified Chinese reference edition: the whole atlas (all 62 chapters, glossary, README/PROGRESS/CLAUDE and the meta/ documents) is mirrored in Simplified Chinese under Chinese translation/. It is for reference; the English text is authoritative.

Public information only. Nothing here is confidential or speculates about non-public Everpure plans. Strategy content is framed as options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information. Every time-sensitive number is footnoted with its source and date. Unverified items are marked [VERIFY: …] and collected in meta/open-questions.md.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text: If you have… Do this 10 minutes Read 0.2 The one-page map: the domain mindmap and "Everpure in 10 diagrams". 2 hours Follow the crash course in 0.1 How to use this atlas: TL;DRs of the key chapters plus the signature figures. 2 days Follow the 2-day ramp in 0.1: the core of Parts 1–4 on day 1; the core of Parts 5–6 plus Ch 53–57 on day 2. 2 weeks Follow the 2-week mastery plan in 0.1, with the question bank and 279 flashcards. A meeting tomorrow Use the Conversation Toolkit and the conversation playbook at the end of each relevant chapter.

docs.title: Learning paths at a glance
docs.text:
• 2-hour crash course: 0.2 map → TL;DRs of Ch 2 media, Ch 13 storage stack, Ch 16 DASE, Ch 24 decision matrix, Ch 26 DirectFlash, Ch 30 AI pipeline, Ch 32 KV cache, Ch 41 why AI-native vendors won and Ch 45 head-to-head → Ch 58 explain it in 30 seconds. The full list (12 TL;DRs plus six signature figures) is in 0.1.
  • 2-day ramp: Day 1 covers the core of Parts 1–4 (fundamentals, protocols, architectures, Everpure). Day 2 covers the core of Parts 5–6 (AI storage, industry and competition) plus Ch 53–57. About six hours on day 1 and five on day 2.
  • 2-week mastery: every chapter, with daily flashcards, the question bank and two "whiteboard rehearsals" per week. The full day-by-day schedule is in 0.1.

docs.title: How the atlas was built and how to trust it
docs.text:
• Sources. Every quantitative or time-sensitive claim carries a footnote with publisher, publication date and retrieval date. The deduplicated bibliography is in meta/sources.md. Private-company figures (VAST, WEKA, DDN and others) are labelled company-stated, reported by press or estimated.
  • Known limits. The build environment could not fetch many primary sites directly, including sec.gov, vendor sites and several trade publications. Those facts were taken from search results that surfaced the primary URL, cross-checked where possible, and otherwise tagged [VERIFY: search-summary only]. See meta/decisions.md D13.
  • Independent review. Each Part was fact-checked by a reviewer that did not draft it, briefed as "a skeptical principal storage engineer and a buy-side analyst". The findings and fixes are in meta/reviews/, and unresolved items are in meta/open-questions.md.
  • Judgment calls. These are logged in meta/decisions.md. Quadrant placements, heatmap ratings and radar scores are the atlas's judgment and are labelled that way.
  • Copyright. All text is original, and all diagrams are original redrawings in Mermaid or SVG. Quotes are under 15 words.

docs.title: Building the site
docs.text:
pip install mkdocs-material pyyaml matplotlib pandas

python3 scripts/make_charts.py && python3 scripts/build_glossary.py && python3 scripts/sync_root.py

mkdocs serve

QA tools:

python3 scripts/wordcount.py

bash scripts/lint_mermaid.sh

python3 scripts/check_links.py

python3 scripts/qa_report.py

The GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/deploy.yml) rebuilds the charts and the site on every push and publishes it to the gh-pages branch. To serve it, the repository owner sets Settings → Pages → Source: Deploy from a branch → gh-pages once. The site URL is then https://frankhuang94.github.io/storage-_db_claude/.

docs.title: Numbers and symbols
docs.text: • 3-2-1-1-0 rule — Backup guideline of three copies, two media, one off-site, one immutable or offline, and zero restore-verification errors. (Ch 6)

docs.title: A
docs.text:
• Accelerator utilisation (AU) — the share of time a simulated accelerator spends computing rather than waiting for data; MLPerf Storage results must stay above a threshold. (Ch 37)
  • Acknowledgement point — the moment a storage system tells the host that a write is durable. (Ch 56)
  • Active recall — Producing an answer from memory before checking it, rather than rereading the material. (Ch 59)
  • Active/non-optimized path — A working path that costs an extra internal hop and is used only when optimized paths fail. (Ch 14)
  • Active/optimized path — A path the array advertises as the preferred, lowest-latency route to a volume. (Ch 14)
  • Active/passive — A controller arrangement in which one controller serves all I/O while the other waits to take over. (Ch 14)
  • Adam optimizer — The standard optimizer for large models, which stores a running mean (first moment) and running variance (second moment) of each parameter's gradient. (Ch 31)
  • AFR (annualized failure rate) — The fraction of devices expected to fail per year of operation. (Ch 20)
  • AFX — NetApp's disaggregated all-flash ONTAP system in which controllers share NVMe enclosures over a fabric. (Ch 46)
  • Agent rollback — Undoing changes an AI agent made to files, databases or configurations, typically by restoring from snapshots or backups. (Ch 39)
  • Agentic AI — AI systems that plan and carry out multi-step tasks by calling tools and data sources, not just answering a single prompt. (Ch 39)
  • Agentic operations — Infrastructure management in which AI agents diagnose and, within limits, act on systems rather than only advise. (Ch 53)
  • AGPLv3 — A copyleft open-source licence that requires sharing source code even when software is offered over a network. (Ch 19)
  • AHV — Nutanix's hypervisor, the main destination for many VMware migrations. (Ch 47)
  • AI agent — An LLM-driven program that plans and executes multi-step tasks by calling tools, APIs and data sources. (Ch 30)
  • AI Data Engine (AIDE) — NetApp's ONTAP extension that indexes, vectorises and governs data for AI pipelines. (Ch 46)
  • AI data pipeline — The end-to-end flow of data through ingest, curation, training, checkpointing, fine-tuning, inference, RAG and agents, each with its own storage I/O pattern. (Ch 30)
  • AI factory — NVIDIA's term for a data centre whose GPUs, networks, storage and software are designed as one production line whose output is AI tokens. (Ch 35)
  • AI infrastructure tracker (IDC) — IDC's quarterly measure of server and storage spending deployed for AI workloads. (Ch 40)
  • AI momentum — The atlas's composite of 2025–26 evidence of AI-driven growth: revenue, bookings, valuation, design wins, benchmarks and shipping AI features. (Ch 49)
  • AI-native depth — How much of the AI data path a vendor serves on architecture it owns and designed for AI workloads. (Ch 49)
  • AI-native storage vendor — A storage company whose growth and roadmap centre on GPU-cluster workloads, such as VAST Data, WEKA and DDN. (Ch 41)
  • AI-Q blueprint — NVIDIA's reference agent workflow that uses NeMo Retriever microservices to search enterprise data. (Ch 34)
  • AI400X series — DDN's 2U all-NVMe EXAScaler appliances (AI400X, AI400X2, AI400X3, AI400X3M), each generation raising bandwidth per box. (Ch 44)
  • AIOps — Use of analytics and machine learning on infrastructure telemetry to predict faults, open tickets and recommend or take corrective actions. (Ch 22)
  • AIStor — MinIO's commercial object storage product, sold as Free and Enterprise editions after the community edition was archived. (Ch 47)
  • All Software Included — Pure Storage's original licensing model in which every Purity software feature came with the array at no extra charge. (Ch 25)
  • Alletra Storage MP — HPE's common storage hardware platform that runs B10000 block and X10000 object/file software. (Ch 46)
  • Alletra Storage MP X10000 — HPE's disaggregated object store with native NFS, aimed at AI data and KV-cache offload. (Ch 46)
  • ALUA (Asymmetric Logical Unit Access) — The SCSI standard by which an array tells hosts which paths to a volume are optimized, non-optimized, standby or unavailable. (Ch 14)
  • ANA (Asymmetric Namespace Access) — NVMe's multipathing mechanism that reports which paths to a namespace are optimized, the counterpart of SCSI ALUA. (Ch 7)
  • ANN (approximate nearest neighbour) search — Similarity search that trades a small loss of recall for orders-of-magnitude speed-ups over scanning every vector. (Ch 33)
  • Antitrust remedy — A divestiture or behavioural commitment that regulators require before clearing a deal. (Ch 54)
  • Anvil — Hammerspace's metadata server that holds the global namespace and hands out pNFS layouts. (Ch 47)
  • Apache Iceberg — An open table format that adds snapshots, atomic commits, schema evolution and time travel to collections of files in object storage. (Ch 33)
  • Apache Parquet — An open columnar file format optimised for analytic scans, storing columns in compressed pages inside large row groups. (Ch 33)
  • Approved vendor list (AVL) — A platform owner's list of qualified component suppliers that reference designs may use. (Ch 34)
  • Approved-vendor list — Board-language shorthand for NVIDIA's storage certifications, which gate entry to most GPU-cluster deals without ranking vendors. (Ch 58)
  • Architectural maximum — the largest configuration a design allows in principle, before testing and support limits. (Ch 56)
  • Architectural pendulum — The recurring swing of storage design between centralized pools, distributed nodes and disaggregated fabrics as media, network and CPU costs change. (Ch 51)
  • Architecture decision matrix — A grid rating each storage architecture against each workload, used to pick a starting design before comparing vendors. (Ch 24)
  • Architecture review — a structured walk through a system's data path, metadata, failure domains, upgrades, scale limits, performance claims and roadmap dependencies. (Ch 56)
  • Archive storage — The tier that retains rarely accessed data for years at the lowest cost per terabyte, often on tape or cloud archive classes. (Ch 1)
  • Areal density — Bits stored per unit area of a disk platter or chip, the main driver of cost per bit. (Ch 2)
  • ARR multiple — A purchase price or valuation divided by the target's annual recurring revenue. (Ch 54)
  • Array controller software — The operating environment of a storage system (e.g., Purity, ONTAP) that runs placement, RAID or erasure coding, snapshots, replication and data reduction. (Ch 13)
  • ASC 606 — The US GAAP revenue-recognition standard that times revenue to the transfer of control of goods or the delivery of services. (Ch 23, Ch 25)
  • ASC 842 — The US GAAP lease standard that puts most leases on the lessee's balance sheet and defines when a contract contains a lease. (Ch 23)
  • Asymmetric active/active — A controller arrangement in which each controller owns some volumes and forwards I/O for volumes it does not own. (Ch 14)
  • Asynchronous checkpointing — Saving training state by copying it quickly to host memory and writing it to storage in the background while training continues. (Ch 11, Ch 31)
  • Asynchronous replication — Replication that acknowledges locally and ships changes later, so recent writes can be lost. (Ch 6)
  • Atlas judgment — a label for the atlas's own synthesis of public facts, such as quadrant placements or threat rankings. (Ch 0.1)
  • Attach rate — The share of an installed customer base that buys an additional product. (Ch 28, Ch 55)
  • Augmented Memory Grid — WEKA's NeuralMesh feature that streams KV cache between GPU memory and shared flash over RDMA and GPUDirect Storage. (Ch 32)
  • Augmented Memory Grid (AMG) — WEKA's KV-cache offload tier that stores evicted attention key/value blocks on pooled NVMe and streams them back to GPUs. (Ch 43, Ch 45)
  • Azure Managed Lustre — Microsoft Azure's managed Lustre parallel file system service. (Ch 36)
  • Azure Native Qumulo — Qumulo's scale-out file service sold and billed inside Microsoft Azure. (Ch 47)
  • A³I (Accelerated, Any-scale AI) — DDN's family of EXAScaler appliances and reference designs sized for NVIDIA GPU clusters. (Ch 44)

docs.title: B
docs.text:
• Back-end compute fabric — The InfiniBand or Ethernet network that carries GPU-to-GPU traffic between racks in an AI cluster, kept separate from storage and front-end traffic. (Ch 35)
  • Back-end fabric — The network that connects storage compute nodes to storage media, separate from the front-end network clients use. (Ch 16)
  • Back-invalidate — A CXL 3.0 mechanism that lets a memory device recall cache lines from hosts, enabling coherent multi-host sharing. (Ch 12)
  • Bandwidth per TB — The throughput a device or system can deliver per terabyte stored, which falls as hard drives grow larger. (Ch 38)
  • Baseline question — A follow-up that asks what a performance or savings claim is measured against. (Ch 57)
  • BeeGFS — A parallel file system developed by ThinkParQ, a 2014 Fraunhofer spin-off, with separate management, metadata and storage services. (Ch 17)
  • Benchmark normalisation — dividing a benchmark result by rack units, power, price or capacity so that differently sized systems can be compared. (Ch 37, Ch 50)
  • BiCS — Toshiba/Kioxia's 3D NAND architecture, announced in 2007 and now built jointly with Sandisk. (Ch 52)
  • Binding constraint — The single requirement in a deal that eliminates most options before price or performance is compared. (Ch 45)
  • Bit growth — The year-on-year increase in total NAND (or DRAM) bits supplied or demanded, the key supply-demand variable in memory markets. (Ch 52)
  • Bit share — a supplier's share of total NAND capacity shipped, as opposed to its share of revenue. (Ch 48)
  • Bits per cell — The number of bits stored in one flash cell (SLC 1, MLC 2, TLC 3, QLC 4, PLC 5), set by how many voltage states the cell must distinguish. (Ch 52)
  • Blast radius — How much data or service a single component failure can take offline or put into rebuild. (Ch 24, Ch 56)
  • Blended gross margin — A company's overall gross margin as the revenue-weighted mix of higher-margin software and lower-margin hardware. (Ch 50)
  • Block protocol — A protocol that lets a host read and write numbered fixed-size blocks on a remote device, with no notion of files. (Ch 7)
  • Block storage — Storage presented as a volume of numbered fixed-size blocks whose meaning is managed by the host's file system or database. (Ch 1)
  • Bloom filter — A compact probabilistic structure that answers "definitely not present" cheaply, used to avoid deduplication index lookups for new data. (Ch 5)
  • BlueField-4 STX — NVIDIA's 2026 modular storage reference architecture in which storage services run on BlueField-4 DPUs. (Ch 10, Ch 34, Ch 45)
  • Board language — Storage jargon restated in terms of cost, risk, speed or revenue quality for a CFO or board audience. (Ch 58)
  • Bounce buffer — A staging area in host (CPU) memory that data passes through on its way between storage or the network and GPU memory. (Ch 11)
  • Bucket — The container in an object store that holds objects and carries policy, region, billing and versioning settings. (Ch 1, Ch 9)
  • Bucket index sharding — Splitting one bucket's key index into multiple shards so that writes and LIST requests spread across servers. (Ch 18)
  • Buffer-to-buffer credits — Fibre Channel's flow-control scheme, in which a sender transmits only as many frames as the receiver has buffers for, so frames are never dropped for congestion. (Ch 7)
  • Build / buy / partner — The three ways a company can obtain a capability: develop it in-house, acquire it, or contract for it with another firm. (Ch 54)
  • Build, partner or defer — the three answers a PM can give to a product gap. (Ch 55)
  • Bulk-data hop — One network traversal that a data byte makes between the flash that stores it and the client that reads or writes it. (Ch 45)
  • Bundled scaling — The constraint that each added node brings a fixed ratio of compute, cache, capacity and network ports. (Ch 15)
  • Busy polling — Having a dedicated CPU core repeatedly check for completed I/O instead of waiting for an interrupt, trading CPU for lower, steadier latency. (Ch 43)
  • Byte-range GET — An S3 read of only a specified byte range of an object, used to parallelise large reads. (Ch 9)
  • Bε-tree (B-epsilon tree) — A write-optimised B-tree whose internal nodes buffer pending updates and push them down in batches, turning small random writes into large sequential ones. (Ch 44)

docs.title: C
docs.text:
• Cached disk array — A storage array that fronts many commodity disks with a large RAM cache so most I/O never waits for a disk (EMC Symmetrix, 1990). (Ch 51)
  • CAP theorem — The result that during a network partition a distributed system must give up either consistency or availability. (Ch 20)
  • Capability heatmap — A vendor-by-capability table using filled, half-filled and empty marks to show how fully each vendor offers each capability. (Ch 49)
  • Capacity buffer — Spare capacity a storage-as-a-service vendor guarantees to keep installed above the customer's current use (25% for Evergreen//One). (Ch 28)
  • Capex discipline — a memory maker's restraint in adding wafer capacity, used to keep supply tight and prices firm. (Ch 48)
  • Capex purchase — Buying storage outright as a capital asset that the customer owns, depreciates and eventually replaces. (Ch 23)
  • Capsule — An NVMe-oF message carrying a command or a response, and optionally in-line data. (Ch 7)
  • Catch-up launch — An incumbent product built to close an architectural gap that challengers opened first. (Ch 41)
  • Causal consistency — A guarantee that no reader sees a write without also seeing the earlier writes it depends on. (Ch 20)
  • CBox — VAST's server chassis containing multiple CNodes. (Ch 16)
  • Ceph RGW — The RADOS Gateway, Ceph's S3-compatible object interface. (Ch 47)
  • CephFS — Ceph's POSIX file system interface. (Ch 47)
  • Ceres — VAST's 2022 storage-enclosure (DBox) design that uses NVIDIA BlueField DPUs as its fabric endpoints. (Ch 42)
  • Chain replication — A replication scheme in which writes flow along an ordered chain of servers (primary to replica) and are acknowledged once the chain has persisted them. (Ch 19)
  • Charge-trap cell — The 3D NAND cell design that stores electrons in a silicon-nitride layer around a vertical channel instead of in a floating gate. (Ch 2)
  • Checkpoint — A periodic snapshot of model weights and optimizer state written during training so a job can restart after a failure. (Ch 30, Ch 31)
  • Checkpoint drain — The background transfer of a checkpoint from host memory or local NVMe to durable shared storage. (Ch 31)
  • Chunk (object store) — A large fixed-size container (128 MB in Dell ObjectScale) into which many objects are packed before erasure coding. (Ch 18)
  • Chunk Store — Tectonic's flat storage layer that holds data chunks on storage nodes. (Ch 36)
  • Chunking — Splitting documents into small passages (typically a few hundred tokens) before embedding them for retrieval. (Ch 33)
  • Clean team — A ring-fenced group allowed to review competitively sensitive material, such as source code, during a deal. (Ch 50)
  • Client eviction — A server's forced removal of an unresponsive client's locks and state, which can lose that client's cached writes. (Ch 17)
  • Client-side NFS multipath — A modified NFS client (for example VAST's) that spreads one mount across many local NICs and many server addresses. (Ch 8)
  • Clone — A writable snapshot that shares unchanged blocks with its source. (Ch 6)
  • Close-to-open consistency — The NFS guarantee that one client's writes become visible to another client only after the writer closes the file and the reader reopens it. (Ch 8)
  • Closed division — the MLPerf category with fixed benchmark code and few tunables, intended for like-for-like comparison. (Ch 37)
  • Cloud block storage — Hyperscaler-run network block volumes, such as AWS EBS, attached to cloud instances. (Ch 24, Ch 60)
  • Cluster map — The authoritative record of a cluster's membership, health and placement rules, versioned by epoch. (Ch 15)
  • ClusterMAX — SemiAnalysis's rating system for GPU clouds, scoring providers on ten criteria including storage. (Ch 35)
  • CMR / ePMR — Conventional (non-overlapping) perpendicular magnetic recording, including energy-assisted variants, the mainstream HDD technology before HAMR. (Ch 2)
  • CMX — NVIDIA's rack-scale context-memory storage platform for KV cache, the first implementation of STX. (Ch 10, Ch 34, Ch 43, Ch 53)
  • CMX (context memory storage) — NVIDIA's BlueField-4-based, Ethernet-attached flash tier for KV cache at pod level, labelled "G3.5". (Ch 32)
  • CNode — VAST's stateless compute node that runs protocols, data reduction and erasure coding but holds no authoritative state. (Ch 16)
  • CNode-X — A VAST compute node with NVIDIA GPUs, announced in February 2026, for GPU-accelerated vector search and SQL inside the storage cluster. (Ch 42)
  • Co-packaged optics (CPO) — Optical engines packaged next to a switch or processor die instead of in pluggable modules, cutting power and laser count. (Ch 53)
  • Colossus — Google's cluster-level distributed file system and the successor to GFS, underpinning Cloud Storage, YouTube and Gmail. (Ch 36)
  • Command set vs. transport — The split between what a storage protocol says (SCSI or NVMe commands) and how it travels (PCIe, FC, RDMA or TCP). (Ch 60)
  • Committed ARR — A private company's own measure of contracted annual recurring revenue (used by VAST); not an audited figure. (Ch 58)
  • Committed ARR (CARR) — The annualised value of signed recurring contracts, including those not yet live, so it runs ahead of ARR. (Ch 41, Ch 42)
  • Commoditisation risk — The danger that a software layer above the arrays (for example a global namespace) makes storage hardware interchangeable. (Ch 58)
  • Community fork — An independently maintained copy of an open-source project created when the original owner stops maintaining or restricts it. (Ch 47)
  • Compaction — Background rewriting of many small data files into fewer large ones to keep table queries fast. (Ch 33)
  • Company-stated — a label for a private company's own unaudited figure. (Ch 0.1)
  • Competitive matrix — A chart or grid placing vendors on chosen dimensions so their relative positions can be compared at a glance. (Ch 49)
  • Computational storage — Placing processing in or beside a storage device to operate on data before it crosses the host interface. (Ch 12)
  • Conditional write — A PUT that succeeds only if a precondition holds (the key is absent or its ETag matches), giving optimistic concurrency control. (Ch 9)
  • Configuration master — A separate service that records which servers form each replication chain and changes membership after failures. (Ch 19)
  • Confused deputy — A security flaw in which a privileged service is tricked into using its authority for a caller who lacks it. (Ch 39)
  • Consensus — A protocol by which a group of machines agrees on one ordered log of operations despite crashes and lost messages. (Ch 20)
  • Consistency model — The contract that defines which version of data a reader may see when copies of it disagree. (Ch 20)
  • Consistent hashing — A placement scheme that maps keys and nodes onto a ring so that adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the data. (Ch 15)
  • Content-aware storage — IBM's Storage Scale capability that embeds and indexes data inside the file system for retrieval-augmented AI. (Ch 46)
  • Content-defined chunking (CDC) — Cutting data where a rolling hash over the content matches a pattern, so chunk boundaries survive insertions. (Ch 5)
  • Content-derived metadata — Metadata produced by reading and classifying the content itself, such as "contains PII" or "EU customer record". (Ch 39)
  • Context memory — A storage tier that holds inference KV cache between GPU memory and shared storage so that long conversations need not be recomputed. (Ch 53)
  • Contract price — the negotiated quarterly or monthly price that large buyers pay NAND or DRAM makers, as distinct from the more volatile spot price. (Ch 48, Ch 52)
  • Control plane — The part of a storage system that holds desired state (volumes, policies, placement) and configures the data plane, operating in seconds rather than microseconds. (Ch 22)
  • Control point — the layer of the stack that owns the customer relationship and the metadata, and so captures most of the value. (Ch 0.2)
  • Controller VM (CVM) — Nutanix's per-node virtual machine that runs the storage service in an HCI cluster. (Ch 19)
  • Converged mode — A deployment in which storage software runs on the same servers as the applications or GPUs, using their local drives. (Ch 43)
  • Conversation playbook — the section of every chapter with questions for PMs and engineers, strong-answer sketches and misconceptions to avoid. (Ch 0.1)
  • Coordinator node — The cluster node a client connects to, which computes data placement and fans reads and writes out to peer nodes. (Ch 15)
  • Copy-on-write (COW) snapshot — Snapshot method that copies an old block to a reserve area before overwriting it in place. (Ch 6)
  • Copyleft — Licence terms, as in GPL and AGPL, that require derived works to be distributed under the same terms with source available. (Ch 50)
  • Copyset — A fixed group of nodes that together hold all replicas of some chunks; limiting copysets makes data loss events rarer. (Ch 20)
  • Correlated failure — Multiple failures with a shared cause (batch, firmware, power, software upgrade) that strike together and break independence assumptions. (Ch 20, Ch 56)
  • Credibility ladder — the progression from L1 to L3 knowledge that sets how far an expert will engage with you. (Ch 0.1, Ch 56)
  • CRUSH — Ceph's placement algorithm, which computes the drives for each placement group from a hierarchical cluster map and failure-domain rules, without a lookup table. (Ch 15)
  • CSI (Container Storage Interface) — The standard plug-in interface through which Kubernetes asks a storage system to create, attach and delete volumes. (Ch 22)
  • cuFile — The programming interface for GPUDirect Storage that applications call instead of POSIX read and write to move file data into or out of GPU memory. (Ch 11)
  • Cumulative bookings — The total value of all contracts a company has ever signed, including multi-year commitments not yet recognised as revenue. (Ch 42)
  • cuObject — NVIDIA's client and server libraries implementing RDMA for S3-compatible object storage. (Ch 9, Ch 11)
  • Curator — A Colossus metadata server; curators store file-system metadata in Bigtable and scale horizontally. (Ch 36)
  • Custodian — A Colossus background service that rebuilds lost data and balances disk usage. (Ch 36)
  • Customer concentration — The share of a vendor's revenue that comes from its largest customers. (Ch 50)
  • CXL (Compute Express Link) — An open interconnect that runs cache-coherent memory and I/O protocols over the PCIe physical layer. (Ch 12)
  • CXL memory — DRAM attached over a Compute Express Link (PCIe-based) connection, adding capacity at roughly two to three times local DRAM latency. (Ch 2)
  • CXL Type 3 device — A CXL memory expander: a controller plus DRAM that the host reaches with ordinary loads and stores. (Ch 12)
  • CXL.mem — The CXL protocol that lets a host read and write a device's memory at cache-line granularity. (Ch 12)

docs.title: D
docs.text:
• D file server — Colossus's simple network-attached disk server, read and written directly by the client library. (Ch 36)
  • 3D NAND deck — One separately etched section of a tall 3D NAND layer stack; high-layer parts stack two or three decks. (Ch 2)
  • 3D XPoint — The phase-change-based persistent memory technology behind Intel Optane, co-developed with Micron. (Ch 12)
  • Dark site — A customer installation that does not phone home, typically for security reasons, and therefore forgoes cloud analytics. (Ch 22)
  • DAS (direct-attached storage) — Storage inside or cabled directly to one server, with no storage network in between. (Ch 13)
  • DASD (direct-access storage device) — IBM's term for mainframe disk storage, as opposed to sequential tape. (Ch 51)
  • DASE (disaggregated shared-everything) — A storage architecture in which stateless compute nodes share access to all media in separate enclosures over an NVMe-oF fabric, so no node owns any data. (Ch 16)
  • Data catalog — An inventory of an organisation's datasets recording their schema, owner, classification and lineage. (Ch 39)
  • Data catalog (table catalog) — The service that maps table names to their current metadata pointer and enforces access, such as Unity Catalog or Apache Polaris. (Ch 33)
  • Data curation — Filtering, deduplicating, cleaning and tokenizing raw data into a training-ready dataset. (Ch 30)
  • Data gravity — The tendency of applications, services and spending to move toward where large volumes of data already sit. (Ch 30)
  • Data lake — A low-cost, usually object-based store that holds raw and curated data for analytics and AI. (Ch 30)
  • Data lifecycle — The progression of data from creation through active use, protection, cooling and archiving to deletion. (Ch 1)
  • Data lineage — The record of where data came from, how it was transformed and which outputs or decisions it fed. (Ch 39)
  • Data loader — The training-framework component that reads, decodes and prefetches batches of samples from storage for the GPUs. (Ch 30)
  • Data node (EXA) — a third-party Linux/NVMe server running Purity//DN that stores FlashBlade//EXA file data and serves it directly to clients. (Ch 27)
  • Data orchestration — Policy-driven movement of files between tiers, sites and clouds without changing how applications address them. (Ch 47)
  • Data plane — The I/O path of a storage system that actually moves and protects bytes, which must keep running even if management services are unreachable. (Ch 22)
  • Data Primacy — Everpure's 2026 strategic framing that puts trusted, classified data rather than applications at the centre of the infrastructure stack. (Ch 28)
  • Data reduction guarantee — A vendor contract promising a minimum reduction ratio or effective capacity, usually on reducible data only, with extra capacity as the remedy. (Ch 5)
  • Data retention — How long NAND holds data without power before charge leakage causes errors; it shrinks as cells wear and as temperature rises. (Ch 2)
  • Data security posture management (DSPM) — Software that discovers and classifies sensitive data across an estate and flags where it is exposed or over-permissioned. (Ch 39)
  • Data services — The "intelligence" of a storage system: data placement, protection, data reduction and metadata management. (Ch 13)
  • Data stall — Time a GPU waits for training data to be fetched from storage or pre-processed. (Ch 11)
  • Data Stream — Everpure's GPU-accelerated pipeline on FlashBlade that ingests, indexes and vectorises data for AI, based on NVIDIA's AI Data Platform design. (Ch 28)
  • Data-in-place upgrade — A controller hardware upgrade that leaves drives, data and configuration in place, so no migration is needed. (Ch 14)
  • Data-loss incident log — A vendor's record of every case of lost or corrupted customer data, with root cause and blast radius. (Ch 50)
  • Data-on-MDT (DoM) — A Lustre feature that stores the first part, or all, of small files on the metadata target to avoid a round trip to a data server. (Ch 17, Ch 21)
  • Data-parallel replica — One full copy of the model in a data-parallel training job; replicas process different data and synchronize gradients. (Ch 31)
  • Data-reduction ratio (DRR) — Logical data stored divided by physical capacity consumed after deduplication and compression. (Ch 4, Ch 5)
  • Data-services breadth — The range of enterprise data services (protocols, replication, ransomware recovery, cloud editions, consumption, cataloguing) delivered on the storage itself. (Ch 49)
  • Datasheet sum vs. system result — The difference between adding up per-box vendor ratings and measuring a whole configured system under a benchmark. (Ch 45)
  • DBox — VAST's storage enclosure holding SCM and QLC SSDs behind redundant DNodes. (Ch 16)
  • DBox-HA — VAST's option that limits strips per enclosure so a cluster survives the loss of an entire DBox. (Ch 16)
  • DCQCN — The standard ECN-based congestion-control algorithm for RoCEv2, in which the sender NIC cuts its rate on congestion notifications. (Ch 10)
  • DDN CORE — DDN's control plane and data fabric, launched in November 2025, that spans EXAScaler and Infinia on-premises and in clouds. (Ch 44)
  • Deal archetype — A recurring buyer profile, such as a neocloud training cluster or a sovereign HPC site, whose dominant requirement predicts which vendor wins. (Ch 45)
  • Declustered RAID — Layout that scatters stripes and spare space across all drives in a pool so rebuilds run in parallel. (Ch 6)
  • Decode — The memory-bandwidth-bound inference phase that generates one token per step while rereading the weights and the full KV cache. (Ch 32)
  • Dedicated mode — A deployment in which storage software runs on separate storage servers rather than on the compute nodes. (Ch 43)
  • Deduplication — Storing identical chunks of data once and replacing repeats with pointers found by fingerprint lookup. (Ch 5)
  • Delegation — An NFSv4 grant that lets one client cache a file exclusively until the server recalls it. (Ch 8)
  • Delta Lake — Databricks-originated open table format that adds a transaction log to Parquet files in object storage. (Ch 33)
  • Dennard scaling — The historical rule that transistor power density stayed constant as transistors shrank, whose end around 2005 made chips power-limited. (Ch 38)
  • Denominator question — A follow-up that asks which population, period and exclusions sit behind a percentage or ratio. (Ch 57)
  • Dentry (directory entry) — A record inside a directory that maps a file or subdirectory name to its inode number. (Ch 21)
  • Depth label — the atlas's three levels of understanding: L1 vocabulary, L2 mechanism and L3 implementation. (Ch 0.1)
  • Design win — A customer's commitment to build its platform around a supplier's technology, ahead of volume revenue. (Ch 29, Ch 55)
  • Design win (hyperscaler) — A hyperscaler's commitment to build its storage on a supplier's technology, in Everpure's case licensed DirectFlash and Purity rather than finished arrays. (Ch 25)
  • DFMD — An Everpure DirectFlash module with built-in NVRAM, so write-log capacity grows with the number of modules. (Ch 14)
  • DGX BasePOD — NVIDIA's reference architecture for enterprise GPU clusters of two to dozens of DGX systems, with a list of validated storage partners. (Ch 34)
  • DGX SuperPOD — NVIDIA's turnkey large-cluster reference architecture, built from scalable units, with storage certified against per-generation performance tables. (Ch 34)
  • Digital Omnibus on AI — EU Regulation 2026/1744, which amended the AI Act and postponed its high-risk obligations to December 2027 and August 2028. (Ch 39)
  • DirectFlash — Everpure's approach of letting Purity manage raw NAND directly instead of going through each SSD's own controller and FTL. (Ch 26)
  • DirectFlash licence — Everpure's hyperscaler model in which the customer licenses DirectFlash software and design and sources its own NAND and hardware. (Ch 26)
  • DirectFlash Module (DFM) — Everpure's proprietary flash module that exposes raw NAND through a thin controller, with no drive-level flash translation layer. (Ch 26)
  • Directory bucket — The S3 bucket type used by S3 Express One Zone, confined to one Availability Zone. (Ch 36)
  • Disaggregated serving — Running prefill and decode on separate GPU pools and transferring the KV cache between them. (Ch 32)
  • DiskANN — Microsoft's SSD-resident graph vector index that keeps compressed codes in DRAM and the full graph and vectors on flash. (Ch 33)
  • Distributed Namespace (DNE) — Lustre's feature for spreading the namespace over multiple metadata targets, via remote directories and striped directories. (Ch 21)
  • DLIO — the deep-learning I/O emulator MLPerf Storage uses to mimic framework data loading and to "sleep" in place of accelerator compute. (Ch 37)
  • DNA data storage — Encoding digital data in synthesized DNA strands; extremely dense and durable but slow and costly to write. (Ch 53)
  • DNE (Distributed Namespace Environment) — Lustre's mechanism for spreading a namespace across several metadata targets to relieve a single metadata server. (Ch 45)
  • DNE (Distributed Namespace) — Lustre's mechanism for spreading the namespace across several MDTs, via remote or striped directories. (Ch 17)
  • DNode — VAST's enclosure fabric endpoint (often a DPU) that exposes an enclosure's SSDs to the NVMe-oF fabric. (Ch 16)
  • Do-nothing option — Continuing the current plan without new acquisitions or major partnerships, evaluated as a real alternative rather than a default. (Ch 54)
  • Doorbell register — A device register that the host writes to tell an NVMe controller that new queue entries are ready or have been consumed. (Ch 7)
  • DPDK (Data Plane Development Kit) — A user-space networking library that lets software drive a NIC directly, bypassing the operating-system network stack. (Ch 43)
  • DPU (data processing unit) — A NIC with its own general-purpose CPU complex and accelerators that can run storage, security or networking software. (Ch 10)
  • DSPM (data security posture management) — Software that finds sensitive data across systems and checks who can access it. (Ch 54)
  • Dual-controller array — A scale-up storage system in which two controllers share dual-ported drives and each can take over the other's work if it fails. (Ch 14)
  • Durability — The property that acknowledged data survives failures and power loss without being lost or corrupted. (Ch 1)
  • DWPD (drive writes per day) — An SSD endurance rating: how many times the drive's full capacity can be written each day over its warranty period. (Ch 2)
  • Dynamic resharding — Automatically increasing a bucket index's shard count as the object count grows, as Ceph RGW does above a per-shard threshold. (Ch 18)

docs.title: E
docs.text:
• E1.S — A small EDSFF form factor suited to dense compute and GPU servers. (Ch 12)
  • E3.L — A long EDSFF form factor with up to 70 W envelope, used for high-capacity QLC drives. (Ch 12)
  • East-west traffic — Traffic between storage nodes, such as replicas, erasure-coded fragments, forwarded reads, rebalancing and rebuilds. (Ch 15)
  • EBox — VAST's packaging that runs CNode and DNode software on the same server, trading independent scaling for hyperscaler and cloud fit. (Ch 16, Ch 42)
  • ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) — Switches mark packets when queues build so senders can slow down before drops occur. (Ch 10)
  • EDSFF — The SNIA family of data-centre SSD form factors (E1.S, E1.L, E3.S, E3.L) designed for density, airflow and scalable power. (Ch 12)
  • Effective $/GB — Storage price divided by logical capacity after data reduction, as opposed to raw or usable capacity. (Ch 52)
  • Effective $/TB — the price per terabyte a customer can actually store after data reduction, rather than per raw terabyte. (Ch 48)
  • Effective capacity — Usable capacity multiplied by an assumed data-reduction ratio. (Ch 4, Ch 43)
  • Effective training time — The share of elapsed time that a training job spends doing useful training, after interruptions, restarts and checkpoint pauses. (Ch 11, Ch 31)
  • elbencho — an open-source distributed storage benchmark tool for file, object and GPU-direct testing. (Ch 37)
  • Element Store — VAST's single metadata and data structure that represents files, objects, block volumes and tables as one kind of "element" underneath every protocol. (Ch 42)
  • Embedding — A fixed-length vector of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of content so similar items can be found by vector search. (Ch 30, Ch 33)
  • Embodied carbon — Greenhouse-gas emissions from manufacturing and shipping hardware, as distinct from emissions from powering it. (Ch 38)
  • Enclosure blast radius — The amount of data and service affected when an entire storage enclosure fails. (Ch 16)
  • Enterprise Data Cloud (EDC) — Everpure's 2025 architecture that uses Pure Fusion to manage a whole on-premises and cloud fleet as one policy-driven pool. (Ch 25, Ch 28)
  • Enterprise level — The middle NVIDIA-Certified Storage tier, simulating workloads of about 1,000 GPUs. (Ch 34)
  • Enterprise storage platform — Gartner's category, created in 2025, covering products that serve block, file and object workloads together. (Ch 24)
  • Enterprise Storage Platforms (Gartner) — Gartner's merged MQ category, from 2025, covering primary block plus file and object storage. (Ch 40)
  • Entity List — The US Commerce Department list of foreign parties subject to export licence requirements, which has included Huawei since 2019. (Ch 46, Ch 48)
  • Erasure coding (k+m) — Scheme that stores k data strips plus m computed parity strips and can rebuild from any k of them. (Ch 6)
  • Erasure set — A fixed group of drives (2–16 in MinIO) across which one object's data and parity fragments are always written. (Ch 18)
  • ETag — An identifier of an object's content or version, returned on writes and used for integrity checks and conditional requests. (Ch 9)
  • Event Broker (VAST) — VAST's Kafka-compatible event-streaming service, implemented as a protocol module so topics can be queried as tables. (Ch 42)
  • Eventual consistency — A guarantee only that all copies converge once writes stop, so reads in the meantime may be stale. (Ch 20)
  • Ever Modern — The Evergreen//Forever entitlement to new-generation controllers with each three-year subscription renewal (six years for //E products). (Ch 23)
  • Evergreen — Everpure's family of subscriptions (//Forever, //Flex, //One) that replaces periodic forklift array replacements with non-disruptive upgrades and consumption options. (Ch 25)
  • Evergreen//Flex — Everpure's fleet-level program that bills capacity per use across a customer's arrays. (Ch 23, Ch 25, Ch 28)
  • Evergreen//Forever — Everpure's subscription for customer-owned arrays that includes in-place controller refreshes at each three-year renewal (formerly Evergreen Gold). (Ch 23, Ch 25, Ch 28)
  • Evergreen//One — Everpure's storage-as-a-service offering (formerly Pure-as-a-Service), with SLAs on performance, availability, capacity and energy. (Ch 23, Ch 25, Ch 28, Ch 29)
  • Evergreen//One for AI — Everpure's storage-as-a-service offering for AI workloads, extended to FlashBlade//EXA in March 2026. (Ch 45)
  • Everpure — the company formerly called Pure Storage, renamed in February 2026 and listed as NYSE: P since 2026-04-17. (Ch 0.2)
  • Everpure Cloud Azure Native — Fully managed Everpure block storage delivered as an Azure Native ISV service, co-developed with Microsoft. (Ch 28)
  • Everpure Cloud Dedicated — Customer-managed Purity running in the customer's own AWS or Azure account; formerly Cloud Block Store. (Ch 28)
  • Everpure Data Intelligence — The data discovery, classification and semantic-context product built from the 1touch acquisition, GA in June 2026. (Ch 25, Ch 28)
  • Everpure Data Stream — Everpure's GPU-accelerated ingest-to-inference data pipeline built on NVIDIA's AI Data Platform reference design. (Ch 25)
  • Everpure Platform — Everpure's name for its whole software and hardware stack (Purity, arrays, Fusion, Pure1, Portworx, Everpure Cloud, Data Intelligence) sold as one platform. (Ch 28)
  • EXAScaler — DDN's commercial distribution of the Lustre parallel file system, with management tooling, usually sold on DDN appliances. (Ch 44)
  • Extent — A contiguous run of physical blocks described by a single map entry, replacing many per-block pointers. (Ch 21)
  • Extent lock — A distributed lock on a byte range of a file, letting several clients write different ranges of one file coherently. (Ch 17)
  • External enterprise storage systems — Branded storage arrays sold as standalone systems to enterprises, the scope of IDC's headline quarterly storage tracker. (Ch 40)
  • External OEM ESS — IDC's label for the external enterprise storage systems market, measured as vendor revenue by brand. (Ch 40)

docs.title: F
docs.text:
• Fabric amplification — The ratio of back-end network traffic to client traffic, raised by mirroring and data migration. (Ch 16)
  • Failover pair — Two servers attached to the same dual-ported storage so either can take over the other's targets if one fails. (Ch 17)
  • Failure domain — A set of components that can fail together, such as a drive, node, enclosure, rack, power zone, site or region. (Ch 20)
  • Fan-out — Splitting one request into many parallel sub-requests, so that the slowest sub-request determines overall latency. (Ch 4)
  • FC-NVMe (NVMe/FC) — The NVMe-oF transport that carries NVMe over Fibre Channel, standardized by INCITS T11 in 2017. (Ch 7)
  • Federation — Managing several arrays or controller pairs as one cluster with volume mobility, without merging them into one system. (Ch 14)
  • Fibre Channel (FC) — A dedicated, lossless storage network using credit-based flow control, the traditional enterprise SAN fabric. (Ch 7)
  • Field failure data — Measured failure rates and rebuild histories from deployed systems, as opposed to modelled reliability. (Ch 50)
  • File handle — An opaque token issued by an NFS server that identifies a file in every subsequent request. (Ch 8)
  • File layout — The map that tells a client which storage targets hold which parts of a file, including stripe size and stripe count. (Ch 17)
  • File storage — Storage presented as a shared tree of named directories and files, with the file system run by the storage system. (Ch 1)
  • Filer — A dedicated network file-server appliance that does nothing but serve files over NFS or SMB (NetApp's original product). (Ch 51)
  • Fingerprint — A cryptographic hash of a data chunk used as its identity in a deduplication index. (Ch 5)
  • fio — the standard open-source I/O load generator used for vendor and customer storage tests, whose job file defines block size, queue depth and data pattern. (Ch 37)
  • First-party cloud storage service — A partner's storage technology sold, supported and billed by a cloud provider as its own service (e.g., FSx for NetApp ONTAP). (Ch 47)
  • FIT (failures in time) — Failures per 10^9 device-hours; a 1% AFR is about 1,140 FIT. (Ch 20)
  • Fixed-block chunking — Cutting data into chunks at fixed offsets such as every 4 KB or 8 KB, which is cheap but misses duplicates after insertions shift the data. (Ch 5)
  • Flash translation layer (FTL) — SSD firmware that maps logical block addresses to physical NAND pages, so erase-before-write flash looks like a rewritable disk. (Ch 3)
  • FlashArray//C — the QLC-based FlashArray that shares //X controllers and targets capacity-oriented tier-2 workloads. (Ch 27)
  • FlashArray//E — the QLC FlashArray tier aimed at replacing disk-based secondary and backup storage. (Ch 27)
  • FlashArray//ST — a latency-optimised, block-only FlashArray that uses commercial SSDs and switches off data reduction to shorten the I/O path. (Ch 27)
  • FlashArray//X — Everpure's mainstream TLC DirectFlash FlashArray for sub-millisecond tier-1 block and file workloads. (Ch 27)
  • FlashArray//XL — Everpure's highest-performance dual-controller FlashArray model for consolidated tier-0/1 block workloads. (Ch 27)
  • FlashBlade//E — the capacity-optimised FlashBlade with CPUs only in a control chassis and storage-only expansion chassis. (Ch 27)
  • FlashBlade//EXA — Everpure's AI/HPC system that splits a Purity//FB metadata core from separately scaled data nodes reached directly by pNFS clients. (Ch 27)
  • FlashBlade//S — Everpure's scale-out file and object performance tier built from blades and DirectFlash Modules. (Ch 27)
  • FlashCore Module — IBM's custom flash module with in-module compression, used in FlashSystem arrays. (Ch 46)
  • FlashStack — The Cisco and Everpure converged-infrastructure stack combining Cisco compute and networking with Everpure storage. (Ch 29)
  • Flat namespace — An addressing scheme with no real directories, where "folders" are only shared key prefixes. (Ch 9)
  • Flex Files layout — The pNFS layout type (RFC 8435, 2018) whose data servers can be ordinary NFSv3 servers and which supports client-side mirroring. (Ch 8)
  • Flexible Data Placement (FDP) — An NVMe feature in which hosts tag writes with placement hints so data with similar lifetimes share erase blocks. (Ch 12)
  • FLIT — The fixed 256-byte transfer unit of PCIe 6.0+ and CXL 3.x, carrying data plus FEC and CRC bytes. (Ch 12)
  • Floor loading — The weight per unit area a datacenter floor can bear, a limit on densely packed disk racks. (Ch 38)
  • Flywheel — A self-reinforcing loop in which early wins produce capital and references that make the next wins easier. (Ch 41)
  • Foreign-investment review — Government screening of cross-border acquisitions on national-security grounds, such as CFIUS in the United States. (Ch 54)
  • Forever Flash — Pure Storage's 2014 maintenance programme that bundled controller refreshes with maintenance renewals, the predecessor of Evergreen. (Ch 25)
  • Forklift upgrade — Replacing an entire storage system and migrating its data, the incumbent refresh model that Evergreen was designed to remove. (Ch 25, Ch 51)
  • Foundation level — The entry NVIDIA-Certified Storage tier, testing workloads that simulate up to 128 GPUs. (Ch 34)
  • FoundationDB — An open-source distributed transactional key-value database used as the metadata store by systems such as DeepSeek's 3FS and Snowflake. (Ch 21)
  • Four-beat answer — The structure of a 30-second explanation: what it is, why it matters, one number, and the implication for the company. (Ch 58)
  • Front-end / back-end network — In AI clusters, the north-south network for users, ingest and often storage, versus the east-west fabric for GPU-to-GPU traffic. (Ch 10)
  • Front-end network — The network that carries traffic between clients and storage nodes (north-south). (Ch 15, Ch 35)
  • 3FS (Fire-Flyer File System) — DeepSeek's open-source all-flash parallel file system for AI training and inference. (Ch 36)
  • FSx for Lustre — AWS's managed Lustre parallel file system service, linked to S3. (Ch 36)
  • FTL mapping DRAM — The DRAM an SSD uses to hold its logical-to-physical page map, roughly 1 GB per TB of flash at 4 KB granularity. (Ch 13)
  • Fusion preset — A named, fleet-wide template in Everpure Fusion that bundles performance limits, protection policy and tags for provisioning workloads. (Ch 28)

docs.title: G
docs.text:
• Garbage collection (GC) — Background work that copies valid pages out of partly stale blocks so the blocks can be erased and reused. (Ch 3)
  • Gating requirement — the one capability or certification without which a deal cannot close. (Ch 55)
  • GB/s per kW — Storage bandwidth delivered per kilowatt of power, an efficiency metric suited to AI workloads. (Ch 38)
  • GDS compatibility mode — The fallback in which cuFile calls still work but data passes through a host-memory bounce buffer because the platform or file system does not support the direct path. (Ch 11)
  • Gemini (VAST) — VAST Data's model in which customers buy certified hardware at cost from a partner and pay VAST a software subscription. (Ch 19, Ch 42)
  • General availability (GA) — the point at which a product is orderable and fully supported, though not necessarily feature-complete. (Ch 55)
  • Geo-distributed erasure coding — Spreading an erasure-coded stripe across several sites so the loss of a whole site is survivable at lower capacity overhead than replication. (Ch 18)
  • Global FTL — a single flash translation layer that maps, garbage-collects and wear-levels across every flash module in an array rather than inside each drive. (Ch 26)
  • Global namespace — A single file tree that spans many storage systems, tiers and sites, so files keep one path wherever their bytes live. (Ch 47)
  • Google Cloud Managed Lustre — Google's first-party managed parallel file system service, built on DDN EXAScaler and generally available since July 2025. (Ch 44)
  • GPLv2 — The GNU General Public License version 2, a copyleft licence used by Lustre and the Linux kernel. (Ch 50)
  • GPU-initiated data access — A data path in which GPU threads issue storage operations directly, without a CPU round-trip for each request. (Ch 44)
  • GPUDirect RDMA — NVIDIA technology that lets a network card read or write GPU memory directly over PCIe, without copying through host memory. (Ch 11)
  • GPUDirect Storage (GDS) — NVIDIA technology that lets storage data move by direct DMA between a NIC or NVMe SSD and GPU memory, bypassing the CPU bounce buffer. (Ch 11)
  • Grace timer — The wait before a missing node is declared failed, so a brief reboot triggers only a resync instead of a full rebuild. (Ch 15)
  • Greedy garbage collection — A GC policy that always reclaims the block with the fewest valid pages, minimising copies under random writes. (Ch 3)
  • GreenLake for File Storage — HPE's file service built on VAST Data software running on Alletra MP hardware. (Ch 46)
  • Grouped-query attention (GQA) — An attention design in which several query heads share one key/value head, shrinking the KV cache per token. (Ch 32)

docs.title: H
docs.text:
• HA interconnect — The dedicated link between two controllers that carries heartbeats and mirrored write data. (Ch 14)
  • HAMR — heat-assisted magnetic recording, which briefly heats the platter with a laser so smaller, more stable magnetic grains can be written, raising HDD density. (Ch 48, Ch 53)
  • HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) — HDD recording that briefly heats a tiny spot with a laser so that very stable, high-density magnetic media can be written. (Ch 2)
  • Hard multi-tenancy — Isolation of many customers' data, performance and administration on one shared system, enforced by the platform rather than by trust. (Ch 35)
  • Hardware compatibility list (HCL) — The vendor-published list of servers, drives, NICs and firmware versions that software-defined storage is supported on. (Ch 19)
  • Hardware-agnostic software — Storage software sold to run on customer-chosen servers, GPU nodes or cloud instances rather than on vendor hardware. (Ch 49)
  • Hashed (striped) directory — A directory whose entries are spread across several metadata servers by hashing names. (Ch 21)
  • HBM (high-bandwidth memory) — Stacked DRAM placed on the same package as a GPU or accelerator, the fastest and most expensive tier of the memory hierarchy. (Ch 2)
  • HCI (hyperconverged infrastructure) — Running storage software on the same servers as the virtual machines, pooling their local drives. (Ch 51)
  • Head server — The server that runs storage software in front of one or more JBOD enclosures. (Ch 38)
  • Headline valuation multiple — A private company's last valuation divided by its latest self-reported revenue or ARR figure; indicative only because definitions differ. (Ch 41)
  • Headroom tax — The capacity a redundant pair leaves unused so a single surviving controller can carry the full load. (Ch 14)
  • Hedged read — Requesting more fragments or replicas than needed and using the first to arrive, to cut tail latency. (Ch 18, Ch 36)
  • Hero configuration — a benchmark system sized to win a headline rather than to match a realistic purchase. (Ch 37)
  • HHI (Herfindahl–Hirschman Index) — A market-concentration measure equal to the sum of squared market shares; above 2,500 is usually treated as highly concentrated. (Ch 52)
  • Hidden over-provisioning — NAND capacity inside an SSD reserved for garbage collection and wear that the host can neither see nor use. (Ch 26)
  • Hierarchical keyspace tenancy — Multi-tenancy implemented by nesting tenants and datasets inside a key-value namespace, with a resource share assigned to each tenant. (Ch 44)
  • High-performance storage (HPS) certification — NVIDIA's certification that a storage system meets the NCP reference architecture's fast-storage tier. (Ch 34)
  • High-risk AI system — Under the EU AI Act, an AI system used in a listed sensitive area (such as hiring or credit) that must meet data-governance, logging and oversight obligations. (Ch 39)
  • Hitachi iQ — Hitachi Vantara's NVIDIA-based full-stack AI infrastructure offering built on VSP One storage. (Ch 46)
  • HNSW — Hierarchical Navigable Small World, a multi-layer proximity-graph vector index that is fast in DRAM but needs one dependent memory access per hop. (Ch 33)
  • Host Memory Buffer (HMB) — An NVMe feature that lets a DRAM-less SSD borrow a slice of host memory to cache its mapping table. (Ch 3)
  • Host-managed device memory (HDM) — Device-attached memory mapped into the host's physical address space, typically exposed as a CPU-less NUMA node. (Ch 12)
  • Hot / warm / cold data — Labels for data by access frequency, from constantly accessed (hot) to rarely accessed (cold). (Ch 1)
  • Hot tier — The high-performance file or flash storage tier that feeds GPUs directly during training and inference. (Ch 30)
  • Hybrid bonding — Joining separately made wafers (such as NAND arrays and their logic) face to face with direct copper connections. (Ch 53)
  • Hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) — An architecture in which every cluster node runs applications (usually VMs), storage software and local drives together. (Ch 19)
  • Hyperscale commercial model — Everpure's arrangement in which hyperscalers buy NAND themselves while Everpure supplies DirectFlash design, Purity software, support and some components. (Ch 29)
  • Hyperscale licensing — Everpure's business of licensing its DirectFlash design, software and support to hyperscalers that buy their own NAND. (Ch 0.2)
  • Hyperscaler licensing — Everpure's model of licensing DirectFlash and Purity technology to hyperscalers, which buy their own NAND and hardware. (Ch 58)
  • Hyperscaler self-build — A hyperscaler designing its own storage software and buying commodity servers and drives instead of branded arrays. (Ch 40)
  • Hyperscaler-native storage — Storage services built and run by AWS, Azure or Google themselves, such as S3, Blob and GCS. (Ch 49)
  • HyperStore — Cloudian's S3-native object storage software and appliance line. (Ch 47)

docs.title: I
docs.text:
• IBM FlashCore Module — IBM's proprietary flash module for FlashSystem that keeps an in-module FTL and adds compression, encryption and threat detection. (Ch 26)
  • IBM Storage Scale (GPFS) — IBM's parallel file system, shipped since 1998 and renamed from Spectrum Scale in 2022, which distributes metadata management across nodes using tokens. (Ch 17)
  • Illustrative chart — a chart of modelled rather than measured data, labelled "Illustrative" in its title. (Ch 0.1)
  • ILM (information lifecycle management) — NetApp StorageGRID's rule engine that decides where and how (replicated or erasure-coded) each object is stored over time. (Ch 18)
  • IMFT (IM Flash Technologies) — The Intel–Micron NAND (later 3D XPoint) manufacturing joint venture in Lehi, Utah, formed in 2006 and unwound in 2019. (Ch 52)
  • Incast — Many senders converging on one receiver port at once, the typical overload pattern in storage networks. (Ch 10)
  • Incumbent (storage) — An established storage vendor with a large installed base and broad portfolio, such as Dell, NetApp, HPE, IBM, Hitachi Vantara or Huawei. (Ch 46)
  • Indirection unit — the granularity at which an SSD's mapping table tracks data; larger units save DRAM but penalise small random writes. (Ch 26)
  • Indirection unit (IU) — The granularity at which an SSD's mapping table tracks data; larger units save DRAM but penalise smaller writes. (Ch 3)
  • Inference Context Memory Storage (ICMS) — NVIDIA's CES 2026 name for its BlueField-4-powered KV-cache storage tier, later delivered as CMX. (Ch 34)
  • Infinia — DDN's software-defined data platform, built on a distributed key-value store, that serves S3, SDK, KV-cache and limited POSIX access. (Ch 44)
  • InfiniBand — A purpose-built, credit-based lossless network fabric for HPC and AI, today supplied effectively only by NVIDIA (Quantum). (Ch 10)
  • InfiniBox — Infinidat's high-end block array that serves most reads from DRAM in front of large media pools; now part of Lenovo. (Ch 47)
  • Infrastructure as code (IaC) — Managing infrastructure through declarative, version-controlled definitions applied by tools such as Terraform or Ansible. (Ch 22)
  • Initiator — The host side of a block-storage session that issues read and write commands. (Ch 7)
  • Inline object — A small object whose bytes are stored inside its metadata record instead of being erasure-coded into separate fragments. (Ch 18)
  • Inline reduction — Data reduction performed before data is written to persistent media. (Ch 5)
  • Innovator's dilemma — The pattern in which incumbents rationally serve their best customers and miss a new segment that later becomes the growth market. (Ch 41)
  • Inode — A per-file record holding a file's attributes (owner, permissions, size, timestamps) and pointers to where its data lives. (Ch 21)
  • Integrated media moat — a competitive advantage from owning flash management down to the media, as with DirectFlash. (Ch 0.2)
  • Integrated memory controller — a DRAM controller built onto the CPU die instead of a separate northbridge chip; the analogy for moving flash control into array software. (Ch 26)
  • Integration seam — One of the places an acquired product must join the acquirer: control plane, data path, licensing or channel. (Ch 50)
  • IntelliFlash — The all-flash array line (ex-Tegile) that DDN bought from Western Digital in 2019. (Ch 44)
  • Interleaving — Mixing topics within one review session instead of drilling one topic at a time. (Ch 59)
  • io2 Block Express — AWS's highest-performance EBS volume type, built on a re-architected back end reached over SRD. (Ch 19)
  • IO500 — A twice-yearly ranking of HPC storage systems, started at SC17, that combines bandwidth and metadata scores via geometric means. (Ch 17, Ch 37)
  • IO500 Production list — the IO500 list restricted to submissions that pass a reproducibility review, separate from the Research list for experimental systems. (Ch 37)
  • IOPS — Input/output operations completed per second, usually quoted for small (4 KiB) random reads. (Ch 4)
  • IOPS per TB — A device's or system's random IOPS divided by its capacity; the metric that falls as hard drives grow. (Ch 4)
  • ior-easy / ior-hard — IO500 bandwidth tests: large, well-aligned sequential I/O versus small, unaligned I/O to a shared file. (Ch 37)
  • iSCSI — SCSI commands carried over TCP/IP on ordinary Ethernet (IETF RFC 3720, 2004). (Ch 7)
  • ISG (Infrastructure Solutions Group) — Dell's reporting segment that contains servers, networking and storage. (Ch 46)
  • Issue fingerprint — A telemetry signature of a known fault that a vendor matches across its connected fleet to prevent recurrences. (Ch 22)
  • IVF (inverted file index) — A vector index that clusters vectors and searches only the few clusters nearest the query. (Ch 33)

docs.title: J
docs.text: • JBOD — "Just a bunch of disks": a drive enclosure with no storage controller logic, attached to a separate head server. (Ch 38)

docs.title: K
docs.text:
• Kernel bypass — Moving data between an application and the NIC without system calls, interrupts or kernel socket buffers on the data path. (Ch 10, Ch 43)
  • Key-person risk — Dependence on a few people, often core code authors, whose departure would stall the product. (Ch 50)
  • Kingmaker risk — Dependence on a platform owner, such as NVIDIA, whose endorsements can be extended to rivals at any time. (Ch 41)
  • Kioxia — The NAND maker formerly called Toshiba Memory, sold to a Bain-led consortium in 2018 and listed in Tokyo in December 2024. (Ch 52)
  • KubeVirt — Open-source project that runs virtual machines as Kubernetes objects, a common VMware-exit path. (Ch 28)
  • KV cache — The per-token attention keys and values an LLM stores during inference so it does not recompute them for each new token. (Ch 30, Ch 32)
  • KV-cache offload — Storing a transformer's key/value tensors outside GPU memory so that a repeated prompt prefix can be reloaded instead of recomputed. (Ch 44)
  • KVBM (KV Block Manager) — The Dynamo component that tiers KV-cache blocks across GPU memory, host DRAM, local SSD and remote storage. (Ch 11, Ch 32)

docs.title: L
docs.text:
• L1 (vocabulary) — the depth at which you can define a term and use it correctly in a sentence. (Ch 0.1)
  • L1 / L2 card — A flashcard that tests vocabulary (L1) or mechanism and trade-off (L2), matching the atlas's depth labels. (Ch 59)
  • L2 (mechanism) — the atlas's default depth: you can whiteboard how something works, name its trade-offs and say why one design wins for a workload. (Ch 0.1)
  • L3 (implementation) — code paths, on-disk formats and kernel internals, covered only as pointers in "Going deeper" boxes. (Ch 0.1)
  • L4 cache — Colossus's machine-learning-driven tier that decides which data is cached or written to SSD instead of HDD. (Ch 36)
  • Lakehouse — An architecture that runs warehouse-style SQL and AI workloads directly on open file and table formats in object storage. (Ch 33)
  • Lance — An open columnar file format, created by LanceDB's founders, designed for both scans and fast random row access to embeddings and multimodal data. (Ch 33)
  • Land motion — the first product sold into a new account, intended to lead to expansion. (Ch 55)
  • Latency — The time from issuing one storage request to its completion, measured in microseconds for flash and milliseconds for disk. (Ch 4)
  • Latency adder — The extra time per I/O that a transport or software layer adds on top of the storage device itself. (Ch 60)
  • Latency-bound workload — A workload whose performance depends on how quickly each small I/O completes, such as an OLTP database. (Ch 24)
  • Layout — The pNFS map telling a client which data servers hold which byte ranges of a file and how they are striped. (Ch 8)
  • LBA (logical block address) — The number that identifies one fixed-size block within a block volume. (Ch 1)
  • LDPC (low-density parity-check) code — The strong error-correcting code that modern SSD controllers apply to every NAND read. (Ch 3)
  • Lease — A time-bounded grant of state (opens, locks) that an NFSv4 client must keep renewing or lose. (Ch 8)
  • Leitner box — A paper spaced-repetition system in which correctly answered cards move to less frequently reviewed boxes and missed cards return to the first box. (Ch 59)
  • Lifecycle policy — A rule that automatically expires, deletes old versions of, or moves objects to another tier after a set age or condition. (Ch 18)
  • Lightning File System — Dell's parallel file system for AI workloads, built on OneFS foundations and previewed as Project Lightning. (Ch 46)
  • Linearizability (strong consistency) — A guarantee that every read sees the latest acknowledged write, as if only one copy existed. (Ch 20)
  • Listen-for note — A one-line description of what a strong answer to a question should contain. (Ch 57)
  • Little's law — The queueing identity L = λW: requests in flight equal arrival rate times time in system, so outstanding I/Os = IOPS × latency. (Ch 4)
  • llm-d — An open-source, Kubernetes-native distributed inference project (CNCF Sandbox) with KV-aware scheduling and offload. (Ch 32)
  • LMCache — An open-source KV-cache layer that offloads and shares KV between inference engines such as vLLM and SGLang and storage tiers. (Ch 32)
  • LNet — Lustre's network layer, which carries traffic over RDMA fabrics such as InfiniBand and RoCE or over TCP and can route between them. (Ch 17)
  • Local checkpointing — Writing each node's checkpoint shard to its own SSD or RAM disk and replicating it to peer nodes before or instead of writing to shared storage. (Ch 31)
  • Locally decodable code — An erasure code that can rebuild a lost strip by reading only a subset of the stripe, cutting rebuild I/O. (Ch 16)
  • Locally decodable erasure code (LDEC) — VAST's wide erasure code that can rebuild a lost strip by reading only a fraction (about a quarter) of the stripe. (Ch 42)
  • Log-on-log — Stacking a log-structured array on top of SSDs that are themselves log-structured, duplicating garbage collection, spare space and mapping. (Ch 3, Ch 26)
  • Log-structured design — A storage design that appends every change to a log and garbage-collects old versions instead of updating in place. (Ch 21)
  • Logical-to-physical (L2P) table — The FTL's map from each logical address to its current physical NAND location, usually held in on-drive DRAM. (Ch 3)
  • Long-term agreement (LTA) — a multi-year memory supply contract, increasingly with prepayments and price floors and ceilings. (Ch 48)
  • LOTA (Local Object Transport Accelerator) — CoreWeave's cache on each GPU node's local NVMe that accelerates reads from its AI Object Storage. (Ch 35)
  • LTO (Linear Tape-Open) — The dominant open tape-cartridge standard; LTO-10 holds 30 TB native per cartridge. (Ch 2)
  • LUN (logical unit number) — The SCSI address of a block volume presented by a target. (Ch 7)
  • LUN (logical unit) — A block volume that a storage array presents to a host as if it were a disk. (Ch 1)
  • Lustre — The open-source parallel file system that runs most of the world's largest supercomputers, now developed mainly by DDN's Whamcloud unit and the community. (Ch 17)

docs.title: M
docs.text:
• Magic Quadrant (MQ) — Gartner's annual vendor assessment plotting ability to execute against completeness of vision; a perception signal, not market share. (Ch 40)
  • Magnum IO — NVIDIA's umbrella name for its GPU input/output software, including GPUDirect RDMA, GPUDirect Storage, NCCL, NVSHMEM and UCX. (Ch 11)
  • Management plane — A fleet-wide layer, often vendor-hosted in the cloud, that aggregates many arrays' control planes for monitoring, analytics and policy. (Ch 22)
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) — An open protocol that lets AI agents connect to tools and data sources, now exposed by several storage management planes. (Ch 22)
  • MCP server — A service that exposes tools and data to AI agents through the Model Context Protocol, here used to let agents query and act on storage fleets. (Ch 28, Ch 39)
  • MDS (metadata server) — The server in a parallel file system that handles namespace operations and hands out file layouts and locks. (Ch 17)
  • MDT (metadata target) — The storage volume behind a Lustre MDS that holds directories, inodes, permissions and file layouts. (Ch 17)
  • mdtest — The metadata benchmark used in IO500, measuring create, stat, read and delete rates in private (easy) and shared (hard) directories. (Ch 21, Ch 37)
  • Mean time between failures (MTBF) — The average time a system or job runs between failures; for large training jobs it shrinks roughly in proportion to GPU count. (Ch 31)
  • Media economics — the cost, density and power advantages a vendor gets from how it manages flash media, not from the NAND price itself. (Ch 0.2, Ch 49)
  • Mediator — Third-party witness that decides which side of a partitioned metro cluster keeps serving I/O. (Ch 6)
  • Memory cycle — The recurring boom-bust pattern in which high memory prices fund new capacity that later overshoots demand and crashes prices. (Ch 52)
  • Memory pooling — Assigning slices of switch-attached memory to different hosts on demand to reduce stranded DRAM. (Ch 12)
  • Memory–storage wall — The roughly 1,000× latency jump between DRAM-class memory (~100 ns) and NAND flash (~100 µs) that storage-system design works to hide. (Ch 2)
  • Metadata — Data about stored data: names, directory structure, permissions, sizes, timestamps and the maps from file offsets to physical blocks. (Ch 21)
  • Metadata bucket — In WEKA, one of thousands of hashed shards of the file-system namespace, each owned by a virtual metadata server. (Ch 43)
  • Metadata core — in FlashBlade//EXA, the FlashBlade blades running Purity//FB that hold the namespace, layouts and locks. (Ch 27, Ch 45)
  • Metadata index (object store) — The replicated, sharded table that maps each bucket, key and version to an object's size, ETag and fragment locations. (Ch 18)
  • Metadata pyramid — Everpure's term for Purity's tiered metadata store, with hot entries in DRAM, in-flight changes in NVRAM and the bulk on flash. (Ch 26)
  • Metadata server (MDS) — The server or service that owns namespace and inode operations in a file system whose data lives elsewhere. (Ch 21)
  • Metadata storm — A burst of creates, opens or stats, such as thousands of ranks writing checkpoint files at once, that saturates the metadata tier. (Ch 21)
  • Metadata/data split — A design that scales metadata servers separately from data nodes, with clients reading data nodes directly, as in pNFS or Lustre. (Ch 16, Ch 45, Ch 60)
  • MGS (management server) — The Lustre server that stores cluster configuration, which clients read when they mount the file system. (Ch 17)
  • Migration (SCM-to-QLC) — The background process that reduces buffered data and writes it to QLC flash in large erasure-coded stripes. (Ch 16)
  • Mirrored write cache — A design in which each write is copied to the partner controller's persistent memory before the host is acknowledged. (Ch 14)
  • Mixed-precision training — Training that computes in low precision (bf16 or FP8) while keeping fp32 master weights and optimizer state for numerical stability. (Ch 31)
  • Mixed-version cluster — a cluster temporarily running two software releases during a rolling upgrade. (Ch 56)
  • Mixture of experts (MoE) — A model design that activates only some of its parameters per token, so compute follows active parameters while checkpoint size follows total parameters. (Ch 31)
  • MLPerf Storage — MLCommons' benchmark that measures how well a storage system feeds AI workloads using software-simulated accelerators instead of real GPUs. (Ch 37, Ch 51)
  • MLPerf Storage checkpointing workload — an MLCommons test that measures how fast a storage system writes and reads emulated LLM training checkpoints. (Ch 27)
  • MLPerf Storage KV-cache workload — an MLCommons v3.0 test that measures how fast storage can deliver inference context (KV cache) to emulated accelerators. (Ch 27)
  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) — Open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in 2024 and now governed under the Linux Foundation, that standardises how AI agents discover and call external tools and data sources. (Ch 39)
  • Model FLOPs utilization (MFU) — The fraction of a GPU's peak arithmetic throughput a training job actually uses on model math. (Ch 31)
  • Monotonic write — a write that only ever appends new data or records and never modifies existing ones in place. (Ch 26)
  • Mountpoint for Amazon S3 — AWS's open-source file client that maps file reads and writes to S3 requests. (Ch 36)
  • Mozaic — Seagate's family of HAMR disk platforms, named by terabytes per platter (Mozaic 3+, 4+, 5). (Ch 53)
  • MTTDL (mean time to data loss) — A modelled estimate of how long a protection scheme runs before enough overlapping failures lose data. (Ch 20)
  • Multi-head latent attention (MLA) — DeepSeek's attention design that caches a compressed latent vector per layer instead of full keys and values, cutting KV size several-fold. (Ch 32)
  • Multipart upload — An S3 method for uploading a large object as many parallel, independently retryable parts that become visible atomically on completion. (Ch 9)
  • Multipath I/O (MPIO) — Host software that spreads I/O over several paths to an array and fails over between them. (Ch 14)

docs.title: N
docs.text:
• Nameplate power — The rated maximum power of a device or power supply, usually well above its typical draw. (Ch 38)
  • Namespace — The NVMe equivalent of a LUN, an addressable block volume exposed by an NVMe controller. (Ch 7, Ch 21)
  • NAND flash — A flash memory architecture with cells wired in series strings, trading random-read speed for much higher density and lower cost per bit. (Ch 52)
  • NAND pass-through — How quickly and fully changes in NAND cost are reflected in a storage vendor's selling prices. (Ch 29)
  • NAND qualification — characterising a new NAND die (read thresholds, retention, program timing) so firmware or software can drive it reliably. (Ch 26)
  • NAND string — A column of NAND cells connected in series along one vertical channel between a bit line and a source line. (Ch 2)
  • NAS (network-attached storage) — A storage system that owns the file system and serves files to hosts over NFS or SMB. (Ch 13)
  • NCCL — NVIDIA's library for collective communication (such as all-reduce) between GPUs within and across servers. (Ch 11)
  • nconnect — A Linux NFS mount option (kernel 5.3+) that opens up to 16 TCP connections per mount to the same server. (Ch 8)
  • NCP (NVIDIA Cloud Partner) — NVIDIA's programme, requirements and reference designs for GPU cloud providers, including a storage certification tier. (Ch 35)
  • Near-synchronous replication — Continuous streaming replication with local acknowledgement, giving an RPO of seconds. (Ch 6)
  • Nearline HDD — high-capacity 7,200 rpm hard drives used for warm and cold data in data centres. (Ch 48)
  • NeMo Retriever — NVIDIA microservices that extract, embed and rerank enterprise data for retrieval-augmented generation. (Ch 34)
  • Neocloud — A GPU-specialist cloud provider that rents AI clusters (bare metal, Kubernetes or Slurm) to labs, enterprises and hyperscalers, e.g. CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda, Crusoe. (Ch 35, Ch 41)
  • Net dollar retention (NDR) — Recurring revenue from an existing customer cohort this year as a percentage of the same cohort's revenue a year earlier. (Ch 23, Ch 28, Ch 29, Ch 55)
  • NeuralMesh — WEKA's software-defined storage platform since June 2025, the re-architected successor to WekaFS and the WEKA Data Platform. (Ch 43)
  • NeuralMesh 6 — WEKA's July 2026 platform release adding multi-tenancy, always-on data reduction and native object access. (Ch 43)
  • NeuralMesh Axon — WEKA's packaging of NeuralMesh to run inside GPU servers on their local NVMe drives and spare CPU cores. (Ch 43)
  • Neutrality — A vendor's ability to serve data stored on rivals' systems, which partners and multi-vendor buyers value. (Ch 54)
