  • NFS (Network File System) — The standard file-sharing protocol on Linux and Unix, in which clients send file-level operations to a server that owns the file system. (Ch 8)
  • NFS over RDMA — NFS carried over RPC-over-RDMA (RFC 8166/8267), letting servers place data directly in client memory with little CPU involvement. (Ch 8)
  • NFSv3 — The stateless 1995 version of NFS (RFC 1813), still the most widely deployed, with locking handled by separate side protocols. (Ch 8)
  • NFSv4.1 — The NFS minor version (RFC 5661, now RFC 8881) that added sessions, trunking and parallel NFS (pNFS). (Ch 8)
  • NFSv4.2 — The NFS minor version (RFC 7862, 2016) that added server-side copy, sparse files, I/O hints and labeled NFS. (Ch 8)
  • NIM — NVIDIA Inference Microservices, packaged containers that serve AI models behind standard APIs. (Ch 34)
  • Nitro card — AWS's custom offload card that, among other jobs, presents EBS volumes to guests as NVMe devices and sends I/O over the network. (Ch 19)
  • NIXL (NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library) — An open-source library that moves KV-cache blocks and tensors between GPU memory, CPU memory and storage through pluggable backends. (Ch 11, Ch 43)
  • NKP — Nutanix Kubernetes Platform, built from the D2iQ acquisition and launched in 2024. (Ch 47)
  • No-regret move — A strategic action that pays off across almost all plausible scenarios. (Ch 53)
  • Non-disruptive upgrade (NDU) — Upgrading array software or controller hardware one controller at a time so hosts keep running. (Ch 14, Ch 23)
  • NOR flash — A flash memory architecture with cells wired in parallel, giving fast random reads at low density; used mainly for code storage. (Ch 52)
  • NQN (NVMe Qualified Name) — The unique name identifying an NVMe host or subsystem for discovery and access control. (Ch 7)
  • Nutanix Unified Storage (NUS) — Nutanix's software storage offering covering Files, Objects and Volumes on its platform. (Ch 47)
  • NVIDIA AI Data Platform — NVIDIA's 2025 reference design for putting GPUs, DPUs and NVIDIA retrieval software inside storage systems. (Ch 34)
  • NVIDIA Cloud Partner (NCP) — NVIDIA's program and reference architectures for GPU cloud providers, including storage uptime, durability and delivery requirements. (Ch 34)
  • NVIDIA Dynamo — NVIDIA's open-source distributed inference-serving framework that routes requests and manages KV cache across GPUs and memory tiers. (Ch 11, Ch 32)
  • NVIDIA STX — NVIDIA's BlueField-4-based storage reference architecture launched at GTC 2026. (Ch 43)
  • NVIDIA-Certified Storage (NVCS) — NVIDIA's storage certification programme with Foundation, Enterprise and NCP levels for AI factory deployments. (Ch 27, Ch 34)
  • NVL72 — NVIDIA's rack-scale system joining 72 Blackwell GPUs by NVLink into one liquid-cooled rack drawing roughly 120–130 kW. (Ch 35)
  • NVMe — A storage interface and command set designed for flash on PCIe, built around many parallel submission and completion queues. (Ch 7)
  • NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF) — The extension of NVMe across a network, using command and response capsules over RDMA, Fibre Channel or TCP. (Ch 7)
  • NVMe/RoCE — NVMe-oF over RDMA on converged Ethernet, in which the target moves data directly to or from host memory without CPU copies. (Ch 7)
  • NVMe/TCP — The NVMe-oF transport that carries capsules and data on ordinary TCP connections, ratified in 2018. (Ch 7)
  • NVRAM — Non-volatile memory in a storage controller that holds acknowledged writes until they are written to flash, surviving power loss. (Ch 13)
  • NVRAM write log — A small battery-, capacitor- or flash-backed persistent buffer that holds acknowledged writes until they are flushed to flash. (Ch 14)

docs.title: O
docs.text:
• Object — An immutable blob of bytes plus metadata, stored and retrieved whole by key through an API such as S3. (Ch 9)
  • Object gateway — A stateless server that terminates S3 requests, checks authentication and policy, and reads or writes object fragments on behalf of clients. (Ch 18)
  • Object key — The string name that addresses an object in a bucket's flat namespace; slashes in it are just characters. (Ch 1, Ch 9)
  • Object storage — Storage presented as flat buckets of objects, each with a key, data and metadata, accessed whole over HTTP APIs such as S3. (Ch 1)
  • ObjectEngine — Pure Storage's short-lived backup appliance built on StorReduce deduplication technology, launched in 2019 and de-emphasised by mid-2020. (Ch 25)
  • OceanStor A-series — Huawei's AI-oriented scale-out storage line, led by the A800. (Ch 46)
  • OceanStor M900 — Huawei's context-memory storage system for sharing KV cache across inference clusters. (Ch 46)
  • ODM direct — Storage or server hardware built by an original design manufacturer to a hyperscaler's own design and sold to it directly, bypassing branded OEMs. (Ch 40)
  • Office of the CTO — the group that frames long-horizon technology bets, standards engagement and external technical strategy. (Ch 56)
  • On-behalf-of authorisation — Access control in which an agent's effective rights are the intersection of the delegating user's rights and the agent's own scope. (Ch 39)
  • One-liner — A 30-second, plain-English answer that states what something is, why it matters and at most one sourced number. (Ch 58)
  • One-page map — the atlas's mindmap of the storage and AI-storage domain, from media to Everpure. (Ch 0.2)
  • Open division — the MLPerf category that allows disclosed changes to loaders, formats or frameworks, so results are not directly comparable with closed ones. (Ch 37)
  • Open Semantic Interchange (OSI) — A Snowflake-initiated, multi-vendor open specification for exchanging semantic-layer definitions, first published in January 2026. (Ch 39)
  • Open-channel SSD — an SSD that exposes NAND geometry to the host so host software performs flash management, the precursor of zoned and placement-hint designs. (Ch 26)
  • Open-core relicensing — Narrowing or restricting a free open-source edition to push users toward paid commercial editions. (Ch 47)
  • Operating lease — Financing in which a lessor owns the hardware and the customer pays periodic rent, recorded under ASC 842 as a right-of-use asset and lease liability. (Ch 23)
  • Operational carbon — Emissions from the electricity a system consumes over its service life. (Ch 38)
  • Optimizer state — The per-parameter values an optimizer such as Adam keeps (fp32 master weights and two moment estimates), which make up most of a checkpoint's size. (Ch 31)
  • OSD (object storage daemon) — The Ceph process that manages one drive and stores, replicates and recovers its objects. (Ch 15)
  • OSS (object storage server) — The Lustre server that serves file data from its object storage targets. (Ch 17)
  • OST (object storage target) — A Lustre data volume, usually a RAID-protected local file system, that stores file data as objects. (Ch 17)
  • Over-provisioning (OP) — Flash installed in a drive but hidden from the host, used as working space for garbage collection, expressed as a percentage of user capacity. (Ch 3)
  • Overall response time (ORT) — SPECstorage's average latency across the load points of a run. (Ch 37)

docs.title: P
docs.text:
• P/E cycle — One program/erase cycle of a NAND block; the unit in which flash wear and endurance are counted. (Ch 2)
  • p99 / p99.9 — The latency that 1% or 0.1% of requests exceed. (Ch 4)
  • PACELC — An extension of CAP: under a Partition choose Availability or Consistency, Else choose Latency or Consistency. (Ch 20)
  • Packaging — how features are bundled into SKUs, tiers and contracts. (Ch 55)
  • PagedAttention — vLLM's technique of storing KV cache in fixed-size pages, like virtual memory, to cut fragmentation and enable block sharing. (Ch 32)
  • PAM4 — Four-level pulse-amplitude modulation, carrying two bits per symbol to double lane rates over NRZ. (Ch 10, Ch 12)
  • Parallel file system — A file system in which clients get a file's layout from metadata servers and then read and write its data directly and in parallel across many storage servers. (Ch 17)
  • Partitioned prefix — The key-prefix unit by which S3 scales request throughput, each supporting at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second. (Ch 9)
  • Partitioned-writer — Everpure's term for the FlashBlade design in which blades own slices of the namespace while flash is managed globally. (Ch 60)
  • Pass-through lag — the delay between a change in component cost and the matching change in a vendor's selling prices. (Ch 48)
  • Pattern removal — Detecting all-zero or repeating-pattern blocks and recording them as metadata instead of storing them. (Ch 5)
  • Paxos — Lamport's majority-based consensus protocol, published in 1998 and used in systems such as Ceph monitors and DynamoDB. (Ch 20)
  • Payback period — The years of incremental gross profit or cash flow needed to recover a purchase price. (Ch 54)
  • PB per rack — Raw or usable petabytes held in one rack, limited in practice by rack power, cooling and floor loading. (Ch 38)
  • Peer-to-peer DMA — A transfer in which one PCIe device (such as a NIC) writes directly into another device's memory (such as a GPU) without involving host memory. (Ch 11)
  • Performance density — Storage throughput or GPUs fed per rack unit or per kilowatt, the metric DDN emphasises in benchmarks. (Ch 44)
  • Performance HDD — 10K and 15K RPM enterprise hard drives optimised for IOPS rather than capacity, largely displaced by flash. (Ch 52)
  • Persistence point — The layer at which a write is durable enough for the system to acknowledge it, typically mirrored NVRAM in an array or power-loss-protected DRAM in an SSD. (Ch 13)
  • Persona — the specific buyer or operator a product is designed and priced for, such as a VMware admin or an AI platform team. (Ch 55)
  • PFC (Priority Flow Control) — An Ethernet mechanism that pauses a link for one traffic class to prevent drops, at the risk of spreading congestion. (Ch 10)
  • Phone-home telemetry — Outbound metrics, logs and health data that an array sends to its vendor's cloud for support and analytics. (Ch 22)
  • Physalia — AWS's configuration-master store for EBS, giving each volume its own small Paxos-replicated cell. (Ch 19)
  • Placeholder score — A neutral score assigned in a scorecard where public data is silent, flagged for diligence access. (Ch 50)
  • Placement group (PG) — Ceph's unit of placement and rebalancing, grouping many objects that are mapped together to the same set of drives. (Ch 15)
  • PLC (penta-level cell) — NAND flash storing 5 bits per cell in 32 voltage states; denser than QLC but slower and less durable. (Ch 53)
  • pNFS (parallel NFS) — An NFSv4.1+ feature in which a metadata server hands clients a layout so they can read and write data servers directly and in parallel. (Ch 8)
  • pNFS Flex Files — The NFSv4.2 parallel-NFS layout that lets clients do I/O directly against data servers after getting a layout from a metadata server. (Ch 47)
  • pNFS layout — the map a pNFS metadata server returns telling a client which data servers hold which parts of a file. (Ch 27)
  • Policy decision point — The component that evaluates an access request against policy and returns allow, deny or mask. (Ch 39)
  • Portworx — Everpure's software-defined data-services layer that gives Kubernetes containers and VMs persistent storage, replication, backup and DR on any infrastructure. (Ch 28)
  • POSIX semantics — The Unix file-system behaviour (open, read, write, rename, byte-range locks, immediate visibility) that applications assume of a local disk. (Ch 8)
  • Post-process reduction — Data reduction performed in the background after data has landed on media. (Ch 5)
  • Post-training — Training steps after pre-training, such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, that adapt a base model. (Ch 30)
  • Power-limited datacenter — A facility whose output is bounded by available electricity rather than by chip supply or floor space. (Ch 38)
  • Power-loss protection (PLP) — On-drive capacitors that hold up power long enough to flush buffered writes and map updates after a power failure. (Ch 3, Ch 13)
  • Powered shell — A datacenter building with grid power and cooling in place, ready for IT equipment to be installed. (Ch 38)
  • Pre-election — Everpure ActiveCluster behaviour that pre-selects a surviving array per pod when both arrays lose contact with the mediator. (Ch 20)
  • Prefetching — Fetching data into a faster tier before it is requested so that the consumer never waits on the slower tier. (Ch 30)
  • Prefill — The compute-bound inference phase that processes the whole prompt in parallel and produces the KV cache. (Ch 32)
  • Prefix caching — Reusing stored KV blocks for the identical leading tokens (system prompt, document, earlier turns) shared by many requests. (Ch 32)
  • Prepayment (supplier) — cash paid to a component maker before delivery to secure allocation, recorded as a prepaid asset rather than inventory. (Ch 48)
  • Preset (Pure Fusion) — A fleet-wide template bundling capacity, QoS, protection and tags that Fusion uses to provision a workload consistently. (Ch 22)
  • Price collar — a contract term that sets both a floor and a ceiling on the price paid, limiting both upside and downside. (Ch 48)
  • Price pass-through — revenue growth that comes from passing higher component (NAND) costs on to customers rather than from shipping more units. (Ch 0.2)
  • Price-led growth — Revenue growth driven by higher component (mainly NAND) prices passed through to customers rather than by more units or capacity shipped. (Ch 58)
  • Price/volume decomposition — Splitting revenue growth into change in price per unit (e.g., per TB) and change in units shipped. (Ch 40)
  • Primary OSD — The OSD that receives a placement group's writes, forwards them to replicas and acknowledges the client. (Ch 15)
  • Primary storage — The tier that serves live applications and is optimised for latency, performance and availability. (Ch 1)
  • Product gross margin — Gross profit on hardware and licence (product) revenue as a percentage of that revenue. (Ch 29)
  • Product quantization (PQ) — Compressing a vector by splitting it into sub-vectors and replacing each with a small codebook index, cutting memory by tens of times. (Ch 33)
  • Program/erase asymmetry — NAND's property that data is programmed page by page but can only be erased a whole (much larger) block at a time, so it cannot be overwritten in place. (Ch 2)
  • Progressive File Layout (PFL) — A Lustre feature that widens a file's stripe count automatically as the file grows. (Ch 17)
  • Project Silica — Microsoft's research program for archival data storage written by laser into quartz or borosilicate glass. (Ch 53)
  • Proof of concept (PoC) — A hands-on test of a vendor's system on the buyer's own workloads, ideally on the buyer's hardware. (Ch 50)
  • Proprietary parallel client — A vendor kernel module or agent that stripes I/O directly across storage servers, as in Lustre, IBM Storage Scale or WEKA. (Ch 60)
  • Protection level (OneFS) — PowerScale's notation for how many drive or node failures a file can survive, e.g., +2d:1n. (Ch 15)
  • Protocol family — The three ways a host sees storage: as a disk (block), a directory tree (file) or a bucket of keys (object). (Ch 60)
  • PUE (power usage effectiveness) — Total facility power divided by IT equipment power; 1.0 would mean zero cooling and distribution overhead. (Ch 4)
  • Pull-forward demand — Orders placed earlier than needed to beat expected price increases, which inflates current growth and borrows from future quarters. (Ch 40)
  • Pure Fusion — Everpure's policy-driven fleet control plane, embedded in Purity, that provisions workloads across FlashArray, FlashBlade and cloud arrays. (Ch 22)
  • Pure Storage Cloud Dedicated — Everpure's customer-managed Purity block service on AWS and Azure, formerly Cloud Block Store. (Ch 24)
  • Pure1 — Everpure's SaaS monitoring, analytics and support portal fed by array phone-home telemetry. (Ch 22)
  • PureKVA — Everpure's KV-cache offload software on FlashBlade (formerly Key Value Accelerator), serving cached LLM attention state over S3 and NFS. (Ch 24, Ch 27, Ch 32, Ch 45)
  • Purity — Everpure's storage operating system for FlashArray (Purity//FA) and FlashBlade (Purity//FB), built as a log-structured, metadata-centric design. (Ch 26)
  • Purity DeepReduce — Everpure's similarity-based, cluster-wide, asynchronous data reduction for FlashBlade, introduced in 2026. (Ch 5)
  • Purity Turbo — An Everpure feature for FlashArray//XL190 that lets the secondary controller serve read I/O. (Ch 14, Ch 27)
  • Purity//DN — Everpure's data-node software for FlashBlade//EXA, running on off-the-shelf servers. (Ch 16, Ch 27, Ch 45)

docs.title: Q
docs.text:
• Quadrant chart — A two-axis chart split into four labelled quadrants, used to group vendors by two strategic dimensions. (Ch 49)
  • Qualification matrix — The set of server, NIC, drive, kernel and cloud combinations a software vendor must test and support. (Ch 50)
  • Question bank — A curated, numbered set of questions tagged by topic and audience, used to prepare for internal meetings. (Ch 57)
  • Queue depth — The number of I/O requests outstanding at a device or system at one time. (Ch 4)
  • Queue pair — The send/receive work-queue pair through which an application posts RDMA operations directly to the NIC. (Ch 10)
  • Quorum — The majority of voting members (e.g., 3 of 5 monitors) required to change cluster state, which prevents split brain. (Ch 15)
  • Quorum (N/W/R) — The replica count N and the number of write (W) and read (R) acknowledgements required; W + R > N ensures reads overlap the latest write. (Ch 20)

docs.title: R
docs.text:
• R-generation — a FlashArray or FlashBlade controller refresh (for example R4, R5) that Evergreen customers can apply in place without migrating data. (Ch 27)
  • R2T (Ready to Transfer) — A target's message inviting the host to send write data, used in iSCSI and NVMe/TCP. (Ch 7)
  • Raft — A consensus protocol (2014) designed to be easy to understand, with leader election by term and majority-committed log replication. (Ch 20)
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) — Answering a prompt by first retrieving relevant documents from an index and feeding them to the model as context. (Ch 30, Ch 33)
  • RAID (redundant array of inexpensive disks) — Combining many cheap drives with mirroring or parity so the group is faster and more reliable than any one drive. (Ch 51)
  • RAID 1 (mirroring) — Protection scheme that writes every block to two drives, giving 50% usable capacity. (Ch 6)
  • RAID 10 — Striping across mirrored pairs; 50% usable capacity with fast, simple rebuilds. (Ch 6)
  • RAID 5 — Striping with one rotating parity block per stripe; survives one drive failure. (Ch 6)
  • RAID 6 — Striping with two independent parity blocks (P and Q) per stripe; survives any two drive failures. (Ch 6)
  • RAID-HA — Purity's dual-parity data protection scheme across flash modules. (Ch 26)
  • RAMAC — IBM's 1956 305 computer and its 350 disk unit, the first commercial hard disk system (about 3.75 MB). (Ch 51)
  • Rapid Bucket — Google Cloud's zonal Cloud Storage bucket on Colossus aimed at AI workloads (formerly Rapid Storage). (Ch 36)
  • Ratable revenue — Revenue recognised evenly over a service period rather than at shipment. (Ch 29)
  • Ratable revenue recognition — Recognizing revenue evenly over the service period rather than upfront at delivery. (Ch 23)
  • Raw capacity — The sum of the drives' capacities in decimal terabytes, before any protection or overhead. (Ch 4)
  • Raw, usable and effective capacity — Capacity before data protection, after protection, and after an assumed data-reduction ratio; vendors' prices differ by which one they quote. (Ch 58)
  • RBD — RADOS Block Device, Ceph's block storage interface. (Ch 47)
  • RDMA (remote direct memory access) — A transport in which the network card moves data directly between registered memory regions on two machines, with no kernel copies and no remote CPU involvement. (Ch 10)
  • Re-mirroring storm — A cascade in which many volumes lose replicas at once and their simultaneous repair traffic exhausts capacity and network. (Ch 19)
  • Read disturb — Gradual shifting of unread NAND cells caused by the pass voltage applied during reads of other cells in the same block, forcing periodic data relocation. (Ch 2)
  • Read retry — Re-reading a NAND page at shifted reference voltages when error correction fails, at the cost of extra latency. (Ch 3)
  • Read-after-write consistency — A guarantee that once a write succeeds, every subsequent read returns the new data. (Ch 9)
  • Read-modify-write penalty — The extra NAND work when a write is smaller than the drive's indirection unit, forcing the whole unit to be read, merged and rewritten. (Ch 3)
  • Real option — A small, early investment that preserves the right to scale up if a trend breaks favorably. (Ch 53)
  • Rebalancing — Background movement of data to restore even placement after nodes are added or removed. (Ch 15)
  • Rebuild storm — The burst of east-west network and drive traffic generated while a cluster restores redundancy after a drive or node failure. (Ch 15)
  • Rebuild window — Time between a drive failure and restored full redundancy, during which further failures risk data loss. (Ch 6)
  • Recall — The share of the true nearest neighbours that an approximate search actually returns. (Ch 33)
  • Recompute-versus-fetch break-even — The per-GPU bandwidth above which loading stored KV is faster than recomputing it with prefill (roughly 2–5 GB/s for a 70B model). (Ch 32)
  • Redirect-on-write (ROW) snapshot — Snapshot method that freezes the pointer map and writes new data to free space. (Ch 6)
  • Reducible data — Data not already compressed or encrypted by the host, which is what most reduction guarantees cover. (Ch 5)
  • Reference-design status — Being named in a platform vendor's validated architecture, which works as a procurement shortlist for buyers. (Ch 41)
  • Remaining performance obligations (RPO) — contracted revenue not yet recognised, including undelivered product and subscription terms. (Ch 55, Ch 58)
  • Reported by press — a label for a figure published by journalists, often from unnamed sources. (Ch 0.1)
  • Reranker — A second, more accurate model that rescores the top candidates from a vector search before they go into the prompt. (Ch 33)
  • Restore storm — The burst of simultaneous reads and metadata operations when every GPU in a job loads the latest checkpoint after a failure. (Ch 31)
  • Retimer — An active chip that recovers and re-transmits a high-speed serial signal to extend link reach. (Ch 12)
  • Revenue inflation — revenue growth driven by higher selling prices rather than more units shipped. (Ch 48)
  • Right-Size Guarantee — Everpure's (originally Pure Storage's, 2016) workload-based guarantee of effective capacity for FlashArray purchases. (Ch 5)
  • RNIC — A network interface card that implements the RDMA transport in hardware. (Ch 10)
  • RoCEv2 — RDMA over Converged Ethernet version 2: the InfiniBand transport carried in routable UDP/IP packets on Ethernet. (Ch 10)
  • Rolling hash — A hash recomputed cheaply as a window slides one byte at a time, used to find content-defined chunk boundaries (e.g., Rabin, Gear). (Ch 5)
  • Royalty / licence revenue — Fees paid to an IP owner per unit deployed, with the customer buying the underlying hardware. (Ch 29)
  • RPO (recovery point objective) — The maximum amount of recent data, measured in time, an organisation can afford to lose. (Ch 6)
  • RPO (remaining performance obligations) — Contracted revenue not yet recognized, disclosed under ASC 606. (Ch 23, Ch 29)
  • RTO (recovery time objective) — The maximum time an organisation can afford a service to be down. (Ch 6)
  • Rule of X — Bessemer Venture Partners' growth-weighted variant of the Rule of 40: revenue growth times a multiplier (about 2–3) plus free-cash-flow margin. (Ch 42)

docs.title: S
docs.text:
• S3 (Simple Storage Service) API — Amazon's HTTP/REST interface for object storage, now the de facto standard implemented by most storage vendors. (Ch 9)
  • S3 Express One Zone — An AWS S3 storage class using single-Availability-Zone directory buckets for single-digit-millisecond access. (Ch 9, Ch 36)
  • S3 over RDMA — A data path in which a normal S3 request carries a memory token over HTTP while the object bytes move by RDMA directly to or from host or GPU memory. (Ch 9, Ch 11)
  • S3 Tables — AWS table buckets that store and automatically maintain Apache Iceberg tables inside S3. (Ch 9)
  • S3 Vectors — An AWS S3 capability that stores and queries vector embeddings natively in vector buckets. (Ch 9, Ch 24)
  • SafeMode — Everpure's snapshot immutability feature, in which deleted snapshots are retained for a set period and cannot be eradicated without support-gated approval. (Ch 6)
  • Sales engineer (SE) — A pre-sales technical specialist who sizes systems, runs proofs of concept and answers technical objections in deals. (Ch 57)
  • SAM (serviceable addressable market) — The part of a TAM a vendor can actually sell into given its products, channels and geographies. (Ch 40)
  • SAN (storage area network) — A dedicated network giving many hosts block-level access to shared arrays. (Ch 13, Ch 51)
  • SBOM (software bill of materials) — A machine-readable list of the components and licences inside a piece of software. (Ch 50)
  • Scalable Reliable Datagram (SRD) — AWS's multipath, reliable but out-of-order transport implemented in Nitro cards and used by EBS io2 Block Express. (Ch 19)
  • Scalable unit (SU) — The 32-node building block of a DGX SuperPOD (256 GPUs with eight-GPU nodes). (Ch 34)
  • Scale-out — Growing a storage system by adding whole nodes rather than upgrading a controller pair. (Ch 15)
  • Scale-out NAS — A file system spread across a cluster of nodes behind one namespace, grown by adding nodes rather than upgrading controllers. (Ch 51)
  • Scale-up — Growing a storage system by adding drives or faster controllers behind a fixed controller pair rather than adding nodes. (Ch 14)
  • Scrubbing — A background process that re-reads stored data and verifies checksums to find and repair silent corruption (bit rot). (Ch 18)
  • SCSI — The Small Computer System Interface command set, standardized in 1986 and still carried over Fibre Channel and iSCSI. (Ch 7)
  • Second-OS problem — The engineering cost and customer confusion of running two storage operating systems after an acquisition. (Ch 54)
  • Secondary storage — The tier that holds backup, disaster-recovery and other copies of primary data, optimised for ingest, restore speed and cost. (Ch 1)
  • Secondary tender — A funding round in which investors buy existing shares from employees or early holders, so the company receives none of that money. (Ch 41, Ch 42)
  • SEDA — HPE's name for the shared-everything disaggregated architecture of its Alletra MP X10000. (Ch 16)
  • Segment-fit heatmap — A vendor-by-buyer-segment table showing where each vendor has proven, partial or little fit. (Ch 49)
  • Sell-through — The share of a neocloud's installed storage capacity actually billed to tenants, which drives its storage gross margin. (Ch 35)
  • Semantic layer — A governed set of business definitions (metrics, dimensions, joins) that maps business terms such as "net revenue" onto underlying tables. (Ch 39)
  • SerDes — Serializer/deserializer circuits whose per-lane rate (e.g., 112G, 224G) determines achievable port speeds. (Ch 10)
  • Server attach — Selling storage as an add-on to a server-led purchase, a key bundling tactic for server-and-storage vendors. (Ch 46)
  • Server-based storage — Drives inside general-purpose servers managed by software (HCI, SDS or a hyperscaler file system) rather than a dedicated array. (Ch 40)
  • Shard — A large file or object that packs many training samples together so storage serves big sequential reads instead of many small ones. (Ch 30)
  • ShardStore — The key-value storage-node engine, written in Rust, that stores object shards on each Amazon S3 storage node. (Ch 18)
  • Shared-nothing cluster — A storage architecture in which each node owns its own CPUs, memory and drives, and nodes cooperate only by sending requests over the network. (Ch 15)
  • Short-stroking — Using only a hard drive's outer tracks to cut seek time, sacrificing most of its capacity for performance. (Ch 52)
  • Signature visual — a diagram marked ★ in the outline that a reader should be able to redraw from memory. (Ch 0.1)
  • Signpost — an observable, dated event that confirms or refutes a long-range technology thesis. (Ch 56)
  • SigV4 — AWS Signature Version 4, which signs each HTTP request with an HMAC-derived key so the server can authenticate it without the secret crossing the wire. (Ch 9)
  • Similarity hash — A fingerprint that gives close values for chunks sharing most of their bytes, unlike a cryptographic hash that changes completely with one byte. (Ch 42)
  • Similarity reduction — Storing near-identical blocks as compressed differences against a reference block found via a locality-sensitive hash. (Ch 5)
  • Similarity-based data reduction — A data-reduction method that groups nearly identical chunks and stores most of them as small deltas against a shared reference chunk. (Ch 42)
  • Simulated accelerator — a software stand-in for a GPU in MLPerf Storage that waits a calibrated time per batch instead of computing. (Ch 37)
  • Single namespace — One file or object directory tree that all clients see, regardless of how many nodes store the data. (Ch 24)
  • Single-head bottleneck — The limit reached when every byte of a NAS mount must pass through one server controller's CPU, memory and NICs. (Ch 8)
  • Single-mount ceiling — The throughput one client mount can reach before extra connections or parallel paths are needed. (Ch 60)
  • Site power cap — The fixed grid allocation, in megawatts, that bounds all IT load a datacenter campus can run. (Ch 38)
  • SLC / MLC / TLC / QLC / PLC — NAND storing 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 bits per cell (2, 4, 8, 16 or 32 voltage states), trading endurance and speed for cost per bit. (Ch 2)
  • SLC cache — Part of a TLC or QLC SSD run in 1-bit mode to absorb incoming writes quickly before they are folded into denser cells. (Ch 2)
  • SLED (single large expensive disk) — The RAID paper's name for the big mainframe drives that arrays of small disks replaced. (Ch 51)
  • Small-file problem — The collapse in effective throughput when files are so small that per-file metadata operations, not bandwidth, limit performance. (Ch 21)
  • Small-object tax — The disproportionate request cost and rate-limit pressure incurred when data is stored as many small objects. (Ch 9)
  • Smart client — A client library that performs data placement, encoding and direct data transfer itself, removing the storage controller from the data path. (Ch 36)
  • SMB Direct — SMB3 running over RDMA (iWARP, InfiniBand or RoCE) for low-latency, low-CPU file access. (Ch 8)
  • SMB Multichannel — An SMB3 feature that automatically spreads one session over several network connections and adapters. (Ch 8)
  • SMB3 — The Windows file-sharing protocol version introduced with Windows Server 2012, adding Multichannel, SMB Direct and transparent failover. (Ch 8)
  • SMR (shingled magnetic recording) — HDD recording that overlaps tracks like roof shingles for more capacity, at the cost of having to rewrite whole bands or zones sequentially. (Ch 2)
  • Software composition analysis — Automated scanning of a code base to inventory its open-source components and their licences. (Ch 50)
  • Software-defined storage — Storage sold as software that runs on partner or customer servers rather than on the vendor's own appliances. (Ch 41)
  • Software-defined storage (SDS) — Storage software sold separately from the hardware it runs on, deployed on commodity servers. (Ch 19)
  • Software-defined wave — A period when storage functions move from proprietary controllers onto commodity servers as software. (Ch 51)
  • Software-only storage — Storage software sold to run on customer- or partner-supplied commodity servers rather than as a vendor appliance. (Ch 13)
  • Solidigm — The SK hynix subsidiary formed from Intel's NAND and SSD business in December 2021. (Ch 52)
  • Sovereign AI — AI infrastructure built so that data, control and operations stay within a given country or jurisdiction. (Ch 53)
  • Sovereign cloud — Cloud services run under local jurisdiction and control, often by domestic providers, to meet data-sovereignty rules. (Ch 53)
  • Sovereign presence — A vendor's ability to win deals that require in-country control of data and supply, typically government and national AI clouds. (Ch 49)
  • Spaced repetition — Reviewing material at increasing intervals, each timed to fall just before it would be forgotten. (Ch 59)
  • SPDK (Storage Performance Development Kit) — A user-space library for driving NVMe devices directly with polling instead of kernel interrupts. (Ch 43)
  • SPECstorage Solution 2020 — SPEC's file-storage benchmark with five workloads (AI_IMAGE, EDA_BLENDED, GENOMICS, SWBUILD, VDA), each scored as a business metric at an overall response time. (Ch 37)
  • SPECstorage Solution 2020 AI_IMAGE — a SPEC storage benchmark workload modelled on image-based AI training, scored in AI_Jobs at a response time. (Ch 27)
  • Spectrum-X — NVIDIA's Ethernet platform pairing Spectrum switches with its NICs for adaptive routing and congestion control on AI fabrics. (Ch 10)
  • Split-brain — Failure state in which two partitioned copies both accept writes and diverge. (Ch 6, Ch 15)
  • Spot price — the price for memory traded in small, immediate lots outside long-term contracts, usually the first to move in a cycle. (Ch 48)
  • SSD controller — The embedded system-on-chip inside an SSD, with processor cores, error-correction engines and flash channel interfaces, that runs the drive's firmware. (Ch 3)
  • STAC-M3 — an audited benchmark of kdb+ tick-data analytics used by financial-services buyers to compare storage and compute stacks. (Ch 37)
  • Stateless controller — A controller that holds no unique data or configuration, so it can be replaced without destaging or migrating anything. (Ch 14)
  • Stock client — the file-system client built into a standard operating system, such as the Linux NFS client, as opposed to a vendor's proprietary driver. (Ch 0.2, Ch 60)
  • Storage as code — Declaring storage resources and policies in version-controlled automation (Terraform, Ansible, Kubernetes manifests) instead of configuring them by hand. (Ch 22)
  • Storage Availability Zone (SAZ) — NetApp AFX's single shared pool of NVMe shelves that every controller can read and write. (Ch 16)
  • Storage network — The network, often converged with the front-end, that links GPU nodes to shared storage for training reads, checkpoints and KV-cache spill. (Ch 35)
  • Storage stack — The ordered layers an I/O crosses from application to physical media: application, file system or object API, volume manager, protocol, network, array controller software, SSD controller/FTL and media. (Ch 13)
  • Storage-as-a-service (STaaS) — A model in which the vendor owns and operates storage at the customer's site and bills for consumption against service-level agreements. (Ch 23)
  • Storage-class memory (SCM) — Persistent media faster than NAND but cheaper than DRAM, such as Intel Optane (3D XPoint). (Ch 12, Ch 16)
  • Storage-only node — An HCI node that contributes capacity but runs no application VMs, used to break coupled scaling. (Ch 19)
  • StorageClass — A Kubernetes object naming a class of storage (performance, protection) that persistent volume claims request by name. (Ch 22)
  • Stranded resources — Compute or capacity that is bought only because a fixed node configuration bundles it with the resource actually needed. (Ch 19)
  • Strategic fit — Whether an option strengthens a layer customers pay for, or protects one they do pay for. (Ch 54)
  • Strategic purchase — buying components well ahead of need to secure supply and lock in cost, at the expense of near-term cash flow. (Ch 48)
  • Stretched (metro) cluster — Two arrays at nearby sites presenting the same volumes active/active over synchronous replication. (Ch 6)
  • Stripe count — The number of storage targets a file's chunks are dealt across, which sets its maximum parallel bandwidth. (Ch 17)
  • Stripe size — The size of each chunk a file is cut into before the chunks are spread across storage targets. (Ch 17)
  • Stripe width — The number of data plus parity strips in one erasure-coded stripe, e.g., 146+4; wider stripes mean lower capacity overhead. (Ch 16)
  • STX — NVIDIA's BlueField-4 storage reference architecture, launched at GTC 2026, on which storage partners build AI storage nodes. (Ch 53)
  • Submission queue / completion queue (SQ/CQ) — NVMe's paired rings in host memory holding 64-byte commands and 16-byte completions. (Ch 7)
  • Subscription ARR — The annualized run rate of recurring subscription revenue at period end. (Ch 23, Ch 25, Ch 29, Ch 58)
  • Substitution right — A supplier's contractual right to swap the underlying asset; if substantive, it can mean a contract contains no lease. (Ch 23)
  • Subtree partitioning — Scaling metadata by assigning whole directory subtrees to different metadata servers, statically or dynamically. (Ch 21)
  • SuperNIC — NVIDIA's term for a high-bandwidth NIC tuned for AI east-west traffic, such as ConnectX-8/9. (Ch 10)
  • Symmetric active/active — A controller arrangement in which every path is optimized and any controller can serve any volume. (Ch 14)
  • Synchronous checkpointing — Pausing training until the checkpoint is fully written to durable storage. (Ch 31)
  • Synchronous replication — Replication that acknowledges a write only after both sites have persisted it, giving zero data loss. (Ch 6)
  • System-level TB/W — Capacity per watt measured for a whole storage system including controllers, fans and networking, rather than for a bare drive. (Ch 38)

docs.title: T
docs.text:
• Tail latency — The latency of the slowest small fraction of requests, expressed as a high percentile such as p99 or p99.9. (Ch 4)
  • Take-or-pay contract — A multi-year commitment in which a customer pays for reserved GPU capacity whether or not it uses it, used by neoclouds to secure financing. (Ch 35)
  • Takeover / giveback — A partner controller assuming a failed or upgrading controller's volumes, then returning them when it rejoins. (Ch 14)
  • TAM (total addressable market) — The total annual spend a product category could capture if it won every deal in its defined scope. (Ch 40)
  • Target — The device or array side of a block-storage session that executes commands from initiators. (Ch 7)
  • TB/RU — Storage capacity per rack unit (1.75 inches of rack height), a density metric. (Ch 4)
  • TB/W — Storage capacity per watt of power drawn, a key efficiency metric for power-constrained data centres. (Ch 4)
  • TCV (total contract value) — The full value of a contract signed in a period, regardless of when revenue is recognized. (Ch 23, Ch 29)
  • Technical due diligence — Verification of a target's technology claims, risks and integration cost before a deal is signed. (Ch 50)
  • Technical fit — Whether an acquired or partnered asset can run on, or beside, the existing operating system and control plane without adding a second data path. (Ch 54)
  • Technology licensing model — A commercial structure in which the customer sources its own hardware and NAND and pays the supplier for software, IP and support. (Ch 25)
  • Technology radar — A chart placing trends by maturity ring and category to show what to adopt now and what to watch. (Ch 53)
  • Tectonic — Meta's exabyte-scale multitenant distributed file system, one cluster per datacenter. (Ch 36)
  • Term (Raft) — Raft's logical clock; each term has at most one leader, and a node seeing a higher term steps down. (Ch 20)
  • Tested limit — the largest configuration a vendor has validated and supports, as opposed to its architectural maximum. (Ch 56)
  • Thin provisioning — Allocating physical capacity to a volume only when data is actually written, rather than at creation. (Ch 5)
  • Throughput — Data moved per second (e.g., GB/s), equal to IOPS multiplied by I/O size; usually quoted for large sequential transfers. (Ch 4)
  • Throughput-bound workload — A workload whose performance depends on aggregate bytes per second across many parallel streams, such as AI training data loading. (Ch 24)
  • TiB (tebibyte) — 2^40 bytes, about 9% smaller than a decimal terabyte (10^12 bytes). (Ch 4)
  • Tier 0 — Hammerspace's shared, protected storage tier built from the local NVMe drives inside GPU servers. (Ch 47)
  • Tiering (lifecycle management) — Policy-driven movement of data between storage tiers as its access pattern or value changes. (Ch 1)
  • Time to first token (TTFT) — The latency from submitting a prompt to receiving the first generated token, the key inference responsiveness metric. (Ch 30, Ch 32)
  • Tintri — A virtualisation-focused storage vendor whose assets DDN bought out of bankruptcy in 2018 and still sells as Tintri VMstore. (Ch 44)
  • Token — The unit of text (roughly a word fragment) that a language model reads and predicts; dataset sizes are usually quoted in tokens. (Ch 30)
  • Token warehouse — WEKA's marketing term for the pooled NVMe store that holds KV-cache blocks for reuse across GPU servers. (Ch 43)
  • Total cost of ownership (TCO) — All costs of a system over a stated period: acquisition, power, space, support, refresh and operations. (Ch 4)
  • Total efficiency — A vendor ratio that adds thin-provisioning and snapshot savings on top of data reduction, and is therefore larger and softer than DRR. (Ch 4, Ch 5)
  • Total enterprise storage systems — External arrays plus server-based storage and ODM-direct hyperscaler purchases; IDC no longer publicises this total. (Ch 40)
  • Tracker estimate — a market figure from an analyst tracker such as IDC's, valid only on that tracker's definitions. (Ch 0.1)
  • TrafficGroup — A Tectonic grouping of tenants that share resource quotas such as IOPS. (Ch 36)
  • TRIM / Deallocate — A host command telling the drive that logical blocks no longer hold useful data, so garbage collection can skip them. (Ch 3)
  • Tuck-in acquisition — A small acquisition that buys a capability or team to fold into an existing product rather than buying a large revenue base. (Ch 25, Ch 54)

docs.title: U
docs.text:
• Ultra Ethernet (UEC / UET) — An industry consortium and its 2025 specification for an Ethernet-based AI/HPC transport that tolerates lossy fabrics. (Ch 10)
  • UltraSMR — Western Digital's shingled magnetic recording technology, which overlaps tracks to raise HDD capacity at the cost of slower random writes. (Ch 48)
  • Unified Cache Manager (UCM) — Huawei's KV-cache tiering software that moves inference context across memory and storage tiers to reduce HBM needs. (Ch 46)
  • Unified storage — A single storage system that serves more than one abstraction (block, file and/or object). (Ch 1)
  • Unified storage platform — A system or product family that serves block, file and object from one software stack or control plane. (Ch 24)
  • Unrecoverable read error (URE) — A sector the drive cannot read back even after retries, specified as a rate per bits read. (Ch 6)
  • Usable capacity — Capacity left after parity, rebuild spares, metadata and system reserves are deducted from raw. (Ch 4)
  • Utilization — The fraction of time a resource (die, CPU, port, disk arm) is busy; latency rises sharply as it approaches 100%. (Ch 4)

docs.title: V
docs.text:
• V-NAND — Samsung's name for its 3D NAND, first mass-produced at 24 layers in 2013. (Ch 52)
  • Value stack — The layers of an industry ranked by where profit is captured, rather than by the technical path an I/O takes. (Ch 54)
  • VAST AgentEngine — VAST's runtime for deploying AI agents with MCP-compatible tool access, announced in May 2025. (Ch 42)
  • VAST AI Operating System (AI OS) — VAST's May 2025 umbrella brand for its storage services (DataStore, DataBase, DataSpace) plus compute engines such as DataEngine, InsightEngine and AgentEngine. (Ch 42)
  • VAST Amplify — VAST's January 2026 programme to assess and reuse customers' installed NVMe SSDs, including competitors', during the NAND shortage. (Ch 41)
  • VAST DataBase — A columnar table store built directly into VAST's Element Store and queried through engines such as Trino and Spark. (Ch 42)
  • VAST DataEngine — VAST's in-cluster event-trigger and serverless-function layer that runs code when data arrives or changes. (Ch 42)
  • VAST DataSpace — VAST's global namespace that spans clusters, sites and clouds. (Ch 42)
  • VAST InsightEngine — VAST's service that embeds and indexes new data as it lands (using NVIDIA NIM) for retrieval-augmented generation. (Ch 42)
  • Vector database — Software that stores embeddings and answers nearest-neighbour similarity queries, usually with metadata filters. (Ch 33)
  • VERIFY tag — an inline marker for a claim not yet confirmed by a primary or second source, collected in the open-questions list. (Ch 0.1)
  • Vertical integration (storage) — Owning several adjacent stack layers, for example array software, flash translation and module design, as one engineered product. (Ch 13)
  • Vertically integrated storage — A storage system whose vendor designs and supplies both the software and key hardware, such as controllers and flash modules. (Ch 49)
  • Virtual metadata server — A software metadata owner running inside WEKA's compute processes on every node, replacing a dedicated metadata server. (Ch 43)
  • Virtual nodes — Many points on a consistent-hashing ring assigned to each physical server to even out load. (Ch 15)
  • VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) — Broadcom's main VMware subscription bundle, licensed per core, combining vSphere, vSAN, NSX and management tools. (Ch 19)
  • Volume manager — Host or hypervisor software that pools and remaps block addresses across devices, such as LVM or software RAID. (Ch 13)
  • vSAN — VMware's HCI storage software, which runs inside the ESXi hypervisor kernel and pools node-local drives. (Ch 19)
  • vSAN Max — A VMware deployment model that builds a storage-only vSAN cluster mounted by separate compute clusters. (Ch 19)
  • VSP One — Hitachi Vantara's storage brand covering block, file and object systems. (Ch 46)

docs.title: W
docs.text:
• Wafer bonding (NAND) — Building the NAND's CMOS control logic on a separate wafer and bonding it to the memory array wafer. (Ch 2)
  • Wafer spot price — The open-market price for unpackaged NAND wafers, quoted per die-equivalent (e.g., per 512Gb unit), a fast-moving indicator of NAND pricing. (Ch 52)
  • Wafer starts — The number of wafers a fab begins processing per month, the physical measure of memory capacity. (Ch 52)
  • Wear levelling — FTL logic that spreads program/erase cycles evenly across blocks so no part of the flash wears out early. (Ch 3)
  • WebDataset — A data-loading format and library that packs training samples into large tar shards so they can be read sequentially. (Ch 21)
  • WekaFS — WEKA's original parallel, POSIX-compliant file system for NVMe flash with tiering to object storage. (Ch 43)
  • WEKApod — WEKA's branded storage appliance line; WEKApod 3 (2026) offers Nitro, Prime and Prime Max configurations. (Ch 43)
  • Whamcloud — The Lustre engineering company bought by Intel in 2012 and revived as a DDN division after DDN bought Intel's Lustre business in 2018. (Ch 44)
  • Whiteboard prompt — a request to sketch a mechanism, such as a write path, to test L2 understanding. (Ch 56)
  • Win/loss review — a structured analysis of why specific deals were won or lost, and on which attribute. (Ch 55)
  • Witness — A data-less third voter, placed outside both sites' failure domains, that breaks ties in a two-site cluster. (Ch 20)
  • Worked example — arithmetic on stated assumptions, shown on the page so it can be checked. (Ch 0.1)
  • Workload fit — How naturally an architecture's design matches a workload's access pattern, protocol, latency and scale needs. (Ch 24)
  • Write amplification factor (WAF) — The ratio of bytes written to NAND to bytes written by the host, driven mainly by garbage collection. (Ch 3, Ch 12)
  • Write buffer — A small persistent tier that absorbs and acknowledges writes before they are reorganized and written to capacity media. (Ch 16)
  • Write quorum — The minimum number of fragment or replica writes that must succeed before a write is treated as durable. (Ch 18)
  • Write-back cache — A cache that acknowledges writes before the slower tier persists them, safe only if the cache is persistent and mirrored. (Ch 20)
  • Write-through cache — A cache that acknowledges writes only after the slower tier has persisted them. (Ch 20)

docs.title: Y
docs.text: • Young's formula — The classic approximation for the optimal checkpoint interval, the square root of two times the checkpoint cost times the mean time between failures. (Ch 31)

docs.title: Z
docs.text:
• Zero-copy — Transferring data between memory and the wire without the CPU copying it between buffers. (Ch 10)
  • ZippyDB — Meta's sharded, replicated key-value store, used by Tectonic to hold its layered metadata. (Ch 36)
  • Zoned Namespaces (ZNS) — An NVMe command set that exposes zones which must be written sequentially and reset by the host. (Ch 12)
  • Zoning — A Fibre Channel switch-level access-control list defining which hosts can see which storage ports. (Ch 7)

docs.title: 0.1. How to use this atlas
docs.text: Depth: L1 · Reading time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: None. Start here, then go to 0.2 The one-page map. Keep the glossary open in a second tab.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• The atlas is a briefing book, not a textbook. It prepares a strategy hire for credible conversations with Everpure PMs, engineering leaders and the Office of the CTO: how storage works, why the trade-offs exist, what they mean.
  • Default depth is L2: mechanism. Whiteboard the design and say why it wins for a workload. L3 detail lives only in "Going deeper" boxes.
  • Every chapter has the same ten sections. TL;DR first, "Core concepts" for the mechanism, the "Conversation playbook" the night before a meeting.
  • Pick a path by time available. A 2-hour crash course, a 2-day ramp and a 2-week mastery plan are laid out below.
  • Every number carries a label. Filed, company-stated, reported by press, tracker estimate, atlas judgment or worked example. Unconfirmed items are given an inline VERIFY tag and collected in one list. Quote a number with its label and date, or not at all.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
A new strategy hire at Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG)1 is judged quickly by career storage people. PMs notice if you confuse an EXA data node with a DirectFlash Module; engineers, if you call write amplification marketing; the CTO's office, if you quote a valuation as if it were revenue. Each slip drops the conversation to a level where you learn nothing; the atlas front-loads what prevents that.

The assumed reader knows NAND, HBM, PCIe and fab economics from semiconductor M&A but is new to storage systems and software. Hence the semiconductor bridges and a business consequence beside every mechanism.

docs.title: What the atlas covers
docs.text: Nine Parts run from physics to strategy: fundamentals, protocols and architectures (1–3), Everpure (4), AI storage (5), competition (6), history and future (7) and the conversation toolkit (8). Parts 1–3 are vendor-neutral, so Parts 4–6 read as applications of mechanisms you already hold, not as competing sales pitches.

docs.title: Depth labels
docs.text:
Label You can… Where it appears Self-test L1 — Vocabulary Define the term and use it correctly in a sentence Key terms, glossary, TL;DRs, Ch 58 one-liners Explain "QLC" to a board member in one sentence L2 — Mechanism (default) Whiteboard how it works, name the trade-offs, say why one design beats another for a workload Core concepts of every chapter Draw a dual-controller write acknowledgment and say where the data sits when the host gets "done" L3 — Implementation Discuss code paths, on-disk formats, kernel internals Only in "Going deeper" boxes, as pointers Not required. Ask about it; never assert it

Table 0.1.1 — Aim for L2 everywhere and L1 on the long tail; treat L3 as territory you ask engineers about, not territory you claim.

At L2 you can put a number on a mechanism and invite correction ("a 4 KB write on a networked array is ~100–250 µs, mostly network and controller software; is that your profile?"). That is when engineers start teaching you: the credibility ladder of Chapter 56.

docs.title: How every chapter is built
docs.text:
Chapters follow one template, so you always know where to look.

Section What it gives you Use it when Header Depth, reading time (prose words ÷ 230), last-verified date, prerequisites Deciding whether to read now or later TL;DR Five bullets to remember Skimming, crash course, the morning of a meeting Why this matters for Everpure strategy The business "so what" in two paragraphs Framing a memo or an exec summary Core concepts The L2 mechanism, worked numbers and most of the diagrams Learning; preparing to whiteboard How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors A comparison table and a steelman of the alternatives Competitive questions, deal reviews History and trajectory How it got here, with dated signals of where it is going Judging whether a trend is early or late Numbers that matter Five to ten sourced or worked figures Building slides; checking a claim Conversation playbook Three PM and three engineer questions, what a strong answer sounds like, and "Don't say this" The night before a meeting Going deeper L3 pointers: papers, specs, talks Only if a conversation goes there Key terms / Sources Glossary entries; footnotes with publication and retrieval dates Checking a definition or a citation

Table 0.1.2 — The template puts the remember-this material first and the evidence last, so a ten-minute skim and a two-hour study use the same page.

The deep dives (Chapters 42–44) add five business sections, from financials to strategic relevance. Every figure's italic caption states its takeaway, so captions alone make a usable summary. Signature diagrams, marked ★ in meta/outline.md rather than in the chapters, are the ones worth redrawing from memory.

docs.title: Three learning paths
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S["How much time before you need to talk credibly?"] --> A["2 hours"]
    S --> B["2 days"]
    S --> C["2 weeks"]
    A --> A1["0.2 one-page map"]
    A1 --> A2["12 TL;DRs plus six signature figures"]
    A2 --> A3["Ch 58 one-liners and the ten numbers"]
    B --> B1["Day 1: Parts 1 to 4"]
    B1 --> B2["Day 2: Parts 5 and 6, Ch 53 to 57"]
    C --> C1["Every chapter, ten days of 3 to 4 hours"]
    C1 --> C2["Daily flashcards, two whiteboard rehearsals a week"]
    A3 --> M["Before any meeting: chapter playbooks plus Part 8"]
    B2 --> M
    C2 --> M

Figure 0.1.1 — All three paths start from the same map and end in the same place: the conversation toolkit and the playbooks of the chapters a meeting touches.

docs.title: 2-hour crash course
docs.text:
1. 0:00–0:15. The map. 0.2: mindmap, ten diagrams, ten numbers.
  2. 0:15–0:50. Twelve TL;DRs, plus "Why this matters". Fundamentals: Ch 2, 3, 13. Architecture: 16, 24. Everpure: 25, 26, 29. AI: 30, 32. Competition: 41, 45.
  3. 0:50–1:30. Six figures, about seven minutes each. Figures 2.1 (media hierarchy), 13.1 (where the intelligence lives), 26.2 (DirectFlash vs. SSD), 30.1 (AI pipeline), 32.3 (KV-cache tiers) and 45.1 (four AI architectures). Read each caption, then explain the figure aloud without looking.
  4. 1:30–1:50. Words and numbers. The "Everpure's model" and "Competition" one-liners in Ch 58, then the 0.2 numbers table, each said with its date.
  5. 1:50–2:00. Behaviour. The credibility ladder in Ch 56 and the matching chapter's "Don't say this" list.

docs.title: 2-day ramp
docs.text:
About six hours on day 1 and five on day 2; header reading times count prose only, so these estimates budget 1.5× for visuals.

  • Day 1, morning: Part 1 in full (Ch 1–6), then Chapters 7, 8, 9 and 11 from Part 2.
  • Day 1, afternoon: Part 3 core (Ch 13–17, 23, 24) and all of Part 4 (Ch 25–29). Close with 30 minutes of flashcards for Parts 1–4.
  • Day 2, morning: Part 5 core (Ch 30–32, 34, 35, 37).
  • Day 2, afternoon: Part 6 core (Ch 40, 41, 45, 46, 49). Deep dives 42–44: TL;DR and business sections only. Then 53 and 54, and Ch 55–56. Finish with ten questions from Ch 57.

docs.title: 2-week mastery plan
docs.text:
Ten working days of 3–4 hours: 15 minutes of review flashcards (Ch 59, organised by Part), the reading (about 1–2 hours at 1.5× header times; days 9 and 10 run longest), then 30–45 minutes of practice, including two whiteboard rehearsals a week.

Day Read Practice Output 1 0.1, 0.2, Ch 1–4 Part 1 flashcards Redraw the media pyramid from memory 2 Ch 5–9 Redo the Ch 4 TCO and Ch 5 data-reduction checks One-paragraph "why the ratio belongs to the data" 3 Ch 10–15 Part 2 flashcards; Rehearsal 1: an NVMe-oF read and the GPUDirect path One-page protocol summary in your own words 4 Ch 16–21 Rehearsal 2: dual-controller write vs. DASE write Compare four architectures on one page 5 Ch 22–24, 51–52 Part 3 flashcards; 30 random cards from week 1 Apply the Ch 24 decision tree to three workloads 6 Ch 25–29, 55 Read the latest Everpure earnings release and prepared remarks One-page company memo with sourced numbers 7 Ch 30–34 Part 4–5 flashcards; Rehearsal 3: a checkpoint write from GPU memory to flash Size a 405B checkpoint and a 128K-token session 8 Ch 35–39, 56, 57 Rehearsal 4: EXA read path vs. VAST read path Seven questions for an engineering meeting 9 Ch 40–45 Part 6 flashcards; 30-second answers from Ch 58 aloud Steelman one competitor against Everpure 10 Ch 46–50, 53–54, 60 Ch 59's 50-card timed mixed test; mock PM meeting Write the ten numbers and five open questions from memory

Table 0.1.3 — The mastery plan alternates reading with output; the outputs, not the reading, are what make the material usable in a meeting.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P0["Part 0 Start here"] --> P1["Part 1 Fundamentals"]
    P1 --> P2["Part 2 Protocols"]
    P1 --> P7a["Ch 51-52 History"]
    P2 --> P3["Part 3 Architectures"]
    P1 --> P3
    P3 --> P4["Part 4 Everpure"]
    P2 --> P5["Part 5 AI storage"]
    P3 --> P5
    P4 --> P6["Part 6 Competition"]
    P5 --> P6
    P6 --> P7b["Ch 53-54 Future and options"]
    P4 --> P8["Part 8 Toolkit"]
    P6 --> P8
    G["Glossary"] -.-> P1
    G -.-> P5

Figure 0.1.2 — Parts 1–3 are the foundation; Everpure and AI storage can be read in either order, but competition and strategy need both.

Three dependencies matter most. Read Chapter 3 (the FTL) before Chapter 26, or DirectFlash looks like marketing. Read Chapter 11 before Part 5, and Chapters 14–17 before Chapter 45. History (51–52) needs only Part 1 and makes good light reading between dense days.

docs.title: Using the conversation toolkit before a meeting
docs.text:
For the 24 hours before a meeting:

  1. Identify the audience and the product line. (Ch 55, Ch 56).
  2. Do the public homework. Latest earnings release plus the chapter's "Numbers that matter"; never spend meeting time on what a 10-Q answers.
  3. Pick five to seven questions, not thirty, from Ch 57 and the chapter playbooks. Give each a hypothesis with a number.
  4. Rehearse two 30-second answers from Ch 58
  5. Re-read "Don't say this" for each chapter in scope, and the cheat sheets for acronyms.

Afterwards, note what contradicted the atlas; those are its most valuable updates.

docs.title: Sourcing, labels and VERIFY
docs.text:
Every time-sensitive or vendor-specific claim has a footnote with publisher, publication date and retrieval date; established engineering facts and on-page arithmetic carry none. Labels say how much weight a number bears:

Label Meaning Example How to say it Filed / company-reported In an SEC filing or earnings release; audited or subject to disclosure rules Everpure subscription ARR US$2.13B (+20%), Q2 FY272 "Everpure reported…" Company-stated A private company's own unaudited figure VAST: committed ARR above US$500M3 "VAST says…" Reported by press Journalists' figures, often from unnamed sources DDN revenue near US$500M in 2025, with conflicting base figures4 "Forbes reported…; numbers conflict" Tracker estimate Analyst trackers with their own definitions Everpure 8.1% of external enterprise storage, 2Q265 "On IDC's definition…" Atlas judgment The atlas's synthesis of public facts Quadrant placements in Ch 49 "My read of public information…" Worked example / illustrative Arithmetic on stated assumptions; charts say "Illustrative" in the title 405B parameters × ~16 bytes ≈ 6.5 TB checkpoint (Ch 31) "Back of envelope…" VERIFY tag (inline, in square brackets) Not confirmed by a primary or second source Figures seen only in a search summary Don't repeat it until checked

Table 0.1.4 — The label is part of the number; dropping it is how a private company's claim turns into "fact" in a deck.

Private figures are never set against public ones without the label. Charts plot only sourced or clearly illustrative data, and each chart's CSV in data/ records its source and as_of date.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Everpure and its competitors face the same standard of evidence; no cheerleading, including for Everpure.

Subject Main evidence Typical weakness How the atlas compensates Everpure 10-K/10-Q, earnings releases, prepared remarks, datasheets Management framing; metrics chosen by the company Same skepticism as for rivals; benchmarks read with the field that entered (Ch 37) Private AI-natives (VAST, WEKA, DDN) Company statements, funding releases, press, MLPerf when they submit Unaudited and selectively disclosed Explicit labels; strongest case stated before the critique Public incumbents (Dell, NetApp, HPE, IBM) Filings, product documentation Storage often buried in a larger segment Profile tables; segment caveats in Ch 46 Hyperscalers Papers, engineering blogs, re:Invent-style talks Selective, years after deployment Treated as architecture evidence, not market data (Ch 36)

Table 0.1.5 — Different competitors leave different evidence trails; the atlas labels each rather than pretending they are comparable.

Strategy content is framed as options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information, never as non-public Everpure plans.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text: The atlas is a snapshot as of 2026-11-01, covering Pure Storage from 2009 and Everpure from the February 2026 rebrand (ticker P since 2026-04-171). Mechanisms (Parts 1–3) and history age slowly; Parts 4–6 date fastest. Each earnings release moves ARR, RPO, margins and guidance; so do MLPerf rounds, NVIDIA certification lists, NAND prices and private funding rounds.

docs.title: How to keep it current
docs.text:
• VERIFY tags sit inline where the doubt lives. scripts/build_meta.py collects them, with staged questions, into meta/open-questions.md; about 200 were open at drafting and 177 after the independent review pass.
  • Per-chapter staging files (meta/open-questions-staging/, meta/glossary-staging/) hold new VERIFY items, questions and terms; scripts/build_glossary.py merges terms into the glossary.
  • The "Last verified" date says when a chapter was last checked. Re-verify "Numbers that matter" first: that is what gets copied into slides.
  • meta/sources.md traces any superseded source to every chapter citing it.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Three questions for a PM

  1. "Which row of the atlas's positioning table for your product line is wrong?" A strong answer names a workload, a competitor and the deciding attribute; a weak one defends the product.
  2. "What metric do you report upward, and what does it hide?" A strong answer separates the public metric (ARR, customer counts) from the operational one it masks, such as time-to-deploy.
  3. "Which competitor claim do customers repeat most, and is it true?" A strong answer concedes the true part first, a sign of a real win/loss loop.

Three questions for an engineer

  1. "Here is my L2 model of the write path. Where is it wrong for your system?" A strong answer corrects a specific step and gives a number, not an adjective.
  2. "What would you want a non-engineer to understand before we evaluate a target in your area?" A strong answer names a wall (metadata, rebuild time, client management) rather than a feature.
  3. "Which benchmark result in our space do you trust least, and why?" A strong answer names the configuration or normalisation that flatters it (Ch 37).

Don't say this:

  • A private company's figure without its label: "VAST has $2B of ARR" is press speculation; the company-stated figure is above US$500M of committed ARR3.
  • "Pure Storage" for post-February-2026 events, or "PSTG" for today's ticker.
  • "We're #1 in MLPerf" without adding that VAST, WEKA, DDN, Dell, IBM and NetApp skipped that round (Ch 27, Ch 37).
  • An L3 assertion you cannot defend; ask it instead.
  • An atlas number without its date; much of Parts 4–6 will be stale within two quarters.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• meta/research/ holds the research notes behind Parts 4–6; cite their underlying sources, not the notes.
  • The SNIA Dictionary (snia.org) is the reference vocabulary when vendor and atlas terms disagree.
  • Each chapter's "Going deeper" box lists the specs, papers and talks (USENIX FAST, Hot Chips, FMS) behind its L3 detail.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Depth label (L1/L2/L3) — vocabulary, mechanism and implementation levels (glossary).
  • Company-stated — a private company's own unaudited figure.
  • Reported by press — a figure published by journalists, often from unnamed sources.
  • Atlas judgment — the atlas's synthesis of public facts, such as quadrant placements.
  • Worked example — arithmetic on stated assumptions, shown on the page.
  • VERIFY tag — an inline marker for a claim not yet confirmed by a primary or second source.
  • Signature visual (★) — a diagram worth being able to redraw from memory.
  • Conversation playbook — each chapter's questions, strong answers and misconceptions.

docs.title: 0.2. The one-page map
docs.text: Depth: L1 · Reading time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: 0.1 How to use this atlas. Nothing else; every section below links to the chapter that explains it.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• The domain is a stack: media, devices, protocols, architectures and data services, stressed by AI workloads and shaped by NVIDIA, hyperscalers and NAND makers.
  • Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG)1 plays unusually low and unusually wide. It owns flash management (DirectFlash), the OS (Purity), two array families and a subscription model (Evergreen) across them.
  • Its distinctive asset is media economics. One flash translation layer over raw-NAND modules yields bigger modules than standard SSDs, a design Everpure licenses to hyperscalers.
  • Its AI position rests on one benchmark lead, with thin references and no completed EXA certification. FlashBlade//EXA led MLPerf Storage v3.0, a round VAST, WEKA, DDN, Dell, IBM and NetApp skipped.
  • The money is still mostly arrays, wrapped in fast-growing subscriptions: US$2.13B of subscription ARR against FY27 revenue guidance of US$5.03–5.07B2.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text: Every deal, partnership or product bet lands on one layer of the map and touches others. A data-intelligence acquisition sits above the array but depends on what the array knows. An NVIDIA reference design sits beside it and decides the shortlist. A NAND price spike sits below it and moves gross margin within a quarter. The ten diagrams below show where Everpure sits, each linked to its evidence.

Figure 0.2.1 — Nine branches cover the domain; Everpure has a product or a dependency on every one of them, which is what makes its strategy a portfolio question.

Parts 1–3 explain the first five branches, Part 5 AI workloads, Parts 4 and 6 the rest; the glossary defines every leaf.

docs.title: 1. Seventeen years, five pivots
docs.text:
timeline
    title Pure Storage to Everpure
    2009 : Incorporated
    2012 : FlashArray GA
    2015 : Evergreen upgrades begin : NYSE IPO
    2017 : FlashBlade GA : FlashArray X with DirectFlash
    2020 : Portworx acquired
    2024 : First hyperscaler design win : CoreWeave stake
    2025 : FlashBlade EXA announced and GA
    2026 : Renamed Everpure : 1touch closes : Second hyperscaler win

Figure 0.2.2 — Each era added a layer to the same Purity and DirectFlash core.

Pure Storage was incorporated in 20093 and shipped FlashArray in 20124. Its pivots stacked rather than replaced each other: the array; the business model (Evergreen in-place upgrades from 20155, IPO the same year6); file and object (FlashBlade, 20177); cloud-native software (Portworx, 20208); IP licensing (a hyperscaler design win, December 20249). Data intelligence (1touch, closed May 202610) arrived with the rebrand11 and a second top-five hyperscaler win12. All were small bets funded by array cash flow. See Chapter 25.

docs.title: 2. Where Everpure plays in the stack
docs.text:
Figure 0.2.3 — Everpure owns three adjacent layers (array software, flash management and media packaging) as one design.

Every I/O crosses eight layers, from application to NAND. Most array vendors keep their intelligence in layer 6, the array software, above SSDs that run their own firmware. Software-only vendors stop above the hardware. Purity also does the SSD controller's job, so one design spans layers 6 to 8. That integration yields density, efficiency and the hyperscaler licence; it costs R&D and the burden of qualifying every NAND generation. See Chapter 13.

docs.title: 3. DirectFlash versus a commodity SSD
docs.text:
Figure 0.2.4 — A commodity-SSD array pays for controllers, DRAM maps, garbage collection and spare flash per drive; DirectFlash pays once.

An SSD is a small computer hiding NAND's erase-before-write physics behind a map. An SSD-based array runs that map, garbage collection and spare capacity twice: in each drive and again in its own log. DirectFlash removes the drive-level brain, so Purity schedules every NAND die globally. The visible result is module size: 300 TB DFMs (released in 2025, per Everpure's FY26 10-K13; "now up to 300 TB" in August 2026 coverage14) against 245.76 TB for the largest standard SSD confirmed shipping15; Sandisk has announced 256 TB16. Power savings beyond that are vendor claims, best checked at system level. It is the integrated-memory-controller move, made by a fabless player buying NAND from SSD-selling IDMs. See Chapter 26.

docs.title: 4. Purity: one OS from protocol to NAND
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    H["Hosts: block, file, S3"] --> NV["NVRAM, write acked"]
    NV --> DR["Inline data reduction"]
    DR --> LS["Log-structured segments"]
    LS --> DF["DirectFlash global FTL"]
    DF --> N["Raw NAND modules"]
    KV[("Metadata key-value store")] <--> DR
    KV <--> LS

Figure 0.2.5 — Purity appends, never overwrites, and keeps every mapping in a metadata store; that one design choice explains snapshots, reduction and DirectFlash.

Purity behaves like a database whose rows are storage blocks. A write is acknowledged once it sits in NVRAM that survives a controller failure, then deduplicated, compressed and packed into large sequential segments with dual parity. Nothing is overwritten in place; a newer version simply wins in the metadata map. Snapshots become nearly free, and small random writes become the large sequential ones QLC tolerates. Purity//FB applies the same ideas across FlashBlade's blades. See Chapter 26.

docs.title: 5. The product lineage
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P["Purity plus DirectFlash"] --> FA["FlashArray, Purity FA: dual controller, block first"]
    P --> FB["FlashBlade, Purity FB: scale-out file and object"]
    FA --> FA1["XL and X: TLC performance"]
    FA --> FA2["C and E: QLC capacity"]
    FA -.-> FA3["ST: commercial SSDs"]
    FB --> FB1["S: performance, QLC"]
    FB --> FB2["E: capacity, QLC"]
    FB --> FB3["EXA: metadata core plus third-party data nodes"]

Figure 0.2.6 — FlashArray splits into TLC performance and QLC capacity tiers; FlashBlade splits by configuration, on QLC throughout; //ST and EXA are the two deliberate exceptions to "all DirectFlash".

FlashArray is scale-up, dual-controller and block-first, with file and S3 added later. FlashBlade is scale-out file and object. FlashArray forked by media: TLC for performance (//X, //XL), QLC for capacity (//C, //E). FlashBlade forked by configuration, not media: //S for performance and //E for capacity, both on QLC modules. FlashBlade//S is not shared-everything; Everpure describes Purity//FB as "partitioned-writer"17, with each blade owning part of the namespace over pooled media (Chapter 15). Two exceptions matter: FlashArray//ST uses commercial SSDs18, and FlashBlade//EXA, announced March 202519 and generally available from June 202520, adds off-the-shelf Linux/NVMe data nodes. Each trades DirectFlash purity for a market: extreme IOPS for //ST, AI-scale throughput for EXA. See Chapter 27.

docs.title: 6. FlashBlade//EXA against the AI-native field
docs.text:
Figure 0.2.7 — Each handles metadata differently: EXA and DDN send bulk data one hop, straight to where it lives; VAST adds a CNode hop for shared, stateless compute; WEKA has no metadata server at all.

EXA keeps metadata on a Purity//FB core of DirectFlash blades and sends bulk data straight to third-party data nodes over stock-client pNFS, so the data tier is not DirectFlash. VAST puts everything on shared media behind stateless compute; WEKA spreads metadata across every node; DDN runs Lustre with a kernel client. EXA's 877.5 GiB/s checkpoint write topped MLPerf Storage v3.021, a round VAST, WEKA and DDN skipped22, as did Dell, IBM and NetApp23. The gaps are references and badges: no public 10,000-GPU EXA site, and NVIDIA's SuperPOD certification belongs to FlashBlade//S24. For EXA, Everpure announced in March 2026 that it was extending NVIDIA-Certified Storage validation, a step toward the NCP level; no completed EXA certification was found by November 202625. See Chapter 45.

docs.title: 7. The platform and Evergreen
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    DI["Data Intelligence and Portworx"] --> CP["Fusion policies plus Pure1 telemetry"]
    CL["Everpure Cloud"] --> CP
    CP --> AR["FlashArray, FlashBlade, EXA"]
    AR --> OS["Purity"]
    OS --> MD["DirectFlash Modules"]
    EV["Evergreen subscription"] -.-> CP
    EV -.-> AR
    CP -.->|"telemetry triggers in-place refresh"| EV

Figure 0.2.8 — One OS on every array, one control plane over every array, and a subscription that refreshes hardware in place because the telemetry says when.

Evergreen makes the platform work. Customers subscribe to an architecture; controllers and media are refreshed in place with no data migration, which works because controllers are stateless and Pure1 watches the fleet. Above the arrays, Fusion turns storage into policy- and API-driven capacity, Portworx extends it to Kubernetes, and Data Intelligence (from 1touch) reads what the data is. Everpure's bet is that switching costs move into the control plane, but adoption is early: Fusion passed 1,200 customers by Q1 FY2726, under a tenth of the installed base on the atlas's estimate (Chapter 28). See Chapter 28.

docs.title: 8. Revenue, ARR and the backlog
docs.text:
Figure 0.2.9 — ARR has compounded at about 21% a year since FY2023 (16% in FY26, 20% at Q2 FY27); RPO stepped up sharply in FY26 as large deals and longer Evergreen terms filled the backlog, partly at the expense of ARR growth.

Two revenue lines hide three businesses: arrays (NAND on Everpure's books), ratable Evergreen subscriptions, and hyperscale DirectFlash licences, plus some parts, where the customer buys the NAND. FY26 revenue was US$3.66B13. At Q2 FY27, subscription ARR was US$2.13B (+20%) and RPO US$4.1B (+44%)2. NAND is the margin risk: non-GAAP product gross margin was 66.2%, against 74.9% for subscriptions27, and DirectFlash's lower bill of materials cushions that squeeze rather than preventing it. FY27 growth is partly price pass-through; watch ARR and units. See Chapter 29.

docs.title: 9. The ecosystem
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    EP(("Everpure"))
    NV["NVIDIA"] ---|"certification, STX co-design"| EP
    EP -->|"DirectFlash licence plus parts"| HS["Two top-five hyperscalers"]
    NAND["NAND makers"] -->|"supply and qualification"| EP
    NAND -.->|"sell NAND direct"| HS
    AZ["Azure and AWS"] ---|"cloud services"| EP
    EP -->|"equity stake, EXA supply"| NEO["Neoclouds incl. CoreWeave"]
    CS["Cisco, GSIs, channel"] -->|"resell, integrate"| EP

Figure 0.2.10 — Most of the ecosystem is distribution and validation; in hyperscale, the NAND makers sell around Everpure straight to its customer.

NVIDIA controls the AI shortlist; Everpure is one of twelve storage co-design partners on its BlueField-4 STX architecture, alongside VAST, WEKA, DDN, Dell and NetApp28. Microsoft co-developed an Azure-native Everpure service29. Cisco and integrators carry enterprise volume. Everpure holds a CoreWeave stake30, but VAST is that neocloud's incumbent (Chapter 35). In hyperscale, NAND makers sell flash directly to the customer, so Everpure is paid for IP, software, support and some non-NAND parts, not for NAND bits. See Chapter 29 and Chapter 34.

docs.text:
quadrantChart

    x-axis Vertically integrated --> Hardware-agnostic software
    y-axis Commodity media handling --> Differentiated media economics
    quadrant-1 Software with media economics
    quadrant-2 Integrated media moat
    quadrant-3 Integrated, commodity media
    quadrant-4 Portable software
