    Hammerspace: [0.96, 0.10]

Figure 0.2.11 — There are two routes to media economics: integrate flash management (Everpure, IBM, Huawei) or extract it in software from QLC (VAST); most vendors take neither.

Placements are the atlas's judgment, drawn from Chapters 42–47. Everpure sits furthest into the integrated-media corner; other placements are more contestable. VAST reaches similar economics from the opposite corner, in software on commodity QLC, which makes it the most direct architectural rival. Dell and NetApp compete on installed base, channel and breadth, not media. Hammerspace's namespace above all arrays would make them interchangeable: does the array stay the control point? See Chapter 49 and Chapter 54.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Layer of the map Everpure VAST Dell / NetApp Hyperscalers Media and devices Own modules on raw NAND (DirectFlash) Commodity QLC plus SCM, made cheap by wide erasure codes Standard SSDs Commodity drives, own designs, licensed IP AI architecture EXA: metadata core, direct data path DASE: stateless compute, shared media New first-generation AI systems (Lightning FS, AFX) Home-grown file systems Data services One OS across both families Climbing into database and AI engines Broadest portfolios, many OSes Rich, but only for data in their cloud Business model Evergreen subscription and IP licensing Software licence, partner hardware Hardware, financing, bundling Pay per use

Table 0.2.1 — Each competitor is strong where Everpure is thin: VAST in AI references, Dell and NetApp in breadth and channel, hyperscalers in data already in the cloud. Atlas judgment; evidence in Chapters 42–47.

Steelman the rivals: VAST's US$30B valuation31 rests on more than US$500M of committed ARR (company-stated)32 and the largest neocloud references; Dell holds about three times Everpure's external-storage share33.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text: The map has redrawn itself three times in Everpure's life: flash replaced performance disk, subscriptions replaced forklift upgrades, and AI now pulls value down into fabrics and up into data services (Chapter 53). Dated signals: second-hyperscaler revenue from FY2812, the next MLPerf Storage round and who enters it, NVIDIA certification for EXA itself, and whether NAND prices let product margin recover.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Three questions for a PM

  1. "Which of these ten diagrams will look most different in two years?" A strong answer picks one and names the driver, such as EXA references or hyperscale mix.
  2. "Where on the mindmap do we lose deals we should win?" Listen for a branch and a named competitor.
  3. "How much of FY27 growth is price and how much is units?" Listen for NAND pass-through versus capacity shipped.

Three questions for an engineer

  1. "What does owning layers 6 to 8 cost you each NAND generation?" Listen for qualification time and supplier count.
  2. "Where does EXA's direct data path hurt, compared with VAST's shared media?" A strong answer concedes something real, such as data-node maturity.
  3. "Which diagram in this chapter is wrong or out of date?" Take any correction back to the chapter.

Don't say this:

  • "Everpure is just a flash array company." Subscriptions and IP licensing matter.
  • "DirectFlash is a big SSD." It has no drive-level FTL.
  • "EXA beat VAST in MLPerf." VAST did not submit to that round.
  • "Hyperscalers buy Everpure arrays." They license the design and buy some parts; the NAND comes from their own suppliers.
  • "EXA is NVIDIA-certified." Everpure announced an extension of validation in March 2026; the certifications on record belong to FlashBlade//S.
  • "FlashBlade is shared-everything." Everpure calls it partitioned-writer; EXA is a metadata/data split, not DASE.

docs.title: 1. What storage does
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: None. This is the first technical chapter. How to use this atlas explains depth labels; the glossary defines every term in bold.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Storage has three jobs: keep bytes safely, find them again, and serve them fast enough. Every product in this atlas trades those three jobs against cost per terabyte.
  • There are three ways to address stored bytes. Block (numbered blocks; the host owns the meaning), file (paths in a tree; the storage system owns the meaning) and object (flat keys plus metadata over HTTP). The abstraction decides who buys the product and how far it scales.
  • Data has a lifecycle. It is created hot, cools as access falls, gets copied for protection and ends in an archive or deletion. Tiers follow it. Primary serves live applications, secondary holds backup and recovery copies, and archive keeps data for years at the lowest cost.
  • Buyers split by workload, not by technology. DBAs and VM admins buy block. Research and HPC groups buy file. Cloud-native, data and AI teams increasingly buy object. Each group uses its own criteria and budget.
  • AI is blurring the old map. Training data needs file-like speed at object-like scale, and "cold" archives are being reheated as training sets. That opens room for flash vendors and AI-native challengers.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
IDC sized the worldwide external enterprise storage systems market at US$10.3 billion in Q2 2026, up 33.6% year on year. All-flash arrays were 52.1% of it. Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) ranked fourth with an 8.1% share and was the fastest grower in the top five, at about +50%12. Those figures exclude hyperscaler internal storage, cloud services, backup software and tape, so "what market are we in?" depends on which abstraction and tier you count.

Everpure's portfolio maps directly onto this chapter's vocabulary. FlashArray began as block storage for databases and virtual machines in 20123 and has since added file and S3 object access4. FlashBlade has served file and object since its 2017 general availability5. Portworx serves container platforms6. Capacity-optimised //E models target secondary storage once dominated by disk7. Every growth argument (AI, hyperscalers, replacing hard drives, data management after the February 2026 rebrand8) is about entering a new tier, abstraction or buyer. This chapter supplies that map.

docs.title: Three jobs: keep, find, serve
docs.text:
A semiconductor person already knows the memory hierarchy: SRAM, then HBM and DRAM, then storage. Storage is the layer that must survive power loss. That one property creates three jobs.

  1. Keep (durability). "Acknowledged" must mean "on persistent media, or in a protected cache that will reach it". Most of the cost and complexity of enterprise storage goes into that promise: mirrored write caches, RAID and erasure coding, replication and snapshots (Chapter 6).
  2. Find (addressing and metadata). Bytes are useless unless something can locate them again. Something keeps the map from names to physical locations. Where that map lives, and how large it grows, is the main difference between architectures (Chapter 21).
  3. Serve (performance). Data must come back at the latency, IOPS or throughput the application needs (Chapter 4).

Every design trades these jobs against cost per terabyte: the familiar density-versus-speed curve, plus an axis for how hard the system works not to lose data. The media physics behind the curve (NAND, HDD and tape) are in Chapter 2.

docs.title: Block, file and object
docs.text:
The same bytes on the same SSD can be exposed in three ways. The choice decides who owns the metadata, which protocols apply and who buys the product.

Figure 1.1 — The three abstractions differ less in where bytes sit than in who keeps the map from names to blocks, and that decides latency, scale and buyer.

Block storage presents a volume (a LUN, or logical unit) that looks like a raw disk: a numbered array of fixed-size blocks, the logical block addresses (LBAs). The host reads and writes by number ("write 8 KB at LBA 6") and the array has no idea what the blocks mean. A database or a host file system on the server keeps that knowledge. That makes block the lowest-latency, most predictable option, which is why databases, ERP and hypervisors want it. Semis bridge: a physical address bus, where the controller moves data and the OS decides what lives there. The protocols are SCSI-family over Fibre Channel and iSCSI, and now NVMe and NVMe-oF (Chapter 7). The limit is sharing: two servers writing one LUN without a cluster file system corrupt each other.

File storage moves the file system into the storage system. Clients see a tree of directories and files and ask for "bytes 4–5 MB of /projects/training/shard-0001.tar". The array keeps names, permissions, locks and the map from file offsets to blocks. Many clients share one namespace safely, which suits home directories, media, HPC and AI training. In virtual-memory terms, the storage system now runs the page tables. The protocols are NFS and SMB, plus parallel file-system clients that stripe one file across many servers (Chapter 8, Chapter 17). The cost is metadata work. Every open, stat and rename hits a shared structure, and billions of small files can choke it.

Object storage drops the tree. A bucket holds objects, and each object is a blob of data, a key (a name that may contain slashes but implies no directory) and a set of user-defined metadata. Clients use HTTP verbs, chiefly PUT, GET, LIST and DELETE, through the S3 API that Amazon launched in 20069. Objects are usually written whole and not edited in place. That removes locking and lets the system spread across thousands of nodes and sites; think hash table, not filesystem. The price is higher per-request latency and no partial overwrite. It suits backups, data lakes, logs, media, model artefacts and AI datasets (Chapter 9, Chapter 18).

Worked example: the same 1 GB, three ways. A database writes a 1 GiB table as 131,072 independent 8 KB block writes (1 GiB ÷ 8 KiB), each at an LBA the database chose and each updatable in place. A training job reads the same gigabyte as a file, in 1 MB requests by path and offset. That is 1,024 reads, each checked against permissions and a shared namespace. An object application issues one PUT, or perhaps 100 parts of 10 MB, and from then on it can only replace the gigabyte whole. Same bytes, different metadata burden, different scaling behaviour.

Two caveats. The layers stack: file systems and object stores sit on blocks internally, and many products serve two or three abstractions from one system (unified storage). And the boundaries move: S3 is becoming the default AI data interface, so file systems are adding S3 front doors. Chapter 13 traces the full stack.

docs.title: The data lifecycle: hot, warm, cold
docs.text:
A fresh order record is read constantly; a quarter later, occasionally; seven years later it exists mainly because a regulator might ask for it. Storage people call this temperature: hot (accessed constantly, latency matters), warm (accessed sometimes, cost and throughput matter), cold (rarely accessed, cost per terabyte is almost everything).

flowchart LR
    A["Create or ingest"] --> B["Hot: active use"]
    B --> C["Protect: snapshots, replicas, backups"]
    B --> D["Warm: occasional access"]
    D --> E["Cold: archive for years"]
    E --> F["Delete or legal hold"]
    C --> E
    E -. "AI reuse reheats old data" .-> B

Figure 1.2 — Data cools as access falls and is copied for protection along the way; AI is adding a return arrow from archive to hot.

Tier placement drives cost. In US East, S3 Standard costs about US$0.023 per GB-month, while S3 Glacier Deep Archive costs about US$0.0009910. For 1 PB (1,000,000 GB) that is roughly US$23,000 a month hot versus US$990 a month cold, a 23x gap. The cold price comes with restore times measured in hours and minimum retention periods10. Moving data between tiers by policy (tiering or lifecycle management) is a large lever on spend, and a source of pain when a "cold" dataset is suddenly needed by 1,000 GPUs on Monday (Chapter 30).

docs.title: Primary, secondary and archive
docs.text:
The industry groups products into tiers by job, not by medium:

Tier Job What the buyer optimises Typical media today Typical abstraction Primary Serve live applications: databases, VMs, AI training and inference Latency, IOPS/throughput, availability (often ≥ 99.999%) TLC/QLC flash; some hybrid Block and file; object growing Secondary Hold backup copies, disaster-recovery replicas, dev/test copies, analytics Ingest speed, fast restore (RTO), immutability against ransomware, $/TB HDD-based appliances, QLC flash, cloud object Object and file Archive Keep data for years for compliance, preservation or future reuse Lowest $/TB, durability, decades-long readability Tape, high-capacity HDD, cloud archive classes Object (or tape library APIs)

Table 1.1 — Tiers are defined by the job the copy does; media and abstraction follow from the job, which is why flash can move "down" into secondary as its cost falls.

The boundaries are soft: "secondary" also means a cheaper capacity tier for cooled primary data. Tape is far from dead. LTO tape shipments were 160.3 EB in 2025, down 9% from a record 176.5 EB in 202411. Those figures assume 2.5:1 compression12, so the native capacity is about 160.3 ÷ 2.5 ≈ 64 EB. Shipments rose 57% year on year in Q1 202611. Data protection, including recovery objectives (RPO and RTO) and ransomware immutability, is covered in Chapter 6. Economic metrics such as $/TB, TB/W and effective capacity are in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Who buys what
docs.text:
The technology map matters commercially because each abstraction and tier has a different buyer, budget and set of criteria:

Buyer Workloads Abstraction Buys on Typical competitive set DBAs and VM / infrastructure admins (enterprise IT) Oracle, SQL Server, SAP, VMware/Hyper-V, Kubernetes Block (some file) Latency consistency, uptime, snapshots, ease of operation, vendor stability Dell, NetApp, Everpure, HPE, Hitachi, IBM, Huawei Backup, security and compliance teams Backup targets, cyber recovery, archive Object and file Restore speed, immutability, $/TB Backup-software vendors plus disk/flash and tape suppliers Research and HPC groups (labs, universities, pharma, energy, media) Simulation, genomics, rendering Parallel file Aggregate throughput per $, open-source fit, scale DDN, IBM, HPE, Dell, WEKA, VAST Cloud-native, platform and data teams Microservices, data lakes, analytics Object (S3), container volumes API compatibility, elasticity, self-service Public cloud first; on-prem object vendors AI infrastructure teams and neoclouds Training, checkpointing, inference/KV cache, RAG Parallel file and object, increasingly both GPU utilisation, TB/s per rack, power, certification by NVIDIA VAST, WEKA, DDN, Everpure, NetApp, Dell

Table 1.2 — Each buyer group judges storage on different criteria, so a vendor strong with DBAs can be invisible to an AI team.

The strategic tension: Everpure built its franchise with conservative enterprise IT buyers who prize operational simplicity. HPC buyers favoured parallel file systems and open source. Cloud-native and AI teams grew up on S3 and on renting. The fastest-growing budgets sit with the last group (Chapter 35, Chapter 41).

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Vendor Block File Object Capacity / secondary angle Everpure FlashArray (//X, //XL, //C, //ST) FlashArray file; FlashBlade//S and //EXA FlashBlade; S3 on FlashArray since 20254 FlashArray//E and FlashBlade//E on QLC713; DirectFlash licensed to hyperscalers for HDD replacement14 Dell PowerStore, PowerMax PowerScale; Lightning parallel file system ObjectScale Separate engines for each abstraction on common hardware15; PowerProtect for backup NetApp ONTAP AFF/ASA ONTAP (unified block, file and S3); AFX disaggregated16 ONTAP S3; StorageGRID One OS across tiers; tiering to cloud HPE Alletra MP B10000 Alletra MP X10000 (native NFS added) Alletra MP X10000 Shared Alletra MP hardware17 VAST Data NVMe/TCP block volumes since early 2025, not the focus18 Core strength Core strength One platform for hot and capacity data on QLC19 Public cloud (AWS as example) EBS EFS, FSx (incl. Lustre) S3 storage classes Archive classes priced ~23x below standard10

Table 1.3 — Everpure covers all three abstractions with two hardware families and one software lineage; Dell sells a product per abstraction, NetApp one unified OS, VAST one platform aimed at file and object at scale.

Everpure's approach. FlashArray (block-first) and FlashBlade (file and object) share the Purity software lineage, DirectFlash modules and Evergreen subscriptions. The bet is that one flash architecture can serve primary and secondary tiers, letting QLC economics pull workloads off disk (Chapter 26, Chapter 27).

Steelman the alternatives. Dell offers breadth: a dedicated, mature product for every abstraction plus the servers and the backup stack, sold through the largest enterprise sales force (IDC's #1 at 23.8% share in Q2 20261). NetApp has long run block, file and object on one OS, ONTAP, which makes "one platform" its home turf. VAST argues that the AI era wants one namespace serving file and object at exabyte scale, not two array families. AWS and other clouds own the cloud-native buyer by default and set the price anchors for cold data. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: how far FlashBlade//EXA and FlashArray S3 carry Everpure into object-first AI buyers, and whether the hyperscaler DirectFlash model extends flash into archive-adjacent tiers that disk still owns.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title How the three abstractions arrived
    1956 : IBM 350 RAMAC ships the first commercial disk drive
    1980s : NFS brings shared file access over networks : RAID turns cheap disks into reliable volumes
    1990s : Fibre Channel SANs pool block storage : NAS filers sell file as an appliance
    2006 : Amazon S3 launches the object API
    2012 : Pure Storage FlashArray brings all-flash block to the mainstream
    2017 : FlashBlade GA for file and object on flash
    2020s : S3 becomes the default AI data interface : Unified and disaggregated designs spread

Figure 1.3 — Each abstraction arrived to solve a sharing problem: block pooled disks, file shared namespaces, object shared the internet.

IBM's 350 disk unit shipped in 1956 with fifty 24-inch platters holding about 3.75 MB20. Networking then turned storage into a shared service. S3's growth shows where scale went. Amazon reported over 280 trillion objects and over 100 million requests per second in 202321. By its twentieth anniversary in March 2026 it cited more than 500 trillion objects and over 200 million requests per second across hundreds of exabytes, with storage prices down from 15 to 2 cents per GB22.

Three trajectories matter for the rest of the atlas:

  1. Object moves up the performance ladder. AI pipelines read training data and write checkpoints through S3, which pushes object stores onto flash and RDMA (Chapter 9, Chapter 11).
  2. Flash moves down the tiers. QLC and very large modules attack secondary storage and parts of the HDD estate. Everpure claims its DirectFlash modules use up to 75% less power than HDD (vendor claim)14. The disk-versus-flash cost gap remains wide (Chapter 2, Chapter 48).
  3. The lifecycle loops back. AI turns archives into training corpora and checkpoints into hot recovery points. Inference adds a new hot tier, KV-cache offload (Chapter 32). The long-run history is in Chapter 51.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Which buyer owns this deal: the DBA, the backup team, the research group or the AI platform team, and how do their criteria differ?" A strong answer names the buying centre, its budget line, the deciding criteria (latency consistency, restore time or TB/s per rack) and the competitors that buyer invites.
  2. "What share of our revenue sits in primary versus secondary versus archive-adjacent use cases, and where is the growth?" A strong answer separates tiers from products (the same FlashBlade can be primary for AI and secondary for backup) and gives a direction even if it cannot give a number.
  3. "When a customer wants S3 and NFS on the same data, how do we serve it, and what breaks?" A strong answer covers semantic mismatches (rename, partial overwrite, permissions) and whether both protocols see one copy or two.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Where does the name-to-block map live for each protocol we serve, and what limits its size?" Strong: the answer separates host-owned metadata (block) from system-owned metadata (file, object) and names the bottleneck, such as directory operations or object-listing rate.
  2. "How fast can a petabyte move from a capacity tier to a performance tier, and what does the application see during the move?" Strong: the answer gives GB/s, whether access is transparent or needs a copy, and what happens to snapshots.
  3. "What does 'acknowledged' mean on our write path: in NVRAM, mirrored, or on flash?" Strong: the answer names the persistence point and its failure domain (Chapter 14).

Don't say this:

  • "Object storage is just cheap, slow storage." Object on flash now feeds GPU clusters; S3 is an interface, not a tier.
  • "File and block are legacy." Databases and VMs still run on block, and most AI training still reads through file systems.
  • "Secondary storage means old hardware." It means a copy doing a protection or analytics job, increasingly on QLC flash.
  • "Tape is dead." It shipped about 160 EB (compressed) in 2025.
  • "Unified storage means everything is equally good at everything." One system serving three protocols usually optimises one and tolerates the others.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• SNIA's dictionary and its "Object Storage" and "File vs Block vs Object" educational webcasts give vendor-neutral definitions.
  • Andy Warfield's FAST '23 keynote and accompanying essay on operating S3 at scale21.
  • The SCSI block command set (T10 SBC) and NVMe base specification for how LBAs are addressed. RFC 8881 (NFSv4.1) for file semantics. The Amazon S3 API reference for object semantics.
  • Chapter 13 for the layer-by-layer stack and Chapter 24 for matching architectures to workloads.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Block storage — a volume of numbered fixed-size blocks; the host owns the meaning.
  • File storage — a shared tree of named files; the storage system owns the file system.
  • Object storage — flat buckets of keyed objects with metadata, accessed over HTTP (S3).
  • LUN / LBA — a block volume and the address of a block within it.
  • Primary / secondary / archive — tiers defined by the job a copy does: serve, protect, retain.
  • Hot / warm / cold — data temperature by access frequency.
  • Unified storage — one system serving more than one abstraction.
  • Lifecycle management (tiering) — policy-driven movement of data between tiers.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 2. Media physics for a semis person
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~14 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: What storage does · NAND basics from semiconductors (assumed)

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Storage is a cache hierarchy with a cliff in the middle. Memory tiers answer in ~100–400 ns, NAND in ~50–150 µs. Most storage-system design is about hiding that ~1,000× wall.
  • NAND is asymmetric by physics. You program pages but erase only whole blocks, and every cell wears out after finite program/erase (P/E) cycles. Hence the flash translation layer (FTL), and why "who runs the FTL" is strategic (Chapter 3, Chapter 26).
  • Each extra bit per cell roughly halves the voltage margin. QLC (16 states) is cheaper per bit but slower, less durable and more fragile than SLC (2 states). It works in enterprise only when software turns small random writes into large sequential ones.
  • Scaling moved from lithography to layers, and from layers to bonding. Leading 3D NAND went from 24 layers in 2013 to 400+ in 2026. Bit density per mm², not layer count, is the number to ask for.
  • HDD is not dead, and the 2026 shortage reset the economics. HAMR ships 40–44 TB drives, and in 2026 enterprise flash cost ~18–23× disk per TB, up from ~6–10×. "Flash replaces disk" now rests on power, density and operations, not purchase price.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Everpure's core technical bet is that whoever manages raw NAND best wins on cost, density and power. Its DirectFlash Modules expose raw NAND to Purity software rather than hiding it behind a per-drive controller, and the same technology underpins its hyperscaler design wins with Meta (December 2024) and a second top-five hyperscaler (August 2026)12. Claims about endurance, QLC viability or "flash cheaper than disk" all trace back to the physics in this chapter; knowing it lets you test them rather than repeat them.

The 2025–26 memory shortage makes this urgent. NAND contract prices rose every quarter of 2026. TrendForce expected another 15–20% rise in 4Q26, with enterprise SSDs up 23–28%3. When flash costs 18× disk per TB instead of 6×, the argument for replacing disk changes from "cheaper to buy" to "cheaper to power, house and run". Chapter 48 covers the supply cycle.

docs.title: The hierarchy: same logic as a CPU cache, wider gaps
docs.text:
Figure 2.1 — Every tier down is roughly 10× cheaper and 10× bigger, but the step from memory to flash costs about 1,000× in latency, and that wall shapes storage architecture.

Sources for the 2026 figures: HBM3E contract pricing is estimated at roughly $8–18 per GB4. In 2026, server DDR5 rose to a similar range: a 64 GB RDIMM ended 1Q26 at about $927, or about $14.5/GB5. The HBM premium over DDR5 was expected to narrow in 20266. A Blackwell Ultra-class GPU carries 288 GB of HBM3E, in 12-high stacks7. HBM is a bandwidth tier, not a latency tier: measured from a GPU core, a dependent load that misses the caches takes roughly 350 ns on an H1008, slower than a CPU's local DRAM. Measured CXL memory expanders show load latencies of about 214–271 ns9. They ship as modules of 256 GB10 and as boxes of up to 16 TB11. NVMe-oF over RDMA adds about 5–15 µs to a local flash access12, and array software adds more. A 30 TB nearline HDD indexed at $1,216 works out to about $0.04/GB13. LTO-10 cartridges hold 30 TB native and sell for about $275–3151415, or about $0.01/GB for media alone.

Three points for a semis reader:

  1. The wall is architectural, not just quantitative. Above it, the CPU issues loads and stores to volatile, byte-addressable media. Below it, the OS queues block I/O to persistent media through a driver. Crossing it costs a software stack and microseconds of overhead. Intel's Optane partly filled the gap but needed new software models to exploit, and Intel wound it down in 202216.
  2. 2026 broke the price ladder at the top. HBM normally costs several times DRAM per GB; the 2026 shortage brought them level. DRAM-heavy designs got far costlier, strengthening the case for pushing KV cache and metadata down to flash (Chapter 32).
  3. Networked flash costs latency, not much else. The fabric adds microseconds against a ~100 µs media read. It buys sharing, protection and independent scaling (Chapter 16).

docs.title: One level deeper on a NAND cell
docs.text:
Modern 3D NAND mostly replaces the floating gate with a charge-trap cell: electrons sit in a silicon-nitride layer wrapped around a vertical polysilicon channel. Word lines are horizontal tungsten plates stacked hundreds high, and a "string" is the column of cells sharing one channel between a bit line and a source line.

Figure 2.2 — Cells sit in series on a vertical string, store charge in a nitride trap, and must fit ever more voltage states into the same few-volt window.

Four behaviours matter for system design:

Program/erase asymmetry. Programming uses incremental step pulses (ISPP) on one word line to tunnel electrons into the trap layer, page by page (~16 kB per plane today; TLC and QLC store several logical pages per word line and often program them in multiple passes). Erase raises the channel to a high voltage relative to every word line in a block. In a charge-trap cell that works mostly by injecting holes that neutralise the trapped electrons, not by pulling electrons back out. Many 3D designs have no body contact under the polysilicon channel, so they generate those holes by gate-induced drain leakage at the select gates. Either way it can only be done for a whole block of many megabytes in current 3D parts. Program takes hundreds of µs (TLC) to a few ms (QLC); erase takes several ms. Above all, you cannot overwrite in place: an update goes to a fresh page, and the old page is garbage until its whole block is reclaimed. That creates the FTL, garbage collection and write amplification, a background housekeeping tax set by cell physics, much as refresh is for DRAM (Chapter 3).

Endurance. Each P/E cycle drives charge through the tunnel oxide and leaves interface and bulk traps behind. The threshold-voltage distributions widen until the controller's error correction (LDPC codes) can no longer separate them. Worked example in drive writes per day (DWPD): DWPD ≈ P/E cycles × (raw ÷ user capacity) ÷ (write amplification × days of warranty). Take a QLC part rated for 1,000 cycles over 5 years (1,825 days), and ignore spare area for simplicity (raw = user). It gives 1,000 ÷ 1,825 ≈ 0.55 DWPD if writes arrive perfectly sequential (WAF = 1). The same drive under random small writes at WAF = 3 gives about 0.18 DWPD. On a 122.88 TB drive, that is the difference between ~67 TB and ~22 TB of host writes per day. A shipping drive shows the same ratio: Micron rates its 245.76 TB QLC 6600 ION at 1.0 DWPD for 128 KB sequential writes but 0.3 DWPD for 16 KB random writes17. The sequential rating also implies that current QLC is good for well over 1,000 cycles, nearer 2,000, so the worked example is conservative.

Retention. Trapped charge leaks, faster when hot and faster in worn cells (the loss is thermally activated, so vendors accelerate it with bake tests). JEDEC's enterprise SSD rating (JESD218) requires only three months of unpowered retention at 40 °C, at the end of rated life. A fresh drive retains far longer, but nobody guarantees how long. Powered drives refresh data in the background, but flash is a poor shelf archive, one reason tape survives.

Read disturb. Cells in a string sit in series, so reading one cell means applying a pass voltage to every other word line in the block. Each read slightly programs the neighbours. After enough reads the controller must relocate the block. AI training rereads the same blocks every epoch, so even a "read-only" workload creates hidden background writes; a good design schedules them away from foreground reads to protect tail latency.

docs.title: Bits per cell: the cost/quality dial
docs.text:
Cell type Bits/cell Voltage states Typical P/E endurance Typical page read (tR) 2026 status SLC 1 2 ~50,000–100,000 ~20–30 µs Caches, write buffers, low-latency SCM-like parts MLC 2 4 ~3,000–10,000 ~50 µs Largely displaced in data centers TLC 3 8 ~3,000–10,000 (enterprise grades at the top) ~40–80 µs Performance tier; the volume workhorse QLC 4 16 ~1,000–3,000 ~100–160 µs Capacity tier; 122–256 TB SSDs181920 PLC 5 32 Lower still (not commercial) Slower still Research only; SK hynix showed a split-cell design at IEDM in December 202521

Table 2.1 — Each added bit gives 100%, 50%, 33% then 25% more bits per cell, while doubling the states to resolve. The cost gain shrinks as the physics penalty grows. Endurance and tR are typical ranges across vendors. NAND makers rarely publish P/E ratings. The TLC and QLC ranges are consistent with the DWPD ratings of the Micron drives cited in this chapter and Chapter 3 once over-provisioning and WAF are backed out, but they are not datasheet values [VERIFY: confirm P/E ranges against 2025–26 NAND vendor disclosures].

TLC→QLC adds ~33% capacity per die, minus extra ECC parity and over-provisioning. QLC→PLC adds only 25% for twice the states, which is why PLC keeps slipping and the industry adds layers rather than bits.

docs.title: Why QLC needs a smart write path
docs.text:
QLC programs slowly, in large units, and wears out quickly. Small random overwrites force the FTL to keep moving valid data out of partly-stale blocks, so write amplification rises, endurance falls and latency turns erratic. Serious QLC systems put a write path in front of the NAND:

flowchart LR
    A["Small random writes from hosts"] --> B["Fast persistent buffer: NVRAM, SCM or SLC-mode flash"]
    B --> C["Coalesce, dedupe, compress"]
    C --> D["Sort by expected lifetime: hot vs cold"]
    D --> E["Large sequential stripes aligned to erase blocks"]
    E --> F["QLC NAND"]
    F -. "occasional garbage collection of cold data" .-> D

Figure 2.3 — QLC is viable in enterprise systems only behind a buffer that turns many small writes into few large, lifetime-sorted ones; the further up the stack this happens, the less the NAND sees.

Commodity QLC SSDs do this inside the drive with an SLC-mode cache, which runs out under sustained writes. Arrays do it one level up: VAST buffers in shared SCM before writing wide QLC stripes (Chapter 16). Everpure's DirectFlash puts the whole job in array software that sees every module's raw NAND (Chapter 26). Hyperscalers push hints down with NVMe Flexible Data Placement so drives can keep data of similar lifetime together22. The semis analogy is a write-combining buffer in front of a DRAM controller.

docs.title: 3D NAND scaling: layers, decks and bonding
docs.text:
Planar NAND stopped shrinking in the mid-teens of nanometres, when cells held too few electrons to count reliably, so the industry turned the array on its side. The critical step is now etching a channel hole through the whole stack at extreme aspect ratio. Long stacks are built as two or three decks that are etched separately and aligned. SK hynix's 321-layer part uses three "plugs" and entered mass production in November 202423. The newest step is wafer bonding: building CMOS periphery on a separate wafer and hybrid-bonding it to the array. Samsung's 400+-layer V10 uses it24.

Figure 2.4 — Layer count rose roughly 17× in 13 years, but it is a poor proxy for cost per bit; density and wafer cost decide competitiveness. Data: data/ch02_nand_layers.csv

Layer count is a marketing number. Kioxia/Sandisk's 332-layer BiCS10 reportedly reaches about 37 Gb/mm² as QLC, which is denser than Samsung's 400+-layer V10 (about 28 Gb/mm² as TLC)2524. Micron's 276-layer G9 is about 21 Gb/mm² in TLC26. Comparing QLC with TLC flatters BiCS10, but the lesson stands: ask for Gb/mm², wafer cost and yield, as for a logic node. Each deck adds deposition and etch steps, so capex per wafer rises even as cost per bit falls, which makes suppliers cautious about adding capacity even in a shortage.

Bigger dies and more layers produce bigger drives. Micron began shipping the 245.76 TB 6600 ION, built on G9 QLC, in May 202618. Sandisk has a 256 TB drive on 218-layer BiCS8 and shows 512 TB on its roadmap for 202720. Everpure's DirectFlash Module is reported at up to 300 TB27 [VERIFY: GA and ship date of the 300 TB DFM].

docs.title: HDD mechanics: capacity keeps rising, performance does not
docs.text:
Random access on a hard drive needs a head seek plus, on average, half a platter rotation. At 7,200 rpm one rotation takes 60 ÷ 7,200 = 8.33 ms, so average rotational latency is ~4.2 ms. Nearline drives have long been specified at ~8 ms average seek, and measured access times run a little higher28. A random read therefore costs ~12 ms, or roughly 80 IOPS per drive at queue depth 1. Command queuing lets the drive reorder requests to shorten seeks, so a 30 TB HAMR drive reaches ~170 random-read IOPS at queue depth 16 (Chapter 4). Those figures have barely moved in 20 years while capacity has grown more than tenfold. A 30 TB drive therefore delivers ~3–6 IOPS per TB. Rebuilding one at an assumed ~250 MB/s sustained takes 30 × 10¹² ÷ 250 × 10⁶ ≈ 120,000 s, about 33 hours at best. Bigger HDDs suit bulk sequential data and get worse at everything else, which is why vendors now pitch bandwidth as well as terabytes29.

Capacity growth depends on areal density, which runs into the magnetic trilemma. Smaller grains store more bits but become thermally unstable. Stable, high-anisotropy grains need a stronger write field than a head can produce. Three recording technologies work around it:

Technology How it adds density The catch 2026 status CMR / ePMR Perpendicular grains; energy-assisted write heads Approaching trilemma limits WD roadmap: ePMR to 60 TB, 40 TB UltraSMR drives in 2H 202630 SMR (shingled) Overlaps tracks like roof shingles, since read heads are narrower than write heads Can't rewrite one track without rewriting its band; host-managed SMR needs sequential zone writes, much like NAND erase blocks Common in hyperscale; WD UltraSMR at 40 TB30 HAMR A laser heats a tiny spot for a nanosecond so a high-anisotropy (FePt) medium can be written, then it cools stably New heads, media and reliability proof; slow volume ramp Seagate Mozaic 3+ at 30 TB from 202431; Mozaic 4+ at up to 44 TB shipping in volume to two hyperscalers from March 202632; WD HAMR ramps 2027, targets 100 TB by 202930

Table 2.2 — HDD makers trade write flexibility (SMR) or manufacturing complexity (HAMR) for capacity; none of it improves random I/O.

Note the SMR/NAND parallel: both prefer large sequential writes into zones that must be reclaimed whole, so the same zoned-storage software ideas (ZNS, FDP, log-structured layouts) apply to both (Chapter 12).

docs.title: Cost-per-bit curves: why the gap moved
docs.text:
Figure 2.5 — Flash's price premium over disk roughly halved between 2017 and 2020, then the 2026 shortage pushed it back to around 20×; the sources use different bases, so read direction, not decimals. Data: data/ch02_hdd_vs_nand_cost.csv

The HDD curve is slow and steady. Backblaze's purchase cost fell from about $0.11/GB in 2009 to $0.014/GB in November 202233, an average decline of ~1.2% a month, or ~14% a year. NAND's curve is steeper but cyclical. In Q2 2020, TrendForce data put enterprise SSDs at about $185/TB against $19/TB for nearline disk, a 9.7× premium34. Seagate said in 2024 that it expected disk to hold a >6:1 advantage through 2027, averaging 6.6:1 (company-stated)35. Then the shortage hit. VDURA's Flash Volatility Index put a 30 TB QLC SSD at 22.6× a 30 TB HDD per TB in Q1 2026, up from 4.9× in Q2 202536, and a 30 TB TLC SSD at 18.6× in Q3 2026 ($22,600 against $1,216)13. The index comes from a hybrid flash-and-disk vendor that does not disclose its price sources, and it has switched between QLC and TLC bases between releases, so read the level with caution [VERIFY: corroborate the 2026 premium with TrendForce or Coughlin data]. Disk rose too: the index's 30 TB HDD went from $668 in Q1 to $1,216 in Q3 2026.

Flash wins elsewhere. Micron rates the 245 TB drive at ~8.2 TB/W against ~4.4 TB/W for a 44 TB HDD (vendor comparison)19. Everpure claims DirectFlash cuts power by up to 75% compared with HDD (vendor claim)37. Where power and space bind, as in AI data centers, TCO can favour flash despite the premium. Chapter 4 works the TCO.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Approach Who Where NAND is managed Strength Weakness Raw NAND under array software Everpure DirectFlash (FlashArray, FlashBlade, hyperscaler DFMs) Purity, globally across modules One FTL for the whole system: lifetime-aware placement, less over-provisioning, very large modules Proprietary module; Everpure carries NAND qualification and supply work Commodity SSDs + SCM buffer VAST SSD FTLs, with an SCM write buffer shaping writes into wide QLC stripes Uses the industry's largest standard drives; buffer absorbs QLC weaknesses Two FTL layers; dependence on an SCM tier38 Commodity TLC/QLC SSDs NetApp, Dell, WEKA, DDN and most others Inside each drive Multi-sourced, fast to adopt new drives Each drive reserves its own spare area and does its own garbage collection Host-guided placement Hyperscalers using FDP Shared: host hints, drive executes Cuts write amplification without custom hardware22 Needs software built for it; hyperscale-specific Disk plus flash cache Hyperscale bulk tiers, HDD vendors' thesis N/A for disk Lowest acquisition $/TB; 6–20× gap Few IOPS per TB, long rebuilds, more power and space per PB

Table 2.3 — The competitive question is not "flash or disk" but where the flash-management intelligence lives and who pays for it.

The steelman for commodity SSDs is supply flexibility: a new 245 TB drive can be qualified quickly, while a module vendor must build its own. The steelman for disk: at an 18× gap, exabyte-scale cold data stays on HDD and tape for years. Two public facts shape Everpure's position. Its Meta and second-hyperscaler deals license DirectFlash technology, and management has said Everpure does not procure the NAND for the hyperscaler business2, which insulates that revenue line from NAND price spikes. It has also qualified multiple NAND sources (Micron G8/G9 QLC, Kioxia BiCS8)39. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: how much of the 2026 NAND price rise flows through array pricing versus margin, and whether a structurally higher flash premium slows HDD-replacement deals while strengthening the power-and-density argument for AI sites.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Storage media milestones
    1956 : IBM RAMAC ships the first hard disk drive
    1987 : Toshiba presents NAND flash
    2013 : Samsung ships first 3D V-NAND at 24 layers
    2022 : Intel winds down Optane
    2024 : Seagate launches 30 TB HAMR drives : SK hynix mass-produces 321-layer NAND
    2025 : LTO-10 30 TB cartridges ship : Sandisk 256 TB QLC SSD announced : SK hynix shows split-cell PLC research
    2026 : Micron ships 245 TB QLC SSD : Samsung unveils 400-plus-layer V10 : NAND contract prices surge : Seagate ships 44 TB HAMR to hyperscalers
    2027-2029 : WD HAMR ramps in 2027 : WD targets 100 TB HAMR by 2029

Figure 2.6 — Flash capacity per device overtook disk by roughly 5× in 2026, while HDD's new technology, HAMR, is only now reaching volume.

The RAMAC date is from the Computer History Museum40; Toshiba's NAND paper (Masuoka et al., IEDM 1987) and Samsung's 24-layer V-NAND (2013) are standard history, and the 2016–2022 layer points in Figure 2.4 are background only. Looking forward: Layer roadmaps target ~500 layers, though vendor timelines conflict26. PLC remains research21. HDD capacity roadmaps (WD: 100 TB by 2029) depend on HAMR ramping on schedule30. Meanwhile the 2026 price shock is a supply-discipline event, not a physics event. AI servers absorbed bits, and TrendForce reported most new supply already committed3. Its length matters for 2027 pricing.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "At today's flash premium over disk, where does an all-flash pitch still win on TCO, and where do we lose?" Strong: names the binding constraint per segment (power, rack space, rebuild risk) and a break-even premium, not "flash is always cheaper".
  2. "How exposed are product margins to the 2026 NAND price rise, and how much is passed through?" Strong: separates arrays (Everpure buys NAND) from hyperscaler licensing (customer buys NAND), and covers contract timing and Evergreen commitments that limit repricing.
  3. "What does QLC let us sell that TLC doesn't, and where would we refuse to put QLC?" Strong: capacity and power wins for file, object and backup; caution for write-heavy, latency-critical block workloads unless the write path absorbs them.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What effective WAF does Purity see on QLC in the field, and how does that translate into DWPD headroom?" Strong: a measured number by workload, and how the system-level FTL keeps WAF near 1.
  2. "How do you handle read disturb and retention on read-mostly AI datasets?" Strong: background scrub and relocation scheduled around foreground I/O, plus telemetry on read-retry rates as a wear signal.
  3. "What changes when you move from a 75 TB to a 300 TB module: rebuild time, blast radius, performance per TB?" Strong: rebuild hours, protection scheme, and how in-module parallelism stops performance per TB collapsing as it does on large HDDs.

Don't say this:

  • "More layers means cheaper flash." Bit density, wafer cost and yield decide cost per bit. A 332-layer part can out-density a 400-layer one.
  • "QLC wears out too fast for enterprise." Behind a good write path it is adequate for most capacity workloads.
  • "Flash is now cheaper than disk." Not on purchase price in 2026, when the premium is roughly 18× or more by one vendor's index. Argue TCO, power and density instead.
  • "SSDs are a good archive." JEDEC-rated unpowered retention at end of life is three months, and nothing guarantees years.
  • "HAMR fixes disk performance." It adds capacity. IOPS per drive stay flat, so IOPS per TB keep falling.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• JEDEC JESD218/JESD219: SSD endurance and retention test conditions.
  • IEDM/ISSCC NAND papers: tR, tPROG and bonding by vendor, e.g. SK hynix's multi-site-cell PLC (IEDM 2025)21.
  • NVM Express FDP (TP4146) and ZNS specifications22.
  • Seagate and Western Digital investor-day decks on HAMR roadmaps.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• P/E cycle — one program/erase cycle of a NAND block; the unit of flash wear.
  • DWPD — drive writes per day sustainable over the warranty.
  • Charge-trap cell — 3D NAND cell storing electrons in a nitride layer.
  • Read disturb — gradual corruption of unread cells caused by reads of neighbours.
  • QLC / PLC — 4 and 5 bits per cell NAND.
  • HAMR / SMR — heat-assisted and shingled magnetic recording.
  • Memory–storage wall — the ~1,000× latency step between DRAM-class memory and flash.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 3. Inside an SSD
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~12 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Media physics for a semis person · What storage does · Glossary

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• An SSD is a small computer wrapped around NAND. A controller SoC (Arm cores, ECC engines, 8–16 flash channels) runs firmware that makes erase-before-write NAND look like a simple disk.
  • The flash translation layer (FTL) is a page table. Its map lives in on-drive DRAM, about 1 GB per TB at 4 KB granularity, which is why the largest QLC drives map 16 KB+ units and penalise small writes.
  • Garbage collection (GC) is the hidden tax. Reclaiming stale pages means copying live data; those extra writes are write amplification (WAF). The main lever against it is over-provisioning (OP), spare flash the host never sees.
  • Spare flash buys endurance. In an illustrative random-write model, WAF falls from ~7.8 at 7% OP to ~2.1 at 37%: most of the gap between "read-intensive" and "mixed-use" drives built from the same NAND.
  • Under a log-structured array, the drive's FTL is mostly duplicated effort: a second map, second spare area and second, unscheduled GC. ZNS and FDP (Chapter 12) and Everpure's DirectFlash (Chapter 26) are three answers to that waste.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Everpure's central technical claim is that an array should buy raw NAND, not commodity SSDs, and run one flash translation layer across the system. Whether that is a durable moat depends on what an SSD's internal FTL actually costs (DRAM, hidden spare flash, write amplification, latency spikes) and how much of that cost standards such as Flexible Data Placement (FDP) claw back for everyone else. This chapter is the mechanism behind DirectFlash (Chapter 26) and the hyperscaler licences (Chapter 29).

It also gives you a test for vendor claims. When a competitor says its 245 TB QLC SSD "just works" for primary storage, or Everpure says DirectFlash "eliminates" overhead, ask about indirection-unit size, over-provisioning, GC isolation and who owns the firmware.

docs.title: A small computer wrapped around NAND
docs.text:
Open an enterprise NVMe SSD and you find a controller ASIC, a few DRAM chips, capacitors and many NAND packages, each stacking dies split into planes, blocks and pages (Chapter 2).

Figure 3.1 — An SSD is an embedded system: Arm cores run the mapping firmware, hardware engines do the error correction, DRAM holds the map, capacitors make it crash-safe, and a slice of the NAND is held back as spare.

The controller is an embedded SoC, much like a baseband modem: general-purpose cores for control flow, fixed-function engines for the heavy maths. Marvell's PCIe Gen5 Bravera SC5 combines Arm Cortex-R8 real-time cores, an LDPC error-correction engine, a DDR4/LPDDR4X interface and 8 or 16 NAND channels1; Silicon Motion's SM8366 drives 16 channels at up to 2,400 MT/s2. Merchant controller vendors sell to SSD makers without their own, while the NAND IDMs mostly design in-house.

Channels are memory channels; dies are banks. One die is slow (a QLC page read takes ~100–160 µs), so bandwidth comes from striping work across 8–16 independent channels, each a shared bus to several dies, and across planes within each die. As with DRAM bank-level parallelism, throughput is a scheduling problem.

DRAM holds the map, the logical-to-physical (L2P) table discussed below. Client drives often skip DRAM and borrow host memory (the NVMe Host Memory Buffer) or cache hot entries in on-chip SRAM.

Power-loss protection (PLP) capacitors keep the drive alive long enough after power fails to flush buffered writes and map updates. PLP lets an enterprise drive acknowledge a write from DRAM and stay crash-safe. Most client drives lack it.

Spare area is NAND that is installed but not sold. A drive built from 8 TiB of NAND (8.80 TB) and sold as 7.68 TB keeps 1.12 TB, or 14.5% of user capacity, as over-provisioning. Sold as 6.4 TB, the same NAND keeps 37%. That is the usual difference between "read-intensive" and "mixed-use" SKUs: Micron's 7450 PRO at 7.68 TB is rated for 1 drive write per day (DWPD), and its 7450 MAX at 6.4 TB for 3 DWPD34 [VERIFY: that both SKUs use the same raw NAND per drive].

docs.title: The FTL: a page table for flash
docs.text:
NAND programs pages (~16 KB) but erases only whole blocks (many MB), so the FTL never updates in place. Every write goes to the next free page of an "open" block, and a table records where each logical block address (LBA) now lives.

flowchart TD
    W["Host writes 4 KB to LBA 1234"] --> B["Buffer in DRAM, protected by PLP"]
    B --> K["Acknowledge host"]
    B --> L["L2P lookup: LBA 1234 is at block 17, page 40"]
    L --> A["Allocate next free page in open block 92"]
    A --> P["Program NAND page"]
    P --> U["Update L2P: LBA 1234 now at block 92, page 7"]
    U --> I["Mark block 17 page 40 invalid"]
    I --> F{"Free blocks below threshold?"}
    F -- "No" --> D["Done"]
    F -- "Yes" --> V["GC: pick victim block with fewest valid pages"]
    V --> C["Copy its valid pages to an open block, update L2P"]
    C --> E["Erase victim, return it to the free pool"]

Figure 3.2 — Every write moves data to a new page and leaves a stale copy behind; garbage collection is the background loop that turns stale pages back into erased blocks, at the cost of extra copies.

The semis bridge is exact. The L2P table is a page table, and the slice cached in controller SRAM is the TLB; a DRAM-less drive takes a TLB miss to host memory on cold lookups. The mapping unit, the indirection unit (IU), is the page size, and choosing it is the huge-page trade: bigger units shrink the table but waste work on smaller accesses.

The FTL does more than map:

  • Garbage collection reclaims blocks full of stale pages (next section).
  • Wear levelling spreads program/erase (P/E) cycles evenly: new writes go to less-worn blocks, and cold data is occasionally moved off young blocks so they share the load (itself extra writing).
  • TRIM (Deallocate in NVMe) tells the drive an LBA is deleted. Without it, GC keeps copying dead files as if live; with it, freed space acts like extra over-provisioning.
  • Bad-block management, read-disturb and retention refresh retire failing blocks and rewrite data that has been read too often or sat too long (Chapter 2).

docs.title: Error correction: LDPC and read retry
docs.text:
Flash is noisy by design: 8 or 16 voltage states share a few volts, and the distributions widen with wear, heat and time. Every read therefore passes through a hardware low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoder. The first attempt is a fast "hard" decode of a single read. If it fails, the controller escalates. First it re-reads the page at shifted reference voltages from a retry table and hard-decodes again. If that also fails, it takes several reads bracketing each reference voltage to build "soft" confidence information (log-likelihood ratios per bit), which lets LDPC correct far more errors. The last resort is parity across dies, a RAID inside the drive.

Each retry costs another full NAND read, so a ~100 µs read can stretch to several hundred µs. This is a major source of tail latency on aged QLC, and why drives with equal headline IOPS differ at the 99.99th percentile. Think of a SerDes receiver re-tuning its equaliser on a marginal link. Controllers that track per-block voltage drift avoid most retries, a quiet advantage of IDMs with process data.

docs.title: Garbage collection and write amplification: a worked example
docs.text:
Take a block of 256 pages. When the FTL needs a free block, it picks the "victim" with the fewest valid pages (greedy GC) and copies those pages elsewhere before erasing it.

  • If the victim is 25% valid, GC copies 64 pages and frees 192 for new host data. NAND writes per host write = (192 + 64) / 192 = 1.33.
  • If the victim is 75% valid, GC copies 192 pages to free just 64. WAF = 256 / 64 = 4.0.

In general WAF = 1 / (1 − u), where u is the valid fraction of the average victim. For uniformly random overwrites on a full drive, a simple model sets u. Assume blocks are cleaned roughly oldest-first, so a block is collected after the log wraps once through all physical pages. During that pass the host writes Nphys × (1 − u) pages. Each lands on a given LBA with probability 1 / Nuser, so a page survives with probability exp(−Nphys(1 − u) / Nuser). Since Nphys / Nuser = 1 + OP:

u = exp(−(1 − u)(1 + OP)), and WAF = 1 / (1 − u).

Solving numerically: at 7% OP, u ≈ 0.87 and WAF ≈ 7.8. At 14.5%, u ≈ 0.76 and WAF ≈ 4.1. At 37%, u ≈ 0.51 and WAF ≈ 2.1. Greedy GC, which is optimal for uniform random writes and has an exact closed-form analysis5, lands within ~5% of this curve in our simulation.

Figure 3.3 — Illustrative model: the first 30 points of over-provisioning cut write amplification by roughly 4×, and returns diminish quickly after that; mixing hot and cold data makes it worse. Data: data/ch03_waf_op.csv

Three lessons follow. OP buys endurance: going from 14.5% to 37% OP halves model WAF, so the same NAND absorbs about twice the host writes, most of the Micron SKUs' 2.5× gap in rated host bytes. Random small writes are the worst case: real workloads are friendlier, and measured WAF usually sits below these models6. Placement beats spare flash: when hot and cold data share blocks, cold pages get copied again and again (the skewed series). A writer that keeps lifetimes apart, or fills whole blocks that later die whole, gets WAF near 1 with little OP. That is the idea behind log-structured arrays, ZNS and FDP.

docs.title: DRAM, indirection units and the small-write penalty
docs.text:
One ~4-byte entry per 4 KB is 1/1,000 of capacity: about 1 GB of DRAM per TB of flash. Harmless at 1 TB; not at 245 TB.

Drive capacity Indirection unit Map entries Map DRAM at ~4 B/entry (floor) 7.68 TB 4 KB 1.9 billion ~7.5 GB 30.72 TB 4 KB 7.5 billion ~30 GB 122.88 TB 16 KB 7.5 billion ~30 GB 245.76 TB 4 KB (hypothetical) 60 billion ~240 GB 245.76 TB 16 KB 15 billion ~60 GB 245.76 TB 64 KB 3.75 billion ~15 GB

Table 3.1 — Worked arithmetic: mapping a quarter-petabyte drive at 4 KB would need ~240 GB of DRAM, more than many servers carry, so large QLC drives coarsen the indirection unit instead.

Two more constraints bite. A 32-bit entry addresses only 2³² × 4 KB ≈ 17.6 TB, so bigger drives need wider entries or a larger IU. Even at 16 KB, a 245.76 TB drive has 15 billion units, more than 2³² (4.3 billion), so its entries need at least 34 bits; the table's ~4 bytes per entry is a floor, not a design value. And at roughly $14.5 per GB for server DRAM in 20267, a 240 GB map would add about $3,500 per drive. Hence larger IUs. Solidigm's 61 TB D5-P5336 uses a 16 KB IU, after its predecessor used 64 KB8. Micron's 245.76 TB 6600 ION uses 16 KB at its top capacity and 4 KB on its 30.72 TB model9. Reviewers report 64 GB of on-drive DRAM, consistent with the table, and credit it with roughly three times the random-write rate of rival 245 TB-class drives that use a 64 KB IU10. (One outlet's headline says 16 GB; its body text and a second review say 64 GB.)

The price is a small-write penalty. A 4 KB write to a 16 KB-IU drive forces a read-modify-write of the whole unit: 4× NAND writes before GC adds its own multiple, and 16× at 64 KB. Large QLC drives therefore suit large aligned writes (object stores, data lakes, AI datasets, checkpoints) or hosts that coalesce writes first.

docs.title: Why the FTL is where commodity SSDs lose efficiency
docs.text:
Most modern all-flash arrays (Purity, WAFL-style designs, VAST's element store) are log-structured: they buffer writes in NVRAM, reduce them, write large sequential segments and run their own garbage collection. The SSD underneath cannot see any of this. Researchers call the result "log-on-log"11:

  • Duplicate GC. The array's cleaning and the drive's GC each rewrite live data, so their amplifications multiply: illustratively 1.5 × 2.0 = 3.0 NAND bytes per host byte.
  • Hidden OP, paid twice. Each drive reserves 7–37% spare; the array keeps its own free space too, and neither can lend to the other.
  • Duplicate DRAM. ~1 GB per TB per drive, about 10 TB across a 10 PB array, to translate addresses the array already translated.
  • Unpredictable latency. Each drive garbage-collects, retries and refreshes on its own schedule, so the array must over-design for tail latency.
  • Lost information. The array knows which data is cold and which segment it will clean next; behind a block interface, the drive cannot use that.

There are three ways out. Zoned Namespaces (ZNS), ratified in June 2020, expose zones the host must write sequentially and reset, removing drive GC12. Flexible Data Placement (FDP), ratified in late 2022 with Meta, Google and Samsung behind it, is gentler: the host tags writes so data of similar lifetime shares erase blocks, and the drive keeps its FTL13. Samsung reported that FDP cut device WAF in Meta's CacheLib from ~1.3 to ~1.0 in the default setup, which keeps half the drive as host-side spare, and from ~3.5 to ~1 when the cache uses the whole drive14. The peer-reviewed version of that work (EuroSys 2025) reports device WAF close to 1 with no host over-provisioning on Meta and Twitter traces15. A FAST '26 study found WAF stays near 1 when lifetimes are classified correctly but degrades when they are not16. Both are covered in Chapter 12. The third way removes the drive FTL: Everpure's DirectFlash modules have no logical-address layer, and one FTL in Purity spans every module17 (Chapter 26).

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Client SSD Enterprise SSD Hyperscale / FDP SSD Everpure DirectFlash Module DRAM for mapping Often none: SRAM cache plus host memory buffer ~1 GB/TB at 4 KB IU; ~0.25 GB/TB at 16 KB on large QLC Same as enterprise None on module; mapping lives in array controller DRAM (size not published) Over-provisioning ~7–10% ~14.5% (read-intensive) to ~37% (mixed-use) Vendor-set; host may add its own spare Pooled once across the array, set by Purity Power-loss protection Usually none Capacitors standard Expected by hyperscale specs18 [VERIFY: OCP spec PLP wording] Writes made durable in array NVRAM; module-level details not public Who owns GC and placement Drive firmware Drive firmware Shared: host hints placement, drive executes Array software Firmware owner Drive maker Drive maker Drive maker, to the hyperscaler's OCP-style spec Everpure Best fit PCs, boot drives Databases, VMs, arrays built on standard drives Caches, log-structured services at fleet scale Everpure arrays and licensed hyperscaler designs

Table 3.2 — Moving left to right, flash-management intelligence migrates from the drive into the host; the cost moves from per-drive DRAM and spare flash into host software and qualification work.

Steelman the standard drive: it is multi-sourced and plug-compatible, its FTL is co-designed with the NAND by firms with fab data, and behind a write-coalescing buffer (VAST's SCM, Chapter 16) a 16 KB-IU QLC drive avoids most of the small-write penalty. FDP recovers much of the WAF benefit with standard parts. DirectFlash instead removes map DRAM, duplicate spare and duplicate GC from the bill of materials and puts latency under one scheduler, at the cost of qualifying every NAND generation itself. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: how much of DirectFlash's advantage survives once FDP is widely deployed, and whether the advantage shifts from "lower write amplification" to "less DRAM and spare flash per TB", which matters more as drives grow and DRAM prices stay high.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title How the drive FTL got challenged
    2009 : TRIM support reaches mainstream operating systems
    2011 : NVMe 1.0 defines a flash-native host interface
    2016 : Linux LightNVM open-channel SSDs merged
    2017 : Pure Storage launches DirectFlash
    2020 : NVMe ZNS ratified
    2022 : NVMe FDP ratified
    2023 : 61 TB QLC drive with 16 KB indirection unit
    2026 : 245 TB QLC drive ships with 16 KB indirection unit

Figure 3.4 — For fifteen years the industry has been pulling flash management out of the drive, through hints, open-channel designs, zones, placement handles and, at Everpure, by removing the drive FTL altogether.

The FTL was the price of making SSDs imitate hard disks so existing software worked unchanged. Since then control has moved steadily to the host. Open-channel SSDs (Linux LightNVM, merged in 2016 and described at FAST 2017) exposed raw geometry19, then fragmented and gave way to standard ZNS and FDP1213. Pure Storage launched DirectFlash in 201720, applying the idea inside one vendor's stack.

Two forces now push harder. Capacity is outrunning DRAM economics: 245.76 TB drives shipped in 202621, with IUs rising in step. And power-bound AI datacentres make spare flash and DRAM that do no user work more visible. Expect larger IUs, wider hyperscale FDP adoption, and continued debate over smart versus thin drives.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "When we compete against arrays built on 122–245 TB QLC SSDs, what happens to their small-write performance and endurance?" Strong answer: names the 16 KB indirection unit and read-modify-write penalty, notes mitigation by SCM/NVRAM write buffers, and separates where that works (large sequential AI and object data) from where it doesn't (small random database writes).
  2. "If FDP becomes standard on hyperscale drives, which parts of the DirectFlash advantage remain?" Strong answer: concedes FDP narrows the WAF gap; argues per-drive DRAM, per-drive spare flash, GC timing and module density remain, with a view on which customers pay for.
  3. "How do we explain to a customer why our usable capacity per raw TB differs from an SSD-based array's?" Strong answer: separates drive OP, array reserve, RAID overhead and data reduction, and avoids double-counting (Chapter 4).

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What WAF does Purity see end to end on a typical customer workload, and how does that compare with the same data on standard SSDs?" Strong answer: measured ranges by workload, how lifetime-aware placement keeps segments dying whole, and candour about where WAF rises.
  2. "Without an on-module DRAM map, where does the mapping state live, and how does it scale per PB?" Strong answer: metadata tiering across controller DRAM, NVRAM and flash, and how map growth stays bounded as modules reach 300 TB.
  3. "How do you handle read retry and LDPC fallback latency on aged QLC?" Strong answer: per-block threshold tracking, scheduling retries away from foreground I/O, and reconstructing from array parity rather than waiting.

Don't say this:

  • "SSDs don't need garbage collection because there's no seek." GC exists because of erase-before-write, not mechanics.
  • "Over-provisioning is wasted capacity." It buys endurance and steady latency; the question is who holds it and whether it is pooled.
  • "TRIM deletes data." It marks LBAs as free so GC can skip them; physical erasure happens later.
  • "Bigger SSDs are just more NAND." Beyond ~30 TB, the map forces coarser indirection units and changes which workloads fit.
