docs.title: 4. Performance and economics metrics
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~12 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Media physics for a semis person · Inside an SSD

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• IOPS, throughput and latency are one equation, not three specs. Throughput = IOPS × I/O size, and Little's law ties IOPS to latency through the requests in flight. A datasheet number means nothing without its I/O size, mix and queue depth.
  • Latency is flat until something saturates, then it hockey-sticks. Past roughly 70% utilization of the bottleneck, queueing dominates and p99/p99.9 blow up long before the average looks bad.
  • The tail, not the mean, sets application speed. Databases chain I/Os and GPU clusters synchronise thousands of workers, so the slowest request governs.
  • Capacity has three prices: raw, usable and effective. Protection and reserves take 20–30% off raw; data reduction multiplies usable by an assumed ratio, so 2:1 versus 4:1 doubles effective $/TB (Chapter 5).
  • TCO at 2026 NAND prices favours disk for cold capacity; flash wins on performance, density and power. In the worked example, all-flash costs ~3.2× hybrid disk over five years for 10 PB of cold data (~2.7× once disk's own 2026 price rise is included), reaching parity only with cheap NAND and ~4:1 reduction. Power and space are under 10% of TCO.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Every competitive claim in storage is a metric choice. Everpure's long-running pitch, that flash can replace disk, rests on effective capacity (data reduction), density (TB per rack unit) and efficiency (TB per watt). AI-native rivals pitch GB/s per rack, and disk vendors pitch $/TB. Each frame is true on its own terms and misleading on someone else's. Translating between them tells you which deals are winnable and which "TCO advantage" slides would not survive a customer's spreadsheet.

The 2026 NAND shortage makes this urgent. TrendForce expects enterprise SSD contract prices to rise another 23–28% quarter on quarter in 4Q261. One vendor's index put a 30 TB QLC SSD at 22.6× the $/TB of a 30 TB nearline disk in Q1 2026, up from 4.9× in Q2 20252, versus about 10× in 20203. When the media gap widens that much, flash's other arguments (performance per TB, power, density and reduction) must carry more of the case, and knowing what each is worth is where credibility lies.

docs.title: IOPS, throughput and latency: one equation
docs.text:
Three numbers describe performance:

  • IOPS: I/O operations completed per second, usually quoted for small (4 KiB) random reads.
  • Throughput (bandwidth): bytes per second, usually quoted for large (128 KiB–1 MiB) sequential transfers.
  • Latency: time from issuing one request to its completion, in microseconds (µs) for flash and milliseconds for disk.

They are linked by two identities. Throughput = IOPS × I/O size. Little's law, proved by John Little in 19614, says the average number of requests in flight (L) equals the arrival rate (λ) times the average time each spends in the system (W). For storage that becomes outstanding I/Os = IOPS × latency.

flowchart LR
    A["Arrivals λ: requests per second"] --> Q["In flight L: queued plus in service"]
    Q --> C["Completions after W seconds each"]
    Q -.-> F["L = λ × W"]
    F --> S1["NVMe SSD: 1M IOPS × 100 µs = 100 I/Os outstanding"]
    F --> S2["DDR5-6400 channel: 51.2 GB/s × 100 ns = 5.1 KB = 80 cache lines in flight"]
    F --> S3["GPU cluster read: 1 TB/s × 2 ms = 2 GB, about 2,000 × 1 MB requests in flight"]

Figure 4.1 — Little's law: to get bandwidth out of any latency-bound device, from a DRAM channel to a storage cluster, you must keep enough requests in flight to cover the latency.

Two consequences follow. First, a device's peak IOPS is reachable only with enough concurrency. A database thread that waits for each read before issuing the next runs at queue depth 1. At 100 µs per read it gets 1 ÷ 100 µs = 10,000 IOPS from an SSD rated at a million. Second, IOPS and throughput are different limits. Micron's PCIe 6.0 9650 is rated at 5.5 million random-read IOPS and 28 GB/s sequential read5. At 4 KiB, 5.5M IOPS is only 22.5 GB/s, so small-block work hits the controller's command-processing limit before it hits the link. A 30 TB HAMR disk is rated at about 170 random-read IOPS6, or 0.7 MB/s at 4 KiB, versus several hundred MB/s sequential, because each random I/O pays a seek and rotation. Since per-drive random IOPS has barely moved in two decades while capacity grew tenfold, a modern disk delivers under 6 IOPS per TB. That is the metric that killed disk for primary storage: performance-bound workloads must buy spindles they do not need for capacity.

Semiconductor bridge: bandwidth versus latency in memory. The same law governs DRAM. A DDR5-6400 channel moves 6.4 GT/s × 8 bytes = 51.2 GB/s. With loaded latency around 100 ns, the controller must keep about 5.1 KB, or 80 64-byte lines, outstanding to fill it. That is why memory controllers have deep request queues and bank-level parallelism, and why one CPU core, limited to a few tens of outstanding misses, cannot saturate a socket's memory bandwidth. HBM raised bandwidth per stack by an order of magnitude while DRAM core latency stayed roughly flat, so GPUs hide latency with tens of thousands of threads in flight. Storage repeats the pattern: each PCIe generation doubles the link, but NAND read time has not improved and is worse for QLC (Chapter 2). Bandwidth scales with parallelism; latency is set by physics.

docs.title: Why latency hockey-sticks under load
docs.text:
Any shared resource, such as a NAND die, a controller CPU, a network port or a disk arm, behaves like a queue. The textbook single-server model (M/M/1) gives mean response time = service time ÷ (1 − utilization). At 50% busy, a 100 µs operation takes 200 µs on average. At 90% it takes 1 ms, and at 95%, 2 ms. Percentiles are worse. In the same model, p99 is about 4.6× the mean and p99.9 about 6.9× at any load, so a 1 ms mean at 90% busy carries a 4.6 ms p99.

Figure 4.2 — Illustrative model: below saturation, more queue depth buys more IOPS; past it, more queue depth buys only more latency, and the tail rises first. Data: data/ch04_latency_load.csv

Panel B shows the knee from the device side. An SSD's parallelism comes from its NAND dies (Chapter 3). With 32 dies and 80 µs reads, perfect parallelism would deliver 400K IOPS at queue depth 32. Requests land on random dies and collide, so at QD32 only about 20 dies are busy: 255K IOPS at 125 µs. Pushing to QD256 squeezes out the last 145K IOPS, but latency rises fivefold. Vendors quote the right-hand end of the curve; latency-sensitive customers live on the left. Garbage collection, which stalls reads behind erases and programs, adds a further tail, so steady-state numbers on a full drive are what matter.

The operating rule: size systems so the bottleneck runs at 50–70% busy at peak.

docs.title: Tail latency: why p99 and p99.9 run the business
docs.text:
Dean and Barroso's "The Tail at Scale" showed that when a request fans out to many servers, rare slowness becomes common7. If each of 100 parallel sub-requests has a 1% chance of being slow, the probability that at least one is slow is 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 63%.

flowchart LR
    R["One user request or training step"] --> F1["I/O 1"]
    R --> F2["I/O 2"]
    R --> F3["..."]
    R --> F4["I/O N"]
    F1 --> W["Wait for the slowest"]
    F2 --> W
    F3 --> W
    F4 --> W
    W --> O["P at least one slow = 1 − 0.99^N: N=10 gives 10%, N=100 gives 63%, N=512 gives 99%"]

Figure 4.3 — When work waits for the slowest of N parallel I/Os, the device's p99 becomes the system's median.

  • Databases. An OLTP commit waits on a log write, and a query plan may chain ten dependent reads. At ten reads, 1 − 0.99¹⁰ ≈ 10% of queries pay at least one p99 penalty. Locks are held longer, others queue behind them, and the hockey stick takes over. Database arrays are therefore judged on p99 at load (Chapter 14).
  • GPU clusters. Synchronous training waits for every rank. If a step needs data for 512 GPUs and each fetch has a 1% chance of a slow read, 99% of steps contain at least one straggler unless prefetch buffers absorb it. Checkpoints are worse: with 1,024 ranks writing shards, training resumes when the last shard lands, so 1 − 0.999¹⁰²⁴ ≈ 64% of checkpoints wait on a p99.9 write. Every stalled second idles the whole cluster, the economic core of Chapter 11 and Chapter 31.

So the question is never "what is your latency?" but "what is your p99.9 at 70% of rated load, on a full system, during a rebuild?"

docs.title: Raw, usable and effective capacity
docs.text:
Capacity is quoted in three layers, and most commercial disputes start in the gaps.

Figure 4.4 — Illustrative: protection and reserves take about 20% off raw; the data-reduction assumption then decides whether "effective" is 1.5× or 3× the raw figure. Data: data/ch04_capacity_waterfall.csv

  • Raw is the sum of drive capacities in decimal terabytes (10¹² bytes). Operating systems report binary tebibytes (2⁴⁰ bytes), so the same capacity reads 9% smaller. The waterfall shows that as a step, but it is a change of units: no bytes are lost.
  • Usable is what remains after parity, rebuild spares, metadata and system reserves. Wide erasure codes (Chapter 6) push usable toward 85–90% of raw; small systems with narrow stripes may get 60–70%. Many systems also run best below ~80% full.
  • Effective is usable × an assumed data-reduction ratio (DRR) from deduplication and compression, sometimes with thin provisioning and snapshots counted on top. Pure Storage has long marketed a fleet-average 5:1 reduction ratio8, and 10:1 "total efficiency" once thin provisioning is counted9, a far softer number.

The DRR is a property of the customer's data, not the array. Databases and VM images typically reduce well; compressed media, encrypted data and most AI training corpora reduce close to 1:1. As reported at launch, Pure Storage stated FlashArray//E's maximum effective capacity at 2:1 but the //C90's at 5:110. VAST cites a median of about 2:1 for its similarity-based reduction (company-stated)11. Chapter 5 covers how to sanity-check a DRR claim.

Worked example ($/TB raw versus effective). A flash system at $450 per raw TB with 80% usable costs $563 per usable TB. At 4:1 it is $141 per effective TB and looks competitive with disk. If the data actually reduces 1.5:1, the same system costs $375 per effective TB, 2.7× the quote. Only the assumption moved.

docs.title: Density and efficiency: TB/W and TB/RU
docs.text:
Two physical metrics matter more each year because power, not floor space, is now the scarce input. Gartner forecasts data-centre electricity use to grow 26% in 202612.

  • TB/W (or its inverse, W/TB): capacity per watt. At the drive level, flash has overtaken disk. Micron rates its 245 TB QLC SSD at about 8.2 TB/W, versus about 4.4 TB/W for a 44 TB HDD (vendor comparison)13. At system level, Pure Storage's FlashBlade//E launched in 2023 at roughly 1 W/TB14. Watch the basis: raw or effective, active or idle, drive or whole system.
  • TB/RU (capacity per rack unit) and its AI cousin GB/s per RU: density per slot of rack space, driven mostly by drive size.

Both flatter large drives and high DRRs and ignore performance: a system can be superb on TB/W and useless for a workload needing 10 GB/s per PB.

docs.title: How vendors pick the metric that flatters them
docs.text:
Headline metric Who leans on it What it flatters What it hides Ask instead Peak IOPS (4 KiB random read, deep queue) SSD and block-array datasheets, e.g., 5.5M IOPS on one SSD5 Parallelism Latency at that load, writes, mixed I/O, a full drive in steady state IOPS at a stated p99 latency, 70/30 read/write, on a full system GB/s per rack unit Parallel file systems for AI, e.g., Dell's claim of up to 150 GB/s per RU15 Front-end bandwidth density Capacity per RU, switches outside the count, write rate GB/s per rack and per kW, including network, at stated capacity Effective PB per rack AI and enterprise vendors, e.g., WEKApod 3 at 1.1 EB effective per rack (company-stated)16 The DRR assumption Usable capacity; whether the data reduces at all Usable PB per rack, plus DRR measured on the customer's data "Up to 75% less power than disk" Flash vendors, including Pure Storage's DirectFlash pitch17 Choice of disk baseline and of reduction Age of the HDD baseline; idle versus active power W per usable TB at the customer's duty cycle $/TB raw Disk vendors and cloud archive tiers Media cost IOPS per TB, rebuild times, power per IOPS $/TB at the required IOPS and GB/s

Table 4.1 — Every headline metric is true at one corner of the operating envelope; the counter-question moves it to the customer's corner.

docs.title: Worked example: five-year TCO, all-flash QLC versus hybrid disk
docs.text:
Requirement: 10 PB of effective capacity for cold-to-warm unstructured data (a data lake or AI dataset archive), held flat for five years in a US colocation facility. Illustrative: the platform costs, power densities and reduction ratios are this atlas's assumptions; market inputs are sourced.

Line item All-flash QLC Hybrid disk (30 TB HDD + 3% flash tier) Basis / assumption Data-reduction ratio 2:1 1.3:1 (compression only) Flash at the 2:1 vendors themselves use for unstructured data1011; disk systems rarely dedupe inline because it fragments reads Usable ÷ raw 80% 75% (8+2 EC, spares) Assumption Raw capacity 6,250 TB 10,256 TB HDD (342 drives) + 288 TB flash 10,000 ÷ DRR ÷ usable ratio Media price $302/TB $22/TB HDD; $302/TB flash tier 122.88 TB QLC SSD at $37,12818; 30 TB nearline HDD ≈ $668 (Q1 2026)19 Platform (controllers, enclosures, software, network) $150 per raw TB $40 per raw HDD TB; $150 per raw TB on the flash tier Assumption Acquisition $2.83M $0.77M Media + platform System power (IT load) 0.40 W/TB → 2.5 kW 0.55 W/TB → 5.8 kW Assumption, cross-checked against ~1 W/TB for 2023-era flash14 and 9.5 W per 30 TB HDD before enclosure overhead6 Energy, 5 years $23K $54K kW × PUE 1.5420 × 43,800 h × $0.1385/kWh21 Space and power capacity, 5 years $29K $68K kW × $196.25 per kW-month colocation22 × 60 Rack units (approx.) ~13 RU ~17 RU 0.5 PB/RU flash; 0.64 PB/RU for 4U 106-bay JBODs plus servers Support, years 2–5 $1.13M $0.31M 10% of acquisition per year Controller/server refresh (year ~4) $0.28M $0.14M 30% of platform cost; bundled into the fee under subscription models (Chapter 23) Five-year TCO $4.29M ($429 per effective TB) $1.33M ($133 per effective TB) Flash ≈ 3.2× Random-read capability Millions of IOPS (controller-bound) ~58K IOPS (342 × 170) Disk fails any random-I/O requirement

Table 4.2 — Illustrative: at 2026 NAND prices, disk wins cold-capacity TCO by about 3×; power and space are under 10% of either total.

Note what the inputs imply: $302 against $22 per TB is a 13.7× media premium, well below the 22.6× index headline, because a 122 TB drive's street price per TB sits below the index's 30 TB QLC drive (about $504/TB in Q1 20262). The base case is therefore kind to flash. Disk prices moved as well: the same index's 30 TB HDD rose to $1,216 (about $40/TB) by Q3 202623. At that disk price, with everything else unchanged, flash costs ~2.7× disk rather than 3.2×. Three sensitivities change the answer. At mid-2025 media prices (about $80/TB for 30 TB QLC and $16.50/TB for HDD19), flash falls to ~2.0× disk. At 2026 prices but with 4:1 reduction on the flash side, it is ~1.6×. With both cheap NAND and 4:1, the two options reach parity (~$1.17M versus $1.16M). Power alone cannot close the gap: even valuing each freed kilowatt at $15,000 a year of GPU output (an assumption), 3.3 kW saved is worth ~$250K over five years. Flash for capacity tiers needs some mix of (a) a performance requirement disk cannot meet without overbuying spindles, (b) reducible data, (c) a power- or space-capped site, and (d) NAND costs below street price, which is the hyperscaler DirectFlash thesis (Chapter 29).

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Vendor Metrics it leads with (public) Why that suits its architecture Steelman / caveat Everpure Effective capacity (fleet-average DRR), TB/W and TB/RU from large DirectFlash modules; contractual watts/TiB Owns the flash translation layer, so it can ship larger modules (Chapter 26); always-on inline reduction Turns metrics into guarantees. The effective numbers still depend on DRR: FlashArray effective capacities assume a 5:1 average, so FlashArray//XL R5's ~1.9 PB raw becomes 7.4 PB effective, ~3.8× raw after RAID, metadata and TiB conversion2425 VAST Data $/TB effective at scale; QLC plus similarity reduction and wide erasure codes Global reduction across a shared pool (Chapter 16) Its own cited median is ~2:111, which is honest; savings need scale WEKA Per-rack IOPS, TB/s and effective capacity Software on dense servers, built for small-file and metadata-heavy AI work Per-rack effective figures carry a DRR assumption16 Dell, DDN GB/s per RU or per appliance (DDN AI400X3M: up to 190 GB/s read26) Parallel file systems for GPU feeding Bandwidth density says nothing about $/TB or tail latency under mixed load Seagate, Western Digital $/TB and TB per drive Disk's media cost advantage, now ~15–23× at the drive2 IOPS per TB keeps falling with each capacity step

Table 4.3 — Each vendor's headline metric is the one its architecture is built to win.

Everpure's distinctive move is contractual. Evergreen//One, its storage-as-a-service offer, added a guaranteed maximum watts per TiB in January 2023, backed by service credits and remediation27. The published figures assume 2:1 reduction on most tiers and none on the capacity tier28. Its subscription is billed on effective used capacity: the customer pays for its reserve commitment whether used or not, plus on-demand usage above it. Separately, Everpure commits to keep a 25% capacity buffer (up to 1 PiB) deployed above the higher of the two29. Pricing per effective TiB shifts DRR risk to the vendor: if data reduces less, Everpure ships more hardware for the same fee, so fleet reduction telemetry becomes a margin input. The steelman for per-usable-TB pricing is transparency. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: how such guarantees hold margin when NAND costs swing 50% in a quarter, and whether AI buyers, whose data reduces poorly, value them at all.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Performance and economics metrics milestones
    1961 : Little proves L equals lambda times W
    2013 : Dean and Barroso publish The Tail at Scale
    2020 : Enterprise SSD about 10x nearline HDD per TB
    2023 : FlashBlade E launches near 1 W per TB : Pure offers a watts per TiB guarantee
    2025 : 122 TB class QLC SSDs ship
    2026 : NAND contract prices surge : QLC 15 to 23x HDD per TB : 245 TB QLC SSD ships

Figure 4.5 — The metrics are old; what changed is that power became the binding constraint just as NAND became expensive again.

Storage marketing moved from IOPS (the disk era) to latency and effective capacity (2010s all-flash), then to GB/s per rack and TB/W (AI). Two forces now pull in opposite directions. Micron's 245 TB QLC SSD began shipping in May 202613, and DirectFlash modules are reported at up to 300 TB30 [VERIFY: official 300 TB DFM availability]. That improves TB/W and TB/RU every year, while NAND contract prices have risen in every quarter of 2026 on AI server demand1, reopening a $/TB gap that flash vendors had expected to keep closing. Expect TCO arguments to lean harder on power, density and guarantees, and buyers to ask for usable rather than effective numbers. Chapter 37 (benchmarks) and Chapter 38 (power) build on this chapter.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What DRR do we assume when we quote effective capacity for an AI data lake, and what does Pure1 telemetry say we actually get?" Strong: measured medians by workload class, candour that AI corpora reduce poorly, and how Evergreen//One absorbs the shortfall.
  2. "Where is the crossover in $/effective TB against a hybrid disk system at today's NAND prices?" Strong: named DRR, density and power assumptions, and candour that cold capacity is hard to win in 2026 without a performance or power constraint.
  3. "Which metric do we lose on in AI bake-offs: GB/s per rack, per kW, or $/TB?" Strong: names competitor, metric and the response.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What is p99.9 read latency at 70% of rated IOPS, on a 90%-full system, during a drive rebuild?" Strong: a number with conditions and the dominant cause (GC, rebuild or controller CPU).
  2. "What queue depth does an application need to reach the rated IOPS?" Strong: Little's-law arithmetic, plus performance at QD1–4, where databases live.
  3. "Is the watts/TiB guarantee measured at the wall or estimated, and on what reduction ratio?" Strong: measurement method, DRR basis, and the incompressible-data case.

Don't say this:

  • "Our array does 2 million IOPS, so it's faster." Ask: at what latency, block size, mix and fill level?
  • "Average latency is 150 µs, so we're fine for databases." Databases and GPU clusters live on p99 and p99.9.
  • "Flash is now cheaper than disk." Not on $/TB in 2026; only under stated reduction, power and performance assumptions.
  • "Effective capacity is what the customer gets." It is what they get if their data reduces as assumed.
  • "Power is the biggest TCO line." Usually under 10%; it dominates only where power is capped.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• Queueing: Harchol-Balter, Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems (Cambridge, 2013), on M/M/c, M/G/1 and why variance in service time drives tails.
  • Dean & Barroso, "The Tail at Scale," on hedged and tied requests, the main software fixes for fan-out tails7.
  • SNIA Solid State Storage Performance Test Specification (PTS), on steady-state preconditioning before measuring SSDs.
  • For DRAM: memory-controller scheduling (FR-FCFS) and miss-status holding registers as the CPU-side analogue of queue depth.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• IOPS / throughput / latency — operations per second, bytes per second, time per operation.
  • Queue depth — I/Os outstanding at once; Little's law links it to IOPS × latency.
  • Tail latency (p99, p99.9) — the latency that 1% or 0.1% of requests exceed.
  • Raw / usable / effective capacity — drive total; after protection and reserves; after assumed data reduction.
  • TB/W, TB/RU — capacity per watt and per rack unit.
  • TCO — total cost of ownership over a stated period, including power, space, support and refresh.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 5. Data reduction
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Inside an SSD · Performance and economics metrics

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Data reduction lets one physical terabyte hold several logical ones. Four techniques stack: pattern removal (zeros and fills), deduplication (identical chunks stored once), similarity reduction (near-identical chunks stored as differences) and compression. The data-reduction ratio (DRR) is logical data written ÷ physical capacity consumed.
  • The ratio belongs to the data, not the array. VDI reaches 12–20:1, SQL Server 2–3:1, and JPEGs, encrypted volumes and most AI data sit near 1:1. The least reducible slice dominates a blend.
  • "Total efficiency" is not data reduction. Counting thin provisioning and snapshots multiplies a headline ratio with no change in the data. Pure Storage's own datasheet separates ~5:1 average reduction from ~10:1 "total efficiency" that includes thin provisioning1.
  • Guarantees transfer risk; the fine print sets the price. Dell (6:1, PowerStore Gen 3), NetApp (4:1 SAN), HPE (4:1) and Everpure (workload-based Right-Size Guarantee) mostly cover "reducible data" only and pay out in capacity.
  • AI is the hard case and the new battleground. Images, tokens and BF16 checkpoints barely shrink with generic tools. Similarity reduction (VAST, WEKA, Everpure's Purity DeepReduce) and format-aware compression are the attempted fixes.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
All-flash arrays beat disk in primary storage partly through data reduction: dividing flash's higher raw $/TB by 4–5:1 closed much of the gap per effective terabyte. Everpure still quotes FlashArray in effective capacity, and Evergreen//One is billed on effective used capacity, measured before data reduction2. DRR is therefore a margin line. When a fleet reduces less than sizing assumed, someone pays for extra DirectFlash Modules, and under a guarantee or subscription that is the vendor.

AI shifts the mix. VMs and databases reduce well; images, tokens and checkpoints do not. In AI deals raw $/TB, density and power matter more, which is where DirectFlash competes (Chapter 26), and near-duplicate reduction becomes a differentiator. VAST built its pitch on it; Everpure answered with DeepReduce on FlashBlade in 2026. A strategy team must separate physics from accounting.

docs.title: Four techniques, one ratio
docs.text:
DRR = logical bytes written by hosts ÷ physical bytes consumed, measured after reduction and before RAID or erasure-coding overhead, which sits elsewhere in the raw-to-effective waterfall (Chapter 4). Savings are 1 − 1/DRR: 2:1 saves 50%, 5:1 saves 80% and 10:1 saves 90%. Returns diminish: doubling 5:1 to 10:1 saves only ten more points, so compare percentages, not ratios.

The pipeline runs cheapest first:

flowchart LR
    W["Host write"] --> NV["Persist in NVRAM, ack host"]
    NV --> P["Pattern removal: zeros, fills"]
    P --> D["Dedupe: chunk, hash, index lookup"]
    D -->|"duplicate"| M["Store pointer only"]
    D -->|"unique"| S["Similarity lookup"]
    S -->|"near match"| DL["Encode delta vs reference"]
    S -->|"no match"| C["Compress, LZ4 or zstd"]
    DL --> PK["Pack variable-size output into log segments"]
    C --> PK
    PK --> F["Write to flash with RAID or EC"]
    F -.->|"later, in background"| DR["Heavier recompression, background dedupe"]

Figure 5.1 — Reduction is a pipeline from cheap to expensive, and where the host acknowledgement sits relative to it is the inline-versus-post-process choice.

docs.title: Deduplication: chunk, fingerprint, look up
docs.text:
Deduplication cuts data into chunks, hashes each into a fingerprint and checks an index. A hit stores only a pointer; a miss writes the chunk and indexes it.

sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant C as Controller
    participant I as Fingerprint index
    participant F as Flash
    H->>C: WRITE 64 KB
    C->>C: split into chunks, fixed or content-defined
    C->>C: hash each chunk with SHA-256
    C->>I: look up each fingerprint
    alt fingerprint found
        I-->>C: existing physical address
        C->>I: increment reference count
    else new fingerprint
        I-->>C: miss
        C->>F: compress and write chunk
        C->>I: insert fingerprint and address
    end
    C-->>H: ACK

Figure 5.2 — Every write becomes an index lookup, so the speed and size of the fingerprint index, not the hash, set the cost of deduplication.

Fixed versus variable chunking. Fixed chunking cuts every 4 KB or 8 KB. It is cheap and aligns with block addresses, but one inserted byte shifts every later boundary and nothing matches. Content-defined chunking (CDC) cuts wherever a rolling hash hits a chosen pattern, so boundaries follow the content and re-synchronise after an insert. LBFS used Rabin fingerprints for this, and FastCDC's cheaper Gear hash runs 3–12× faster at about the same dedupe ratio3. Backup appliances use CDC because backup streams shift; primary arrays mostly use aligned chunks because databases overwrite pages in place. Purity on FlashArray is a hybrid: variable 4–32 KB chunks scanned at 512-byte granularity, which catches misaligned copies4.

The index is the real problem. 1 PB of unique data in 8 KB chunks is 10¹⁵ ÷ 8,192 ≈ 1.2 × 10¹¹ chunks. At ~40 bytes per entry (32-byte SHA-256 plus address) the index is ~5 TB, far more than a controller pair's DRAM. Data Domain kept a Bloom filter in RAM to answer "definitely new" cheaply, laid chunks out in stream order and prefetched neighbouring fingerprints, removing 99% of index disk accesses5. Many primary arrays keep a partial index and treat dedupe as best-effort. VAST keeps reduction metadata in shared storage-class memory6 (Chapter 16). Larger chunks shrink the index but find fewer duplicates.

Semiconductor bridge. The fingerprint index is the tag RAM of a huge cache where every write is a lookup, and the Bloom filter is its snoop filter. Collisions are not a practical risk: for 1.2 × 10¹¹ chunks and a 256-bit hash, n² ÷ 2²⁵⁷ ≈ 10⁻⁵⁵.

docs.title: Compression: redundancy inside the chunk
docs.text:
LZ-family compressors replace repeated strings with back-references, then entropy-code. Speed trades against ratio: on the Silesia corpus LZ4 reaches ~2.1:1 at ~700 MB/s per core and zstd level 1 ~2.9:1 at ~510 MB/s, both decompressing above 1.5 GB/s7. Arrays run a fast codec inline and recompress cold data in the background (Purity's "deep reduction"4). Offload engines are the analogue of an SSD controller's LDPC block (Chapter 3): fixed-function logic wins on throughput per watt.

Granularity is the subtle trade-off. 32 KB units compress better than 4 KB units, but a 4 KB random read must decompress the whole unit. Compressed output varies in size, so it is packed into log-structured segments and garbage-collected later, adding write amplification. That is why compression bolted onto update-in-place designs struggled and why Purity and VAST were log-structured from the start.

docs.title: Similarity reduction: storing only the difference
docs.text:
One changed byte defeats exact-match deduplication. Similarity reduction uses a locality-sensitive hash so near-identical blocks collide. The first block with a hash becomes the reference; later matches are compressed with it as a dictionary, storing only differences8. VAST dedupes first, then applies compression or similarity, whichever saves more, while data migrates from the SCM buffer to QLC, off the write path9. Hash tables in shared SCM make the scope cluster-wide6.

VAST's figures are company-stated: ~3:1 across its installed base in 202210, 8:1 on one quant firm's market data6, and a ~2:1 median in a later webinar11. Everpure's Purity DeepReduce is also similarity-based, cluster-wide and asynchronous12. It reached FlashBlade in February 2026, and at the end of September Everpure announced an always-on version for October. Everpure cites a ~2:1 median, measured on top of data that was already compressed, so it is incremental to conventional reduction rather than a total ratio1314. The costs: reading a delta block may also require its reference, and referenced blocks cannot be freed, which complicates garbage collection. Semiconductor bridge: this is video coding's P-frame, encoded as a difference from an I-frame.

docs.title: Inline versus post-process
docs.text: Inline reduction runs before data reaches flash: fewer NAND writes, no landing space, but CPU work in the write path, and some systems defer it under load, so the ratio can depend on load. Post-process lands data raw or lightly compressed and reduces later: lowest write latency and room for heavier algorithms, but it needs landing capacity and the ratio lags ingest. Most systems are hybrids that acknowledge from NVRAM, reduce lightly inline and work harder in the background. Purity's deep reduction4, ONTAP's inline-plus-background deduplication and its temperature-sensitive efficiency for cold data15, VAST's reduction at migration9 and WEKA's background similarity reduction16 all follow this pattern. Ask what the ratio is in migration week versus month three.

docs.title: Pattern removal, thin provisioning and the "total efficiency" trick
docs.text:
Pattern removal records all-zero or repeating-pattern blocks as metadata4. The saving is real, but zero-filled thick VM disks and preallocated database files "reduce" without limit, so some VM-estate ratios are partly zeros.

Thin provisioning allocates capacity only on write. That is capacity efficiency, not data reduction, as Pure Storage's own blog argues: 8 TB on a 10 TB thin LUN "saves" 20%, on a 100 TB LUN 92%17. Snapshots and clones are metadata copies (Chapter 6); counting each at full logical size inflates further.

Worked example: hosts write 100 TB that reduces 3:1, so 33.3 TB physical. Provisioned at 400 TB, "total efficiency" is 400 ÷ 33.3 = 12:1. Add seven daily snapshots counted at 100 TB each, with 1% daily change (7 TB written, 2.3 TB physical): (400 + 700) ÷ 35.6 ≈ 31:1. The data has not changed.

xychart-beta
    title "Illustrative: same 100 TB of data, three headline ratios"
    x-axis ["Data reduction only", "Plus thin provisioning", "Plus 7 snapshots as copies"]
    y-axis "Reported ratio x to 1" 0 --> 35
    bar [3, 12, 31]

Figure 5.3 — Illustrative worked example: counting thin provisioning and snapshots turns a 3:1 reduction into a 31:1 headline with no change to the data.

docs.title: What different data reduces to
docs.text:
Data type Typical reduction Why Source SQL Server databases 2.2–2.9:1 Page compression; little duplication unless copies are present Everpure guidance based on Pure1 telemetry18 Oracle databases 3.5–4.1:1 Same, with more compressible block formats Everpure guidance18 Server VMs (VSI) 6–8:1 Common OS and application images deduplicate Everpure guidance18 VDI 12–20+:1 Near-identical desktop images Everpure guidance18 Already-compressed media and backups (JPEG, MP4, zstd Parquet) ~1.0–1.1:1 Already entropy-coded Engineering estimate Host-encrypted data 1.0:1 Ciphertext looks random Engineering fact AI training images (JPEG/PNG shards) ~1.0–1.1:1 Already compressed; duplicates are rare after curation Engineering estimate Tokenized text (uint16 shards) ~1.1–1.5:1 The tokenizer has already removed much of the redundancy Author estimate; raw text gets ~1.9:1 with zstd19 BF16 checkpoints, format-aware lossless ~1.5:1 Skewed exponent bits; mantissas look random ZipNN, 33% savings20 Successive dense checkpoints, dedupe ~1:1 Every weight changes each step; deltas compress better ZipNN20

Table 5.1 — Reduction is a property of the data. AI data is near the bottom of the range unless the reduction is format-aware.

Blended ratios are harmonic, not arithmetic. Physical = Σ(logical share ÷ DRR). An estate of 80% VMs at 6:1 and 20% images at 1:1 needs 0.8/6 + 0.2/1 = 0.333 of its logical size: 3:1, not the 5:1 an average suggests.

For AI, tokenizers are themselves compressors: raw English text compresses ~1.9:1 with zstd and token-ID packing alone ~2.25:119, so stored shards have little redundancy left. In BF16 weights, half the bits are exponent; a format-aware coder such as ZipNN exploits their skew to save ~33%, beating generic codecs20. The big AI wins sit in the application: Check-N-Run's incremental, quantized checkpoints cut capacity 2.5–8× for recommendation models21, but that is lossy, app-side and invisible to array DRR (Chapter 31).

docs.title: Interrogating a vendor DRR claim
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Vendor quotes X to 1"] --> B{"Includes thin provisioning, snapshots or clones?"}
    B -->|"yes"| B1["Ask for reduction-only ratio"]
    B -->|"no"| C{"Measured on your data or close peers?"}
    B1 --> C
    C -->|"no"| C1["Run assessment tool or POC on a data copy"]
    C -->|"yes"| D{"Any host-compressed or encrypted share?"}
    C1 --> D
    D -->|"yes"| D1["Carve it out at 1 to 1 and re-blend"]
    D -->|"no"| E{"Mean or median, and what spread?"}
    D1 --> E
    E --> F{"Guarantee covers your mix with capacity remedy?"}
    F -->|"yes"| G["Size at guaranteed ratio plus headroom"]
    F -->|"no"| H["Size at your own blended ratio"]

Figure 5.4 — A defensible sizing ratio comes from stripping accounting effects, carving out incompressible data, and only then deciding how much to trust the vendor's guarantee.

The six questions to put to any vendor:

  1. What is in the numerator and denominator? Written or provisioned capacity? Zero-filled, snapshot or clone space?
  2. Whose data? Which workload, median not mean, and the 25th-percentile customer.
  3. How much of mine is already compressed or encrypted? Backups, media, Parquet, AI shards, host-encrypted volumes.
  4. Inline or post-process, and under load? The ratio in migration week one and at 80% utilisation.
  5. What does reduction cost? Latency and throughput with it on and off, and index DRAM or SCM per petabyte.
  6. What does the guarantee promise? Scope ("reducible data"), measurement point, remedy (capacity or refund) and duration.

docs.title: Worked example: $/effective TB
docs.text:
A buyer needs 1,000 TB logical: 400 TB databases, 400 TB VMs, 200 TB AI images and checkpoints. Prices are illustrative.

Vendor X Vendor Y Price per usable TB $600 $450 Headline DRR → headline $/effective TB 5:1 → $120 3:1 → $150 Assumed DRR: databases / VMs / AI 2.5 / 6 / 1.2 2.2 / 4.5 / 1.1 Physical needed (Σ logical ÷ DRR) 160 + 66.7 + 166.7 = 393 TB 181.8 + 88.9 + 181.8 = 453 TB Blended DRR 2.54:1 2.21:1 Usable bought (+20% headroom) 472 TB → $283k 543 TB → $244k Realistic $/effective TB $283 $244

Table 5.2 — Illustrative worked example: the headline makes X 20% cheaper, but on this data mix X costs 16% more.

The guarantee changes the answer. If X's 5:1 guarantee covered the 800 TB of databases and VMs, the shortfall (226.7 − 160 = 66.7 TB) would be free capacity worth ~$40k, bringing X to ~$243 per effective TB, level with Y. A guarantee's scope is worth as much as its ratio.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
System Dedupe Compression / similarity When it runs Guarantee (current public terms) Everpure FlashArray (Purity Reduce) Inline, global; variable 4–32 KB, 512 B scan Inline plus post-process deep reduction; pattern removal; copy reduction4 Hybrid Right-Size Guarantee: workload-based effective capacity, 12 months, //X and //XL, signed agreement22 Everpure FlashBlade Not in DeepReduce materials DeepReduce similarity, cluster-wide12 Asynchronous, off the write path None found [VERIFY: any FlashBlade data-reduction guarantee] VAST Data Global Compression or similarity, whichever saves more9 During SCM→QLC migration No formal program found [VERIFY: any VAST data-reduction guarantee] Dell PowerStore Always-on inline Always-on inline Inline 6:1 on Gen 3 (PowerStoreOS 5.0+); 5:1 on Gen 2 and PowerMax; reducible data only2324 NetApp AFF (ONTAP) Inline plus background, cross-volume Inline compression and compaction; TSSE for cold data15 Hybrid 4:1 SAN, 3:1 virtualization on NAS, 1.5:1 NAS2526 HPE Alletra MP Yes Yes Inline StoreMore: ≥4:1 effective vs usable on reducible data, for the support term27 WEKA (NeuralMesh) Cluster-wide, at 4 KB block level Similarity grouping plus delta compression16 Post-process, per file system, licensed option None found

Table 5.3 — Everyone reduces data. The real differences are scope (per volume versus global), similarity versus exact matching, and how carefully each guarantee is written.

Guarantee mechanics matter more than headlines. Dell's PowerStore terms exclude host-compressed and host-encrypted data, require reduction to stay on, and accept claims only once half the physical capacity is written28. In Dell's favour, its 6:1 needs no assessment and no signed agreement23. HPE's remedy (expertise, capacity or other compensation) is at its discretion27. Everpure inverts the fixed-ratio promise: it sizes each customer's workloads and guarantees the resulting effective capacity, under a signed agreement2229. For mixed or AI-heavy estates that fits the data better than a banner ratio. The catch is that the vendor sets the sizing ratio, and a conservative sizer can make any guarantee safe, so the buyer should compare the sized capacity, not the existence of a guarantee.

Steelman VAST. Global similarity finds savings exact-match dedupe misses, and running it at migration keeps it off the latency path. FlashArray's strength is mature inline reduction on well-understood block workloads. Putting DeepReduce on FlashBlade concedes that similarity matters for unstructured and AI data. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: extending similarity reduction to FlashBlade//EXA data nodes, and format-aware codecs for checkpoints and KV cache (Chapter 42, Chapter 45).

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Data reduction milestones
    2001 : LBFS popularises content-defined chunking
    2008 : Data Domain paper shows dedupe at disk speed
    2016 : Pure Storage Right-Size Guarantee : NetApp 4 to 1 AFF guarantee : FastCDC
    2018 : Pure Storage buys StorReduce
    2019 : VAST launches with similarity reduction
    2023 : WEKA 4.2 adds similarity-based data reduction
    2026 : DeepReduce on FlashBlade : DeepReduce always-on

Figure 5.5 — Reduction moved from backup (2000s) to primary flash (2010s) to unstructured and AI data (2020s), and the guarantees followed it.

Deduplication grew up in backup, where Data Domain showed it could run at disk speed5; flash's raw $/TB then made it a primary-storage feature. Guarantees followed in 2016 from Pure Storage30 and NetApp31. Pure bought StorReduce in 2018 for US$20.5 million in cash, net of cash acquired, to bring deduplication to cloud object storage32. VAST launched in 2019 with similarity reduction33. WEKA added post-process similarity reduction in its 4.2 release in 202316 and featured data reduction again in NeuralMesh 6, launched in July 202634. In 2026 Everpure followed on unstructured and AI data with DeepReduce on FlashBlade13. Next is format awareness: codecs that understand tensors, token streams and KV-cache blocks20.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What is the median and 25th-percentile DRR across the fleet for each workload, excluding thin provisioning and snapshots?" Strong: a telemetry distribution by workload, with "total efficiency" called out as a different metric.
  2. "How does the Right-Size Guarantee price AI datasets and checkpoints?" Strong: how near-1:1 data is carved out, historical payout, and how that cost is reserved.
  3. "Where does DeepReduce win against VAST similarity reduction, and where does it lose?" Strong: ratios on the same datasets, scope, and candour about EXA data nodes.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "How big is the dedupe index per petabyte, and where does it live?" Strong: bytes per entry, placement (DRAM, NVRAM, flash) and miss behaviour.
  2. "Under what load does inline reduction defer, and how fast does post-process catch up?" Strong: thresholds, a backlog metric, worst-case landing capacity.
  3. "What is the read amplification of a 4 KB random read on compressed or similarity-encoded data?" Strong: compression unit size, reference-block reads, cache hit rate.

Don't say this:

  • "Our arrays get 10:1." Say whether that is reduction or total efficiency, and for which workload.
  • "Dedupe works on AI data." Exact duplicates are rare after curation; gains come from similarity or format-aware coding.
  • "Higher ratio is always better." 5:1 to 10:1 saves ten more points and may cost latency.
  • "The guarantee covers us." Most exclude host-compressed and encrypted data and pay only in capacity.
  • "Encryption doesn't affect reduction." Host-side encryption drops it to 1:1; only array-side encryption after reduction preserves it.

  • Colgrove et al., SIGMOD 2015, on Purity's log-structured design.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• DRR — logical written ÷ physical consumed.
  • Content-defined chunking — boundaries set by a rolling hash.
  • Similarity reduction — near-duplicates stored as deltas.
  • Total efficiency — DRR plus thin provisioning and snapshots.
  • Right-Size Guarantee — Everpure's workload-based capacity guarantee.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 6. Data protection and resilience
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~13 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Media physics · Inside an SSD · Performance and economics metrics

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Protection is layered; each layer covers one failure. RAID/erasure coding handles broken drives, snapshots handle bad writes, replication handles a lost site, and immutable, separately administered copies handle an attacker with your admin password.
  • Erasure coding is RAID generalised. A k+m code survives any m failures. Wide stripes cut overhead (8+2 costs 25% extra raw, 146+4 under 3%), but a rebuild reads k strips for every strip it recreates.
  • Rebuild time grows with drive size. A 245 TB QLC SSD rebuilt onto a single spare at 1 GB/s takes about 68 hours, longer than a 30 TB hard drive did. Declustering, evacuation and dual parity are the responses.
  • Synchronous replication buys RPO = 0 by adding a round trip to every write. At about 1 ms per 100 km, that confines it to metro distances.
  • Ransomware turned storage into a security product. Snapshots even an administrator cannot delete early, plus contractual recovery SLAs (Everpure, NetApp, Dell), are now part of the sale.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Resilience used to be a checkbox. Ransomware changed the buyer: the CISO now joins storage decisions, and the question became "can I be back in business by Monday, with data I trust?" Recovery is still slow. In Sophos's 2025 US survey only 51% of hit organisations had fully recovered within a week1. Victims with compromised backups recovered within a week far less often (26% versus 46%)2. Regulators now require tested recovery capability: the EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) has applied to financial entities since 17 January 20253.

For Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) this is an opening and a positioning choice. Its May 2026 messaging calls storage "the last line of defense"4, and its snapshot immutability (SafeMode) and Evergreen//One recovery SLA are among its most concrete differentiators. Backup vendors (Veeam, Rubrik, Cohesity, Commvault) claim the same role, so who owns the recovery budget is a live strategic question, and most incumbents (Chapter 46) now market a ransomware guarantee.

docs.title: Four failures, four tools
docs.text:
Failure Example Primary defence What it does not fix Media / component SSD dies, controller fails RAID / erasure coding, dual controllers Deleted or corrupted data (it faithfully protects the corruption) Logical Bad script deletes a volume, app bug corrupts a DB Snapshots, clones, backups Losing the whole array or site Site Fire, flood, power, regional outage Replication (sync, near-sync, async), stretched clusters Corruption, which replicates instantly to the other site Adversarial Ransomware, malicious insider with admin rights Immutable snapshots, isolated or offline copies, separation of duties Data you never captured (the RPO gap)

Table 6.1 — Each layer of protection covers one class of failure and is blind to the others, which is why "we have RAID and replication" is not a ransomware plan.

The bottom rows interact badly: replication copies encrypted blocks at full speed, so a synchronous mirror of an attack is just a second encrypted copy.

docs.title: RAID: redundancy inside the box
docs.text:
The 1988 Berkeley paper by Patterson, Gibson and Katz proposed building reliable storage from arrays of cheap disks5. Four levels survive in practice (Figure 6.1):

  • RAID 1 (mirroring) writes every block twice: 50% usable, and a rebuild just copies the surviving twin.
  • RAID 10 stripes across mirrored pairs: 50% usable, fast rebuilds, survives one failure per pair.
  • RAID 5 adds one rotating XOR parity block: a 7+1 group is 87.5% usable, survives one failure, and a rebuild reads all seven survivors.
  • RAID 6 adds a second, independent parity (the Reed–Solomon "Q" syndrome): 8+2 is 80% usable and survives any two failures.

Figure 6.1 — Classic RAID binds a stripe to a fixed set of drives; declustered erasure coding scatters stripes and spare space across the whole pool, so every drive helps rebuild.

Semiconductor bridge. Parity is ECC one level up. RAID 5 is a parity bit; RAID 6 resembles chipkill ECC, which survives losing a whole DRAM device. Inside each SSD the controller already runs LDPC across pages and often parity across dies (Chapter 3); array RAID protects against losing the whole drive.

docs.title: Erasure coding: RAID generalised, and made wide
docs.text:
An erasure code takes k data strips, computes m parity strips and can rebuild from any k of the k+m. RAID 5 is k+1 and RAID 6 is k+2. Scale-out and object systems (Chapter 18) push k much higher and spread stripes across nodes, enclosures or sites.

Scheme Raw : usable Raw for 10 PB usable Failures survived Strips read to rebuild one lost strip 3-way replication 3.00× 30.0 PB 2 1 RAID 10 / 2-way mirror 2.00× 20.0 PB 1 (guaranteed) 1 RAID 6, 8+2 1.25× 12.5 PB 2 8 EC 16+2 1.125× 11.25 PB 2 16 EC 146+4 (VAST maximum width)6 1.027× 10.27 PB 4 ~37 with locally decodable codes7

Table 6.2 — Wider stripes cut raw capacity by up to 2.2 PB per 10 PB usable, but each lost strip costs more reads to rebuild unless the code is designed around that.

That last column is the hidden cost. With a plain Reed–Solomon 16+2 code, rebuilding one 245 TB drive means reading 16 × 245 TB ≈ 3.9 PB across the cluster. Locally decodable or locally repairable codes compute parity over sub-groups so that a repair reads only part of the stripe. VAST says its codes read about a quarter of the stripe7. The trade-off is the classic one: capacity efficiency against repair bandwidth. Chapter 20 covers the durability arithmetic (nines, mean time to data loss).

docs.title: Why big drives make rebuild time a strategic problem
docs.text:
Rebuild time ≈ capacity to reconstruct ÷ effective rebuild rate. The exposure is the window in which another failure, or an unreadable sector, can cause data loss.

Worked example (single spare). A 30 TB HAMR hard drive8 rebuilt at 200 MB/s takes 30×10¹² ÷ 2×10⁸ = 150,000 s ≈ 42 hours. A 245.76 TB QLC SSD9 rebuilt to one replacement at 1 GB/s (a throttled rate, because the array is still serving production) takes 245,760 s ≈ 68 hours. A 300 TB-class module10 takes ≈ 83 hours. Capacity grew about eight-fold; single-drive write bandwidth did not.

Worked example (declustered). Rebuilding is limited by reads, not writes: every reconstructed byte needs k bytes read from survivors. Suppose 100 surviving drives each devote 4 GB/s of read bandwidth to the rebuild (400 GB/s in all) and stripes are 8+2. The pool then reconstructs 400 ÷ 8 = 50 GB/s into spare space spread across all drives, and the 245 TB drive is restored in 245,760 ÷ 50 ≈ 4,900 s ≈ 1.4 hours. With 16+2 stripes the same read budget takes twice as long; with plain Reed–Solomon at 146+4 it would take about 18 times as long, which is why very wide stripes need locally decodable codes. The price is that read load and a performance dip while it runs.

Figure 6.2 — Illustrative: QLC-era capacities push classic single-spare rebuilds past three days, which is why large-drive systems decluster, evacuate or add parity. Data: data/ch06_rebuild.csv

Two risks grow with the window: further drive failures (drives in a group share age, batch and workload) and unrecoverable read errors. Enterprise HDDs are typically specified at one unrecoverable error per 10¹⁵ bits read. A RAID 5 rebuild that reads seven 30 TB survivors reads 210 TB = 1.7×10¹⁵ bits, so at the specified rate it should hit more than one error. The specification is a worst-case ceiling and field rates are usually lower, but the arithmetic is the 2007 "RAID 5 stops working" argument11, and it is why dual parity became the large-drive minimum. Enterprise SSDs are specified about ten times better, but are growing faster.

Everpure's answer has two parts: dual-parity protection across DirectFlash Modules, with host I/O given priority during a rebuild12, and evacuating a failing module rather than rebuilding it after it dies. Because Purity knows which parts of a degrading module are still good, it copies that data to a new device instead of reconstructing it from parity, which Everpure says cuts time to full protection by 95% or more (company-stated, no baseline published)13 [VERIFY: rebuild-versus-evacuation hours for a 150 TB DFM; copying 150 TB in under an hour would need ~40 GB/s, above a single module's likely read rate]. Managing raw NAND directly (Chapter 26) gives Purity early sight of a degrading module.

docs.title: Snapshots and clones
docs.text:
A snapshot is a point-in-time image of a volume. There are two ways to build one.

Figure 6.3 — Copy-on-write pays one read and two writes on the first overwrite of each block; redirect-on-write pays one write plus a pointer update, which is why flash-native systems take thousands of snapshots without measurable penalty.

  • Copy-on-write (COW) keeps live data in place and copies each old block to a reserve area before it is overwritten. Its cost grows with snapshot count and write rate.
  • Redirect-on-write (ROW) freezes the metadata map and sends new writes to free space. Write-anywhere designs such as Purity (log-structured), NetApp WAFL and ZFS never overwrite in place anyway, so a snapshot is close to free: a copy of a pointer tree plus reference counts. Terminology trap: ZFS and WAFL documentation call themselves "copy-on-write" file systems, although their snapshots work the redirect-on-write way described here. The cost moves to metadata and garbage collection, because space frees only when no snapshot references a block.

A clone is a writable snapshot. Ten copies of a 20 TB database for dev and test consume almost no extra capacity until the copies diverge.

The limit: a snapshot lives on the same array as its data, so it does not survive losing the array, or an attacker who can delete snapshots.

docs.title: Replication: synchronous, asynchronous and in between
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant A as Array A, site 1
    participant B as Array B, site 2
    H->>A: WRITE block
    A->>A: persist in NVRAM
    A->>B: forward write over metro link
    B->>B: persist in NVRAM
    B-->>A: ack
    A-->>H: ACK only after both sites hold it
    Note over H,B: Every write pays one inter-site round trip, about 1 ms per 100 km of fibre

Figure 6.4 — Synchronous replication acknowledges only after both sites persist the write: RPO is zero, and the inter-site round trip is added to every write.

sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant A as Primary array
    participant B as DR array
    H->>A: WRITE block
    A->>A: persist in NVRAM
    A-->>H: ACK immediately
    loop every replication interval
        A->>A: snapshot, compute changed blocks
        A->>B: ship delta only
        B-->>A: delta applied
    end
    Note over A,B: Writes since the last shipped delta are lost if site 1 fails, and that gap is the RPO

Figure 6.5 — Asynchronous replication keeps local write latency and works at any distance, at the price of a non-zero RPO set by the interval and the link.

Worked example (the physics tax). Light in fibre travels at about 200,000 km/s, or 5 µs per km. A 100 km separation adds about 1 ms of round trip, before switch and protocol overhead. NetApp's guidance uses the same rule of thumb14. An all-flash write that takes 150–300 µs locally becomes about 1.15–1.3 ms, roughly four to eight times slower: fine for most databases, fatal for latency-sensitive trading. Protocols that need two round trips per write, such as Fibre Channel without write acceleration, double the adder.

Near-synchronous sits between the two. Writes are acknowledged locally and streamed continuously, not in periodic batches, so the RPO is seconds and host latency is untouched. Everpure's ActiveDR (2020) uses this model15. Journal-based continuous data protection (CDP) products such as HPE's Zerto quote RPOs in seconds and can rewind to any point in the journal16.

docs.title: Stretched and metro clusters
docs.text:
A stretched (metro) cluster presents one volume, writable at both sites, over synchronous mirroring with automatic failover. The hard problem is split-brain: if the link drops, both healthy arrays could keep accepting writes and diverge. A third-party witness (mediator) decides which side keeps serving. Everpure's ActiveCluster uses Pure1 Cloud Mediator, a SaaS witness, so customers need no third site17.

The main implementations are Everpure ActiveCluster (FlashArray), NetApp MetroCluster (supported up to 700 km for the IP version, subject to latency limits) and SnapMirror active sync (formerly SnapMirror Business Continuity)1418, Dell SRDF/Metro on PowerMax19, and HPE Active Peer Persistence on Alletra20.

Figure 6.6 — Illustrative: the further down the protection ladder you go, the more data you lose and the longer you are down. Ransomware is the outlier, with a short-ish RPO but the longest RTO, because forensics, scanning and clean infrastructure dominate the recovery. Data: data/ch06_rpo_rto.csv

RPO (recovery point objective) is how much recent data you can afford to lose. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long you can afford to be down. Each step better costs more bandwidth, licences and standby hardware, so mature shops tier applications into 0/0, minutes/hours and day/days classes.

docs.title: Immutability and ransomware
docs.text:
Modern attackers log in with stolen admin credentials, delete snapshots and backups, then encrypt. Sophos found that 94% of victims in its 2024 survey reported that attackers had tried to compromise their backups2. The storage response is immutability backed by separation of duties:

  • Everpure SafeMode. Deleted snapshots enter an eradication-pending state, and eradication cannot be forced. The default delay is 24 hours, configurable to 30 days on FlashArray2122. Changing or disabling SafeMode requires Everpure Support plus pre-registered customer contacts, not just an admin login21. Since Purity//FA 6.4.10 new volumes join a SafeMode-protected group by default ("Auto-on SafeMode")23. 2026 additions include Fusion "Security Presets" that keep it on424.
  • Equivalents elsewhere. NetApp offers tamperproof snapshots, locked with the SnapLock Compliance clock so that neither an administrator nor NetApp support can delete them early, plus SnapLock WORM volumes and multi-admin verification for destructive commands25. Dell offers PowerMax Secure Snaps and an isolated PowerProtect Cyber Recovery vault. HPE offers Virtual Lock on Alletra MP B10000. S3 Object Lock provides the same for object stores. The real differences are defaults and who can override a lock: SafeMode can be changed with Everpure Support's help, while a NetApp compliance lock cannot be shortened by anyone.

An array can also help detect an attack. Encrypted data does not compress or dedupe, so a sudden collapse in data-reduction ratio, or a spike in overwrite rate, is a strong signal (Chapter 5). Vendors productise this: NetApp's Autonomous Ransomware Protection analyses NAS workloads inside ONTAP and takes snapshots when it suspects an attack25, Dell's Cyber Recovery vault offers CyberSense content analytics, and Everpure flags anomalies through Pure1.

flowchart TD
    A["Detect: DRR collapse, overwrite spike, EDR alert"] --> B["Contain: isolate hosts, revoke and rotate admin credentials"]
    B --> C["Preserve: infected array is now evidence"]
    C --> D{"Clean recovery hardware on hand?"}
    D -->|No| E["Ship or procure clean arrays"]
    D -->|Yes| F["Choose last-known-good immutable snapshot"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["Restore into isolated clean room"]
    G --> H{"Scan and validate data and apps"}
    H -->|Infected| I["Step back to an older snapshot"]
    I --> G
    H -->|Clean| J["Promote to production, re-seed replication"]
    J --> K["Lengthen retention, tighten MFA and duty separation"]

Figure 6.7 — Recovery is a loop, not a button: the bottleneck is usually finding a clean point and clean hardware, which is exactly what immutability and recovery SLAs target.

Note "Preserve": investigators often want the attacked array untouched, so you need clean hardware to restore to. Everpure's Evergreen//One SLA addresses exactly that (below).

docs.title: The 3-2-1(-1-0) rule
docs.text: The backup rule of thumb, usually credited to photographer Peter Krogh's The DAM Book26, is 3 copies of data, on 2 different media, with 1 off-site. The ransomware-era extension popularised by Veeam adds 1 copy that is immutable, air-gapped or offline, and 0 errors on automated restore verification27. Array snapshots are the fast first tier of such a design, not a substitute for it.

docs.text:
Vendor Metro / sync Near-sync / async Immutable copies Recovery guarantee Everpure (FlashArray, FlashBlade) ActiveCluster: active/active, Pure1 Cloud Mediator17 ActiveDR near-sync; snapshot-based async15 SafeMode: 24 h to 30 days on FlashArray, auto-on for new volumes2123 Evergreen//One Cyber Recovery and Resilience SLA (add-on): clean arrays shipped next business day, recovery plan in 48 h, 8 TiB/h transfer; covers ransomware and other disasters2829 NetApp (ONTAP) MetroCluster; SnapMirror active sync, symmetric active/active since ONTAP 9.15.118 SnapMirror async Tamperproof snapshots, SnapLock Ransomware Recovery Guarantee (2023); requires SnapLock Compliance volumes on eligible new arrays3031 Dell (PowerMax) SRDF/Metro, Smart DR to a third array19 SRDF/A; 4-site topologies Secure Snaps; up to 65 M snapshots per array (company-stated)19 Cyber Recovery Guarantee up to US$10 M, for PowerProtect Cyber Recovery vaults on DD appliances (not PowerMax itself), with purchase, Retention Lock and services conditions32 HPE (Alletra) Active Peer Persistence, RPO and RTO zero claimed20 Remote Copy; Zerto CDP (seconds)16 Virtual Lock snapshots33 [VERIFY: search-summary only] None verified for primary storage Backup software (Rubrik, Veeam, Cohesity) n/a Backup schedules Immutable backup repositories Rubrik warranty up to US$5 M for Cloud Vault (2022)34

Table 6.3 — On replication and immutability the incumbents are close; the differences are in defaults, in who can override a lock, and in what the vendor contractually commits to after an attack.

Where Everpure is differentiated. The edge is the operating model more than the replication technology. Its ROW snapshots, like NetApp's, are nearly free, which lets SafeMode default on. The Evergreen//One SLA then turns "you'll get clean hardware" into a contractual commitment within a subscription. NetApp's guarantee is narrower (SnapLock Compliance snapshots on new arrays) and Dell's covers a backup vault rather than the primary array, so of the three guarantees described here, only Everpure's commits to shipping clean replacement arrays. It complements a joint Veeam offer35 and 1touch-based data discovery for working out what was hit36.

Steelman the alternatives. Dell PowerMax's SRDF has three decades of mainframe and multi-site deployments that ActiveCluster has never targeted. NetApp's SnapLock is a regulator-recognised WORM implementation. Backup vendors argue, credibly, that a copy on a different system with different credentials beats any same-array snapshot. The honest framing: SafeMode shortens RTO in the common case; an isolated backup covers a lost or untrusted array. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: whether to extend recovery SLAs to FlashBlade//EXA-scale AI datasets, where a 5 PB restore at 8 TiB/h would take about 24 days, and how far to build into the backup layer versus partner with it.

Figure 6.8 — The centre of gravity moved from surviving hardware failure (1988–2010) to surviving site loss (2010s) to surviving an adversary (2020s).

ActiveCluster arrived with Purity//FA 5.0 in 201717, and ActiveDR followed with Purity 6.0 in June 202015. The 2023 guarantees from Pure Storage28 and NetApp30 moved resilience into the contract. Looking forward, 300 TB-plus drives push designs toward declustering and locally repairable codes, and petabyte-scale AI datasets will judge recovery guarantees on restore bandwidth, not just immutability.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "When a customer is hit, what fraction of the RTO is storage, and what fraction is forensics and clean-room work?" Strong: real incident timelines, an admission that the restore is rarely the bottleneck, and which features shorten the other phases.
  2. "How many Evergreen//One customers buy the Cyber Recovery SLA, and has it ever been invoked?" Strong: attach rate, claim history, fulfilment cost and preconditions.
  3. "Where do we lose to Veeam, Rubrik or Cohesity in the 'last line of defense' conversation?" Strong: concedes the separate-system argument and names joint designs (snapshot as tier one, backup as tier two).

Questions for an engineer

  1. "A 150 TB DFM fails outright, with no evacuation possible. What is the time to full redundancy at 80% fill under production load, and what does the host see?" Strong: it gives hours, the performance dip as a percentage and the rebuild-rate policy.
  2. "How does ActiveCluster behave if the mediator and the inter-site link fail together?" Strong: it gives the pre-election behaviour, which side survives and why, and what the host multipathing sees.
  3. "What stops a stolen-credential attacker from shortening SafeMode retention?" Strong: it names the out-of-band authentication path, how many approvers are required, and the audit trail.

Don't say this:

  • "RAID is a backup." It protects against drive failure and faithfully preserves every deletion and every encrypted block.
  • "We replicate, so we're ransomware-proof." Replication copies the encryption to the other site within seconds.
  • "Snapshots slow arrays down." That is true for copy-on-write. On redirect-on-write flash systems the cost is mostly metadata and garbage collection.
  • "Erasure coding is always cheaper than RAID." It is cheaper in capacity. It costs more in rebuild reads, network traffic and minimum cluster size.
  • "Sync replication works anywhere." It adds about 1 ms per 100 km to every write, so it is a metro-distance tool.

docs.text:
• The original RAID paper5; Huang et al., "Erasure Coding in Windows Azure Storage" (USENIX ATC 2012) on local reconstruction codes.
  • Everpure ActiveCluster documentation (mediator logic, pre-election) and the SafeMode technical brief1721.
  • VAST's resilience blog series on locally decodable codes7. NetApp's SnapMirror active sync architecture docs18.
  • Chapter 20 for durability math (MTTDL, nines) and Chapter 14 for mirrored NVRAM write paths.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• RAID 1/5/6/10 — mirroring, single parity, dual parity, and striped mirrors.
  • Erasure coding (k+m) — k data plus m parity strips; survives any m losses.
  • Declustered RAID — stripes and spares spread over all drives.
  • Redirect-on-write / copy-on-write — the two ways to implement snapshots.
  • RPO / RTO — data you can lose, and time you can be down.
  • Mediator — tie-breaker that prevents split-brain.
  • SafeMode — Everpure's snapshot immutability with delayed, support-gated eradication.
  • 3-2-1-1-0 — three copies, two media, one off-site, one immutable, zero restore errors.
  • See the glossary for the rest.
