docs.title: 7. Block protocols
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: What storage does · Inside an SSD · Performance and economics metrics

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A block protocol is a command set riding a transport (plus fabric services for discovery and access control). SCSI rode parallel cables, Fibre Channel (FC) and TCP/IP (iSCSI). NVMe replaced it, and NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF) carries NVMe over FC, RDMA or TCP.
  • NVMe's advantage is its queue model, not raw bandwidth. Up to 65,535 I/O queues of up to 64K entries, one or more per core, driven by doorbell registers with no shared lock.
  • NVMe/TCP is the enterprise default trajectory. It runs on any Ethernet NIC and every major OS and array, and adds roughly 20–35 µs, small next to a flash read.
  • NVMe over RoCE (RDMA on Ethernet) wins AI back-ends. GPU servers already carry 400G RDMA NICs, and copy-free data movement keeps GPUs fed.
  • Fibre Channel is not dying. FC sales grew in 2025 and 128G switches launched. Most FC estates will move to NVMe/FC on the same hardware.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
FlashArray is a block array, so its revenue rides on whichever wire the customer's servers use. Transport transitions are when customers re-platform and incumbents lose share. Two current examples: VMware-exit projects, where Everpure's May 2025 Nutanix partnership attaches FlashArray to AHV hosts over NVMe/TCP1, and AI clusters, where storage must sit on the RDMA fabric the GPUs already use.

Protocol support is now table stakes. The strategic questions are subtler. Which transport will buyers standardize on for a decade? Who controls discovery and automation? Does end-to-end NVMe (Everpure's DirectFlash, see Chapter 26) become a measurable edge once the front end is NVMe too?

docs.title: What a block protocol does
docs.text:
A block protocol lets a server (the initiator, or host) read and write numbered fixed-size blocks on a remote device (the target). It asks for "block 1,000,000, 256 blocks long" and knows nothing about files, which are the job of the file system above (see Chapter 1). Every block protocol has three layers:

  1. Command set. READ, WRITE, FLUSH and error reporting. SCSI uses a Command Descriptor Block (CDB) addressed to a LUN. NVMe uses a 64-byte Submission Queue Entry (SQE) addressed to a namespace.
  2. Transport. How commands, data and status cross the wire: parallel SCSI, FC, TCP/IP, PCIe or RDMA.
  3. Fabric services. Discovery, naming, access control and multipathing: FC zoning, iSCSI qualified names (IQNs), NVMe Qualified Names (NQNs) and discovery controllers.

The command set and the transport evolve on different clocks.

docs.title: SCSI: a command set that outlived its cable
docs.text:
SCSI was standardized in 1986 for disks on a ribbon cable2. Its command model is rich (sense codes, persistent reservations that clusters use for fencing) and was designed when a disk access took about 5 ms. A 20 µs software stack was then 0.4% of the I/O; against an 80 µs flash read it is 25% (worked example).

The bigger problem is queuing. SCSI-era stacks present roughly one queue per device per path, and cores contend for its lock. SATA's AHCI is the extreme: one queue, 32 commands deep. Sustained IOPS ≈ outstanding commands ÷ latency, so 32 commands at 100 µs caps a device at 32 ÷ 0.0001 s = 320,000 IOPS, however fast the NAND behind it. Linux later retrofitted multi-queue layers (blk-mq, scsi-mq) and modern FC and SAS HBAs expose several hardware queues, but per-LUN queue depths and the heavier SCSI command path still cap concurrency well below NVMe's.

docs.title: Fibre Channel and iSCSI: two ways to network SCSI
docs.text:
Fibre Channel (FC-PH, 19943) built a dedicated, lossless network for SCSI. Lossless is the defining property. Each link uses buffer-to-buffer credits: a sender transmits only as many frames as the receiver has advertised buffers for, so congestion never drops frames. Semiconductor bridge: this is PCIe's flow-control credit scheme stretched across a building. FC adds a name server and zoning (an access-control list on the switch) and maps SCSI onto frames through FCP. The result is deterministic, offloaded in HBAs and run by the storage team. It also needs its own switches (in practice Broadcom's Brocade or Cisco MDS), HBAs and skills.

iSCSI (RFC 3720, April 20044) put the same SCSI commands into TCP/IP, so any Ethernet network and any server NIC could build a SAN. It made SANs affordable for the mid-market, at the cost of host CPU for TCP and Ethernet's lossy, shared nature.

sequenceDiagram
    participant I as Initiator host
    participant T as iSCSI target array
    Note over I,T: READ
    I->>T: SCSI Command PDU with READ CDB
    T->>I: Data-In PDUs carry the blocks
    T->>I: SCSI Response PDU with status
    Note over I,T: WRITE
    I->>T: SCSI Command PDU with WRITE CDB
    T->>I: R2T, ready to transfer
    I->>T: Data-Out PDUs carry the blocks
    T->>I: SCSI Response PDU with status

Figure 7.1 — SCSI over iSCSI (or FC, where the same steps are FCP_CMND, FCP_XFER_RDY, FCP_DATA and FCP_RSP): by default a write costs an extra round trip because the target must invite the data before the host sends it. iSCSI immediate/unsolicited data and FC first burst can skip that step for the first chunk, if both ends negotiate it.

docs.title: NVMe: a protocol designed around queues
docs.text:
NVMe 1.0 (March 20115) was written for flash on PCIe and organizes the interface around paired rings in host memory:

  • A submission queue (SQ) holds 64-byte commands. A completion queue (CQ) holds 16-byte completions.
  • The host may create up to 65,535 I/O queue pairs, each up to 64K entries deep6. The driver typically gives each CPU core its own pair, so no core waits on another's lock.
  • The command set is small and fixed-format, so the controller parses commands in hardware without walking variable-length CDBs.
flowchart LR
    subgraph LEG["Legacy SCSI or AHCI host model"]
        A0["Core 0"] --> LK["Shared lock"]
        A1["Core 1"] --> LK
        A2["Core N"] --> LK
        LK --> Q["One queue per device, 32 deep on SATA"]
    end
    subgraph NV["NVMe host model"]
        B0["Core 0"] --> P0["SQ 0 and CQ 0"]
        B1["Core 1"] --> P1["SQ 1 and CQ 1"]
        B2["Core N"] --> P2["SQ N and CQ N"]
    end
    Q --> HBA["HBA or SATA controller"]
    P0 --> CTL["NVMe controller, up to 65,535 queues x 64K entries"]
    P1 --> CTL
    P2 --> CTL

Figure 7.2 — NVMe replaces one lock-protected queue with a private queue pair per core; parallelism comes from the interface, not from heroic per-command speed.

Little's law again: 64 cores each keeping 32 commands in flight gives 2,048 outstanding. At 100 µs that is about 20 million IOPS of addressable concurrency, far beyond any single SSD. The interface stops being the bottleneck.

Semiconductor bridge: NVMe is a DMA engine with descriptor rings. The host writes a descriptor (the SQE) into a ring in DRAM, then performs one memory-mapped write to a doorbell register in the SSD's PCIe BAR to announce the new tail pointer. The SSD, a PCIe bus master, fetches the descriptor by DMA, moves the data by DMA to or from the host buffers the descriptor points to, writes a completion entry into the CQ (with a phase bit so the host can tell new entries from stale ones), and raises an MSI-X interrupt. The host consumes completions and rings a second doorbell to free CQ slots. PCIe is NVMe's native transport: the protocol assumes the device can reach host memory directly.

sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Host driver on core k
    participant R as SQ k and CQ k in host DRAM
    participant C as NVMe SSD controller
    D->>R: write 64 B READ command into SQ k
    D->>C: MMIO write to SQ k tail doorbell
    C->>R: DMA fetch the command
    C->>R: DMA write data into host buffer
    C->>R: write 16 B completion into CQ k
    C->>D: MSI-X interrupt to core k
    D->>C: MMIO write to CQ k head doorbell

Figure 7.3 — Local NVMe over PCIe: one doorbell write starts the I/O and the device does the rest by DMA, which is why the host-side cost is a few microseconds.

docs.title: NVMe-oF: stretching the rings across a network
docs.text:
A remote SSD cannot DMA descriptors out of host DRAM, so NVMe-oF (1.0 in June 2016, with RDMA and FC bindings7) sends them. The 64-byte SQE travels in a command capsule, optionally with small-write data inside, and the completion returns in a response capsule. Each NVMe queue pair maps onto one transport connection (an RDMA queue pair, a TCP connection or an FC-NVMe connection within an association), preserving per-core parallelism end to end. Multipathing uses ANA (Asymmetric Namespace Access), NVMe's equivalent of SCSI ALUA (see Chapter 14).

The transports differ mainly in how bulk data moves:

  • RDMA (RoCEv2 on Ethernet, or InfiniBand). The capsule carries the address and key of a registered host buffer; the target RDMA-WRITEs read data into it, or RDMA-READs write data out of it. No host CPU copies a byte, and the adder is about 5–15 µs over local NVMe8. The price is RDMA NICs and, for RoCE, carefully tuned Ethernet (see Chapter 10).
  • TCP. Capsules and data travel as PDUs on a TCP stream: reads return as C2HData PDUs (the last one may carry a success flag so the target can skip the response capsule), and writes larger than the in-capsule limit wait for an R2T, as in iSCSI, then send H2CData PDUs. The kernel copies payloads and runs TCP; early Linux tests showed 20–35 µs added9. Under heavy load the gap widens: one 2018 vendor test measured 183 µs average for TCP versus 107 µs for RoCE, although single-I/O latency was within a few microseconds10.
  • FC (FC-NVMe, standardized by T11 in 201711). Capsules ride FC frames on the same HBAs, switches, zoning and lossless credits as SCSI-FC, with data movement offloaded to the HBA.
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host NVMe-oF driver
    participant T as Target array controller
    participant M as Flash media
    H->>T: command capsule READ 128 KB, buffer address and key
    T->>M: read blocks
    M-->>T: data
    alt RDMA transport
        T->>H: RDMA WRITE data directly into host buffer
        Note over H: NIC places data, no host CPU copy
    else TCP transport
        T->>H: C2HData PDUs on the TCP stream
        Note over H: kernel reassembles and copies into buffer
    end
    T->>H: response capsule with 16 B completion

Figure 7.4 — NVMe-oF read: the command and completion are identical across transports; only the data leg changes, and that leg is where RDMA saves CPU and microseconds.

sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host NVMe-oF driver
    participant T as Target array controller
    participant W as NVRAM write cache
    alt Small write, in-capsule data
        H->>T: command capsule WRITE with 4 KB data inside
    else Large write over RDMA
        H->>T: command capsule WRITE, buffer address and key
        T->>H: RDMA READ pulls data from host memory
    else Large write over TCP
        H->>T: command capsule WRITE
        T->>H: R2T, ready to transfer
        H->>T: H2CData PDUs carry the data
    end
    T->>W: persist to mirrored or shared NVRAM
    W-->>T: durable
    T->>H: response capsule with completion

Figure 7.5 — NVMe-oF write: in-capsule data (up to a size the target advertises) lets small writes finish in one round trip on RDMA or TCP, while large writes are pulled by the target (RDMA) or invited by an R2T (TCP). FC-NVMe has an analogous first-burst option.

docs.title: The transports compared
docs.text:
Transport Latency adder vs local NVMe Hardware needs Ecosystem Typical buyer FC-NVMe (NVMe/FC) Low; HBA-offloaded. Vendor claims ~50% lower end-to-end latency than SCSI-FC12 FC HBAs (32G+), FC switches, zoning Brocade/Cisco fabrics; VMware, Linux, Windows; all major arrays Enterprises with an existing FC estate and a storage team that owns it NVMe/RoCE ~5–15 µs8 RDMA NICs (ConnectX/BlueField class), switches tuned for RoCE NVIDIA networking, Linux, VMware; DASE back-ends AI clusters, neoclouds, latency-critical databases NVMe/TCP ~20–35 µs in early Linux tests9; wider under load10 Any Ethernet NIC; offloads optional Linux kernel, VMware since 2021, every major array Greenfield Ethernet SANs, VMware/Nutanix refreshes, cloud and SDS iSCSI Highest: TCP plus SCSI translation. Vendor claims NVMe/RoCE has ~50% lower latency13 Any Ethernet NIC Universal, 20+ years of tooling Mid-market and branch; the long tail of installed SANs

Figure 7.6 — The four transports trade the latency adder against hardware specialization; the buyer's existing fabric usually decides more than the microseconds do.

docs.title: Why NVMe/TCP is the enterprise default trajectory
docs.text:
NVMe/TCP was ratified in November 2018 (TP 8000)14, reached upstream Linux in 5.015 and VMware in vSphere 7 Update 3 in late 202116. Four reasons it is winning new Ethernet SANs:

  1. No special hardware. It runs on existing NICs and routes like any TCP traffic; RoCE needs RDMA NICs and carefully engineered switches.
  2. The penalty is small where it counts. A 20–35 µs adder over a 100–200 µs array round trip is real but rarely decisive for databases or VMs. A 2021 SNIA talk reported realistic performance similar to RoCEv217.
  3. CPU cost is falling. More cores and NIC/DPU offloads shrink the copy overhead.
  4. It replaces iSCSI without retraining. Same network, same team, better queue model.

The gaps are operational: discovery at scale (Dell's SmartFabric Storage Software is a centralized discovery controller for this18), authentication and TLS, and tail latency on congested networks.

docs.title: Why RoCE wins AI back-ends
docs.text: In an AI cluster the economics flip. GPU servers already carry several 400G RDMA NICs, so RDMA is free, and at hundreds of gigabits per server CPU copies would burn host cores. GPUDirect Storage needs an RDMA-capable path to land data directly in GPU memory (see Chapter 11). Disaggregated back-ends such as VAST's use NVMe over RDMA internally (see Chapter 16). NVIDIA claims its Spectrum-X adaptive routing gives almost 50% more storage read bandwidth than plain RoCEv2, in its own tests19.

docs.title: Why Fibre Channel persists
docs.text: FC's survival is organizational as much as technical: a separate lossless fabric with a small blast radius, change control owned by the storage team, and mature diagnostics under decades of mission-critical databases. Its NVMe upgrade path is cheap, because NVMe/FC runs on the same 32G-and-later HBAs and switches. Crehan Research reported FC networking sales up 6% in 2025, with 64G about half of shipments20 [VERIFY: search-summary only], and Broadcom launched Gen 8 128G Brocade switches in November 202521.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Vendor / array NVMe/RoCE NVMe/FC NVMe/TCP Notable angle Everpure FlashArray 2019, Purity 5.2 "DirectFlash Fabric"13 Feb 2021, Purity 6.112 Purity 6.4.2, 2022 [VERIFY: exact GA month; sources conflict]22 NVMe end to end internally (DirectFlash); Nutanix AHV over NVMe/TCP1 NetApp ONTAP (AFF/ASA) Not supported on ONTAP, which offers NVMe/FC and NVMe/TCP only23; the separate E-Series/EF line has RDMA options ONTAP 9.4, 201824 ONTAP 9.10.1, late 202125 Unified file+block; large FC base Dell PowerStore Not found in public PowerStore material; Dell chose NVMe/TCP for Ethernet hosts26 PowerStoreOS 2.0, 202127 PowerStoreOS 2.1, early 202228 SmartFabric Storage Software for NVMe/TCP discovery18

Figure 7.7 — Everpure shipped RoCE early and followed on TCP; by 2026 the three vendors are at parity on NVMe/FC and NVMe/TCP (only Everpure offers RoCE on these lines), so differentiation sits in the internal data path and the automation around discovery.

Everpure shipped RoCE first, a bet on latency-sensitive databases. Its structural argument is that DirectFlash already speaks NVMe from controller to raw NAND, so an NVMe front end removes the last SCSI translation (see Chapter 26). The steelman for competitors is strong. Dell's centralized discovery addresses a real NVMe/TCP pain point at scale, NetApp's unified ONTAP serves FC, NVMe and NAS from one estate, and because FC customers rarely change fabric, the incumbent with the deepest FC relationships often holds the account. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: owning NVMe/TCP automation in VMware-exit and Nutanix deals, and judging how much AI back-end RoCE demand reaches block arrays rather than file and object (FlashBlade; see Chapter 27).

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Block protocol lineage
    1986 : SCSI-1 standard for parallel disks
    1994 : Fibre Channel FC-PH, a lossless SAN for SCSI
    2004 : iSCSI RFC 3720 puts SCSI on TCP
    2011 : NVMe 1.0 for PCIe flash
    2016 : NVMe-oF 1.0 with RDMA and FC bindings
    2017 : FC-NVMe standard completed in T11
    2018 : NVMe over TCP ratified as TP 8000
    2021 : NVMe 2.0 library and vSphere NVMe over TCP
    2025 : 128G Gen 8 Fibre Channel switches

Figure 7.8 — The command set changed once in 25 years (SCSI to NVMe); transports keep multiplying because each buyer segment brings its own fabric.

A command set is born on a local bus, then re-ridden across every network: SCSI from ribbon cable to FC to TCP, NVMe from PCIe to RDMA and FC to TCP. The June 2021 NVMe 2.0 refactor made each transport its own specification29.

Signals to watch: NVMe/TCP offload on DPUs (erasing its CPU penalty), better Ethernet RDMA congestion control (making RoCE easier outside AI), FC's move to 128G, and whether hyperscaler-style block services (see Chapter 19) pull enterprise buyers toward NVMe/TCP-only designs.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In new FlashArray deals, what share of hosts attach by NVMe/TCP versus FC versus iSCSI, and how has that shifted in two years?" Strong: a measured mix from telemetry, by segment, and whether NVMe/TCP is displacing iSCSI or FC.
  2. "When a VMware customer moves to Nutanix or another hypervisor, does the storage protocol change, and who decides?" Strong: names the decision-maker and whether NVMe/TCP automation shortens the cycle.
  3. "Where do we lose block deals on protocol grounds?" Strong: specific cases (a missing automation integration, an FC estate locked to a competitor), not "we support everything."

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What is the latency delta between NVMe/TCP and NVMe/RoCE on FlashArray at queue depth 1 and at saturation?" Strong: both numbers, host CPU per IOPS, and where tail latency diverges.
  2. "How do ANA paths and controller failover behave on NVMe-oF versus ALUA on SCSI?" Strong: path-state transitions and failover time.
  3. "Does the array's internal NVMe path change how many queue pairs per host you can serve?" Strong: concrete queue and connection limits per port, and behaviour with thousands of Kubernetes hosts.

Don't say this:

  • "NVMe-oF is faster because the wire is faster." The wire is the same; the gain is the queue model and no SCSI translation.
  • "Fibre Channel is dead." Sales grew in 2025 and 128G is shipping. Say "shrinking share, durable base."
  • "NVMe/TCP is too slow for real work." It adds tens of microseconds, not milliseconds.
  • "RoCE is the same as InfiniBand." RoCE shares RDMA semantics but runs on Ethernet and depends on congestion management.
  • "iSCSI and NVMe/TCP are interchangeable." Same network, different command set and queue model.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• NVM Express base and transport specifications (2.x library): capsule formats, SGLs, ANA.
  • Linux nvme-tcp, nvme-rdma and nvmet drivers, and blk-mq queue-to-CPU mapping.
  • iSCSI RFC 7143 and T11 FC-NVMe-2 (transport error recovery).
  • Kernel-bypass storage stacks (SPDK) and NVMe/TCP offload on DPUs.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Initiator / target — host issuing block commands; device executing them.
  • LUN / namespace — the SCSI and NVMe names for an addressable block volume.
  • SQ / CQ — NVMe's command and completion rings.
  • Doorbell — device register announcing new queue entries.
  • Capsule — NVMe-oF command or response message.
  • ANA — Asymmetric Namespace Access, NVMe's multipath path-state mechanism.
  • R2T — Ready to Transfer, a target's invitation for the host to send write data.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 8. File protocols
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: What storage does · Block protocols and NVMe-oF · Datacenter networking (helpful)

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• File protocols carry operations on names, not blocks. The server owns the namespace, locks and byte placement. NFS rules Linux and AI clusters; SMB rules Windows.
  • NFSv3 is stateless; NFSv4.x is stateful, with leases, delegations and integrated locks. v4.1 added sessions and pNFS; v4.2 added server-side copy and sparse files.
  • Classic NAS has a "single head" problem. Each mount goes to one server, so every byte crosses one controller. The fixes, from least to most disruptive: nconnect, RDMA, client multipath, pNFS, a proprietary parallel client.
  • pNFS separates the control path from the data path. The client gets a layout from a metadata server, then does I/O directly and in parallel to the data servers. The Flex Files layout (2018) lets those data servers be plain NFSv3 servers.
  • Vendors are converging on "parallel, with the stock Linux client." Hammerspace, Everpure FlashBlade//EXA, Dell and NetApp bet on pNFS; VAST on its multipath NFS client; Lustre, GPFS and WEKA on proprietary clients.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
GPU servers mount data, checkpoints and home directories as a POSIX file system, which on Linux usually means NFS, FlashBlade's main front door. The protocol therefore gates the deal. A proprietary parallel client is fastest but costs an install, kernel lock-in and a security review on every GPU node. Standard NFS is easy to adopt but tops out at the server head.

FlashBlade//EXA (March 2025) is Pure Storage's (now Everpure's) bet on a middle path. It speaks pNFS, with metadata over NFSv4.1/TCP to a FlashBlade metadata core and data over NFSv3/RDMA directly to data nodes, and needs no proprietary client1. Rivals are making the same bet. In September 2026 NetApp announced its intent to acquire PEAK:AIO (not yet closed) to bring parallel NFS to ONTAP2, and Dell is adding pNFS Flex Files to PowerScale3. Judging EXA means knowing where pNFS beats VAST's multipath NFS or a Lustre client, and where it falls short; see Chapter 17 and Chapter 16.

docs.title: What a file protocol actually carries
docs.text:
A block protocol says "read 8 blocks at LBA 1,000,000" and leaves meaning to the host's file system. A file protocol says "look up shard-00042.tar" and "read 1 MiB at offset 64 MiB". Because the server owns namespace and locks, many clients can share data safely, which is the point of NAS. The cost: every client depends on the server to turn names into bytes.

Semiconductor bridge. In directory-based cache coherence, a home node tracks where each line lives. A file server is that home node, and classic NAS also pushes the data through it. pNFS tells the requester where the line is and lets it fetch peer-to-peer.

docs.title: NFSv3: stateless by design
docs.text:
NFSv3 (RFC 1813, 1995)4 runs over Sun RPC. Each request carries an opaque file handle and stands alone; the server tracks no opens, so after a reboot clients just retry. That simplicity keeps v3 the most widely deployed version. Statelessness has three costs:

  • Locking sits outside the protocol, in fragile NLM/NSM side protocols.
  • Consistency is "close-to-open". Clients cache attributes for a few seconds, revalidate on open() and flush on close(). Another client is guaranteed to see your writes only after you close the file and it reopens it.
  • Every path component costs a round trip. A LOOKUP per component, plus GETATTRs, comes before the first READ.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Linux client
    participant S as NAS head
    participant D as Drives behind head
    C->>S: LOOKUP data then train then shard file
    S-->>C: file handle
    C->>S: GETATTR file handle
    S-->>C: size, mtime, permissions
    loop for each 1 MiB chunk
        C->>S: READ handle, offset, 1 MiB
        S->>D: fetch blocks
        D-->>S: data
        S-->>C: data over one TCP connection
    end

Figure 8.1 — In NFSv3 every metadata step and every data byte goes through the one server that owns the mount, so that server's CPU and NICs set the ceiling.

docs.title: NFSv4.0, 4.1 and 4.2: state, sessions, layouts
docs.text:
NFSv4.0 (RFC 3530 in 2003, revised as RFC 7530)5 made NFS stateful. Clients OPEN files under renewable leases, and locking became part of the protocol. Delegations give one client exclusive caching rights to a file until the server recalls them. COMPOUND bundles several operations, such as LOOKUP, GETATTR and READ, into one round trip. It runs on one port with Kerberos and ACLs. The price is a grace period after restarts while clients reclaim state.

NFSv4.1 (RFC 5661 in 2010, now RFC 8881)6 added sessions, which make retries exactly-once; trunking, which spreads one session over several connections; and pNFS. NFSv4.2 (RFC 7862, 2016)7 added server-side copy, sparse files, I/O hints, labeled NFS, and layout statistics and error reporting that pNFS servers use to steer clients. The Flex Files layout (RFC 8435, 2018)8 lets data servers speak plain NFSv3 and lets clients mirror writes.

docs.title: The single-head bottleneck and the escalation ladder
docs.text:
Each end of a TCP connection is served by roughly one core and one NIC queue. VAST's documentation puts a plain NFS/TCP mount on a 100 Gb/s NIC at about 2–2.5 GB/s9 [VERIFY: search-summary only]. Worked example: a GPU server with two 400 Gb/s storage ports can absorb 2 × 50 = 100 GB/s, the equivalent of 100 ÷ 2.25 ≈ 44 such connections. Across 500 servers that is 50 TB/s, far beyond any controller pair, and scale-out NAS nodes often relay data east-west behind the scenes. Five fixes, in rising order of disruption (Figure 8.2):

  1. nconnect (Linux 5.3, 2019) opens up to 16 TCP connections per mount to the same server address10. VAST cites about 11 GB/s on one 100 Gb/s NIC9: more pipes, same head.
  2. NFS over RDMA (RFC 8166/8267, 2017)11 has the server place bulk data directly into client memory, which saves copies and CPU. It is also how GPUDirect Storage runs over NFS: NVIDIA's GDS driver supports NFS/RDMA12. VAST cites about 8–8.5 GB/s per RDMA connection on 100 GbE9.
  3. Client multipath spreads one mount over many local NICs and many server IPs. VAST ships its own build of the Linux NFS client for this, covering NFSv3 and NFSv4.1 over TCP or RDMA, and reported 162 GiB/s into one DGX A100 with eight 200 Gb/s NICs and GDS (company-stated)13. The wire protocol is standard; the client module is VAST's. It works because in DASE any node can serve any file.
  4. pNFS changes the protocol so that data bypasses the head (Figure 8.3).
  5. Proprietary parallel clients (Lustre, IBM Storage Scale/GPFS, WEKA, BeeGFS) replace NFS on the client entirely.

Figure 8.2 — The escalation ladder moves from "more pipes into the same head" (A to B) to "take the head out of the data path" (C).

docs.title: How pNFS works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Linux client
    participant M as Metadata server
    participant D1 as Data server 1
    participant D2 as Data server 2
    participant D3 as Data server 3
    C->>M: OPEN shard file over NFSv4.1
    M-->>C: stateid and delegation if granted
    C->>M: LAYOUTGET byte range 0 to 3 GiB
    M-->>C: layout, stripe unit and data server list
    C->>M: GETDEVICEINFO
    M-->>C: data server addresses, TCP or RDMA
    par direct parallel I/O
        C->>D1: READ stripe 0 over NFSv3 RDMA
        C->>D2: READ stripe 1 over NFSv3 RDMA
        C->>D3: READ stripe 2 over NFSv3 RDMA
    end
    D1-->>C: data
    D2-->>C: data
    D3-->>C: data
    Note over M,D3: If data moves or a server fails, M recalls the layout and the client asks again
    C->>M: LAYOUTRETURN and CLOSE

Figure 8.3 — pNFS touches the metadata server once per file or range, then streams data from many servers in parallel, so throughput scales with the number of data servers, not with the metadata server.

Three properties matter. First, the client does the striping arithmetic: from the stripe unit and server list it works out which server holds offset X, as a Lustre client does with its stripe map. Second, layouts are recallable leases: a rebalance, failure or conflicting writer triggers a recall, and the client re-fetches or sends I/O via the metadata server. Third, layout types differ. The "files" layout needs data servers that speak NFSv4.1, and the block and SCSI layouts point at LUNs. Flex Files accepts plain NFSv3 servers, which is why Hammerspace and FlashBlade//EXA use NFSv3 on the data leg18.

docs.title: SMB3: the Windows side
docs.text: SMB 3.0 (Windows Server 2012) added Multichannel, which spreads one session over several NICs automatically; SMB Direct, SMB over RDMA on iWARP, InfiniBand or RoCE; and transparent failover1415. Multichannel also detects RDMA adapters, and SMB Direct gained encryption in Windows Server 202214. SMB3 is capable but rare on Linux GPU nodes; it matters for media, Windows analytics and as a multiprotocol checkbox.

docs.title: POSIX semantics, and why AI loaders want them
docs.text:
AI software is written against POSIX: open, random-offset read, mmap, fsync, atomic rename. Loaders read random samples inside shards; checkpointers write a temp file and rename it. NVIDIA's NIXL and Dynamo KV tiers use a POSIX backend for disk, and NVIDIA's cloud-partner rules require NFSv4 home directories with POSIX access control16. S3 is gaining: about one-sixth of MLPerf Storage v3.0 submissions (September 2026) used S317. But S3 has no rename, append or partial overwrite, so most training code still expects a mount (Chapter 9).

How much POSIX matters depends on the access pattern. Read-mostly datasets and write-then-rename checkpoints are safe under close-to-open. Many processes writing one shared file at once are not, for example 1,024 ranks writing a single checkpoint file. That needs byte-range locks and immediate cross-client visibility, which Lustre, GPFS and WEKA clients provide via distributed lock managers. That is what the proprietary install buys.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Protocol State model Locking Parallel data path RDMA Client Best fit NFSv3 Stateless Side protocols (NLM) No: one server per mount (multipath needs vendor client) Yes (NFS/RDMA) In every OS Simple shared data, legacy apps, pNFS data leg NFSv4.1 / 4.2 (no pNFS) Stateful: leases, delegations, sessions Integrated, leased Trunking only; still one server's data Yes In every modern Linux Home dirs, secure multi-tenant NAS pNFS (v4.1+, Flex Files) Stateful on metadata server; data servers simple Via metadata server Yes: direct to many data servers Yes on data leg Stock Linux NFSv4.1/4.2 client AI training/inference at scale without custom clients SMB3 Stateful sessions, leases Integrated (oplocks/leases) Multichannel across NICs, same server SMB Direct Windows native; Linux CIFS Windows, media, VDI, enterprise shares Proprietary parallel (Lustre, GPFS, WEKA) Stateful, distributed lock manager Full POSIX byte-range Yes: client stripes across storage servers Native (IB/RoCE; WEKA DPDK) Vendor kernel module or agent Largest HPC/AI clusters, shared-file writes

Table 8.1 — Only pNFS and proprietary clients remove the server head from the data path; pNFS does it with the client already in the kernel.

The proprietary route has a cost. The Lustre client left the Linux staging tree in 2018 and lives out of tree18, so every GPU-fleet kernel update waits for a matching client build. WEKA's client can bypass the kernel network stack with DPDK19, trading dedicated cores for speed.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Vendor / product Client-facing approach Client software Notes Everpure FlashBlade//S NFSv3/4.1, SMB, S3; nconnect; NFS over RDMA Stock Scale-out NAS; Everpure documents nconnect on kernels ≥ 5.320; NFS over RDMA with GDS reported from Purity//FB 4.3.4 (late 2023)21 [VERIFY: search-summary only; confirm in Purity//FB release notes] Everpure FlashBlade//EXA pNFS: NFSv4.1/TCP to metadata core, NFSv3/RDMA to data nodes Stock Linux client Metadata core of 1–10 FlashBlade chassis; off-the-shelf data nodes at launch122 VAST Data NFSv3/4.1, NFS/RDMA, SMB, S3 Optional VAST NFS multipath client No public pNFS support found: its NFS client documentation (v4.5, 2026) lists multipath for NFSv3 and v4.1, not pNFS23; DASE makes any node a valid target13 Hammerspace pNFS Flex Files over existing NFS storage Stock NFSv4.2 client Metadata on Anvil servers24; parallel NFS co-developed for Meta's 24k-GPU clusters25 Dell PowerScale / Lightning FS pNFS Flex Files with separate metadata server (2026) Stock Lightning FS aimed at >16k-GPU / 4 TB/s sites3 NetApp ONTAP / AFX NFSv4.1 pNFS, trunking; PEAK:AIO scale-out metadata to come Stock Deal announced 2026-09-25; terms undisclosed226 WEKA, DDN EXAScaler, IBM Storage Scale Proprietary POSIX client (plus NFS/SMB/S3 gateways) Vendor client Highest per-client throughput and full POSIX; heaviest footprint19

Table 8.2 — Three answers to the single head: a better client on standard NFS (VAST), the pNFS standard (Everpure EXA, Hammerspace, Dell, NetApp), or a proprietary client (WEKA, DDN, IBM).

Steelmen. Proprietary clients remain safest for shared-file writes. VAST's multipath gets most of pNFS's bandwidth without a metadata server on every open, with a far lighter client than Lustre's. pNFS is the only option that takes the head out of the data path using the client already in the distro. Hammerspace cites a 10-node production IO500 result on the upstream NFSv4.2 client (company-stated)27.

Where pNFS is weaker. It is only as good as each distro's Linux client, one of whose upstream maintainers is Hammerspace's CTO28. Layout recalls under churn can stall clients, and metadata becomes the scaling point. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information:

  • how well EXA's NFSv3/RDMA data leg delivers GDS into GPU memory: Portworx documentation describes GDS for EXA file systems over RDMA NFS29 [VERIFY: search-summary only], but NVIDIA certification for EXA and measured per-client numbers are not yet public;
  • whether FlashBlade//S should add pNFS, giving one protocol story from enterprise to EXA;
  • how much Everpure should invest upstream in the Linux pNFS client, which every pNFS vendor shares.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title File protocol milestones
    1984 : Sun designs NFS
    1995 : NFSv3 RFC 1813
    2003 : NFSv4 RFC 3530 adds state and locking
    2010 : NFSv4.1 RFC 5661 adds sessions and pNFS
    2012 : SMB 3.0 adds Multichannel and SMB Direct
    2016 : NFSv4.2 RFC 7862
    2017 : RPC over RDMA v1 RFC 8166
    2018 : Flex Files layout RFC 8435 : Lustre client leaves Linux staging
    2019 : Linux 5.3 adds nconnect
    2024 : Meta uses Hammerspace parallel NFS for GenAI clusters
    2025 : Pure Storage announces FlashBlade EXA on pNFS : Dell previews PowerScale pNFS
    2026 : NetApp agrees to buy PEAK AIO

Figure 8.4 — The pNFS standard existed from 2010, but AI-scale adoption came only after Flex Files (2018) and an upstream Linux client matured; 2024–2026 is when the major vendors committed.

For 15 years pNFS was a standard in search of a market while HPC ran Lustre or GPFS. Then Flex Files and a better upstream client removed the need for special data servers, and AI buyers, especially neoclouds with thousands of GPU nodes, resisted proprietary kernel modules. Watch upstream NFSv4.2 client work (attribute delegations, faster failover and client-side erasure coding were in progress in 202428), GDS on pNFS data legs, and whether S3-over-RDMA absorbs checkpoint and KV-cache traffic (Chapter 32).

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Why pNFS for EXA rather than a proprietary or multipath client?" Strong: adoption friction (no kernel module on GPU nodes, faster neocloud security review), plus candour on costs: shared-file writes and distro-client dependence.
  2. "Which distros and kernels do we validate, and what happens on older RHEL?" Strong: minimum versions, known client bugs, fallback path.
  3. "Against VAST, where does multipath NFS match us and where does the direct path win?" Strong: per-client and aggregate numbers, with GDS on or off stated for both.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "A data node fails mid-checkpoint: what happens to in-flight I/O?" Strong: layout recall, retry or fallback, time to a new layout, and how writes were protected.
  2. "Which layout type do we hand out, and who does striping and redundancy?" Strong: names Flex Files or the files layout, gives the stripe unit, and says whether the client mirrors.
  3. "What create/open rate can the metadata core sustain, and what saturates first?" Strong: a per-chassis number, plus whether opens, layouts or directory locks hit the limit first (Chapter 21).

Don't say this:

  • "pNFS is new." It was standardized in 2010. Flex Files, a mature client and AI demand are new.
  • "NFS can't do RDMA." NFS/RDMA is standardized and is a common GDS path.
  • "nconnect makes NFS parallel." Same server, more connections.
  • "NFS is POSIX." It is close-to-open: fine for reads, not for concurrent shared-file writes.
  • "VAST uses pNFS." Its parallelism comes from multipath into a shared-everything back end.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• RFC 8881 §12–13 (pNFS and the file layout), RFC 8435 (Flex Files), RFC 8166/8267 (RPC-over-RDMA).
  • Trond Myklebust, "Advancements in pNFS and NFSv4.2," SNIA SDC 202428.
  • Linux fs/nfs/flexfilelayout/ and net/sunrpc/xprtrdma/; nfs(5) on nconnect, actimeo, nocto and proto=rdma.
  • Full parallel file systems (Lustre MDS/OSS, GPFS tokens): Chapter 17.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• File handle — opaque server token naming a file in NFS.
  • Close-to-open consistency — writes visible to others only after close and reopen.
  • Lease / delegation — NFSv4 time-bounded state; recallable exclusive caching rights.
  • pNFS layout — map of which data servers hold which byte ranges.
  • Flex Files — pNFS layout whose data servers can be plain NFSv3.
  • nconnect — Linux option for up to 16 TCP connections per mount.
  • SMB Multichannel / SMB Direct — SMB3 multi-connection and RDMA transport.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 9. Object storage and S3
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: What storage does · File protocols · Datacenter networking for storage

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• S3 is a REST API over HTTP. You PUT whole objects into a bucket under a key and GET them back; every request is signed (SigV4) and priced. No directories, in-place edits or locks: that is why it scales.
  • The namespace is flat; LIST and small objects are the weak spots. "Folders" are key prefixes. LIST pages through an index 1,000 keys at a time, and per-request fees can exceed the storage bill.
  • AWS S3 has been strongly consistent since December 2020. Other S3-compatible systems vary, especially across sites.
  • S3 is becoming the default AI data interface. Lakehouses, data loaders, checkpoint libraries and KV-cache tiers target it, and AWS keeps adding Express One Zone, S3 Tables and S3 Vectors.
  • S3 over RDMA removes the performance excuse. HTTP keeps the control path while RDMA moves bytes straight into GPU memory, via NVIDIA's cuObject libraries (adopted by Cloudian, Dell and HPE) and separate implementations such as MinIO's.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
For AI buyers the question is shifting from "file or object?" to "how fast is your S3?". MLPerf Storage v3.0 (September 2026) added an S3 access layer, and about one-sixth of submissions used it1. Pure Storage built FlashBlade as unified fast file and object, and added S3 to FlashArray in June 20252, which suits an S3-first world.

The threat is commoditisation from two sides. With RDMA, object-native vendors (Cloudian, MinIO, HPE, Dell) can bid for GPU-feeding work that used to need a parallel file system. Meanwhile AWS pulls table management, vector search and low-latency tiers into S3 itself. The questions are how good Everpure's S3 is on small objects, LIST and RDMA, and whether its value lies in the protocol or the data services behind it. Internal object-store design is in Chapter 18.

docs.title: The model: buckets, keys, whole objects
docs.text:
An object is a blob of bytes plus metadata (size, ETag, checksum, user tags). Objects live in buckets, the unit of policy, region, billing and versioning, and are addressed by a key of up to 1,024 bytes. s3://training/imagenet/train/0001.jpg looks like a path, but the slashes mean nothing: it is one key in a flat namespace, and console "folders" are just listings by prefix.

Three choices separate this from a file system (Chapter 8):

  1. Whole-object writes. A PUT atomically creates or replaces an entire object. There is no writing bytes 4,096–8,191 in place and no cheap rename: "renaming a folder" copies and deletes every key under it.
  2. No sessions or locks. Each request stands alone. Conditional writes (If-None-Match: *, If-Match: <ETag>) let the first writer win while later ones get 412 Precondition Failed3.
  3. Thin metadata. No POSIX permissions, hard links or mtime semantics; access is governed by bucket policy and IAM.

Semiconductor bridge: S3 is an FTL at planetary scale. NAND cannot overwrite a page, so the FTL writes elsewhere, remaps and garbage-collects later (Chapter 3). An S3 overwrite is likewise a new immutable version plus a pointer swap in the index. A file system with in-place edits is closer to byte-addressable DRAM. Immutability is what lets object stores erasure-code aggressively, cache anywhere and replicate without coherence traffic.

docs.title: Anatomy of a PUT
docs.text:
AWS does not publish S3's internals; this is the generic pattern (component names illustrative):

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client SDK
    participant F as Front end
    participant A as Auth and policy
    participant S as Storage nodes
    participant I as Metadata index
    C->>C: hash payload, derive SigV4 key, sign canonical request
    C->>F: PUT /bucket/key with Authorization, checksum, body
    F->>A: verify signature and IAM or bucket policy
    A-->>F: allowed
    F->>S: stream body, erasure-coded or replicated across failure domains
    S-->>F: fragments durable
    F->>F: verify checksum, compute ETag
    F->>I: commit key to new version and fragment locations
    I-->>F: committed, now visible to all readers
    F-->>C: 200 OK with ETag and version id

Figure 9.1 — A PUT becomes visible only when the index commit lands, after the data is durable; that ordering gives atomic replace and read-after-write consistency.

SigV4 signs a canonical form of the method, path, headers and payload hash with a key derived by chained HMAC-SHA256 (secret → date → region → service). The server recomputes it, so no secret crosses the wire and requests expire quickly. The price is CPU hashing at both ends on every request.

docs.title: Anatomy of a GET
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client SDK
    participant F as Front end
    participant I as Metadata index
    participant S as Storage nodes
    C->>F: signed GET /bucket/key, optional Range bytes
    F->>F: verify SigV4 and policy
    F->>I: look up latest committed version
    I-->>F: version, size, ETag, fragment locations
    F->>S: read needed fragments in parallel
    S-->>F: fragments
    F->>F: reconstruct and verify checksum
    F-->>C: 200 or 206 Partial Content with bytes and ETag

Figure 9.2 — Every GET pays an auth check and an index lookup before any data moves, so small reads are dominated by fixed per-request cost.

Byte-range GETs are the main lever: split a 1 GB object into 64 parallel 16 MB ranges over many connections, because one HTTP stream runs far below NIC line rate.

docs.title: LIST, prefixes and the small-object tax
docs.text:
Two numbers shape S3 workload design. AWS supports at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per partitioned prefix, splitting prefixes as load grows and returning 503 Slow Down meanwhile4. And requests are billed: in S3 Standard (us-east-1), $0.0004 per 1,000 GETs and $0.005 per 1,000 PUTs or LISTs, against $0.023 per GB-month of storage for the first 50 TB5.

LIST is a paged scan of a sorted index, 1,000 keys per call. Enumerating 1 billion objects takes 1,000,000 calls: $5, but at an assumed ~20 ms per call, 5.6 hours single-threaded. That is why lakehouse formats keep their own manifests instead of listing.

Figure 9.3 — Illustrative: at 4 KB per object, request charges and per-prefix limits dominate; at ≥16 MB they vanish, which is why AI datasets are packed into large shards. Data: data/ch09_small_object_tax.csv

Writes are worse. Storing 1 PB as 4 KB objects takes 2.5e11 PUTs × $0.005 / 1,000 = $1.25 million in fees, against ~$21,550 a month to store it (tiered $0.023/$0.022/$0.021 per GB5): 58 months of storage. Hence tar shards, Parquet row groups and checkpoint files of hundreds of MB.

docs.title: Multipart upload
docs.text:
Large objects upload as parallel, individually retryable parts that become visible atomically:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as S3 endpoint
    C->>S: CreateMultipartUpload bucket key
    S-->>C: UploadId
    par parallel streams
        C->>S: UploadPart 1 of N, 5 MiB to 5 GiB
        S-->>C: ETag 1
    and
        C->>S: UploadPart 2 of N
        S-->>C: ETag 2
    and
        C->>S: UploadPart N, last part may be small
        S-->>C: ETag N
    end
    C->>S: CompleteMultipartUpload with part numbers and ETags
    S-->>C: 200 OK, object visible atomically
    Note over C,S: On failure call AbortMultipartUpload, or a lifecycle rule deletes stale parts that are still billed

Figure 9.4 — Multipart turns one fragile multi-terabyte stream into thousands of independent, retryable parts committed by a single atomic step.

Limits are 10,000 parts of 5 MiB–5 GiB6; in December 2025 AWS raised the maximum object from 5 TB to 50 TB7, which is roughly 10,000 × 5 GiB. A 6.5 TB checkpoint (405B parameters × 16 bytes) therefore needs parts of at least 650 MB; at 64 streams × 200 MB/s it writes in about 8.5 minutes (Chapter 31).

docs.title: Consistency models
docs.text:
Until 2020, S3 guaranteed read-after-write only for new keys; overwrites, deletes and LIST were eventually consistent8. On 1 December 2020 AWS made all of them strongly consistent at no extra cost9, retiring workarounds such as Hadoop's S3Guard metadata tables.

System Read-after-write (new and overwrite) LIST after write Across regions / sites Caveats Amazon S3, before Dec 2020 New keys only; overwrites and deletes eventual Eventual Async replication Readers could see stale data or missing keys8 Amazon S3, since Dec 2020 Strong Strong Cross-region replication is asynchronous Bucket-configuration changes still propagate eventually9 Google Cloud Storage Strong, global Strong Strong even for multi-region buckets ACL changes take ~1 minute; cached public objects may be stale10 Azure Blob Storage Strong Strong Geo-redundant secondary is asynchronous ETag If-Match for optimistic concurrency11 Ceph RGW Strong within a zone Strong within a zone Multisite is asynchronous and eventual; last writer wins Non-zero RPO between sites12 MinIO AIStor Strict read-after-write (company-stated)13 Strict list-after-write (company-stated)13 Site replication asynchronous Erasure-set quorum writes

Table 9.1 — Strong consistency within a site is now standard; across sites almost everyone is asynchronous.

Strong consistency means the index commit in Figure 9.1 is one linearisation point every reader sees. At S3's scale (over 350 trillion objects and 100 million requests per second in 202414 [VERIFY: search-summary only]) that needs a replicated, coherent metadata layer (Chapter 20).

docs.title: AWS is pulling functions into S3
docs.text:
• S3 Express One Zone (November 2023): single-AZ "directory buckets", up to 10× faster than S3 Standard with 50% lower request cost (AWS-stated)15, aiming at single-digit-millisecond latency. April 2025 cuts took storage from $0.16 to $0.11 per GB-month and GETs down 85%16. The trade-off is one-AZ durability.
  • S3 Tables (December 2024): managed Apache Iceberg tables with automatic compaction, moving lakehouse upkeep into the storage service17.
  • S3 Vectors (preview July 2025, GA December 2025): 2 billion vectors per index, 20 trillion per bucket, up to 90% cheaper than dedicated vector databases (AWS-stated)18; see Chapter 33.

docs.title: Why S3 became the AI data interface
docs.text: Four forces converged. Lakehouses: Iceberg, Delta and Hudi tables are Parquet files plus manifests in object storage. Data loaders: PyTorch S3 connectors and WebDataset-style libraries stream shards without mounting anything. Checkpoint libraries: distributed checkpoints are large files, ideal for parallel multipart PUTs. Inference: NVIDIA Dynamo's KV Block Manager uses remote object storage as its fourth cache tier after HBM, DRAM and local SSD19, and CoreWeave puts an object cache (LOTA) on every GPU node, claiming up to 7 GB/s per GPU (company-stated)20. One API runs on every cloud, neocloud and on-prem system with no client kernel modules. What was missing was GPU-feeding bandwidth.

docs.title: S3 over RDMA
docs.text:
Classic S3 pushes every byte through TCP, TLS, HTTP parsing and a host-memory bounce, so both CPUs touch every byte and throughput hits a CPU and DRAM wall before a 400 GbE link fills. S3 over RDMA splits the request in two:

Figure 9.5 — S3 over RDMA keeps HTTP for authentication and metadata but hands bulk bytes to the NICs, removing the CPU and bounce-buffer copies from the data path.

The client registers a GPU or host buffer and puts a token describing it in a header (x-amz-rdma-token) of a normal SigV4-signed request. The server authenticates and looks up metadata as usual, then moves the bytes to or from that buffer by RDMA over RoCEv2 or InfiniBand; the HTTP reply just confirms completion21. Some servers fall back to HTTP bodies for non-RDMA clients21; MinIO instead returns x-amz-rdma-reply: 50122. It is PIO versus DMA: the CPU issues a descriptor, the DMA engine moves the payload, as in GPUDirect Storage for files (Chapter 11).

Who is doing it. MinIO shipped S3 over RDMA in November 202423, and Cloudian showed GPUDirect for object the same month (>200 GB/s claimed)24. NVIDIA productised the pattern as "RDMA for S3-compatible storage" (cuObject libraries), naming Cloudian, Dell and HPE as adopters, in mid-November 2025, with general availability promised via the CUDA Toolkit in January25. cuObject 1.0 release notes date from January 202626; by autumn 2026 NVIDIA called the libraries generally available and was working with Google Cloud and Microsoft on standardisation (xio-sig)27. IBM Storage Scale (June 2026)28, Dell ObjectScale 4.329 and the open-source Versity gateway, which also has an experimental AMD variant21, followed. Vendor numbers are not comparable: Cloudian claims 35 GB/s per node and 90% lower CPU30; MinIO reports a 16 GiB checkpoint loading in 0.65 s versus 12.16 s over tuned HTTP31.

The caveat is fragmentation: these headers are ecosystem conventions, not AWS's API, and AWS does not offer RDMA to S3. For now it is an on-prem and neocloud GPU-fabric protocol.

Table 9.2 — Everyone speaks S3; differentiation is moving to RDMA, small-object and LIST performance, and data services.

Steelman for object-native vendors: built for S3 semantics from day one, now with RDMA throughput, usually cheaper per TB. Steelman for unified platforms (FlashBlade, VAST): AI pipelines mix POSIX tools and object-native lakehouses over the same data, and copying between silos is costly. Everpure's own read of re:Invent 2025 treated AWS's S3 moves as evidence that enterprise AI is converging on object37. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: publishing FlashBlade S3-over-RDMA results (MLPerf Storage now has an S3 path1), on-prem equivalents of S3 Tables/Vectors, and positioning against HPE and Dell bundles with NVIDIA certification.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title S3 from web storage to AI data plane
    2006 : Amazon S3 launches with a simple REST API
    2020 : S3 becomes strongly consistent for all operations
    2023 : S3 Express One Zone and directory buckets
    2024 : S3 Tables for Iceberg : MinIO and Cloudian ship S3 over RDMA
    2025 : Pure Storage announces FlashBlade S3 over RDMA : S3 Vectors preview then GA : NVIDIA RDMA for S3 with Cloudian, Dell, HPE : S3 objects up to 50 TB
    2026 : cuObject 1.0 then GA : IBM Storage Scale S3 with RDMA : MLPerf Storage v3.0 adds S3

Figure 9.6 — S3 went from web-backup API to the interface AI frameworks target first, and gained a GPU-native data path in 2024–2026.

S3 launched in March 2006 and held over 100 trillion objects by 202138. Its API became a de facto standard without a standards body: vendors cloned it, and compatibility is defined by test suites. Forward signals: GPU-native data paths (cuObject standardisation), Google's zonal Rapid Storage replacing plain HTTP with a stateful gRPC protocol39, and S3 absorbing tables and vectors. The contest is moving from "do you support S3?" to small-GET latency, LIST rate and what runs inside the bucket.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "When a neocloud asks for S3 over RDMA, what do we ship, on which FlashBlade models, with which client libraries?" Strong: GA status, cuObject compatibility, supported NICs and measured GB/s per node.
  2. "How do we beat an object-native vendor with RDMA and lower $/TB?" Strong: unified file and object on the same data, small-object and LIST performance, data reduction, with a deal example.
  3. "Which AWS S3 features do customers want on-prem: conditional writes, low latency, Iceberg tables, vectors?" Strong: prioritised by deal impact, gaps admitted.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What is our LIST rate on a 1-billion-key bucket, and how does it scale?" Strong: keys per second and how the index is sharded.
  2. "Where is a PUT's linearisation point, and what does another reader see mid-upload?" Strong: index commit, atomic multipart completion, conditional-write enforcement.
  3. "In S3 over RDMA, how is the token secured and what happens to TLS?" Strong: auth stays on HTTP, tokens are scoped and expiring, and the answer explains how an unencrypted fabric payload is mitigated.

Don't say this:

  • "S3 is slow, cold storage." Express One Zone targets single-digit ms; RDMA-attached S3 feeds GPUs at tens of GB/s per node.
  • "S3 is eventually consistent." Not on AWS since December 2020; ask about cross-site consistency.
  • "Object storage has folders." It has prefixes; renaming one copies every object.
  • "S3-compatible means identical." Consistency, limits and RDMA headers vary.
  • "S3 over RDMA is an AWS feature." It is an NVIDIA and vendor ecosystem for on-prem GPU fabrics.

docs.title: 10. Datacenter networking for storage
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Block protocols and NVMe-oF · File protocols · Performance and economics metrics

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• In an AI cluster the network is part of the storage system. Fabric design, congestion behaviour and NIC offloads decide delivered throughput as much as the array does.
  • RDMA is DMA stretched across a fabric. The NIC moves data between registered memory regions with no kernel copies and no remote CPU.
  • Ethernet has won the volume argument against InfiniBand. Dell'Oro reports Ethernet took more than two-thirds of AI back-end switch sales in 2025, up from about 20% two years earlier1. InfiniBand still anchors many of the largest training clusters.
  • RoCE's weak spot is congestion. Classic RoCEv2 assumes a lossless fabric (PFC pauses plus ECN-driven DCQCN). Spectrum-X, Ultra Ethernet (UEC 1.0, June 2025) and Meta's 2026 MetaRoCE all try to escape that fragility23.
  • The DPU is moving storage logic into the NIC. NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX reference architecture (March 2026) runs storage services on an 800G DPU. Everpure is a named co-design partner, alongside nearly every competitor45.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
In AI deals, the storage vendor is a guest at a table NVIDIA sets. NVIDIA also sells the NIC, the DPU, the switches and the reference architectures that say which storage plugs in where. NVIDIA's networking revenue reached a reported US$14.8 billion in the quarter to April 2026, up 199% year on year6. Storage that performs well and is certified on NVIDIA's fabric makes the shortlist.

Three questions follow. Does Everpure's Ethernet-only posture cost it InfiniBand-built clusters, or save engineering spend on a shrinking fabric? Does BlueField-hosted storage software commoditize the array controller, where Purity creates value? And which network camp should Everpure lean toward: NVIDIA, Cisco (where CEO Charles Giancarlo spent 14 years7), Arista, or UEC? See Chapter 11 for the GPU data path and Chapter 34 for certifications.

docs.title: Three networks, not one
docs.text:
AI clusters run separate fabrics because traffic patterns conflict:

flowchart LR
    U["Users, data sources, internet"] --> FE["Front-end network: north-south, 100-400G Ethernet"]
    FE --> N1["GPU node A"]
    FE --> N2["GPU node B"]
    N1 <--> BE["Back-end compute fabric: east-west GPU-to-GPU, 400-800G per GPU, InfiniBand or RoCE"]
    N2 <--> BE
    N1 --> SN["Storage network: 2 x 200-400G per node, RoCE or TCP"]
    N2 --> SN
    SN --> S1["Shared file and object storage"]
    SN --> S2["Context-memory tier, KV cache"]
    N1 -.-> NV["Scale-up domain inside the rack: NVLink, not storage"]

Figure 10.1 — Storage traffic usually rides its own fabric (or a converged front-end), sized at a fraction of the GPU-to-GPU back-end but with nastier traffic patterns.

  • Front-end (north-south): user requests, ingest, management, and in many designs storage too (a "converged" front-end).
  • Back-end compute fabric (east-west): GPU collectives such as all-reduce, usually one NIC per GPU. It is the costliest network and the one InfiniBand-versus-Ethernet fights are about. Meta runs a dedicated training back-end so it can evolve independently8.
  • Storage network: feeds datasets, absorbs checkpoints and increasingly serves KV cache (Chapter 32).

Worked example (illustrative). Take a 1,024-GPU cluster: 128 nodes of 8 GPUs. If each GPU has an 800G back-end NIC, injection bandwidth is 128 × 8 × 800 Gb/s ≈ 819 Tb/s. If each node has 2 × 400G storage ports, the storage side is 128 × 800 Gb/s ≈ 102 Tb/s (12.8 TB/s), about one-eighth as much. Now checkpoint a 405B-parameter model with optimizer state, roughly 405e9 × 16 bytes ≈ 6.5 TB, in 60 seconds. That needs 108 GB/s ≈ 0.86 Tb/s, under 1% of the client-side storage capacity. The bottleneck is the storage-side ports: 0.86 Tb/s lands on a handful of 400G ports (two to three at line rate). On writes, many clients converge on a few storage ports; on reads, each client striping across many storage nodes receives from all of them at once. Both are incast (many senders, one receiving port), the defining pathology of storage networks.

docs.title: RDMA: DMA across a fabric
docs.text:
On a chip, a DMA engine moves blocks between memory and a peripheral while the CPU does other work. RDMA (remote direct memory access) gives the NIC a DMA engine whose address space spans the fabric. The application registers a memory region once (the kernel pins it and gives the NIC the translation), then posts work requests to a queue pair by ringing a doorbell. The RDMA NIC (RNIC) does the transport in silicon.

Figure 10.2 — RDMA removes the kernel copies and the remote CPU from the data path; the kernel only sets up memory registration and queue pairs.

Three properties matter for storage:

  1. Zero-copy. No CPU copy between application (or GPU) memory and the wire.
  2. Kernel bypass. No system call, interrupt or socket per I/O.
  3. One-sided operations. An RDMA READ or WRITE completes without the target's CPU, which disaggregated designs rely on (Chapter 16).

Worked example (illustrative arithmetic): why the copy matters at 400G. A 400 Gb/s port carries 50 GB/s. On kernel TCP receive, the NIC DMAs 50 GB/s into kernel buffers, and the CPU then reads 50 GB/s and writes 50 GB/s to copy into user space. That is ~150 GB/s of DRAM traffic per port. A server socket with 12 channels of DDR5-4800 peaks at 12 × 38.4 ≈ 461 GB/s. Two 400G ports running TCP at line rate would use ~65% of that before the application touches a byte. With RDMA, the same two ports cost ~100 GB/s of DMA. Per-I/O overhead compounds this: at 4 KiB, 50 GB/s is ~12 million I/Os per second; at an assumed 2 µs of kernel CPU each, that is ~24 busy cores. WEKA gets a similar effect without RDMA by running its own user-space stack over DPDK9.

The transports differ in what carries the RDMA:

  • InfiniBand: a purpose-built fabric with credit-based flow control (send only when the receiver has buffer) and a central subnet manager.
  • RoCEv2 (2014): InfiniBand's transport inside routable UDP/IP packets on ordinary Ethernet. Meta uses it for most of its AI capacity8; Microsoft reported RDMA carrying ~70% of Azure's traffic10.
  • TCP options: iWARP has lost the market; NVMe/TCP and NFS over TCP remain the "no special network" choices (Chapter 7).
Dimension InfiniBand (NVIDIA Quantum) Ethernet with RoCEv2 (standard switches) Ethernet, AI-tuned (Spectrum-X, UEC) Loss handling Lossless by design: link-level credits Needs PFC to be lossless; drops hurt older RNICs badly Spectrum-X: lossless RoCE plus adaptive routing. UEC: lossy or lossless11 Congestion control Built-in, centrally managed DCQCN (ECN + rate cuts); hard to tune at scale8 Telemetry-driven (Spectrum-X); new UET congestion control (UEC) Multipath Adaptive routing in switches Per-flow ECMP hashing; elephant flows collide Per-packet spraying, NIC reorders packets In-network compute SHARP reductions in switches None Limited; vendor-specific Suppliers Effectively NVIDIA only Broadcom, NVIDIA, Cisco, Marvell, others; many OEMs NVIDIA (Spectrum-X); Broadcom, AMD, Cisco and others (UEC) Operations Separate skills and tooling Same as rest of datacenter, but PFC/ECN tuning is specialist Ethernet tooling plus vendor-specific features Storage support Long native support in HPC file systems (Lustre, GPFS) Broadest: NVMe/RoCE, NFS over RDMA, S3 over RDMA Spectrum-X storage results from DDN, VAST, WEKA, Everpure1213 2025 AI back-end share Under one-third of switch sales Ethernet more than two-thirds combined1 (included at left)

Table 10.1 — InfiniBand sells predictability from a single vendor. Ethernet sells supplier choice and operational familiarity, and has had to bolt on what InfiniBand had natively.

docs.title: Congestion control: why "lossless" matters for RoCE
docs.text:
TCP treats a drop as normal. RNICs were designed for InfiniBand's lossless links, and many generations recover with go-back-N: one drop forces retransmission of everything sent after it, so even 0.1% loss can collapse goodput. RoCE fabrics are therefore engineered not to drop:

sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Storage senders
    participant SW as Switch egress queue
    participant R as Receiving client RNIC
    S->>SW: incast burst from many storage nodes
    Note over SW: queue passes ECN threshold
    SW->>R: forward packets marked Congestion Experienced
    R->>S: Congestion Notification Packet
    S->>S: DCQCN cuts sending rate, then probes back up
    Note over SW: if queue still passes PFC XOFF threshold
    SW->>S: PFC PAUSE for this priority class
    Note over S,SW: upstream link stops, which can spread congestion to innocent flows
    SW->>S: PFC RESUME when queue drains

Figure 10.3 — ECN plus DCQCN is the first, end-to-end brake; PFC is the emergency brake that prevents drops but can freeze whole links.

  • ECN + DCQCN. Switches mark packets as queues build; the receiver echoes a notification and the sender's NIC cuts its rate. DCQCN (Microsoft and Mellanox, 2015) became the default RoCE algorithm14.
  • PFC (Priority Flow Control). If a queue keeps growing, the switch sends a pause frame upstream for that traffic class. Nothing drops, but the paused link stops unrelated flows too: head-of-line blocking, congestion spreading and, rarely, deadlock14.

Worked example (illustrative): lossless costs buffer. After sending PAUSE, a switch must absorb whatever is already in flight. On a 400G link with 100 m of fibre (≈0.5 µs each way), the round trip alone is about 1 µs; take ~1 µs as a floor, since switch and NIC reaction time adds more. That is 50 GB/s × 1 µs = 50 KB, plus a maximum-size frame in each direction, or about 70 KB of reserved headroom per port per lossless class. A 64-port switch reserves ~4.5 MB just for this, and twice that at 800G. In shallow-buffer AI switch ASICs, that is buffer unavailable for absorbing incast.

There are three answers. Tune harder, though Meta found DCQCN difficult to tune for its training collectives8. Make the fabric smarter: Spectrum-X pairs NVIDIA switches with SuperNICs that spray packets across all paths, reorder them and apply telemetry-based rate control. NVIDIA reports 20–48% higher storage reads than standard RoCE with DDN, VAST and WEKA12; Everpure reports +25% reads, +23% writes and better noisy-neighbour isolation on FlashBlade//EXA13 [VERIFY: search-summary only]. All are vendor-run tests. Stop needing lossless: UEC 1.0 (published 11 June 2025) defines a new transport, UET, with per-packet multipathing, out-of-order delivery and support for lossy fabrics, plus optional link-level retry and credit-based flow control211. Meta's August 2026 MetaRoCE likewise treats Ethernet as lossy, with no PFC3 [VERIFY: search-summary only].

docs.title: The DPU in the storage path
docs.text:
A SmartNIC offloads fixed functions (checksums, RoCE, encryption). A DPU adds a general-purpose CPU complex and memory, so it can run a storage client, a storage target or a firewall. It is the server's I/O die becoming a programmable chiplet.

BlueField-3 is a 400G part with 16 Arm cores. BlueField-4, announced October 2025 for 2026, combines an 800G ConnectX-9 with a 64-core Grace CPU, which NVIDIA claims is 6× BlueField-3's compute1516.

flowchart LR
    subgraph GPU["GPU server"]
        G["GPUs, HBM"] --- C["Host CPU"]
        G --- B1["BlueField DPU or SuperNIC"]
    end
    B1 -->|"Spectrum-X storage fabric, RDMA"| B4
    subgraph STX["BlueField-4 STX storage node"]
        B4["BlueField-4: storage software, KV-cache manager, encryption, tenant isolation"] --- SSD["NVMe SSDs: CMX context-memory tier"]
    end
    B4 -->|"miss or persist"| SH["Shared storage: FlashBlade, VAST, DDN, WEKA and others"]
    B1 -.->|"offloads on client side: NVMe-oF initiator, crypto, multi-tenant policy"| C

Figure 10.4 — DPUs sit at both ends of the storage path: on the client they hide storage from the host, and in STX they become the storage controller.

DPUs play three storage roles:

  1. Client-side offload. The DPU terminates storage protocols and enforces encryption and tenant isolation, which matters to neoclouds renting bare metal.
  2. Target-side controller. VAST has used BlueField DPUs as the fabric endpoints inside its DBox enclosures since 202217.
  3. Storage software on the DPU. At CES 2026, NVIDIA announced a BlueField-4-based context-memory storage tier for KV cache18. At GTC on 16 March 2026 it generalized this into BlueField-4 STX, a modular storage reference architecture on Vera Rubin, BlueField-4 and Spectrum-X, whose first rack-scale implementation is the CMX context-memory platform4. The named co-design partners are Cloudian, DDN, Dell, Everpure, Hitachi Vantara, HPE, IBM, MinIO, NetApp, Nutanix, VAST and WEKA5. VAST says it will run its CNode software natively on BlueField-419. Everpure says it is aligning FlashBlade//EXA with STX20.

The tension: STX makes NVIDIA the reference controller hardware, so vendors compete on software running on NVIDIA silicon, which favours software-defined players over those differentiated by controller hardware.

docs.title: Link speeds and the SerDes engine underneath
docs.text:
Port speed is lane rate × lane count, and SerDes generations set the lane rate:

SerDes class Lane rate, modulation 4-lane port 8-lane port First IEEE standard 28G 25G NRZ 100GbE — 802.3bm-era 100GbE optics 56G 50G PAM4 200GbE 400GbE 802.3bs, Dec 201721 112G 100G PAM4 400GbE 800GbE 802.3ck, Sep 202222; 802.3df, Feb 202423 224G 200G PAM4 800GbE 1.6TbE 802.3dj, still in ballot Oct 202624

Table 10.2 — Each SerDes doubling yields the next port speed; PAM4 doubled bits per symbol at the price of tighter signal integrity, which is why reach shrinks and co-packaged optics arrive.

Figure 10.5 — Products now ship ahead of standards: NVIDIA's 800G InfiniBand and 1.6T-capable Ethernet silicon arrived before IEEE finished 1.6TbE. Data: data/ch10_link_speeds.csv

The 224G generation has arrived in silicon. Quantum-X800 (March 2024), whose 800G ports run on 200G-per-lane SerDes, was among the first switches of that generation25. Broadcom's Tomahawk 6 (June 2025) and NVIDIA's Spectrum-6 (CES 2026) both reach 102.4 Tb/s per chip2627. An 800G client port ingests 100 GB/s, more than a whole mid-range array, so arrays must scale out or sit behind a caching tier.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Vendor Fabric posture (public) NVIDIA networking alignment Other network alignment Everpure Ethernet only: NVMe/RoCE on FlashArray since Purity 5.2 (2019)28; FlashBlade on RoCE at 400GbE, 16 ports per FlashBlade//S R2 in SuperPOD designs29 SuperPOD-certified over Ethernet (2024)30; Spectrum-X testing13; STX co-design partner5 Cisco FlashStack and Secure AI Factory3132 VAST Data NFS over RDMA; BlueField DPUs inside DBoxes17 Spectrum-X tested12; CNode on BlueField-419 Cisco UCS and Nexus HyperFabric33 DDN Lustre heritage on InfiniBand (EXAScaler); Infinia on Ethernet Spectrum-X "Inferno" bundle (GTC 2025)34 HPC system integrators WEKA DPDK user-space stack over Ethernet or InfiniBand9 Spectrum-X tested12; STX integration Cloud-native networking (AWS, OCI) HPE Slingshot HPC fabric; claims ~75% of UEC's transport came from Slingshot2 STX partner5 UEC camp

Table 10.3 — Everpure is closely aligned with NVIDIA on Ethernet but, unlike DDN, VAST and WEKA, has no public InfiniBand story.

Steelman for Everpure's Ethernet-only stance. The market is moving its way: Ethernet has passed two-thirds of AI back-end switch sales1, one fabric family keeps engineering focused, and Cisco offers a route into enterprise AI factories.

Steelman for the competitors. In the largest InfiniBand training clusters, DDN, VAST and WEKA can attach natively and Everpure cannot [VERIFY: whether any FlashBlade model offers InfiniBand connectivity]. VAST's BlueField head start (DBoxes since 2022) gives it a natural STX story. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: whether Purity's metadata and data-reduction engines could run on BlueField-4 as an STX "personality"; how much Spectrum-X certification depth matters versus UEC neutrality as Broadcom-based fabrics grow; and whether a deeper Cisco or Arista alignment hedges against NVIDIA's dual role as partner and reference-architecture gatekeeper.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title RDMA and AI fabrics for storage
    2000 : InfiniBand 1.0 specification
    2014 : RoCEv2 makes RDMA routable over UDP and IP
    2015 : DCQCN congestion control published
    2017 : IEEE 400GbE approved
    2019 : Pure Storage ships NVMe over RoCE on FlashArray : NVIDIA agrees to buy Mellanox
    2022 : VAST puts BlueField DPUs in DBoxes
    2024 : IEEE 800GbE approved : Quantum-X800 InfiniBand : Meta details RoCE for AI training
    2025 : Spectrum-X storage results : Tomahawk 6 ships : UEC 1.0 published : BlueField-4 announced : Ethernet passes two-thirds of AI back-end sales
    2026 : BlueField-4 STX and CMX : Spectrum-6 : MetaRoCE goes lossy : 1.6TbE in final ballot

Figure 10.6 — RDMA spent 20 years as an HPC niche, then AI made it the default storage transport, and the argument shifted from "InfiniBand or Ethernet" to "which kind of Ethernet".

InfiniBand began around 2000 as an effort to replace server I/O and survived in HPC, where Mellanox made it the default. Buying Mellanox (announced 11 March 2019 at US$6.9 billion; closed April 2020) gave NVIDIA both the leading InfiniBand stack and the leading RNIC line35. The Ultra Ethernet Consortium formed in July 2023 as a Linux Foundation (Joint Development Foundation) project, founded by AMD, Arista, Broadcom, Cisco, Eviden, HPE, Intel, Meta and Microsoft, to bring InfiniBand-like behaviour to open Ethernet36. NVIDIA was not a founder. SNIA's Storage.AI project (August 2025) lists UEC as a partner, hinting that storage protocols will be profiled for UET37.

Three signals for 2026–2028: (1) 1.6T client ports on 224G SerDes as 802.3dj completes24; (2) lossy-tolerant RDMA (UEC, MetaRoCE) easing PFC tuning; (3) storage software moving onto DPUs via STX, with 2H 2026 hardware4.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In which AI deals do we lose because the customer's fabric is InfiniBand?" A strong answer quantifies lost opportunities and knows whether those customers run a separate Ethernet storage network anyway, which is common.
  2. "What does BlueField-4 STX mean for our controller roadmap: partner, port or compete?" A strong answer separates the CMX context-memory tier from the full controller role and has a view on Purity running on Arm/Grace.
  3. "How much of a FlashBlade//EXA bill of materials is networking, and who supplies it?" A strong answer gives a percentage and says whether the customer's fabric is reused.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Do we require PFC for RoCE, and what happens on a lossy fabric?" Strong: it names the RNIC's loss-recovery mode, the throughput drop at 0.01–0.1% loss, and recommended ECN and PFC thresholds.
  2. "How does a 128-client checkpoint burst behave at our storage-side ports?" Strong: it quotes incast measurements and whether packet spraying helps or hurts NFS-over-RDMA.
  3. "What is our UEC plan?" Strong: it knows which NICs ship UET and how NFS, NVMe-oF and S3 over RDMA would map onto it.

Don't say this:

  • "RDMA is just faster Ethernet." RDMA is a transport that runs over InfiniBand or Ethernet.
  • "InfiniBand is dead." It still anchors many of the largest training clusters and grew strongly in Q2 20251.
  • "Lossless means no congestion." PFC prevents drops by pausing links, which can spread congestion.
  • "800G means 800 GB/s." It is 800 Gb/s, which is 100 GB/s before protocol overhead.
  • "A DPU is a SmartNIC." A DPU runs general-purpose software; that distinction is the whole STX argument.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• RDMA / RNIC — remote direct memory access; the NIC that implements it in hardware.
  • RoCEv2 — RDMA transport carried in UDP/IP over Ethernet.
  • PFC, ECN, DCQCN — pause frames, congestion marking and RoCE rate control.
  • Incast — many senders converging on one receiver port.
  • DPU / SuperNIC — NIC with its own CPU complex; NVIDIA's AI-tuned NIC.
  • UEC / UET — Ultra Ethernet Consortium and its transport.
  • SerDes, PAM4 — the lanes and four-level signalling behind port speeds.
  • See the glossary for the rest.
