docs.title: 11. The GPU data path
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Block protocols and NVMe-oF · File protocols · Datacenter networking for storage · Performance and economics metrics

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• The GPU is the expensive asset; storage's job is to keep it busy. At US$2.00–6.16 per H100-hour, each second a 1,024-GPU cluster waits on I/O costs US$0.57–1.75. Storage earns its keep through utilization, not its own price.
  • GPUDirect Storage (GDS) removes the CPU "bounce buffer". The NIC or SSD writes straight into GPU memory over PCIe, freeing CPU and DRAM bandwidth. It raises the per-node ceiling; it does not make the storage system faster.
  • Most LLM training is compute-bound. A 70B model on 1,024 GPUs reads a few MB/s of tokens. Storage matters in bursts: checkpoints, restores, multimodal loading and inference KV-cache loads.
  • Know the stack. Magnum IO is the umbrella, GPUDirect RDMA the primitive, cuFile the GDS API, NIXL the inference transfer library, Dynamo the orchestrator that calls NIXL.
  • GDS is table stakes. Nearly every AI storage vendor, including Everpure's FlashBlade//S, claims it. Deals turn on aggregate throughput, checkpoint behaviour and KV-cache integration.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
In AI deals the largest line item is GPUs, so storage is sold as "we keep your US$50 million of GPUs busy", not "we are cheaper per terabyte". Every vendor therefore stakes out the GPU data path: GDS certification, RDMA protocols and now NIXL plugins for KV cache. Failing these checks costs a place in NVIDIA reference architectures (Chapter 34); passing them wins nothing by itself.

The path has moved from bulk file reads (GDS, 2019–2021) to object over RDMA (2024–2025) to latency-sensitive KV-cache tiers orchestrated by Dynamo (2025–2026). That last step makes storage part of inference serving, which is recurring spend, and it is where Everpure's PureKVA, WEKA's Augmented Memory Grid and DDN's Infinia now compete (Chapter 32).

docs.title: "Keep the GPU fed" is the whole game
docs.text:
A GPU cluster is a fab: a fixed-cost machine whose margin is set by utilization. Its cost accrues by the hour whether or not it computes, and storage, a small share of capex, can idle all of it. CoreWeave lists an 8× HGX H100 node at US$49.24 per hour, or US$6.16 per GPU-hour1. Specialist clouds and marketplaces span roughly US$1.49 to US$6.982. A 1,024-GPU cluster at US$3.99 per GPU-hour, Lambda's 2026 on-demand 8× H100 rate as reported by several price trackers3 [VERIFY: Lambda's own pricing page has also shown US$2.99], costs 1,024 × 3.99 = US$4,086 per hour, or about US$35.8 million a year. One percent idle is US$358,000 a year.

At scale, a large share of idle time comes from interruptions. Meta's Llama 3 run on 16,384 H100s logged 466 interruptions in 54 days yet exceeded 90% effective training time, partly by cutting job-startup and checkpoint time4. Each interruption reloads the last checkpoint, so storage sets the restart cost.

docs.title: Where storage actually stalls a GPU
docs.text:
Steady-state LLM training needs far less bandwidth than people assume. Take a 70B dense model on 1,024 H100s. At 40% utilization of the ~989 dense BF16 TFLOPS of an H100, the cluster processes about 1,024 × 989×10¹² × 0.4 ÷ (6 × 70×10⁹) ≈ 0.96 million tokens per second. At ~4 bytes per token ID, that is ~4 MB/s for the whole cluster. Any NAS serves that; GDS does nothing for it. Storage stalls GPUs in four places:

  1. Checkpoint saves. With Adam in mixed precision, the full training state is about 16 bytes per parameter: bf16 weights (2) and gradients (2), fp32 master weights (4) and two fp32 Adam moments (4 + 4). Gradients are usually not saved, so a real checkpoint is closer to 14 bytes per parameter (Chapter 31 walks through the variants); this example uses 16 as a round upper bound. A 70B model therefore checkpoints up to 70×10⁹ × 16 = 1.12 TB. Written synchronously at 20 GB/s, that takes 56 s. Every 30 minutes, that is 3.1% of wall-clock time spent idle.
  2. Checkpoint restores. Every GPU reads its shard at once, the burstiest read storage sees.
  3. Multimodal data loading. Samples are megabytes. For many vision and audio models, Mohan et al. found training time dominated by "data stalls" (fetch plus pre-processing)5.
  4. Inference KV-cache loads. A Llama 3 70B token needs 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dimensions × 2 (key and value) × 2 bytes ≈ 320 KiB of KV cache4. A 32K-token context is ~10.7 GB, and fetching it must beat recomputing ~2 × 70×10⁹ × 32,768 ≈ 4.6×10¹⁵ FLOPs (a second or more even on eight GPUs). The load is latency-critical and repeats for every returning user (Chapter 32).

Figure 11.1 — Worked example: storage stalls cost seven figures a year on a mid-sized cluster, but software (async checkpointing) removes more of that cost than faster hardware does. Data: data/ch11_gpu_idle_cost.csv

The nuance: raising checkpoint bandwidth from 20 to 100 GB/s saves ~US$0.9 million a year at mid-tier pricing, but asynchronous checkpointing saves nearly all of it in software. GPUs copy state to host DRAM in a second or two and keep training while the CPU drains it, so storage need only absorb the checkpoint within the interval. Chapter 31 works through the 405B and 1T cases.

docs.title: The traditional path: the bounce buffer
docs.text:
On a standard Linux server, read() lands data in host DRAM (page cache or a pinned staging buffer); cudaMemcpy then moves it to GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Each byte crosses the memory bus twice, and the CPU pays for system calls, copies and cache management.

Figure 11.2 — GPUDirect replaces two trips through host DRAM with one peer-to-peer DMA across the PCIe switch; the CPU keeps control but stops touching data.

Worked example (why the bounce buffer bites). Give a GPU node 200 GB/s of storage-facing network, for example four 400 Gb/s ports. Bounce-buffering 200 GB/s generates about 400 GB/s of DRAM traffic. A dual-socket server with eight channels of DDR5-4800 per socket has 2 × 8 × 38.4 ≈ 614 GB/s of theoretical peak. Staging copies would consume about two-thirds of it, competing with data-loader processes; if NIC and GPU sit on different sockets, every byte also crosses the inter-socket link. It is the classic case for peer-to-peer DMA past the host bridge: stop using scarce memory bandwidth as a transit lounge.

NVIDIA's original GDS write-up made the point at system scale: on a DGX-2, CPU memory could feed GPUs at ~50 GB/s, while drives and NICs reaching GPUs directly could aggregate to nearly 200 GB/s6.

docs.title: GPUDirect RDMA and GPUDirect Storage
docs.text:
GPUDirect RDMA is the primitive: the GPU exposes a window of its memory on PCIe, nvidia-peermem registers it with the RDMA stack, and a NIC DMAs straight into HBM. NCCL moves gradients this way (Chapter 10).

GPUDirect Storage applies it to file and block I/O. The application calls cuFile (cuFileRead with a GPU buffer instead of read); the file-system client turns the offset into a storage request with a GPU address as DMA target; the NIC or local NVMe SSD writes directly into GPU memory7.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as App on CPU
    participant K as FS client
    participant H as Host DRAM
    participant N as RDMA NIC
    participant S as Storage
    participant G as GPU HBM
    Note over A,G: Traditional path
    A->>K: read 64 MB into host buffer
    K->>S: request over fabric
    S->>N: data
    N->>H: DMA into bounce buffer
    K-->>A: read complete
    A->>G: cudaMemcpy host to device
    H->>G: second copy over PCIe
    Note over A,G: GPUDirect Storage path
    A->>K: cuFileRead into GPU buffer
    K->>S: request tagged with GPU address
    S->>N: data
    N->>G: RDMA write straight into HBM
    K-->>A: complete with no host copy

Figure 11.3 — The two paths issue the same storage request; GDS changes only where the bytes land, which is why it needs file-system client support but not a new storage protocol.

GDS's limits, which engineers will expect you to know:

  • The array's ceiling does not move. GDS raises what one client absorbs; a 100 GB/s array still delivers 100 GB/s.
  • Topology matters. Gains are largest when NIC or SSD and GPU share a PCIe switch; unsupported setups fall back to a bounce-buffer "compatibility mode"7.
  • The client must support it. NFS over RDMA, Lustre, WekaFS, IBM Storage Scale and BeeGFS clients do; NFS over TCP does not.
  • Data must arrive GPU-ready. CPU-side JPEG decode or augmentation forces a trip through host memory anyway. GDS helps when the GPU decodes (e.g., DALI) or the bytes are already tensors, as with checkpoints and KV blocks.

docs.title: The layer stack: Magnum IO, cuFile, NIXL and Dynamo
docs.text:
The names nest; confusing them loses an engineer fast.

flowchart TB

        PT["PyTorch and data loaders"]
        INF["vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM"]
    end
    subgraph ORCH["Inference orchestration"]
        DYN["Dynamo: KV-aware routing, KVBM tiers"]
    end
    subgraph LIB["Transfer libraries"]
        NIXL["NIXL: KV and tensor moves"]
        CUF["cuFile API = GDS"]
        CUO["cuObject: S3 over RDMA"]

    end
    subgraph DRV["Primitives and drivers"]
        RDMA["GPUDirect RDMA, nvidia-peermem"]
        UCX["UCX and libfabric"]
        NVFS["nvidia-fs, POSIX fallback"]
    end
    subgraph HW["Hardware and storage"]
        NIC["ConnectX or BlueField NICs, PCIe switches"]
        ST["File, NVMe-oF and object storage"]
    end
    INF --> DYN
    DYN --> NIXL
    PT --> CUF
    PT --> NCCL
    NIXL --> UCX
    NIXL --> CUF
    NIXL --> CUO
    CUF --> NVFS
    CUF --> RDMA
    CUO --> RDMA
    NCCL --> RDMA
    UCX --> RDMA
    RDMA --> NIC
    NVFS --> ST
    NIC --> ST
    classDef mio fill:#E6F0F8,stroke:#0072B2,stroke-width:2px
    class CUF,NCCL,RDMA,UCX,NVFS,CUO mio

Figure 11.4 — Magnum IO, shaded blue, is the I/O plumbing; NIXL and Dynamo sit above it for inference, so a storage vendor's integration point has moved up from "GDS-capable file system" to "NIXL backend".

  • Magnum IO is NVIDIA's umbrella for GPU I/O software (GPUDirect RDMA, GDS, NCCL, NVSHMEM, UCX), launched at SC19 in November 2019 with GDS in early access8. GDS 1.0 followed in 2021 with about a dozen storage partners9.
  • cuFile is the GDS API that data loaders and checkpoint writers call instead of POSIX.
  • cuObject does the same for S3: control stays in S3 calls, payload moves over RDMA; client SDK and object server both need changes10.
  • NIXL is an open-source (Apache 2.0) point-to-point library that moves KV blocks and tensors between GPU memory, CPU memory and storage via plug-ins including UCX, POSIX, GDS, object, Azure Blob, 3FS, Mooncake and libfabric11.
  • Dynamo is NVIDIA's open-source inference framework. Its KV Block Manager (KVBM) tiers KV cache across HBM (G1), host DRAM (G2), local SSD (G3) and remote storage (G4), with disk I/O through NIXL, using GDS where available12. Dynamo 1.0 shipped 2026-03-1613.

Semiconductor bridge: Magnum IO is the DMA engine and bus fabric, cuFile and NIXL the driver API, and Dynamo the memory controller's page policy, deciding what stays in "HBM" and what is evicted to "flash".

docs.text:
Vendor / system GPU-direct path claimed Inference / KV integration Notes DDN EXAScaler (Lustre) GDS, listed in NVIDIA partner tables since early releases14 Dynamo/NIXL KV cache on EXAScaler and Infinia (June 2026)15 Kernel Lustre client; HPC heritage WEKA NeuralMesh (WekaFS) GDS since 1.014 Augmented Memory Grid over RDMA and GDS; open-sourced a NIXL plugin16 Own kernel-bypass client VAST Data GDS via NFS over RDMA14 Dynamo integration [VERIFY: VAST NIXL backend status] Standard NFS client with RDMA and multipath IBM Storage Scale GDS (5.1.2 and newer)14 — GPFS client NetApp ONTAP GDS via NFS over RDMA; 171 GiB/s in an eight-node demo (company-stated)17 — AFX disaggregated line (2025) Dell PowerScale GDS via NFS over RDMA (OneFS 9.2 and newer)14 — pNFS "Lightning" variant (2025) Everpure FlashBlade//S GDS over NFS over RDMA, reported from Purity//FB 4.3.4 (October 2023)1819 [VERIFY: search-summary only; not seen in NVIDIA GDS release-note partner tables] PureKVA: KV cache on FlashBlade over NFS and S3, Dynamo integration, RDMA into GPU memory20 S3 over RDMA announced for the object store21 Everpure FlashBlade//EXA NFSv3 over RDMA data path to data nodes22; Portworx documents GDS on EXA file systems over RDMA NFS23 [VERIFY: search-summary only] Via PureKVA [VERIFY: EXA support] NVIDIA certification of EXA still in progress as of March 2026 (Chapter 34) Hammerspace GDS validation (company-stated, 2024)24 — NFS-based global namespace AWS FSx for Lustre GDS with EFA (Nov 2024)25 — First major cloud file service with GDS Cloudian HyperStore GPUDirect for object, S3 over RDMA (Nov 2024)26 — Object-first

Table 11.1 — Every serious AI storage vendor claims a GPU-direct path; the competitive frontier has moved to S3 over RDMA and KV-cache integration with Dynamo and NIXL.

The real trade-off is client architecture, not GDS. WEKA, DDN (Lustre) and IBM ship their own clients that open many RDMA connections per node and stripe across servers, giving the highest per-node throughput at the price of a kernel module to qualify on every GPU server. Everpure, VAST, NetApp and Dell use the standard Linux NFS client over RDMA: nothing to install, historically less per-client parallelism. FlashBlade//EXA narrows the gap with pNFS, sending clients directly to data nodes over NFSv3 on RDMA22 (Chapter 16).

Steelman the proprietary clients: on a 2,000-GPU checkpoint restore, per-node absorption and client striping set time-to-resume. Steelman the standard clients: operators of thousands of heterogeneous GPU servers save real effort by not qualifying a client, and compute-bound training rarely hits per-node peak.

Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: upstreaming a FlashBlade NIXL backend (WEKA open-sourced one), bringing S3 over RDMA and cuObject compatibility to EXA, and positioning PureKVA on latency versus capacity economics once NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX/CMX context-memory tier ships27.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title The GPU data path
    2019 : Magnum IO launched at SC19 : GDS in early access
    2021 : GDS 1.0 with a dozen storage partners
    2024 : FSx for Lustre adds GDS : GPUDirect for object storage over S3 RDMA
    2025 : Dynamo and NIXL arrive : FlashBlade EXA uses NFSv3 over RDMA data path : WEKA AMG ships with NIXL plugin
    2026 : Dynamo 1.0 in production : BlueField-4 STX and CMX context memory : DDN KV cache via Dynamo

Figure 11.5 — The GPU data path moved from bulk file reads to object over RDMA to latency-critical KV-cache tiers in about six years.

GPUDirect RDMA dates from Kepler-class GPUs and CUDA 5.0 (2012)28; GDS carried it into storage. Pure Storage said in 2022 that FlashBlade//S would support GDS the following year29 [VERIFY: search-summary only], and trade press reports support arriving with Purity//FB 4.3.4 in October 202319. Dynamo, announced at GTC on 18 March 202530, reached 1.0 in March 202613.

Three trends point forward. Object over RDMA: cuObject standardizes S3 over RDMA10, and Cloudian26 and Everpure21 have announced it, eroding the "file for performance, object for capacity" split (Chapter 9). A context-memory tier: NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX and CMX (GTC 2026) put KV-cache storage inside each pod, with Everpure, DDN, VAST, WEKA, NetApp and others as partners27; whoever supplies the software decides whether that commoditizes hardware or opens a new socket. GPU-initiated I/O: research systems let GPU threads issue NVMe commands without the CPU, which would move the storage client into the GPU.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In our last five lost AI deals, did GPU data path features decide it, or aggregate throughput and price?" Strong: separates checkbox items (GDS, certification) from deciding factors, with named cases.
  2. "What is PureKVA's measured time-to-first-token gain versus recompute and versus local NVMe, and on which model and context length?" Strong: gives model, context, concurrency and network, separates vendor from customer numbers, and says where the benefit vanishes.
  3. "Where does FlashBlade sit relative to Dynamo's G3 and G4 tiers and NVIDIA's CMX tier?" Strong: says whether Everpure competes with, supplies or sits behind CMX, and the revenue-per-GPU effect.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "With GDS on FlashBlade, what single-node read rate do we reach on a current HGX node, and what limits it: NIC, NFS client concurrency or the array?" Strong: a GB/s figure, the named bottleneck, and the nconnect/multipath settings.
  2. "How does a 4,000-GPU checkpoint restore behave: per-node rate, metadata load, time to resume?" Strong: time-to-resume, not peak bandwidth, including the open/stat storm on thousands of shard files.
  3. "Do we ship a NIXL backend, and is it the POSIX, GDS or OBJ plugin path?" Strong: the plugin, whether it is upstream, and block size and latency per KV fetch.

Don't say this:

  • "GDS makes storage faster." It removes a host copy; array throughput is unchanged.
  • "LLM training needs huge read bandwidth." Text needs MB/s; bursts come from checkpoints, restores and multimodal data.
  • "Magnum IO is a product you buy." It is a family of free NVIDIA libraries.
  • "NIXL is a storage protocol." It is a transfer library; underneath sit UCX/RDMA, POSIX, GDS or S3.
  • "Having GDS is a differentiator." Almost every vendor in Table 11.1 has it.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• NVIDIA GDS Overview, Design and Best Practices guides: topology rules, compatibility mode, gdsio, alignment7.
  • The NIXL repository and Dynamo's KVBM design document: plugins, memory registration, G1–G4 policy1112.
  • Mohan et al., "Analyzing and Mitigating Data Stalls in DNN Training," PVLDB 2021, on fetch versus pre-processing stalls5.
  • On GPU-initiated storage access: Qureshi et al., the BaM system (ASPLOS 2023).

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Bounce buffer — host-memory staging on the way to the GPU.
  • GPUDirect RDMA / GDS / cuFile — NIC or storage DMA into GPU memory, and the GDS API.
  • Magnum IO — NVIDIA's GPU I/O library umbrella.
  • NIXL / Dynamo / KVBM — inference transfer library, inference framework, KV tier manager.
  • cuObject — NVIDIA's S3-over-RDMA libraries.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 12. Interfaces and emerging tech
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Media physics for a semis person · Inside an SSD · Block protocols and NVMe-oF · The GPU data path

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• PCIe doubles every generation; the drive link is rarely the bottleneck. A PCIe 6.0 x4 link carries ~29.5 GB/s each way, so in shared storage the network and software set throughput.
  • CXL turns PCIe wires into a load/store memory bus. Expanders ship; pooling is starting; multi-host sharing is still in labs.
  • EDSFF replaced the 2.5-inch drive in hyperscale and AI servers, fixing watts and NAND per bay. Everpure's proprietary DirectFlash Module (DFM) sidesteps some of those limits.
  • FDP is commodity flash catching up with host-managed flash. It cuts write amplification without breaking software; Purity has managed raw NAND directly since DirectFlash launched.
  • Optane is the case study for any new memory tier: good physics, but a thin price gap, a CPU-locked ecosystem and one fab. CXL memory and KV-cache tiers face the same tests.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Interfaces decide what can be commoditised. With standard form factors and placement hints, a hyperscaler can buy flash from four NAND makers and run its own software. That is the alternative Everpure's DirectFlash licensing has to beat at Meta and at the second top-five hyperscaler announced in August 20261. FDP and EDSFF narrow the gap between proprietary modules and commodity SSDs.

AI inference adds a second contest: the KV-cache tier between GPU HBM and networked flash, where CXL memory, local NVMe and shared flash such as PureKVA compete (Chapter 32). Optane shows how such tiers fail.

docs.title: PCIe: the doubling machine
docs.text:
PCIe is a serial link of SerDes lanes: x4 for SSDs, x16 for GPUs and NICs. Each generation doubles the per-lane rate. The cadence stalled after PCIe 3.0 (November 2010)2. PCIe 4.0 took until October 20173, because 16 GT/s needed retimers and better board materials. Cloud and AI demand then restored a three-year rhythm: 5.0 in May 20194, 6.0 in January 20225, 7.0 in June 20256. PCIe 8.0, at 256 GT/s, is targeted for 20287.

Figure 12.1 — Each generation doubles the x4 link a drive uses; the first PCIe 6.0 SSD in volume reads at ~95% of its link, four years after the spec. Data: data/ch12_pcie_bandwidth.csv

Per direction, bandwidth = lanes × rate × encoding efficiency ÷ 8. PCIe 6.0 x4 gives 32 GB/s raw, ~29.5 GB/s after flit overhead. Micron's 9650, the first Gen6 data-centre SSD in mass production, reads at 28 GB/s8.

The consequence is counter-intuitive. A 2U server with 24 such drives holds 24 × 29.5 ≈ 708 GB/s of drive bandwidth; two 400 GbE ports carry ~100 GB/s. In an array, the network (Chapter 10), CPUs and software bind long before the drive link. Faster links matter most for GPU-local NVMe holding checkpoints and KV cache (Chapter 11).

docs.title: PCIe 6.0 one notch deeper: PAM4 and FLIT
docs.text:
With NRZ (one bit per symbol), 64 GT/s would push Nyquist to 32 GHz, where board losses are unmanageable. PCIe 6.0 adopted PAM4 (two bits per symbol), as 56G/112G Ethernet SerDes did earlier. The symbol rate stays at 32 GBaud, so the channel looks like PCIe 5.0's, but the three stacked eyes are each a third of the height. The raw error rate rises to roughly 10⁻⁶, against 10⁻¹² for NRZ generations.

Forward error correction (FEC) needs fixed-size blocks, so PCIe 6.0 introduced the FLIT. Each 256-byte flit carries 236 bytes of transaction data, a 6-byte link field, an 8-byte CRC and 6 bytes of FEC9. The FEC is deliberately light, single-symbol-correcting across three interleaves, so it adds only nanoseconds. The CRC catches the rest and triggers a flit replay10. For storage, dropping per-packet framing means small transfers (doorbells, completions, 64-byte CXL lines) waste less link, and PCIe and CXL now share one PHY and roadmap.

PCIe 5.0 PCIe 6.0 PCIe 7.0 Per-lane rate 32 GT/s 64 GT/s 128 GT/s Signalling NRZ PAM4 PAM4 Encoding 128b/130b + framing tokens 256-byte FLIT, FEC + CRC 256-byte FLIT x16, raw, both directions 128 GB/s 256 GB/s 512 GB/s x4 SSD, per direction ~15.75 GB/s ~29.5 GB/s ~59 GB/s

Table 12.1 — PCIe 6.0 changed modulation and encoding at once; PCIe 7.0 kept both and doubled the symbol rate (x16 from PCI-SIG456; x4 is worked arithmetic).

docs.title: CXL: memory semantics over PCIe wires
docs.text:
Compute Express Link runs three protocols on the PCIe PHY11: CXL.io (ordinary PCIe), CXL.cache (a device coherently caches host memory) and CXL.mem (the host loads and stores device memory). Type 1 devices (io + cache) are caching SmartNICs; Type 2 (all three) are accelerators whose memory joins the coherent space; Type 3 (io + mem) are memory expanders.

CXL.mem for the semis reader. The host's home agent sends 64-byte cache-line reads and writes, and the device returns data or completions. The device's DRAM is mapped into physical address space as host-managed device memory (HDM), usually exposed as a CPU-less NUMA node that software reaches with plain loads and stores. Passive expanders are host-coherent (HDM-H). CXL 3.0 added back-invalidate (HDM-DB). The device keeps a snoop filter and can recall lines from host caches, which is what lets several hosts share one region coherently11. Microsoft's Pond team measured direct-attached CXL memory at roughly 70–90 ns over local DRAM. That is a NUMA-hop penalty, not a storage one, and switches add more12.

flowchart LR
    subgraph HA["Host A"]
        CPUA["CPU + local DDR5"]
    end
    subgraph HB["Host B"]
        CPUB["CPU + local DDR5"]
    end
    T1["Type 1 SmartNIC<br/>CXL.io + CXL.cache"]
    T2["Type 2 accelerator with own memory<br/>io + cache + mem"]
    T3["Type 3 expander, direct attach<br/>CXL.io + CXL.mem"]
    SW{{"CXL switch"}}
    P1["Pooled Type 3<br/>slices assigned per host, CXL 2.0"]
    P2["Shared Type 3<br/>same lines visible to both hosts, CXL 3.x"]
    CPUA --- T1
    CPUA --- T2
    CPUA --- T3
    CPUA --- SW
    CPUB --- SW
    SW --- P1
    SW --- P2

Figure 12.2 — Direct-attached expansion ships, switched pooling is starting, and multi-host sharing (which needs CXL 3.x back-invalidate) is the frontier.

The spec runs well ahead of deployment. CXL 4.0 (November 2025) reached 128 GT/s on the PCIe 7.0 PHY, or 256 GB/s per direction on a x16 link, and added bundled ports that gang several links into one logical port (the consortium's white paper illustrates 768 GB/s per direction)13. Deployment lags:

  • Direct attach: Azure's M-series preview (November 2025) uses Astera Labs' CXL 2.0 controllers, up to 2 TB each14.
  • Pooling: Marvell has a CXL 2.0 switch in production and its next one sampling in Q3 202615.
  • Rack-scale AI pooling: demonstrations, such as Samsung with AMD at OCP 202616.

The economics are modest: Pond estimated a 16-socket pool trims DRAM needs by about 7%17. CXL memory is DRAM at DRAM prices.

docs.title: EDSFF: the form factor is a power contract
docs.text:
SNIA's EDSFF family replaced the 2.5-inch U.2 shape with ones designed for airflow, with power envelopes that scale with thickness. A form factor fixes watts and NAND packages per bay, and so fixes TB per rack unit.

Form factor Size (W × L; thickness) Max sustained power (air) Largest capacity seen (2026) Typical use U.2 (2.5-inch) 70 × 100 mm; 15 mm ~25 W [VERIFY: U.2 power class] 245.76 TB (Micron 6600 ION)18 ~24 bays per 2U; legacy servers and arrays E1.S 33.75 × 118.75 mm; 9.5 / 15 / 25 mm ~12 W (5.9 mm) to ~25 W (25 mm heat sink)19 [VERIFY: largest shipping E1.S] Dense compute and GPU nodes, e.g. Meta's GenAI clusters20 E1.L ("ruler") 38.4 × 318.75 mm; 9.5 / 18 mm ~25–40 W21 122.88 TB (Solidigm D5-P5336)22 Up to ~32 bays per 1U [VERIFY]; capacity JBOFs E3.S 76 × 112.75 mm; 7.5 mm (1T) / 16.8 mm (2T) 25 W (1T) / 40 W (2T)23 [VERIFY: largest shipping E3.S] Mainstream PCIe 5/6 servers; CXL memory modules E3.L 76 × 142.2 mm; 7.5 / 16.8 mm 40 W (1T) / 70 W (2T)23 245.76 TB (Micron 6600 ION)18 Capacity QLC in storage servers

Table 12.2 — EDSFF replaced one universal bay with shapes sized to their power envelope; capacity now concentrates in E3.L and U.2, density in E1.S.

Two constraints bind at the top end. First, controller DRAM: a conventional SSD's flash translation layer keeps ~4 bytes of map per 4 KiB page, i.e. 1 GB of DRAM per TB, or ~245 GB for a 245 TB drive. Big QLC drives therefore map in coarser units, and small random writes pay in read-modify-write amplification. Second, the standard's power and volume per bay.

Everpure's DirectFlash Module escapes both because it is not an SSD. Purity runs one global FTL and treats modules as raw NAND, so no drive-sized DRAM map is needed, and Everpure sets the module's shape and thermals (Chapter 26). DFMs reached 300 TB by 202624, on a roadmap first set in 202325, while the largest standard drives ship at 245.76 TB. The price: only Purity can drive a DFM. Meanwhile, in July 2025 the SFF TA reopened the E1/E3 power and thermal specs26.

docs.title: Data placement: ZNS, FDP and host-managed flash
docs.text:
NAND erases in large blocks, so when data with different lifetimes share a block, garbage collection (GC) must first copy the still-valid pages. If a block is 75% valid when collected, each host write costs 1 ÷ (1 − 0.75) = 4 NAND writes. That is a write amplification factor (WAF) of 4. The cure is to group data by lifetime so whole blocks die at once, which needs the host to tell the drive.

flowchart TB
    subgraph CONV["Conventional SSD"]
        direction LR
        C1["Host writes LBAs, no hints"] --> C2["Drive mixes hot and cold in one block"] --> C3["GC copies live pages, WAF up to 3-4x"]
    end
    subgraph ZNS["Zoned Namespaces"]
        direction LR
        Z1["Host writes each zone sequentially"] --> Z2["Host resets zones and runs GC"] --> Z3["WAF near 1, software must be rewritten"]
    end
    subgraph FDP["Flexible Data Placement"]
        direction LR
        F1["Host tags writes with a placement handle"] --> F2["Drive steers handles to separate reclaim units"] --> F3["Blocks die together, hints optional"]
    end
    subgraph DF["Host-managed raw flash, DirectFlash style"]
        direction LR
        D1["Array software sees NAND blocks"] --> D2["One global map and GC schedule"] --> D3["Placement and wear decided with full knowledge"]
    end

Figure 12.3 — ZNS and FDP move placement knowledge from drive to host by degrees; host-managed flash such as DirectFlash moves all of it.

ZNS (NVMe TP4053, ratified June 202027) exposes zones that must be written sequentially. Software must become zone-aware, so adoption stayed niche. FDP (NVMe TP4146, ratified late 2022) was driven by Meta and Google with Samsung. Writes carry a placement identifier, and the drive keeps identifiers in separate reclaim units. A drive that ignores the hints still works2829, which is why hyperscalers chose FDP.

Semis bridge. ZNS is a software-managed scratchpad; FDP is a hardware cache with hints, like non-temporal stores; DirectFlash is one memory controller managing every bank. For Everpure, FDP gives commodity SSDs much of DirectFlash's WAF benefit while keeping drives multi-sourced.

docs.title: Computational storage: why it stalled
docs.text:
Computational storage puts FPGAs or Arm cores in the drive to filter, compress or search data before it crosses PCIe. SNIA defined an architecture for it, and NVM Express added computational-program command sets [VERIFY: SNIA CS architecture v1.0 (2022) and NVMe computational command sets (2024)]. Outside transparent in-drive compression, and vendor-integrated modules such as IBM's FlashCore Modules (compression plus ransomware-detection statistics inside the array's own module30), adoption is thin:

  1. Data is striped. Erasure coding spreads a record across 10+ drives, so no single drive can filter it.
  2. Fragmentation. Every vendor shipped its own accelerator and toolchain.
  3. Procurement. Drive buyers pay for $/TB and reliability, not lock-in features.
  4. Compute moved up. Controllers, DPUs and GPUs took the offload; NVIDIA's BlueField-4 context-memory platform is computational storage at system level31.

Near-data compute wins in the array or DPU, where whole objects are visible, not in the drive.

docs.title: Optane: the lessons for any new memory tier
docs.text:
timeline
    title Optane and 3D XPoint, 2015 to 2025
    2015 : Intel and Micron announce 3D XPoint
    2017 : First Optane data-centre SSDs ship
    2019 : Optane persistent-memory DIMMs launch with Intel Xeon Scalable
    2021 : Micron exits 3D XPoint and sells its Lehi fab
         : VAST qualifies Kioxia SLC flash as a second SCM source
    2022 : Intel announces Optane wind-down with a 559 million dollar charge
    2025 : Final Optane DIMM shipments scheduled

Figure 12.4 — Optane went from launch to wind-down in about seven years; storage vendors that had a second source survived it.

The July 2022 wind-down and US$559 million charge are documented3233, as are Micron's March 2021 exit and June 2021 sale of the Lehi fab to Texas Instruments for US$900 million34; the 2015–2019 milestones are from background knowledge [VERIFY: Optane milestone dates 2015–2019]. Optane failed three non-technical tests:

  1. Price gap. Too dear against NAND, too slow against DRAM, while NAND $/GB kept falling.
  2. Ecosystem. The DIMMs needed Intel Xeons, and full value needed software rewritten for persistent memory, which few applications did.
  3. Single supplier. One fab, effectively one platform vendor. When Micron left in 2021 there was no second source; VAST had already qualified Kioxia SLC flash35.

What this implies for CXL memory and KV-cache tiers.

  • Price gap. CXL memory is DRAM: a bigger tier, not a cheap one. Flash keeps a wide gap below DRAM, and TrendForce links part of 4Q26 SSD demand to hyperscalers buying QLC for KV cache36. Synopsys claims CXL offloads KV 3.6× faster than SSDs37; the test is cost per token.
  • Ecosystem. CXL runs on Intel and AMD, an improvement. KV-cache frameworks (Dynamo, KVBM, LMCache) are this cycle's persistent-memory rewrite: the tier is only as useful as the software driving it.
  • Single supplier. The risk moved from media to platform: NVIDIA's BlueField-4 design sets the KV-tier reference31, and every vendor's KV product, PureKVA included38, must fit it.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Topic Everpure VAST WEKA / DDN Hyperscaler DIY Drive form factor Proprietary DFM, up to 300 TB24 Standard QLC SSDs in DBoxes Standard NVMe in partner servers E1.S / E3 standard drives20 Data placement Purity global FTL on raw NAND SCM write buffer, then wide sequential stripes File-system layout over drive FTLs FDP hints on commodity drives28 SCM / Optane exposure DirectMemory Cache (2019) used Intel Optane SSDs as an optional read cache in FlashArray//X70/X9039; not Optane-dependent today Optane at first; Kioxia SLC second source since 202135 None DRAM + flash KV-cache tier PureKVA on FlashBlade, RDMA into GPU memory38 CNode software on BlueField-4 DPUs31 WEKA Augmented Memory Grid; DDN Infinia Local NVMe; CXL pilots (Azure)14 Supply chain NAND from Micron and Kioxia; licence model at hyperscalers1 Partner hardware, multi-vendor SSDs Any qualified server/SSD Multi-sourced standard SSDs

Table 12.3 — Everpure is the only major vendor whose own flash module has no drive-level FTL (IBM also designs its FlashCore Modules, but they keep an in-module controller); that buys capacity, power and write-amplification advantages at the cost of a non-standard part.

Steelman the standard route. EDSFF plus FDP gives much of DirectFlash's benefit with four suppliers and no licence; the toll is per-drive DRAM and controllers. The 300 TB versus 245 TB lead must be re-earned each generation, and Sandisk's roadmap shows 512 TB in 202740. Steelman DirectFlash. A global FTL removes per-drive DRAM, controllers and over-provisioning, an edge that compounds as capacity grows. Two top-five hyperscalers have signed1.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
NVMe flash arrays, DirectFlash included, grew up on PCIe 3.0; GPUs then pulled the 2017–2025 sprint. Optane rose and fell in that window, and Intel redirected its memory-tier ambitions to CXL33. CXL went from direct attach (1.0, March 2019) to pooling (2.0, November 2020)41 and fabrics/sharing (3.0, August 202242; 3.1, November 2023 [VERIFY: 3.1 release day]), reaching 4.0 in November 202513. FDP displaced ZNS at hyperscale after 2022.

Watch through 2027: Gen6 platform volume, CXL 3.x switches leaving sampling, a bigger E3 power envelope, 512 TB standard drives, and KV tiers converging on NVIDIA's interfaces (Chapter 53).

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "If a hyperscaler can get FDP on 245 TB E3.L drives from four suppliers, what keeps DirectFlash ahead next cycle?" Strong: quantifies the gap per generation (TB per module, W per TB, DRAM avoided) and why it widens with capacity.
  2. "Where does PureKVA sit against CXL memory and local NVMe, on cost per token?" Strong: $/GB and latency per tier, and the hit rates that justify shared flash.
  3. "Which components are single-sourced today, and what did Optane teach us?" Strong: names NAND, controllers and DPUs, each with a mitigation.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What does PCIe 6.0 change inside an array?" Strong: fewer lanes, switches and watts per GB/s, not headline throughput, because the network binds first.
  2. "Would CXL memory help a controller with dedup tables or metadata?" Strong: separates capacity (tables grow with TB) from persistence (CXL DRAM is volatile).
  3. "How does Purity's WAF compare with FDP drives on a mixed workload?" Strong: measured WAF, and what system-wide GC scheduling buys.

Don't say this:

  • "PCIe 6.0 doubles array performance." The network and software usually bind first.
  • "CXL makes memory cheap." It makes memory poolable. The bits are still DRAM.
  • "Optane failed technically." It failed on economics, ecosystem and supply.
  • "DFMs are just big SSDs." They have no drive FTL.
  • "ZNS is the placement standard." Hyperscalers chose FDP.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• PCIe 6.0 flit layout and FEC: Cadence's flit-mode walkthrough9 and Lockwood's notes10.
  • CXL internals: Das Sharma, Blankenship and Berger43; the Linux back-invalidate work11.
  • CXL pooling economics: Pond17. FDP design: the NVM Express blog28.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• PAM4 — four-level signalling, two bits per symbol.
  • FLIT — fixed 256-byte PCIe 6.0+ transfer unit with FEC and CRC.
  • CXL Type 1/2/3 — caching device, accelerator with memory, memory expander.
  • CXL.mem / HDM — load/store protocol and the device memory it maps.
  • Back-invalidate — CXL 3.0 mechanism enabling multi-host sharing.
  • Memory pooling — assigning slices of switched memory to hosts.
  • EDSFF — data-centre SSD form factors (E1.S/E1.L/E3.S/E3.L).
  • FDP / ZNS — NVMe placement hints / sequential-write zones.
  • WAF — NAND writes per host write.
  • SCM — persistent media between DRAM and NAND, such as Optane.

docs.title: 13. The storage stack, layer by layer
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: What storage does · Inside an SSD · Block protocols and NVMe-oF · File protocols · Datacenter networking

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Every I/O crosses eight layers: application, file system or object API, volume manager, protocol, network, array software, SSD controller/FTL, media. Architectures differ in which layer holds the "intelligence": placement, protection, reduction and metadata.
  • Storage history is that intelligence moving: from the host (DAS), into a shared networked box (SAN and NAS, 1990s), across commodity server clusters (2000s), then into stateless compute over shared flash (late 2010s on).
  • Each layer crossed costs latency; each layer owned earns margin. A 4 KB database write takes ~20–40 µs on a local SSD and ~100–250 µs on a networked array. The extra microseconds buy shared, protected, reduced data.
  • Everpure owns three adjacent layers. Purity array software also does the FTL's job on raw NAND inside DirectFlash modules. Most rivals stop at array software; software-only vendors stop higher.
  • Vertical integration is a bet, not a default. It buys density, efficiency and a separately licensable layer (the hyperscaler wins), at the cost of more R&D and NAND supply exposure.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Part 3 compares architectures: dual-controller arrays, shared-nothing clusters, DASE, parallel file systems, object stores and HCI. Each is best read as an answer to one question: which layer does the clever work, and on whose hardware? That question maps onto the business. Owners of a scarce layer set prices; assemblers of commodity layers compete on cost. Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) reported a 70.4% GAAP gross margin for fiscal 20261; Supermicro, which builds servers largely from bought-in parts, reported 11.1% for fiscal 20252.

The stack is also a map of adjacencies. Everpure's hyperscaler wins license the bottom layers (DirectFlash modules and flash management) without the array software, on hardware the customer sources34. WEKA attacks from the top, selling software for partners' servers5.

docs.title: Eight layers, one I/O
docs.text:
Read the stack top to bottom as the path of a write:

  1. Application. A database, hypervisor or training job decides what must be durable, and when (for a database, at commit).
  2. File system or object API. Turns names (/db/redo01.log, a bucket and key) into blocks or objects and keeps the namespace, which is metadata (Chapter 21).
  3. Volume manager. Pools and remaps block addresses: LVM, software RAID, a hypervisor's storage layer.
  4. Protocol. SCSI or NVMe for blocks, NFS or SMB for files, S3 for objects (Chapters 7–9).
  5. Network. Fibre Channel, Ethernet or InfiniBand; in DAS, a PCIe slot (Chapter 10).
  6. Array controller software. Purity, ONTAP, VAST and the like: placement, RAID or erasure coding, snapshots, replication, reduction.
  7. SSD controller and FTL. Maps logical blocks to NAND pages, levels wear, collects garbage (Chapter 3).
  8. Media. NAND, storage-class memory or disk (Chapter 2).

Figure 13.1 — Every architecture has the same layers; what differs is which row holds the intelligence, and Everpure is unusual in owning rows 6 through 8 as one design.

"Intelligence" means four jobs: placing, protecting, shrinking and tracking data. Where an architecture puts them decides what its network carries and where it hits its scaling wall.

Semiconductor bridge: the compute stack. Computing runs from application to compiler to ISA to microarchitecture to memory controller to DRAM cells, and profit follows layer ownership. NVIDIA owns CUDA, the compiler and the silicon, and posted a 71.1% GAAP gross margin in fiscal 20266; a server assembler owning none of those layers earns about a sixth of that. In storage the FTL plays the memory controller's role: address mapping and wear management that hide media physics behind a clean interface. Whoever owns it decides how much raw NAND capability reaches the customer, and at what DRAM and spare-capacity cost. (Layers are not the whole margin story; R&D intensity and scale matter too.)

docs.title: Tracing one 4 KB database write
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["1 Database commit: 4 KB log write + fsync<br/>~1–5 µs"] --> B["2 File system and block layer in kernel<br/>~5–20 µs"]
    B --> C["3 Volume manager remaps address<br/>~1 µs"]
    C --> D["4 NVMe-oF initiator builds command<br/>RDMA ~5–15 µs, TCP ~20–35 µs adder"]
    D --> E["5 NIC and 2–3 switch hops<br/>~1–5 µs"]
    E --> F["6 Array software: map, hash, persist<br/>to mirrored or shared NVRAM ~30–100 µs"]
    F --> G["ACK back up the stack<br/>end to end ~100–250 µs"]
    F -.-> H["7 Later: array or FTL writes full stripe<br/>off the critical path"]
    H -.-> I["8 NAND program: TLC hundreds of µs,<br/>QLC longer"]
    J["DAS comparison: local NVMe SSD acks<br/>from protected DRAM, ~20–40 µs total"]

Figure 13.2 — Illustrative, order-of-magnitude latencies: on a networked array the network, protocol and controller software dominate a small write, and NAND programming is hidden behind NVRAM.

Walk the numbers. A networked array acknowledges the write once it sits in two NVRAM locations (mirrored to the partner controller, or in NVRAM modules both controllers can reach, as on FlashArray; see Chapter 14), not when it reaches NAND. The critical-path steps sum to roughly 45–165 µs one way; with the return trip and queueing, a 4 KB write lands near 100–250 µs, consistent with the 150 µs quoted for FlashArray//XL170 (company-stated, conditions unspecified)7. A local NVMe SSD skips layers 4–6 and acknowledges from power-loss-protected DRAM.

Three lessons follow. NAND is not on the write critical path: NVRAM or SSD DRAM absorbs the write and the slow program happens later. Network and software dominate small-I/O latency, which is why transport matters for databases: NVMe-oF over RDMA adds about 5–15 µs over local NVMe8, NVMe/TCP roughly 20–35 µs in early tests9, and the host kernel path becomes a large share of latency on very fast SSDs10. The extra ~100 µs buys what DAS lacks: one copy shared by many hosts, surviving controller loss, deduplicated, snapshotted and replicated.

docs.title: Where the intelligence lives
docs.text:
Architecture Where data services run Where metadata and state live What the network carries Examples Chapter DAS Host file system, volume manager, RAID In the host Nothing (PCIe inside the server) Local NVMe in a database server 1 SAN array (scale-up) Dual controllers in the array Controller DRAM plus mirrored or shared NVRAM Block commands (FC, NVMe-oF, iSCSI) FlashArray, PowerStore, PowerMax, ONTAP AFF 14 NAS filer Controllers, which also own the file system In the filer File operations (NFS, SMB) ONTAP, FlashBlade, PowerScale 8 Shared-nothing Distributed software on every node Partitioned across nodes Client traffic plus east-west replication PowerScale, WEKA, Ceph 15 DASE Stateless compute nodes Shared SCM and flash enclosures Front end plus all back-end media I/O VAST, NetApp AFX, HPE X10000 16 Parallel FS Metadata servers plus the client library Metadata servers Layout from metadata, data direct to storage nodes Lustre, Storage Scale, FlashBlade//EXA 17 Object Gateways and a metadata database Metadata database across nodes S3 over HTTP; erasure-coded fragments east-west S3, Ceph RGW, MinIO, FlashBlade 18 HCI / SDS Software inside each hypervisor host Spread across hosts VM I/O plus replicas between hosts Nutanix, vSAN 19

Table 13.1 — Where the intelligence lives decides what crosses the network and where each architecture hits its scaling wall.

For any architecture, two diagnostic questions apply: where does metadata live, and how many hops does a write cross before it is safe?

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Player Layers owned Hardware model Strategic implication Everpure FlashArray / FlashBlade 6, 7 and module design for 8 (Purity + DirectFlash); buys NAND Own controllers and modules Density and efficiency gains; NAND supply exposure Everpure hyperscaler deals 7 and module design (DirectFlash, flash management) Customer sources hardware; Everpure does not procure the NAND4 A layer sold on its own, without the array IBM FlashSystem 6 and 7 (own FlashCore Modules) Own modules with on-module compression11 The closest integrated rival Dell, NetApp arrays 6 Standard third-party SSDs (Dell contrast noted by TechTarget11) Multi-source drives; adopt each SSD generation quickly VAST 6, plus enclosure designs Commodity SSDs; servers via Supermicro, HPE, Cisco12 Software margin on partner hardware WEKA, Ceph, Nutanix 6 (or 3 in HCI) Software on commodity servers51314 Ride server cost curves; no hardware inventory AWS All eight Own Nitro SSDs with a rewritten FTL15 Proof that the largest buyers can build layer 7 themselves

Table 13.2 — Everpure and IBM integrate down to the flash; most rivals stop at array software, and software-only players stop above the hardware entirely.

Why collapse layers 6 and 7? A standard SSD's FTL works blind: it does not know which blocks the array will soon overwrite, so it may copy dead-to-be data during garbage collection, and it carries its own spare area and DRAM. With DirectFlash, Purity drives raw NAND and handles placement, garbage collection and wear levelling across all modules at once16. The DRAM arithmetic matters as drives grow: a 4-byte map entry per 4 KB page is 1 TB ÷ 4 KB × 4 B ≈ 1 GB of DRAM per TB, or ~150 GB for a 150 TB drive. Folding mapping into array software, which already keeps metadata for deduplication and snapshots, lets module capacity scale without that DRAM bill. DFMs went from 75 TB in 2023 to 150 TB, with 300 TB reported in August 20261718 [VERIFY: official 300 TB DFM GA date].

Steelman the alternatives. Software-only vendors ride server and SSD cost curves for free, run in any cloud and focus R&D on one layer. Array vendors on standard SSDs multi-source drives and adopt each SSD generation once qualified, while Everpure must engineer modules for each NAND generation and carries supply risk: it raised prices in February 2026 as NAND costs surged19. AWS's Nitro SSD, claimed at 60% lower latency than OEM drives, proves hyperscalers can build layer 7 themselves15. The licensing thesis therefore rests on staying ahead in time-to-capacity, not on the layer being unreplicable.

Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: how far to license layers 7 and 8; whether FlashBlade//EXA's third-party data nodes (Chapter 16) dilute the integration thesis or extend Purity's reach; and which layer becomes contestable as DPUs absorb storage services.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Where the storage intelligence lived, 1956 to 2026
    section Direct-attached
        1956 : IBM 350 RAMAC ships, the first commercial disk
        1988 : Berkeley RAID paper puts protection in a controller
    section SAN and NAS
        1990 : EMC Symmetrix cached disk array
        1992 : NetApp founded to build dedicated file servers
        1994 : ANSI approves Fibre Channel FC-PH
    section Distributed
        2003 : Google File System paper
        2006 : Amazon S3 launches : Ceph paper at OSDI
        2011 : Nutanix ships hyperconverged software
    section Flash and disaggregated
        2012 : Pure Storage ships FlashArray
        2016 : NVMe over Fabrics 1.0 published
        2017 : DirectFlash moves flash management into array software
        2019 : VAST Data emerges with a disaggregated design
        2025 : FlashBlade EXA and NetApp AFX disaggregate
        2026 : NVIDIA STX puts storage services on BlueField-4 DPUs

Figure 13.3 — Each era moved the intelligence to a new layer; the current era splits metadata, data and fabric into separately scaled pieces.

Sources for Figure 13.3: 20212223242526131427282930313233.

Each move answered a bottleneck: stranded DAS capacity, then controller limits, then (with flash) the network and software themselves. Two signals point to the next re-cut. NVIDIA's 2026 STX design runs storage services on DPUs, pulling parts of layer 6 into the NIC33. NVMe Flexible Data Placement lets any array steer placement on standard SSDs, narrowing, not erasing, the advantage of owning layer 7 (Chapter 12).

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In hyperscaler deals, which layer are we monetizing, and what stops the customer building it?" Strong: flash management and module design; AWS Nitro proves in-sourcing is possible; the moat is time-to-capacity per NAND generation and exabyte-scale qualification.
  2. "When a customer insists on software-only, what do we offer and what do we give up?" Strong: names the cases (sovereign cloud, standard server fleets, public cloud), the products that serve them, and the density lost off DirectFlash.
  3. "In latency-driven deals, which layer is the bottleneck?" Strong: host stack, transport and controller software, with NVMe/TCP versus RDMA numbers; not NAND.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Walk a 4 KB write: where is the persistence point, and what is each layer's p99 contribution?" Strong: names the NVRAM mirror point, per-layer microseconds, and which layer degrades first under load.
  2. "What does Purity know that a drive FTL cannot, and what does that do to write amplification at 90% full?" Strong: a quantified write-amplification or over-provisioning comparison plus the mechanism.
  3. "If Flexible Data Placement lets any array steer placement on standard SSDs, what DirectFlash advantage remains?" Strong: separates what FDP closes (placement) from what it does not (DRAM, density, power, global wear management).

Don't say this:

  • "Flash latency is the bottleneck." On networked arrays, network and software dominate small writes; NAND programming is off the critical path.
  • "DirectFlash is an SSD without the case." It removes the drive-level FTL; flash management moves into Purity.
  • "Software-defined means no hardware." Someone's hardware always runs it; the question is who carries inventory and earns margin.
  • "SAN and NAS are different hardware." They differ mainly in who owns the file system: host or array.
  • "Disaggregation is new." Every era re-cut the stack.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Storage stack — the eight layers from application to media.
  • Data services ("intelligence") — placement, protection, reduction, metadata.
  • Persistence point — where a write becomes safe to acknowledge.
  • Vertical integration — owning adjacent layers, e.g. array software, FTL and module.
  • See the glossary.

docs.title: 14. Scale-up dual-controller arrays
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: The storage stack · Inside an SSD · Data protection and resilience · Block protocols

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A dual-controller array is two servers sharing one set of dual-ported drives. If one dies, the other takes over. FlashArray, PowerStore, NetApp AFF, IBM FlashSystem and HPE Alletra all work this way.
  • A write is acknowledged once it sits in two persistent places, not on flash. It lands in mirrored or shared NVRAM; flash is written later in batches.
  • "Active/active" is a spectrum; ALUA tells hosts where an array sits. The real question is how much performance remains with one controller gone.
  • A non-disruptive upgrade is two planned failovers. Everpure's stateless controllers turned that into a commercial product: Evergreen.
  • The wall is one pair's CPU and memory. Beyond it, vendors federate pairs, which is not the same as one bigger system.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
FlashArray, Everpure's founding product, is a dual-controller design, and so are its main block rivals. Enterprise block deals are fought on p99 latency, behaviour during failure, upgrade disruption and refresh economics. Evergreen//Forever's promise of new controllers at each three-year renewal1 works only because the controller holds no data: the business model is an architectural property.

The tension is that AI and large file workloads pull spending toward designs with no central pair (Chapter 15, Chapter 16). Knowing where scale-up still wins is how to judge FlashArray's runway and FlashBlade's role (Chapter 27).

docs.title: The idea in one picture
docs.text:
Each controller is a server with x86 CPUs, DRAM, front-end ports (FC, iSCSI or NVMe-oF) and back-end links to the drives. Hosts cable into two independent fabrics, so any single component can fail without losing access. Only the passive midplane and the software are not doubled.

Figure 14.1 — Two controllers, one set of drives: every path, controller and drive connection is redundant, but the software and chassis are shared.

Semiconductor bridge: hot standby, not lockstep. ASIL-D automotive SoCs run two cores in lockstep and a comparator flags divergence. A controller pair compares nothing; the partner holds just enough state (the mirrored write log) to resume. Lockstep buys fault detection, HA buys availability; both share one weakness: a bug hits both copies.

docs.title: Where state lives
docs.text:
Data and metadata sit on RAID-protected drives (Chapter 6), in-flight writes in small, durable NVRAM, and rebuildable caches in controller DRAM. The key choice is where NVRAM sits.

  • Inside each controller, mirrored to the partner. ONTAP logs each write in local NVRAM and mirrors it to the HA partner, which replays it on takeover2. If the mirror falls out of sync, ONTAP blocks takeover3. The entry PowerStore 500 mirrors into its peer's DRAM4.
  • In the chassis, reachable by both. FlashArray//m dual-homed its NVRAM modules to both controllers over PCIe5. FlashArray//XL moved it onto DirectFlash modules ("DFMD"), so log capacity and bandwidth grow with module count6. Larger PowerStore models keep mirrored pairs of NVRAM drives in the base enclosure4. With nothing unique in the controller, Pure Storage called the design "stateless": a controller can be swapped without destaging anything5.

Semiconductor bridge. NVRAM is array-scale power-loss protection: DRAM or SRAM held up by capacitors or batteries long enough to dump to flash, as in an SSD (Chapter 3).

docs.title: Tracing a write ★
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant A as Owning controller A
    participant N as NVRAM log
    participant B as Partner controller B
    participant F as Flash drives
    H->>A: WRITE 32 KB to LUN 7
    A->>A: validate, checksum, place in DRAM
    A->>N: append to NVRAM write log
    A->>B: mirror log entry over HA interconnect
    B-->>A: mirror persisted
    A-->>H: ACK
    Note over A,F: Later, off the latency path
    A->>A: dedupe, compress, fill a RAID stripe
    A->>F: write full stripe to flash
    A->>N: release log space

Figure 14.2 — The ACK waits for two persistent copies of the write log, never for flash. With chassis NVRAM, as on FlashArray, the mirror step becomes a write into NVRAM that both controllers can read.

Worked example (illustrative). Wire and protocol ~20 µs, NVRAM append ~10 µs, mirror hop ~15 µs, software ~50 µs: the ACK leaves in roughly 100 µs. One TLC page program takes hundreds of microseconds, so waiting for NAND would multiply write latency. NVRAM is a buffer, not a cache. At 4 GB/s of sustained writes a 32 GB log holds 32 ÷ 4 = 8 seconds; if the flush falls behind, the log fills and hosts are throttled to flash speed, a latency cliff. Those 4 GB/s also cross the mirror path, which is why interconnects are PCIe or 100 Gb-class RDMA.

docs.title: Tracing a read
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant A as Owning controller A
    participant D as DRAM cache in A
    participant F as Flash drives
    H->>A: READ 64 KB from LUN 7
    A->>D: look up block map and cache
    alt cache hit
        D-->>A: data
    else cache miss
        A->>F: read needed blocks through the midplane
        F-->>A: compressed blocks
        A->>A: verify checksum and decompress
    end
    A-->>H: data
    Note over H,A: A read arriving at controller B is forwarded over the interconnect, adding one hop

Figure 14.3 — Reads skip NVRAM unless the data is still in the log. Arriving at the "wrong" controller costs one interconnect hop, and ALUA path states advertise exactly that.

Most flash-array reads miss DRAM: latency is a metadata lookup, a NAND read and decompression, and at high IOPS controller CPU is the limit.

docs.title: Active/active, active/passive and ALUA
docs.text:
Model How it works Examples Active/passive One controller serves everything; the other waits Older midrange arrays Asymmetric active/active Each controller owns some LUNs; I/O sent to the non-owner is forwarded NetApp AFF before 9.19.1; IBM FlashSystem preferred node; Dell PowerStore, whose two nodes both serve I/O7 [VERIFY: PowerStore per-volume node affinity and ALUA path states] Symmetric active/active Every path optimized; any controller serves any LUN via a coherent shared cache NetApp ASA8 and AFF from 9.19.19; HPE Alletra 9000 "all-active"10; PowerMax global cache11 Single-envelope (FlashArray) All ports active, but only the primary controller processes I/O; the secondary relays its ports' I/O and keeps a DRAM mirror of transactions1213 FlashArray; since January 2026, XL190 Purity Turbo lets the secondary serve reads14

Table 14.1 — "Active/active" covers three different designs; FlashArray is its own category.

FlashArray is the outlier, and current Everpure material still describes it this way: active/active for host connectivity, with workload processing on one controller12. Pure's own taxonomy calls Purity//FA a "single-writer" design, against the "partitioned-writer" Purity//FB in FlashBlade15. Critics called it active/passive in disguise16; Pure Storage's answer is that capping performance at one controller's worth means nothing is lost on failure17.

How ALUA works. Asymmetric Logical Unit Access is a SCSI standard (SPC-3). Each port group reports a per-LUN state: active/optimized, active/non-optimized, standby or unavailable. Hosts use optimized paths and fall back only when needed; on failover the array flips states. NVMe's equivalent is ANA18, which ONTAP has supported since 9.519. Symmetric designs mark every path optimized, so hosts never wait for a transition8.

flowchart LR
    H["Host multipath driver"]
    PA1["Controller A port 1"]
    PA2["Controller A port 2"]
    PB1["Controller B port 1"]
    PB2["Controller B port 2"]
    CA["Controller A owns LUN 7"]
    CB["Controller B"]
    L[("LUN 7 on shared drives")]
    H -->|"optimized, fabric A"| PA1
    H -->|"optimized, fabric B"| PA2
    H -.->|"non-optimized, fabric A"| PB1
    H -.->|"non-optimized, fabric B"| PB2
    PA1 --> CA
    PA2 --> CA
    PB1 --> CB
    PB2 --> CB
    CB -->|"forward over interconnect"| CA
    CA --> L

Figure 14.4 — The host spreads I/O across optimized paths and keeps non-optimized paths in reserve. If controller A dies, the array marks B's paths optimized and B takes ownership.

Semiconductor bridge. ALUA is NUMA advertised to the host: a non-optimized path is a remote-socket access over UPI, and the port-group report plays the role of the SRAT/SLIT distance tables.

Worked example (the headroom trap). Two controllers each deliver 500k IOPS, so a vendor can market 1M. Run at 800k and lose one: the survivor faces 800k against 500k of capacity, and latency hockey-sticks (Chapter 4). Riding through undegraded requires ≤500k total, or 50% per controller. Failure-safe performance of any two-controller array is one controller's capacity. Active/active lets customers run hotter and accept degradation; FlashArray makes that choice for them.

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text:
Failure What happens Blast radius / cost Drive RAID or erasure-coded rebuild onto spare capacity; both controllers can read every drive Small. Rebuild CPU competes with host I/O Controller Partner takes ownership and replays the mirrored log. ONTAP I/O pause is "generally measured in seconds"2; Everpure cites a short pause during local HA failover20 Hosts must tolerate the pause. With active/active run hot, performance drops NVRAM module or mirror link Redundant module or mirror continues. ONTAP refuses takeover while the log is unsynchronized3 Window of reduced protection Path (HBA, cable, switch, port) Multipath driver retries on surviving paths. ONTAP SAN LIFs do not move, so hosts must switch paths2 None if hosts are dual-fabric and timeouts are set correctly Expansion shelf or shelf module Second shelf I/O module keeps the drives reachable. Losing a whole shelf depends on how RAID groups span shelves Large: one shelf can hold hundreds of TB Software bug, chassis, site Both controllers share code and chassis. Protection needs a second array (sync replication such as ActiveCluster) Whole array

Table 14.2 — The pair removes hardware single points of failure; the shared software and chassis remain, which is why synchronous replication between arrays exists.

HPE sells this as a 100% availability guarantee on Alletra 9000 and B10000, conditional on a support contract and a case opened within seven days21. For scale, six nines is 1e-6 × 31.5M s ≈ 32 seconds a year, about one takeover.

docs.title: Non-disruptive upgrades
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Both controllers serving" as Normal
    state "Pre-checks" as Check
    state "Partner B offline, A serves all" as BOut
    state "B upgraded or replaced, resyncs" as BNew
    state "B owns all LUNs, A offline" as AOut
    [*] --> Normal
    Normal --> Check: upgrade requested
    Check --> Normal: health check fails
    Check --> BOut: take B down
    BOut --> BNew: new software or new controller
    BNew --> AOut: planned failover to B
    AOut --> Normal: A upgraded, rejoins, paths rebalance

Figure 14.5 — An upgrade is two planned failovers. Hosts see two path flips, and the risky window is while one controller is out and the array has no redundancy.

The same choreography covers software and hardware. With stateless controllers, a technician pulls the secondary, inserts a newer controller, fails over and repeats; drives, NVRAM and configuration never leave the chassis22. One integrator reported an //X90R2-to-R4 swap on live workloads in business hours23. PowerStore's data-in-place upgrades work one node at a time4; ONTAP controller replacement relocates aggregates between nodes24.

docs.title: How it scales and where it hits walls
docs.text:
• Capacity. Shelves add drives until back-end ports or controller DRAM (which must hold block maps and dedupe tables) run out. FlashArray//XL R5 tops out near 1.9 PB raw, 7.4 PB effective25.
  • Performance. One pair's CPUs, memory bandwidth and PCIe lanes set the limit. Moving FlashArray//X R5 and //C R5 to Intel Emerald Rapids raised performance ~30% and ~40%35: the array roadmap is largely Intel's. Scale-up is a monolithic die riding process nodes; scale-out is the multi-die answer.
  • Federation. PowerStore clusters up to four appliances and migrates volumes between them4, with ML rebalancing in Prime26. ONTAP ASA clusters reach 12 nodes27 and HPE's B10000 six nodes28. IBM went the other way: from Storage Virtualize 8.7.1, a FlashSystem can no longer scale out by adding control enclosures, and IBM points customers to FlashSystem grid, which federates separate systems (up to 32 for the FlashSystem 7600, per a reseller datasheet)29. A volume still lives on one pair; federation adds mobility and one management plane, not a bigger volume.
  • The exception. PowerMax 8500 scales to 16 nodes sharing a global cache over a 100 Gb/s NVMe/InfiniBand fabric3011, a scale-up machine built from many controllers.

docs.title: Pros, cons and fit
docs.text:
Strength Weakness Latency Sub-millisecond, consistent; ACK from NVRAM Every I/O funnels through one pair's CPUs Simplicity No cluster network, no quorum, small footprint Scaling past the pair means federation and data moves Resilience Mature failover; hardware fully redundant Shared software and chassis; no redundancy during upgrades Economics Low entry cost; stateless designs enable in-place refresh Failure-safe design idles half the CPU Scale Effective capacity of several PB per array Throughput tops out far below TB/s scale-out systems

Table 14.3 — Scale-up trades a hard ceiling for low latency, low entry cost and operational simplicity.

Best fit: OLTP databases, hypervisor estates, VDI, SAP and mid-size Kubernetes volumes. Worst fit: multi-petabyte namespaces read at TB/s by GPU clusters (Chapter 31), cheap-and-deep archives, and workloads that will outgrow one pair.

docs.title: Cost and operational implications
docs.text: Entry is cheap and operations simple. The hidden cost is the headroom tax of paying for two controllers to get one's failure-safe performance. Traditional refreshes replace the array and migrate data every three to five years; Evergreen-style swaps turn that capital event into a subscription line (Chapter 23). Many outages start on the host: single-fabric cabling or timeouts shorter than a takeover.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
System Controllers Write log Path model Beyond one pair Everpure FlashArray //X, //C, //XL 2, stateless NVRAM in chassis; on //XL, on DFMDs6 All ports active; one controller does back-end work; XL190 Turbo lets secondary serve reads14 No clustering; ActiveCluster sync replication between arrays; fleet management Dell PowerStore T 2 nodes per appliance Mirrored NVRAM drives; 500 mirrors to peer DRAM4 Both nodes serve I/O7; ALUA Up to 4 appliances per cluster4 Dell PowerMax 2500/8500 2–16 nodes Global cache shared via RDMA11 All-active 8 node pairs on Dynamic Fabric30 NetApp AFF / ASA HA pairs Per-node NVRAM mirrored to partner2 ALUA on AFF until 9.19.1; symmetric on ASA89 ONTAP clusters of HA pairs27 HPE Alletra 9000 / MP B10000 2–4 (9000)10; up to 6 (B10000)28 Not verified All-active 100% availability guarantee21 IBM FlashSystem 2 canisters per I/O group Write cache mirrored across the pair31 Preferred node per volume One I/O group per system from 8.7.1; FlashSystem grid federates systems29

Table 14.4 — Everyone ships two controllers; the differences are where the write log lives, whether both controllers do real work, and how many pairs can be federated.

Everpure's bet is a single-controller envelope with stateless controllers: predictable performance through failure and swaps cheap enough to bundle into a subscription. The cost is a lower per-array ceiling and a partner CPU that relays front-end I/O and mirrors transactions but does no back-end work; Purity Turbo relaxes that on reads. Steelmen: PowerMax has the highest single-system ceiling, NetApp one OS for NAS and SAN with cluster mobility, HPE a guarantee that shifts risk to the vendor. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: how far Turbo-style active/active can go before "no loss on failover" needs caveats, and whether customers outgrowing an //XL are better served by fleet management or FlashBlade.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Dual-controller milestones
    2015 : Pure Storage launches FlashArray m with Evergreen controller upgrades
    2021 : FlashArray XL moves NVRAM onto DirectFlash modules
    2022 : PowerMax 2500 and 8500 scale to 16 nodes
    2024 : Dell PowerStore Prime adds ML rebalancing across appliances
    2025 : HPE B10000 runs four nodes switchless : FlashArray X R5 and C R5 move to Emerald Rapids
    2026 : FlashArray XL190 Purity Turbo lets the secondary serve reads

Figure 14.6 — The architecture is old; what changed recently is where NVRAM lives and how much work the second controller does.

The pattern dates to 1990s RAID arrays; flash moved the bottleneck from drives to controllers. In 2015 Pure Storage paired FlashArray//m with Evergreen, selling statelessness as a refresh model32. Looking forward, symmetric active/active is becoming the default (ASA, then AFF 9.19.19), and NVMe-oF shelves blur scale-up into shared-everything: HPE's B10000 is described as disaggregated33, and FlashArray attaches DirectFlash shelves over NVMe-oF/RoCE34.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What does a customer lose, in IOPS and p99, while one controller is out during an Evergreen swap, and for how long?" Strong: "nothing by design", the window in minutes, and which Purity Turbo read gains vanish during failover.
  2. "When a block customer outgrows one //XL, what do we sell?" Strong: thresholds for a second array, ActiveCluster or FlashBlade, and candour that there is no scale-out block namespace.
  3. "How do Dell, NetApp and HPE upgrade programs differ from Evergreen//Forever?" Strong: refresh clocks, trade-in credits, who does the swap, and the architecture behind each.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Where is the persistence point, how many copies exist, and in which failure domains?" Strong: NVRAM location, copy count, power-loss behaviour, single-device failure.
  2. "With Purity Turbo, how is the secondary's read cache kept coherent with the primary's writes?" Strong: invalidation protocol, interconnect cost, failover behaviour.
  3. "What is the CPU cost per I/O, and is the next ceiling CPU, memory bandwidth or PCIe?" Strong: names the bottleneck and how the next CPU generation moves it.

Don't say this:

  • "Active/active doubles performance." Failure-safe, it is one controller's worth.
  • "The array waits for flash before acknowledging." The ACK comes from mirrored NVRAM.
  • "Dual controllers mean no single point of failure." Software, chassis and the upgrade window are shared.
  • "FlashArray is scale-out." It is scale-up.
  • "ALUA is a NetApp feature." It is a SCSI standard; NVMe calls it ANA.
