docs.title: 15. Scale-out shared-nothing clusters
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Data protection and resilience · Datacenter networking · Scale-up dual-controller arrays

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A shared-nothing cluster is identical servers that each own their CPUs, memory and drives. The scaling unit is a whole node. PowerScale (Isilon), WEKA, Ceph, Qumulo and Nutanix work this way; ONTAP does at the level of HA pairs.
  • Placement is computed, not looked up. A consistent-hashing ring or CRUSH-style function maps data to nodes, so adding a node moves only about 1/(N+1) of the data.
  • The network does the real work. Replicas, erasure-coded fragments, forwarded reads and rebuilds travel east-west. At 16 nodes, ~94% of read bytes come from a peer.
  • The cluster heals itself. An odd-numbered quorum owns the cluster map, lost nodes are rebuilt many-to-many, and a partition's minority side stops writing.
  • The walls are bundled scaling, rebuild storms, hot spots and node limits. It is the incumbent design that disaggregated systems define themselves against.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Most scale-out file and object storage Everpure competes against is shared-nothing. PowerScale is the unstructured-data incumbent, WEKA the software-defined challenger in GPU clusters, and Ceph the open-source default for operators building their own. Deals against PowerScale, WEKA or "Ceph on our own servers" turn on this chapter's strengths and walls.

The architecture also explains a partnership. Hyperconverged (HCI) clusters such as Nutanix are shared-nothing, so storage grows only when compute grows. In 2025 Pure Storage and Nutanix announced FlashArray as external storage for Nutanix AHV, Nutanix's first major certified external-storage integration1. That deal sells against the bundled-scaling wall.

docs.title: The idea in one picture
docs.text:
Each node is a full server: CPUs, DRAM cache, an NVRAM or journal device, and NVMe drives no other node can address. Clients connect to any node over the front-end network; nodes talk over a back-end network. A few nodes run a quorum service, the authoritative record of membership and ownership.

Figure 15.1 — Data is never shared, only requested: reaching another node's bytes means asking its CPU over the back-end.

Semiconductor bridge: a multi-socket NUMA server. Each socket has local DRAM; a remote access crosses UPI or Infinity Fabric to another socket's memory controller, slower and bandwidth-hungry. Shared-nothing storage is NUMA at datacenter scale. The coherence parallel is closer still. In directory-based coherence, every cache line has a home node whose directory tracks sharers, and a contended line serializes there. In a cluster, every object has an owner or primary node, and a hot key serializes on it the same way. Chapter 16 is the UMA alternative.

docs.title: Where state and metadata live
docs.text:
Everything lives on the nodes. Data is striped across nodes under replication or erasure coding (EC); OneFS spreads data, metadata and parity across nodes, using Reed-Solomon EC for data and mirroring for metadata2. Metadata (inodes, directories, block maps) is sharded too, and designs differ in how: WEKA spreads it across all nodes3, while Ceph's file layer adds separate metadata servers.

The one piece of state that cannot be sharded is the cluster map: membership, health and placement rules. Ceph keeps it in a few monitors that agree on changes by Paxos and majority vote4. Nodes and smart clients cache the map and tag requests with its version (epoch), so stale views are caught.

docs.title: Placement: hash it, don't look it up
docs.text:
A central table of every object's location would become the bottleneck, so shared-nothing systems compute placement instead.

  • Consistent hashing (Karger et al., 19975) puts nodes and keys on a ring; each key belongs to the next node clockwise. Amazon's Dynamo (2007) added many "virtual nodes" per server to even out load6.
  • CRUSH (Weil et al., 20067) hashes objects into placement groups (PGs), then maps each PG to drives by walking a host-and-rack hierarchy under a rule such as "three copies in three racks". Anyone with the same map computes the same answer, and map changes move little data7.

Figure 15.2 — Computed placement needs no directory and moves only about the new node's fair share of data.

Semiconductor bridge: address interleaving. Memory controllers hash physical addresses across channels, banks and LLC slices so no channel becomes a hot spot; clusters hash keys across nodes for the same reason. The difference: a memory system never re-interleaves at run time, while a cluster must, under live I/O.

docs.title: Tracing a write
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant K as Coordinator node
    participant P as Primary or owner node
    participant R as Peer nodes
    C->>K: WRITE 1 MB to file F
    K->>K: hash file and offset against cluster map
    alt replicated pool
        K->>P: forward write unless K is the primary
        P->>P: persist to local NVRAM or journal
        P->>R: send two replica copies
        R-->>P: persisted
        P-->>K: committed
    else erasure-coded layout
        K->>K: split into 8 data and 2 parity strips
        K->>R: send strips to 10 nodes in distinct failure domains
        R-->>K: each strip persisted
    end
    K-->>C: ACK after all copies or strips are durable

Figure 15.3 — The ACK waits until every copy or strip is durable on peers, so write latency includes at least one back-end round trip.

OneFS follows the EC branch: the node a client connects to computes parity and commits strips to peers, journaling in NVRAM. Ceph skips the coordinator: clients run CRUSH themselves and write to the primary OSD (the daemon managing one drive), which replicates and acknowledges once all copies are stored4.

Worked example (east-west on writes). A client writes 1 GB/s. Under three-way replication the primary sends 2 GB/s to replicas, plus up to 1 GB/s if the coordinator forwards first: 2–3 GB/s of back-end traffic. Under 8+2 EC the coordinator sends 10/8 = 1.25 GB/s of strips. Against roughly 4× in DASE, shared-nothing is cheaper on writes; its cost shows up on reads.

docs.title: Tracing a read
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant K as Coordinator node
    participant L as Local drives on K
    participant R as Owner peer nodes
    C->>K: READ offset X of file F
    K->>K: check DRAM cache and resolve layout
    alt strip is local
        K->>L: NVMe read
        L-->>K: data
    else strip lives on peers
        K->>R: back-end read request
        R->>R: read from their drives or cache
        R-->>K: data
    end
    K-->>C: reassembled data

Figure 15.4 — Whichever node holds the data serves it; the coordinator mostly stitches together peers' answers.

With data spread evenly over N nodes, a client finds only 1/N locally. At 16 nodes, 15/16 ≈ 94% of read bytes cross the back-end, which must be sized at least as large as the front-end. Smart clients (Ceph's, WEKA's) skip this hop by reading straight from owners; Nutanix's data locality instead keeps a VM's data on its own node.

docs.title: Rebalancing: node add and node loss
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    E["Topology change"] --> Q["Quorum commits new cluster map epoch"]
    Q --> D{"Node added or lost?"}
    D -->|added| A1["Each node computes which PGs or stripes move"]
    A1 --> A2["Throttled background copy to new node"]
    A2 --> A3["Old copies deleted after new ones are durable"]
    D -->|lost| L1["Grace timer: is it a reboot?"]
    L1 -->|back in time| L2["Resync only changes made while away"]
    L1 -->|timer expires| L3["Mark out and serve reads degraded"]
    L3 --> L4["Many-to-many rebuild into spare space on survivors"]
    A3 --> H["Cluster healthy"]
    L2 --> H
    L4 --> H

Figure 15.5 — Adding a node is a throttled migration; losing one starts a race to restore redundancy before a second failure.

Figure 15.6 — Illustrative: computed placement keeps adds cheap, but rebuild time grows with node size and shrinks only as clusters widen. Data: data/ch15_rebalance_rebuild.csv

Panel B's math: a node of 24 × 30.72 TB drives at 80% full holds 590 TB. Under 8+2 EC each rebuilt strip reads 8 strips and writes 1, so 9 bytes cross the network per byte restored. If each survivor donates 2 GB/s, a 10-node cluster restores 9 × 2 ÷ 9 = 2 GB/s: about 82 hours. At 64 nodes it is ~12 hours; with 122.88 TB drives, four times longer.

docs.title: How it scales and where it hits walls
docs.text:
1. Bundled scaling. Each node adds fixed CPU, cache, capacity and ports. Capacity-heavy workloads pay for idle CPUs; throughput-heavy ones pay for idle terabytes. Mixed node pools only soften this.
  2. East-west amplification. Reads cross the back-end (N−1)/N of the time; rebuilds multiply traffic by the code width.
  3. Rebuild storms. Bigger drives make every node loss longer and noisier. At Facebook, recovering Reed-Solomon-coded data added more than 100 TB a day of cross-rack network traffic8; locally repairable codes roughly halve repair traffic9.
  4. Hot spots. Hashing spreads keys, not load. A million-file directory, or one checkpoint read by 1,000 GPUs, lands on its owner, like a contended line stalling at its home directory.
  5. Membership limits. Failure detection and all-to-all connections grow with node count. PowerScale tops out at 252 nodes on an Ethernet leaf-spine back-end10; ONTAP at 24 nodes for NAS and 12 for SAN11.

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text:
Failure What happens Blast radius / cost Drive Strips rebuilt from peers into spare space on many nodes Small. Parallel rebuild; brief extra east-west load Node Grace timer, then many-to-many rebuild. OneFS +2d:1n survives 2 drives or 1 node; N+M EC needs ≥2M+1 nodes2 1/N of capacity and performance lost; hours to days to rebuild (Figure 15.6) Back-end link or switch Dual back-end fabrics with failover; a node cut off from peers is fenced out of the cluster A flapping link can trigger repeated mark-out and resync churn Front-end link Client IPs move to surviving nodes (for example, OneFS SmartConnect) Brief stall or reconnect for clients on that node Partition (split brain) Only the side holding a quorum majority keeps the map and accepts writes. 5 monitors tolerate 2 failures The minority side goes read-only or offline, by design

Table 15.1 — There is no partner controller in this design: the cluster heals itself, and the price is rebuild traffic and a quorum that must be protected.

docs.title: Pros, cons and fit
docs.text:
Shared-nothing strength Shared-nothing weakness Scaling Linear add-a-node growth; commodity servers; no special fabric Capacity and performance bundled; membership limits (24–252 nodes) Performance Local reads possible; writes cheaper on the network than DASE Most reads hop through a peer unless clients are smart Resilience No single controller pair; parallel, many-to-many rebuild Node loss is a big rebuild; partitions need quorum discipline Efficiency EC across nodes; per-TB software pricing Small clusters need narrow stripes or replication (≥2M+1 nodes) Lifecycle Rolling, node-by-node upgrades; mixed generations Every reboot creates a window of reduced redundancy

Table 15.2 — Shared-nothing trades bundled scaling and network-heavy recovery for simplicity, commodity hardware and no controller bottleneck.

Best fit: large file shares, media and genomics archives, analytics lakes, HCI VM estates, and GPU clusters whose throughput-to-capacity need matches a server's built-in ratio; software-defined variants suit operators who pick their own servers. Worst fit: latency-critical block databases (dual-controller arrays are simpler), very capacity-heavy archives (idle CPUs; see object storage), sites under about 3–5 nodes, and namespaces that must outgrow the node limit.

docs.title: Cost and operational implications
docs.text: Commodity hardware shifts value to software, which is why WEKA, Qumulo and Ceph vendors price per terabyte or node. Operations get harder in three places: back-end network sizing, free-space reserve (often one node's worth, to absorb a rebuild), and rolling upgrades that reboot nodes one by one. Incremental growth is the strong suit: add a node, rebalance, retire the oldest later.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
System Node model Placement and protection Notes Dell PowerScale (OneFS) 3–252 nodes, each with its own drives Reed-Solomon EC across nodes; metadata mirrored210 OneFS 9.15 claims up to 35 GB/s reads per node on next-gen nodes and makes pNFS GA12 WEKA NeuralMesh Software on commodity or cloud servers Stripes of 3–16 data plus 2–4 parity strips; N+4 aimed at 100+ servers13 Data and metadata on all nodes; NeuralMesh 6 announced July 2026314 Ceph RADOS OSD per drive, monitors for quorum CRUSH placement; replicas or EC; "FastEC" in Tentacle (2025)715 Open source; Red Hat bought Inktank for ~US$175M in 201416 NetApp ONTAP cluster HA pairs federated over a cluster interconnect Each pair owns its aggregates; volumes move between pairs Up to 24 NAS nodes11; AFX (2025) moves ONTAP to shared media17 Qumulo Software on commodity or cloud nodes Erasure-coded block layer across nodes [VERIFY: current protection scheme] Became software-only under CEO Doug Gourlay (2024)18 Nutanix One controller VM per HCI node Replication factor 2 or 3 across nodes19 Supports FlashArray as external storage since 20251 Everpure FlashBlade//S Chassis of 7–10 blades; each blade takes 1–4 DirectFlash Modules, so compute and capacity are sized separately Global EC and flash management in Purity//FB; namespace split into "authorities" that run on blades2021 Pure calls Purity//FB "partitioned-writer" and rejects the binary label22 [VERIFY: multi-chassis data placement]

Table 15.3 — Every major scale-out incumbent is shared-nothing at heart; Everpure's file platforms sit between the patterns rather than in one.

Everpure sells no classic shared-nothing product. FlashArray is dual-controller (Chapter 14). FlashBlade//S scales out blades in a chassis. Pure Storage describes Purity//FB as a "partitioned-writer" design and argues that the shared-nothing versus shared-everything label obscures more than it reveals22. Metadata and write ownership are partitioned into "authorities" running on each blade, much like shared-nothing owners, while Purity manages DFM flash and NVRAM globally2120. One Pure data sheet even calls FlashBlade "shared-nothing"23. The fair summary is a partitioned scale-out design with pooled media management, not shared-everything in the DASE sense. FlashBlade//EXA splits metadata from data, yet its data nodes each own their NVMe, giving the data tier a shared-nothing flavour (Chapter 16).

The steelman for PowerScale is maturity: two decades of OneFS, a vast installed base, and now pNFS and a parallel "Lightning" tier on common hardware24. For WEKA and Ceph it is freedom over hardware and clouds. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: attacking the bundled-scaling wall in HCI estates, and leading with rebuild-time and failure-domain math against large-drive clusters.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Shared-nothing storage milestones
    1997 : Consistent hashing paper at MIT
    2003 : NetApp buys Spinnaker for clustering
    2006 : CRUSH paper describes Ceph placement
    2007 : Amazon Dynamo popularises virtual nodes
    2010 : EMC buys Isilon for 2.25B dollars
    2014 : Red Hat buys Inktank, the Ceph company
    2025 : Ceph Tentacle ships FastEC : NetApp AFX and Dell Lightning add disaggregated options
    2026 : WEKA NeuralMesh 6 : OneFS 9.15 adds pNFS

Figure 15.7 — The algorithms date from 1997–2007; since 2025 incumbents have added disaggregated or parallel tiers beside them.

EMC paid about US$2.25 billion for Isilon in 201025; NetApp paid ~US$300 million in stock for Spinnaker in 2003 to cluster beyond two nodes26. Since 2025 the trend is hybridization: NetApp AFX17 and Dell Lightning24 add shared-media or parallel paths beside shared-nothing cores, while WEKA's NeuralMesh refines the mesh itself3.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Against PowerScale, where does FlashBlade win on architecture, not price?" Strong: rebuild time on large drives, bundled-scaling waste, back-end cost; concedes PowerScale's installed base and pNFS moves.
  2. "Which customers does HCI's bundled scaling block, and how big is the Nutanix external-storage opportunity?" Strong: segments by capacity-to-compute ratio and VMware-exit timing.
  3. "A neocloud says 'we'll just run Ceph'. What is our TCO counter?" Strong: staff, rebuild windows, free-space reserve and watts per usable TB, not list price.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Where is a write's persistence point, and how many back-end hops precede the ACK?" Strong: names the NVRAM or journal, the fan-out and the failure-domain rule.
  2. "A 1 PB node dies at 80% full. How long until redundancy is restored, and what do clients see meanwhile?" Strong: hours, rebuild throttle, degraded-throughput percentage.
  3. "How do you handle one file read by thousands of GPUs?" Strong: metadata sharding, client caching or hot-data replication, not "we hash it".

Don't say this:

  • "Shared-nothing has no network bottleneck." Most reads and every rebuild cross the back-end.
  • "Add a node, get linear scaling." Only until hot keys, node limits or back-end bandwidth bite.
  • "Ceph is free." The operators, spare capacity and rebuild risk are not.
  • "ONTAP is fully shared-nothing." Drives belong to HA pairs, which federate.
  • "Consistent hashing balances load." It balances keys, not skewed access.
  • "FlashBlade//S is shared-everything, like VAST." Pure calls Purity//FB a partitioned-writer design: blades own slices of the namespace, while media management is global.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Shared-nothing — nodes own their CPU, memory and drives and cooperate only over the network.
  • Coordinator node — the node a client contacts, which computes placement and fans out I/O.
  • Placement group (PG) — Ceph's unit of placement and rebalancing.
  • Rebuild storm — heavy east-west traffic while lost redundancy is restored.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 16. Disaggregated shared-everything architectures
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Inside an SSD · Block protocols and NVMe-oF · Scale-up dual-controller arrays · Scale-out shared-nothing clusters

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• DASE splits a storage system into stateless compute nodes and shared enclosures of flash, joined by an NVMe-oF fabric. Every compute node can read and write every SSD, so no node "owns" any data. VAST Data built the category and coined the acronym.
  • The trick is where state lives. Data and all metadata sit on persistent media that every node shares: a small storage-class-memory (SCM) tier for the write buffer and metadata, and QLC flash for everything else. Compute nodes can fail, be added or be replaced without moving data.
  • Performance and capacity scale independently. That matters most when a workload's throughput-to-capacity mix is far from what a fixed server bundles; near that ratio the advantage is small.
  • The walls are the fabric, the enclosure and the minimum size. Every I/O crosses the back-end network. A whole enclosure is a failure domain. Wide, cheap erasure coding only kicks in at scale.
  • Disaggregation is becoming table stakes, but vendors implement it differently. NetApp (AFX) and HPE (X10000) ship shared-media designs. Everpure's FlashBlade//EXA separates metadata from data but sends clients directly to data nodes, which makes it closer to a parallel file system than to pure DASE.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
VAST grew with neocloud AI clusters, buyers who want one namespace at hundreds of GB/s to several TB/s without paying for CPUs they don't need. In November 2025 CoreWeave signed a reported US$1.17 billion commercial agreement with VAST1, and in April 2026 Reuters reported a ~US$30 billion valuation2 (both reported by press). Each enterprise-AI deal Everpure competes in is now partly an argument about this architecture.

Everpure's answer, FlashBlade//EXA, was announced by Pure Storage in March 2025. It disaggregates differently3. Judging that bet requires knowing what DASE gets right, where it is fragile, and whether a metadata/data split with a direct data path is a better trade or merely a different one. Chapter 42 covers VAST as a company, and Chapter 45 covers the head-to-head.

docs.title: The idea in one picture
docs.text:
Earlier architectures tie compute to media. A dual-controller array puts two controllers in front of one shelf of drives. A shared-nothing cluster builds servers that each own their drives, so reaching another node's data means asking that node's CPU. DASE removes the ownership:

  • Compute nodes ("CNodes" in VAST's terms) run the file, object and block protocols, data reduction and erasure coding. They hold no authoritative state.
  • Data enclosures ("DBoxes") hold SSDs behind small, dumb-by-design fabric endpoints ("DNodes"). Each DBox has at least two for redundancy. The original DBox used two x86 DNodes; the 1U Ceres DBox uses four NVIDIA BlueField DPUs, each fronting about a quarter of the SSDs4.
  • The back-end fabric, NVMe-oF over RDMA, makes every SSD look roughly local to every CNode5.

Figure 16.1 — In DASE, compute is a stateless pool and all state lives on shared media, so every CNode is one fabric hop from every byte.

Semiconductor bridge: NUMA versus UMA. Shared-nothing is NUMA. Each socket (node) has local memory (drives), and remote accesses go through the owner. DASE is UMA. Every core is equidistant from every memory bank, at the price of never being local. As with UMA, the interconnect becomes the critical resource. The chiplet parallel is just as useful. AMD separated compute dies from the I/O die so cores and memory/IO could scale and refresh on different cadences and processes. DASE does the same with CPUs, which follow Intel/AMD roadmaps, and NAND, which follows the flash cost curve.

docs.title: Where state and metadata live
docs.text:
DASE works only because a small, fast, persistent tier is shared by everyone. VAST began with Intel Optane SSDs as SCM and qualified Kioxia's SLC-based FL6 in 2021 as a second source6, a year before Intel announced the Optane wind-down7. The SCM holds two things. The first is the write buffer. The second is all metadata: the file system tree, block maps and locks8. The tier is tiny. A current DF-3060V2 DBox pairs 12 TB of SCM with 1,352 TB of QLC9, so SCM is 12 ÷ 1,364 ≈ 0.9% of raw capacity.

Because metadata sits in shared persistent media, CNodes coordinate through it, not with each other: a lock is a write into SCM, much as cores coordinate through atomics on a shared last-level cache. No CNode-to-CNode cache-coherence traffic exists to scale. The cost is that every metadata lookup is a fabric round trip. RDMA NVMe-oF adds roughly 5–15 µs per access over a local drive5. That is small next to a QLC read, which is on the order of 100 µs, but it is visible on metadata-heavy, small-file work (see Chapter 21).

docs.title: Tracing a write
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant CN as Any CNode
    participant S1 as SCM in DBox 1
    participant S2 as SCM in DBox 2
    participant Q as QLC across many DBoxes
    C->>CN: WRITE 1 MB to a file
    CN->>S1: RDMA write data and metadata update
    CN->>S2: RDMA write mirror copy
    S1-->>CN: persisted
    S2-->>CN: persisted
    CN-->>C: ACK after two persistent copies
    Note over CN,Q: Later, asynchronously, any CNode migrates the buffer
    CN->>S1: read buffered data
    CN->>CN: dedupe, similarity reduction, compress
    CN->>Q: write wide erasure-coded stripe
    CN->>S1: update metadata pointers and free buffer

Figure 16.2 — A write is acknowledged once it is mirrored in SCM on two enclosures; reduction and wide-stripe erasure coding happen later, off the latency path.

The persistence point is the mirrored SCM copy, with the two copies placed in different DBoxes and DNodes810. The expensive work happens during migration, when a CNode reduces data and lays it onto QLC in large stripes11. Big sequential stripes match QLC's large program and erase units and keep write amplification low (see Chapter 3). This is the storage version of a write-combining buffer.

Worked example (fabric amplification). A client writes 1 GB/s. The front-end network carries 1 GB/s. The back-end carries 2 GB/s into SCM for the two mirror copies, about 1 GB/s back out during migration, and about 1.03 GB/s into QLC once a 146+4 stripe is added. That is roughly 4 GB/s of back-end traffic per 1 GB/s of client writes, before data reduction, which shrinks only the QLC leg. Sustained writes are therefore bounded by SCM write bandwidth and fabric capacity, not by QLC.

docs.title: Tracing a read
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant CN as Any CNode
    participant M as Metadata in SCM
    participant Q as QLC SSDs
    C->>CN: READ offset X of file F
    CN->>M: walk metadata tree via RDMA
    M-->>CN: block location and reduction info
    alt data still in write buffer
        CN->>M: read from SCM
    else data already migrated
        CN->>Q: NVMe-oF read of needed strips
    end
    Q-->>CN: compressed blocks
    CN->>CN: decompress and rehydrate
    CN-->>C: data

Figure 16.3 — Any CNode can serve any read with no help from other CNodes, which is why adding CNodes scales read performance almost linearly until the fabric or media saturates.

docs.title: How it scales and where it hits walls
docs.text:
Adding CNodes buys protocol and reduction horsepower without moving data. Adding DBoxes buys capacity and media bandwidth, and also makes erasure coding cheaper. VAST caps a stripe at twice the number of DBoxes when enclosure-level protection is on. A 20-DBox cluster therefore runs 36+4 stripes (10% overhead), and at 75+ DBoxes it reaches 146+4 (2.7%)1012. Compare a typical shared-nothing 8+2 (20%). For 10 PB usable, 8+2 needs 10 ÷ 0.8 = 12.5 PB raw, while 146+4 needs 10 ÷ 0.973 ≈ 10.3 PB. That is ~18% fewer drives, the largest single capacity-side saving.

Figure 16.4 — Illustrative: decoupling pays off when the workload's throughput-to-capacity ratio is far from what a fixed server bundles; near that ratio, shared-nothing can be as cheap or cheaper. Data: data/ch16_scaling.csv

In panel A, 800 GB/s on 5 PB forces shared-nothing to buy 40 full nodes (cost 1,320); DASE buys 40 CNodes plus 16 DBoxes for media bandwidth (754). In panel B the gap at 30 PB is ~13%, almost all of it from erasure-coding efficiency. The walls:

  1. Fabric bandwidth. All traffic is east-west on the back-end. A 1 TB/s read target needs ≥1 TB/s of back-end bisection bandwidth as well as front-end bandwidth, which means dozens of 400 GbE switch ports.
  2. Fabric cost and lock-in. Back-end switches are usually specified, and sometimes supplied, by the vendor. NetApp supports only approved switches for the AFX back-end13.
  3. Enclosure blast radius. A DBox holds hundreds of TB. Surviving its loss requires spreading each stripe thinly (see below).
  4. Minimum size. Cheap, wide stripes and enclosure protection need many DBoxes. Small clusters pay more overhead or accept less resilience.
  5. SCM write ceiling. The persistent tier is a shared write funnel, and supply has already been disrupted once.

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text:
Failure What happens Blast radius / cost SSD Rebuilt from erasure-coded strips. Locally decodable codes read ~1/4 of the stripe instead of all of it14. Every CNode helps. Small. Rebuild is many-to-many and fast. CNode Clients fail over to another CNode's address. No data lost, because the node had no authoritative state. In-flight operations retried. Lose 1/N of compute. DNode / DPU Another DNode in the same DBox takes over its SSDs. Reduced enclosure bandwidth until replaced. Whole DBox Survivable only if each stripe has ≤2 strips per DBox ("DBox-HA", ≥8 DBoxes)12. Rack-level protection needs ≥7 racks15. Without HA: data unavailable. With HA: higher erasure-coding overhead on small clusters. Fabric link / switch Dual fabrics and multipathing reroute. A partition between compute and media halts I/O on the affected side. A switch pair is a shared dependency for everything.

Table 16.1 — DASE makes compute failures trivial and moves the risk to enclosures and the fabric.

docs.title: Pros, cons and fit
docs.text:
DASE strength DASE weakness Scaling Compute and capacity independent; no rebalancing when adding compute Fixed cost floor: fabric and minimum enclosure count Efficiency Wide stripes (≈3–10% overhead), global reduction across all data Gains need scale; small systems see little Resilience Compute failure is cheap; rebuilds are parallel Enclosure and fabric are large shared failure domains Performance Uniform: any node, any data, one hop Never local; extra µs per metadata access; back-end fabric amplification on writes Lifecycle Refresh CPUs and NAND on separate cycles Proprietary enclosures/fabric specs; SCM supply dependency

Table 16.2 — The architecture trades locality and a higher entry cost for uniformity, efficiency at scale and cheap compute failures.

Best fit: large shared namespaces read by many GPU nodes (training data, checkpoints, model repositories), mixed file and object estates where global reduction pays, and multi-tenant neocloud storage where demand shifts between throughput and capacity. Worst fit: small deployments under ~1 PB, latency-critical block databases that dual-controller arrays serve at a lower cost floor (Chapter 14), and edge sites without a dedicated fabric.

docs.title: Cost and operational implications
docs.text: Steady-state operations get simpler (no rebalancing when adding compute; CNode upgrades never touch media), while network engineering gets harder, because the back-end fabric is now storage. The commercial consequence is subtle. Because compute is stateless, it can be sold as software on someone else's servers, which is what VAST's EBox and its OEM and cloud routes do16. Gross margin then depends on software pricing rather than on enclosure markup.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
System Compute / metadata tier Data tier Shared-everything? Notes VAST (CBox + DBox) Stateless CNodes DBoxes: SCM + QLC behind DPUs Yes, the reference design Metadata in shared SCM; any CNode reaches any SSD8 VAST EBox CNode and DNode software on one server Same server's SSDs, pooled Logically yes; physically converged Gives up independent scaling for hyperscaler/cloud fit16 Everpure FlashBlade//EXA FlashBlade running Purity//FB as metadata core Off-the-shelf Linux/NVMe data nodes managed by Purity//DN tooling; DirectFlash nodes planned No. Metadata/data split; clients read data nodes directly pNFS: metadata over TCP, data over NFSv3/RDMA317 NetApp AFX AFX 1K controllers running ONTAP NX224 NVMe-oF shelves in one shared pool Yes (shared pool) Design maximum 128 controllers, 52 enclosures1813; 32 controllers supported in ONTAP 9.19.1, per WWT19 HPE Alletra MP X10000 Containerized compute nodes JBOF nodes Yes (HPE: "shared-everything") Log-structured KV store; object plus native NFS since Release 42021 HPE GreenLake for File VAST software on Alletra MP compute Alletra MP JBOFs Yes (VAST-based) Launched 202322 Dell Lightning FS / PowerScale pNFS Metadata server + storage nodes Server-attached flash No, parallel file system pNFS with Flex Files layout23

Table 16.3 — "Disaggregated" covers two distinct designs: shared media (VAST, NetApp, HPE) and split metadata with a direct data path (FlashBlade//EXA, Dell).

How close is FlashBlade//EXA to DASE? It shares the motivation: scale metadata performance separately from data capacity and bandwidth. It differs on the key property. In EXA no compute tier can reach all media. Clients receive a layout from the metadata core and then talk directly to data nodes over RDMA17. Architecturally that is the Lustre MDS/OSS pattern (Chapter 17) with a far stronger metadata engine. The steelman for EXA is that it removes a hop. VAST's data path is client → CNode → DBox; EXA's is client → data node. EXA also reuses years of hardened Purity metadata code and lets customers source data-node hardware. Pure Storage reported that 60 data nodes exceeded 5 TB/s of reads (about 83 GB/s per node; the brief cites "upwards of" 85 GB/s per node), scaling linearly3. The often-quoted ">10 TB/s" figure was a launch-time claim from preliminary testing, not a published configuration24.

The steelman for VAST: shared media makes cluster-wide reduction, wide erasure codes and multi-protocol access natural. EXA's data-node protection also appears to be maturing. One hands-on review reported hardware HA with software erasure coding planned25 [VERIFY: current FlashBlade//EXA data-node protection scheme and release]. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: how fast DirectFlash-based data nodes close the media-efficiency gap, and whether EXA's design wins the >1 TB/s single-namespace deals while FlashBlade//S and FlashArray hold the enterprise.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Disaggregated shared-everything milestones
    2016 : VAST founded with separate compute and storage tiers
    2019 : VAST emerges from stealth
    2021 : VAST qualifies Kioxia FL6 SLC as second SCM source
    2022 : Ceres DBox with BlueField DPUs : Intel winds down Optane
    2023 : HPE GreenLake for File runs VAST software
    2025 : HPE X10000 shared-everything object : Pure Storage announces FlashBlade EXA : VAST EBox ships in v5.2 : NetApp AFX disaggregates ONTAP : CoreWeave signs 1.17B dollar VAST deal
    2026 : VAST valuation reported near 30B dollars

Figure 16.5 — A single start-up's design (2016–2019) became an industry pattern in 2025, when three incumbents shipped disaggregated systems within eight months.

The roots are older: VAXclusters and Oracle RAC were "shared-disk" designs that choked on lock traffic and slow SANs. What changed was NVMe-oF making remote flash nearly local, and SCM giving a shared, persistent place for metadata266. Two trends point forward. Packaging is converging: VAST's EBox16 and Dell's Exascale "personalities" on common PowerEdge hardware27 blur the hardware line while keeping the logical split. And CXL memory pooling applies the same disaggregation logic one level down, inside the server.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In which deals does EXA beat a shared-media design, and where does it lose?" A strong answer names thresholds (throughput, GPU count, namespace size). It credits the direct data path and metadata performance, and it is candid about features that apply to the metadata core but not yet to data nodes.
  2. "What share of a 2 TB/s bill of materials is back-end networking, and who supplies the switches?" A strong answer gives a percentage, port count and supplier, and says whether the customer's fabric can be reused.
  3. "What is the smallest configuration we can sell profitably against a VAST EBox?" A strong answer knows the minimum node counts on both sides and where erasure-coding overhead and fixed fabric cost bite.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Trace a write from client to persistence: how many fabric crossings, and in which failure domains do the two copies land?" Strong: it gives the persistence point, the anti-affinity rule and the amplification factor.
  2. "An enclosure or data node dies at 80% full during a checkpoint. What does the client see, and for how long?" Strong: it gives the degraded throughput percentage, the rebuild time and whether the outcome is unavailability or only slowdown.
  3. "Where is the serialization point for metadata: sharding, locks in shared memory, or an owner node?" Strong: it gives a create/s figure for small files and what limits it.

Don't say this:

  • "DASE eliminates east-west traffic." It moves all traffic onto the back-end fabric and multiplies it for writes.
  • "Stateless compute means a node failure is free." It is cheap, not free: in-flight operations retry and capacity drops by 1/N.
  • "FlashBlade//EXA is Everpure's version of VAST." It disaggregates metadata from data, but clients go directly to data nodes. Say "metadata/data split" instead.
  • "Disaggregated is always cheaper." It is cheaper only when the workload is far from a server's built-in ratio, or at a scale where wide erasure codes apply.
  • "This is new." Shared-disk clusters are 40 years old. What is new is NVMe-oF plus shared persistent metadata.

docs.text:
• VAST's architecture white paper and its KB pages on DBox-HA and rack resiliency (similarity reduction, locally decodable codes, stripe rules).
  • Lockwood et al., PDSW'21, which benchmarks a VAST system independently8.
  • Everpure's FlashBlade//EXA technical brief and "Metadata Advantage" white paper. NetApp's AFX technical reports on the Storage Availability Zone.
  • For code theory: Huang et al., "Erasure Coding in Windows Azure Storage" (USENIX ATC 2012) on local reconstruction codes.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• DASE — disaggregated shared-everything: stateless compute sharing all media over a fabric.
  • CNode / DNode / DBox — VAST's compute node, enclosure fabric endpoint and storage enclosure.
  • Storage-class memory (SCM) — persistent media much faster than NAND, used here for write buffer and metadata.
  • Locally decodable code — erasure code that rebuilds a strip from a subset of the stripe.
  • Enclosure blast radius — the data affected when a whole shelf fails.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 17. Parallel and distributed file systems
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: File protocols · Scale-out shared-nothing clusters · Disaggregated shared-everything

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A parallel file system splits "where is it?" from "give me the bytes." A metadata server (MDS) answers once per file; clients then stripe data directly across many object storage servers (OSSs).
  • The client is the smart part. A kernel module on every node stripes, locks and speaks RDMA. That gives Lustre and IBM Storage Scale (GPFS) multi-TB/s, and makes them hard to run.
  • HPC built them and still runs on them. Lustre is on more than 60% of the Top5001. Early GPU clusters inherited them from HPC teams.
  • The walls are metadata, small files and client management. One MDS serialises its namespace, and every kernel upgrade waits for a matching client build.
  • The pattern is being rebuilt on standard clients. pNFS designs such as Everpure's FlashBlade//EXA and Hammerspace keep the split but use the stock NFS client2, trading some coherency for easier operations.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Every large AI storage deal is partly a referendum on the parallel file system. DDN (Lustre as EXAScaler), IBM (Storage Scale) and WEKA all sell parallel file systems with NVIDIA certifications and HPC references. Buyers raised on Lustre judge everything by its bandwidth; those who have run it remember evictions, MDS hot spots and client builds.

FlashBlade//EXA copies Lustre's architecture (a metadata tier, data streamed directly from data nodes) but swaps the proprietary client for pNFS2. Which pain a buyer weighs more decides the deal. Chapter 8 covers the pNFS protocol; Chapter 44 covers DDN.

docs.title: The components
docs.text:
Lustre is the reference design, with five parts29:

  • Clients run a kernel module that presents an ordinary POSIX mount.
  • The MGS (management server) holds configuration; clients read it at mount.
  • The MDS serves MDTs (metadata targets) holding the namespace: directories, inodes, permissions and each file's layout, the list of OST objects holding its data.
  • The OSS serves OSTs (object storage targets): local ldiskfs or ZFS file systems on RAID-protected devices, holding file data as objects.
  • LNet is the network layer: RDMA over InfiniBand or RoCE, or TCP, with routing between fabrics.
flowchart LR
    subgraph CL["Compute and GPU nodes"]
        C1["Client 1"]
        C2["Client 2"]
        C3["Client N"]
    end
    NET["LNet fabric: IB, RoCE or TCP"]
    C1 --- NET
    C2 --- NET
    C3 --- NET
    NET --- MGS["MGS + MGT: config"]
    NET --- MDS1["MDS 1: MDT0 namespace"]
    NET --- MDS2["MDS 2: MDT1 via DNE"]
    NET --- OSS1["OSS 1: OST0, OST1"]
    NET --- OSS2["OSS 2: OST2, OST3"]
    MDS1 -. "failover pair" .- MDS2
    OSS1 -. "failover pair" .- OSS2

Figure 17.1 — Lustre separates a small metadata tier from a wide data tier, and both sit behind the same RDMA fabric that clients reach directly.

The ratio is the design: Frontier's 679 PB Orion file system has 40 metadata servers and 450 storage servers3.

docs.title: Striping: memory interleaving for files
docs.text:
A layout has two main parameters: stripe size, the chunk size (commonly 1 MiB by default), and stripe count, how many OSTs the chunks are dealt across (commonly 1)4. Both are set per file or directory; Progressive File Layouts (2.10) widen the count as a file grows5.

Figure 17.2 — The client computes which OST holds any byte without asking a server, exactly as a memory controller picks a DRAM channel from address bits.

Semiconductor bridge. This is channel interleaving: consecutive lines spread across channels so a stream uses all of them. The failure modes match. Interleave too finely and every access touches every bank; let an access stride align with the pattern and all clients hammer one OST, the "partition camping" GPU programmers know.

Worked example (why stripe count matters). Assume each OST sustains 5 GB/s (illustrative). A 405B-parameter checkpoint is about 6.5 TB. As one shared file with stripe count 1, it lands on one OST: 6.5 TB ÷ 5 GB/s ≈ 1,300 s, 22 minutes of idle GPUs. Stripe count 64 gives 320 GB/s and about 20 s. Wider is not free: every client then locks every OST, and one slow OST stalls the write, so checkpoint libraries usually write one file per rank.

docs.title: Tracing a write
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant M as MDS and MDT
    participant O1 as OSS 1 OST0
    participant O2 as OSS 2 OST2
    C->>M: open with create intent
    M->>M: allocate inode, choose OSTs, assign precreated objects
    M-->>C: file handle, layout, metadata lock
    C->>C: map offsets to OSTs from stripe size and count
    par stripes in parallel over RDMA
        C->>O1: extent lock, then write stripes 0, 4, 8
        C->>O2: extent lock, then write stripes 2, 6, 10
    end
    O1-->>C: reply with transaction number
    O2-->>C: reply with transaction number
    Note over C,O2: Client keeps data until OSTs report the commit, for replay after a crash
    C->>M: close

Figure 17.3 — The MDS is touched at open and close; the bytes flow straight from client to many OSSs at once.

OSTs grant byte-range extent locks through Lustre's distributed lock manager, so clients writing different ranges of one file proceed in parallel and stay coherent. That POSIX coherency for shared-file writes is what the kernel module buys; NFS's close-to-open model is weaker (Chapter 8).

docs.title: Tracing a read
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant M as MDS and MDT
    participant O1 as OSS 1 OST0
    participant O2 as OSS 2 OST2
    alt layout not cached
        C->>M: lookup and open
        M-->>C: layout and read lock
    else layout cached under a valid lock
        C->>C: no MDS round trip needed
    end
    par read stripes in parallel
        C->>O1: read lock, read stripes 0, 4, 8
        C->>O2: read lock, read stripes 2, 6, 10
    end
    O1-->>C: RDMA bulk data
    O2-->>C: RDMA bulk data
    C->>C: reassemble in page cache

Figure 17.4 — With the layout cached, a read never touches the metadata server, which is why large sequential reads scale almost linearly with OSS count.

Semiconductor bridge. The MDS is the directory or tag lookup before the data access; the cached layout is a TLB entry, and a lock callback is a TLB shootdown.

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text:
Failure What happens Blast radius / cost Drive RAID or ZFS under the OST rebuilds locally. Lustre itself does not see it. Degraded OST bandwidth during rebuild; one slow OST slows every file striped over it. OSS server Its partner in the failover pair mounts the OSTs from shared, dual-ported storage. Clients reconnect and replay uncommitted requests6. I/O to those OSTs pauses for the recovery window. Pairs need shared enclosures and fencing. MDS Same pattern, with a standby or a DNE peer taking over the MDT. Namespace operations stall cluster-wide while it recovers. Client or its link If a client misses a lock callback before the timer expires, the server evicts it and reclaims its locks7. Dirty data in that client's cache is lost and applications see I/O errors, a frequent operational complaint. Whole OST lost Data striped over it is gone unless the file was mirrored. File Level Redundancy has existed since Lustre 2.11, but it is opt-in5. Protection is per-server, not cross-server erasure coding as in shared-nothing systems.

Table 17.1 — Classic Lustre protects data inside each server pair and relies on fast failover. The client, not the hardware, is the weakest link in daily operation.

docs.title: Where it hits walls
docs.text:
1. Metadata serialisation. One MDT handles every create, open and stat in its namespace slice. Distributed Namespace (DNE) added remote directories in 2.4 and directories striped across MDTs in 2.85, yet ORNL still found shared-directory workloads bottlenecked on one MDT8. Scaling needs the workload to spread out.
  2. Small files. Worked example: a billion 100 KB images (100 TB) read in 100 s at 1 TB/s. At an illustrative 50,000 opens/s per MDT [VERIFY: representative per-MDT open rate on current hardware], the opens take 20,000 s (5.6 hours), 200 times longer. Data-on-MDT (2.11) keeps tiny files on the MDT to save a round trip5. AI training looks exactly like this (Chapter 21).
  3. Client software management. The client left mainline Linux in 2018; a 2025 effort aims to upstream it again9. Meanwhile every kernel update waits for a matching client build.
  4. Kernel dependence and tenancy. A kernel module on thousands of GPU nodes is a security and change-control burden neoclouds dislike, and multi-tenancy came late: Lustre 2.17 (December 2025) headlined dynamic nodemaps10.

docs.title: Pros, cons and fit
docs.text:
Strength Weakness Bandwidth Near-linear with OSS count; RDMA end to end Sensitive to stripe settings and to the slowest OST Semantics Full POSIX, coherent shared-file writes Locks require eviction to resolve dead clients Metadata Simple and fast per MDT Serialisation point; DNE needs workload cooperation Cost Open source (Lustre) on commodity or appliance hardware Specialist staff; pair-wise HA hardware; little data reduction Operations Mature tooling, 25 years of HPC experience Kernel client lifecycle; tuning is a craft

Table 17.2 — Parallel file systems trade operational simplicity for raw, coherent bandwidth.

Best fit: large-file streaming (simulation output, checkpoints, video), many ranks writing one file, sites with an HPC operations team. Worst fit: billions of tiny files, multi-tenant clouds with mixed kernels, enterprise shares needing SMB, snapshots and data reduction, and small clusters where fixed MDS and failover-pair costs dominate.

docs.title: Why HPC built them and AI inherited them
docs.text:
Late-1990s simulations on thousands of nodes dumped memory simultaneously, overwhelming NFS's single head. Lustre began as a Carnegie Mellon research project in 19991; IBM's GPFS shipped in 199811. The IO500 list, started at SC17, ranks systems by a geometric mean of bandwidth and metadata scores12; Lustre accounts for nearly half its entries [VERIFY: search-summary only]13.

Early AI training looked like HPC: synchronous jobs, giant checkpoints, InfiniBand, lab-trained buyers. NVIDIA reference architectures and the clouds followed: AWS launched FSx for Lustre in 201814, Google's Managed Lustre runs DDN EXAScaler15, and Azure Managed Lustre entered MLPerf Storage in 202616. AI added what HPC tolerated badly: billions of small files, churning inference fleets, tenants refusing kernel modules. WEKA, VAST and pNFS designs compete in that gap.

docs.title: Cost and operational implications
docs.text: Lustre is free; expertise is not. Sites pay for appliance support or a managed service, buy paired servers on shared enclosures, accept RAID overhead (20% for 8+2) with little data reduction, and absorb hidden costs: GPU time lost to evictions and MDS stalls, and staff time tuning stripes.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
System Metadata design Client / data path Protection AI positioning Lustre / DDN EXAScaler MDS/MDT, scaled by DNE Kernel client, LNet RDMA RAID under OSTs, failover pairs AI400X-series appliances; Google Cloud Managed Lustre1715 IBM Storage Scale (GPFS) Distributed: any node can manage metadata, with token-based locking Kernel client; shared-disk (NSD) or shared-nothing RAID or erasure coding NVIDIA-certified "AI Data Platform" (6.0.1, June 2026)1118 BeeGFS (ThinkParQ) Separate metadata services, namespace split by directory Kernel client Buddy mirroring of targets v8.2 (Nov 2025) added background rebalancing19 WEKA NeuralMesh Metadata sharded into "buckets" across all nodes, with no dedicated MDS Proprietary client: user-space DPDK data path plus a WEKA kernel driver for the POSIX mount Distributed erasure coding Converged and cloud modes; KV-cache extension2021 Hammerspace Anvil metadata servers pNFS Flex Files, stock Linux client Delegated to underlying NFS storage Parallel NFS co-developed for Meta's GenAI clusters22 Everpure FlashBlade//EXA FlashBlade metadata core running Purity pNFS: metadata over NFSv4.1/TCP, data over NFSv3/RDMA to data nodes; stock client Data-node scheme maturing [VERIFY: current data-node protection] MLPerf Storage v3.0 checkpoint result216

Table 17.3 — Every design keeps the metadata/data split. They differ in where metadata lives, how heavy the client is, and who protects the data.

Is FlashBlade//EXA a parallel file system? Architecturally, yes: the metadata core plays the MDS role, data nodes play the OSS role, and clients move bytes directly to data nodes2. The differences are deliberate: metadata runs on Purity across a scale-out blade cluster, not one MDT, and the client is stock Linux NFS. In MLPerf Storage v3.0, 30 EXA data nodes posted 877.5 GiB/s of checkpoint writes (327.6 GiB/s with 10 data nodes) against Azure Managed Lustre's 642.2 GiB/s from 128 clients, on different configurations1623.

Steelman the incumbents. Lustre and Storage Scale give coherent shared-file writes NFS lacks, plus decades of exascale references; Lustre's open-source license appeals to sovereign and lab buyers; WEKA sidesteps the MDS bottleneck by sharding metadata across every node. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: target HPC-heritage AI buyers whose pain is client management and metadata; publish IO500-style metadata results beside bandwidth; and address shared-file-write semantics before they become a late objection.

docs.text:
timeline
    title Parallel file system milestones
    1998 : IBM ships GPFS on AIX
    1999 : Lustre starts as a Carnegie Mellon research project
    2007 : Sun acquires Cluster File Systems
    2012 : Intel buys Whamcloud
    2013 : Lustre 2.4 adds DNE remote directories

Figure 17.5 — Lustre outlived four changes of owner and kept its HPC lead; managed cloud services now extend it while standard-client designs attack it from below.

IBM dropped the Spectrum brand in 2023, making GPFS "IBM Storage Scale"24. Lustre changed hands four times: Cluster File Systems to Sun (2007), Oracle (2010, with Sun), Intel (2012, via Whamcloud) and DDN (2018)252627. In 2020 it ran on 77 of the top 100 systems, Spectrum Scale on 2328. Going forward, clouds absorb the operational burden, upstreaming may end the kernel-module tax, and pNFS rebuilds the architecture on standard clients.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "When a Lustre shop evaluates EXA, what is the first objection?" Strong: names shared-file writes, shows where close-to-open is safe (per-rank checkpoints, read-mostly data), cites a reference.
  2. "Do buyers value metadata rate or bandwidth more?" Strong: EXA creates and opens per second at a stated size, beside bandwidth, tied to a billion-file dataset.
  3. "How do we beat Google or Azure Managed Lustre for cloud-adjacent buyers?" Strong: data gravity, egress, price per TB/s, as-a-service.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What is EXA's equivalent of a Lustre eviction? What does a client see if it hangs mid-write?" Strong: layout recall, lease expiry, recovery time, fate of in-flight writes.
  2. "Does one hot directory scale across the metadata core?" Strong: says whether a single directory spans blades, unlike Lustre's single-MDT limit.
  3. "Who sets stripe width, and can a bad user setting hurt neighbours?" Strong: server-chosen layouts versus Lustre-style user tuning.

Don't say this:

  • "Lustre is legacy." It runs most of the largest systems, and three hyperscalers sell it as a managed service.
  • "Parallel file systems can't scale metadata." DNE, GPFS and WEKA distribute it; the question is how evenly the workload spreads.
  • "pNFS is Lustre with NFS." It drops the kernel module but also Lustre's coherent shared-file locking.
  • "Wider striping is always faster." It multiplies locks and makes the slowest OST everyone's problem.
  • "GPFS is IBM's Lustre." GPFS has no dedicated metadata server; it uses distributed tokens on a shared-disk heritage.

docs.text:

  • Lustre's LDLM lock manager, imperative recovery and Progressive File Layouts; IOR and mdtest, the IO500 tools.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• MDS / MDT — metadata server and its target holding namespace and layouts.
  • OSS / OST — object storage server and its targets holding file data.
  • MGS — Lustre's configuration server.
  • LNet — Lustre's RDMA-capable network layer.
  • Stripe size / count — chunk size; number of OSTs a file spans.
  • DNE — namespace spread across several MDTs.
  • Client eviction — a server dropping an unresponsive client's locks.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 18. Object storage architecture
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Object storage and S3 · Data protection and resilience · Scale-out shared-nothing clusters

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• An object store has three planes: stateless S3 gateways, an index mapping keys to fragments, and data nodes holding erasure-coded fragments, with background services behind them.
  • The index decides most outcomes. A sharded metadata database makes LIST cheap. Hashing the key to compute placement (MinIO) removes the database bottleneck but turns LIST into a cluster-wide fan-out.
  • Erasure coding across sites is the capacity lever. 6+3 over three sites stores 1.5× raw versus 2–3× for replication, at the price of WAN reads and multi-day site rebuilds.
  • The scaling walls are object count, small objects and tail latency. Disks are rarely the limit.
  • Object storage is moving from cheap-and-deep to fast. On all-flash object, the metadata engine matters more than $/TB.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Chapter 9 showed S3 becoming the default AI data interface. Behind the API, systems differ sharply: a fast endpoint over a slow index still lists a billion keys slowly. When an AI buyer weighs FlashBlade against MinIO AIStor, Cloudian or Dell ObjectScale, deals turn on internals: objects per bucket, LIST rate, the cost of a small PUT, and what happens when a node dies.

Pure Storage built FlashBlade as all-flash object while object still meant disk archives. Now that rivals are on flash too, does its metadata engine still differentiate?

docs.title: The idea in one picture
docs.text:
Figure 18.1 — Gateways, index and data nodes scale independently: gateways for request rate, the index for object count and LIST, data nodes for capacity and bandwidth.

  • Gateways terminate HTTPS, check SigV4 and policy, choose placement and erasure-code; they hold no durable state.
  • The index is a replicated, sharded table keyed by bucket + key + version, holding size, ETag and fragment map, sorted so LIST is a range scan.
  • Data nodes map fragments to disk extents with a local engine. AWS's engine, ShardStore, is a key-value store of roughly 40,000 lines of Rust, validated with lightweight formal methods1. It is LSM-based but keeps shard data outside the tree to limit write amplification2.

S3's index design is unpublished; its scale is not: over 500 trillion objects and 200 million requests per second (March 2026)3.

docs.title: Where metadata lives: a database or a hash
docs.text:
1. A separate metadata database. Cloudian HyperStore uses Cassandra for metadata and small objects4. StorageGRID uses Cassandra with three copies per site5. Ceph RGW keeps bucket indexes in RocksDB-backed omap, resharding above 100,000 objects per shard67. FlashBlade runs a distributed key-value database across its blades8.
  2. Computed placement, with metadata stored beside the data. MinIO hashes the object name to pick an erasure set of 2–16 drives and has no metadata database910. Objects under about 128 KiB are stored inline in the metadata file11. Scality RING places keys on a Chord-style ring12. So does Ceph's CRUSH (Chapter 15).

Semiconductor bridge: page table versus set-associative cache. An index database is a page table, with the gateway cache as its TLB: data can live anywhere, but a miss costs a walk. Hash placement is a set-associative cache: address bits pick the set, no table needed. But a cache cannot be enumerated in address order, so LIST on a hash-placed store queries every erasure set and merge-sorts the replies.

docs.title: Tracing a PUT
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant LB as Load balancer
    participant G as S3 gateway
    participant A as IAM and policy cache
    participant I as Index shard
    participant D as 12 data nodes
    C->>LB: PUT bucket/key with 64 MB body
    LB->>G: route to any healthy gateway
    G->>A: verify SigV4 and bucket policy
    A-->>G: allow
    G->>I: get placement for bucket/key
    I-->>G: erasure set or chunk allocation
    alt object below inline threshold
        G->>I: store bytes inside the index record
    else large object
        G->>G: cut into 8 data and 4 parity fragments
        G->>D: stream fragments with checksums, one per failure domain
        D-->>G: write quorum reached
    end
    G->>I: conditional commit of new version and fragment map
    I-->>G: committed on index quorum
    G-->>C: 200 OK with ETag
    Note over I,D: Later - scrub, rebalance, lifecycle, GC of old versions

Figure 18.2 — Data becomes durable first and visible second: the index commit is the single point where a new version appears to every reader.

Worked example (write amplification). A 64 MB PUT under 8+4 coding writes twelve 8 MB fragments, 96 MB in all (1.5×). Gateway NICs carry 64 MB in and 96 MB out, 2.5× the client bandwidth. A 4 KB object under the same code would make 512 B fragments, each padded to a 4 KiB sector: 48 KiB on disk (12×) and 12 drive writes. So systems inline small objects (MinIO, Cloudian) or mirror first and erasure-code later. Dell ObjectScale triple-mirrors until a 128 MB chunk fills, then converts it to 12+413.

docs.title: Tracing a GET
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as S3 gateway
    participant K as Gateway metadata cache
    participant I as Index shard
    participant D as Data nodes
    C->>G: GET bucket/key, optional Range
    G->>G: verify SigV4 and policy
    G->>K: location cached and still current?
    alt miss or stale
        G->>I: read latest committed version
        I-->>G: version, ETag, fragment map
    end
    G->>D: request 8 data fragments plus 1 hedge
    D-->>G: first 8 fragments to arrive
    G->>G: decode only if a data fragment is missing, verify checksum
    G-->>C: 200 or 206 with bytes

Figure 18.3 — A GET waits for the slowest of k fragment reads, so tail latency comes from the wide stripe, not the average drive.

Worked example (tail latency). Suppose each node stalls 1% of the time. Waiting on 8 specific fragments, 1 − 0.99⁸ ≈ 7.7% of GETs stall. Asking 9 nodes and using the first 8, a GET stalls only if two are slow: 1 − (0.99⁹ + 9 × 0.01 × 0.99⁸) ≈ 0.34%. Spending 12% more reads buys a roughly 20× better tail.

docs.title: Erasure coding across nodes and sites
docs.text:
Semiconductor bridge: chipkill. Server ECC spreads each codeword across DRAM chips so a dead chip is correctable; object stores spread stripes across nodes, racks or sites. Wider spread means cheaper protection and dearer reconstruction.

flowchart TB
    subgraph A["A. Three full copies, one per site"]
        A1["Site 1: copy"] --- A2["Site 2: copy"] --- A3["Site 3: copy"]
    end
    subgraph B["B. Local 12+4 at two sites, mirrored"]
        B1["Site 1: 16 fragments"] --- B2["Site 2: 16 fragments"]
    end
    subgraph C["C. Geo 6+3 across three sites"]
        C1["Site 1: fragments 1-3"] --- C2["Site 2: fragments 4-6"] --- C3["Site 3: fragments 7-9"]
    end
    A --> AR["3.0x raw, local reads, async copy lag"]
    B --> BR["2.67x raw, local reads, survives site plus 4 nodes"]
    C --> CR["1.5x raw, every read crosses WAN, zero margin after site loss"]

Figure 18.4 — Geo-dispersed erasure coding halves raw capacity against replication but puts the WAN on every read and every rebuild.

10 PB usable Raw capacity Survives site loss? Normal GET Rebuild after a site loss A. 3 copies, 3 sites 30 PB Yes, 2 copies left Local Re-copy 10 PB B. 12+4 per site, 2 sites 26.7 PB Yes, plus 4 node losses Local Re-copy 10 PB from one site C. 6+3 across 3 sites 15 PB Yes, zero margin left ≥3 of 6 fragments over WAN Read 10 PB over WAN to rebuild 5 PB

Table 18.1 — Worked example: geo-EC saves 15 PB raw per 10 PB usable, but leaves data unprotected during a multi-day rebuild.

StorageGRID documents 1.5× for 6+3 over three sites and advises against it above 100 ms inter-site latency1415. A site rebuild pulls twice the lost data over the WAN16. In case C, rebuilding 5 PB moves 10 PB: 800,000 s (~9.3 days) at 100 Gb/s. AWS spreads S3 Standard across at least three Availability Zones, targeting eleven nines17; metro distances keep the penalty small.

docs.title: How it scales and where it hits walls
docs.text:
1. Index and LIST. Index size grows with object count, not bytes. At an illustrative ~500 bytes per record and 3 replicas, 100 billion objects need ~150 TB of index flash. LIST speed depends on index design and client parallelism: Pure Storage listed a 67-billion-object FlashBlade bucket in ~43 hours with a parallel Go client18, which works out to 67e9 ÷ 154,800 s ≈ 433,000 keys/s. A single thread at 20 ms per 1,000-key page would need ~15.5 days.
  2. Small objects multiply records, drive I/Os and request overhead (see the 12× example).
  3. Hot shards. Sequential keys such as timestamps pile onto one index range. Ceph briefly blocks a bucket's writes while it reshards6.
  4. Background debt. Scrubbing, rebuild, expiry and garbage collection compete with clients.

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text:
Failure What happens Cost Drive Fragments rebuilt from k survivors onto many drives in parallel Background bandwidth; degraded reads decode on the fly Data node Its fragments rebuilt elsewhere; GETs read other fragments meanwhile Rebuild traffic ≈ k × lost data Gateway Load balancer drops it; clients retry In-flight requests retried; no data at risk Index replica Quorum continues on remaining replicas Lose quorum and that shard's keys are unwritable though data is intact Network partition Minority side cannot commit; quorum prevents split-brain Writes fail on one side, CAP in practice (Ch 20) Site Replication fails over; geo-EC serves degraded reads See Table 18.1

Table 18.2 — Data-node failures are routine; losing index quorum is the outage that matters.

docs.title: Pros, cons and fit
docs.text:
Strength Weakness Scale Hundreds of trillions of objects, exabytes, no directory tree to lock Object count stresses the index; LIST is the slowest operation Efficiency Wide and geo erasure codes (1.3–1.5×) on commodity servers Small objects defeat erasure coding; need inlining or packing Resilience Node and site loss survivable by design Rebuilds are long and wide; index quorum is a single point of logic Performance Bandwidth scales with nodes; parallel range GETs Per-request fixed cost; tail latency from wide stripes Semantics Immutable whole objects, simple consistency No in-place updates, no rename, thin metadata

Table 18.3 — Object storage trades rich semantics for scale and capacity efficiency.

Best fit: sharded AI datasets, checkpoints, lakehouse tables, backup, archive, media. Worst fit: in-place-write databases and VMs, tiny files renamed often, POSIX tools that need directories.

docs.title: From cheap-and-deep to fast
docs.text:
HDD-era object stores were built around a disk's ~100–200 random IOPS: big chunks, metadata on a thin flash slice, tens of milliseconds of latency. Flash removes the IOPS-per-TB constraint, so metadata and small objects share fast media. Falling QLC $/TB, S3-native AI pipelines and RDMA into GPU memory make it pay (Chapter 9).

Signal (vendor-stated, not comparable) Claim Source MinIO on NVMe 325 GiB/s GET from 32 nodes MinIO19 Cloudian HyperStore on flash ~200 GiB/s from 6 nodes (~35 GiB/s each) Cloudian20 Scality RING XP Microsecond-level 4 KB PUT/GET latency Scality, 2024-10-3021 Dell ObjectScale XF960 All-flash appliance positioned for AI Dell, 202522 FlashBlade//E >3 trillion objects in one array Pure Storage23

Table 18.4 — Every major object vendor now markets flash performance; object count and latency claims are the new battleground.

docs.title: Cost and operational implications
docs.text: Software-defined object storage on dense HDD servers is still the lowest $/TB. Its hidden cost is operations: index repair and compaction, rebalancing, scrubbing and multi-site networking. In StorageGRID, the smallest node caps a site's metadata capacity5. Licensing can also shift: MinIO's community edition entered maintenance mode in December 202524. Appliances cost more per TB but remove most of it (Chapter 19).

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
System Index / metadata Placement and protection Media Public data point Everpure FlashBlade Distributed key-value metadata across blades, shared with NFS/SMB NVRAM write staging, then wide N+2 erasure coding across blades825 All-flash (DirectFlash) 3 T objects on one //E23; 67 B-key LIST in ~43 h18 AWS S3 Not published ≥3 AZs; ShardStore on storage nodes117 Not disclosed 500 T+ objects, 200 M+ req/s3 MinIO AIStor None; xl.meta beside data Hash to 2–16-drive erasure set10 NVMe or HDD 325 GiB/s GET, 32 nodes19 Cloudian HyperStore Cassandra; small objects inline4 Replication or EC per policy HDD and flash ~35 GiB/s per node claimed20 Ceph RGW Sharded bucket index in RocksDB omap7 4 MB RADOS objects; replicated or EC pools7 Any 100 k objects per index shard6 NetApp StorageGRID Cassandra, 3 copies per site5 ILM rules; 6+3 across 3 sites14 HDD and flash appliances Geo-EC below 100 ms latency14 Dell ObjectScale Chunk-based store 128 MB chunks, 12+4 or 10+213 XF960 all-flash22 ECS heritage Scality RING Chord-style key ring12 Replication or EC RING XP all-flash21 µs-level 4 KB latency claimed

Table 18.5 — Every vendor now has a flash object story; they differ in where the index lives and how protection crosses failure domains.

FlashBlade bets that object metadata is a database problem, solved in flash and NVRAM, shared with file. A 2023 analyst report describes writes mirrored to NVRAM on two other blades before acknowledgement8. On current DFM-based systems, Everpure says Purity distributes the DFMs' NVRAM and flash among "authority" processes running on each blade, each owning a slice of the namespace26 [VERIFY: current Purity//FB PUT write path and copy count]. Steelman for software-defined rivals: cheaper capacity, geo-EC and free choice of servers. FlashBlade's multi-site protection appears to be replication between arrays rather than geo-EC [VERIFY: FlashBlade multi-site object options in 2026]. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: publishing LIST and small-object benchmarks, and testing whether FlashBlade//E with DeepReduce wins capacity deals now lost to Ceph or MinIO on HDD.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Object storage internals, from disk archive to AI data path
    2006 : Amazon S3 launches
    2010 : Scality RING built on a Chord-style ring
    2017 : Pure Storage adds S3 object features to FlashBlade
    2020 : S3 becomes strongly consistent
    2021 : ShardStore paper wins SOSP best paper
    2024 : Scality RING XP all-flash object
    2025 : Cloudian about 200 GiB/s from six flash nodes : FlashBlade E passes 3 trillion objects : MinIO community edition enters maintenance
    2026 : S3 turns 20 with over 500 trillion objects

Figure 18.5 — Object storage spent 15 years optimising for cheap disk; since 2024 the contest has moved to flash, latency and object count.

S3's 2020 strong consistency (Chapter 9) pushed compatible vendors toward linearisable indexes. Pure Storage announced FlashBlade object features in 201727. Next, indexes absorb tables, vectors and richer metadata (Chapter 33): the index is becoming the product.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What is our largest production bucket by object count, and its LIST rate?" Strong: objects, keys/s, client parallelism, a competitor comparison.
  2. "Where do we lose object deals to MinIO, Ceph or Cloudian?" Strong: $/TB, geo-EC and server choice, then where small-object and LIST speed flip it.
  3. "What share of FlashBlade capacity is accessed via S3 rather than NFS?" Strong: a trend and its workloads (lakehouse, checkpoints, KV cache).

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Trace a 4 KB PUT: where do the bytes land, how many drive writes, when is it erasure-coded?" Strong: inline or staging path, amplification, conversion trigger.
  2. "What happens when one index shard gets hot?" Strong: how it splits, whether writes block, for how long.
  3. "How do we bound tail latency on wide stripes?" Strong: hedged reads, fragment sizing, p99 by object size.

Don't say this:

  • "Object storage is cheap and slow." It increasingly runs on flash and feeds GPUs.
  • "Geo-EC is free durability." It puts the WAN on every read and leaves a multi-day exposed rebuild.
  • "Object stores have no metadata bottleneck." The index is the bottleneck, and LIST exposes it.
  • "MinIO has a metadata database." It deliberately does not; hence both its write scaling and its LIST cost.
  • "AWS S3 runs on X." Its internals are mostly unpublished; cite ShardStore and stop.

docs.text: • Gateway, metadata index, erasure set, inline object, bucket index sharding, geo-distributed erasure coding, hedged read, scrubbing, lifecycle policy, ShardStore. Definitions in the glossary.
