docs.title: 19. Software-defined storage and HCI
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Scale-up dual-controller arrays · Scale-out shared-nothing clusters · Block protocols and NVMe-oF · Data protection and resilience

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Software-defined storage (SDS) sells the storage OS without the box (Ceph, MinIO, VAST, WEKA). Hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) runs it on the same nodes as the VMs (Nutanix, vSAN).
  • HCI's wall is coupled scaling. Every node adds compute and capacity in a fixed ratio, stranding whatever the estate did not need.
  • Cloud block storage is SDS at hyperscale. EBS replicates volumes inside one Availability Zone, with a separate configuration service and Nitro-card offload.
  • Broadcom's VMware licensing reset (from December 2023) reopened "HCI vs. array" and pushed customers toward Nutanix, public cloud and external arrays.
  • Software-only buys margin %, no NAND inventory and fast iteration; appliances buy gross profit per deal and control of the media.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) mostly sells appliances built on its own DirectFlash modules. Yet it already runs every other model here: Portworx (Kubernetes SDS), Purity on cloud instances, and a Meta DirectFlash technology licence with no Everpure hardware1.

Broadcom forces the choice: every VMware renewal must stay on vSAN, switch HCI stacks, or split compute from storage. Everpure's May 2025 Nutanix partnership, with FlashArray as external storage for the AHV hypervisor, is a bet on the third2.

docs.title: Three ways to package the same software
docs.text:
Figure 19.1 — The software is similar in all three; what changes is who supplies hardware and what must scale together.

In the appliance model (Chapter 14) one vendor designs, qualifies, ships and supports the whole box. SDS runs on commodity servers from a hardware compatibility list (HCL), usually as a shared-nothing cluster. HCI folds storage into the hypervisor cluster: each node gives CPU and memory to a storage service (Nutanix's controller VM, or vSAN inside the ESXi kernel) that replicates each VM's writes to other nodes' drives.

Semiconductor bridge. An appliance vendor is an IDM: it owns design and integration, carries inventory and captures integration margin. A software-only vendor is an IP licensor like Arm, collecting a high-margin fee on hardware others build. VAST's "Gemini" model is fabless: VAST specifies the hardware, a manufacturing partner sells it to the customer at cost, and VAST books only software3.

docs.title: Where HCI hits the wall
docs.text:
State and metadata. Data sits on node-local drives (replication factor 2–3, or erasure coding across nodes); metadata is distributed across the cluster. A node is at once compute host, storage target and metadata participant, so losing it touches all three.

Worked example: stranded resources. An illustrative node has 64 cores and 8 × 15.36 TB SSDs (123 TB raw, ~61 TB usable at RF2). An estate needs 400 cores and 2 PB usable. Sized for compute, ⌈400 ÷ 64⌉ = 7 nodes give only ~430 TB. Sized for capacity, ⌈2,000 ÷ 61⌉ = 33 nodes give 2,112 cores, 81% idle. Under per-core subscriptions such as VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), idle cores still need licences; VCF's bundled 1 TiB of vSAN per licensed core4 softens this without fixing it. The fix is un-converging: Nutanix storage-only and compute-only nodes; vSAN Max (2023), a storage-only cluster of up to 8.6 PB that other clusters mount5; or an external array behind HCI compute2. Each concedes HCI's one-building-block promise.

Two more walls follow. East-west amplification: at RF2 every write crosses the cluster network again, and rebuilding a failed 123 TB node at ~5 GB/s of spare bandwidth takes 123,000 ÷ 5 ≈ 6.8 hours. Noisy neighbours: busy VMs starve their node's storage service.

Failure HCI (Nutanix / vSAN-style) EBS-style cloud block Drive Rebuild that drive's data from replicas on other nodes; VMs keep running Invisible to tenant; storage fleet re-replicates Node VMs restart elsewhere (hypervisor HA) and its data re-replicates; two recoveries at once Storage server loss: chain reconfigured, new replica re-mirrored; brief I/O pause Storage controller CVM or kernel module failure: I/O redirected to another node's storage service Nitro card failure is a host failure; volume can attach to a new instance Network link / partition Minority side loses quorum; a split cluster can halt writes Chain cannot complete writes until configuration service picks a new replica set6

Table 19.1 — HCI couples application and data recovery on the same nodes; cloud block moves that complexity into a control plane.

docs.title: Inside an EBS-style cloud block service
docs.text:
From AWS's public papers and docs: an EBS volume lives in one Availability Zone, replicated across several servers there7. On Nitro instances the guest sees an ordinary NVMe device8, emulated by a Nitro card that turns block commands into network requests. Classic EBS keeps each volume on a replication chain (client → primary → replica). A separate configuration master, Physalia, records chain membership in a seven-node Paxos "cell" per volume, so one failure cannot strand many volumes' configuration6. The io2 Block Express back end talks to Nitro over Scalable Reliable Datagram (SRD)9, a multipath transport in the Nitro card that sprays packets across many network paths10.

flowchart LR
    VM["Guest VM: NVMe driver"] --> NC["Nitro card: NVMe emulation, encryption, SRD"]
    NC --> NET["AZ network: multipath"]
    NET --> P["Storage server: primary"]
    P --> R["Storage server: replica"]
    P -.-> CM["Configuration master: Physalia cells"]
    R -.-> CM
    NC -.-> CM
    P --> S3["Snapshots to S3, multi-AZ"]

Figure 19.2 — The configuration master sits off the data path and matters only when a chain changes.

sequenceDiagram
    participant G as Guest VM
    participant N as Nitro card
    participant P as Primary server
    participant R as Replica server
    G->>N: NVMe WRITE 16 KiB
    N->>P: encrypted write over SRD
    P->>R: forward along chain
    R-->>P: persisted
    P-->>N: persisted on both copies
    N-->>G: NVMe completion

Figure 19.3 — A write is acknowledged only after both chain copies persist it; network round trips, not flash, dominate latency.

sequenceDiagram
    participant G as Guest VM
    participant N as Nitro card
    participant P as Chain member
    participant C as Configuration master
    G->>N: NVMe READ 16 KiB
    N->>P: read request over SRD
    P-->>N: data
    N-->>G: decrypted data and completion
    Note over N,C: Only if a member fails
    N->>C: who owns this volume now
    C-->>N: new chain membership

Figure 19.4 — Reads need one copy; the configuration master must survive partitions, when membership changes.

Block Express internals are public only at a high level, so the read diagram leaves the serving copy generic. AWS rates io2 Block Express at 256,000 IOPS, 4,000 MB/s and 64 TiB per volume, under 500 µs average for 16 KiB I/O, and 99.999% durability9. The fleet-level lesson came in April 2011: a network change cut many volumes off from their replicas, all re-mirrored at once, and the "re-mirroring storm" exhausted the zone's spare capacity11. It is the HCI rebuild problem at cloud scale: rate-limit repair and reserve capacity, or recovery becomes the outage.

docs.title: Pros, cons and fit
docs.text:
Appliance SDS on commodity servers HCI Cloud block service Strength Predictable latency; one support owner; media co-design Hardware choice; scale-out; no vendor box markup One building block; simple ops for VM estates No hardware; elastic; API-driven Weakness Box markup; vendor lock on media Customer owns integration and HCL drift Coupled scaling; rebuilds hit apps Single-AZ volumes; egress and per-IOPS pricing Best fit Databases, mixed enterprise block, consolidation Large object and file, AI data lakes, hyperscale Edge, ROBO, mid-size VM clusters Elastic cloud apps; dev/test Worst fit Very small sites; extreme-scale cheap capacity Small teams without storage skills Capacity-heavy or GPU-heavy estates Steady, large, high-IOPS estates (cost) Examples FlashArray, PowerStore, NetApp AFF Ceph, MinIO, VAST, WEKA, Portworx Nutanix, vSAN EBS, Azure Disk, Pure Storage Cloud Azure Native

Table 19.2 — No model dominates; fit depends on how stable the compute-to-capacity ratio is and who owns integration risk.

docs.title: The business-model trade-off
docs.text:
Dimension Software-only subscription Appliance Cloud service Gross margin structure Very high %, on software revenue only (Nutanix non-GAAP 88.0%, FY2026)12 Lower %, on full system revenue (Everpure product 66.2%, subscription 74.9%, Q2 FY27, non-GAAP per earnings summaries)13 Bundled into the provider's service margin; per-GB-month and per-IOPS pricing Support burden Highest: any HCL server, firmware and NIC combination can fail Lowest per system: vendor controls the whole bill of materials Provider absorbs it; customer sees only the SLA Hardware qualification matrix Large (servers × drives × NICs × firmware), or narrowed with "ready node" programmes Small and vendor-owned Single fleet design per generation NAND / component exposure Passed to customer or OEM On the vendor's P&L (Everpure raised prices in early February 2026, and again later, citing NAND and component costs)1415 On the provider's capex Pricing power Depends on lock-in: high for VMware (VCF), eroded for open-source-based products Earned through efficiency (TB/W, data reduction) and lifecycle programmes Strong for small users; weak against large customers who can repatriate Public examples Nutanix; VAST Gemini3; WEKA; MinIO AIStor; IBM Storage Ceph Everpure FlashArray/FlashBlade; Dell; NetApp; DDN appliances AWS EBS; Pure Storage Cloud Azure Native16

Table 19.3 — Software-only maximizes margin percentage and iteration speed; appliances maximize gross profit per deal and media control.

Worked example (illustrative split). On a US$1M system, an appliance vendor books US$1M at 66%: US$660k gross profit. A software-only vendor might book US$400k at 88%: US$352k, with the OEM taking US$600k of hardware. In exchange it carries no inventory or NAND risk and ships on new CPUs immediately. Open source caps pricing from below; a free tier that is good enough must be fenced, as MinIO did with AGPLv3 in 202117, a stripped community console in 202518 and maintenance mode in December 202519.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Everpure's centre of gravity is the appliance, justified by DirectFlash's density and power advantage over commodity SSDs (Chapter 26). At the edges it runs software-only motions: Portworx, container-native SDS bought for about US$370M in 202020; Purity on cloud infrastructure16; off-the-shelf FlashBlade//EXA data nodes (Chapter 16); and the Meta technology licence1.

Steelman the alternatives: Nutanix runs ~88% gross margins on US$2.55B ARR growing 16%12; VAST scales on OEM supply chains without inventory3; IBM's 2022 absorption of Red Hat's Ceph team21 keeps "free and good enough" alive. The appliance reply: HCL support is costly and AI-era power limits reward co-designed media. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: more "array behind someone else's HCI" partnerships; DirectFlash licensing as a repeatable IP business; and Portworx against VMware for VMs moving to Kubernetes.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Software-defined storage, HCI and the Broadcom shock
    2008 : AWS launches EBS
    2011 : EBS re-mirroring storm in US East
    2020 : Physalia and SRD papers published
    2021 : MinIO completes AGPLv3 move : VAST exits hardware
    2022 : Red Hat Ceph team moves to IBM
    2023 : vSAN Max disaggregates vSAN : Broadcom closes VMware and ends perpetual licences
    2024 : AT&T sues over a 1050 percent renewal quote
    2025 : Nutanix and Pure Storage partner : vVols deprecated in VCF 9 : Gartner sees 35 percent of VMware workloads moving by 2028
    2026 : Nutanix with FlashArray generally available : Nutanix ARR reaches 2.55B dollars

Figure 19.5 — SDS and HCI matured quietly; Broadcom's 2023 licensing reset made platform choice a board-level cost decision.

Broadcom closed VMware on 22 November 2023, then ended perpetual licences and folded thousands of SKUs into two bundles, VCF and vSphere Foundation22. AT&T's 2024 lawsuit cited a proposed 1,050% increase; it later settled23. Much of the base paid: Broadcom reported ~US$27B of FY2025 infrastructure-software revenue24 [VERIFY: FY2025 infrastructure-software total, transcript summaries only], and in June 2025 its CEO said over 87% of its 10,000 largest customers had adopted VCF25.

Storage felt it. Gartner expects over a third of VMware workloads to move by 202826. Nutanix's FlashArray integration reached GA around the turn of 2026227. It was not Nutanix's first external storage: Dell PowerFlex took that slot in May 2025, and Dell PowerStore followed in 202628. VCF 9 deprecated vVols, the main external-array hook, with removal planned for 9.12930. The trajectory is un-convergence: split node types, arrays behind HCI, Kubernetes-native SDS for VMs. Cloud block storage has been SDS since EBS was built in 200831.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In a VMware renewal, when do we win behind Nutanix rather than against vSAN?" Strong: capacity-heavy estates, stranded-core licence cost, data reduction; concedes edge and small clusters to HCI.
  2. "What is our gross profit per deal, not margin %, against a software-only rival?" Strong: splits software and hardware dollars and NAND risk.
  3. "What breaks first if Purity ships as software on customer-chosen servers?" Strong: HCL support cost, lost DirectFlash density, Evergreen economics.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What happens to a database VM's p99 latency during an HCI node rebuild?" Strong: rebuild bandwidth caps, throttling policy, time to full redundancy.
  2. "How does a cloud block service avoid a re-mirroring storm?" Strong: reserved spare capacity, rate-limited repair, a small-blast-radius configuration service.
  3. "What does NVMe/TCP to an external array cost versus local HCI reads?" Strong: tens of microseconds, offset by avoided replica writes.

Don't say this:

  • "HCI is just SDS." It is SDS sharing nodes with applications; that coupling is its defining weakness.
  • "Software-only is always better economics." Higher percentage, smaller revenue base, support shifted to the HCL.
  • "EBS is a SAN in the cloud." It is a replicated service with a separate configuration plane, scoped to one zone.
  • "Broadcom killed vSAN." VCF bundles vSAN capacity, so many customers now own more of it.
  • "Ceph is free." The software is; people, testing and hardware qualification are not.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• SDS — storage software sold apart from its hardware.
  • HCI — compute, storage software and media in every node.
  • Stranded resources — capacity or compute bought only because the node bundles it.
  • Chain replication — writes flow along an ordered server chain; a configuration master tracks membership.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 20. Distributed-systems fundamentals for storage
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Data protection and resilience · Object storage and S3 · Scale-out shared-nothing clusters

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• With more than one copy, a system must define "the latest write": its consistency model. Primary storage chooses strong consistency and pays in latency.
  • Consensus (Paxos, Raft) needs 2f+1 voters to survive f failures. Two-site clusters therefore need a third vote, a witness, against split brain.
  • CAP in practice is PACELC. The everyday trade is latency versus consistency, chosen per feature: sync metro picks consistency, async DR picks latency.
  • "Eleven nines" of durability is a model output, not a measurement. Parity, rebuild time and assumed independence drive it; correlated failures are what lose data in practice.
  • Availability nines are measured; durability nines are modelled. Ask which is quoted.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text: Headline claims such as "zero RPO", "six nines", "11 nines durability" and "strongly consistent S3" each rest on a quorum rule, a failure model and a consistency choice. Knowing which separates an engineering guarantee from a marketing number. The stakes are rising: disaggregated and parallel systems (Chapters 16 and 17) spread metadata and erasure codes across hundreds of nodes, where the hard engineering and the outage risk now live.

docs.title: Consistency models: what a reader is promised
docs.text:
A consistency model is the contract about what a reader may see when copies disagree.

Model Promise to a reader Cost Who uses it Strong / linearizable Every read sees the latest acknowledged write, as if there were one copy Each write waits for a quorum or synchronous mirror; minority side stops during a partition Block arrays (FlashArray, PowerMax, ONTAP); metro clusters; Spanner; DynamoDB strongly consistent reads1 Strong read-after-write (per object) Once a PUT or DELETE is acknowledged, every later GET or LIST by any client reflects it; no multi-object transactions Index commit must be a single linearisation point per key Amazon S3 since Dec 2020, Azure Blob, GCS (Chapter 9) Causal If write B depends on write A, nobody sees B without A Track dependencies (version vectors) Some geo-distributed databases; rare as a storage product guarantee Close-to-open A file reopened after another client closes it shows that client's writes Client caches revalidated on open NFS (Chapter 8) Eventual All copies converge if writes stop; reads may be stale meanwhile Cheapest and fastest; conflicts need resolution (last-writer-wins) Cross-region and asynchronous replication; Dynamo-style stores at low quorum settings2

Table 20.1 — Strong consistency is the norm inside one system or one metro; almost everything across regions is eventual.

Semiconductor bridge: MESI versus consensus. MESI already enforces single-writer, multiple-reader per cache line, which is exactly the strong-consistency invariant. But a coherence fabric assumes no lost messages or independent core failures; a storage cluster must survive both. Consensus is coherence that tolerates faults. A directory maps onto a metadata server; an Exclusive line maps onto a lease or NFS delegation.

docs.title: Consensus at L2: Raft on a whiteboard
docs.text:
Paxos (published 1998)3 and Raft (2014)4 solve the same problem: replicas agree on one ordered log, so all apply the same commands in the same order. Ceph's monitors run Paxos and need a strict majority5; DynamoDB replicates each partition with Multi-Paxos1.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Node A
    participant B as Node B
    participant D as Node D
    Note over A,D: Term 4. Leader has crashed. Followers wait a random timeout.
    A->>A: timeout fires first, become candidate for term 5
    A->>B: RequestVote term 5, my log ends at index 6
    A->>D: RequestVote term 5, my log ends at index 6
    B-->>A: vote granted
    Note over A: 2 of 3 votes is a majority, A is leader for term 5
    A->>B: heartbeat AppendEntries, empty
    A->>D: heartbeat AppendEntries, empty
    C->>A: write X to 5
    A->>A: append entry 7 to own log
    A->>B: AppendEntries entry 7
    A->>D: AppendEntries entry 7
    B-->>A: stored entry 7
    Note over A: Majority holds entry 7, so it is committed
    A->>A: apply to state machine
    A-->>C: ACK
    A->>D: next heartbeat carries commit index 7
    D-->>A: stored entry 7, slow but caught up

Figure 20.1 — Raft in two phases: a randomised timeout elects one leader per term by majority vote, then a write commits once a majority has logged it, so the slowest replica never sets latency.

A strong whiteboard answer makes three points. Terms are a logical clock: a node seeing a higher term steps down, so a stale leader cannot commit. Voters reject candidates with staler logs, so a new leader holds every committed entry. Commit needs a majority, not all, so three nodes tolerate one failure.

docs.title: Quorum math: N, W, R
docs.text:
Leaderless, Dynamo-style systems use quorums directly2. With N replicas, writes wait for W acknowledgements and reads query R. W + R > N makes every read overlap the latest write (N=3, W=2, R=2 is classic). W > N/2 stops two conflicting writes both succeeding. N=3, W=1, R=1 is fast but only eventually consistent.

Surviving f failures needs 2f+1 voters, so four voters are no better than three5. Without a majority you get split brain: both halves of a partitioned pair accept writes and diverge. Two-site clusters add a witness (or mediator): a data-less third vote, outside both sites' failure domains, that decides which side keeps serving.

docs.title: CAP and PACELC: what storage actually chooses
docs.text:
CAP (Brewer, 2000; proved by Gilbert and Lynch, 20026) says that during a partition a system gives up consistency or availability. Partitions are not optional, so it is not "pick two". Abadi's PACELC7 adds: else, trade latency against consistency.

Storage chooses per feature. Synchronous metro clusters are PC/EC: each write pays an inter-site round trip, and in a partition the side that loses the mediator race stops serving. Asynchronous DR is PA/EL: local acknowledgement, remote copy lags by the RPO. Spanner is formally CP, yet Brewer argued it exceeds five nines because Google's network rarely partitions8.

docs.title: Durability nines versus availability nines
docs.text:
Availability is the fraction of time data can be served; six nines is ~31.5 seconds of downtime a year, measurable from telemetry. Pure Storage (now Everpure) claimed 99.9999% across the FlashArray//m installed base in 2016, including upgrades, and repeats six nines for later FlashArrays9 (company-stated).

Durability is the probability of not losing data in a year. S3 is designed for eleven nines10; Azure states 11, 12 and 16 nines for locally, zone- and geo-redundant storage11. Nobody can observe a 10⁻¹¹ event on one system, so these are model outputs. (At 100 trillion objects it still implies ~1,000 losses a year.)

The standard model is mean time to data loss (MTTDL). A group of n drives tolerating m failures loses data when m+1 failures overlap. With λ = AFR ÷ 8,766 h and μ = 1 ÷ rebuild time, MTTDL ≈ μᵐ ÷ [n(n−1)…(n−m) λᵐ⁺¹].

Figure 20.2 — Illustrative model: extra parity moves durability by many nines, AFR and rebuild time by fewer, and correlated failures can erase the gain. Data: data/ch20_durability.csv

Worked example (10 PB usable, 30 TB drives, Backblaze's 2025 HDD AFR of 1.36%12). RAID 6 (8+2) with a 42-hour single-spare rebuild models at 5.8 nines. The same code rebuilt declustered in 4 hours reaches 7.8: RAID 6 and 8+2 EC are identical maths, differing only in rebuild speed. Three-way replication reaches 9.0; EC 16+4 reaches 15.1. Device reliability helps less. Backblaze's SSDs ran at 0.9%13; Everpure states 0.15% for DirectFlash Modules14 (NetApp disputes it15). Cutting AFR from 1.36% to 0.15% adds 2.9 nines to RAID 6; moving from 8+2 to 16+4 adds 7.3. Rule of thumb: each tenfold cut in AFR is worth m+1 nines, each tenfold cut in rebuild time m. One caveat on the declustered lines: the model treats each group of k+m drives as independent. In a declustered layout, almost any m+1 failed drives share some stripe, which in this example costs back roughly three nines for 8+2 and five for 16+4. Rebuilding first the few stripes that have lost the most strips recovers much of that, and declustered systems generally do so.

docs.title: Correlated failures and failure domains
docs.text:
The model assumes independence. If each further failure during a rebuild is ten times likelier, because drives share a batch, firmware or power feed, MTTDL falls by 10ᵐ: the dashed line in Figure 20.2 shows 16+4 losing four nines. In 2019 HPE warned that certain SAS SSDs would die at exactly 32,768 power-on hours without a firmware fix16. Drives installed together fail together. Google's 2010 fleet study named planned kernel upgrades a major source of correlated failure17. Random replica placement compounds it; copyset placement cut modelled data-loss probability in a 5,000-node power outage from 99.99% to 0.15%18.

flowchart LR
    D["Drive<br/>media wear, firmware batch"] --> N["Node or controller<br/>CPU, DIMM, NIC, software crash"]
    N --> E["Enclosure or shelf<br/>backplane, PSU pair"]
    E --> R["Rack<br/>top-of-rack switch, PDU"]
    R --> P["Power and cooling zone<br/>UPS, chiller"]
    P --> S["Site or availability zone<br/>utility, fire, fibre cut"]
    S --> G["Region<br/>disaster, regulation"]
    D -.-> D2["Protect: parity within group"]
    E -.-> E2["Protect: stripe across enclosures"]
    S -.-> S2["Protect: sync metro or async DR"]

Figure 20.3 — Each level up is rarer but takes out everything beneath it; protection is only as good as the highest domain a stripe or replica set spans.

The design rule is anti-affinity: at most m strips of a stripe in any domain you intend to survive. Ceph's CRUSH map encodes the hierarchy; VAST's DBox-HA caps strips per enclosure (Chapter 16).

Semiconductor bridge: FIT, AFR and chipkill. One FIT is one failure per 10⁹ device-hours, so 1% AFR ≈ 0.01 ÷ 8,766 × 10⁹ ≈ 1,140 FIT: Backblaze's 1.36% is ~1,550 FIT, a 0.15% module ~170. Erasure coding is chipkill one level up: Reed–Solomon across devices survives a dead chip or drive, until "independent" devices share a defect.

docs.title: Caching and tiering design
docs.text:
Storage caches face the CPU's write-back versus write-through choice, with durability added.

Policy Acknowledge when Risk Typical use Write-through Slower tier has persisted Latency of the slow tier Simple caches, client-side read caches Write-back, volatile Data is in DRAM cache Loss on power or node failure Unsafe for primary storage Write-back, persistent and mirrored Two NVRAM/SCM copies exist Mirror link and NVRAM capacity Dual-controller arrays (Chapter 14); DASE SCM (Chapter 16) Tiering (move, not copy) Data placed by temperature Fast tier may hold the only copy Hot/cold flash and HDD/cloud tiers

Table 20.2 — Write-back is safe only when the cache is itself a durable, mirrored copy; a tier holding the only copy needs the same parity as any other.

Read caches add a coherence cost: every client or node cache needs invalidation, leases or timeouts, which is why NFS settles for close-to-open.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
System Agreement mechanism Partition / PACELC behaviour Durability or availability claim Everpure ActiveCluster (FlashArray) Synchronous mirror, Pure1 Cloud Mediator or on-premises mediator; pre-election if mediator lost PC/EC: up to 11 ms RTT between arrays; loser of mediator race stops serving the pod19 Six nines availability, installed base (company-stated)9 NetApp SnapMirror active sync / MetroCluster ONTAP Mediator; ONTAP Cloud Mediator for SnapMirror active sync from ONTAP 9.17.120 PC/EC; automatic unplanned failover via mediator21 See Chapter 6 Ceph Paxos monitors hold cluster map; CRUSH places data by failure domain PC/EC inside a cluster; multisite asynchronous Depends on pool rule and EC profile5 Amazon S3 / DynamoDB Replicated metadata; DynamoDB Multi-Paxos per partition Strong within region; cross-region asynchronous S3: designed for 11 nines101 Dynamo-style (Cassandra) Leaderless quorums, tunable N/W/R PA/EL by default; PC with QUORUM settings Operator-defined

Table 20.3 — Nearly everyone converges on strong consistency inside a site and a witness for two-site clusters; claims differ in whether they are measured (availability) or modelled (durability).

Everpure's distinctive choice was a cloud-hosted witness, removing the need for a third site19. Steelman for rivals: NetApp has shipped a cloud mediator since ONTAP 9.17.120, and Dell's SRDF family has three decades of deployments. An option a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: publishing durability assumptions beside availability telemetry, making a modelled number defensible.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Distributed-systems ideas in storage
    1998 : Paxos paper published after an eight-year delay
    2000 : Brewer states the CAP conjecture
    2002 : Gilbert and Lynch prove CAP
    2007 : Amazon Dynamo popularises N W R quorums
    2010 : Google quantifies correlated failures in its fleet
    2012 : PACELC and Spanner
    2013 : Copysets placement
    2014 : Raft published
    2017 : ActiveCluster with cloud mediator
    2020 : Amazon S3 becomes strongly consistent

Figure 20.4 — Theory came first; products adopted strong consistency and cloud witnesses once networks made the latency affordable.

Direction: strong consistency wherever latency allows, wider codes with declustered rebuilds, cloud witnesses. AI scale puts metadata consensus and lease managers on the critical path (Chapter 21).

docs.text: Metric Value Context Source / date HDD fleet AFR, 2025 1.36% 344,196 drives; 1.55% in 2024 Backblaze, 2026-02-12<sup>12</sup> SSD lifetime AFR 0.9% Backblaze boot SSDs to mid-2023 The Register, 2023-09-26<sup>13</sup> DirectFlash Module AFR 0.15% Company-stated; disputed by NetApp Everpure blog<sup>14</sup><sup>15</sup> ActiveCluster max RTT 11 ms Synchronous, mediator-arbitrated Everpure docs<sup>19</sup> S3 / Azure LRS / ZRS / GRS durability 11 / 11 / 12 / 16 nines Design targets, not SLAs AWS<sup>10</sup>, Microsoft<sup>11</sup> FlashArray availability 99.9999% (~31.5 s/yr) Company-stated, measured on installed base Pure Storage, 2016<sup>9</sup> AFR to FIT 1% ≈ 1,140 FIT 0.01 ÷ 8,766 h × 10⁹ Worked example RAID 6 vs 16+4 nines ~5.8 vs ~15.1 10 PB, 1.36% AFR, 42 h vs 4 h rebuild Worked example (Figure 20.2)

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What is in the denominator of our six nines?" Strong: installed-base telemetry, the outage definition, whether upgrades count, the window.
  2. "What do we tell a customer who asks for our durability number?" Strong: a model with stated parity and rebuild times, plus the caveat that bugs and humans dominate real loss, hence SafeMode snapshots.
  3. "Where does the mediator run for a customer with no internet egress?" Strong: an on-premises mediator VM in a third failure domain; pre-election if it is lost.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Which FlashBlade or EXA components run consensus, with how many voters?" Strong: names the service, quorum size and what stalls without a majority.
  2. "How long does rebuilding our largest DirectFlash Module take at 80% full under load?" Strong: hours, throttle policy, declustered or not.
  3. "How do we prevent correlated failures?" Strong: telemetry-staged firmware rollout, batch mixing, anti-affinity.

Don't say this:

  • "CAP means pick two." Partitions are not optional.
  • "Eleven nines means we never lose data." It models independent drive failures, not bugs or people.
  • "A two-node cluster can vote." It needs a witness.
  • "RAID 6 and 8+2 erasure coding differ in durability." Same code; rebuild speed and placement differ.
  • "Eventual consistency is a bug." It is a deliberate latency trade.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• Raft paper4 and Lamport's "Paxos Made Simple".
  • Ford et al.17 and Cidon et al.18 on correlated failures and placement; Abadi7 and Brewer8 on CAP.
  • Greenan, Plank and Wylie (HotStorage 2010) on MTTDL's limits.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Raft / Paxos — majority-based consensus on one ordered log.
  • Quorum (N/W/R) — W + R > N makes reads see the latest write.
  • Linearizability — behaves as if there were one copy.
  • PACELC — partition: availability or consistency; else: latency or consistency.
  • Witness / mediator — data-less third vote against split brain.
  • MTTDL — modelled mean time to data loss.
  • FIT — failures per 10⁹ device-hours.
  • Copyset — node group holding all replicas of some chunks.
  • See the glossary.

docs.title: 21. Metadata: the hidden bottleneck
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: File protocols · Object storage and S3 · Disaggregated shared-everything · Parallel file systems

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Metadata is the data about data: names, directories, permissions, sizes and block maps. Open, stat, list, create and rename are metadata operations; only read and write move payload.
  • Metadata operations are small, latency-bound and serialized on shared structures such as a directory lock. Systems sized in GB/s routinely stall on operations per second.
  • AI is metadata-heavy. Millions of ~100 KB samples and checkpoints that create a file per GPU turn a bandwidth problem into a metadata problem.
  • Metadata has moved from one server to a distributed database: hashed directories, shared SCM (VAST), key-value stores on flash (Everpure FlashBlade), FoundationDB (DeepSeek's 3FS).
  • Metadata performance is now a buying criterion. Ask for creates/s and stats/s, not just TB/s.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text: Everpure's top-end AI system, FlashBlade//EXA, is a metadata argument. The namespace lives in a FlashBlade "metadata core" built on a distributed key-value store, while commodity data nodes stream the bytes (Chapter 8, Chapter 16). Pure Storage pitches the core as serving thousands of clients and billions of items1. If AI pipelines stay metadata-bound, that is a durable differentiator. If data teams pack samples into large shards, the advantage narrows to checkpoints, curation, inference caches and enterprise file estates. Which workloads stay metadata-bound sizes the prize.

docs.title: Names, inodes and maps
docs.text:
A POSIX file system keeps three layers of metadata. The namespace is the directory tree, whose dentries (directory entries) map names to inode numbers. The inode holds owner, permissions, size and timestamps. The extent map translates file offsets to physical locations; one extent replaces thousands of per-4 KB pointers.

flowchart LR
    subgraph NS["Namespace: directory tree"]
        R["/"] --> D["data/"] --> T["train/"]
    end
    T --> DE["dentry: img_0001.JPEG maps to inode 48213"]
    DE --> I["inode 48213: owner, mode, size 113 KB, mtime"]
    I --> E["extent map: offset 0 to 113 KB at device 7, block Y"]
    E --> B[("data blocks on flash")]
    classDef meta fill:#E69F00,stroke:#222222,color:#222222
    classDef data fill:#56B4E9,stroke:#222222,color:#222222
    class R,D,T,DE,I,E meta
    class B data

Figure 21.1 — Reaching one file's bytes takes a chain of dependent metadata lookups, then a single data access.

Distributed systems add layouts, leases, locks, dedup tables and reference counts. On a modern flash system, metadata is a large, hot, constantly mutating database.

Semiconductor bridge. The metadata service is the file system's tag array and page-table walker. Data reads resemble DRAM burst streaming: wide and bandwidth-bound. Metadata lookups are pointer chasing: each step needs the previous result, so latencies add serially and extra bandwidth buys nothing. Client metadata caches are TLBs; a random shuffle over a billion files blows through them, and every miss becomes a page walk across the network. A rename needs invalidations, the analogue of a TLB shootdown.

docs.title: Why AI training is metadata-heavy
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Job start: list dataset directories"] --> B["Build index of N sample paths"]
    B --> C{"Next sample in shuffled order"}
    C --> D["lookup: resolve path"]
    D --> E["open: permission check, layout"]
    E --> F["stat: size"]
    F --> G["read: one ~113 KB data I/O"]
    G --> H["close"]
    H --> C
    S1["Sharded loader: open one 256 MB shard"] --> S2["stream ~2,000 samples sequentially"] --> S3["close"]
    classDef meta fill:#E69F00,stroke:#222222,color:#222222
    classDef data fill:#56B4E9,stroke:#222222,color:#222222
    class A,B,D,E,F,H,S1,S3 meta
    class G,S2 data

Figure 21.2 — A per-file data loader pays about four metadata operations (orange) for every data read (blue); a sharded loader pays them once per thousands of samples.

ImageNet-1k is the canonical case: 1,281,167 training JPEGs, 144.8 GB, averaging ~113 KB2. One epoch is ~5.1 million metadata operations, in an order that random shuffling makes unprefetchable.

Figure 21.3 — Illustrative: below the crossover size S* = k × B / M, effective throughput is metadata IOPS times file size, and bandwidth sits idle. Data: data/ch21_small_file_throughput.csv

Worked example. Effective throughput = min(B, M × S / k): B is data bandwidth, M metadata ops/s, S file size, k metadata ops per file. With B = 500 GB/s, M = 1 million and k = 4, the cluster opens 250,000 files/s; 250,000 × 113 KB ≈ 28 GB/s, 6% of the bandwidth paid for. Saturating 500 GB/s with 113 KB files needs ≈17.7 million metadata ops/s.

Mitigations. Pack samples into large sequential containers. WebDataset uses plain tar shards, grouping a sample's files by basename3; TFRecord and Parquet do the same, and LLM corpora are tokenized into large binary shards. A 256 MB shard holds ~2,265 such images, cutting metadata operations ~2,000-fold, at the price of coarser shuffling and a repacking step. Curation and deduplication still run on raw files, and RAG corpora and enterprise data often cannot be repacked.

docs.title: Checkpoint metadata storms
docs.text: PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint writes at least one file per rank plus a .metadata file4. A 16,384-GPU job creates 16,384 files in one directory almost simultaneously; on one metadata server they serialize on the directory lock, and one-file-per-tensor mode multiplies the count. Closing costs too: 3FS notes that a striped file's exact length must be queried from storage at close5. Bandwidth for a 405B model's ~6.5 TB checkpoint is the headline (Chapter 31); the create burst decides whether the first second is wasted.

docs.title: Why ls on a billion files is hard
docs.text: ls -l reads directory entries in batches, stats each, then sorts in client memory. Serially, at ~100 µs per round trip, 10⁹ stats take 10⁵ s, about 28 hours. At 1 million stats/s in parallel it is ~17 minutes, and sorting 10⁹ names of ~50 bytes needs ~50 GB of client RAM. The fix is to scan the metadata store in parallel, not walk the tree. In 2011 IBM's GPFS, with metadata on flash, scanned 10 billion files in 43 minutes, versus 1 billion in about three hours on disk in 20076. Single servers hit memory walls first: an HDFS NameNode spends ~150 bytes of heap per file, directory or block7, so a billion single-block files need ~300 GB.

docs.title: Log-structured designs
docs.text: Metadata updates are small random writes, the worst pattern for flash (Chapter 3). Log-structured designs append every change, index the latest version and garbage-collect the rest, an idea dating from 19918. Pure Storage described Purity's metadata as a key-value store that minimizes overwrites and writes in erase-block multiples9. The gains are sequential writes, cheap snapshots and simple crash recovery; the costs are read amplification, compaction and background work competing with foreground I/O. An SSD's FTL is itself log-structured metadata; doing it once at the array level, not twice, is part of the DirectFlash case (Chapter 26).

docs.title: Metadata scaling strategies
docs.text:
Strategy How it works Wall / trade-off Examples Single metadata server One server holds the whole namespace, often in RAM RAM and one CPU's lock throughput; ~150 B/object for HDFS7 HDFS NameNode, classic NAS head Active/standby Same, plus a failover partner Adds availability, not performance Lustre single MDT with failover Static subtree partitioning Admin pins directories to different servers Hot directories still hit one server Lustre DNE1 remote directories (2.4)10 Dynamic subtree partitioning Servers migrate busy subtrees among themselves Balancer complexity; locality kept CephFS MDS cluster11 Hash-distributed directories Entries hashed across servers or virtual shards Rename and readdir span shards Lustre DNE2 striped directories (2.8)12; WEKA virtual metadata servers13; Meta Tectonic14 Metadata in shared SCM Stateless nodes read/write one persistent tree over RDMA Fabric round trip per lookup; SCM capacity VAST V-tree15 Distributed KV store on flash Namespace as key-value records spread over blades Compaction; a dedicated metadata tier to buy Everpure Purity//FB, FlashBlade//EXA core1617 Transactional KV database, stateless servers Inodes and dentries stored as keys in a serializable database Transaction conflicts and retries; database operations DeepSeek 3FS on FoundationDB5; Snowflake18; Google Colossus on Bigtable19

Table 21.1 — Metadata scaling has moved from bigger servers to partitioned servers to a database underneath stateless servers.

The core trade-off is locality versus spread. Subtree partitioning keeps listings and renames local but bottlenecks on hot directories; hashing spreads load but makes them multi-server operations. Weil's 2004 simulations favored dynamic subtrees11. Newer systems push consistency into a transactional database: in 3FS a directory is one contiguous key range, so listing is a range scan, and conflicting writes retry5.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
System Where metadata lives How it scales AI-relevant notes Everpure FlashBlade//S, //E Distributed key-value database across blades Add blades Company-stated "billions of files"1617 Everpure FlashBlade//EXA FlashBlade metadata core; separate data nodes Metadata core and data nodes scale independently MLPerf Storage v3.0 config: 30 EXA blades with 120 DFMs for metadata, 30 data nodes20; company-stated ">20× more files per namespace" than "the leading parallel file system", a namespace-size claim, not a metadata ops/s multiple21 VAST V-tree in SCM shared by stateless CNodes Any CNode serves any operation No lock manager; locks are SCM writes15 WEKA Thousands of virtual metadata servers on all cores Hash-sharded buckets Journals to its own storage13 DDN EXAScaler (Lustre) MDS/MDT servers DNE remote and striped directories Data-on-MDT keeps small files on metadata targets22 DDN Infinia Key-value object platform Software-defined Claims sub-1 ms lookups vs >10 ms (vendor)23

Table 21.2 — Every AI-native contender now treats metadata as a distributed database; they differ in where it sits and how far it is from the data.

Steelmen. VAST avoids partitioning decisions, since any node serves any operation, at a fabric round trip per lookup. WEKA's hashing across every core scales creates with the cluster. Lustre was the weakest small-file default, but DNE plus Data-on-MDT closed much of the gap; a 2025 user-group talk called the small-file problem a myth (site-reported)24. EXA's case is a hardened metadata engine scaled separately from data; its open questions are pNFS layout recalls under churn and whether a dedicated FlashBlade core beats software-only rivals on cost. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: publishing per-chassis create/stat curves (IO500 weights metadata equally with bandwidth25), and exposing the metadata database for search and governance (Chapter 39).

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Which workloads stay metadata-bound after customers shard their datasets?" Strong: checkpoint bursts, curation on raw files, RAG corpora, KV caches, with ops/s from real deals.
  2. "What are creates/s and stats/s per metadata chassis, in one directory and in many?" Strong: a scaling curve for both cases, not one hero number.
  3. "Can the metadata engine become a search and governance product?" Strong: what is queryable today and the foreground-latency cost.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What happens when 16,384 ranks create files in one directory in the same second?" Strong: whether the directory is hashed, lock granularity, creates/s and p99 latency.
  2. "Walk me through a rename across metadata shards." Strong: the transaction protocol and crash recovery mid-rename.
  3. "How does metadata compaction behave under sustained create/delete churn?" Strong: a write-amplification figure and worst-case latency.

Don't say this:

  • "We do X TB/s, so small files are fine." Below the crossover size, bandwidth is irrelevant.
  • "Object storage has no metadata problem." It has LIST and per-request overhead (Chapter 9).
  • "Faster flash fixes metadata." The hard parts are serialization and distribution, not media latency.
  • "Sharding solves it." Not for checkpoints, curation or inference.

docs.title: 22. Control planes and fleet management
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~5 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: The storage stack · Scale-up dual-controller arrays · Consumption models

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• The data plane moves bytes in microseconds. The control plane decides what should exist (volumes, policies, placement) and runs in seconds. Good designs keep the control plane out of the I/O path, so a cloud outage never stops storage.
  • Fleet management moved to the cloud in the mid-2010s. Arrays phone home telemetry; the vendor's analytics predict failures, open tickets and size upgrades before the customer notices.
  • Telemetry compounds with fleet size. Rare faults are only learnable when you watch many systems, so the biggest installed bases learn fastest. That is a support-cost moat and a sales-signal moat.
  • "Storage as code" changes the buyer. Platform engineers declare storage in Terraform, Ansible or Kubernetes manifests; API quality now wins deals that GUIs used to.
  • Everpure's bet is Pure1 (cloud analytics) plus Fusion (policy control plane built into Purity). Dell, NetApp and HPE all ship equivalents, and all four now add AI copilots.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text: The control plane is where hardware becomes a service. Evergreen//One's SLAs (Chapter 23) are only insurable because Everpure sees every array's capacity, performance and health in near real time. The control plane is also the integration surface for Everpure's platform pitch, the Enterprise Data Cloud, launched in June 2025 with Fusion at its core1 (Chapter 28). If customers automate against Everpure's APIs, switching costs migrate from the box to the policy layer, which survives every hardware refresh.

docs.title: Three planes, three clocks
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Cloud["Vendor cloud: management plane"]
        T["Telemetry lake and analytics"]
        P["Fleet policy and AI copilot"]
    end
    subgraph Site["Customer site"]
        CP["Control plane: config, placement, policies"]
        DP["Data plane: Purity I/O path on controllers"]
    end
    H["Hosts and GPUs"] -->|"reads and writes, microseconds"| DP
    DP -->|"metrics and logs, outbound only"| T
    P -->|"recommendations and workflows"| CP
    CP -->|"create volume, set QoS, seconds"| DP
    A["Terraform, Ansible, Kubernetes CSI"] -->|"REST API calls"| CP

Figure 22.1 — The data plane must keep serving if every arrow to the cloud is cut; the control plane decides, the data plane executes.

The data plane is the I/O path: protocol handling, deduplication, RAID and flash management (Chapter 14). The control plane holds desired state, such as "this database gets three volumes, a 50,000-IOPS limit and hourly snapshots replicated to site B", and pushes it to the data plane. The management plane aggregates many control planes. Semiconductor bridge: the data plane is the chip's datapath; the control plane is the on-die power-management microcontroller setting voltages and clocks; the management plane is the out-of-band BMC that a fleet operator scripts. Nobody puts the BMC on the critical path of a load instruction.

Unreachable cloud services must degrade gracefully. Pure1's terms allow "dark sites" with phone-home disabled, at the cost of manual log collection2.

docs.title: The telemetry loop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Arrays phone home metrics and logs"] --> B["Cloud telemetry lake"]
    B --> C["Fingerprint and forecast models"]
    C --> D["Predictive support: auto-ticket, ship part"]
    C --> E["Recommendations: capacity, workload placement"]
    D --> F["Policy actions: firmware hold, rebalance, upgrade quote"]
    E --> F
    F --> A

Figure 22.2 — Each incident becomes a fingerprint that protects the rest of the fleet, so the loop improves with every array connected.

Pure Storage launched Pure1 META in 2017, claiming more than a trillion telemetry data points a day in a ~7 PB lake3 and over 500 prevented Severity-1 incidents by then4 (company-stated). Today a detected hardware fault opens a support case automatically and can trigger a replacement shipment5. HPE bought Nimble Storage in 2017 largely for InfoSight6 and claims it predicts and auto-resolves 86% of issues (company-stated, Nimble base)7.

Why scale is a moat (worked example). Take a firmware-and-drive interaction that strikes 1 in 10,000 arrays a year. A vendor with 1,000 connected arrays sees it once a decade, which is too rare to model. A vendor with 50,000 sees it five times a year, fingerprints it after the first, and blocks that firmware fleet-wide. This mirrors fab yield learning: more wafer starts surface defect signatures sooner. The same data cuts support cost (fewer engineers per installed array), feeds capacity planning (forecast fill dates per array) and gives sales a list of customers about to run out of space.

docs.title: Storage as code
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant E as Platform engineer
    participant G as Git and CI pipeline
    participant T as Terraform or Ansible
    participant F as Fleet API endpoint
    participant X as Selected array
    E->>G: commit storage class gold-db, 3 volumes
    G->>T: plan and apply
    T->>F: POST workload from preset
    F->>F: check policy, pick array with headroom
    F->>X: create volumes, QoS, snapshot schedule
    X-->>F: volume IDs
    F-->>T: desired state reached
    Note over T,X: Kubernetes CSI follows the same path when a pod claims a volume

Figure 22.3 — Declarative automation means the engineer names an outcome and the control plane chooses the array, so placement logic becomes the vendor's product.

Pure Fusion's presets bundle QoS, protection and tags into a fleet-wide template8. In September 2025 Pure Storage (now Everpure) announced cross-array provisioning through storage classes9. Automation hooks include a Terraform provider for Fusion (the newest release found dates from 2023 and targets the original Fusion service)10, certified Ansible collections11 and Portworx CSI for Kubernetes12. The buyer changes: platform engineering teams judge API coverage, idempotency and provider maturity; a slick GUI matters less. CSI is double-edged. It makes arrays substitutable behind one Kubernetes interface, so differentiation must live above it, in fleet policy.

Everpure's distinctive choice is putting Fusion inside the array OS, so there is no separate control plane to license or deploy13. The steelman for NetApp: its console manages ONTAP inside all three hyperscalers, a broader hybrid reach than Everpure's cloud offerings. HPE's InfoSight claims cross-stack (server and storage) correlation that a storage-only vendor cannot match. Dell spans the widest hardware portfolio, so one AIOps console covers servers, storage and networking.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text: Per-array element managers gave way to cloud analytics (Nimble InfoSight, Pure1) and ML prediction (Pure1 META, 2017), then cloud consoles (HPE 2021), then policy control planes (Fusion embedded 2024; Enterprise Data Cloud 2025). The 2025–26 signal is agentic: Pure1's copilot and HPE's GreenLake Intelligence both expose MCP so AI agents can query and act on fleets924. The open question is how much write access customers will grant an agent.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What share of Sev-1 cases are opened by Pure1 before the customer calls?" Strong: a measured percentage, trend and cost-per-case impact.
  2. "Which Evergreen//One SLAs depend on telemetry, and what happens at dark sites?" Strong: names the SLAs that need phone-home and the contractual fallback.
  3. "How do Fusion presets show up in Terraform, and who owns the provider?" Strong: a supported, versioned provider with release cadence and coverage gaps listed.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "If Pure1 and Fusion are both unreachable, what still works?" Strong: all I/O and local admin; only fleet placement and analytics pause.
  2. "How does Fusion pick an array for a new workload?" Strong: concrete inputs (headroom, forecast fill, latency class, failure domains) and conflict handling.
  3. "What stops a copilot or agent from deleting production volumes?" Strong: scoped tokens, approval gates, SafeMode-style immutability underneath.

Don't say this:

  • "AIOps is just monitoring." It acts: tickets, part shipments, firmware holds.
  • "The cloud manages the array." It advises; the array runs alone.
  • "CSI support is a differentiator." Every major vendor has it.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Control plane / data plane / management plane — deciding, doing, and fleet-wide oversight.
  • Phone-home telemetry — outbound metrics and logs sent to the vendor's cloud.
  • Issue fingerprint — a telemetry signature of a known fault, matched across the fleet.
  • Storage class / preset — a named policy bundle that automation requests by name.
  • See the glossary.

docs.title: 23. Consumption models
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Performance and economics metrics · Scale-up dual-controller arrays · Control planes and fleet management

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Storage is bought four ways: outright capex, a lease, capex plus an upgrade subscription (Evergreen//Forever-style), or storage-as-a-service (STaaS), where the vendor owns the hardware and bills for consumption against SLAs.
  • Total cost over five years can be similar; the cash-flow shape, balance-sheet treatment and risk allocation differ. STaaS turns a lumpy purchase into a usage-tracking fee and moves overprovisioning and refresh risk to the vendor.
  • For the vendor, STaaS trades upfront product revenue for ratable revenue. A mix shift toward it depresses reported growth while lifting ARR, RPO and TCV, which is why Everpure leads with those metrics.
  • The business model is an architecture requirement. A credible subscription needs non-disruptive upgrades, stateless controllers and fleet telemetry; bolting a subscription onto a forklift-upgrade array just finances the forklift.
  • Everpure was early (Evergreen, 2015). Dell, NetApp and HPE now match the contract terms; matching the architecture is harder.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text: Subscription services were 46% of Everpure's FY2026 revenue, and subscription ARR reached $1,924.3M with 113% net dollar retention1. By Q2 FY2027 ARR was $2.13B (+20%) and RPO $4.1B (+44%)2. Storage-as-a-service TCV, led by Evergreen//One, grew 121% to $277M in that quarter, a run rate above $1B a year3. Management says this acceleration "dilutes reported near-term revenue growth"3. Reading Everpure's financials or pricing a deal against Dell APEX requires knowing what each model does to cash, revenue and architecture.

docs.title: Four ways to pay for the same petabyte
docs.text:
Model Who owns the asset How upgrades work Vendor revenue (ASC 606) Customer accounting (US GAAP) Examples Capex purchase + maintenance Customer Forklift refresh every 4–6 years, with data migration Product upfront at transfer of control; support ratable PP&E, depreciated; support is opex Any array Operating lease Lessor (bank or captive finance arm) As capex; asset returned or refinanced at term end Upfront if sold to a third-party lessor Right-of-use asset and lease liability on balance sheet (ASC 842); straight-line cost Any array via leasing partner Capex + upgrade subscription Customer Controllers refreshed in place at renewal; media expanded with credits Product upfront; subscription ratable4 PP&E plus opex subscription Evergreen//Forever5; NetApp Storage Lifecycle Program / Advance6; Dell Future-Proof7 Storage-as-a-service Vendor Vendor's problem; SLA-backed Over time, on a consumption basis; contracts usually set a minimum usage commitment plus fees for usage above it8 Usually a service contract, so opex and off balance sheet, if the vendor's substitution rights are substantive9 Evergreen//One; Dell APEX; NetApp Keystone; HPE GreenLake

Table 23.1 — Moving down the table shifts asset ownership, refresh risk and revenue timing from the customer's books to the vendor's.

The lease-versus-service line is an audit judgment. Under ASC 842, a contract contains a lease if there is an identified asset the customer directs. A vendor's right to swap hardware is only "substantive" if it is practical and economic for the vendor9. STaaS contracts sell capacity and performance, not specific boxes. One EBITDA nuance: STaaS fees and US GAAP operating-lease cost both sit above EBITDA, whereas purchased hardware depreciation sits below it.

docs.title: Cash-flow shapes
docs.text:
Figure 23.1 — Illustrative: the three models land within ~15% of each other in nominal five-year cost; what differs is timing, who carries idle capacity, and who pays for the refresh. Data: data/ch23_cashflow.csv

Assumptions. Demand starts at 1.0 PB effective and grows 20% a year. The capex buyer sizes for year 3 (1.5 PB at an assumed $400K per PB), expands 0.6 PB in year 4 at prices 15% a year lower, and pays 12% a year for support. The lease finances the same hardware at 7%. STaaS charges an assumed $144K per PB-year on actual usage. Discounting at 8% with payments at the start of each year, present costs are capex ~$969K, lease ~$1,007K and STaaS ~$899K. Three things the nominal totals hide: the capex buyer runs one-third idle in year 1 (1.0 of 1.5 PB used); its controllers are five years old at the end and due for a forklift refresh that STaaS already includes; and the STaaS rate is the negotiated variable that decides the winner. Semiconductor bridge: STaaS is a foundry capacity reservation. The customer commits to a minimum take, and the vendor owns the fab, the utilization risk and the node upgrades.

docs.title: What the vendor's P&L sees
docs.text: Take a three-year, $1.2M deal. Sold as capex, perhaps $0.9M is product revenue in the quarter it ships and $0.3M of support is recognized at $25K a quarter, so year-one revenue is about $1.0M. Sold as STaaS, it is roughly $100K a quarter, $0.4M in year one. Same economics, 60% less year-one revenue, while the vendor pays for hardware up front. Hence Everpure's emphasis on ARR, RPO and TCV, and its CEO's claim that growth adjusted for the Evergreen//One shift exceeded 40%3. Its subscription gross margin (74.9% in Q2 FY2027, non-GAAP) exceeds product (66.2%)10, but STaaS hardware costs sit inside the subscription line.

docs.title: Why the business model shapes the architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S["Subscription promise: no migrations, upgrades included, SLAs"] --> N["Non-disruptive upgrades"]
    N --> C["Stateless controllers: state lives in NVRAM and flash"]
    N --> F["Data layout readable by every controller generation"]
    N --> M["Modular media swapped in place"]
    S --> T["Fleet telemetry"]
    T --> U["Meter usage, enforce SLAs, forecast capacity"]
    C --> V["Vendor bears refresh and idle-capacity cost"]
    M --> V
    U --> V
    V --> D["Incentive to maximize density and minimize watts per TB"]
    D -->|"lower cost to serve"| S

Figure 23.2 — A subscription is only profitable if upgrades are cheap and risks are measurable, so the contract pushes engineering toward stateless controllers, modular media and telemetry.

A subscription that promises "never migrate again" is a liability unless swapping controllers is routine. That works only if controllers hold no unique state (Chapter 14) and new controllers read old layouts. Think of a CPU socket kept compatible across generations: chassis as motherboard, controller as chip. Pure Storage had delivered more than 10,000 non-disruptive controller upgrades to more than 3,000 customers by 202211. SLAs require measurement, so Evergreen//One's guarantees run on Pure1 telemetry (Chapter 22), including a watts-per-TiB energy guarantee introduced in January 202312. Once the vendor pays for power and hardware, density is margin, which ties DirectFlash to the subscription model (Chapter 26).

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Everpure's Evergreen family has three tiers. Evergreen//Forever is owned hardware with a subscription and a controller refresh at each three-year renewal ("Ever Modern"; six years for the //E lines)13. Evergreen//Flex bills capacity per use across a fleet; its product revenue is recognized when the subscription starts, and its subscription fees ratably, as for Forever8. Evergreen//One is full STaaS, formerly Pure-as-a-Service5. Its SLAs cover performance, availability, capacity, energy and cyber recovery14. Gartner named Pure Storage a Leader in its 2025 consumption-services Magic Quadrant15.

Steelman the competitors. HPE launched GreenLake pay-per-use in 201716, earlier than most, and covers compute and networking as well as storage. NetApp Keystone (2019)17 runs across on-premises and hyperscaler ONTAP. Dell APEX (2021)18 can wrap the broadest hardware portfolio. On contracts, NetApp's and Dell's controller-refresh programs now mirror Evergreen//Forever67. Everpure's edge lies in architecture and track record, not contract terms: one OS lineage designed for in-place upgrades, and a decade of refreshes delivered. A vendor that must migrate data to refresh carries that cost inside every STaaS contract.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Consumption models at Pure Storage and Everpure
    2015 : Evergreen Gold subscription with in-place controller upgrades
    2017 : HPE launches GreenLake pay-per-use
    2019 : Pure-as-a-Service name in use : NetApp Keystone
    2021 : Dell APEX storage services
    2022 : Evergreen family formalised as Forever, Flex and One
    2023 : Evergreen One energy-efficiency SLA
    2026 : Evergreen One TCV above 1B dollar run rate

Figure 23.3 — Subscriptions moved from a Pure Storage differentiator (2015) to an industry norm (2021); the competition shifted to SLAs and architecture.

Next: Evergreen//One Overdrive, letting customers burst above their subscribed level, was announced in 202619 [VERIFY: terms and GA]. Contract lengths are reported at three to four years3.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What is Evergreen//One's gross margin by contract year?" Strong: a curve showing early-year hardware drag and later payback, plus the utilization assumption.
  2. "How much headroom above commitment do we deploy, and who pays when it sits idle?" Strong: a percentage, the forecasting model, and redeployment practice.
  3. "Why do customers choose Forever over One?" Strong: accounting, data-sovereignty and procurement reasons by segment.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What breaks a non-disruptive upgrade?" Strong: specific generation-boundary constraints and how they are tested.
  2. "Which SLA is hardest to meet?" Strong: names the metric and the telemetry used to police it.
  3. "How is consumption metered: provisioned, written or effective capacity?" Strong: the exact counter and how data reduction enters it.

Don't say this:

  • "STaaS is always cheaper." It moves risk; the price decides.
  • "Subscription means off balance sheet." Only if no embedded lease exists.
  • "Lower revenue growth means weaker demand." Check TCV and RPO first.

docs.title: 24. Architecture decision matrix
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: The storage stack · Scale-up dual-controller · Scale-out shared-nothing · DASE · Parallel file systems · Object storage · SDS and HCI

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Seven architectures cover almost every deal. Each has a home workload and a wall (Chapters 14–19).
  • Five questions decide most deals: how big, which protocol, latency or throughput, how large a failure domain the customer accepts, and who operates it at what cost. Vendor features come after.
  • The deepest split is latency-bound versus throughput-bound. Databases and VMs want sub-millisecond block; AI training and HPC want TB/s into one namespace.
  • AI is not one workload. Data loading, checkpointing, KV-cache serving and RAG land in different cells, so "AI storage" is a portfolio question.
  • The boundaries are blurring. Everyone now sells "unified" block, file and object, and Gartner's 2025 Magic Quadrant merged them into one category1. Underneath, the architectures, and their walls, have not converged.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Everpure sells three architectures: scale-up (FlashArray); a partitioned blade scale-out (FlashBlade//S and //E), which Everpure's engineers call "partitioned-writer", arguing that neither the shared-nothing nor the shared-everything label fits2 (Chapter 15); and a pNFS-style parallel design that splits metadata from data (FlashBlade//EXA, Chapter 17). It adds container-native SDS (Portworx) and Purity in public clouds. It sells no DASE system, because in EXA no compute tier reaches all media (Chapter 16), and no general-purpose HCI. A strategy team needs to know which cells Everpure covers natively, where it partners, and where rivals fit better by design, because discounting won't win those cells.

The matrix also guards against category errors: an enterprise "AI storage" request is often mostly a capacity and governance problem.

docs.title: The heatmap
docs.text:
Architecture OLTP databases VMs / VDI Containers Backup / restore HPC simulation AI training (data load) AI checkpointing AI inference / KV cache RAG / vector Archive Scale-up dual-controller ● sub-ms, sync replication, mature ● clones dedupe, deep hypervisor integration ◐ CSI works, one array's ceiling ◐ fast restores, pricey per TB ○ one pair caps bandwidth ○ one pair caps GB/s ◐ fine for small clusters ◐ low latency, little shared scale ● vector DB is a database ○ $/TB too high Scale-out shared-nothing (incl. partitioned) ◐ east-west hop adds latency ◐ works; rebuilds hit tail latency ◐ Ceph/Rook common, ops-heavy ● capacity grows node by node ◐ strong in WEKA, weaker NAS ● bandwidth grows per node ● every node absorbs writes ◐ NVMe near GPUs, vendor-dependent ◐ corpus fine, index elsewhere ◐ HDD nodes, bundled scaling DASE ◐ block new, fabric hop ◐ NFS datastores; young block ◐ CSI fine, large minimum ● QLC plus reduction, fast restore ● one namespace, multi-TB/s ● built for GPU-cluster reads ● SCM buffer absorbs bursts ● any node reaches shared flash ◐ corpus fits; engines vendor-specific ◐ cheap only at scale Parallel file system (incl. pNFS split) ○ wrong semantics and latency ○ not a datastore ◐ shared mounts, client friction ○ costly, complex target ● its home ground ● striping feeds thousands of GPUs ● clients write servers directly ◐ bandwidth fits, integrations maturing ○ small files strain metadata ○ flash tier too costly Object ○ no in-place updates ○ not block ◐ cloud-native apps use S3 ● immutability, cheap, geo-EC ○ no POSIX, needs staging ◐ fine with streaming loaders ◐ async upload, slow sync ◐ latency-tolerant KV tiers ● data-lake corpus, native vectors ● lowest $/TB, geo-EC SDS / HCI ◐ local reads, coupled scaling ● HCI's original use case ● container-native data services ◐ small sites only ○ coupled nodes, no striping ○ GPU servers aren't HCI ○ not built for bursts ○ not on GPU fabric ◐ vector DB pods fine ○ flash HCI costly per TB Cloud block (EBS-style) ● sub-ms io2, pay per IOPS ● native boot volumes ◐ CSI works, AZ-pinned volumes ◐ snapshots to S3, egress ○ per-volume throughput caps ○ single-attach, volume caps ○ ~4 GB/s per volume ○ no shared namespace ◐ vector DB on volumes ○ use object tiers instead

Legend: ● natural fit, what the architecture was built for · ◐ workable with caveats or vendor-dependent · ○ poor fit, usually the wrong tool. Ratings are the atlas's judgment for typical 2026 deployments, not benchmarks; a strong product can beat its row. The SDS / HCI row rates HCI and container-native SDS; SDS sold as software for commodity servers (WEKA, Ceph, VAST's software-only route) is rated in the row of its architecture (Chapter 19).

Figure 24.1 — Read the heatmap by row for an architecture's home turf and by column for which architectures compete for a workload. Most columns have two or three credible answers, not one.

Where Everpure's products sit. FlashBlade//S and //E belong in the scale-out row. Namespace and write ownership are partitioned into "authorities" that run on blades, much like shared-nothing owners, while Purity manages DFM flash and NVRAM across the chassis (Chapter 15). Pooled media management softens the row's rebuild and hot-spot caveats but does not change its OLTP or archive cells. FlashBlade//EXA belongs in the parallel-file-system row, not DASE. Clients get a layout from the metadata core and then move data directly to data nodes, the Lustre MDS/OSS pattern (Chapter 17). Its stock pNFS client eases the row's "client friction" caveat, and its Purity metadata core is pitched at the small-file weakness (company-stated, Chapter 21). Its failure-domain story is weaker: data-node protection is not yet publicly documented.

docs.title: The five questions that decide a real deal
docs.text:
Question What to ask Pushes toward Scale Capacity today and in three years; how many clients <~2 PB, tens of hosts → scale-up; multi-PB, thousands of clients → scale-out, DASE, parallel FS, object Protocol Block, NFS/SMB, POSIX shared-file, S3 Block → scale-up or cloud block; S3 → object; shared-file writes from many nodes → parallel FS Latency vs throughput p99 latency target, or aggregate GB/s Latency → fewest hops (scale-up); throughput → most parallel paths (parallel FS, DASE) Failure domain What may one fault take down, and how long is a rebuild? Small blast radius → many small arrays; wide EC → big shared pools Operating model and economics Who runs it, kernel clients allowed, capex vs service Thin team → appliance or cloud; HPC team → parallel FS; cost per TB → object/QLC

Figure 24.2 — The first three questions narrow the matrix to one or two rows; the last two usually choose between them.

Latency versus throughput is the deepest split, and it is physics. A 4 KB database write on a networked all-flash array completes in roughly 100–250 µs (Chapter 13). Each extra fabric hop or forwarded request adds tens of microseconds, so the latency winner is the design with the fewest hops between host and NVRAM. Throughput is the reverse problem. A 405B-parameter checkpoint is about 405e9 × 16 bytes ≈ 6.5 TB. At 20 GB/s (an illustrative single-array figure) the write takes 6.5e12 ÷ 20e9 ≈ 325 s. At the 877.5 GiB/s that 30 FlashBlade//EXA data nodes posted in MLPerf Storage v3.03 (≈ 942 GB/s), it takes ≈ 7 s. That gap is the whole case for parallel paths. The semiconductor bridge is the HBM-versus-DRAM trade: HBM wins on bandwidth by going wide, DDR wins on cost and capacity, and no single interface wins both.

Failure domain costs money a spec sheet hides. A dual-controller array loses at most itself; a failed DASE enclosure or shared-nothing node puts a slice of a giant namespace into rebuild (Chapter 20).

docs.title: The decision tree
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Workload in hand"] --> B{"Latency-critical block or VM data?"}
    B -- "Yes" --> C{"Lives in a public cloud?"}
    C -- "Yes" --> D["Cloud block, EBS-style"]
    C -- "No" --> E["Scale-up dual-controller"]
    B -- "No" --> F{"Hundreds of GB/s to TB/s into one namespace?"}
    F -- "Yes" --> G{"POSIX shared-file writes and an HPC team?"}
    G -- "Yes" --> H["Parallel file system"]
    G -- "No, mixed protocols" --> I["DASE or pNFS-style split"]
    F -- "No" --> J{"Compute and storage run as one estate?"}
    J -- "Yes" --> K["SDS or HCI"]
    J -- "No" --> L{"S3 API, retention or PB-scale capacity?"}
    L -- "Yes" --> M["Object storage"]
    L -- "No" --> N["Scale-out NAS, shared-nothing"]

Figure 24.3 — The tree picks a starting row; failure-domain and economics questions then test it, and real estates usually end with two or three rows.

docs.title: Justifying the contentious cells
docs.text:
• Scale-up gets ● for RAG/vector. A vector database is a database. Its hot index lives in DRAM or on low-latency block, which arrays serve well. The source corpus belongs in object or file, which is why object also gets ●, helped by AWS making S3 Vectors generally available in December 2025 with up to two billion vectors per index4.
  • Shared-nothing and DASE get ◐, not ○, for OLTP, even though Chapters 15 and 16 list latency-critical block among their worst fits. Block SDS such as Dell PowerFlex runs production databases, and VAST added NVMe/TCP block in 20255. But every I/O still crosses a back-end hop, and few banks yet run tier-1 databases on either.
  • Object gets ◐ for training and checkpointing, although Chapter 18 lists sharded datasets and checkpoints among its best fits. Many labs stream shards from S3 through caching loaders and upload checkpoints asynchronously from local NVMe. The ◐ reflects synchronous checkpoint writes and small-file random access, which drops training to ○.
  • Parallel FS gets ◐ for KV cache. The bandwidth is there, and EXA led the v3.0 KV-cache read test3, but serving millions of small, latency-sensitive KV blocks is newer ground than streaming checkpoints (Chapter 32).
  • Cloud block gets ● for OLTP despite cost. io2 Block Express promises under 500 µs average at 16 KiB and 256K IOPS per volume6. The objection is price per IOPS, not fit.

docs.title: The quadrant view
docs.text:
quadrantChart
    title Performance scalability vs operational simplicity
    x-axis Bounded scale --> Massive scale
    y-axis Expert operations --> Simple operations
    quadrant-1 Scales and stays simple
    quadrant-2 Simple but bounded
    quadrant-3 Niche or legacy
    quadrant-4 Scales with expert care
    Scale up: [0.22, 0.85]
    Cloud block: [0.30, 0.93]
    SDS HCI: [0.40, 0.62]
    Shared nothing: [0.60, 0.48]
    Object: [0.70, 0.40]
    DASE: [0.85, 0.68]
    pNFS split: [0.86, 0.52]
    Parallel FS: [0.92, 0.15]

Figure 24.4 — Placement is the atlas's judgment: the commercial prize is the top-right quadrant, which DASE occupies and pNFS-style splits are trying to reach, so that is where the AI-era competition concentrates.

Object sits low because self-run PB-scale object needs expertise; managed S3 would sit near cloud block. DASE scores well because stateless compute nodes make upgrades routine. The pNFS split (FlashBlade//EXA's design) sits between DASE and classic parallel file systems. The stock NFS client removes Lustre's kernel-module lifecycle, but customers still run an RDMA data fabric and, for EXA, source and operate the data-node servers (Chapter 17).

docs.title: Where the boundaries are blurring
docs.text:
Three forces are blurring the rows. First, protocol unification: FlashArray gained S3 in 20257, VAST added block5, WEKA's NeuralMesh 6 unified file and object8, and HPE positions its Alletra Storage MP family as one platform for block (B10000) and file and object (X10000)9. Second, control-plane unification: Everpure's Enterprise Data Cloud10 and DDN's CORE layer over EXAScaler and Infinia11 present several architectures as one pool. Third, hybrids: FlashBlade//EXA is a parallel file system on a scale-out metadata engine (Chapter 17). NetApp's AFX is shared-media but documented for NAS and object, not block12.

Test any "unified" claim against the matrix: which column was the protocol added for, and do its latency and failure domain match a native design?

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Architecture Everpure Incumbent competitors AI-native, software and cloud competitors Scale-up dual-controller FlashArray //X, //C, //XL, //E, //ST7 Dell PowerStore, PowerMax; NetApp AFF/ASA; HPE Alletra MP B10000; IBM FlashSystem — Scale-out shared-nothing or partitioned FlashBlade//S, //E (partitioned scale-out: per-blade authorities, pooled media management; Everpure says "partitioned-writer"2) Dell PowerScale; NetApp ONTAP clusters WEKA NeuralMesh, Qumulo, Ceph DASE None; EXA splits metadata from data instead (Chapter 16) NetApp AFX12; HPE Alletra MP X100009 VAST Data Parallel file system FlashBlade//EXA (pNFS metadata/data split)13 Dell PowerScale pNFS / Lightning; HPE Cray E2000 (Lustre)14; IBM Storage Scale DDN EXAScaler, BeeGFS, Hammerspace Object FlashBlade S3; FlashArray S37 Dell ObjectScale; NetApp StorageGRID; HPE X10000 AWS S3, MinIO AIStor, Cloudian, Scality, DDN Infinia SDS / HCI Portworx; FlashArray behind Nutanix15 Nutanix; VMware vSAN (Broadcom) Ceph, Red Hat and IBM distributions Cloud block Pure Storage Cloud Dedicated (ex-Cloud Block Store) and Azure Native16 NetApp ONTAP in hyperscaler clouds AWS EBS, Azure Managed Disks, Google Hyperdisk

Table 24.5 — Everpure covers five of the seven rows natively, plus the SDS half of the SDS / HCI row with Portworx and the HCI half by partnership; DASE is the row it competes against rather than in.

The steelman for VAST: one DASE system covers most of the heatmap's right half with one namespace and reduction domain, which suits neoclouds. For Dell and NetApp: a native product in nearly every row under one contract. Everpure's counter is one OS family (Purity) across FlashArray and FlashBlade, including EXA's metadata core though not its Linux data nodes, and one control plane (Pure1, Fusion), with media economics from DirectFlash (Chapter 26). Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: closing the KV-cache cell faster (PureKVA for FlashBlade was announced in September 2026 for October availability17); using Portworx's Kubernetes VM-migration cell to pull through arrays; and keeping "unified" messaging behind per-workload proof points.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text: Until about 2010 the matrix had three rows: SAN arrays, NAS filers and tape. Shared-nothing and object came with web-scale data, HCI with 2010s virtualization, DASE and pNFS revivals with GPUs. In 2025 the market started folding rows together: Gartner's new Enterprise Storage Platforms category1, NetApp AFX in October 202512, and DDN CORE in November 202511. The signal to watch in 2027 is whether buyers run one platform across columns, as CoreWeave's reported US$1.17B VAST agreement suggests for neoclouds18, or keep best-of-breed per column, as most enterprises still do.
