docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM 1. "Which cells do we lose on architecture rather than price?" Strong answer: names them (shared-file-write HPC, multi-site geo-EC object) and a plan for each: partner, roadmap or walk away. 2. "Where does 'unified' help a buyer?" Strong answer: one control plane and support contract, with honesty about which protocol is native. 3. "What is our AI-inference story by cell?" Strong answer: separates KV cache (PureKVA) from RAG corpora (FlashBlade S3/NFS) from vector-DB block (FlashArray).

Questions for an engineer 1. "What is the p99 penalty of block through a scale-out design?" Strong answer: the extra hop in microseconds, plus rebuild effects on tail latency. 2. "How big is the failure domain in EXA's data tier today?" Strong answer: states the current data-node protection scheme [VERIFY: current FlashBlade//EXA data-node protection] and rebuild time per node. 3. "Where does the decision tree break?" Strong answer: small-file AI datasets look throughput-bound but are metadata-bound (Chapter 21).

Don't say this: - "One platform for every workload." No architecture rates ● in every column, including Everpure's. - "Object is just for archive." It is the default RAG and data-lake substrate. - "Parallel file systems are legacy HPC." They lead AI checkpointing benchmarks. - "DASE can't do block." It can; the question is latency and maturity. - "FlashBlade is Everpure's shared-everything answer to VAST." FlashBlade//S is a partitioned scale-out design and EXA a metadata/data split; neither is DASE.

docs.title: 25. Company history and strategy, 2009–2026
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Data reduction · Consumption models · Purity and DirectFlash

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Pure Storage was founded in 2009 on one insight: consumer-grade flash plus aggressive data reduction could match disk's cost per usable terabyte. FlashArray reached GA in May 2012; the IPO followed in October 2015.
  • Its durable moat was a business model, not a box. Forever Flash (2014) and Evergreen (2015) turned controller upgrades into a subscription; subscription ARR was $1.92B at FY2026.
  • Acquisitions were small and capability-driven. StorReduce, Compuverde, Portworx and 1touch together cost about $0.6B in disclosed consideration, less than one year of free cash flow. One (StorReduce) produced a product that was quietly withdrawn.
  • The newest growth leg is selling IP rather than arrays. DirectFlash licensing wins with Meta (December 2024) and a second top-five hyperscaler (August 2026) are real, but hyperscale is still a small slice of FY2027 revenue guidance of $5.03–5.07B (about +38%).
  • The February 2026 rebrand to Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) is a claim, not yet a result. It bids for a data-platform valuation while revenue is still mostly arrays and attached subscriptions.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Strategic conversations inside Everpure carry this history. PMs defend Evergreen because it built the installed base; engineers trust Purity because it has survived 14 years of NAND generations; corporate development inherits a pattern of small tuck-ins that bought capabilities, not revenue. Which bets paid off, ran late or died tells you how the organisation weighs a new one.

The rebrand, the 1touch acquisition and hyperscaler licensing all move away from "we sell the best flash array". Is that the fifth pivot in a consistent line, or a break? The record suggests the first, with one caveat: past pivots were underwritten by array cash flows, and the newest ones still are.

docs.title: Seventeen years in one picture
docs.text:
timeline
    title Pure Storage to Everpure, 2009-2026
    2009 : Incorporated as OS76 in Sutter Hill offices
    2012 : FlashArray 300 series GA with Purity
    2014 : Forever Flash maintenance model
    2015 : Evergreen Storage with FlashArray m : NYSE IPO at 17 dollars a share
    2016 : FlashBlade unveiled : EMC litigation settled for 30M dollars
    2017 : FlashBlade GA : Charles Giancarlo becomes CEO
    2018 : StorReduce acquired
    2019 : Compuverde acquired
    2020 : Purity 6 brings file to FlashArray : Portworx acquisition closes
    2022 : Meta RSC built on FlashArray and FlashBlade : Evergreen family relaunched
    2024 : Top-four hyperscaler DirectFlash design win : CoreWeave investment
    2025 : FlashBlade EXA announced : Enterprise Data Cloud : Meta volume deployment
    2026 : Rebrand to Everpure : Ticker changes to P : 1touch closes : Second hyperscaler win

Figure 25.1 — Each era added a layer on top of the same Purity and DirectFlash core: array (2012), business model (2014–15), file and object (2016–20), cloud-native software (2020), IP licensing (2024) and data intelligence (2026).

docs.title: Era 1, 2009–2015: the all-flash disruptor
docs.text:
The company was incorporated in Delaware in October 2009 as OS76, Inc. and renamed Pure Storage in January 20101. Its founders, John Colgrove (from Veritas) and John Hayes (from Yahoo), were incubated by Sutter Hill Ventures2. In 2009 enterprise flash meant expensive SLC drives for a few hot databases. Pure bet that consumer MLC flash, managed by software that deduplicated, compressed and spared the cells, could replace disk for primary storage. Illustratively, if a 5:1 data-reduction ratio turns raw flash at five times disk's $/TB into parity per effective terabyte, the speed comes almost free (Chapter 5).

Think of a fabless start-up winning with design on a cheap, mature node. After a two-year beta, the FlashArray 300 series reached general availability in May 2012, running the Purity operating environment3. It shipped with "All Software Included" licensing1.

The second insight was commercial. Incumbents earned much of their margin from forklift upgrades every three to five years. In February 2014 Pure launched Forever Flash, which included a controller refresh with maintenance renewal4. In June 2015 it widened this into the Evergreen Storage programme, launched alongside FlashArray//m5. Four months later the IPO priced at $17, raising $425M (25M shares)6. The stock closed its first day at $16.017. Incumbents fought back in court: Pure settled EMC's patent and trade-secret litigation in October 2016 with a $30M payment to Dell, EMC's new owner8.

docs.title: Era 2, 2016–2020: second product, new CEO, first deals
docs.text:
FlashBlade, a scale-out file and object system for unstructured data, was unveiled in March 2016 and reached GA on 25 January 20179. In August 2017 the board appointed Charles Giancarlo, previously CTO of Cisco, as CEO, succeeding Scott Dietzen10. DirectFlash modules, which put raw NAND under Purity's direct control instead of behind an SSD controller, followed with FlashArray//X in April 201711 (Chapter 26).

Three acquisitions followed in 26 months (Table 25.1).

Target Announced → closed Price (disclosed) Rationale What became of it StorReduce Aug 2018 $20.5M cash, net of cash acquired12 Cloud-native dedupe for object and backup data Became the ObjectEngine backup appliance (2019). It disappeared from Pure's product pages by mid-2020, with no formal EOL announcement found13 Compuverde (Sweden) Apr 2019 $47.9M net, plus $15.9M paid to former holders over two years14 File-system software and a team for FlashArray Basis of native file services in Purity//FA 6.0 (June 2020)15 Portworx Sep 2020 → Oct 2020 $352.9M consideration plus $32.2M retention (about $370M as announced)1416 Kubernetes persistent storage and data services Sold as Portworx by Everpure. Release 3.6 (Mar 2026) targets VMs on Kubernetes (KubeVirt)17 CoreWeave (minority stake) Nov 2024 Undisclosed Channel into GPU clouds A preferred storage option at CoreWeave18. CoreWeave later signed a $1.17B platform deal with VAST19 1touch 23 Feb 2026 → 7 May 2026 $125.0M cash; $101.2M of it booked to goodwill20 Data discovery, classification and semantic context Relaunched as Everpure Data Intelligence, GA June 202621

Table 25.1 — Everpure buys capabilities, not revenue; the one clear miss (StorReduce) was also the cheapest.

Disclosed consideration for the four acquisitions is 20.5 + 47.9 + 15.9 + 352.9 + 32.2 + 125.0 ≈ $594M over eight years, less than FY2026 free cash flow of $616M22. No deal bought a large installed base; each had to fit Purity or sit beside it.

docs.title: Era 3, 2020–2023: subscription and the first Meta relationship
docs.text:
FY2021 revenue grew only 2%, which the company attributed to COVID-19. FY2022 then rose 29% to $2.18B23. Meta became the showcase AI customer: its AI Research SuperCluster, unveiled in January 2022, used 175 PB of FlashArray and 10 PB of FlashBlade24. In June 2022 Pure reorganised Evergreen into //Forever, //Flex and //One (storage-as-a-service)25 (Chapter 23).

In May 2023 a Pure executive predicted that no new hard drives would be sold after 2028. Analysts such as Coughlin Associates disputed it2627. It was a marketing line that pointed to the real strategy: QLC DirectFlash at hyperscale.

docs.title: Era 4, 2024–2025: from array vendor to IP licensor
docs.text:
On 3 December 2024 Pure announced a DirectFlash design win with a "top-four hyperscaler"28. The FY2025 10-K later named the customer as Meta29. The hyperscaler sources its own hardware and NAND; Pure licenses Purity and DirectFlash technology and provides support28. It is an Arm-style IP licence: Pure trades hardware revenue for margin and reach. Volume deployment began in Q2 FY2026, and the CFO targeted 1–2 EB shipped by the end of that year30.

2025 added FlashBlade//EXA for AI-scale throughput (March)31 and the Enterprise Data Cloud, which uses Fusion to run a fleet as one policy-driven pool (June)32 (Chapter 28).

docs.title: Era 5, 2026: Everpure
docs.text: On 23 February 2026 Pure Storage renamed itself Everpure and announced the 1touch acquisition the same day33. On 7 April it said the NYSE ticker would change from PSTG to P, effective 17 April 202634. At Pure//Accelerate in June it made Data Intelligence (formerly 1touch) and Data Stream, a GPU ingest-to-inference pipeline, generally available21. On 10 August a second, unnamed top-five hyperscaler signed a DirectFlash design-win and supply agreement. Meaningful revenue is expected from FY202835.

docs.title: The numbers behind the eras
docs.text:
Figure 25.3 — Revenue compounded about 24% a year over a decade, but unevenly. Two near-flat years show the cost of transitions, and FY2027 guidance would add more revenue in one year than FY2021–FY2024 added in three. Data: data/ch25_revenue.csv

Worked numbers: FY2016 revenue was $440.3M and FY2026 was $3,662.8M3637. That is (3,662.8 ÷ 440.3)^(1/10) ≈ 8.32^0.1 ≈ 1.236, or about 23.6% CAGR. FY2027 guidance of $5.03–5.07B38 implies about $1.39B of new revenue at the midpoint. FY2021 to FY2024 added only $1.15B (2,830.6 − 1,684.2). FY2017–FY2018 are shown as originally reported, before the ASC 606 accounting change, so they are not strictly comparable.

docs.title: What worked, what took longer, what the rebrand signals
docs.text:
Worked: Evergreen, which made subscription services $1,691M, or 46% of FY2026 revenue, with ARR of $1,924M37; Purity's single code base across FlashArray and FlashBlade; and the hyperscaler licence, which reached volume shipments within a fiscal year, though its revenue is still small.

Took longer or landed narrower: native file on FlashArray took a year from the Compuverde deal to Purity 6.0, and one report says two more years to mature [VERIFY: Purity//FA 6.4 as the release in which file services matured]. Portworx has no disclosed revenue line, and its pitch moved from containers to VM migration off VMware. Hyperscaler revenue was described as small in Q1 FY2027 and back-half-weighted39. The 2028 "end of disk" call is still unproven.

What the rebrand signals: the old name tied the company to flash media just as its pitch moved to software, data services and licensing. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: whether data-intelligence revenue can be disclosed separately enough to support a platform multiple; whether further 1touch-sized deals (governance, vector, lakehouse connectors) are needed to make "data primacy" credible against VAST's AI OS; and how to keep the array franchise funding all of this while NAND costs rise. Everpure raised prices in February 202640, and Q2 FY2027 free cash flow was −$238M after strategic NAND and component purchases41.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Company Starting point Platform move AI move Capital model Everpure All-flash arrays, one OS (Purity) Evergreen subscriptions; Fusion/EDC; data intelligence via 1touch FlashBlade//EXA; DFM licensing to hyperscalers Public; small tuck-ins funded from FCF NetApp Unified file/block (ONTAP), hybrid then flash Cloud-native ONTAP services AFX disaggregated ONTAP plus AI Data Engine (Oct 2025)42 Public; history of software acquisitions Dell Broadest portfolio after acquiring EMC Multiple OSes by product line PowerScale parallel NFS ("Lightning")43 Public conglomerate; channel scale VAST Data Disaggregated software platform (2016) Rebranded as "AI Operating System" (May 2025)44 GPU clouds and neoclouds Private; $30B valuation (Apr 2026, reported by CNBC)45 DDN HPC parallel file systems "AI and data intelligence" positioning NVIDIA SuperPOD incumbency Blackstone $300M at $5B (Jan 2025)46

Table 25.2 — Everyone is converging on "data platform for AI". Everpure is unusual in reaching it through one OS and a subscription base rather than through a portfolio (Dell) or a clean-sheet AI design (VAST).

The steelman for the alternatives: VAST's single-namespace, database-in-storage design was built for AI pipelines, while Everpure is adding equivalent functions after the fact through EXA and Data Stream. Dell and NetApp own larger installed bases and channel reach, and NetApp's ONTAP served file and block from one OS long before Purity 6.0. Everpure's counter-argument is consistency: one OS, one upgrade model and fleet telemetry across 14 years of installed systems (Chapter 46, Chapter 42).

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
Dated, public signals to watch through 2027:

  • Q3 FY2027 results, due late November 2026, are the first quarter in which management expects hyperscale revenue to rise significantly39.
  • Second hyperscaler revenue is expected from FY202835. A third win would prove a repeatable model.
  • NAND pricing: the 2026 component spike tests whether Evergreen contracts protect or squeeze product margins (Chapter 48).
  • Data Intelligence adoption: no metrics are disclosed yet; the first customer count or ARR figure will be the real test of the rebrand (Chapter 39).

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Which Evergreen promise costs us the most in a NAND upcycle, and how is it priced?" Strong: names the entitlement (controller refresh, capacity guarantees, //One effective-capacity metering), quantifies exposure and cites contract protections.
  2. "What would make Data Intelligence a separately disclosed line, and when?" Strong: gives attach rates, standalone versus bundled pricing and a reportable metric, not just "platform".
  3. "Where did Portworx win in FY2026: containers, VM migration or both?" Strong: separates KubeVirt and VMware-exit deals from cloud-native ones and cites customer counts.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What changed in Purity to serve a hyperscaler that owns the hardware?" Strong: describes the split between licensed firmware/software and customer-built systems, and who owns failure analysis.
  2. "How much of the Compuverde code still runs in FlashArray file services?" Strong: candid about the rewrite share and what was kept.
  3. "What did the StorReduce/ObjectEngine exit teach about integrating acquired data paths?" Strong: names the integration cost and the backup-ISV overlap that made it redundant.

Don't say this:

  • "Pure invented all-flash storage." Other flash-system vendors were selling before FlashArray reached GA (Chapter 52). Pure's edge was flash-for-disk economics plus the business model.
  • "Everpure is a new company." It is a rename. The legal entity, CUSIP and products carried over.
  • "The Meta deal is a hardware sale." It is technology licensing plus support. Meta sources its own hardware and NAND.
  • "Pure is an acquisitive company." It has done four small deals in 17 years.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• The 2015 Form S-1 (risk factors and the early Evergreen description) and the FY2021 and FY2026 10-Ks (purchase accounting for Portworx and 1touch).
  • Chapter 29 for revenue mix and margin drivers, and Chapter 54 for the option map.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Evergreen — Everpure's subscription family (//Forever, //Flex, //One) that replaces forklift upgrades.
  • Forever Flash — the 2014 predecessor programme bundling controller refreshes with maintenance.
  • Design win (hyperscaler) — a customer's commitment to build on a supplier's technology, here licensed DirectFlash and Purity.
  • Enterprise Data Cloud (EDC) — Everpure's 2025 architecture for managing a fleet as one policy-driven pool.
  • Data Intelligence — the ex-1touch discovery and classification product.
  • ASC 606 — the revenue-recognition standard that restated pre-FY2019 figures.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 26. Core technology: Purity and DirectFlash
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Media physics for a semis person · Inside an SSD · Data reduction · Interfaces and emerging tech · Glossary

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Purity is a log-structured, database-like storage OS. It appends instead of overwriting, reduces data inline, and keeps all mappings in a key-value metadata store.
  • DirectFlash removes the SSD's own brain. Purity runs one flash translation layer (FTL) across raw-NAND modules. That gives one log, one garbage collector and one pool of spare flash, where an SSD-based array has one per drive.
  • That is why DFMs ship bigger than SSDs: 300 TB per module by 20261, against 245.76 TB for the largest standard SSD confirmed shipping2 (Sandisk has announced 256 TB3). Everpure's power advantages are vendor claims, best checked at system level.
  • Semis frame: it is the integrated-memory-controller move, made by a fabless-style player. Global scheduling is the gain; qualifying every NAND generation itself, with NAND bought from IDMs that also sell finished SSDs, is the cost.
  • Exposure cuts both ways. Everpure buys NAND for its enterprise arrays, and strategic NAND purchases turned Q2 FY27 operating cash flow negative4. It does not buy NAND for hyperscaler licences5. Flexible Data Placement (FDP) SSDs and hyperscaler do-it-yourself designs are the main threats to the moat.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
DirectFlash is the technical root of three things investors pay Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) for. The first is product gross margin, which a lower bill of materials supports but does not protect: non-GAAP product GM fell to 66.2% in Q2 FY27 from a royalty-flattered 72.9% in Q3 FY26 as NAND costs rose67. The second is the hyperscaler licensing business: Meta, then a second unnamed top-five hyperscaler in August 20268. The third is the power-and-density pitch to replace disk in power-constrained AI datacenters (Chapter 38). If FDP gives commodity SSDs most of the benefit, or a hyperscaler builds its own equivalent, all three weaken together.

The strategy question is which moat layer is durable: the global FTL, module design, NAND qualification know-how or supply relationships. Owning the module also makes Everpure a direct raw-NAND buyer in the 2026 shortage, competing for allocation with the IDMs' own SSD businesses.

docs.title: Purity in one picture
docs.text:
Purity was built in 2009–2012 to make commodity SSDs behave like enterprise storage, borrowing from databases and key-value stores. Every write is monotonic (append-only), and deletes are recorded as predicates that hide old records rather than overwriting them9. That one choice explains most of the product.

flowchart TB
    H["Hosts and apps"] --> FE["Protocol front-ends<br/>FC, iSCSI, NVMe-oF, NFS, SMB, S3"]
    FE --> NV["NVRAM reachable by both controllers<br/>write acknowledged here"]
    NV --> DR["Inline data reduction<br/>pattern removal, dedupe, compression"]
    DR --> LS["Log-structured segment writer<br/>append only, never overwrite"]
    LS --> RH["RAID-HA<br/>dual parity across modules"]
    RH --> DF["DirectFlash software<br/>global FTL, GC, wear, scheduling"]
    DF --> M1["DFM raw NAND"]
    DF --> M2["DFM raw NAND"]
    DF --> M3["DFM raw NAND"]
    KV[("Metadata key-value store<br/>hot tiers in DRAM, rest on flash")]
    DR <--> KV
    LS <--> KV
    DF <--> KV

Figure 26.1 — Purity is a pipeline from protocol to raw NAND. The metadata store, not the data layout, is the centre of gravity, and DirectFlash is its lowest layer.

A write lands in persistent NVRAM that both controllers can reach (dual-homed chassis modules on earlier models, NVRAM on DirectFlash modules on //XL) and is acknowledged there10 (Chapter 14). Purity then removes patterns such as zeros, deduplicates, and compresses into variable-size blocks of roughly 4–32 KB, matching duplicates at 512-byte alignment11 (Chapter 5). Reduced data is packed into large segments written sequentially across modules with dual parity (RAID-HA)12. Overwrites never happen in place: a newer version simply wins in the metadata map, which is why snapshots are nearly free (Chapter 6).

The metadata store is the hard part. Everpure describes a tiered "pyramid": hot metadata in controller DRAM, in-flight changes journalled in NVRAM, the bulk on flash13. Purity//FB spreads the same ideas across FlashBlade's blades (Chapter 27).

docs.title: The problem DirectFlash solves: a log on top of a log
docs.text:
An SSD is itself a log-structured system. NAND programs pages but erases only whole blocks, so the drive's FTL appends writes, remaps addresses in DRAM, and garbage-collects (GC) stale pages (Chapter 3). Put Purity on top and you have two logs. Each has its own map, its own GC and its own reserved spare space, and neither can see the other's state. Academic work calls this "log-on-log" and shows the layers' write amplification compounding14.

Figure 26.2 — A commodity-SSD array pays for controllers, DRAM maps, garbage collection and spare flash once per drive and again at array level; DirectFlash pays once.

Three worked numbers show the cost of the stack:

  • Spare flash, paid twice. A drive built from 8 TiB of NAND (8.80 TB) sold as 7.68 TB hides 1.12 TB, or 14.5% of user capacity. Sold as a 6.4 TB mixed-use drive, it hides 2.40 TB, or 37%. The array then keeps its own free space for segment cleaning on top.
  • Write amplification multiplies. Illustrative: if array GC rewrites 1.5 bytes per host byte, and the drive's GC independently doubles that, NAND absorbs 3 bytes per host byte. QLC, with roughly a third of TLC's endurance, cannot afford that.
  • DRAM scales with capacity. A page-level FTL stores ~4 bytes per 4 KiB page, i.e. 1 GB of DRAM per TB. A 245 TB SSD mapped that finely would need ~245 GB of on-drive DRAM. Big QLC drives therefore map coarser units and pay read-modify-write penalties on small writes. A 10 PB array mapped at 4 KiB would carry ~10 TB of drive DRAM, Everpure's own argument15.

DirectFlash deletes the inner layer. The DirectFlash Module (DFM) is a PCIe/NVMe card of raw NAND behind a thin controller. It has no logical address abstraction of its own10, so Purity addresses NAND blocks directly. Purity then does wear levelling, GC and over-provisioning once, at array level15. The precise split of functions such as error correction between module and Purity is not public [VERIFY: which NAND functions run on the DFM controller versus in Purity].

docs.title: The semiconductor lens: on-die memory controllers and IDM versus fabless
docs.text:
Moving the memory controller on-die. Until the mid-2000s, x86 CPUs reached DRAM through a northbridge chip. AMD (2003) and Intel (2008) pulled the memory controller onto the CPU die. Latency fell and the CPU could schedule DRAM banks knowing its own request stream. DirectFlash is the same move: the "flash northbridge" inside every SSD is absorbed into the array CPU. So is the price: as an on-die controller ties CPUs to DRAM generations, DirectFlash ties Purity releases to NAND generations, each of which must be characterised in software.

IDM versus fabless. The SSD makers (Samsung, SK hynix/Solidigm, Micron, Kioxia, Sandisk) are IDMs. They own the NAND fab, design the controller and tune firmware with privileged process data. Everpure behaves like a fabless system house: it buys the "wafer" (raw NAND), designs the module, differentiates in software and skips the SSD maker's controller, DRAM and firmware margin. The classic fabless trade-offs apply:

  • Upside: freedom to qualify several suppliers on one design, faster architectural iteration, and capital-light scale.
  • Downside: no process insight, dependence on suppliers that also sell competing finished products, and weaker allocation leverage in shortages.
flowchart LR
    subgraph IDM["SSD maker: IDM model"]
        direction TB
        F1["Own NAND fab"] --> C1["Own controller ASIC + firmware FTL"] --> S1["Finished SSD sold to any array vendor"]
    end
    subgraph FAB["Everpure: fabless-style model"]
        direction TB
        F2["Buy raw NAND from several fabs"] --> C2["DFM design, thin controller"] --> P2["Purity global FTL in array software"]
    end
    S1 --> A1["Dell, NetApp, HPE, VAST arrays"]
    P2 --> A2["FlashArray, FlashBlade, hyperscaler licence"]

Figure 26.3 — SSD makers integrate vertically from fab to firmware; Everpure integrates from module to software and buys NAND from those same IDMs.

docs.title: What owning the FTL buys
docs.text:
Density. Without a per-drive DRAM map, module capacity is limited by NAND packages and power, not controller memory, which is why DFMs have led the largest standard SSD at each step (Figure 26.4).

Power. Everpure's CTO put the 75 TB DFM under 10 W, against a 25 W maximum for a 61.44 TB Solidigm SSD22: about 0.13 W/TB against 0.41 W/TB, though comparing a typical draw with a maximum flatters the DFM. At system level, Everpure claims HDD-based and 15.36 TB-SSD systems need 2.4× the power of its 75 TB-DFM system and 4.8× that of its 150 TB-DFM system16, and up to 75% less power than disk in hyperscale use17. NetApp's rebuttal is fair: compare whole systems, not modules18.

Endurance and QLC viability. With one GC that knows which data is cold, Purity can group data by lifetime so whole blocks die together. That makes low-endurance QLC usable for enterprise primary storage.

Failure behaviour. Purity sees per-block health, so it can retire blocks and evacuate a degrading module before it fails rather than rebuild afterwards19. A commodity SSD fails as a black box. Its firmware is a fleet-wide correlated risk: in 2019 HPE warned that certain SAS SSDs would fail at exactly 32,768 power-on hours without a firmware update20. DirectFlash concentrates that risk in Everpure's own code instead of eliminating it.

Consistency. Drive GC fires on its own schedule, causing latency spikes; one scheduler can defer GC around host I/O.

docs.title: DFM capacity roadmap
docs.text:
Figure 26.4 — DFMs went from 75 TB to 300 TB in about two years and stayed above the largest standard SSD; the next steps, 600 TB and 1 PB, are undated ambitions. Data: data/ch26_dfm_capacity.csv

The 75 TB QLC DFM launched with FlashArray//E in 202321. In March 2023 Pure Storage set targets of 150 TB in 2024 and 300 TB in 202622. The 150 TB module was announced in September 2024 for availability by year-end23. Everpure's FY2026 10-K says the 300 TB DFM was released in 2025, ahead of target24 [VERIFY: search-summary only], and trade press confirmed 300 TB modules in August 20261. A co-founder has spoken of 600 TB and then 1 PB-plus modules without dates25. The commodity side is closing in: Sandisk shows 512 TB on its 2027 roadmap3, and Meta plans QLC drives up to 512 TB26.

docs.title: NAND supplier exposure and the 2026 shortage
docs.text:
Everpure qualified Micron's G8 QLC for the 150 TB DFM and is taking Micron G9 QLC into future DFMs, including hyperscaler ones27. Kioxia, whose BiCS8 generation includes a 2 Tb QLC die, is a long-standing partner28. Two suppliers give leverage and resilience at the cost of qualifying each new die.

Everpure raised prices on 9 February 2026, citing component costs29. Strategic NAND and component purchases in Q2 FY27 took operating cash flow to −$136M and free cash flow to −$238M; a ~$577M build in prepaid expenses has been read as advance NAND buying30 [VERIFY: prepaid figure from third-party reading of the 10-Q]. Management said cash flow should normalise over two quarters4. TrendForce forecasts NAND contract prices up another 15–20% quarter on quarter in Q4 2026, with enterprise SSDs reportedly up 23–28%3132.

The hyperscaler model sidesteps this: the customer licenses the design and buys its own NAND and hardware, so Everpure procures no NAND for it15. That is closer to Arm than to a fabless chip vendor (Chapter 29).

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Dimension Everpure DirectFlash Commodity-SSD array (Dell, NetApp, HPE, VAST) Hyperscaler DIY with FDP SSDs DRAM for flash mapping None on module; array-level metadata in controller DRAM (size not published) ~1 GB per TB per drive at 4 KiB mapping, less with coarse mapping Same as commodity SSDs Over-provisioning Pooled once at array level Hidden per drive (~15–37%) plus array reserve Per drive, though FDP reduces need Write amplification One GC layer; data placed by lifetime Array GC × drive GC (log-on-log) FDP lets host separate lifetimes; near-1 when used well33 Power and density 300 TB modules; vendor claims 2.4–4.8× system power advantage16 61–245 TB standard drives; standard power envelopes Same drives; host software tuned Failure behaviour Per-block visibility; evacuation before failure Drive fails as unit; firmware bugs correlated across fleet Same, mitigated by scale and diversity Supply flexibility Qualify any NAND die, but each needs Purity support Four-plus drive suppliers, plug-compatible Four-plus suppliers; maximum leverage Who carries NAND qualification Everpure Drive maker Drive maker

Table 26.1 — DirectFlash wins on DRAM, spare flash and write amplification; commodity SSDs win on supply flexibility and on who carries the qualification burden.

Middle paths exist. IBM builds its own FlashCore Modules for FlashSystem, putting compression, encryption and threat detection inside the module, so it keeps an in-module FTL and adds compute instead of removing it34. Everpure itself uses commercial SSDs in FlashArray//ST35 and in FlashBlade//EXA's launch data nodes36. DirectFlash is a choice made per product, not a dogma.

Steelman the counter-case:

  1. FDP closes much of the gap without lock-in. NVMe FDP, ratified in 2022 and backed by Meta and Google with Samsung, lets hosts tag writes so drives keep lifetimes apart, cutting write amplification while drives stay standard3337. Meta is deploying standard QLC SSDs alongside DFMs38.
  2. R&D scale. Each NAND IDM funds controller and firmware teams from a far larger SSD revenue base, with process data first.
  3. Single-design risk and qualification burden. One module design and one FTL serve FlashArray, FlashBlade and two hyperscalers, so a latent bug or NAND-generation defect is correlated across the base; and each new die must be characterised without fab data.
  4. Hyperscalers can build it. Open-channel SSDs (LightNVM) were the industry's attempt at host-managed flash, and they were set aside in favour of zoned and placement-hint designs39. Yet when Meta wanted raw-flash control at scale, it licensed rather than built38.

docs.text:
timeline
    title DirectFlash and Purity milestones
    2012 : FlashArray ships with Purity on commodity SSDs
    2016 : FlashBlade puts raw NAND on blades
    2017 : DirectFlash Module launches with FlashArray X
    2020 : QLC DFMs reach 49 TB in FlashArray C

Figure 26.5 — Purity began by taming commodity SSDs, then spent a decade replacing them, and is now licensing the replacement to hyperscalers.

Sources for the timeline: FlashBlade's 2016 blades already carried raw NAND chips, not SSDs40; DirectFlash arrived in FlashArray//X in April 201741; QLC DFMs reached 24.7 TB and then 49 TB in FlashArray//C4243. In December 2024 a "top-four hyperscaler" licensed DirectFlash44, and the FY2025 10-K later named it as Meta45. The second top-five win (August 2026) is expected to matter from FY20288.

Signals to watch: a date for 600 TB DFMs, standard SSDs reaching 512 TB, FDP adoption, and NAND costs in product margin.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "When a 512 TB standard SSD ships, what keeps DFMs ahead?" Strong answer: a dated next module step and the system-level gap in W/TB, TB/RU and DRAM avoided.
  2. "How does NAND inflation flow through Evergreen//One pricing versus capex sales?" Strong answer: separates pass-through on new sales from absorption on fixed-price subscriptions, and how the Q2 FY27 NAND buys hedge the gap.
  3. "Why does FlashArray//ST use commercial SSDs?" Strong answer: small latency-optimised configurations where DFM capacity is overkill, with a clear rule for when DirectFlash wins.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "How long does qualifying a new NAND die take, and what fails most often?" Strong answer: months, with specifics on read-retry, retention and error-correction margins.
  2. "Under FDP, what write amplification can a commodity-SSD array reach, and what is Purity's?" Strong answer: measured fleet numbers, plus the part FDP cannot fix (per-drive DRAM, hidden spare, opaque failure handling).
  3. "What is the blast radius of a DFM firmware or FTL bug?" Strong answer: staged rollouts, version diversity across the fleet, and a fallback when a NAND lot misbehaves.

Don't say this:

  • "DFMs are just big SSDs." They have no drive FTL; that is the entire point.
  • "DirectFlash makes Everpure immune to NAND prices." Enterprise arrays still consume purchased NAND; only the hyperscaler licence model avoids it.
  • "Everpure makes its own flash." It designs modules and software; Micron and Kioxia make the NAND.
  • "Up to 75% less power" as a fact. It is a vendor claim against disk, sensitive to the baseline.

docs.text:
• Colgrove et al., SIGMOD 20159: Purity's monotonic writes, predicate deletion and metadata design.
  • Yang et al., INFLOW 201414: the log-on-log argument.
  • Bjørling et al., FAST 201739: open-channel SSDs, the precursor of ZNS and FDP.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• DirectFlash Module (DFM) — Everpure's raw-NAND module, with no drive-level FTL.
  • Global FTL — one flash translation layer for every module in an array.
  • Log-on-log — stacked log-structured layers whose GC and write amplification compound.
  • RAID-HA — Purity's dual-parity protection across modules.
  • FDP — NVMe Flexible Data Placement: host hints that let drives separate data lifetimes.
  • Indirection unit — the granularity an SSD's map tracks; larger units cut DRAM but penalise small writes.
  • NAND qualification — characterising a new NAND die so firmware or software can drive it reliably.

docs.title: 27. Product portfolio: FlashArray and FlashBlade
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Core technology: Purity and DirectFlash · Scale-up dual-controller arrays · Scale-out shared-nothing clusters · Disaggregated shared-everything

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Two product families, two operating systems, one media strategy. FlashArray runs Purity//FA on a dual-controller, scale-up design and serves block storage first (file and S3 were added later). FlashBlade runs Purity//FB on scale-out blades for file and object. Almost every model uses Everpure's own DirectFlash Modules (DFMs). The exceptions are FlashArray//ST and the FlashBlade//EXA data nodes.
  • Models differ mainly in media and controller size. //XL, //X and //ST are TLC performance tiers. //C and //E are QLC capacity tiers. FlashBlade//S is the performance tier and FlashBlade//E the capacity tier. "R-numbers" (R4, R5) are controller refreshes that customers can apply in place.
  • FlashBlade//EXA is the AI-scale outlier. A Purity//FB metadata core sits on DFM blades, and separate third-party Linux/NVMe data nodes hold the data. Clients use pNFS to fetch a file's layout from the metadata core, then move data directly to and from the data nodes. Chapter 16 explains why this is a metadata/data split rather than DASE.
  • EXA posted the top numbers in MLPerf Storage v3.0 (September 2026), with 877.5 GiB/s of checkpoint write and 1,623.4 GiB/s of KV-cache read. VAST, WEKA, DDN, Dell, IBM and NetApp did not submit to that round, so "#1" means first among the systems that entered.
  • The AI certification gap has narrowed but not closed. FlashBlade//S holds DGX SuperPOD and NCP high-performance-storage certification. For EXA, Everpure announced in March 2026 that it was extending NVIDIA-Certified Storage validation to the platform as a step toward the NCP level; no completed EXA certification had been published by November 2026.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
The portfolio is the revenue engine: product revenue grew 54% year on year in Q2 FY27, to US$687 million1, and the mix within that growth shows where the business is heading. Each FlashArray tier meets a different incumbent, each FlashBlade tier a different challenger. EXA is the entry ticket to the GPU-cluster deals that VAST, WEKA and DDN have been winning (Chapter 41).

Placing a model against a workload is the minimum for credible PM conversations; knowing what the benchmarks actually measured is the minimum for the Office of the CTO. The technology underneath is in Chapter 26, the software layer on top in Chapter 28.

docs.title: The lineage in one picture
docs.text:
Pure Storage launched FlashArray in May 20122. For its first five years it had one product line built on SAS SSDs. Two changes reshaped it. The first was DirectFlash: FlashArray//X (April 2017) talked NVMe directly to raw NAND on Pure's own modules3. The second was media tiering: QLC-based //C arrived in September 20194 so that one controller design could serve both performance and capacity. FlashBlade began as a separate scale-out file and object system. It was unveiled in 2016 and generally available in January 20175. It later forked the same way: //S for performance (June 2022)6 and //E for capacity (March 2023)7.

flowchart LR
    subgraph FA["FlashArray - Purity//FA, dual controller, block first"]
        A1["FA-300 series 2012"] --> A2["FlashArray//m 2015"]
        A2 --> A3["//X all-NVMe DirectFlash 2017"]
        A3 --> A4["//C QLC 2019"]
        A3 --> A5["//XL 2021"]
        A4 --> A6["//E QLC disk-replacement 2023"]
        A3 --> A7["//X and //C R4 2023"]
        A5 --> A8["//XL R5 2025"]
        A7 --> A9["//X and //C R5 Sep 2025"]
        A8 --> A10["//XL190 with Purity Turbo GA Jan 2026"]
        A3 -.-> A11["//ST commercial SSDs Jun 2025"]
    end
    subgraph FB["FlashBlade - Purity//FB, scale-out file and object"]
        B1["FlashBlade 2016 to 2017 GA"] --> B2["FlashBlade//S 2022"]
        B2 --> B3["FlashBlade//E 2023"]
        B2 --> B4["//S R2 2025"]
        B2 --> B5["FlashBlade//EXA announced Mar 2025"]
    end

Figure 27.1 — Both families now span performance and capacity tiers on shared software; media by model is in Table 27.1. //ST (dotted) is the only FlashArray that leaves DirectFlash, and EXA is the only FlashBlade that adds third-party hardware.

Sources for the nodes: FA-300 and //m8; //XL9; //E, //X R4 and //C R410; //XL R5, //ST and //S R211; //X R5 and //C R512; //XL19013; EXA14.

Semiconductor bridge. Read the R-numbers as die shrinks on a stable instruction set. Purity is the ISA. A new controller generation (newer Intel Xeon, more PCIe lanes) is a new stepping. Because Evergreen subscriptions swap controllers in place without moving data (Chapter 23), a 2019 //X customer can be running R5 controllers today.

docs.title: FlashArray: one controller design, five media personalities
docs.text:
Every FlashArray is a two-controller, scale-up system (Chapter 14). The models differ in three things: controller horsepower, media and which data services stay switched on.

  • //X and //C share controllers. In the R5 refresh (September 2025) both moved to Intel Emerald Rapids. Pure reported //X about 30% faster and //C about 40% faster than R4. The default 3RU chassis grew to 28 drive slots12. //X uses TLC DFMs for sub-millisecond tier-1 work. //C uses QLC for capacity at millisecond-class latency.
  • //XL is the big-controller variant. It launched in December 2021 at up to 5.78 PB effective, with NVRAM moved onto the flash modules9. The R5 datasheet cites up to 7.4 PB effective and 45 GB/s, a large-block (512 KB) read figure15. The XL190, GA in January 2026, adds Purity Turbo, which lets the secondary controller serve reads13. That is a notable change for an active/passive-style design (Chapter 14).
  • //E is the disk-replacement tier. It launched in June 2023 with 75 TB QLC DFMs and an entry size of about 1 PB10.
  • //ST is the deliberate exception. It uses commercial PCIe SSDs, not DFMs. It is block-only. It turns off deduplication, compression and synchronous replication to shorten the I/O path. Everpure claims more than 10 million IOPS per 5RU16.

Worked example: what //ST's design choice costs. Take 400 TB of logical database data that reduces 4:1 on a normal FlashArray. A //X stores it on about 100 TB of physical flash. //ST does not reduce data, so it needs the full 400 TB, roughly four times the NAND. With NAND prices up sharply in 2026 (Chapter 48), //ST makes sense only for data that barely reduces anyway (encrypted or compressed tablespaces near 1:1) or where each microsecond has a dollar value (trading, large OLTP, log writes).

Model Target workloads Media Performance / capacity tier Competitor it most often meets FlashArray//XL (R5, XL190) Consolidated tier-0/1 databases, large virtualisation estates TLC DFMs, NVRAM on modules Top of scale-up block; up to 7.4 PB effective (R5) Dell PowerMax, Hitachi VSP, NetApp high-end AFF/ASA FlashArray//X (R5) Mainstream tier-1 block and file: VMs, databases, VDI TLC DFMs Sub-ms performance, midrange to upper midrange Dell PowerStore, NetApp AFF/ASA, HPE Alletra MP FlashArray//ST In-memory DBs, large OLTP, logging Commercial PCIe SSDs, no data reduction Latency and IOPS-density specialist Server-local NVMe; high-end PowerMax/VSP FlashArray//C (R5) Tier-2 consolidation, dev/test, VM capacity, backup QLC DFMs Capacity block/file, ms-class latency NetApp AFF C-Series, Dell PowerStore, hybrid arrays FlashArray//E Disk replacement, backup and secondary copies QLC DFMs (75 TB and up) Lowest $/TB FlashArray, about 1 PB entry Hybrid and HDD arrays FlashBlade//S (S100/S200/S500 R2) Analytics, EDA, rapid restore, AI training and inference on SuperPOD QLC DFMs Scale-out file and object performance tier Dell PowerScale, NetApp ONTAP NAS, VAST FlashBlade//E Data lakes, archives, backup repositories QLC DFMs; storage-only chassis behind a control chassis Capacity file and object Dell PowerScale archive tiers, HDD object (Cloudian, Scality), Qumulo FlashBlade//EXA GPU clusters, neoclouds, HPC: checkpoints, training reads, KV cache DFM metadata blades plus third-party NVMe data nodes Multi-TB/s single namespace VAST, WEKA, DDN EXAScaler, IBM Storage Scale

Table 27.1 — Positioning by workload. Competitor pairings are the atlas's judgement from public positioning, not Everpure win/loss data. Specs: 15161013717.

docs.title: FlashBlade//S and //E: scale-out with a capacity fork
docs.text:
FlashBlade//S separates per-blade compute from DirectFlash capacity inside a 5U chassis. This lets customers add blades for performance or larger DFMs for capacity6. Partner listings for the R2 generation cite up to 1,200 TB per blade with 300 TB DFMs and 400GbE networking13 [VERIFY: per-blade figure is a partner claim]. FlashBlade//E keeps CPUs only in a control chassis and adds storage-only chassis behind it. That design lowers $/TB for cold unstructured data7. Purity DeepReduce reached //E in early 202613. In September 2026 Everpure made it always-on, with a median 2:1 global reduction expected on //E and //S200 R218.

In AI, FlashBlade//S is the workhorse. FlashBlade//S500 earned DGX SuperPOD certification over Ethernet in November 202419. In March 2025 FlashBlade earned NVIDIA-Certified Storage at the Foundation and Enterprise levels, plus NCP high-performance-storage certification for HGX B200/H200 reference architectures20. Everpure says the //S R2 platform is certified for GB200 and GB300 SuperPODs21 [VERIFY: search-summary only].

docs.title: FlashBlade//EXA: metadata core plus data nodes
docs.text:
EXA was announced on March 11, 2025, for AI and HPC at a scale beyond what a FlashBlade//S cluster reaches14, and declared generally available at Accelerate in June 202522. The design starts from a diagnosis: at thousands of GPUs, the bottleneck is metadata and coordination, not raw media bandwidth (Chapter 21). EXA therefore splits the system into two independently scaled tiers1722:

flowchart LR
    subgraph CL["GPU servers - pNFS clients"]
        C1["Client 1"]
        C2["Client N"]
    end
    subgraph MD["Metadata core - Purity//FB"]
        M1["EXA blades with DFMs"]
        M2["Namespace, layouts, locks"]
    end
    subgraph DN["Data nodes - Purity//DN"]
        D1["Linux server + NVMe SSDs"]
        D2["Linux server + NVMe SSDs"]
        D3["Planned: DFM-based nodes"]
    end
    C1 -->|"NFSv4.1 over TCP: open, LAYOUTGET"| M1
    C2 -->|"metadata ops"| M1
    C1 ==>|"data over RDMA, direct"| D1
    C2 ==>|"data over RDMA, direct"| D2
    M1 -.->|"health and capacity control"| D1
    M1 -.-> D2
    M1 -.-> D3

Figure 27.2 — Clients go to the metadata core only for the map. Bulk data travels straight between GPU servers and data nodes, so throughput scales with data-node count while metadata scales with blades.

  1. The metadata core is FlashBlade hardware running Purity//FB. It holds the namespace, file layouts and locks on DFM blades. Pure Storage's launch materials described one to ten chassis of ten blades each17.
  2. Data nodes at launch were off-the-shelf Linux servers with NVMe SSDs, running Everpure's Purity//DN stack1723. Under the EXA terms of use, a data node is a third-party server paired with the metadata core. Each node comes with a 160 TiB usable-capacity entitlement, and larger capacity is licensed per TB24. The SPECstorage submission used Supermicro ASG-1115S-NE316R servers as data nodes23.
  3. DFM-based data nodes, with 75 TB and 150 TB modules and up to 24 per server, were planned for 2H 202525. No public source found confirms they are GA as of November 2026: the terms of use still describe third-party servers24, and the September 2026 MLPerf submission used Linux/NVMe data nodes26 [VERIFY: DFM data-node GA status].
sequenceDiagram
    participant G as GPU server
    participant M as Metadata core
    participant D as Data nodes
    G->>M: OPEN file and LAYOUTGET over TCP
    M-->>G: layout listing which data nodes hold which stripes
    G->>D: parallel RDMA reads to many data nodes
    D-->>G: data, with no metadata hop
    G->>M: LAYOUTRETURN or CLOSE

Figure 27.3 — The pNFS read path: one metadata round trip, then many parallel direct transfers. This is the parallel-file-system pattern of Chapter 17 with Purity as the metadata server.

Clients speak standard pNFS. Metadata travels as NFSv4.1 over TCP, and data moves over RDMA27. No proprietary client driver is needed, which helps in locked-down GPU images. That is a fair point against WEKA and Lustre, whose clients buy finer client-side control in exchange; VAST makes the same standard-client argument with NFS over RDMA. Two consequences matter for the portfolio. First, EXA's data-node hardware is customer-sourceable, which helps neoclouds with server supply deals. Second, EXA's data services, including protection, reduction and multi-tenancy, mature on a separate release train (Purity//DN) from Purity//FB23. Multi-tenancy and QoS for neoclouds arrived at Accelerate 2026 in June28.

docs.title: What the benchmarks actually measured
docs.text:
MLPerf Storage emulates accelerators in software. A run passes if the storage keeps every simulated GPU above a utilisation threshold. No real GPUs are involved (Chapter 37)29. Round v3.0, published September 1, 2026, moved the simulated accelerator from H100 to B200. It also added KV-cache and vector-database workloads30. Everpure was one of 11 first-time submitters30; DDN, Dell, Huawei, IBM, NetApp, VAST and WEKA were absent31. Earlier "v2.0 results" from Pure Storage were a white paper, not an MLCommons-listed entry32 [VERIFY: whether any v2.0 result was officially submitted].

Figure 27.4 — Checkpoint write scales nearly linearly with data nodes, but at 30 nodes per-node throughput is about 11% below the 10-node rate. Data: data/ch27_mlperf_checkpoint_scaling.csv

Worked check on the headline. Everpure reported 877.52 GiB/s for 17.74 seconds on the largest checkpoint model33. That is 877.52 × 17.74 ≈ 15,570 GiB, or about 16.7 TB. That fits the round's 1.25-trillion-parameter checkpoint at about 13 bytes per parameter for weights plus optimizer state (Chapter 31). Scaling efficiency is (877.52 ÷ 30) ÷ (327.65 ÷ 10) = 29.25 ÷ 32.77 ≈ 89%. In converted units, 877.52 GiB/s × 1.074 ≈ 942 GB/s. A cluster checkpointing every 30 minutes would stall for about 17.74 ÷ 1,800 ≈ 1% of wall-clock time, before any asynchronous checkpointing.

Data nodes are not DFMs. Reported read figure conflicts (588.3 vs 833.0 GiB/s)2633 Near-linear scaling, 327.6 → 877.5 GiB/s Same 2026-09-01 10 → 30 data nodes Per-node rate down ~11%. 15- and 20-node points from one secondary source 1,623.4 GiB/s KV-cache read MLPerf Storage v3.0, KV cache 2026-09-01 51-host EXA configuration26 First round of a new workload. docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Everpure's portfolio argument is one software lineage per family, own media everywhere, upgrade in place. Rivals beat it in specific places:

Line Everpure's best argument Where a rival genuinely wins Rival FlashArray//XL In-place controller upgrades, high reduction, operational simplicity Mainframe (FICON) attachment and decades of multi-site replication practice; FlashArray has no mainframe answer Dell PowerMax, Hitachi VSP, IBM DS8000 FlashArray//X, //C DFM density, shared controllers, block + file + S3 on one OS NAS depth and installed base (ONTAP replication, caching, multiprotocol); FlashArray file services are younger NetApp FlashArray//ST Microsecond-class latency with array-grade availability Server-local NVMe with database-native replication beats any networked array on latency and cost for one application DIY / HCI //E and FlashBlade//E Power, footprint and flash reliability for "cold" data Raw $/TB. QLC was roughly 15× HDD per GB in 2026 per TrendForce38 [VERIFY: single-vendor-derived index] HDD object and hybrid arrays FlashBlade//S SuperPOD-certified scale-out file/object with Evergreen PowerScale's installed base and mixed flash/HDD tiers in one cluster; VAST's global similarity reduction and database features Dell, VAST FlashBlade//EXA Purity metadata engine, standard pNFS client, customer-sourced data nodes, top v3.0 results NVIDIA flagship references (DDN's ~4 TB/s on Eos)39; WEKA's software-anywhere and cloud reach; VAST's neocloud scale (US$1.17B CoreWeave deal, reported by press)40; SuperPOD certification held by all three VAST, WEKA, DDN

Table 27.3 — Steelman by product line. FlashArray's exposures are breadth (mainframe, NAS heritage). FlashBlade//EXA's are references and certification maturity.

Everpure is strongest where one OS stretches across tiers (FlashArray from //ST to //E) and most exposed where buyers want an ecosystem badge or a reference customer first: at EXA scale, "who runs this on 10,000 GPUs?" comes before speed. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: whether DFM data nodes (closing the media-cost gap) or NCP/SuperPOD certification for EXA (closing the badge gap) matters more to neocloud win rates, and whether //ST and //E justify their SKU complexity or should fold into //X and //C over time.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
The portfolio grew by forking, not acquiring (Figure 27.1), and the forks track the NAND roadmap: QLC density made //C and //E viable, and the 75 → 150 → 300 TB DFM progression (Chapter 26) lets the capacity tiers compete with disk.

Signals for 2026–2027: in March 2026 Everpure said it was extending NVIDIA-Certified Storage validation to EXA, a step toward the NCP level that Blocks & Files reported for "later this year"41, and aligned EXA with NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX reference architecture42. Neither an EXA entry on NVIDIA's certified-storage list nor an NCP certification had been found by 2026-11-01. PureKVA and always-on DeepReduce were announced on 30 September 202618. The first enterprise EXA customer was reported in Q4 FY2643. Watch for three things: DFM data-node GA, NCP and SuperPOD badges for EXA, and an MLPerf v4.0 round that VAST, WEKA or DDN actually enter.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Where does //ST win deals that //XL190 with Purity Turbo would lose, and how big is that pool?" Strong: separates latency-bound from IOPS-bound buyers, gives the reduction ratio at which //ST's lack of reduction stops mattering, and admits overlap with //XL.
  2. "What share of EXA pipeline needs DFM data nodes or NCP certification before signing?" Strong: splits enterprise from neocloud buyers, with the gating requirement and a date for each.
  3. "Which competitor shows up most against FlashBlade//E, and on what metric do we lose?" Strong: HDD-based object on $/TB, plus the power, rack and refresh numbers that flip TCO at a stated capacity and term.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "In the 30-node MLPerf run, what limited per-node throughput: data-node NICs, SSDs or metadata?" Strong: names the bottleneck, says what changes with DFM nodes, and explains the read-figure discrepancy.
  2. "How are data nodes protected today, and what does a data-node loss during a checkpoint look like to the client?" Strong: names the protection scheme, the degraded-mode throughput and the rebuild time.
  3. "What does Purity Turbo change in controller cache coherence when the secondary serves reads?" Strong: explains how the two caches stay consistent, how failover behaves, and why this is XL190-only.

Don't say this:

  • "EXA beat VAST and WEKA in MLPerf." They did not submit to v3.0.
  • "Every Everpure product runs on DirectFlash." //ST and EXA data nodes use commercial SSDs.
  • "FlashBlade//EXA is SuperPOD-certified." The public record shows //S, not EXA, as of this writing.
  • "R5 is a new product." It is a controller refresh that Evergreen customers can apply in place.
  • "877 GiB/s means 877 GB/s." GiB is about 7% larger, so the figure is ≈942 GB/s.

docs.text:
• The MLCommons v3.0 results tables and Everpure's submission system description (closed division, per-workload configurations).
  • The SPECstorage Solution 2020 full disclosure for the EXA result (Purity//FB 4.6.4, Purity//DN 1.0, network topology).
  • RFC 8881 (NFSv4.1) on pNFS layouts, and RFC 8435 (Flex Files), for the client path in Figure 27.3.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• R-generation — a FlashArray controller refresh (for example R5) applied in place.
  • Purity Turbo — XL190 feature letting the secondary controller serve reads.
  • Metadata core / data node — EXA's Purity//FB blade tier and its Purity//DN Linux data servers.
  • pNFS layout — the map a metadata server returns so clients can read data servers directly.
  • MLPerf Storage checkpointing / KV-cache workloads — emulated tests of checkpoint bandwidth and inference-context reads.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 28. Platform and software
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Control planes and fleet management · Consumption models · Purity and DirectFlash · FlashArray and FlashBlade

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• One software stack, many kinds of hardware. Purity runs on every array, Fusion and Pure1 manage the fleet, Portworx and Everpure Cloud extend it to Kubernetes and public cloud, and Data Intelligence (ex-1touch) reads what the data is. Umbrella names: Enterprise Data Cloud (2025), "Data Primacy" (2026).
  • Evergreen is the business model that makes the platform work. Customers subscribe to an architecture; controllers and media are refreshed in place with no data migration. Subscription ARR reached $2.13B (+20%) in Q2 FY271.
  • Switching costs now live in the control plane. Fusion presets and automation outlast any hardware refresh. Over 1,200 customers used Fusion by Q1 FY27, double the prior quarter2, still under a tenth of the base.
  • 1touch ($125.0M, closed 2026-05-07)3 bets that storage metadata plus content classification becomes a governance and AI-readiness product. It is small next to Portworx (~$353M, 2020)4 but enters categories owned by data catalogs and data-security vendors.
  • Every incumbent is making the same pitch. Dell, NetApp, HPE and VAST all sell a "data platform"; the differences are what sits beneath (one OS or a portfolio), reach beyond own hardware, and whether customers buy the top layers.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Hardware margins ride the NAND cycle; Everpure raised prices in February 2026 as component costs surged (Chapter 29). Subscription gross margin was 74.9% in Q2 FY27 against 66.2% for product (both non-GAAP)5. The platform aims to make revenue compound through attach and expansion. Subscription net dollar retention was 113% in FY266, so a cohort paying $100 one year paid $113 the next.

The risk: if Fusion, Portworx and Data Intelligence mostly ship inside array deals rather than winning standalone budgets, "data management company" is a rebrand on a storage P&L. The options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information, turn on that distinction.

docs.title: The stack, layer by layer
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    DI["Data intelligence: Everpure Data Intelligence, Data Stream"]
    PX["Portworx: Kubernetes data services"]
    CL["Everpure Cloud: Dedicated, Azure Native"]
    CP["Control plane: Fusion policies plus Pure1 telemetry and AIOps"]
    AR["Arrays: FlashArray, FlashBlade, FlashBlade EXA"]
    OS["Purity operating system"]
    MD["Media: DirectFlash Modules on raw NAND"]
    EV["Evergreen subscriptions wrap every layer"]
    DI --> CP
    PX --> CP
    CL --> CP
    CP --> AR
    AR --> OS
    OS --> MD
    EV -.-> CP
    EV -.-> AR

Figure 28.1 — One OS on every array, one control plane over every array, and the newest layers (Portworx, cloud, data intelligence) plugged into that control plane rather than into individual boxes.

The bottom three layers are covered in Chapter 26, Chapter 27 and Chapter 22. The layers above need no Everpure hardware: Portworx serves Kubernetes anywhere, Everpure Cloud runs Purity in AWS and Azure, and Data Intelligence classifies data wherever it lives.

Semiconductor bridge: this is Synopsys and Cadence moving from point tools to flows. A simulator is easy to swap; a sign-off flow with years of scripts and qualified recipes is not. Fusion presets and automation are Everpure's "flow"; the arrays are the tools.

Naming has shifted, so be precise. The Enterprise Data Cloud (June 2025) was a unified on-premises-plus-cloud control plane with Fusion at its core7; the CEO tied the February 2026 Everpure name to it and to Evergreen8. Counsel and filings now say "Everpure Platform"9. At Accelerate 2026 the framing became Data Primacy, trusted data rather than applications at the centre10, with pillars of data management, a unified data plane and an intelligent control plane11. "Pure Storage Cloud" is now Everpure Cloud12.

docs.title: Evergreen: subscribing to an architecture
docs.text:
Evergreen began in 2015; Evergreen Gold became Evergreen//Forever in the 2022 restructuring13 that produced today's three tiers14.

Tier Who owns the hardware What you pay for Refresh mechanics Key guarantees (company-stated) Evergreen//Forever Customer Array purchase plus a recurring subscription Controller refresh tied to three-year renewals, subject to program terms1516 Non-disruptive upgrades; no re-buying capacity already owned Evergreen//Flex Customer Capacity actually used, with fleet-level pooling Same as //Forever; capacity can be moved across the fleet Pay-per-use on owned arrays15 Evergreen//One Everpure A performance tier, priced per unit of used capacity, with a minimum commit Everpure's responsibility, invisible to the customer Up to ten SLAs, including 99.9999% availability, a 25% capacity buffer, energy efficiency, zero planned downtime and zero data loss1718

Table 28.1 — The three Evergreen tiers move risk progressively from the customer (owns and plans) to Everpure (owns, plans and guarantees).

The enabler is architectural. In a Purity dual-controller array, persistent state (data, metadata, write log) lives on flash modules and NVRAM in the chassis, not in the controllers (Chapter 14), so controllers swap one at a time while the partner serves I/O, and media is replaced by adding modules and evacuating old ones.

flowchart LR
    S["Subscription signed: Forever, Flex or One"] --> T["Pure1 telemetry: capacity, load, health"]
    T --> F["Forecast: fill date, performance headroom"]
    F --> D{"Trigger"}
    D -->|"renewal or SLA breach risk"| C["Ship new controllers"]
    D -->|"capacity or density need"| M["Ship new DirectFlash Modules"]
    C --> N["Swap one controller at a time, I/O continues"]
    M --> E["Add modules, evacuate and retire old ones"]
    N --> R["Same array, same data, newer hardware"]
    E --> R
    R --> T

Figure 28.2 — The Evergreen loop: telemetry tells Everpure when to ship hardware, and the architecture lets that hardware go in with no data migration, which is what makes the subscription renewable.

By July 2021 Pure Storage cited more than 7,000 non-disruptive controller upgrades for over 2,700 customers since 2015 (company-stated)19. Evergreen//One's SLAs are underwritable only because Pure1 watches every array; the buffer is sized from historical growth via Pure1's workload planner17. Overdrive, announced for Q3 2026, allows bursts up to 25% above the subscribed level20 [VERIFY: Overdrive terms from secondary summaries only].

Worked example (illustrative). A customer uses 800 TiB under Evergreen//One. With a 25% buffer, Everpure keeps at least 1,000 TiB effective on site, on hardware it owns; if data reduces worse than planned, it adds flash at its own cost. The vendor carries utilisation and data-reduction risk a capex buyer would carry, priced into the per-TiB rate and profitable only if telemetry keeps forecasts accurate. Chapter 23 covers the cash-flow side.

Evergreen//One bookings growth is tracked in Chapter 29.

docs.title: Fusion and Pure1: the control plane as the product
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    U["Admins, Terraform, Ansible, AI agents via MCP"] --> API["Fusion API and Pure1 Manage MCP"]
    API --> PS["Presets: QoS, protection, tags, compliance"]
    PS --> PL["Placement engine picks array with headroom"]
    PL --> A1["FlashArray fleet"]
    PL --> A2["FlashBlade fleet"]
    PL --> A3["Everpure Cloud Dedicated"]
    A1 --> P1["Pure1 telemetry and AIOps"]
    A2 --> P1
    A3 --> P1
    P1 -->|"forecasts, drift alerts, triage"| PL

Figure 28.3 — Users and agents ask for an outcome through one API; presets encode policy, Pure1 telemetry informs placement, and the arrays become interchangeable capacity behind it.

Fusion has been embedded in Purity since 2024, with nothing separate to deploy21. Its central object is the preset, a fleet-wide template of performance limits, snapshot and replication policy, and tags22, much like a Kubernetes storage class. Pure1 supplies forecasts, workload planning and predictive support. In 2026 both became agent-addressable: Everpure offers a Pure1 Manage MCP server and a Fusion MCP server, so AI tools can query fleet state and carry out supervised actions23. Fusion Compliance and Agentic Triage (configuration-drift detection with AI root-cause suggestions) and Workload Rebalance and Mobility were slated for Q4 202624 [VERIFY: GA status].

Watch adoption: over 1,200 Fusion customers against roughly 14,500–15,000 in total [VERIFY: two different base figures] is about 8%, and control-plane lock-in is real only for them.

docs.title: Portworx: storage for Kubernetes, then for VMs
docs.text:
Portworx (acquired October 20204) pools whatever disks or cloud volumes sit under a Kubernetes cluster and gives containers persistent volumes, replication, snapshots, backup and DR, on any hardware or cloud, or directly on FlashArray. Everpure books Portworx term licences as product revenue and its other offerings as subscription services revenue3, so no standalone Portworx revenue figure is public.

Portworx's second act came from Broadcom, whose post-2023 VMware licensing changes raised many renewal bills25 and pushed enterprises to evaluate KubeVirt, which runs VMs as Kubernetes objects (often via OpenShift Virtualization). Portworx Enterprise 3.6 (March 2026) added validated KubeVirt frameworks and a VM-readiness tool; customers run over 100,000 VM volumes on it (company-stated)26. Everpure's own IT moved more than 5,000 VMs to KubeVirt on Portworx (company-stated)27. An OpenShift plugin and an Edge SKU followed at Red Hat Summit 202628.

Everpure hedges the VMware exit both ways: Portworx for Kubernetes, and the May 2025 Nutanix partnership (FlashArray as external AHV storage) for another hypervisor29. Either way the array can stay Everpure.

docs.title: Everpure Cloud
docs.text: Everpure Cloud Dedicated (ex-Cloud Block Store) is customer-managed Purity in the customer's AWS or Azure account, with replication and snapshot parity with on-premises arrays12. Everpure Cloud Azure Native, co-developed with Microsoft and launched September 202530, is a fully managed Azure Native ISV service, first for Azure VMware Solution31, with Azure VM support GA from June 202620 [VERIFY: Azure VM GA date]. The role is mainly defensive: a workload moving to cloud can stay under Fusion and Evergreen-style billing rather than native EBS or Azure Disk. Against NetApp's first-party ONTAP services in all three hyperscalers, Everpure's reach is narrower (Chapter 46).

docs.title: 1touch and the data-intelligence thesis
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    SM["Storage metadata: volumes, files, objects, owners, snapshots, access"] --> KG["Knowledge graph of data"]
    CC["Content classification: entities, PII, PHI, business meaning"] --> KG
    EX["Other estates: databases, SaaS, public cloud, third-party storage"] --> CC
    KG --> GV["Governance: residency, attribute-based access, lineage"]
    KG --> CY["Cyber: what was exposed, recover what matters first"]
    KG --> AI["AI readiness: Data Stream ingest, index, vectorize via MCP"]

Figure 28.4 — The thesis: the storage layer already knows where every byte is and who touched it; add knowledge of what the bytes mean, and you can sell governance, cyber recovery and AI-ready data from the same graph.

1touch closed on 2026-05-07, the $125.0M subject to adjustments and escrow3. As Everpure Data Intelligence (GA June 2026)10 it discovers structured and unstructured data, classifies it at entity level (flagging PII and PHI) into a semantic knowledge graph, tracks lineage, and enforces attribute-based access and residency policy32. Analysts also describe it as reaching databases, SaaS and third-party storage, not only Everpure arrays11. Native MCP support (September 2026) lets agents query it33. Data Stream, on FlashBlade with NVIDIA GPUs and NVIDIA's AI Data Platform reference design, ingests, indexes and vectorises that data for RAG and inference34 (Chapter 39, Chapter 33).

Why a storage company? The array already holds the inventory (every volume, file, object, snapshot and access) and sits on the write path, so classification can trigger as data lands rather than by weekly crawls, as a catalog above storage must. Semiconductor bridge: on-die telemetry sees every transaction; external test equipment only samples.

docs.title: How "storage vendor → data platform" is meant to work commercially
docs.text:
The model has three levers:

  1. Attach. Each layer sells into ~15,000 customers who already trust the vendor and run Pure1. Illustrative: if 5% of 15,000 customers attach Data Intelligence at an assumed $150k ARR, that is 750 × $150k ≈ $113M of ARR, about 5% on top of the $2.13B base. That is roughly one year's revenue to recover the $125M price.
  2. ARR quality. Software raises subscription mix, margin and net retention beyond capacity growth alone.
  3. Switching costs. They shift from the box (which Evergreen makes easy to refresh) to policy, automation and the knowledge graph, which are costly to rebuild elsewhere.

Where it may not work. First, crowding: catalogs and lakehouse governance (Databricks Unity Catalog, Snowflake's governance features, Microsoft Purview) own "what is this data" for analytics, and data-security vendors (BigID, Varonis, Cyera) sell discovery to the CISO, a different buyer. Second, neutrality is unproven. One analyst said the case beyond Everpure hardware becomes "a bigger question mark", noting Everpure is outside the Open Semantic Interchange metadata effort11 [VERIFY: search-summary only]. Third, storage sellers are paid on arrays; software covering rival storage needs separate incentives. Futurum's open question: how quickly customers follow32.

docs.text:
Vendor Platform pitch (2025–26) What's underneath Data-intelligence / AI layer Consumption Steelman Weak spot Everpure Enterprise Data Cloud → Data Primacy710 One OS (Purity) across all arrays and cloud Data Intelligence (ex-1touch), Data Stream34 Evergreen //Forever, //Flex, //One Simplest single-OS stack; mature non-disruptive refresh Narrow cloud reach; DI unproven off Everpure gear; software mostly sold with arrays Dell AI Data Platform with NVIDIA35 Several OSes: PowerScale, Lightning FS, ObjectScale, PowerStore, PowerMax Data orchestration within the AI Data Platform APEX36 Sells servers, networking and storage on one PO Portfolio sprawl; control plane less unified NetApp Intelligent data infrastructure; AFX + AI Data Engine37 ONTAP on-premises and as first-party service in all three hyperscalers AI Data Engine (ONTAP extension on NVIDIA AI Data Platform) Keystone36 Deepest hybrid-cloud reach; long data-management heritage AFX/AIDE new; ONTAP complexity HPE GreenLake cloud with GreenLake Intelligence38 Alletra MP (block, file, object), Zerto, Data Fabric39 Inline metadata enrichment on X10000; agentic ops GreenLake36 Full-stack (compute, networking via Juniper) under one cloud console Storage is a small slice of HPE; many products VAST AI Operating System40 One software stack (DASE) on partner hardware DataBase, DataEngine, InsightEngine, AgentEngine, PolicyEngine in-platform Software subscription Most integrated: database and compute live in the storage layer Asks customers to replace analytics tools too; private-company disclosure

Table 28.2 — All five vendors call themselves data platforms; Everpure's distinctive claim is one OS plus a non-disruptive subscription, while VAST goes furthest up the stack and NetApp furthest across clouds.

Dell and HPE stitch several OSes under one console; NetApp has one OS but a less clean refresh subscription; VAST puts database and functions inside storage (Chapter 42), where Everpure stops short. The strongest steelman is NetApp: first-party ONTAP services in all three hyperscalers against Everpure's one native service plus a customer-managed virtual array.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What share of Data Intelligence deals cover data that is not on Everpure storage?" Strong: a number, named estate types (Oracle, SaaS, rival NAS), and how it integrates with an existing catalog or DSPM tool.
  2. "Is Fusion adoption counted as customers who enabled it or customers running presets in production?" Strong: separates "turned on" from "automating against it" and ties the latter to renewal and NDR.
  3. "What does Evergreen//One's 25% buffer cost us in deployed capacity, and how has NAND inflation changed that?" Strong: quantifies buffer and data-reduction risk and how pricing or Overdrive recovers it.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "How does Data Intelligence classify on the write path without adding latency to Purity?" Strong: asynchronous, off the I/O path, triggered by snapshot or metadata events, with bounded controller resources.
  2. "What can an agent do through the Fusion MCP server without human approval?" Strong: scoped credentials, read-only default, approval gates on destructive actions, immutable snapshots as backstop.
  3. "When Portworx runs on non-Everpure disks, what do customers lose versus Portworx on FlashArray?" Strong: candid about data reduction, snapshot offload and replication efficiency.

Don't say this:

  • "Evergreen means free hardware." The subscription funds upgrades, with eligibility terms.
  • "Everpure is now a data-management company like Databricks." It manages data infrastructure and metadata, not analytics engines.
  • "Portworx only works with Everpure arrays." It is hardware-agnostic by design.
  • "1touch is Everpure's biggest software deal." Portworx cost almost three times as much.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Everpure Platform / Enterprise Data Cloud / Data Primacy — names for the stack and strategy.
  • Evergreen//Forever, //Flex, //One — owned, owned pay-per-use, and as-a-service subscription tiers.
  • Fusion preset — a fleet-wide policy template for provisioning.
  • Portworx — Kubernetes data services that run on any infrastructure.
  • KubeVirt — runs VMs as Kubernetes objects.
  • Everpure Cloud Dedicated / Azure Native — customer-managed and fully managed cloud Purity.
  • Everpure Data Intelligence — discovery and classification product from 1touch.
  • See the glossary.
