docs.title: 29. Hyperscaler business, ecosystem and financials through a tech lens
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Purity and DirectFlash · Consumption models · Company history and strategy

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Two revenue lines, three businesses. Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) sells arrays with NAND on its own books, Evergreen subscriptions recognised ratably, and hyperscale DirectFlash licences where the customer buys the NAND. Each has a different margin profile.
  • The hyperscaler model licenses flash-management IP; it does not sell boxes. The first customer, Meta (named in the FY25 10-K), passed 2 EB in FY26. A second top-five hyperscaler signed on 2026-08-10, with revenue from FY28.
  • Recurring revenue keeps compounding. At Q2 FY27 (ended 2026-08-02), subscription ARR was $2.13B (+20%) and RPO $4.1B (+44%).
  • Technology choices set margins. DirectFlash removes SSD controllers and DRAM from the bill of materials. The 2026 NAND spike has pushed non-GAAP product gross margin (GM) down to 65–66%, subscription GM runs about 75%, and hyperscale licensing is accretive but lumpy.
  • The ecosystem is mostly distribution. NVIDIA certifications gate AI deals, Cisco and GSIs carry enterprise volume, and NAND makers sell directly to Everpure's hyperscale customers.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Everpure raised its FY27 revenue guidance from $4.3–4.4B in February 2026 to $5.03–5.07B in August. The new midpoint is about 38% above FY26's $3.66B12. A dollar of hyperscale licence, FlashArray//C or Evergreen//One revenue differs in cost, cash timing and durability, so the source of growth matters. This chapter links the architecture in Chapter 26 to the numbers analysts model.

Whether the licensing model reaches more than two hyperscalers, and whether it complements or cannibalises arrays, sits near the centre of the equity story.

docs.title: Three revenue engines on one technology stack
docs.text:
The 10-K has two revenue lines, product and subscription services. Three engines feed them:

  1. Arrays sold outright (FlashArray, FlashBlade, FlashBlade//EXA). Everpure buys NAND, builds DirectFlash Modules (DFMs) and books product revenue at shipment; the attached Evergreen//Forever support-and-upgrade subscription is ratable.
  2. Consumption services, mainly Evergreen//One, an SLA-backed storage-as-a-service priced on capacity used. Everpure keeps the hardware and revenue is ratable, which is why FY24 product revenue fell 9% while subscription rose 26%; the 10-K partly blamed Evergreen//One's consumption model3.
  3. Hyperscale. DirectFlash and Purity technology is licensed to hyperscalers that buy their own NAND, and the revenue lands in product. Q3 FY26 product revenue was $534.8M (+17.6%) and included royalties from hyperscaler shipments4.

Figure 29.1 — Evergreen//One pulled the mix toward subscription through FY25. In FY27 product revenue is growing faster again, driven by price, large deals and hyperscale. Data: data/ch29_revenue_mix.csv

Subscription's share of revenue rose from 35% in FY23 to 46% in FY25 and FY26. It then slipped to 44% in H1 FY27, and to 42% in Q2 alone5, because product revenue grew 55% in Q1 and 54% in Q261. The causes: price increases after NAND costs surged (list prices rose on 2026-02-097), larger deals and, from H2 FY27, hyperscale. The recurring base is not weakening; subscription services still grew 17% in Q1 and 20% in Q2.

docs.title: The hyperscaler model: licensing a controller, not selling a box
docs.text:
Semiconductor bridge. DirectFlash takes the SSD's controller ASIC and FTL DRAM out of the drive and moves flash management into Purity (Chapter 26). The hyperscale deals sell that capability the way an IP vendor sells a design: the customer buys the "wafers" (NAND); Everpure supplies design, software and some non-NAND parts, and is paid as capacity deploys.

flowchart LR
    EP["Everpure: DirectFlash design + Purity software"]
    NAND["NAND makers"]
    INT["Integrator / ODM"]
    HS["Hyperscaler data centres"]
    EPPARTS["Everpure: some non-NAND components"]
    NAND -->|"NAND sold directly to hyperscaler"| INT
    EPPARTS -->|"parts supply"| INT
    EP -->|"design + software licence"| INT
    INT -->|"assembled flash shelves"| HS
    HS -->|"licence, royalty and support fees per deployment"| EP

Figure 29.2 — In hyperscale, the NAND never appears on Everpure's books. Everpure is paid for IP, software, support and some components, so revenue per exabyte is low but gross margin is high.

What is public, in date order:

  • Design win (December 2024). With Q3 FY25 results, Pure Storage announced a DirectFlash win with an unnamed top-four hyperscaler. Hardware was excluded: the customer buys from its integrator, and Pure earns licence, software and support fees89. Analysts identified Meta, which the FY25 10-K later named11; the CEO cited Meta's choice of DFMs at the March 2025 FlashBlade//EXA launch10, and the FY2025 10-K names Meta11.
  • Volume (FY26). Pure recognised its first revenue in Q2 FY26. The FY26 plan assumed 1–2 EB of DirectFlash deployed12, and by Q3 FY26 Pure said it had beaten its 2 EB forecast4. For scale, 2 EB is about 26,700 modules at 75 TB or 13,300 at 150 TB (deployed sizes undisclosed).
  • Standardised model (February 2026). Management said hyperscale terms were now standard: Everpure procures some components, and hyperscalers keep buying NAND through their own supply chains. Revenue follows data-centre build-outs, with most of FY27's expected in Q3–Q413. [VERIFY: search-summary only]
  • Second hyperscaler (2026-08-10). Everpure announced a design win and supply agreement with a second unnamed top-five hyperscaler, built on DirectFlash. It contributes little to FY27 and is expected to matter from FY281415. Management said it mirrors the first, and that DirectFlash is mostly replacing SSDs, not disks, for now16. The release itself warns that the customer may not order or deploy the volumes contemplated14.

Worked example (illustrative): why hyperscale lifts margin only at scale. Everpure does not disclose hyperscale gross margin. Analyst commentary puts it around 75–85% (some notes say above 90% for pure royalties)17 [VERIFY: analyst estimates, search-summary only]. Suppose hyperscale is 5% of quarterly revenue at 85% GM and everything else runs at Q2 FY27's 69.9% non-GAAP GM18. Blended GM = 0.95 × 69.9% + 0.05 × 85% = 66.4% + 4.25% ≈ 70.7%, a lift of about 0.8 points. At a 10% share it is 0.90 × 69.9% + 0.10 × 85% ≈ 71.4%. Hyperscale moves the blend only at double-digit revenue share. Q3 FY26 is the real-world version: royalties helped lift non-GAAP product GM to 72.9% (from 67.4%) and GAAP GM to 72.3%419. But management said the newer models, with Everpure supplying components, bring hyperscale margins closer to the company average19, so 85% is an upper case.

docs.title: Subscription ARR and RPO: what the backlog says
docs.text:
Everpure defines subscription ARR as the annualised contract value of active subscriptions at quarter-end plus that quarter's on-demand revenue × 43. RPO (remaining performance obligations) is contracted revenue not yet recognised: undelivered product plus the unexpired years of multi-year subscriptions.

Figure 29.3 — ARR has compounded at about 21% a year, while RPO stepped up sharply in FY26 as large deals and longer Evergreen terms added to the backlog. Data: data/ch29_arr.csv

How to read it:

  • Growth rate. (2.13 ÷ 1.10)^(1/3.5 years) ≈ 1.21, about 21% a year31.
  • The RPO step. RPO grew 40% in FY26 (14% in FY25) on large deals and longer Evergreen contracts20. Some growth was borrowed: longer renewals slowed ARR growth to 16% and net dollar retention fell from 117% to 113%21.
  • Sanity check. Q2 subscription revenue of $499M × 4 ≈ $2.0B sits just below $2.13B ARR, which includes on-demand run-rate and late-quarter starts. RPO is about 1.9× ARR.

Tech lens. In Evergreen//One, Everpure owns the hardware and charges per TB used, so DFM density, data reduction and watts per TB set its margin, and non-disruptive upgrades make multi-year SLAs workable. Evergreen//One sales grew 73% in Q1 FY276, and storage-as-a-service total contract value (TCV) was $277M in Q2 (+121%)16 [VERIFY: TCV from call summaries].

docs.title: Gross-margin drivers tied to technology
docs.text:
Driver Technology mechanism Margin effect Public evidence DirectFlash vs SSD bill of materials No per-drive controller ASIC or FTL DRAM. An SSD needs about 1 GB of DRAM per TB, because it keeps a 4-byte map entry for each 4 KiB page. Purity manages NAND globally, with less hidden over-provisioning Lower $/TB than buying finished SSDs, which supports product GM while Everpure prices aggressively Q4 FY26 product GM 67.3%, up more than 400 bp on mix22 NAND pricing pass-through Everpure buys NAND for enterprise arrays. NAND contract prices rose steeply through 2026, with TrendForce forecasting another +15–20% QoQ for 4Q26 (enterprise SSDs reportedly +23–28%)23 Costs rise before price lists do. Margin lags and then recovers. Securing supply uses cash Price rise on 2026-02-097; non-GAAP product GM 65.5% in Q1 and 66.2% in Q2 FY27618; Q2 free cash flow (FCF) –$238M on strategic NAND buys24 Evergreen//Forever and //One Software-heavy support plus non-disruptive upgrades. With //One, Everpure also carries the hardware Subscription GM about 75%. Hardware-heavy //One mix can dilute it relative to pure support [VERIFY: //One cost composition] Non-GAAP subscription GM 75.6% in Q1 and 74.9% in Q2 FY27618 Hyperscale licensing The customer buys the NAND. Everpure supplies IP, software, support and some non-NAND parts Royalty-like and margin-accretive, but lumpy and tied to customers' build-outs Q3 FY26 GAAP GM 72.3%, helped by royalties4; model standardised in Feb 202613 Deal and product mix Large AI and enterprise deals; QLC capacity tiers (//C, //E) priced against disk Management says it is deliberately running near the bottom of the 65–70% product GM range to win share Long-term product GM range 65–70%25 Software attach Portworx, Fusion, Data Intelligence (ex-1touch) Close to pure software, but too small today to move the blend Not separately disclosed

Table 29.1 — Every margin line traces back to a technology choice: who owns the NAND, how much of the drive Everpure designs, and who owns the hardware after the sale.

Figure 29.4 — Most of the ecosystem is distribution and validation, not revenue. The hyperscaler edges are the exception: there the NAND makers sell around Everpure, straight to its customer.

  • Validation (NVIDIA). SuperPOD (November 2024)26, NVIDIA-Certified Storage and NCP high-performance storage (March 2025)27 for FlashBlade//S; Data Stream on the AI Data Platform design28; BlueField-4 STX partner29. No fees, but no shortlist without them (Chapter 27, Chapter 34).
  • Converged distribution. FlashStack joined Cisco's Secure AI Factory with NVIDIA in late 2025, sold via AHEAD, ePlus, SHI and WWT30.
  • Hyperscalers, two roles. DirectFlash customers, and cloud channels: Everpure Cloud Azure Native, co-developed with Microsoft31, and Cloud Dedicated on AWS and Azure32 (Chapter 28).
  • Neoclouds. A November 2024 CoreWeave stake made Pure a preferred storage option there33, though Evercore noted investors rated it below a tier-1 hyperscaler win34; CoreWeave later signed a far larger deal with VAST35. STN's GPU cloud runs on FlashBlade//EXA36, and Evergreen//One reached EXA in March 202637 (Chapter 35).
  • NAND. Micron and Kioxia supply and co-qualify DFM NAND (Chapter 26)38.
  • ISVs and platforms. Veeam (Fusion plug-in)39, Commvault (IntelliSnap)40, Rubrik and CrowdStrike (Enterprise Data Cloud)41, and Nutanix AHV external storage (May 2025)42.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Which hyperscale components do we procure, and which does the customer source?" Strong answer: NAND stays with the customer; Everpure supplies parts where its design adds value, trading margin percentage for revenue per exabyte.
  2. "What drives Evergreen//One cost per TB, and how does the DFM roadmap change it?" Strong answer: density, data reduction, power and refresh cadence under the SLA.
  3. "Which certification has moved the most AI pipeline?" Strong answer: specific (NCP for neoclouds, Cisco Secure AI Factory for enterprise), tied to win rates, not logos.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What changes when Purity runs on a hyperscaler's hardware and fleet tooling?" Strong answer: telemetry, firmware updates, and the boundary with the hyperscaler's own storage software.
  2. "Why is DirectFlash replacing SSDs before HDDs at hyperscale?" Strong answer: performance tiers adopt first; the $/TB gap with disk delays displacement.
  3. "How exposed is DFM qualification to one NAND supplier?" Strong answer: Micron and Kioxia dual-sourcing, and qualification lead times per NAND generation.

Don't say this:

  • "Everpure sells Meta storage arrays." It licenses technology and supplies some parts. Meta buys the NAND.
  • "Subscription share fell, so recurring is weakening." It grew about 20%; product grew faster.
  • "Hyperscale will lift margins immediately." Not until it reaches double-digit revenue share.
  • "RPO is all subscription." It includes undelivered product.
  • "Everpure has named the second hyperscaler." It has not; only Meta is named.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Subscription ARR — annualised value of active subscriptions plus on-demand run-rate.
  • RPO — contracted revenue not yet recognised.
  • Design win — a customer's commitment to build its platform around a supplier's technology.
  • Royalty / licence revenue — fees paid per unit deployed for the use of IP.
  • TCV — total contract value over a contract's life.
  • NAND pass-through — how quickly NAND cost changes reach customer prices.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 30. The AI data pipeline end to end
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: What storage does · Object storage and S3 · The GPU data path · Parallel file systems

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• "AI storage" is at least eight workloads, not one. Ingest is write-heavy and cost-bound, training reads are throughput-bound, checkpointing is a write burst, and inference, RAG and agents are latency-bound small I/O.
  • Data shrinks, then grows again. More than 10 PB of web crawl1 filters down to tens of TB of training text and under 1 TB of weights. Then the pipeline makes new data: multi-TB checkpoints, KV caches, embeddings and logs.
  • Capacity lives in object storage; performance lives in file and flash next to the GPU. Object is the cheapest durable TB and every tool speaks S3. Training and checkpoint code expects POSIX paths and RDMA-fed bandwidth. The two are converging.
  • In LLM training, checkpoints stress storage more than the training data does. Newer spending sits further down the pipeline, in KV cache and in data intelligence for RAG and agents.
  • Treat the pipeline as a memory hierarchy with a prefetcher. Training access order is known in advance; inference and agent access depends on users. Every hop costs energy.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Every storage vendor now says "AI", but the money sits in different places at each stage: the lake pays for cheap capacity, the training tier pays a premium for bandwidth, and inference and agents pay for new software. Everpure has products at most stages: FlashBlade//E and S3 for capacity, FlashBlade//S and FlashBlade//EXA for training and checkpoints, PureKVA for inference, and Data Stream plus Data Intelligence (formerly 1touch) for RAG and agents234. DDN and WEKA start from the high-performance tier, hyperscalers own the cloud lake, VAST spans the stack, and database vendors contest RAG and agents.

The real questions: which stages to compete in, where a multi-stage platform beats point products, and where data gravity lets the lake owner capture downstream stages. This chapter maps Part 5; later chapters cover training, inference and KV cache, RAG and lakehouses, NVIDIA's ecosystem, neoclouds, hyperscalers, benchmarks, power and agents.

docs.title: Eight stages, eight I/O signatures
docs.text:
Figure 30.1 — The pipeline moves from write-heavy, cost-bound bulk I/O on the left to read-heavy, latency-bound small I/O on the right, then feeds its own outputs back into the lake.

Ingest. Crawls, documents, images, video and logs arrive as large write-once objects. Common Crawl's January 2025 crawl alone held 3.0 billion pages and 460 TiB uncompressed5. Ingest needs cheap durable capacity and aggregate write bandwidth; latency barely matters.

Curation and preprocessing. Extraction, language identification, quality filtering, deduplication, PII scrubbing and tokenization are repeated full scans that rewrite shards into formats such as Parquet. This is AI's closest cousin to analytics, bound by scan throughput and CPU or GPU. It is also power-hungry: Meta found that for some production recommendation models, storage plus preprocessing drew more power than training itself6.

Training: data loading. Thousands of GPUs read shuffled samples and almost never write. Image and video datasets mean floods of small reads; LLM text is packed into large shards and is light. The danger is tail latency, because a synchronous step waits for its slowest loader.

Checkpointing. Every GPU dumps its state at once: a write burst, read back only after a failure (Chapter 31).

Fine-tuning and post-training. Supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and distillation run many smaller jobs that re-read base weights repeatedly; RL even runs inference inside training. To storage it looks like a busy multi-tenant file share.

Inference. Two kinds of I/O. Weight loading is large sequential reads and a cold-start problem when services autoscale: 810 GB at 10 GB/s takes 81 seconds. The KV cache is per-token attention state that spills from HBM into DRAM, local NVMe and shared flash (Chapter 32).

RAG and agents. Retrieval searches a vector index and fetches chunks: small random reads on a millisecond budget, plus re-embedding writes as documents change. Agents chain many such steps across files, databases and APIs, adding governance and a trail of state and logs. Here storage becomes data management (Chapter 39).

Stage Dominant pattern Read / write Interface Typical I/O or file size Most sensitive to Typical tier Ingest Sequential, append-only Write-heavy Object (S3 PUT, multipart) MB–GB objects $/TB, aggregate write GB/s Object lake on HDD or QLC Curation / preprocessing Repeated full scans + rewrites Read-heavy, large writes Object + Parquet / table formats 100 MB–1 GB shards Scan throughput, CPU/GPU Lake + flash scratch Training data loading Random reads of shuffled samples/shards ~100% read POSIX / NFS / parallel FS, or S3 with cache KB samples to GB shards Throughput and tail latency Hot flash + GPU-local NVMe Checkpointing Bursty large sequential writes ~95% write Parallel FS or object GBs per GPU, TBs per checkpoint Burst write bandwidth Local NVMe → flash → object Fine-tuning / post-training Many concurrent medium jobs Mixed File, object, model hub GB–TB base weights Multi-tenancy, QoS Shared flash + object Inference Weight loads + KV block reads/writes Read-heavy File/S3; KV over RDMA GB–TB weights; KB–MB KV blocks Latency (time to first token) HBM → DRAM → NVMe → shared flash RAG retrieval Small random reads, background re-indexing ~95% read Vector DB, lakehouse, object 1–6 KB vectors; KB–MB chunks Query latency (ms), freshness DRAM/flash index; object corpus Agents Small, metadata-heavy, many sources Mixed (state, logs) APIs, MCP, file, object, DB KB records Latency, permissions, lineage All tiers + metadata catalog

Table 30.1 — No single row resembles another closely enough for one tuning to serve all eight; read/write mixes are indicative.

docs.text:
quadrantChart

Figure 30.2 — The stages scatter across all four quadrants, which is why "AI storage" deals are really multi-tier deals.

The stages pull a design in opposite directions:

  • Cost versus speed. The lake wants the cheapest durable TB (HDD or QLC, wide erasure codes); the hot tier wants flash, RDMA and a metadata engine that pays only if GPUs stay busy.
  • Large versus small I/O. Wide stripes suit multi-MB writes and punish 4 KB random updates (Chapter 6).
  • Metadata. A checkpoint is a few huge files; an image dataset is billions of tiny ones; agents generate lookups (Chapter 21).
  • Semantics. POSIX offers rename, append and locks; S3 offers immutable objects over HTTP.

Buyers run several tiers or buy a platform that credibly spans several; that choice is the vendor battleground.

docs.title: Why the lake is object and the hot tier is file
docs.text:
Object storage wins the lake on cost, scale and reach. AWS says S3 holds more than 500 trillion objects and serves over 200 million requests per second7. Erasure coding makes durability cheap, write-once data fits immutable objects, and every tool from Spark to PyTorch loaders speaks S3. The weaknesses: millisecond latency, no append or rename, and a tax on small objects (Chapter 9).

File and parallel file systems win the hot tier because training and checkpoint code writes to paths. Parallel file systems stripe each file across many servers that a client reads at once (Chapter 17); RDMA and GPUDirect Storage skip the CPU bounce buffer (Chapter 11).

The boundary is blurring. S3 Express One Zone (2023) claims 10x faster access than S3 Standard8; CoreWeave caches object data on every GPU node with LOTA9; MLPerf Storage v3.0 added an S3 path that about one-sixth of submissions used10. File systems are adding S3 front ends, and multiprotocol platforms (VAST, FlashBlade) serve both. The useful distinction is becoming tier, not protocol.

flowchart LR
    SRC["Sources: crawl, docs, logs, sensors"] --> LAKE["Object data lake: HDD or QLC, EB-scale"]
    LAKE -->|"stage curated shards"| HOT["High-performance file or flash tier"]
    HOT -->|"prefetch batches"| NVME["GPU-server local NVMe"]
    HOT -->|"RDMA or GPUDirect reads"| HBM["GPU HBM"]
    NVME --> DRAM["Host DRAM"]
    DRAM --> HBM
    HBM -->|"checkpoint drain"| DRAM
    DRAM -->|"async flush"| HOT
    HOT -->|"age out old checkpoints"| LAKE
    HBM <-->|"KV cache spill and reload"| NVME
    HBM <-->|"shared KV tier"| HOT
    HOT -->|"weights and indexes"| APP["Serving: inference, RAG, agents"]
    APP -->|"logs, feedback, synthetic data"| LAKE

Figure 30.3 — Bulk data flows inward from the lake toward HBM; checkpoints and KV state flow back outward; the lake both starts and ends the loop.

docs.title: Worked numbers: where the bytes and the stress are
docs.text:
Figure 30.4 — Illustrative: filtering shrinks petabytes to terabytes, then training produces artefacts larger than the model itself. Data: data/ch30_data_funnel.csv

From crawl to weights. DataComp-LM's pool holds 240T tokens of Common Crawl text11. FineWeb filtered and deduplicated 96 snapshots into 15T tokens, about 44 TB on disk1213, with a 1.3T-token educational subset12. Llama 3 trained on about 15.6T tokens14; as 4-byte token IDs that is 15.6e12 × 4 ≈ 62 TB. Filtering, not tokenization, does the shrinking, so curation is where the lake's capacity and scan bandwidth earn their keep.

Tokens are cheap to stream. Llama 3's batch grew to 16M tokens per step14: 64 MB at 4 bytes per token, so even one step per second is about 64 MB/s for the whole cluster. Multimodal is different; video can need GB/s per node.

Checkpoints are not cheap. A 405B model at 14–16 bytes per parameter (weights plus Adam state) needs 5.7–6.5 TB. Meta built Llama 3's storage on its Tectonic file system at 240 PB across 7,500 SSD servers, sustaining 2 TB/s with 7 TB/s peaks, and named bursty checkpoint writes a major challenge14. At 2 TB/s, 6.5 TB takes about 3.3 s; at 100 GB/s, 65 s, with a 16K-GPU job like Llama 3's14 idle throughout.

Inference creates new state. Llama 3 70B's KV cache costs 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dimensions × 2 (K and V) × 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes, or about 320 KiB per token. A 128K-token context is about 40 GiB, half an 80 GB GPU's HBM. RAG adds more: 1 billion chunks × 1,024-dimension float32 embeddings is 4 TB of vectors before any index overhead.

docs.title: Semiconductor bridge: a memory hierarchy with a prefetcher
docs.text:
Read the tiers as a cache hierarchy:

AI pipeline tier CPU analogue HBM Register file / L1 Host DRAM L2 GPU-local NVMe Last-level cache Shared flash Main memory Object lake Disk

Each step outward adds capacity and loses bandwidth per GPU; as in CPU design, the craft is hiding the next level's latency with prefetching and buffering.

Training is the friendly case. The shuffle order comes from a seed, so the loader knows exactly which samples come next: a perfect prefetcher, like a DMA engine walking a known descriptor list rather than a speculative stream prefetcher. Checkpoints use a write-back buffer: state drains from HBM to host DRAM or local NVMe in seconds, then flushes asynchronously, as a store buffer does.

Inference is a cache whose reuse distance depends on users: hit rate depends on how often prompts share prefixes. NVIDIA's KV Block Manager names its tiers G1 (HBM) through G4 (remote storage)15. Agents are least predictable of all. Downstream, value shifts from raw bandwidth to caching policy, placement and metadata.

Moving data costs energy. At 45 nm, Horowitz put a 64-bit DRAM access at roughly 1.3–2.6 nJ against 0.4–3.7 pJ for a floating-point operation, a gap of hundreds to thousands of times16. Every NIC, switch and SSD hop adds more. With data-centre electricity forecast at 565 TWh in 202617, there are three responses:

  1. Keep hot data close, in local NVMe caches and KV tiers.
  2. Move compute to the data. NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX18 and VAST running its storage controllers on BlueField-4 DPUs19 both do this.
  3. Move fewer bytes, by filtering early and reducing data (Chapter 38).

Table 30.2 — Everpure has a product at every stage, but its strongest positions are the flash tiers in the middle; the lake and the agent layer are contested by players who do not sell arrays.

Steelman the specialists. DDN and WEKA win the hot tier through focus, HPC heritage and early NVIDIA alignment. Hyperscalers win the lake through gravity: egress fees and tooling keep petabytes in S3. VAST argues one shared-everything platform should span lake, hot tier and database, the most direct challenge to a product-family approach (Chapter 42). Everpure's counter-thesis is one operating environment and control plane across stages, with DirectFlash pulling lake capacity from HDD onto flash. The risk is being second-best at every stage.

Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information:

  • Lead with checkpoint and KV-cache performance, where MLPerf v3.0 gives comparable evidence.
  • Use Data Intelligence to own the metadata layer that RAG and agents depend on.
  • Partner rather than compete for the cloud lake.

Figure 30.5 — The industry's attention has moved stage by stage down the pipeline, from feeding training to serving inference.

Small image files were the first AI storage problem; LLMs made checkpoints the bandwidth problem; deployment made inference context the latency problem. MLPerf Storage followed: v1.0 (September 2024) measured training reads27, v2.0 (August 2025) added checkpointing28, v3.0 (September 2026) added KV cache, vector database and S310. So did hardware: GPUDirect Storage 1.0 in 202129, NVIDIA's AI Data Platform in March 202520, BlueField-4 STX in March 202618. TrendForce attributes part of 4Q26 enterprise SSD demand to hyperscalers buying QLC for KV cache30. A likely next step is agent memory and state as a named workload.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Which stages does our AI revenue come from today, and which are we betting on?" Strong: revenue split by stage, where attach happens (does KVA ride on existing FlashBlade deals?), and candour about which wins are still pilots.
  2. "If the lake is already in S3, how do we win the hot tier, and ever win the lake back?" Strong: data gravity, egress economics, the caching or tiering mechanism, and the NVIDIA certifications that get Everpure onto the bill of materials.
  3. "What must PureKVA prove to become a standard tier, not a feature?" Strong: independent results (MLPerf v3.0 KV cache), integrations (Dynamo, vLLM, llm-d), hit-rate assumptions and tokens per dollar versus no offload.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Walk me through a 6 TB checkpoint on FlashBlade//EXA. Where does the burst land, what is the persistence point, and how many seconds are GPUs blocked?" Strong: async staging via host DRAM or local NVMe, write GB/s per data node, blocked time versus time to durability.
  2. "What happens when a dataset of billions of small files is reshuffled every epoch?" Strong: metadata operations per second, client caching, and advice to pack data into shards.
  3. "For a KV block fetch, what is the latency budget and where does it break: network, metadata or media?" Strong: microsecond figures, the RDMA path, block sizes, and the concurrency where tail latency climbs.

Don't say this:

  • "AI storage is all about throughput." Inference, RAG and agents are latency- and metadata-bound.
  • "LLM training needs huge read bandwidth for the dataset." Text tokens are tiny. Checkpoints and multimodal data drive bandwidth.
  • "Object storage is too slow for AI." Nearly every lake is object storage, and S3 is now inside MLPerf Storage.
  • "Data shrinks through the pipeline, so storage demand falls." Checkpoints, KV caches, embeddings, logs and retained versions grow it again.
  • "GPUDirect makes storage latency irrelevant." It removes a CPU copy; it does not remove the network or the media.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Data lake — low-cost, usually object-based store for raw and curated data.
  • Hot tier — high-performance file or flash tier feeding GPUs.
  • KV cache — per-token attention state reused during inference.
  • Data gravity — the pull of applications and spend toward where large data already sits.
  • More in the glossary.

docs.title: 31. Training storage
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: The GPU data path · The AI data pipeline end to end · Performance and economics metrics · Parallel file systems

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Checkpoints, not training data, set the performance spec for LLM training storage. A 405B-parameter model reads roughly 11 MB/s of text tokens across 16,384 GPUs, yet its full training state is about 6.5 TB. Writing that in 60 seconds takes about 108 GB/s.
  • Size the checkpoint at roughly 14–16 bytes per parameter, not 2. Mixed-precision Adam keeps fp32 master weights and two fp32 optimizer moments next to the bf16 weights. Weights alone are one-seventh of what gets saved.
  • Failures set the checkpoint frequency. Meta's Llama 3 run saw 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days, about one every 3.1 hours. With synchronous saves, the best interval wastes about 10% of the cluster. At 100,000 GPUs it would waste about a quarter.
  • Asynchronous and tiered checkpointing turn a peak-bandwidth problem into a sustained-bandwidth one. GPUs dump state to host DRAM or local NVMe in seconds and drain to shared storage in the background; software removes most of the stall.
  • The hardest moment is the restore. Every GPU reads at once after a failure, and at large scale restart time costs more than save time. Ask about cold read bandwidth and metadata storms, not only write GB/s.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
In training-cluster deals, the checkpoint is the requirement that turns "a few MB/s of tokens" into "hundreds of GB/s of writes", and it decides which architectures get shortlisted. In its first MLPerf Storage entry (v3.0, September 2026), Everpure's FlashBlade//EXA posted the top checkpoint-write result among submitters12, a credible public data point in exactly this argument (Chapter 27).

The tension: asynchronous saves, node-local tiers and in-memory replicas keep shrinking the peak storage must absorb, so a pitch built on burst write bandwidth sells into an eroding requirement. Durable value moves to sustained drain bandwidth, restore speed and efficient checkpoint retention. These are options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information.

docs.title: Two very different I/O jobs
docs.text: Data loading is a steady, read-mostly stream of often small, random samples. Checkpointing is a periodic burst of large, mostly sequential writes; its mirror image, the restore, is a read burst from every GPU at once. Chapter 30 places both in the pipeline and Chapter 11 explains how bytes reach GPU memory; this chapter sizes them.

docs.title: How big is a checkpoint?
docs.text:
A checkpoint is everything needed to resume training exactly. With the Adam optimizer in mixed precision, each parameter carries:

Component Bytes per parameter In GPU memory? Usually saved? bf16 working weights 2 Yes Yes (or re-derived from fp32 master) fp32 master weights 4 Yes Yes Adam first moment (m), fp32 4 Yes Yes Adam second moment (v), fp32 4 Yes Yes bf16 gradients 2 Yes, transient Rarely Total 16 16 ~12–14

Table 31.1 — Weights are only about one-eighth of training state; the optimizer is most of what a checkpoint writes.

So full training state = parameters × 16 bytes, and a typical saved checkpoint = parameters × ~14 bytes. Variations: gradients are transient and rarely saved; dropping the bf16 copy (rebuilt from fp32 on load) gives 12 bytes; fp32 gradients push in-memory state to 18; 8-bit or bf16 optimizer moments can halve the optimizer share. Data-loader and RNG state add only megabytes.

MLPerf Storage's checkpoint workload lands in the same range. IBM reports 105 GB for the 8B case and 15 TB for the 1T case, of which 13.2 TB is optimizer state3. That is roughly 13–15 bytes per parameter.

Figure 31.1 — Worked example: a checkpoint is roughly 7–8× the model's inference weights, so a 1T-parameter model saves 14–16 TB every time. Data: data/ch31_checkpoint_size.csv

One subtlety: for mixture-of-experts models, checkpoint size follows total parameters, while compute follows active parameters. A 1T-total MoE activating a few tens of billions of parameters per token computes like a mid-size model but checkpoints like a 1T one, raising storage bandwidth per unit of GPU compute.

docs.title: Throughput math: bytes ÷ window
docs.text:
The core formula is required bandwidth = checkpoint bytes ÷ the time you allow the write to take. The window is a business choice: allowed GPU idle time (synchronous) or time until the checkpoint is safe (asynchronous).

Model (full state) Assumed GPUs Per-GPU shard Sync, 60 s window Sync, 300 s window Async, drain within 30 min Per 8-GPU node, 60 s 70B (1.12 TB) 1,024 1.09 GB 18.7 GB/s 3.7 GB/s 0.6 GB/s 0.15 GB/s 405B (6.48 TB) 16,384 395 MB 108 GB/s 21.6 GB/s 3.6 GB/s 0.05 GB/s 1T (16 TB) 32,768 488 MB 267 GB/s 53 GB/s 8.9 GB/s 0.07 GB/s 2T (32 TB) 65,536 488 MB 533 GB/s 107 GB/s 17.8 GB/s 0.07 GB/s

Table 31.2 — Worked example: sharding makes each client's job trivial; the hard part is the aggregate burst landing on shared storage, which asynchronous drain cuts by 30×.

Two lessons follow. First, sharding spreads the bytes but does not shrink them. Every GPU writes its own slice, so no single NIC is the bottleneck; Meta reports per-GPU checkpoint state of 1 MB to 4 GB for Llama 34, which brackets the 395 MB average above. If only one model replica wrote (16 nodes in Llama 3 405B's tensor-by-pipeline layout4), each node would push 405 GB, 6.75 GB/s for a minute. Either way, storage sees the full aggregate plus thousands of simultaneous file creates, a metadata event (Chapter 21).

Second, the asynchronous column matters most for sizing, because modern frameworks lean toward it.

docs.title: Synchronous vs asynchronous checkpointing
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant G as GPU HBM
    participant H as Host DRAM
    participant L as Local NVMe
    participant S as Shared storage
    Note over G,S: Synchronous save - training paused throughout
    G->>S: write shard over storage network
    S-->>G: durable ACK after 60 s at 108 GB/s aggregate
    Note over G: training resumes
    Note over G,S: Asynchronous save - training paused only for the copy
    G->>H: copy shard over PCIe in about 1 to 2 s
    Note over G: training resumes immediately
    H->>L: optional fast local persist
    L->>L: optional replica to a peer node
    H->>S: background drain over minutes
    S-->>H: durable ACK - previous checkpoint can be deleted

Figure 31.2 — Asynchronous checkpointing cuts the GPU stall to a PCIe copy and moves the storage write off the critical path, at the cost of a window in which the newest checkpoint is not yet durable.

In an asynchronous save, each GPU copies its shard into pinned host memory (about a second for a few hundred MB over PCIe) and resumes while CPU threads write it out. With PyTorch's 2024 asynchronous mode, IBM measured a 7B model's checkpoint downtime falling from 148.8 to 6.3 seconds5. Tiered variants add an intermediate stop. NVIDIA's NeMo local checkpointing writes each node's part to local SSD or RAM disk and replicates it to peer nodes6. The Gemini research system (Rice University and AWS) keeps checkpoints in peer CPU memory and reported over 13× faster recovery7.

The costs: a node lost mid-drain falls back to the previous checkpoint; host DRAM must hold the shard; the drain must finish before the next save; and background writes compete with training traffic unless they use a separate storage fabric.

Semiconductor bridge. A checkpoint is a power-gating state save. Context goes to retention flops before a domain is gated, and designers trade save/restore cost against leakage saved, a break-even calculation. Synchronous checkpointing is an all-bank DRAM refresh, blocking every bank for tRFC; asynchronous checkpointing is per-bank refresh, hiding the burst behind useful work.

docs.title: Frequency vs failure rate
docs.text:
Checkpoint frequency trades time spent saving against work redone after a failure. Young's approximation gives the optimal interval as τ ≈ √(2 × C × M), where C is the GPU stall per checkpoint and M is the mean time between job-killing failures8. Overhead is then roughly C/τ + τ/(2M), plus restart time per failure.

During a 54-day snapshot of Llama 3 405B pre-training on 16,384 H100s, Meta logged 466 interruptions: 47 planned and 419 unexpected. About 78% of these were attributed to confirmed or suspected hardware, led by faulty GPUs and HBM349. That is one unexpected stop every 54 × 24 ÷ 419 ≈ 3.1 hours. In Meta's research clusters a 1,024-GPU job's mean time to failure was 7.9 hours, against 47.7 days for an 8-GPU job10. Scaling that linearly predicts about 30 minutes at 16K GPUs; the authors' own model projects about 1.8 hours (as summarized in secondary sources), and Llama 3's production fleet managed 3.1 hours.

Scenario (405B, 6.48 TB state) MTBF M Stall per save C Optimal interval τ Save + rework overhead Drain bandwidth needed 16K GPUs, sync at 108 GB/s 3.1 h 60 s 19 min 10.4% 108 GB/s burst 16K GPUs, sync at ~1 TB/s 3.1 h 6.5 s 6.3 min 3.4% ~1 TB/s burst 16K GPUs, async 3.1 h 2 s 3.5 min 1.9% 31 GB/s sustained 100K GPUs, sync at 108 GB/s 30 min* 60 s 7.8 min 25.6% 108 GB/s burst 100K GPUs, async 30 min* 2 s 1.4 min 4.7% 76 GB/s sustained

Table 31.3 — Worked example using Young's formula: at 100K GPUs synchronous checkpointing wastes a quarter of the cluster, while asynchronous saves keep overhead under 5% but demand steady drain bandwidth. *Assumes failures scale linearly with GPU count from the Llama 3 rate.

At 16K GPUs, 10.4% overhead idles ~1,700 GPUs, tens of millions of dollars a year at the rental rates in Chapter 11. The trap: restart time is paid per failure however checkpoints are written. A 5-minute restart costs 2.7% at 16K GPUs and 16% at 100K.

docs.title: Restore storms
docs.text:
After a failure, bad nodes are swapped and every rank reads the latest checkpoint at once. Three things make this harder than the save:

  1. Read amplification. The optimizer state is sharded, but the bf16 weights are replicated across data-parallel groups. In the naive approach every replica reads its own copy. For Llama 3 405B with 128 data-parallel replicas, that is 0.81 TB × 128 of bf16 weights plus 4.86 TB of sharded fp32 master weights and moments ≈ 109 TB of reads to recover ~5.7 TB of unique checkpoint data. Good frameworks read each byte once and broadcast it over the faster GPU fabric.
  2. Cold reads and metadata. Caches may no longer hold the checkpoint, and thousands of ranks open and stat files simultaneously. In Everpure's own MLPerf Storage v3.0 result, checkpoint read was 588 GiB/s against 877 GiB/s write1. Restore was the slower direction even for the leader.
  3. Everything else restarts too. Container images and Python environments hit shared storage at the same moment; Meta cut job-startup time to keep effective training time above 90%4.

A useful sizing target is a restore time, not a bandwidth. Reading 5.7–6.5 TB of unique data in two minutes needs 47–54 GB/s. The same restore with naive replica reads needs about 900 GB/s.

docs.title: Data loading: tokens are cheap, pixels are not
docs.text:
The data-loading requirement is tokens/s per GPU × bytes per token × GPUs. Llama 3 405B ran at about 41% of the H100's ~989 dense BF16 TFLOPS on 16,384 GPUs4. At 6 FLOPs per parameter per token, each GPU consumes 989×10¹² × 0.41 ÷ (6 × 405×10⁹) ≈ 167 tokens/s. At 4 bytes per token ID, that is 0.7 KB/s per GPU and about 11 MB/s for the cluster. (Over 15.6T tokens that is ~66 days, consistent with the run4.) Yet Meta's Tectonic storage for Llama 3 offered 240 PB on 7,500 SSD servers, 2 TB/s sustained and 7 TB/s peak, and Meta still called bursty checkpoint writes "a major challenge"4. It was sized for checkpoints, not tokens.

Workload Per-GPU input rate Bytes per GPU per second 1,024 GPUs Basis 405B dense text LLM 167 tokens/s ~0.7 KB/s ~0.7 MB/s Worked example from Llama 3 MFU 8B dense text LLM 8,450 tokens/s ~34 KB/s ~35 MB/s Same formula, smaller model Image model, ~100 KB JPEGs 1,000 images/s (illustrative) ~100 MB/s ~100 GB/s Illustrative assumption Video model, 20 MB clips 2 clips/s (illustrative) ~40 MB/s ~40 GB/s Illustrative assumption MLPerf Storage 3D U-Net ~2.7 GiB/s per simulated H100 ~2.7 GiB/s ~2.8 TiB/s DDN v1.0 result11

Table 31.4 — Text training barely touches storage; image, video and scientific volumes can need five to six orders of magnitude more bytes per GPU.

Teams often pre-encode video into compact latents, trading storage bandwidth for an offline compute pass. The MLPerf 3D U-Net row is deliberately storage-bound (tiny model, large volumes), a stress test rather than a typical workload (Chapter 37).

docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Model size and optimizer"] --> B["Checkpoint bytes"]
    C["GPU count and failure rate"] --> D["Checkpoint interval"]
    B --> E["Drain or burst write GB/s"]
    D --> E
    B --> F["Restore read GB/s"]
    G["Target restart time"] --> F
    H["Data modality and tokens/s"] --> I["Data-loading read GB/s"]

    E --> M["Storage performance spec"]
    F --> M
    I --> M
    J --> N["Storage capacity spec"]

Figure 31.3 — For text LLMs, the performance spec comes from checkpoint save and restore; for multimodal training, data loading can dominate.

Capacity example: the last 10 checkpoints of a 405B run plus 20 evaluation milestones is 30 × 5.67 TB ≈ 170 TB, modest next to a multimodal corpus but hot data readable at restore speed. NVIDIA's DGX SuperPOD (H100) reference architecture's "best" storage tier asks for 40 GB/s read and 20 GB/s write per node, and 125/62 GB/s read/write per 32-node scalable unit12 [VERIFY: the 125 GB/s per-SU read appears in a search snippet of the RA's Table 6 (good/better/best = 15/40/125 GB/s); per-node and write figures still search-summary only]. Scaled linearly to 64 units (16,384 GPUs), that is about 4 TB/s of write, the same order as Meta's 7 TB/s peak.

docs.text:
Approach Where the checkpoint burst lands Strength Weakness Examples (public) Shared all-flash, metadata/data split Shared namespace, clients write data nodes directly High aggregate write; one copy visible to every node for restore Must be sized for the burst or the drain Everpure FlashBlade//EXA: 877.5 GiB/s checkpoint write in MLPerf Storage v3.012 Parallel file system Object storage targets via striping Mature at HPC scale; strong streaming Metadata server limits on file-per-rank storms DDN EXAScaler (>2× checkpoint speedup, company-stated)13; Azure Managed Lustre 642.2 GiB/s in v3.02 Disaggregated shared-everything SCM/flash write buffer, migrated to QLC later Absorbs bursts into a fast tier; global reduction Write path amplifies back-end traffic VAST (no MLPerf Storage submission)214 Software-defined parallel FS Commodity NVMe servers or cloud instances Scales per node; cloud and neocloud fit Customer owns hardware integration WEKA (company-stated checkpoint focus)15 Node-local tier GPU servers' own NVMe, then drained Removes network from the critical path Durability depends on replication; capacity stranded in servers Hammerspace Tier 016; NVIDIA NeMo local checkpointing6 Self-built Hyperscaler or lab file system Tuned to one workload; no vendor margin Engineering headcount; not for sale Meta Tectonic4; DeepSeek 3FS (~6.6 TiB/s reads across 180 storage nodes)17

Table 31.5 — Every architecture can absorb checkpoints; they differ in whether the burst lands on shared flash, a fast buffer tier, or the GPU servers themselves.

Everpure's position. FlashBlade//EXA pitches aggregate write through a direct client-to-data-node path plus a metadata core for mass file creates. The v3.0 submission wrote a 1.25T-parameter checkpoint emulation from 1,024 simulated accelerators in 17.74 seconds1. That implies roughly 16–17 TB per checkpoint (atlas arithmetic), consistent with Figure 31.1. Everpure also markets FlashBlade with PyTorch asynchronous checkpointing and claims at least 10× lower checkpoint overhead (company-stated)18. Most of that gain is the software pattern, which works on any storage.

Steelman the alternatives. DDN's Lustre lineage has absorbed file-per-process checkpoint storms in national labs for two decades. VAST's write buffer absorbs bursts without sizing QLC for them. Node-local tiers attack the root: if checkpoints rarely leave GPU servers, shared storage holds only slower, durable copies. And VAST, WEKA and DDN did not submit to v3.02, so Everpure's lead covers the submitters, not the market.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Checkpointing for large-scale training
    1974 : Young publishes the optimal checkpoint interval formula
    2006 : Daly refines it for HPC restart dumps
    2023 : Gemini keeps checkpoints in peer CPU memory
    2024 : PyTorch ships asynchronous distributed checkpointing : Llama 3 paper reports 419 unexpected stops in 54 days
    2025 : MLPerf Storage v2.0 adds Llama 3 checkpoint workloads : DeepSeek open-sources 3FS
    2026 : MLPerf Storage v3.0 runs a 1.25T checkpoint case : Everpure tops checkpoint write in its first submission

Figure 31.4 — Checkpoint theory is 50 years old; what changed is scale, which pushed checkpointing into the storage benchmark and the storage RFP.

HPC solved this first: supercomputer restart dumps drove the parallel file systems of the 2000s (Chapter 17). MLPerf Storage made checkpointing a scored workload in v2.0 (August 2025), using Llama 3 8B, 70B, 405B and 1T models19. Its metrics are deliberately pessimistic: duration is the slowest process and throughput is the minimum across processes, over 10 checkpoints written and read20.

Three trends point forward: checkpoints move closer to the GPU (host DRAM, local NVMe, peer replicas), with shared storage as durable backstop; lower-precision optimizer states shrink bytes per parameter while total parameter counts keep growing; and as failures scale with GPU count, time-to-resume becomes the metric vendors are judged on.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In the last five training deals we lost, was the checkpoint requirement written as burst GB/s, drain rate or time-to-resume?" Strong: knows the customer's framework (sync or async), checkpoint size and interval, and whether the RFP number was real or copied from a reference architecture.
  2. "How do we size a cluster for a customer running asynchronous checkpointing to local NVMe?" Strong: sustained drain, restore bandwidth and retained-checkpoint capacity, not peak write, and how pricing compensates when that shrinks the deal.
  3. "What's our answer when VAST or WEKA says MLPerf Storage doesn't reflect real customers?" Strong: concede it is synthetic, then cite the 1.25T case, the pessimistic min-throughput metric and references at similar scale.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Walk me through a 16K-rank restore after the cache has been dropped: files opened per second, read GB/s and time to first step." Strong: separate metadata and data numbers, broadcast versus per-replica reads, and the slowest-client tail.
  2. "What happens to a running checkpoint drain when a data node fails?" Strong: degraded write bandwidth as a percentage, stall-or-retry behaviour, and time to full speed.
  3. "Where does the checkpoint's write amplification come from on our platform: erasure coding, metadata, reduction?" Strong: a back-end-bytes-per-client-byte figure, and candour that optimizer state barely compresses.

Don't say this:

  • "LLM training needs huge read bandwidth." Text needs MB/s. Checkpoints, restores and multimodal data drive bandwidth.
  • "A 405B checkpoint is 810 GB." That is the bf16 weights. With optimizer state it is about 5.7–6.5 TB.
  • "Faster storage is the only way to cut checkpoint overhead." Asynchronous and tiered checkpointing remove most of the stall in software.
  • "Checkpoint data dedupes well." Successive checkpoints differ in almost every fp32 value; expect little reduction.
  • "The MLPerf leader is the fastest system on the market." Major competitors didn't submit to v3.0.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Checkpoint — a saved copy of all training state needed to resume a run.
  • Optimizer state — Adam's per-parameter moments and fp32 master weights, most of a checkpoint's size.
  • Asynchronous checkpointing — copying state to host memory, then writing to storage in the background while training continues.
  • Restore storm — every GPU reading the latest checkpoint at once after a failure.
  • Young's formula — the optimal checkpoint interval, √(2 × save cost × MTBF).
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 32. Inference and KV cache
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Media physics · The GPU data path · Interfaces and emerging tech (CXL) · Training storage

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• The KV cache is a conversation's working memory: the attention keys and values of every token so far. A Llama 3.1 70B-class model needs 320 KiB per token, so one 128K-token session is about 43 GB; a fleet of retained sessions reaches petabytes.
  • Prefill is compute-bound; decode is memory-bound. Decode rereads the whole cache for every new token, so active KV must sit in HBM. Storage can only hold KV that is not being decoded right now.
  • It is a recompute-or-fetch trade. Rebuilding a 128K context costs an 8-GPU node ~2.6 s of compute; fetching it over 8 × 400 Gb/s NICs takes ~0.13 s. Fetching wins above roughly 2–5 GB/s per GPU, so hit rate and bandwidth decide the economics.
  • NVIDIA has standardized the hierarchy. Dynamo's KV Block Manager (KVBM) defines tiers G1 (HBM) to G4 (networked storage), NIXL moves the bytes, and BlueField-4 STX/CMX adds a pod-level "G3.5" flash tier. Storage vendors, Everpure included, compete to be the G3.5/G4 backend.
  • Discount the multipliers. Everpure, WEKA, DDN and HPE each claim 20× or more faster time to first token, mostly against a no-cache baseline; VAST and NVIDIA claim power and throughput gains instead. MLPerf Storage v3.0 (September 2026) added the first neutral KV-cache test1.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Training storage is a one-time sale per cluster; inference spending recurs, and KV caching is the first inference workload that needs shared-storage capacity and bandwidth on every user request. If a cache tier lets a GPU fleet serve more conversations per GPU, storage is paid for out of the GPU budget, the most persuasive argument a storage vendor has (Chapter 11). Everpure has entered with PureKVA on FlashBlade, led the MLPerf Storage v3.0 KV-cache runs it entered2 (company-stated) and is a named partner in NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX architecture3.

The risk is equally direct. NVIDIA is defining the tier (names, software, and now a reference rack, CMX), in which storage can become a commodity flash shelf behind NVIDIA's DPUs. The strategic question: is KV cache a new socket for Everpure, or a feature that NVIDIA, local NVMe and leaner model architectures will absorb?

docs.title: What the KV cache is, and how big it gets
docs.text:
A transformer generates one token at a time. At each step, every layer's attention compares the new token's query with the keys of all earlier tokens and blends their values. Caching each token's K and V avoids recomputing the whole history every step. The cost is memory:

KV bytes per token = 2 (K and V) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per value.

Llama 3.1 70B has 80 layers and uses grouped-query attention (GQA): 64 query heads share 8 KV heads, each of dimension 128 (8,192 ÷ 64)4. At fp16 that gives 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes (320 KiB) per token. Llama 3.1 405B (126 layers, 8 KV heads) needs 504 KiB per token. DeepSeek-V3 uses multi-head latent attention (MLA). It caches one compressed 512-wide latent plus a 64-wide positional key per layer, so 61 layers come to about 69 KiB per token despite 671B parameters5. Without GQA, the 70B model would need 8× more (2.5 MiB per token). Model architects keep shrinking KV, and any storage pitch has to survive that.

Figure 32.1 — Worked example: KV size is linear in context and in sessions, so a few hundred retained long conversations already exceed everything one 8-GPU node holds. Data: data/ch32_kv_size.csv

Compare the hardware. An H200 has 141 GB of HBM6; a Rubin GPU has 288 GB of HBM47. A DGX B200 node has 1,440 GB of HBM, 2 TB of host DRAM and 8 × 3.84 TB of local NVMe8. After 71 GB of fp8 weights for a 70B model, ~1.37 TB remains for KV: about 31 sessions at 128K, fewer after activations (fp8 KV doubles it).

docs.title: Prefill versus decode: two different machines
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P["Prompt: system prompt, documents, chat history"] --> PF["PREFILL: all prompt tokens in parallel<br/>compute-bound, high FLOPs per byte"]
    PF --> KV[("KV cache in HBM")]
    PF --> T1["First token: TTFT ends here"]
    T1 --> DC["DECODE: one token per step<br/>reads all weights and all KV every step"]
    KV --> DC
    DC -->|"appends K,V per new token"| KV
    DC --> OUT["Streamed answer: inter-token latency"]

Figure 32.2 — Prefill creates the KV cache in one compute-heavy burst; decode then rereads it once per generated token, which is why active KV must live in the fastest memory.

Prefill processes the whole prompt at once, matrix-multiply heavy and near the compute roofline; its latency is time to first token (TTFT). Decode produces one token per step, and each step reads the weights and the entire KV cache of every sequence in the batch: the low-arithmetic-intensity, memory-bound corner of a roofline plot. A worked example: 16 sessions at 128K on a 70B model hold 687 GB of KV. Spread across eight B200s, each GPU reads ~86 GB of KV per step, about 11 ms at B200's 8 TB/s of HBM bandwidth8. Reading the weights takes only ~1 ms. At long context, KV bytes set decode speed and HBM capacity caps batch size. Streaming that 86 GB from a 50 GB/s link would take 1.7 s per token. Hence the hard limit: storage holds inactive KV (between turns, while an agent waits on a tool, or a shared prefix not yet in use), never the working set.

Because the phases want different hardware, disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate GPU pools and ships the KV cache between them, an idea published in 2024 as DistServe (OSDI)9 and Splitwise (ISCA)10. Moonshot AI's Mooncake (serving Kimi) pooled KV on spare CPU DRAM and SSDs and won Best Paper at USENIX FAST 2025, subtitled "trading more storage for less computation"11. Disaggregation turns KV from a private GPU buffer into data that crosses the network, where storage vendors operate.

docs.title: Prefix caching: the hit-rate game
docs.text:
Requests often share a beginning (system prompt, document, repository, earlier turns). Prefix caching stores KV in fixed-size blocks keyed by a hash of the tokens up to that block, so a new request reuses the longest matching prefix and prefills only new tokens. vLLM's PagedAttention (SOSP 2023) enabled this by paging KV like virtual memory, cutting fragmentation waste and raising throughput 2–4×12. SGLang's RadixAttention extended the idea to a prefix tree13.

The semiconductor bridge is direct: the block hash is a cache tag, eviction is LRU with a frequency filter, and average access time is hit rate × fetch time + miss rate × recompute time. The quirk is that misses are recomputable: losing a block costs time and money, never correctness, so durability matters far less than throughput and tail latency. Hit rates are fragile: context truncation can halve them14, and a model update invalidates the entire cache.

docs.title: Recompute or fetch: the break-even
docs.text:
Worked example (128K-token context, Llama 3.1 70B, 8-GPU B200-class node). Recompute needs about 2 × 70.6×10⁹ × 131,072 ≈ 1.85×10¹⁶ FLOPs for the linear layers, plus about 2.25×10¹⁶ for causal attention (2 × n² × 8,192 × 80 layers), so ≈ 4.1×10¹⁶ FLOPs. Assume the node delivers 16 PFLOPS (2 PFLOPS per GPU, an assumption well below peak). Recompute then takes ≈ 2.6 s and ≈ 21 GPU-seconds. Fetching 43 GB over eight 400 Gb/s NICs at ~80% efficiency (320 GB/s) takes ≈ 0.13 s with the GPUs free. A 70B model spends 0.5–1 million FLOPs to recreate each byte of KV, so at 2 PFLOPS per GPU fetching wins above ~2–5 GB/s per GPU: a low bar for RDMA flash, and why KV offload works at all.

Figure 32.3 — The KV hierarchy is a cache hierarchy with a ~1,000× latency cliff between memory and flash; storage vendors compete below the cliff, where capacity and sharing matter more than nanoseconds.

Path for a 128K-context hit (70B, 43 GB) Time to restore GPU time burned Capacity at that tier (one node) Cost to hold 43 GB for 1 hour Miss: recompute prefill ≈ 2.6 s ≈ 21 GPU-s (≈ US$0.02 at US$4/GPU-h, assumed) n/a n/a G2 host DRAM over PCIe 5 (~440 GB/s per node) ≈ 0.1 s ~0 2–4 TB → ~45–90 sessions ≈ US$0.01 (DRAM at ~US$10/GB, 4-yr life, assumed) G3 local NVMe (8 drives, ~56 GB/s) ≈ 0.8 s ~0 ~31 TB → ~700 sessions, this node only ≈ US$0.0006 (flash system at ~US$0.50/GB, assumed) G3.5 / G4 networked flash (~320 GB/s to the node) ≈ 0.13 s + lookup ~0 PB per pod or cluster, any node ≈ US$0.0006 plus network and software Miss on a 1M-token context (343 GB) ≈ 100 s recompute (attention dominates) ≈ 800 GPU-s ~4 sessions per node's HBM after weights; exceeds one GPU's 180 GB n/a

Table 32.1 — Worked example, not vendor data: one recompute costs about as much as holding the same KV in DRAM for two hours or on flash for ~40 hours, so the economics come down to hit rate and fetch bandwidth.

Three conclusions. First, eight 400G NICs out-run eight local U.2 drives, which is why NVIDIA put its context tier on Ethernet. Second, DRAM and CXL memory win on speed for the hottest evicted blocks but cost ~20× more per GB-hour; Synopsys claims CXL offloads KV 3.6× faster than SSDs15 (vendor claim), but the test is tokens per dollar. Third, the shared tier's main advantage is invisible per node: any GPU can hit any session's prefix, so the router can send a returning user to whichever node is free.

docs.title: Why long context and agents turn KV into a storage problem
docs.text: Agents are long and stop-start. A coding agent that runs 50 turns, growing to 100K tokens and waiting seconds to minutes on tools between turns, would re-prefill its history every turn without a cache: about 50 × 50K ≈ 2.5 million prefill tokens, 25× the work with perfect reuse. Across thousands of agents the retained state is the right-hand side of Figure 32.1: tens of TB to PB, reused within minutes, recomputable but expensive to lose. That is the profile of a shared flash cache. TrendForce attributes part of 4Q26 enterprise SSD demand to QLC purchases for KV cache16. DeepSeek moved its API cache to disk in 2024, pricing hits at one-tenth of a miss, and reported that first-token latency on a heavily reused 128K prompt fell from 13 s to about 0.5 s17 (company-stated). Anthropic bills cache reads at 0.1× the base input price18. Prompt-cache pricing is the market's own valuation of a KV hit.

docs.title: The software stack: Dynamo, KVBM, NIXL, LMCache, llm-d
docs.text:
NVIDIA unveiled Dynamo, its open-source distributed inference framework, at GTC on 2025-03-1819 and declared it production-ready (1.0) on 2026-03-1620. It does KV-aware routing and disaggregated serving across TensorRT-LLM, vLLM and SGLang. Its KVBM tiers KV blocks across G1 (HBM), G2 (host DRAM), G3 (local SSD) and G4 (remote storage, treated as an opaque blob store), with disk I/O through NIXL and GPUDirect Storage where available21. To spare SSD endurance, recent versions write a block from DRAM to disk only after it has been reused at least twice (a version-dependent default)22. NIXL, the transfer library underneath, has plug-in backends (UCX/RDMA, POSIX, GDS, object, vendor); that socket is where storage vendors integrate23.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User or agent
    participant R as Dynamo router
    participant W as GPU worker
    participant K as KVBM
    participant S as G3 or G4 tier
    U->>R: request with long shared prefix
    R->>K: hash prefix blocks and look up
    alt prefix found in G3 or G4
        K->>S: locate blocks
        S-->>W: NIXL transfer via RDMA or GDS into HBM
        W->>W: prefill only the new tokens
    else miss
        W->>W: full prefill recompute
        W->>K: register new blocks
        K->>S: offload later if reused
    end
    W-->>U: first token then decode stream
    Note over W,S: active decode KV stays in HBM throughout

Figure 32.4 — On a hit, the expensive step becomes a bulk DMA from flash into HBM; on a miss, the GPU recomputes and the new blocks become tomorrow's hits.

Open-source layers keep the tier vendor-neutral. LMCache moves KV from vLLM and SGLang into shared tiers; its authors report up to 15× throughput on multi-round and document workloads14. vLLM itself now offloads to host memory, storage and remote peers24. llm-d, launched in May 2025 by Red Hat, Google Cloud, IBM Research, CoreWeave and NVIDIA and a CNCF Sandbox project since March 2026, brings KV-aware scheduling to Kubernetes25. A vendor supporting NIXL, LMCache and llm-d reaches nearly every serving stack.

docs.title: Where storage vendors can, and can't, add value
docs.text: Can: capacity at flash cost; a namespace shared across nodes (higher hit rates, free routing); persistence across restarts; tenant isolation and encryption of sensitive user context; and bandwidth to feed hundreds of GPUs (FlashBlade//EXA's MLPerf v3.0 entry read KV at 1,623.4 GiB/s on 51 hosts26, vendor-submitted; the standard-scale leaders, UBIX and FarmGPU, posted ~444 GiB/s on much smaller configurations, so compare per host, not headline). Can't: touch the decode loop; beat DRAM or CXL for blocks reused within seconds; charge for durability on recomputable data; or stop model-side shrinkage (MLA, fp8/fp4 KV, hybrid attention), which moves the break-even toward local memory. The defensible position is the shared, pod-to-cluster tier: too big for DRAM, too shared for local NVMe.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Vendor Offering Integration path Headline claim (vendor claim) Caveat Everpure PureKVA on FlashBlade (S3 and NFS); EXA for scale vLLM and Dynamo; RDMA pre-staging into GPU memory27 Up to 20× faster TTFT; DeepReduce always-on; availability announced for October 202628 Test details unpublished; MLPerf v3.0 KV results are its neutral data point2 WEKA Augmented Memory Grid on NeuralMesh RDMA + GDS; open-sourced NIXL plugin; GA 2025-11-18, OCI launch partner29 "1000×" GPU memory extension; up to 20× lower TTFT29 Longest commercial track record; NeuralMesh 6 claims lack a reproducible method30 VAST Data VUA (open source, Apr 2025); CNode software on BlueField-4 (CES 2026) vLLM, LMCache, Dynamo31 75% lower power for KV operations; hardware 2H 202632 Strongest fit with NVIDIA's DPU-centric CMX design DDN KV cache on Infinia and EXAScaler via Dynamo/NIXL Dynamo-integrated since June 202633 Up to 55× faster KV loading (2026); 27× faster, 75% lower input-token cost (2025)3334 Multipliers vary widely by baseline HPE Alletra MP X10000 KV offload Kamiwaza-validated test on H20035 Up to 20× faster TTFT, 17× effective throughput35 Sponsored content NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX / CMX "G3.5" tier Native to Dynamo, Spectrum-X, BlueField-4336 5× tokens/s and 5× power efficiency vs traditional storage37 Defines the socket; partners supply software and flash

Table 32.2 — Every claim here is vendor-reported, most against a no-cache baseline; comparable numbers exist only in MLPerf Storage v3.0.

Steelmanning the alternatives. WEKA moved first (AMG at GTC 2025, OCI as launch partner) and has production references Everpure is still building. VAST running its software on the BlueField-4 DPU inside GPU servers fits NVIDIA's CMX blueprint most closely, which can decide NVIDIA-led deals (Chapter 34). The simplest rival is the "free" one: a DGX already ships with ~31 TB of local NVMe, and LMCache can use it at no extra licence cost.

Everpure's case. PureKVA reuses FlashBlade's existing shared, multi-tenant, high-bandwidth position rather than adding a silo, and its MLPerf v3.0 KV results are benchmark evidence, not a marketing multiplier, though WEKA, VAST and DDN did not enter that round26. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: an upstream NIXL backend and LMCache/llm-d connectors so PureKVA reaches every serving stack; positioning EXA as the software layer for STX/CMX racks rather than a rival to them; and pricing KV capacity by GB-hour or tokens served, as inference buyers already price cache hits.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title KV cache becomes a storage workload
    2023 : vLLM PagedAttention pages KV like virtual memory
    2024 : Disaggregated prefill and decode papers : SGLang RadixAttention : DeepSeek moves API context cache to disk
    2025 : Mooncake wins FAST best paper : Dynamo and NIXL launched : WEKA AMG announced then GA : VAST open-sources VUA : llm-d launched : Pure KVA integrates Dynamo
    2026 : NVIDIA context memory storage at CES : Dynamo 1.0 and BlueField-4 STX with CMX : DDN KV cache on Infinia : MLPerf Storage v3.0 adds KV cache : PureKVA announced

Figure 32.5 — In three years KV cache went from a GPU memory-management trick to a named storage tier with a reference rack and a benchmark.

Three forces point forward. Standardization: NVIDIA named the tiers and shipped the library and a rack; MLCommons defined a test. Commoditization: with NIXL as the interface, backends are interchangeable unless they differ on throughput, sharing or price. Model-side shrinkage: MLA-style compression and low-precision KV cut bytes per token 4–10× while contexts and agent counts rise. Whether total KV demand outruns the shrinkage decides if this tier becomes a revenue line or stays a feature (Chapter 53).

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What hit rate and context length does PureKVA's 20× TTFT figure assume, and what is the baseline: recompute, local NVMe or LMCache on DRAM?" Strong: model, context, concurrency and baseline, plus where the benefit vanishes (short contexts, low reuse).
  2. "Are we a supplier to NVIDIA's CMX racks, a competitor to them, or the G4 tier behind them?" Strong: a position per NVIDIA deal type and what Everpure adds beyond a BlueField-4 flash shelf (sharing, tenancy, operations).
  3. "How would we price a KV tier: per TB, per GB-hour or per token served?" Strong: anchors price to the customer's recompute cost, visible in API prompt-cache pricing.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What restore bandwidth per GPU, and what p99 latency per KV block, does PureKVA deliver at 1,000 concurrent sessions?" Strong: GB/s per GPU well above the ~2–5 GB/s break-even, block size, and tail latency under mixed offload and onload.
  2. "What happens to the cache when the model is updated or a node restarts?" Strong: model version in the cache key, invalidation, warm-up, and loss meaning recompute, not data loss.
  3. "Do we have an upstream NIXL backend, and does PureKVA work with LMCache and llm-d without our own client?" Strong: names the plugin, upstream status and supported engine versions.

Don't say this:

  • "Storage extends GPU memory." It holds inactive KV; decode rereads every active token each step and cannot run from flash.
  • "KV cache needs enterprise-grade durability." It is recomputable. Value comes from throughput, sharing and cost per GB-hour, not eleven nines.
  • "Local NVMe is enough." Sometimes, but only its own node sees it, which caps hit rates; it also restores slower than eight 400G NICs.
  • "20× faster TTFT" without stating the baseline, context length and hit rate.
  • "CXL solves this." CXL memory is DRAM at DRAM prices: faster, but roughly 20× the GB-hour cost of flash.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• KV cache — stored per-token attention keys and values.
  • Prefill / decode — compute-bound prompt phase; memory-bound generation phase.
  • TTFT — time to first token.
  • Prefix caching — reusing KV for identical leading tokens.
  • GQA / MLA — attention designs that shrink KV per token.
  • KVBM, NIXL, CMX — Dynamo's tier manager, transfer library, pod context-memory tier.
  • See the glossary for the rest.
