docs.title: 33. RAG, vector databases and AI-native data formats
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Object storage and S3 · Metadata · The AI data pipeline end to end · Inference and KV cache

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• RAG turns a company's documents into an LLM's working memory. Chunks are embedded as vectors; at question time the closest chunks are pasted into the prompt. Storage sits on three steps: vector search, chunk fetch and, increasingly, KV-cache reuse.
  • Vector indexes are a memory-capacity problem. One billion 1,024-dimension vectors are ~4.1 TB raw. Held in DRAM, that costs ~16× more media than an SSD-resident design such as DiskANN, so billion-scale indexes are moving to flash and object storage.
  • AI-native formats change the I/O pattern. Parquet is built for scans; Lance for scans and random row reads (shuffled training, embeddings, multimodal blobs). Iceberg adds transactions and a catalog over plain files in object storage.
  • Every storage vendor now ships a "data engine". VAST, NetApp, Dell, Everpure and AWS have all moved embedding, vector search or table management into or next to storage. Meanwhile vector search has become a feature of Postgres, Elastic, Databricks, Snowflake and S3 itself.
  • The strategic question is who owns the control point. Bytes are replaceable; catalogs, metadata and governance are sticky. Value accrues to whoever owns the metadata and the query, unless the data cannot leave the building.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text: Enterprise AI is mostly inference over private data, and RAG is the default way to connect the two. That creates a storage workload of small random reads against huge indexes, plus a lakehouse of Parquet, Lance and Iceberg files in S3 buckets. It also creates a land grab. AWS put vector search and Iceberg tables inside S312. VAST added a vector-capable database3. NetApp's AI Data Engine generates embeddings "at the storage layer"4, and Dell bundled Elastic and Starburst engines into its AI Data Platform5. Everpure's answer is FlashBlade as substrate, Data Stream (ingest-to-vector pipeline, GA June 2026)6 and Data Intelligence (ex-1touch). Whether these moves capture value or merely defend share depends on a market where data platforms dwarf any storage vendor's data-services business: Databricks reported a >US$7 billion run-rate at a US$190 billion valuation (company-stated, August 2026)7, and Snowflake booked US$4.47 billion of FY2026 product revenue8.

docs.title: Embeddings in one paragraph
docs.text:
An embedding model maps a chunk of text, an image or a video frame to a fixed-length vector, say 1,024 floats, trained so that similar meanings land close together. Similarity is then geometry: a cosine or dot product. For a semis reader, an embedding is a learned fingerprint, and search is a giant matrix-vector multiply (GEMV) against every stored vector, unless an index lets you skip most of them.

Embeddings can outweigh the source. A 512-token text chunk is about 2 KB (~4 bytes per token), but its 1,024-dim fp32 embedding is 4 KB. A 10 TB text corpus becomes ~5 billion chunks and ~20 TB of vectors, twice the source, before any index. For images and video the ratio flips.

docs.title: The RAG request path
docs.text:
RAG was named in a 2020 Facebook AI paper9. Documents are chunked, embedded and indexed offline; at query time the system embeds the question, retrieves the nearest chunks and conditions the LLM on them.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User or agent
    participant A as RAG app
    participant E as Embedding model on GPU
    participant V as Vector index
    participant O as Object or file store
    participant R as Reranker on GPU
    participant L as LLM on GPU
    U->>A: question
    A->>E: embed query, 10-30 ms
    E-->>A: 1024-dim query vector
    rect rgb(225, 238, 250)
    A->>V: STORAGE - top-50 ANN search plus access filter, 2-50 ms in DRAM or SSD, 100-500 ms object-native
    V-->>A: chunk IDs and scores
    A->>O: STORAGE - 50 parallel GETs of chunk text, 5-50 ms
    O-->>A: chunks plus metadata
    end
    A->>R: score 50 candidates, 20-100 ms
    R-->>A: best 8 chunks
    A->>L: prompt with 8 chunks, prefill 200-800 ms
    rect rgb(225, 238, 250)
    Note over L,O: STORAGE - reused prompt prefixes can load KV cache from flash, see Ch 32
    end
    L-->>U: streamed answer, first token under about 1 s

Figure 33.1 — Illustrative latency budget: in a well-built RAG stack, storage-bound steps take 10–30% of time-to-first-token, but a cold object-store index can make retrieval the single largest step.

The budget is a worked illustration, not a benchmark. Object-native search ranges come from vendor documentation: Databricks quotes ~250 ms for storage-optimized endpoints10, AWS ~100 ms for frequently queried S3 Vectors indexes and sub-second otherwise11, and turbopuffer hundreds of milliseconds cold versus under 10 ms from its NVMe cache12. The lesson: retrieval is latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound. Fifty 2 KB chunks is 100 KB, but each GET pays a full round trip: about a millisecond on all-flash object storage, tens of milliseconds on a disk-based cloud tier.

docs.title: Vector indexes: trading memory for recall
docs.text:
A flat scan of every vector is exact but O(N). Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes give up a few percent of recall (the share of true neighbours returned) for orders-of-magnitude speed-ups.

Index How it works Memory footprint (1B × 1,024-dim) Recall / latency SSD-friendly? Flat (brute force) Scan every vector, often on GPU 4.1 TB fp32, wherever it sits 100% / seconds per query at 1B Only as a sequential scan IVF (inverted file) Cluster vectors; probe the nearest few clusters Centroids small; lists = full data 90–98% tunable / ms if lists in RAM Yes: clusters are contiguous reads (SPANN keeps lists on SSD13) HNSW (graph) Multi-layer proximity graph; greedy walk Vectors + ~264 B/vector of links ≈ 4.4 TB 95–99% / ~1 ms in DRAM Poor: one dependent random read per hop DiskANN / Vamana Flat graph on SSD; PQ codes in DRAM steer the walk ~64 GB DRAM + ~4.4 TB SSD >95% 1-recall@1, <3 ms on SIFT1B14 Designed for it: beam search issues parallel 4 KB reads PQ / binary quantization Compress each vector to 8–128 B codes; ADC look-up tables 64–128 GB for 1B Lower alone; re-rank fixes it Codes in RAM, originals on SSD

Table 33.1 — Index choice is a placement decision: which bytes must sit in DRAM and which can live on flash.

Worked example (the 4 TB problem). 1 billion vectors × 1,024 dimensions × 4 bytes = 4.1 × 10¹² bytes ≈ 4.1 TB raw. An HNSW graph (M = 32) adds up to 64 four-byte neighbour IDs per vector, ~264 GB. At ~US$14.5/GB for 2026 server DRAM15, an in-memory replica carries ~US$63,000 of DRAM, plus ~US$3,000 for a persisted fp32 copy on SSD. DiskANN keeps only 64-byte PQ codes in DRAM (64 GB, ~US$900) and the 4.4 TB graph on SSD at ~US$0.75/GB16 (~US$3,300). That is ~US$66k versus ~US$4k of media per replica.

Figure 33.2 — Worked example: moving the bulk of a billion-vector index from DRAM to flash cuts media cost per replica by roughly 16× at 2026 prices. Data: data/ch33_vector_memory.csv

docs.title: Why graph search on SSD works, and why it is pointer chasing
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Q["Query vector"] --> P["Approximate distances<br/>from PQ codes in DRAM"]
    P --> B["Pick best W = 4<br/>unvisited frontier nodes"]
    B --> S["Read 4 nodes from SSD in parallel<br/>vector + neighbour list, ~8 KB each"]
    S --> X["Exact distances on full vectors<br/>push neighbours onto frontier"]
    X -->|"repeat ~30 rounds"| B
    X --> T["Top-k chunk IDs"]

Figure 33.3 — DiskANN hides SSD latency by issuing a small batch of reads per hop, the same trick an out-of-order core uses to keep several cache misses in flight.

Semiconductor bridge. An HNSW walk is a linked-list traversal: the next address depends on data not yet loaded, so prefetchers cannot help and the walk is bound by latency. It is the irregular-access profile of graph analytics that caches handle badly. DiskANN's beam width W is memory-level parallelism. With ~30 dependent rounds at ~100 µs per NVMe read, a query takes ~3 ms, consistent with the paper. At 5,000 queries/s, 30 × 4 nodes × two 4 KB sectors is ~1.2 million random reads per second, within reach of a few data-centre NVMe SSDs. Behind a networked array adding ~0.5 ms per round trip, a query takes ~15–18 ms; behind a 20 ms object GET, ~600 ms. That is why object-storage-native engines (turbopuffer, Pinecone serverless) prefer clustered IVF/SPANN-style layouts, which need a few large reads instead of dozens of dependent small ones1217.

PQ is weight quantization for vectors. Product quantization splits a 1,024-dim vector into 64 sub-vectors and replaces each with a 1-byte codebook index: 4,096 bytes → 64 bytes. Distances come from table look-ups, as palettized or INT4 weights trade accuracy for memory in inference. The fix for lost accuracy is re-ranking top candidates with full-precision vectors from SSD. Elastic's "BBQ" pushes this to 1 bit per dimension and claims ~95% memory reduction18.

Production systems combine these. Milvus offers a DiskANN index19; Pinecone serverless keeps immutable "slabs" in object storage, cached on executor SSDs17; S3 Vectors scales to 2 billion vectors per index and 20 trillion per bucket1. The direction is clear: DRAM for steering, flash for the index, object storage for durability.

docs.title: File formats: Parquet versus Lance
docs.text:
Parquet groups rows into large row groups and stores each column in compressed pages of roughly a megabyte. That suits scans, but fetching one row means decompressing a whole page per column. Reading 1 million random 4 KB embeddings that way could drag ~1 TB off storage to deliver 4 GB: 250× read amplification. It is the DRAM problem of activating a whole row to read one cache line.

Lance, an open columnar format from LanceDB's founders, adapts its encoding to the data's width. Wide values such as embeddings and image bytes are laid out so one row costs about one I/O; narrow values are packed into small blocks for fast scans. The authors' 2025 paper reports that tuned Parquet can get >60× better random access than its defaults, at a cost in scan speed and memory, and that Lance targets that random-read performance without those costs20. Lance also versions datasets and adds columns (say, a new embedding model's output) without rewriting the table, suiting shuffled training loaders and RAG stores whose small random reads NVMe flash serves well. LanceDB raised a US$30 million Series A in June 2025 led by Theory Ventures, with Databricks Ventures participating, and positions itself as a "multimodal lakehouse"21 (company-stated).

docs.title: Table formats, catalogs and the lakehouse
docs.text:
A folder of Parquet files has no transactions, schema enforcement or safe concurrent writers. Apache Iceberg (like rivals Delta Lake and Hudi) adds a metadata tree: a table points to a snapshot, which lists manifests, which list data files with column statistics. A commit writes new files, then atomically swaps one pointer in a catalog. That compare-and-swap on a root pointer gives snapshot isolation, time travel and engine independence, and avoids slow LIST calls (Chapter 9). Iceberg v3 added deletion vectors and a variant type for semi-structured data22.

flowchart TB
    C["AI and ML consumers<br/>RAG retrievers, training loaders, feature stores, agents"]
    E["Engines<br/>Spark, Trino and Starburst, DuckDB, Databricks, Snowflake, Dremio"]
    K["Catalogs<br/>Unity Catalog, Apache Polaris, AWS Glue and S3 Tables"]
    T["Table formats<br/>Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi, Lance datasets"]
    F["File formats<br/>Parquet, ORC, Lance"]
    O["Object storage<br/>AWS S3, FlashBlade, VAST, ObjectScale, MinIO"]
    C --> E --> K --> T --> F --> O
    V1["Control point: identity, permissions, lineage"] -.-> K
    V2["Commodity pressure: S3 API is the contract"] -.-> O

Figure 33.4 — In a lakehouse, storage is the bottom layer behind a standard S3 contract; the catalog above it is where lock-in and governance concentrate.

The catalog is the prize. In June 2024 Snowflake announced Polaris as an open Iceberg catalog, and a day later Databricks bought Tabular, founded by Iceberg's creators, for a reported US$1–2 billion23, then open-sourced Unity Catalog24. In 2026 SAP agreed to buy Dremio to make its Business Data Cloud Iceberg-native25. Storage's part is real but narrow: fast small-object GETs and PUTs, high LIST rates and, as S3 Tables showed (claimed up to 3× faster queries and 10× more transactions per second than self-managed Iceberg), automatic compaction of the small files streaming writers leave behind2.

Figure 33.5 — Illustrative judgment, not measured data: storage vendors cluster on the left and climb, data platforms own the upper right, and pure vector databases are squeezed from both sides.

Does value accrue to storage or to data vendors? The steelman for data vendors is strong. Vector search became a feature within about two years, in Postgres, Elastic, Databricks, Snowflake and S3. The best-funded specialist, Pinecone (US$100 million Series B at a US$750 million valuation in 202331), replaced its founder-CEO in September 202532 and was reported to be weighing options including a sale33 [VERIFY: date and status of the reported Pinecone sale exploration]. Revenue pools differ by an order of magnitude, and catalogs, not bytes, carry permissions and lineage (Chapter 39).

The steelman for storage vendors: most enterprise unstructured data sits on on-premises file and object systems, kept there by sovereignty or cost. Embedding it in place avoids the expensive copy, and SSD-resident indexes expand flash demand. Everpure read AWS's 2025 S3 moves as evidence that enterprise AI is converging on object storage34.

Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: (1) make FlashBlade the best on-prem target for Iceberg and Lance, with managed compaction, published small-object and LIST performance, and results on MLPerf Storage v3.0's new vector-database workload35; (2) partner with engines and catalogs rather than build a database, as Snowflake external tables on FlashBlade (2022) and Dremio briefs already did36; (3) treat Data Intelligence's metadata as the control point that makes FlashBlade the system of record for what the data is; (4) watch format companies, where LanceDB's size makes it a partner- or investment-scale asset, not a platform bet.

The arc runs from DRAM-resident specialist databases (2019–2023), through storage-compute separation onto object stores (2024), to absorption (2025–2026), where vectors became a column type, a bucket type or a storage feature. Watch GPU-accelerated indexing (NVIDIA cuVS in VAST, Dell and the AI Data Platform, Chapter 34) and IBM's 100-billion-vector demonstration on content-aware storage37, a scale only flash holds economically.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "When a customer runs RAG on FlashBlade, where does the vector index live, and whose software is it?" Strong: validated engines named, DRAM- or SSD-resident, who owns support, and where Data Stream ends and a partner begins.
  2. "Which engines read Iceberg on FlashBlade S3 in production, and how do our small-object GET latency and LIST rate compare with S3 Tables?" Strong: named engines, measured numbers, a compaction view.
  3. "How does Data Intelligence's metadata make us harder to replace than an S3 endpoint?" Strong: a concrete workflow (classification feeding RAG access filters) and Unity or Polaris integration.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "For a 1B-vector DiskANN index on FlashBlade, what is per-hop read latency and sustainable queries per second per chassis?" Strong: µs, IOPS per TB, and the network round trip's effect on 30 dependent hops.
  2. "How do we serve Lance-style random reads and Parquet scans from one bucket without one starving the other?" Strong: QoS, per-request overhead, small-I/O efficiency.
  3. "Where does embedding run in Data Stream, and what happens when the customer changes embedding model?" Strong: GPU placement, re-embedding throughput, and versioned columns rather than full rewrites.

Don't say this:

  • "Vector databases are a new storage tier." They are software indexes; storage holds their files.
  • "RAG is bandwidth-hungry." Retrieval is latency-bound; ingest and re-embedding need the bandwidth.
  • "HNSW runs fine on network storage." Each hop is a dependent read.
  • "Iceberg is a storage product." It is a table format; the catalog, not the bucket, holds the power.
  • "Quantization ruins recall." With full-precision re-ranking, 64× compression typically loses little.

docs.text:
• Embedding — fixed-length vector representing the meaning of a chunk of data.
  • ANN index — approximate nearest-neighbour structure (IVF, HNSW, DiskANN).
  • Product quantization (PQ) — compression into codebook indices.
  • Lance, Apache Iceberg, catalog — see the glossary.

docs.title: 34. NVIDIA's ecosystem and certifications
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Datacenter networking for storage · The GPU data path · Inference and KV cache

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• NVIDIA runs the approved-vendor list for AI storage. Each of its reference designs (BasePOD, SuperPOD, NVIDIA Cloud Partner, Enterprise) names storage that passed NVIDIA's tests. A vendor missing from the list is usually not in the deal.
  • The program is a set of tiers ordered by scale. NVIDIA-Certified Storage has Foundation (up to 128 simulated GPUs), Enterprise (about 1,000) and NCP (up to 10,000) levels. SuperPOD certification adds per-GPU-generation throughput tiers. NCP certification adds cloud-grade uptime, durability and delivery-time rules.
  • Certification sets a floor. It does not rank vendors. The SuperPOD B200 "enhanced" tier works out to under 0.5 GB/s of read per GPU. About a dozen vendors hold NVIDIA storage certifications. Certification proves interoperability and minimum throughput. It says nothing about price, data reduction, operations or failure behaviour.
  • NVIDIA keeps moving into the storage box. The AI Data Platform (2025) put GPUs and NVIDIA retrieval software inside storage. BlueField-4 STX and CMX (2026) standardize the KV-cache tier on NVIDIA silicon, with 12 storage vendors as co-design partners.
  • NVIDIA invests in some of the vendors it certifies. It holds equity in VAST and WEKA, and NVIDIA's own clusters run on DDN. Everpure has every major certification for FlashBlade//S. It has none NVIDIA-granted yet for FlashBlade//EXA, and it has no reported NVIDIA equity tie.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Storage is a small slice of an AI cluster's bill of materials, but the GPU vendor sets the architecture, picks the reference partners and often owns the customer conversation. For Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG), certification is the gate to compete; the competition happens after it. The strategic questions: how fast each new product clears NVIDIA's gates, how much deal flow runs through server OEMs that sell their own storage, and what happens to array economics if NVIDIA's reference storage (STX) absorbs functions storage software performs today.

The semiconductor parallel is close. Being on a foundry's IP ecosystem list (TSMC's Open Innovation Platform) or a reference board's approved vendor list does not win a socket, but being off it loses one. The platform owner also decides when the list is re-qualified: usually every product generation.

docs.title: Five programs, one gatekeeper
docs.text:
NVIDIA publishes five overlapping structures that matter for storage:

  1. DGX BasePOD. Enterprise clusters from two DGX nodes to dozens1; storage partners pass a validation-and-approval process. Launched with storage partners in September 20222.
  2. DGX SuperPOD. NVIDIA's turnkey large cluster, built from 32-node scalable units (SUs). Each GPU generation's reference architecture publishes a storage performance table to certify against3.
  3. NVIDIA Cloud Partner (NCP) reference architectures. GPU-cloud blueprints; storage earns "high-performance storage" (HPS) certification, and NCPs must meet NVIDIA's Requirements for AI Clouds4.
  4. NVIDIA-Certified Storage (NVCS). Launched at GTC in March 2025 for enterprise AI factories on NVIDIA-Certified servers5, with Foundation, Enterprise and NCP levels6.
  5. AI Data Platform and STX. Reference designs for what storage itself should contain, not test suites. NVCS is the prerequisite for building on the AI Data Platform5.
flowchart LR
    G["GDS support or self-certification"] --> F["NVCS Foundation: simulates up to 128 GPUs"]
    F --> E["NVCS Enterprise: about 1,000 GPUs"]
    E --> B["DGX BasePOD validation: 2 to dozens of DGX nodes"]
    B --> S["DGX SuperPOD: per-SU read and write tiers, re-run per GPU generation"]
    S --> N["NCP HPS and NVCS NCP level: up to 10,000 GPUs, uptime, durability, early delivery"]

Figure 34.1 — Each rung simulates or deploys more GPUs and adds tests; the programs are parallel, not formal prerequisites, but buyers read them as a ladder.

docs.title: What the tests actually require
docs.text:
Most test details sit on partner portals. Three public anchors show the bar:

  • NVCS scale. Foundation tests simulate workloads of up to 128 GPUs, Enterprise about 1,000 and NCP up to 10,0006 [VERIFY: Foundation 128 and the 10,000-GPU top of the ladder are corroborated by NVIDIA docs summaries; the ~1,000-GPU Enterprise figure is not]. NVIDIA's framework covers training, fine-tuning, inference, KV cache and retrieval I/O profiles, including synchronous and asynchronous checkpoints6.
  • SuperPOD throughput. The DGX B200 reference architecture asks, per 256-GPU SU, 40/20 GB/s read/write at "standard" and 125/62 GB/s at "enhanced", scaling linearly to four SUs3. The B300 version asks 640 and 2,000 GB/s read for eight SUs7.
  • NCP operations. High-speed file storage at roughly 99.5% uptime and 99.999% annual durability per PB, NFSv4 home directories, and storage live with API integration eight weeks before the GPUs arrive4 [VERIFY: thresholds quoted from v2.2; current is v2.4]. The detailed GB300 NVL72 storage design is on NVIDIA's non-public partner portal8.

Worked example: how high is the floor? Enhanced B200 read is 125 GB/s ÷ 256 GPUs ≈ 0.49 GB/s per GPU; standard is 40 ÷ 256 ≈ 0.16 GB/s. NVIDIA's own guidance says read-dominant work (image or video training) wants about 4 GB/s per GPU3, eight times the enhanced tier, or ~1 TB/s per SU. WEKA claimed 720 GB/s of read from one eight-node WEKApod at its 2024 SuperPOD certification9, beating the four-SU enhanced target with a single small appliance. Certification says the system won't starve a text-LLM training job; it does not separate the top vendors.

What certification does and doesn't prove

Certification shows Certification does not show Interoperates with NVIDIA's stack (GDS, RDMA, Spectrum-X or InfiniBand, Base Command) Price-performance, $/TB or power per TB Meets a published throughput floor at a stated scale Behaviour at 80% full, during rebuilds, or under mixed tenants NVIDIA support and sales teams know the configuration Effective capacity after data reduction The vendor will re-qualify on the next GPU generation Long-run reliability, upgrade disruption, operations staffing Inclusion in reference bills of materials Any ranking: the list is unordered and non-exclusive

Table 34.1 — Certification is a gate, not a grade. Everything in the right column is where deals are actually won (see Chapter 37 on reading benchmarks).

docs.title: The AI Data Platform: NVIDIA's blueprint for the storage box itself
docs.text:
In March 2025 NVIDIA presented the AI Data Platform, a reference design that puts accelerated compute and AI agents into the storage layer so data is extracted, embedded and indexed where it lives rather than copied to a separate RAG pipeline. NVIDIA named ten launch partners, Pure Storage among them10. The hardware recipe pairs RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs with BlueField DPUs and Spectrum-X Ethernet. The software recipe is the AI-Q blueprint, which calls NeMo Retriever microservices for extraction and retrieval11. Later implementations go further: Hammerspace's platform (GA March 2026) bundles NIM and NeMo Retriever12, and Everpure's Data Stream (June 2026) is an ingest-to-inference pipeline on the same design13.

    subgraph NVSW["NVIDIA AI Enterprise software running in the storage layer"]
        NR["NeMo Retriever: extract, embed, rerank"]
        NIM["NIM inference microservices"]
        VI["GPU-accelerated vector index"]
    end

Figure 34.2 — NVIDIA supplies GPUs, DPUs, network and retrieval software; the partner's differentiated layer, data services and metadata, is the middle of the sandwich.

The bargain cuts both ways: partners get a ready-made RAG answer (Chapter 33), NVIDIA gets GPUs and software subscriptions in every storage rack, and every partner's AI story converges on the same NVIDIA parts.

docs.title: STX and CMX: the reference storage server
docs.text:
NVIDIA went a step further at CES in January 2026 with the Inference Context Memory Storage (ICMS) platform, a BlueField-4-powered KV-cache tier inside each pod14. It sits between Dynamo's local-SSD (G3) and networked-storage (G4) tiers, hence the "G3.5" label in Chapter 32. At GTC in March 2026 it widened this into BlueField-4 STX, a modular storage reference architecture built on Vera Rubin, BlueField-4 and Spectrum-X. The first rack-scale implementation is the CMX context memory storage platform, effectively the CES platform under a new name15. Twelve storage vendors, including Everpure, VAST, WEKA, DDN, Dell and NetApp, are co-design partners; AIC, Supermicro and QCT build hardware; CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius, OCI and four others are early adopters16. STX is a blueprint NVIDIA distributes, not a box it sells17. KV-cache mechanics are in Chapter 32, and the DPU's place in the network is in Chapter 10.

The strategic point is where value moves. If the controller is a BlueField-4 running NVIDIA's DOCA software on ODM-built servers, storage software becomes a tenant on NVIDIA's controller silicon, as fabless designs build on a foundry's process and IP. One analyst firm argues vendors not optimized for inference and context memory face margin pressure as NVIDIA standardizes the data path, while noting those vendors are STX partners18. Opinion, but the right risk.

docs.text:
flowchart TB
    RA["NVIDIA reference design: SuperPOD, BasePOD, NCP RA, Enterprise RA, AI Data Platform, STX"]
    CL["NVIDIA certified-storage list"]
    RA --> CL
    CL --> P1["Path 1: NVIDIA-led DGX SuperPOD sale"]
    CL --> P2["Path 2: server OEM AI factory - Dell, HPE, Cisco, Lenovo, Supermicro"]
    CL --> P3["Path 3: NCP or neocloud build"]
    P1 --> D1{"Storage choice"}
    P2 --> D2{"Storage choice"}
    P3 --> D3{"Storage choice"}
    D1 -->|"customer picks from list, NVIDIA team influences"| BUY["Buyer: enterprise, sovereign, lab"]
    D2 -->|"OEM's own storage is the default"| BUY
    D3 -->|"neocloud runs bake-offs, often multi-vendor"| NEO["Buyer: neocloud tenant capacity"]
    GSI["Integrators: WWT, SHI, ePlus, AHEAD"] --> P2

Figure 34.3 — Storage is chosen at three points: the certified list sets the field in NVIDIA-led deals, the OEM's own storage starts ahead in OEM deals, and neoclouds run their own tests.

The paths have different economics. Dell bundles PowerScale, ObjectScale and its Lightning parallel file system into its AI Data Platform with NVIDIA19, so an independent vendor in a Dell-led deal starts behind. HPE sells its own X10000 alongside GreenLake for File, which runs VAST software20. Cisco has no storage, so its Secure AI Factory with NVIDIA lists partners (Pure Storage, Hitachi Vantara, NetApp, VAST, later Nutanix)21, which is why Everpure's FlashStack CVD in the Cisco AI PODs matters22. Neoclouds qualify several vendors: CoreWeave lists VAST, WEKA, DDN, IBM and Pure Storage23, and its US$1.17 billion VAST agreement shows how large one decision can be24. See Chapter 35.

docs.title: Kingmaker or toll booth? NVIDIA's investments
docs.text:
NVIDIA also invests in some listed vendors. It participated in VAST's 2021 Series D25 and its 2026 Series F at a US$30 billion valuation (company-stated)26. Secondary sources also list NVIDIA in VAST's December 2023 Series E, but VAST's own release names other investors [VERIFY: NVIDIA in VAST Series E]. NVIDIA was in WEKA's US$140 million Series E in 2024 (company-stated)27. DDN has no reported NVIDIA equity; its tie is operational, running NVIDIA's Selene and Eos clusters (Eos: 48 AI400X2 units, ~4 TB/s, company-stated)28. No public evidence shows certifications favour NVIDIA's portfolio companies; the pass lists include almost everyone. The investments buy something less formal: early roadmap access, joint launches (VAST's CNode-X, February 2026) and the "NVIDIA-backed" label in every press article.

Read honestly, NVIDIA is less a kingmaker than a toll booth with favoured lanes. It rarely picks one winner; it sets the entry fee (re-certify every GPU generation, adopt each new NVIDIA interface) and profits from a crowded field of compliant suppliers. That is a platform owner commoditizing its complements.

Table 34.2 — Nearly every vendor holds nearly every badge; the differences are timing and product-line coverage. "None found" means no public source located, not confirmed absence.

Everpure's position. FlashBlade//S holds the full set. The gap is FlashBlade//EXA, aimed at the largest AI and neocloud deals. In March 2026 Everpure said it was extending NVCS validation to EXA as a step toward the NCP level, and aligning EXA with STX31. Trade press reported NCP certification for "later this year", but no completed EXA certification had been published by 2026-11-01. Until one is, competitors can call EXA uncertified in exactly the deals it targets. Everpure's distinctive move is public, peer-reviewed benchmarking: it submitted to MLPerf Storage v3.0 in September 2026, while VAST, WEKA and DDN did not45 (DDN and WEKA entered earlier rounds; VAST never has44). The results are vendor-run, so they show what each submitter's configuration can do, not a market ranking.

Steelmanning the others. DDN's claim is strongest: NVIDIA runs its own clusters on DDN, which no certificate matches. VAST and WEKA have equity ties and usually ship NVIDIA's new interfaces first. Dell and HPE own the server sale. Everpure's counter is what certification doesn't measure: Evergreen economics, power and density (Chapter 38) and enterprise data services.

Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information:

  1. Certification velocity as a KPI. Treat "days from NVIDIA GPU launch to certified on each tier" as a product metric, with EXA at the NCP level as the near-term gap.
  2. Be an early STX/CMX implementer so Purity's data services run on whatever controller NVIDIA standardizes, rather than defending x86 controllers.
  3. Diversify routes to market beyond NVIDIA-led deals: Cisco, integrators, hyperscaler marketplaces, and non-NVIDIA accelerator and Ultra Ethernet ecosystems as hedges.
  4. Compete on what certificates don't measure: independent benchmarks, effective $/TB, TB per watt and non-disruptive upgrades.
  5. Weigh a deeper NVIDIA commercial or equity tie against the cost: dependence on one supplier's roadmap and less neutrality with AMD and hyperscaler buyers.

Supermicro has shown a prototype CMX server and is validating STX SSD requirements with Micron, Samsung and Phison, for 2H 2026 shipments46. The 2027 signal: whether NCP designs make CMX-class context storage a required line item, and whether CMX nodes come from storage vendors or straight from ODMs.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "When will FlashBlade//EXA appear on NVIDIA's certified list, at which level, and which deals are we losing until then?" Strong: a level, a GPU generation, a target quarter, and the deal types where the gap is used against EXA.
  2. "In a Dell- or HPE-led AI factory, how do we get in?" Strong: separates customer-mandated storage from OEM default, cites Cisco and integrator routes, and sizes each path.
  3. "What does STX/CMX do to our bill of materials and gross margin?" Strong: whether Purity runs on BlueField-4, who builds the hardware, and whether CMX is new revenue or cannibalizes array capacity.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "How much headroom do we have over the SuperPOD enhanced tier per SU, and what limits us first?" Strong: a multiple (say 3× or 5×) and the first bottleneck (front-end ports, metadata, back-end fabric).
  2. "What did certification testing not exercise that customers hit in production?" Strong: rebuild under load, full-system behaviour, multi-tenant QoS, upgrade under load.
  3. "What would it take to run our data path on a BlueField-4 controller?" Strong: core-count and memory constraints, which Purity services fit on the DPU, and what stays on x86.

Don't say this:

  • "We're NVIDIA-certified, so we're as good as VAST." Everyone is; it is the entry ticket.
  • "SuperPOD certification proves top performance." It proves a floor of about 0.5 GB/s per GPU on B200 enhanced.
  • "NVIDIA picks the storage winner." NVIDIA usually lists a dozen. OEMs, integrators and neocloud bake-offs decide most deals.
  • "STX means NVIDIA is entering storage." It is a partner-built reference architecture; the risk is a commoditized controller, not an NVIDIA storage brand (yet).

docs.text:

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• DGX BasePOD / SuperPOD — enterprise and large-cluster reference architectures.
  • Scalable unit (SU) — the 32-node building block of a SuperPOD.
  • NCP / HPS — NVIDIA Cloud Partner program, and its high-performance storage certification.
  • NVIDIA-Certified Storage — tiered storage certification (Foundation, Enterprise, NCP).
  • AI Data Platform — NVIDIA's reference design for GPU-accelerated retrieval inside storage.
  • BlueField-4 STX / CMX — NVIDIA's storage reference architecture, and its context-memory rack implementation.
  • AI-Q, NeMo Retriever, NIM — agent blueprint, retrieval and inference microservices.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 35. AI factories and neoclouds
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: The GPU data path · Consumption models · Training storage · NVIDIA's ecosystem and certifications

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Neoclouds are GPU-specialist clouds that rent accelerator capacity to AI labs, enterprises and even hyperscalers. The leaders now operate at utility scale: CoreWeave ended 2025 with more than 850 MW of active power in 43 data centres1 and guides 2026 capex to US$35–39 billion2.
  • They buy storage as a product to resell, not as infrastructure to consume. It must be multi-tenant, API-provisioned and metered in $/GB-month, and it must clear a margin over its own cost.
  • The largest disclosed storage contract is about 1% a year of its customer's capex, and storage is about 4% of a GPU row's power, but it can idle 100% of the GPUs. Neoclouds therefore weight reliability, time-to-deploy and NVIDIA alignment above price.
  • VAST is the incumbent of record. Its US$1.17 billion CoreWeave agreement is the largest disclosed deal3. WEKA and DDN hold multi-vendor positions, and the biggest neoclouds increasingly build their own object tier.
  • Everpure is a challenger here. It has a CoreWeave equity stake, small FlashBlade//EXA neocloud wins and a fitting consumption model, but no large anchor account.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Neoclouds are the fastest-growing new class of storage buyer, and they buy differently from the enterprises that built Everpure's franchise. CoreWeave alone had a backlog of roughly US$104 billion in August 20262. The storage chosen there shapes reference designs, benchmarks and buyer expectations far beyond their own data centres. VAST's rise (Chapter 42) is in large part a neocloud story.

The strategic question is which neocloud business is worth winning. Mega-neocloud deals are huge, concentrated and increasingly contested by in-house builds. Tier-2, sovereign and inference neoclouds are smaller, more numerous and less locked up. Each needs a different product, pricing and financing posture.

docs.title: Neoclouds, AI factories and the foundry analogy
docs.text:
An AI factory is NVIDIA's term for a data centre whose output is tokens: GPUs, networks, storage and software designed as one production line. A neocloud rents out such factories. It sells bare-metal or Kubernetes/Slurm GPU clusters by the hour or under multi-year take-or-pay contracts, to labs, start-ups, enterprises and capacity-short hyperscalers. Microsoft's contract with Nebius is worth about US$17.4 billion4.

The semiconductor bridge is the foundry model. Hyperscalers resemble IDMs: they design their own storage stacks (Chapter 36), much as an IDM runs its own process. Neoclouds resemble a young pure-play foundry: they buy tools and compete on capacity, time-to-volume and yield (here, utilisation). They adopt whatever tool the reference flow qualifies, and NVIDIA Cloud Partner (NCP) reference designs play the role of the PDK. A storage vendor outside the qualified flow rarely gets evaluated.

Scale has moved fast. CoreWeave reported a fleet of about 250,000 GPUs and 360 MW of active power at its 2025 IPO5. It ended 2025 with more than 850 MW active and about 3.1 GW contracted1. By June 2026 it had about 1.5 GW active and 3.7 GW contracted, and it targets more than 1.85 GW active by end-202662. Nebius raised its end-2026 contracted-power target to 5 GW in August 2026; contracted power means land and power commitments, not running capacity, and Nebius expects 0.8–1 GW connected by then7. Oracle acts as a quasi-neocloud: its remaining performance obligations passed US$455 billion in fiscal Q1 20268. Fluidstack is building data centres for Anthropic's US$50 billion programme9.

docs.title: Anatomy of an AI-factory row
docs.text:
Figure 35.1 — In an AI-factory row, storage is a small slice of racks and power on its own network, yet every GPU depends on it for data, checkpoints and context.

A liquid-cooled GB200 NVL72 rack joins 72 GPUs by NVLink into one scale-up domain and draws roughly 120 kW (vendor ratings up to 130 kW)1011. Eight of them make a 576-GPU unit drawing about 1 MW. Three networks leave the row:

  • Back-end compute fabric (InfiniBand or Spectrum-X Ethernet) carries GPU-to-GPU collectives between racks. Storage normally stays off it.
  • Storage network (Ethernet with RoCE) carries training reads, checkpoints and KV-cache spill. It is often converged with the front-end on the same NICs or DPUs.
  • Front-end network carries tenant access, APIs, dataset ingest and management.

How much storage does the row need? Reference designs disagree. Cisco's NCP high-performance storage design sizes 180 GB/s of read for 1,152 GPUs, about 0.16 GB/s per GPU [VERIFY: search-summary only]12. WEKA's NCP-certified designs cite roughly 1 GB/s per GPU13. For our 576 GPUs that is 90–576 GB/s, a sixfold spread. The gap is mostly checkpoint bursts and tolerated write stall (Chapter 31). NVIDIA's NCP requirements add an operational bar: end-to-end uptime above 99.5% per PB for the high-speed file system, an NFSv4 shared home-directory tier held to a higher (99.99%) availability target, and a readiness timeline in which data-movement systems must be in place about eight weeks before GPU handover14.

docs.title: How a neocloud buys differently from an enterprise
docs.text:
1. Storage is resold, so it is priced per GB-month. CoreWeave lists Distributed File Storage at US$0.07/GB-month. Its AI Object Storage is US$0.06 hot, US$0.03 warm and US$0.015 cold, with no egress or request fees15. US$0.07/GB-month is US$840 per TB-year. Assume, for illustration only, an all-in cost of US$1,000 per usable TB over four years. At list price and 100% sold, revenue is US$3,360 against US$1,000 of cost, a 70% gross margin. At 50% sold the margin falls to about 40%, and at 30% sold it is roughly breakeven. The neocloud's storage P&L is a utilisation business. Hence the premium on thin provisioning, data reduction and capacity-on-demand pricing. An enterprise sees only the US$1,000.

2. Multi-tenancy is the product. An enterprise array serves one company with trusted administrators. A neocloud serves hundreds of tenants who must not see each other's data or noisy I/O. That means hard isolation (namespaces, VRF separation, per-tenant keys), QoS, quotas, metering and self-service APIs. Crusoe, for example, exposes VAST-backed shared disks through its API, CLI and Terraform16.

3. Reliability and time-to-deploy beat price. Storage is a rounding error in neocloud capex. The VAST–CoreWeave agreement is US$1.17 billion over what VAST describes as typical 3–5-year terms17, or about US$0.23–0.39 billion a year. Against CoreWeave's US$35–39 billion of 2026 capex that is roughly 0.6–1.1% (Figure 35.3). Yet a storage outage idles every GPU attached to it (Chapter 11 prices GPU idle time). Blocks & Files summarised the neocloud view: reliability beats storage price because GPU downtime costs far more18.

4. Power per rack is the binding constraint. Using the Figure 35.1 assumptions, three storage racks at about 15 kW draw 45 kW. That equals 45 ÷ 125 ≈ 0.36 of an NVL72 rack, about 26 GPUs' worth of power. Where contracted megawatts cap revenue, TB/W and TB per rack matter even when storage $/TB does not (Chapter 38).

5. NVIDIA alignment is the entry ticket. Neoclouds want storage certified at NVIDIA's NCP tier and present in NCP reference designs (Chapter 34). They also want it on NVIDIA's roadmap: CoreWeave, Crusoe, Lambda, Nebius, OCI and others are named early adopters of the BlueField-4 STX context-memory architecture19. And buyers rank neoclouds with SemiAnalysis's ClusterMAX ratings, whose ten criteria include storage20.

6. Software-defined is preferred. Large neoclouds want storage on the same qualified servers, spares and automation as their compute. WEKA, for example, runs natively on Nebius's servers21. Appliances win when they are the fastest route to a certified configuration.

7. Financing shapes the deal. Neoclouds fund GPUs with debt secured on customer contracts, plus customer prepayments and convertible bonds. Nebius expects more than US$9 billion of customer prepayments in 2026, covering roughly 50–60% of the capex on the related deals7. It also priced US$2.75 billion of convertible notes in September 2025, up to about US$3.16 billion if the purchasers' option was exercised in full22. Vendors are asked to match with consumption pricing or deferred payments, and they take counterparty risk.

Criterion Why it matters to a neocloud Architectures that score well Hard multi-tenancy and QoS Hundreds of tenants share a cluster; a noisy or leaky neighbour is a lost customer VAST (built-in tenancy); WEKA; FlashBlade//EXA since 2026 multi-tenancy/QoS release23 API/Terraform provisioning and metering Storage is sold self-service and billed per GB-month In-house object stores; VAST; WEKA Throughput per rack and per watt Power caps revenue; checkpoint bursts set sizing Disaggregated flash (VAST, FlashBlade//EXA); DDN appliances for raw GB/s NVIDIA NCP certification and STX roadmap Entry ticket to reference designs and NVIDIA-led deals VAST, WEKA, DDN, Everpure, IBM, NetApp all pursue it19 Runs on the neocloud's own hardware One supply chain, spares pool and automation stack Software-defined (WEKA, VAST software, Lightbits, in-house) Time-to-deploy at scale Storage readiness milestones run weeks ahead of GPU handover; revenue starts at handover Vendors with pre-validated racks and field teams at scale Consumption pricing and financing Matches debt- and prepayment-funded capex Subscription models (Evergreen//One, VAST/WEKA licences) Hybrid tiering to cheap capacity Margin on cold data, free-egress positioning Object-native designs; cloud capacity partners (Backblaze)

Table 35.1 — Neocloud buying criteria: price per TB matters less than tenancy, power, NVIDIA alignment and speed, which favours software-defined, disaggregated designs.

docs.title: The build-it-yourself threat
docs.text:
The largest neoclouds are copying the hyperscaler playbook. CoreWeave's AI Object Storage runs LOTA (Local Object Transport Accelerator), a cache on every GPU node's local NVMe, and claims up to 7 GB/s per GPU25. Nebius's own shared filesystem now has validated cluster sizes of 100 PB [VERIFY: search-summary only]30. The emerging pattern is in-house object for bulk data, third-party file for the hottest tier and a cheap partner for capacity, such as CoreWeave's five-year, multi-exabyte deal with Backblaze, which supplies HDD-based tiers behind CoreWeave AI Object Storage (about US$335 million over the initial orders)27. Vendors keep the performance tier only while measurably better than a commodity-flash build, the dynamic that led Everpure to license DirectFlash to Meta rather than sell arrays37 (Chapter 29).

Figure 35.3 — The largest disclosed neocloud storage deal is about 1% a year of its customer's capex, which is why neoclouds buy storage on risk and speed, not price.

Data: data/ch35_neocloud_capex.csv

docs.text:
Vendor Neocloud position (public) Fit to neocloud criteria Weak spot VAST Data Primary platform at CoreWeave (US$1.17B); Lambda, Crusoe, Nebius, many tier-2s331 Native multi-tenancy, software on partner hardware, NVIDIA closeness Concentration in one customer; neoclouds building their own object tier WEKA Nebius premium tier; CoreWeave option; OCI launch partner2133 Software-defined, runs on neocloud servers, strong KV-cache story Smaller scale and balance sheet; client software on GPU nodes DDN CoreWeave option, Nebius, OCI; xAI heritage2834 Raw throughput, HPC credibility, NVIDIA reference designs Appliance-centric; Lustre operations burden for multi-tenant service Everpure (FlashBlade//EXA) CoreWeave equity stake and dedicated option; STN, beyond.pl wins2638 Standard pNFS client, DirectFlash density in the metadata tier, Evergreen//One for EXA38, NCP reference architecture39 Multi-tenancy only arrived in 202623; EXA data nodes are still third-party NVMe servers, so DFM power density does not yet reach the data tier (Chapter 37); no mega-neocloud anchor In-house / open CoreWeave AI Object Storage, Nebius filesystem, Lightbits at Crusoe2532 Lowest cost, full control, same hardware Engineering burden; harder for hottest file tier

Table 35.2 — VAST holds the neocloud anchor accounts, WEKA and DDN hold multi-vendor seats, and Everpure enters as a challenger whose levers are financing and, once DFM data nodes ship, power density.

Steelman VAST. VAST got there first with a design that matches neocloud economics. Its stateless compute and shared QLC let a neocloud scale performance and capacity separately. It had multi-tenancy early, sells software on commodity servers, and its CoreWeave reference makes it the safe choice for smaller neoclouds, none of whom wants to experiment during a GPU ramp.

Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information:

  1. Software-first EXA. License EXA software on neocloud-qualified servers, as with hyperscalers, trading gross dollars for presence.
  2. Finance the ramp. Evergreen//One already covers EXA38. Terms tied to tenant sell-through would address criteria 1 and 7, at the cost of credit exposure.
  3. Lead on power. Publish TB/W and TB/rack against NCP sizings.
  4. Target tier-2, sovereign and inference neoclouds. Demand is shifting towards enterprise inference18, where KV-cache tiers (PureKVA, STX) are new and contested (Chapter 32).
  5. Use the CoreWeave relationship. Aim for a tier or region, not head-on displacement.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
• 2023–2024: H100 scarcity creates the boom. VAST becomes CoreWeave's and then Lambda's storage platform (2023)40. Crusoe launches VAST-backed shared disks in September 202416. Pure Storage invests in CoreWeave in November 202426.
  • 2025: CoreWeave IPOs (March) and launches AI Object Storage with LOTA25. Nebius adds DDN (May) and WEKA (June)2821. In September Nebius signs the Microsoft contract4. In October Microsoft contracts Nscale for about 200,000 GB300 GPUs (company-stated; no value disclosed)41. In November VAST expands its CoreWeave relationship into the US$1.17 billion agreement3 and Anthropic picks Fluidstack9.
  • 2026: NVIDIA's STX names neocloud early adopters (March)19. Everpure reports EXA neocloud wins and extends Evergreen//One to EXA (March)38, then adds EXA multi-tenancy (June)23. CoreWeave signs a US$335M capacity deal with Backblaze (June)27 and raises capex guidance to US$35–39B (August)2.
  • Where it goes: inference over training, KV-cache tiers, more in-house object storage at the top, and credit stress among weaker neoclouds if GPU rental prices fall faster than debt amortises.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What does a neocloud's storage P&L look like on EXA versus VAST at 50% sell-through?" Strong: $/TB-month cost against tenant list price, including data reduction.
  2. "Which tenancy features block us in neocloud bake-offs today?" Strong: specific gaps (keys, VRF, QoS floors, metering, Terraform) with ship dates.
  3. "How do we get into NCP reference designs for GB300 and Vera Rubin, not just certification?" Strong: separates certification from being the named design.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Size storage for 1,152 GB300 GPUs at 0.16 versus 1 GB/s per GPU. What changes in racks, kW and switch ports?" Strong: node counts, kW and ports for both, and which tenants need.
  2. "How do we stop one tenant's checkpoint burst from starving another's training reads?" Strong: QoS at metadata and data layers, with measured tail latency.
  3. "Could EXA data nodes run on a neocloud's own server SKU?" Strong: qualification steps, firmware dependencies, support model.

Don't say this:

  • "Neoclouds are price-driven buyers." Not for storage: the largest disclosed deal is about 1% a year of capex, so risk, speed and power dominate.
  • "VAST owns all neoclouds." CoreWeave and Nebius run several vendors plus in-house storage.
  • "NCP certification wins the deal." It qualifies you. Reference-design placement and the anchor account win it.
  • "Multi-tenancy is a feature." For a neocloud it is the product.
  • "CoreWeave is a hyperscaler." It buys and finances third-party storage like a foundry buys tools.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Neocloud — GPU-specialist cloud provider renting AI clusters.
  • AI factory — data centre designed end to end to produce AI tokens.
  • NCP (NVIDIA Cloud Partner) — NVIDIA's programme and reference designs for GPU clouds.
  • LOTA — CoreWeave's node-local cache for its AI Object Storage.
  • Sell-through — share of installed storage capacity actually billed to tenants.
  • ClusterMAX — SemiAnalysis's rating system for GPU clouds.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 36. How hyperscalers build AI storage
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Parallel file systems · Object storage architecture · Metadata · Training storage · Purity and DirectFlash

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Hyperscalers build the file system and buy the parts. Google (Colossus), Meta (Tectonic) and AWS (S3) run home-grown software that turns a datacenter of commodity drives into one pool. They buy no arrays for their own workloads.
  • The designs are close cousins. A smart client library, metadata on a scalable database (Bigtable for Colossus, ZippyDB for Tectonic) and simple data servers, with no controller in the data path.
  • AI pushed them from disk toward flash. Built on HDDs with a little flash, these systems met GPU clusters that need far more bandwidth per terabyte. Meta's GenAI clusters run on flash-optimized Tectonic; Google, AWS and Azure sell zonal, GPU-adjacent tiers.
  • Where hyperscalers do buy, they buy components and IP, not systems. Meta and a second top-five hyperscaler licensed Everpure's DirectFlash design while buying their own NAND. Cloud services do resell partners (DDN Lustre at Google, VAST listings) for tenants.
  • It is the same logic as TPU, Trainium and Nitro. Build where volume amortizes engineering and the part differentiates. Buy where a merchant supplier has more scale. Vendors win at the seams.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
The top hyperscalers are the largest buyers of storage media on earth, yet almost closed to storage-system vendors. For Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) that matters three ways. Its hyperscaler revenue exists only because Pure Storage found a seam: a licence for flash-management software and module design, with the customer buying its own NAND12. Hyperscaler designs set the reference architecture that neoclouds and enterprises copy. And whether hyperscalers keep cold data on HDD or move it to QLC is the largest swing factor in flash-versus-disk demand (Chapter 48).

Which layers hyperscalers build, which they buy, and why the boundary moves defines the addressable surface for licensing deals. Chapter 29 covers the deal financials; this chapter covers the engineering behind the boundary.

docs.title: The common pattern: one disaggregated file system per datacenter
docs.text:
An enterprise array puts intelligence in a controller between host and drives (Chapter 14). Hyperscale file systems remove that box:

  • A client library in every application encodes data, finds where it lives and streams it directly to or from storage servers.
  • A metadata service runs as a sharded application on a scalable database; file names and block maps are just rows.
  • Thin data servers expose local disks over the network, while background workers repair and rebalance.

Semiconductor bridge. Moving the RAID logic into the client is like moving the memory controller onto the CPU die. It removes a hop and a box, but only works if you control every application and its libraries. Hyperscalers do; enterprise vendors don't, so they sell controllers and standard protocols.

docs.title: Google Colossus
docs.text:
Colossus succeeded GFS as Google's cluster-level file system and sits under Cloud Storage, Firestore, YouTube, Drive and Gmail3. Its control plane is a pool of Curators, which store file-system metadata in Bigtable. That change let Colossus scale metadata more than 100× beyond the largest GFS clusters. Data flows directly between the client library and D file servers, which are network-attached disks. Custodians handle rebuilds and disk balancing3.

flowchart LR
    subgraph HOST["Application host"]
        APP["App: Spanner, Cloud Storage, training job"]
        CL["Colossus client library: encoding, software RAID"]
        APP --> CL
    end
    CL -- "control: open, create, locate" --> CU["Curators: scalable metadata service"]
    CU <--> BT[("Bigtable: file metadata")]
    CL == "data: direct" ==> DH["D file servers on HDD"]
    CL == "data: direct" ==> DS["D file servers on SSD"]
    L4["L4: ML-driven SSD cache index"] -.-> CL
    CUS["Custodians: rebuild, rebalance"] -.-> DH
    CUS -.-> DS

Figure 36.1 — Colossus keeps metadata in a database and data on simple disk servers; the client library, not a controller, owns the data path.

Two Colossus file systems each hold more than 10 exabytes; the largest regularly exceed 50 TB/s of reads and 25 TB/s of writes, and the busiest cluster serves over 600 million IOPS4. At ~250 MB/s per HDD, 50 TB/s is the streaming bandwidth of 200,000 drives.

The economics come from mixing media: Google buys just enough flash to lift I/O density to what applications need, and just enough disk for capacity3. A tier called L4 decides which data earns SSD, running a read cache and a writeback policy that simulates options such as "SSD for one hour" per file category. The same simulations drive SSD purchasing4. Semiconductor bridge: L4 is a last-level cache with a learned replacement policy, sized by simulating hit rates before buying silicon.

For AI, Rapid Bucket (GA April 2026) is a zonal Cloud Storage bucket on Colossus; Google claims more than 15 TB/s, 20 million requests per second and sub-millisecond latency in one bucket. Rapid Cache (formerly Anywhere Cache) adds up to 2.5 TB/s of read cache in front of existing buckets5. For POSIX users Google sells Managed Lustre, built with DDN's EXAScaler, now claimed at up to 10 TB/s per instance, about 10× its 2025 launch figure56. All three figures are Google's own.

docs.title: Meta Tectonic
docs.text:
Tectonic, Meta's exabyte-scale multitenant file system (USENIX FAST '217), runs one cluster per datacenter. It replaced separate systems for photo and video blobs (Haystack and f4) and many HDFS clusters for the data warehouse78. Warehouse clusters fell 10×8.

flowchart TB
    subgraph TEN["Tenants"]
        BLOB["Blob storage"]
        DWH["Data warehouse"]
        AIT["AI training via FUSE"]
    end
    TEN --> CLB["Client library: per-tenant tuning, EC or replication"]
    CLB --> MS
    subgraph MS["Metadata Store, hash-partitioned layers"]
        NL["Name layer"] --> FL["File layer"] --> BL["Block layer"]
    end
    MS --> ZDB[("ZippyDB: sharded key-value store")]
    CLB == "data: direct" ==> CS["Chunk Store: flat chunk storage on storage nodes"]
    BG["Background services: repair, rebalance"] -.-> CS
    TG["TrafficGroups: shared quotas across tenants"] -.-> CLB

Figure 36.2 — Tectonic splits metadata into layers on a shared key-value store and gives each tenant its own client-side tuning over a common chunk pool.

Two ideas matter. Disaggregated metadata: names, files and blocks are separate layers, each hash-partitioned into a key-value store, so a hot directory does not overload the servers holding block maps78. Multitenancy without per-tenant clusters: tenants share a few dozen traffic groups, so the blob store's peak no longer strands disks the warehouse could use8, while tenant-specific tuning such as erasure-code width lives in the client library. It is the hyperscale version of the consolidation argument (Chapter 19).

AI changed the media. Meta's two 24,576-GPU GenAI clusters (2024) use a home-grown FUSE client on a flash-optimized Tectonic, plus a parallel NFS deployment co-developed with Hammerspace, both on YV3 Sierra Point servers with high-capacity E1.S SSDs9. A worked number shows why. A 405B-parameter checkpoint with optimizer state is ~405e9 × 16 bytes ≈ 6.5 TB. Writing it in 60 seconds needs ~108 GB/s. That is ~430 HDDs at ~250 MB/s streaming flat out, before erasure-coding overhead, or ~22 NVMe SSDs at ~5 GB/s.

Meta's July 2026 "AI storage blueprint" adds regional, flash-backed BLOB storage colocated with GPUs, a client SDK embedding Tectonic's block client to skip proxies, hedged reads against tail latency, and GPU-host memory and local flash as L1/L2 caches10: a cache hierarchy around one source of truth (Chapter 31).

In March 2025 Meta argued for QLC flash as a middle tier, because HDD bandwidth per terabyte falls as drives grow. Meta places QLC at workloads that still need about 10 MB/s per TB, between HDD and TLC; some batch workloads at 15–20 MB/s/TB sit on TLC today11. The arithmetic: a ~250 MB/s drive gives 12.5 MB/s/TB at 20 TB at best, but only 8.3 MB/s/TB at 30 TB. Under mixed access real HDD clusters deliver less: a 2025 Meta conference deck put HDD-cluster supply at 5–7 MB/s/TB12. Meta named Pure Storage's DirectFlash Module and standard QLC SSDs from other vendors1113.

docs.title: AWS: object store at the centre, file and cache at the edge
docs.text:
AWS builds a layered stack around S3, which AWS said at re:Invent 2025 holds more than 500 trillion objects and hundreds of exabytes14. A peak near 1 PB/s is cited from an earlier AWS talk15 [VERIFY: S3 ~1 PB/s peak bandwidth, secondary source only].

flowchart TB
    subgraph EC2["EC2 GPU and Trainium instances"]
        MPT["Mountpoint for S3 and PyTorch connector"]
        LCL["Lustre client with EFA and GPUDirect Storage"]
    end
    MPT --> S3X["S3 Express One Zone: same-AZ directory buckets"]
    MPT --> S3S["S3 Standard: regional data lake"]
    LCL --> FSX["FSx for Lustre: POSIX training and checkpoint tier"]
    FSX <-- "lazy load and export" --> S3S
    S3S --- TBL["S3 Tables: managed Iceberg"]
    S3S --- VEC["S3 Vectors: vector indexes"]

Figure 36.3 — AWS keeps S3 as the system of record and adds zonal object, parallel file and client-side layers to bring bandwidth next to the GPUs.

  • S3 Express One Zone (November 2023) puts directory buckets in the compute's Availability Zone for single-digit-millisecond access. AWS claimed 10× faster access than S3 Standard at launch16, then cut storage prices 31% and GET prices 85% in April 202517.
  • FSx for Lustre, a managed parallel file system linked to S3, has since November 2024 supported EFA and GPUDirect Storage at up to 1,200 Gbps (150 GB/s) per client, 12× the earlier 100 Gbps TCP limit18.
  • Mountpoint for S3 (GA August 2023), an open-source client, maps file reads to S3 GETs at up to 100 Gb/s per instance19.
  • S3 Tables (Iceberg, December 2024) and S3 Vectors (GA December 2025, up to 2 billion vectors per index) pull analytics and RAG data into the object layer2021 (Chapter 33).

AWS did not invent a new file system for AI. It runs open-source Lustre as a service and keeps proprietary effort where scale pays: the object store, the EFA network and Nitro offload cards.

docs.title: Azure: Blob at exabyte scale plus managed Lustre
docs.text: Microsoft centres on Blob, whose "scaled accounts" let OpenAI run exabyte-scale datasets across regions22. For POSIX, Azure Managed Lustre's AMLFS 20 SKU (preview, November 2025) reaches 25 PiB and 512 GB/s in one namespace, which is 20 MB/s per TiB: a bandwidth-light, capacity-heavy tier, with one extra metadata server per 5 PiB23. Azure was the first hyperscale service submitted to MLPerf Storage, at 642 GiB/s checkpoint write in v3.024 (Chapter 37). Azure also offers VAST through its Native ISV Service25.

docs.title: DeepSeek 3FS: the open hyperscale design
docs.text: DeepSeek open-sourced its Fire-Flyer File System (3FS) in February 202526. Its design follows the same pattern: stateless metadata services on a transactional key-value store (FoundationDB), chain replication (CRAQ) for strong consistency, and storage nodes shared by all clients. A 180-node cluster, each node with 2×200 Gb/s InfiniBand and sixteen NVMe SSDs, reached ~6.6 TiB/s aggregate reads27. Per node: 6.6 TiB/s ÷ 180 ≈ 37.5 GiB/s, against a line rate of 400 Gb/s ≈ 46.6 GiB/s, or ~80% of the NIC. Built for AI rather than photo archives, it is all-flash. It shows an AI lab can build hyperscaler-class storage and give it away, which pressures proprietary software pricing.

docs.title: Build versus buy, and the custom-silicon parallel
docs.text:
Buyer Builds Buys Why Top hyperscalers (Google, Meta, AWS, Microsoft) File system, metadata, erasure coding, caching, client libraries; servers to OCP-style specs HDDs, NAND/SSDs, NICs; selective IP licences (DirectFlash); partner software inside some cloud services Exabyte scale amortizes large teams; control of the whole stack; media is a commodity where suppliers have scale AI labs with own clusters (DeepSeek, Meta FAIR-type) Lean parallel FS (3FS) or a tuned hyperscaler FS Servers, SSDs, InfiniBand Workload is narrow and known; talent concentrated Neoclouds (CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda) Object layer and GPU-side caches (e.g., CoreWeave LOTA)28 Dedicated file systems from VAST, WEKA, DDN, Everpure28 Time to market; customer demand for certified, known systems; small storage teams (Chapter 35) Large enterprises Almost nothing below the data platform Arrays and SDS (Everpure, NetApp, Dell, VAST) or cloud services No scale to amortize a storage team; need support, SLAs, features

Table 36.1 — The build boundary falls as scale rises: hyperscalers build everything except media, neoclouds build only the GPU-side glue, and enterprises buy systems.

The logic mirrors silicon. Google ran the TPU for about a year before announcing it in May 201629. AWS bought Annapurna Labs in 2015 to build Nitro, then Graviton and Trainium (announced December 2020)30. The design is proprietary; the wafers come from a foundry. In storage, the file system is the chip design and NAND and HDDs are foundry capacity bought on the merchant market. A DirectFlash licence is like licensing a SerDes or CPU core: IP that speeds up an in-house design without ceding control to a system vendor.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Vendor How it reaches hyperscalers What the hyperscaler gets Strength Weakness Everpure DirectFlash software and module design licence plus non-NAND parts; the customer buys NAND12 Raw-NAND management at high density under its own file system The only array vendor publicly known to sit inside a top-five hyperscaler's own storage; no NAND inventory risk Two customers; a hyperscaler could rebuild the function with FDP SSDs DDN Engine of a first-party cloud service (Google Cloud Managed Lustre)6 Proven Lustre for cloud tenants Lustre depth; Google brand Sells to the cloud service, not Google's internal storage VAST Managed marketplace services on Google Cloud and Azure2531 A turnkey AI data platform for tenants Fast GTM; same software as on-prem Marketplace revenue, not internal infrastructure Hammerspace Co-developed parallel NFS for Meta's GenAI clusters9 Standards-based NFS over existing storage Inside Meta's AI stack Software layer over others' storage Commodity SSD makers (Samsung, Solidigm, Micron) Direct supply; standards such as FDP Standard QLC/TLC SSDs Scale, multiple sources Little differentiation

Table 36.2 — Vendors enter hyperscalers either through internal infrastructure as IP or components, or through cloud services as managed partners; only the first touches the exabytes.

The steelman against Everpure is that hyperscalers can build it. NVMe Flexible Data Placement, driven by Meta and Google, lets standard SSDs take placement hints and removes much of the write amplification DirectFlash targets (Chapter 26). Meta runs standard QLC SSDs alongside DFMs11. The counter-argument is revealed preference: when Meta wanted raw-flash control at scale, it licensed it, and a second top-five hyperscaler followed in August 2026, with revenue expected from FY20282. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: which other hyperscaler file systems face the same HDD-to-flash pressure, and whether the licence can extend to software above the FTL.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline

    2003 : Google publishes the GFS paper
    2015 : Amazon buys Annapurna Labs
    2016 : Google announces the TPU
    2021 : Tectonic at FAST and Colossus blog

    2026 : Rapid Bucket GA : Meta AI storage blueprint : Second hyperscaler signs DirectFlash

Figure 36.4 — The disk-era file systems of 2003–2021 were rebuilt around flash and GPU locality in 2023–2026.

Two signals point forward. Storage is moving next to the GPUs: zonal buckets, regional BLOB stacks and host-memory caches trade durability domain for latency and bandwidth. Flash is advancing into capacity tiers: in August 2025 Pure Storage expected to ship 1–2 exabytes of DirectFlash to Meta by the end of FY2632. HDDs still dominate hyperscale exabytes, and bears argue disk keeps a large TCO edge (Chapter 48); the debate is how fast flash takes share.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Which hyperscaler file systems besides Tectonic hit the same HDD bandwidth-per-TB wall?" Strong: names workloads (warm blob, AI data lakes) and how the licence fits each file system, not just the Meta story.
  2. "What do we deliver to a hyperscaler that FDP plus a standard QLC SSD doesn't?" Strong: numbers on density per rack, power, write amplification and the software the customer would otherwise maintain.
  3. "Could the licence model sell to tier-2 clouds or neoclouds that lack a Tectonic?" Strong: the licence assumes the buyer has its own file system; others need a full system such as FlashBlade//EXA.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Where does DirectFlash sit relative to the hyperscaler's file system?" Strong: at the media and flash-management layer under the storage servers, with the file system still owning placement, erasure coding and metadata (public sources don't detail the integration).
  2. "How do hyperscalers stop GPU stalls from tail latency?" Strong: hedged reads, client-side concurrency control, host-memory and local-NVMe caches, and zonal placement, as in Meta's 2026 blueprint.
  3. "What would it take for Colossus's L4 tier to move bulk data from HDD to QLC?" Strong: cost per unit of bandwidth versus cost per TB; once HDD must be over-provisioned for bandwidth, flash wins.

Don't say this:

  • "Hyperscalers buy storage arrays." Internally they buy media and occasional IP.
  • "Meta replaced its disks with Pure." Meta adds QLC as a middle tier alongside HDDs and also uses standard QLC SSDs.
  • "We compete with Colossus or Tectonic." They are internal; we compete with services built on them, such as Rapid Bucket.
  • "3FS proves storage software is worthless." A lab with a narrow workload can build its own; enterprises still pay for support and features.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• Tectonic FAST '21 paper: layered metadata and consistency semantics7.
  • CacheSack, cited in the 2025 Colossus post: the admission policy behind L44.
  • 3FS design notes: CRAQ and the USRBIO zero-copy client API27.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Colossus / Curator / D file server — Google's cluster file system, its metadata servers (on Bigtable) and its simple disk servers.
  • L4 cache — Colossus's ML-driven SSD caching and placement tier.
  • Tectonic / ZippyDB / Chunk Store — Meta's multitenant file system, the key-value store holding its metadata, and its flat data layer.
  • S3 Express One Zone / Rapid Bucket — AWS and Google zonal, low-latency object tiers built for AI.
  • Smart client — a client library that does placement and encoding itself, so no controller sits in the data path.
  • Hedged read — a duplicate request sent to a second replica to cut tail latency.
  • See the glossary for the rest.
