docs.title: 37. Reading benchmarks critically
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Performance and economics metrics · Training storage · Inference and KV cache · FlashArray and FlashBlade

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Storage benchmarks mostly measure how much hardware was submitted. Scale-out systems scale, so the biggest configuration wins. A number means little until divided by rack units, kilowatts or dollars at the buyer's capacity point.
  • MLPerf Storage uses no real GPUs. Simulated accelerators "compute" by sleeping; the score is how many the storage keeps above a utilisation threshold. That is bandwidth divided by per-accelerator demand, so results do not compare across versions.
  • Each benchmark has a blind spot. SPECstorage AI_IMAGE has few contenders; IO500 mixes units and splits production from research systems; STAC-M3 reports "X of Y" wins; vendor fio runs are only as honest as their job files.
  • Absence is data. VAST, WEKA and DDN skipped MLPerf Storage v3.0 (September 2026). Everpure's first-place checkpoint and KV-cache results are peer-reviewed and real, and they came in a field without its strongest rivals.
  • Benchmarks shortlist; proofs of concept decide. Ten questions (below) separate engineering results from marketing.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Benchmarks are how AI-storage vendors, Everpure included, turn engineering into sales claims. FlashBlade//EXA's MLPerf Storage v3.0 and SPECstorage AI_IMAGE results anchor Everpure's case for neocloud and AI-factory deals (Chapter 27), and competitors will attack them as Everpure attacks theirs. Pricing a benchmark claim separates a durable technical lead from a configuration choice, which also matters when a diligence target (Chapter 50) leads with a "world record".

Participation is itself a strategic choice: costs (engineering weeks, hardware, a possible public loss) against credibility with buyers who cannot test for themselves. Which tests to enter, and how to frame results, are options a strategy team might evaluate from public information.

docs.title: Why storage benchmarks are harder than chip benchmarks
docs.text: A CPU benchmark runs on one part. A storage benchmark runs on a system (servers, drives, network, clients, software), all chosen by the submitter. It is like a memory-bandwidth claim for a self-chosen number of HBM stacks, with no die area or power attached. Scale-out storage is near-linear by design (Chapter 15), so "fastest" usually means "largest configuration". The useful content is the result's shape: per-node rate, scaling efficiency, latency under load.

docs.title: How MLPerf Storage works
docs.text:
MLPerf Storage, from MLCommons, uses no accelerators. A tool called DLIO runs on ordinary client hosts, reads data with real data-loader behaviour, then sleeps for the time a real GPU would take to compute each batch1. The v2.0 rules list A100, H100, B200 and AMD MI3552, and v3.0 submissions simulate B200 or MI3553.

The key metric is accelerator utilisation (AU): the share of time a simulated accelerator spends "computing" rather than waiting for data. The submitter adds accelerators until AU falls below threshold and reports the largest passing count and its throughput. Under the v2.0 rules the thresholds were 90% for 3D U-Net and ResNet-50 and 70% for CosmoFlow2. In v3.0 the closed training workloads are 3D U-Net (90%) and RetinaNet (85%)43. CosmoFlow, ResNet-50, DLRM and Flux moved to an unranked "whatif" category5.

flowchart TD
    A["Client hosts run DLIO"] --> B["N simulated accelerators per host"]
    B --> C["Each step: read batch from storage, then sleep for calibrated B200 compute time"]
    C --> D{"AU at or above threshold? 90% U-Net, 85% RetinaNet"}
    D -->|"yes"| E["Add accelerators, rerun"]
    E --> B
    D -->|"no"| F["Report last passing N and samples/s"]
    F --> G["Training score: accelerators supported and MiB/s"]
    H["Checkpoint: fixed ranks 8, 64, 512, 1,024"] --> I["Write 10 checkpoints, clear cache, read 10"]
    I --> J["Score: GiB/s and duration"]
    K["v3.0 KV cache: emulated inference context reads"] --> L["Score: tokens/s or conversations"]
    M["v3.0 vector DB: DiskANN index"] --> N["Score: queries/s at stated recall"]

Figure 37.1 — MLPerf Storage turns storage bandwidth into "accelerators kept busy" by sleeping in place of compute. Checkpoint, KV-cache and vector tests score bandwidth, tokens and queries directly.

"Accelerators supported" is bandwidth in disguise. In v1.0 Huawei's OceanStor A800 fed 255 simulated H100s on 3D U-Net at 679 GB/s1. That is 679 ÷ 255 ≈ 2.7 GB/s per accelerator. DDN's EXAScaler AI400X2T reached 99,018 MiB/s with 36 H100s from 18 clients6, or ≈2.9 GB/s each. So the count is roughly throughput ÷ 2.7 GB/s. A faster simulated GPU needs more bandwidth each, so the same storage "supports" fewer, and a v3.0 B200 count cannot be set against a v2.0 H100 count7.

Anti-gaming rules. The dataset must be at least five times total client memory, so it cannot sit in page cache. Results are the mean of consecutive runs after a warm-up, with no cherry-picking, reproducible within 5%2. Checkpointing uses fixed process counts for Llama 3 8B, 70B, 405B and 1T (8 to 1,024 ranks; about 105 GB to 18 TB per checkpoint), and hosts must clear file cache between write and read when the checkpoint is under three times client memory2. Submissions disclose topology and, for on-premises systems, rack units and the full list of powered hardware; measured power is not required, so watts must still be estimated2. Peer review is closed: submitters object to each other's results, which can be fixed, moved to the open division or withdrawn2.

Closed versus open. The closed division fixes the code and allows a few tunables such as reader threads; storage-side optimisation is unrestricted. The open division allows disclosed custom loaders, formats and framework changes2. Quoting an open result beside closed ones mixes categories.

What v3.0 added. The September 2026 round drew 143 results from 19 organisations, 11 of them first-time submitters such as Everpure, Azure, Nebius and NVIDIA. Absent were VAST, WEKA and DDN, plus v2.0 submitters such as Huawei, Hammerspace and Lightbits87. It added a KV-cache test (a working-group emulation scoring how fast storage feeds inference context), a Milvus-based vector-database test that scores queries per second at stated recall, and an S3 object path beside POSIX849. Reports differ on the vector dataset size: 10 million vectors in the closed configuration versus 1 million at 1,536 dimensions [VERIFY: vector DB dataset size and index type in v3.0 rules]49. Power and rack-space efficiency began to be tracked as reported metrics7 [VERIFY: search-summary only].

docs.title: The other benchmarks
docs.text:
Benchmark What it measures Who runs / audits it Main metric How gameable Best used for MLPerf Storage (MLCommons) Training reads, checkpoint write/read, KV-cache reads, vector search, all with simulated accelerators Vendor runs; closed peer review among submitters2 Accelerators supported, GiB/s, tokens/s, QPS Medium: config size, client count, choosing which workloads to enter AI training and checkpoint shortlisting SPECstorage Solution 2020 (SPEC) Five file workloads: AI_IMAGE, EDA_BLENDED, GENOMICS, SWBUILD, VDA Vendor runs; SPEC review before publication Business metric (e.g., AI_Jobs) at an overall response time (ORT)10 Medium: thin fields per workload, cross-workload comparisons barred by SPEC10 File-system latency under rising load IO500 IOR easy (large sequential) and hard (small, shared-file) bandwidth, mdtest easy/hard metadata, parallel find Sites or vendors submit; committee scores reproducibility11 Geometric mean of a bandwidth score and a metadata score12 High: metadata-heavy tricks, research-grade software, client count (hence the 10-node list) HPC parallel file systems, metadata stress STAC-M3 (STAC) kdb+ tick-data analytics (Antuco, Kanaga suites) STAC audits vendor-sponsored runs Mean response times across dozens of tests13 Medium: "best in X of Y" reporting, full reports often subscriber-only Financial time-series buyers Vendor fio / elbencho / GDSIO Whatever the job file says Vendor, unaudited GB/s, IOPS, latency Very high: block size, queue depth, compressible buffers, cache-resident working sets Engineering tuning and POC scripts, never as a claim

Table 37.1 — The five benchmark families an AI-storage buyer meets. Gameability rises as audit and fixed rules fall away.

SPECstorage Solution 2020 replaced SPEC SFS 2014 in late 202014. Each workload scales "business units" until response time collapses, yielding a load-latency curve, which says more than a single peak. The AI_IMAGE field is thin. WEKA on HPE hardware topped all five workloads in February 2025, including 5,000 AI_Jobs15. FlashBlade//EXA posted 6,300 AI_Jobs at 0.97 ms ORT in February 2026, using 30 blades, 60 data nodes and 80 client hosts1617.

IO500 scores bandwidth tests in GiB/s and metadata tests in kIOPS, then takes a geometric mean. The mixed units have no physical meaning, and strong metadata can carry weak bandwidth12. Write phases must run at least 300 seconds18. Since ISC23 a reproducibility questionnaire splits a Production list from a Research list11. That rule bit at ISC26. Sugon's ParaStor F9000 entry, scoring 79,110 (on 500 client nodes) against Aurora's 32,166, was moved to the Research list for lack of widely available architecture details1920. Sugon's press release had claimed No. 1 on both production lists; always ask which list, and when. DDN's ISC25 "#1" claim concerned the 10-node production list, where Argonne's DAOS systems actually held the top two places and a DDN EXAScaler system was third; WEKA disputed the claim21.

STAC-M3 is audited, but results are framed as wins on subsets, for example "19 of 24 Kanaga benchmarks" and "1.77× faster than a Pure Storage based SUT" on one metric13, or "12 of 17 Antuco" for Dell PowerScale22. Ask which tests were lost.

docs.title: Where a v3.0 headline comes from
docs.text:
Figure 37.2 — The same EXA design gives 327.6 or 877.5 GiB/s depending on how many data nodes were submitted. The ranking is mostly a ranking of configuration size. Data: data/ch37_mlperf_v3_checkpoint.csv

Change the denominator and the story changes. EXA delivers 877.52 ÷ 30 ≈ 29.3 GiB/s per data node, or ≈14.6 if its 30 metadata blades count too23. NVIDIA's AIStore delivers 133.27 ÷ 12 ≈ 11.1 GiB/s per node, at about 95% of nominal NIC bandwidth: a network-bound, well-tuned cloud result24. Alluxio's 147 GiB/s used the smaller 405B model through a cache over Amazon S325. Azure publishes no node count and warns against normalising by clients26; for a cloud service the honest denominator is provisioned capacity and price. The choice of denominator is the argument.

docs.title: How vendors game benchmarks
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Vendor benchmark claim"] --> B{"Audited and peer-reviewed?"}
    B -->|"no: own fio or elbencho"| C["Treat as marketing; ask for job files"]
    B -->|"yes"| D{"Closed division, current version?"}
    D -->|"no"| E["Open division or old round: not comparable"]
    D -->|"yes"| F{"Workload matches yours?"}
    F -->|"no"| G["Cherry-picked test: ask what was not entered"]
    F -->|"yes"| H{"Config, clients, RU, power disclosed?"}
    H -->|"no"| I["Hero config suspected"]
    H -->|"yes"| J["Normalize per RU, kW and dollar at your capacity"]
    J --> K{"Did the main rivals submit?"}
    K -->|"no"| L["Rank is within entrants only"]
    K -->|"yes"| M["Shortlist, then POC on your data"]

Figure 37.3 — A claim has to survive five gates before it says anything about your deployment. Most fail at "workload matches yours" or "rivals submitted".

The recurring tactics:

  1. Hero configurations. Submit the largest system you can borrow; none of these benchmarks reports price.
  2. Client inflation. More clients bring more DRAM and NICs. DDN's 36-accelerator v1.0 result used 18 clients6.
  3. Caching and compressible data. Vendor working sets that fit in DRAM, or fio buffers that are zero-filled or highly compressible on arrays with inline reduction, Everpure's included (Chapter 5).
  4. Division and version mixing. Open next to closed, H100 next to B200, GiB next to GB (1 GiB/s ≈ 1.074 GB/s).
  5. Workload cherry-picking. Enter checkpointing and skip training, or report "#1 on every test entered". Everpure uses that framing for v3.027.
  6. Flattering denominators. Per data node excluding metadata servers, per client, per undefined "rack".
  7. Unverified previews. Hammerspace's v1.0 records were first reported before verification28. Pure Storage published a v2.0 white paper that was not an official listed submission29.
  8. Not submitting. Absence avoids a public loss. StorageReview lists no published MLPerf result for VAST in any round30, and VAST, WEKA and DDN all skipped v3.07.

docs.title: Worked normalisation example (illustrative assumptions)
docs.text:
Two hypothetical submissions; every figure is an assumption, realistic in shape but not any product's data.

Metric Submission A (60 servers) Submission B (10 servers) Arithmetic Checkpoint write 900 GB/s 300 GB/s Assumed Rack units incl. switches 130 U 24 U Assumed: 2U servers + network Power 70 kW 15.5 kW Assumed Price (3-year, installed) $9.0M $2.4M Assumed Usable capacity 4.0 PB 0.5 PB Assumed GB/s per RU 6.9 12.5 900/130; 300/24 GB/s per kW 12.9 19.4 900/70; 300/15.5 GB/s per $M 100 125 900/9.0; 300/2.4 Cost to meet 900 GB/s + 4 PB $9.0M (1 unit) $19.2M (8 units, capacity-bound) 4.0/0.5 = 8 Cost to meet 900 GB/s + 1 PB $9.0M (1 unit) $7.2M (3 units, bandwidth-bound) 900/300 = 3

Table 37.2 — B wins every ratio, but A is cheaper once the buyer needs 4 PB. Normalise at the customer's requirement point, not at the vendor's.

The semiconductor parallel is perf-per-watt at a fixed workload versus peak TOPS. What predicts the buyer's bill is cost at their bandwidth-to-capacity ratio, exactly the axis on which architectures differ (Chapter 16; Chapter 38).

docs.title: Ten questions to ask any vendor benchmark claim
docs.text:
1. Which benchmark, version and division, and is the result listed by the benchmark body?
  2. What exact hardware ran it: storage nodes, metadata nodes, drives, NICs, switches?
  3. How many client hosts, with how much DRAM, and was the dataset larger than their combined memory?
  4. What is the per-node, per-RU and per-kW figure, and what does that configuration cost?
  5. Was the tested media the media you would buy (for example DFMs versus commodity NVMe)?
  6. Which workloads did you skip, and why?
  7. Which competitors were in the same round?
  8. Is this read or write, peak or sustained, GB or GiB?
  9. How did throughput scale from the smallest configuration tested to the largest?
  10. Will you run the same harness on our data, at our scale, in a POC?

docs.text:
Vendor MLPerf Storage SPECstorage 2020 IO500 STAC-M3 Reading Everpure v3.0 first submission: top checkpoint write and KV-cache results237; v2.0 white paper only29 AI_IMAGE #1, 6,300 AI_Jobs (Feb 2026)16 None found Pure Storage-based SUT cited as a comparison point13 Strong, audited numbers in rounds rivals skipped VAST Never submitted30 None found None found None found Sells on references, POCs and NVIDIA alignment WEKA v0.5 and v1.0; not v2.0 or v3.03132 All five workloads #1 (Feb 2025); AI_IMAGE since passed by EXA1517 Customer submissions, e.g., 665.49 at a cancer research centre (company-stated)33 kdb+ on AWS (2021)34 Prefers benchmarks it can win broadly DDN v0.5, v1.0 and v2.0; skipped v3.0316357 None found Frequent; "#1" claims on the 10-node list21 EXAScaler AI400X (2020)36 HPC-native benchmark culture Azure, NVIDIA, Nebius First-time v3.0 entrants8 n/a n/a n/a Clouds now benchmark managed storage too

Table 37.3 — Who enters which benchmark is itself a positioning signal.

Apply the same scrutiny to Everpure. The case for its v3.0 result is strong: peer-reviewed, the round's largest checkpoint write, about 89% per-node efficiency from 10 to 30 data nodes (Chapter 27), and 1,623.4 GiB/s of KV-cache read on 51 hosts7. That KV-cache lead is partly scale: the best standard-scale entries (UBIX, FarmGPU) reported about 444 GiB/s on smaller configurations, so normalise per host before quoting a multiple. The caveats:

  • The data nodes were third-party Linux/NVMe servers, so the result says little about DirectFlash economics.
  • No price was disclosed.
  • Checkpoint read was 588.3 GiB/s, below the 877.5 GiB/s write, per Everpure's release and Blocks & Files; one StorageReview passage gives 833.0 GiB/s, apparently in error239. A restore-heavy buyer should anchor on the read figure.
  • KV cache is a first-round workload with few entrants.
  • Coverage shows no EXA training-workload result: YanRong (543.9 GiB/s on 3D U-Net) and HPE led the training tables7 [VERIFY: confirm on the MLCommons results table that EXA entered no training workload].

The abstainers' steelman is real: neocloud-scale buyers run their own acceptance tests, a run costs engineering weeks, and a loss is public forever. So is the counter: enterprise buyers without test labs lean on audited results.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Storage benchmarks that matter for AI buyers
    2017 : IO500 first list at SC17
    2020 : SPECstorage Solution 2020 replaces SPEC SFS 2014
    2023 : MLPerf Storage v0.5 : IO500 splits Production and Research lists
    2024 : MLPerf Storage v1.0 - 13 organisations
    2025 : MLPerf v2.0 adds checkpointing - 26 organisations : WEKA tops all SPECstorage workloads
    2026 : EXA tops SPEC AI_IMAGE : IO500 moves Sugon to Research list : MLPerf v3.0 adds KV cache, vector DB and S3

Figure 37.4 — Benchmarks have moved from HPC file I/O toward the AI pipeline. Each round adds a stage, from training reads to checkpointing to inference context.

IO500's first list was released at SC17 in November 201737, and MLPerf Storage v0.5 published its first results, from five submitters including DDN and WEKA, in September 202331. MLPerf Storage grew from 13 organisations in v1.0 (September 2024)32 to 26 in v2.0 (August 2025), when checkpointing arrived38, then shrank to 19 in v3.0 even as it added inference workloads8. Benchmarks follow the I/O hot spot, which in 2026 is KV-cache offload (Chapter 32) and S3 access9. Watch whether VAST, WEKA or DDN enter v4.0, whether power and rack-unit efficiency become ranked metrics, and whether IO500's reproducibility gate spreads.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Why did we enter checkpointing and KV cache in v3.0 but not training?" Strong answer: names the target buyer and says what a training entry would have shown.
  2. "How do sellers answer 'VAST and WEKA didn't need MLPerf'?" Strong answer: concedes POCs dominate at neocloud scale; positions peer-reviewed results as risk reduction for enterprises without test labs.
  3. "What is EXA's cost per GB/s at a customer's capacity point?" Strong answer: a range at two or three bandwidth-to-capacity ratios, not a headline.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "In the 30-node checkpoint run, what was the bottleneck?" Strong answer: names NICs, SSDs or metadata with per-node numbers, and explains the 11% per-node falloff.
  2. "Why did checkpoint read (588 GiB/s) trail write (878 GiB/s)?" Strong answer: cites the 3×-memory cache-clear rule and client DRAM sizes, and names the read-path bottleneck (metadata, data-node NICs or client parallelism).
  3. "What would change with DFM-based data nodes?" Strong answer: separates media from network and software effects, and admits the current result does not test DirectFlash.

Don't say this:

  • "EXA beat VAST and WEKA in MLPerf." They did not enter v3.0.
  • "MLPerf Storage tested real B200s." The accelerators are simulated.
  • Comparing v3.0 with v2.0 results. The simulated accelerator changed, and Pure's v2.0 numbers were not an official submission.
  • "IO500 #1" without naming the list (production or research, full or 10-node) and the date.
  • Quoting GiB/s and GB/s in the same comparison.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Accelerator utilisation (AU) — share of time a simulated accelerator computes rather than waits.
  • Closed / open division — fixed-code results versus disclosed modifications.
  • Hero configuration — a system sized to win a headline, not to match a purchase.
  • See the glossary for MLPerf Storage, DLIO, SPECstorage, IO500, STAC-M3 and the rest.

docs.title: 38. Power, density and the AI datacenter
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Media physics · Performance and economics metrics · Purity and DirectFlash · AI factories and neoclouds

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• AI datacenters are power-limited, not chip-limited. NVIDIA, Microsoft, AWS, Meta and CoreWeave have all said so publicly. A site's grid connection caps its GPUs, so every storage watt is a watt that cannot run a GPU.
  • QLC flash beats disk about 2× per watt at the drive (~8.2 against ~4.4 TB/W for the best of each). At system level the gap depends on drive size and on what sits in the box. A 2022-era flash enclosure can lose to a modern disk JBOD.
  • Density is where flash pulls away. A rack of 245 TB QLC drives holds roughly 5× the raw petabytes of a rack of 44 TB disks. It also needs 2–3× the power per rack, which many halls cannot feed.
  • At grid prices, power savings never pay for the flash premium. Storing 100 PB for five years on QLC rather than disk saves about 1.2 GWh, or roughly $170K, against a media premium of $8–37M on Chapter 4's inputs, and more at index prices. Flash wins when bandwidth per TB is required or when NAND is bought at hyperscaler cost; turning freed watts into GPUs helps but rarely closes the gap on its own.
  • Disk still wins cold data at rest, on $/TB and on embodied carbon. HAMR roadmaps (100 TB by 2029) improve disk's TB/W every generation. Vendor power claims from both camps need system-level, same-basis checks.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
"Flash replaces disk" used to be a cost-curve argument. With enterprise QLC at 15–23× disk per TB in 2026 (Chapter 2), it is now a power argument. Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) has made that argument central. Its DirectFlash hyperscaler wins were explained in terms of footprint and power (Chapter 29), and it sells a contractual watts-per-TiB guarantee. If power stays the binding constraint for AI build-outs, a vendor with the best system-level TB/W has a demand driver that is independent of the NAND price cycle. If grid supply loosens, or HAMR closes the gap, the pitch falls back to $/TB, where disk wins.

This chapter gives the arithmetic to tell which world a deal is in. It builds on the metrics in Chapter 4 and the module design in Chapter 26, and does not repeat them.

docs.title: The site power cap is the budget everything else comes out of
docs.text:
An AI campus starts from a fixed grid allocation, measured in megawatts and set years ahead by utilities and permits. GPUs are the revenue engine, so operators hand them as much of that allocation as possible. Networking, cooling overhead and storage share what is left. The leaders say this openly.

Company Who / where What was said Date NVIDIA Jensen Huang, GTC keynote "We are now a power-limited industry"; revenue tracks available power1 2025-03 AWS Andy Jassy, Q2 2025 earnings call "The single biggest constraint is power"2 2025-07-31 Microsoft Satya Nadella, Bg2 podcast GPUs sit in inventory for lack of powered shells to install them in3 late 2025 Meta Mark Zuckerberg, Dwarkesh podcast Energy, not chips, would bound cluster build-out4 2024-04 CoreWeave Q2 2026 results 1.5 GW active, 3.7 GW contracted; >1.85 GW active targeted by end-20265 2026-08-11 Meta storage team FMS 2025 talk on QLC QLC racks exceed 10 PB, but power is still higher than Meta would like6 2025-08-06

Table 38.1 — Hyperscaler and neocloud leaders frame power, not silicon, as the binding constraint, and even flash's champions at Meta still want lower watts.

Gartner expects datacenter electricity use to grow 26% in 20267. That gives a decision chain:

flowchart TD
    A["Grid allocation per site, MW"] --> B["GPU racks: about 120 kW per NVL72"]
    A --> C["Cooling and distribution overhead, PUE"]
    B --> D["Residual IT power for storage and network"]
    D --> E{"Is storage power binding?"}
    E -->|"No: power is plentiful"| F["Optimise $/TB: disk for cold, flash for hot"]
    E -->|"Yes: every kW is a GPU"| G{"Bandwidth per TB needed?"}
    G -->|"Low, cold data"| H["HDD plus flash cache, accept racks"]
    G -->|"High, AI data"| I["QLC flash for capacity tier"]
    I --> J["Vendor choice on system TB/W, TB per rack, GB/s per kW"]
    H --> K["Vendor choice on $/TB, rebuild time, weight"]

Figure 38.1 — The site power cap flows down to storage; the flash-versus-disk choice turns on whether storage watts displace GPUs and how much bandwidth each terabyte must serve.

At about 120 kW per GB200 NVL72 rack8, one GPU and its share of the rack draws roughly 1.7 kW. Chapter 35 works out storage at about 4% of a GPU row's power. Small, but not free.

docs.title: Semiconductor bridge: storage after the end of frequency scaling
docs.text: This is the move chip design made around 2005, when Dennard scaling ended. Once power density stopped falling with each node, clock frequency stopped being the goal. Designs became power-limited, and perf/W became the metric that sold chips. In a fixed-TDP SoC, watts saved in the uncore (I/O, fabric, memory controllers) become turbo headroom for the cores. Storage is the AI campus's uncore. Every watt it saves goes to the "cores", the GPUs, and Huang's framing makes tokens per watt the revenue metric. Storage vendors are being pulled into perf/W thinking the way CPU vendors were twenty years ago.

docs.title: TB per watt: what the datasheets actually say
docs.text:
Figure 38.2 — At the drive, QLC is about 2× disk per watt; at system level, older flash enclosures and performance appliances can trail a modern disk JBOD. Data: data/ch38_tb_per_watt.csv

Three readings matter. First, drive-level TB/W tracks capacity per device, because power per device barely changes. A nearline disk draws about 9.5–10 W whether it holds 30 or 44 TB910. A large QLC drive draws 25–30 W whether it holds 122 or 245 TB1110. Everpure's 75 TB module was stated at under 10 W12. Second, system overhead swamps drive differences. Controllers, fans, NICs and DRAM cut TB/W 2–10×. VAST's 1U DBox reaches about 1.9 TB/W before its CNodes13. A WD 102-bay JBOD of 22 TB disks reaches about 1.7 TB/W before its head server14; filled with 44 TB disks at similar watts it would reach about 3.5 TB/W (illustrative), ahead of the DBox. Everpure's FlashBlade//E (0.83 W/TB per expansion) and FlashBlade//S500 (1.3 W/TB) include their compute1516. Third, performance boxes sit in a different class. DDN's 2U AI400X3 is rated at 2,400 W17, about 0.2 usable TB/W on an implied ~500 TB [VERIFY: usable capacity per appliance]. It is built for GB/s per kW, not TB/W, and its TB/W depends on the drives fitted: the AI400X3M variant launched in June 2026 offers up to 2 PB usable per appliance18, so read the DDN bar as one configuration, not a ceiling.

The lesson: compare systems at the same scope, watts basis and drive generation.

docs.title: Rack density: petabytes per rack
docs.text:
Configuration (42U rack, ~36U for storage) Devices Raw PB per rack IT kW per rack Basis 7 × 4U 106-bay JBOD + 4 head servers, 44 TB HDD 742 32.6 ~11 Worked example: 15 W per bay all-in Same, 100 TB HAMR (WD 2029 roadmap19) 742 74.2 ~11 Illustrative 30 × 1U servers, 24 × 122.88 TB QLC 720 88.5 ~32 Worked example: 25 W/drive + 450 W/server 30 × 1U servers, 24 × 245.76 TB QLC 720 176.9 ~32 Matches Micron's 720-drive rack10 Deployed hyperscale QLC rack (Meta) n/d >10 n/d FMS 20256

Table 38.2 — Illustrative: QLC holds about 5× the petabytes per rack of 44 TB disk, but at about 3× the kW, so real racks are often power-capped far below the theoretical maximum.

Two caveats keep this honest. A full flash rack at ~32 kW exceeds the 10–15 kW many air-cooled halls feed, so operators spread it across racks. And deployed racks, such as Meta's ">10 PB", run well below the theoretical ceiling because of power, cooling, network ports and drive generation. Disk racks hit a different wall: floor loading. A rack of 742 nearline drives weighs well over a tonne.

docs.title: Worked example: 100 PB for five years
docs.text:
Requirement: 100 PB usable, held flat for five years, read-mostly. Illustrative: per-bay and per-server watts, PUE and usable ratios are this atlas's assumptions; prices are sourced.

Line HDD (44 TB) QLC (245.76 TB) Basis Raw capacity at 75% usable 133.3 PB 133.3 PB 8+2 erasure coding plus spares, assumption Devices 3,030 drives 543 drives in 23 servers Raw ÷ drive size IT power 45.5 kW 23.9 kW HDD 15 W/bay all-in (WD JBOD ≈12.7 W/bay14 + head share); QLC 25 W/drive + 450 W/server Racks 5 1 (2 if capped at ~15 kW) Table 38.2 Facility power at PUE 1.3 59.1 kW 31.1 kW Assumption for a new AI-class hall Energy, 5 years 2.59 GWh 1.36 GWh × 43,800 h Energy cost at $0.1385/kWh $359K $189K US commercial average20; at Chapter 4's PUE of 1.54 the saving is ~$200K Media cost, 2026 prices $2.9M ($22/TB, Q1); ~$5.4M (~$40/TB, Q3) $40.3M ($302/TB) HDD2122; QLC23; a 13.7× premium versus the 22.6× index Media cost, mid-2025 prices $2.2M ($16.50/TB) $10.7M ($80/TB) 21 Embodied carbon, media ~2.7 kt CO2e ~21.3 kt CO2e 0.16 kg/GB flash, about 1/8 for disk24

Table 38.3 — Illustrative: QLC halves the power and cuts racks 5×, but the ~$170K energy saving is two orders of magnitude smaller than the media premium.

The media inputs are the same as Chapter 4's and are kind to flash. $302 against $22 per TB is a 13.7× premium, below the 22.6× index headline, because a 122 TB drive's street price per TB sits under the index's 30 TB QLC drive (about $504/TB in Q1 2026)25. At that index price the QLC media would cost ~$67M. Disk moved too: the same index put a 30 TB HDD at about $1,216 (~$40/TB) by Q3 202622, which lifts the HDD media line to ~$5.4M and leaves the 2026 premium at ~$35M. Every variant leaves the energy saving two orders of magnitude below the premium.

The flash case has three escape routes from that table.

1. Freed watts become GPUs. The 21.6 kW of IT power saved is about 13 GPU slots at 1.7 kW each. At CoreWeave's US$6.16 H100 list price per GPU-hour26, 13 GPUs would bill about $3.5M over five years. That is gross rental, before the GPUs' own capex, financing and operating cost, and it prices a GB200-class power slot at an H100 rate, so treat it as an upper bound. Chapter 4 values a freed kilowatt at an assumed $15,000 a year, which puts the slot at about $1.6M. Either figure beats the electricity saving many times over. Neither covers the ~$37M premium at 2026 NAND prices, and even the upper bound covers under half of the ~$8.5M premium at mid-2025 prices. Premium and freed watts both scale with capacity, so scale alone does not close the gap: this route works only alongside routes 2 or 3.

2. Bandwidth per TB is required. Meta's argument for QLC is that disk bandwidth per TB keeps falling as drives grow27. Meta places QLC at workloads needing about 10 MB/s per TB. For 100 PB usable that means 1 TB/s. A nearline disk streams perhaps 250 MB/s at best and far less under mixed access. At an assumed 125 MB/s effective, you need about 8,000 drives instead of 3,030, roughly 120 kW. That is 5× the flash option's power, the regime where vendor claims of "75% less power" become plausible.

3. NAND at hyperscaler cost. In Everpure's second hyperscaler deal the customer buys its own NAND28. The NAND then reaches the buyer near contract price, not array street price, which shrinks the media premium. That is why hyperscalers move first.

docs.title: Where disk still wins
docs.text: Disk wins cold data at rest: archives, backup copies and data lakes read rarely. There the bandwidth requirement is low and $/TB dominates. It also wins on embodied carbon. Tannu and Nair estimated about 0.16 kg CO2e per GB to manufacture flash, about 8× disk per unit of capacity24. In the example above, the embodied gap (~18.6 kt) dwarfs the operational savings (1.23 GWh, or 120–620 t at any grid intensity from 0.1 to 0.5 kg/kWh). That 2022 figure predates today's denser NAND, so treat it as an order of magnitude. Flash's carbon case leans on longer service life and on avoided racks and buildings.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Camp Headline power/density claim Basis Steelman or caveat Everpure DFMs use up to 75% less power than disk in hyperscale (company-stated)29; disk and 15 TB-SSD systems draw 2.4× its 75 TB-DFM system and 4.8× its 150 TB-DFM system (company-stated)30; watts/TiB guarantee on Evergreen//One31 Own system models; guarantee is contractual Strongest when DFM size leads commodity SSDs; guarantee assumes data reduction on most tiers (Chapter 4) Commodity QLC (Micron, Solidigm) ~8.2 vs ~4.4 TB/W drive-level (vendor)10; 1 EB study: 77% less power, 90% less space than HDD on Ceph (vendor)32 Drive max watts; 10-year model Credible at drive level; system results depend on the software vendor VAST ~500 W per PB with 30 TB QLC (company-stated, 2021)33 DBox plus CNodes Pioneered QLC at scale; the 61 TB-drive DBox in Figure 38.2 trails 245 TB-class designs, and its TB/W rises with larger drives HDD vendors (Seagate, WD) Disk more cost- and energy-efficient per TB for mass data (Seagate CEO)34; Mozaic 3+ cuts power per TB 40% and embodied carbon per TB 55%, the latter against a 16 TB PMR drive (vendor)35 Per-drive, own baseline Right on $/TB and embodied carbon; weak on bandwidth per TB VDURA (hybrid) HDD systems lower total carbon (vendor)36; QLC at 22.6× HDD $/TB in Q1 202625 Hybrid flash plus HDD Price data is real; argues mixed fleets

Table 38.4 — Every camp's power claim is true at its chosen scope; the counter-question is always "whole system, same watts basis, same drive generation, your bandwidth per TB".

Everpure's structural edge is that it owns the flash translation layer, so its module capacity can run ahead of commodity SSDs. That edge narrows whenever a 245 TB drive ships (Chapter 26). The steelman for VAST and WEKA is that commodity 245 TB QLC brings much of the TB/W benefit with a broader supply base. The steelman for disk is the table above: at 2026 prices, cold exabytes stay on HDD. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: publishing audited system-level TB/W and GB/s per kW against NVIDIA reference sizings, and pricing guarantees per usable TiB for AI data that does not reduce.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
In 2021, flash vendors like VAST argued density per rack unit33. In 2023, Pure Storage added a watts-per-TiB SLA31 and showed roughly 1 W/TB with FlashBlade//E15. In 2024–25 power entered the CEO vocabulary: Zuckerberg4, Huang1, Jassy2. Meta published its QLC case27, widely read as pointing to DirectFlash, and Pure's hyperscaler revenue began. In 2026, 245 TB QLC drives shipped10 while NAND prices rose every quarter37. That widened the $/TB gap just as the power argument peaked.

Disk is not standing still. Western Digital targets HAMR at 100 TB by 202919. At constant ~10 W per drive that is ~10 TB/W, about today's best QLC at the drive. Expect flash to answer with 512 TB-class drives and larger modules (Chapter 53), and the contest to shift from TB/W to GB/s per kW, where disk cannot follow.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In a power-capped AI deal, what is our system TB/W and GB/s per kW at the customer's real configuration, including compute?" Strong: a number with scope and watts basis stated, and a named competitor configuration.
  2. "Where do we lose to disk, and do we walk away?" Strong: cold archive and backup at 2026 NAND prices; a break-even $/TB premium per segment.
  3. "How does the watts-per-TiB guarantee behave on AI data that does not reduce?" Strong: the usable-capacity figure and who bears the risk.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What fraction of system power is NAND, and what is controller, DRAM, fans and NICs?" Strong: a breakdown showing where DFM design saves watts, not just "bigger modules".
  2. "What do our boxes draw idle, at read-mostly load and during rebuild?" Strong: measured curves, not nameplate.
  3. "How does QLC write power scale with sustained ingest?" Strong: watts per GB/s written, and how the write path limits it.

Don't say this:

  • "Flash saves so much power it pays for itself." Not at grid prices: about $170K against tens of millions for 100 PB.
  • "Our TB/W beats disk," comparing a drive with an enclosure. Compare whole systems.
  • "HDD is dead." Disks are shipping at 40–44 TB, with HAMR targeting 100 TB.
  • "Storage power is a big share of an AI datacenter." It is a few percent; it matters only because the cap is hard.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• Meta's QLC case and E2 form-factor work276: bandwidth per TB as the tiering criterion.
  • Tannu and Nair, "The Dirty Secret of SSDs"24: embodied-carbon method and its sensitivity to refresh cycles.
  • Chapter 48 for how NAND pricing moves the break-even.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Power cap (site) — the fixed grid allocation that bounds all IT load.
  • TB/W — capacity per watt; drive-level and system-level figures differ widely.
  • PB per rack — rack density, limited by power, cooling and floor loading.
  • GB/s per kW — bandwidth per kilowatt, the AI-era storage efficiency metric.
  • Bandwidth per TB — throughput a device delivers per unit of capacity; falls as disks grow.
  • HAMR — heat-assisted magnetic recording, disk's capacity roadmap.
  • Embodied carbon — emissions from manufacturing hardware.
  • Dennard scaling — the historical rule that kept power density constant as transistors shrank.
  • Powered shell — a datacenter building with grid power and cooling ready for IT.

docs.title: 39. Agentic AI and data intelligence
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Metadata · Control planes · Platform and software · The AI data pipeline end to end · RAG, vector databases and AI-native data formats

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Agents turn metadata into a product. An agent can only use data it can find, interpret and is allowed to touch, so knowing what exists, what it means and who may use it becomes as valuable as the bytes.
  • MCP is becoming the agent's I/O bus. The Model Context Protocol (open-sourced November 2024, given to a Linux Foundation fund in December 2025, >10,000 servers) standardises how agents call tools1. Bulk data still moves over S3, NFS and SQL.
  • Agents change the access pattern. An agent fans one question out into dozens of tool calls and hundreds of small reads, each needing a delegated permission decision and a log line.
  • Every storage vendor now claims this layer. VAST, NetApp, Dell, Hammerspace, Cohesity and Everpure (Data Intelligence, from the US$125.0M 1touch deal2) all pitch it, against far larger catalog and data-security vendors.
  • The strategic question is neutrality. Storage vendors see every write; data and security vendors see every vendor's storage and own the buyer. A storage vendor wins only if it covers data not on its own arrays.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Everpure's "Data Primacy" pitch and its 1touch purchase rest on one bet: in an agentic enterprise, the scarce asset is trusted context about data, not capacity. If agents become the main consumers of data, control moves to whoever answers three questions per request: what is this, may this agent see it, and what did it do with it. A vendor that answers them stays sticky as hardware commoditises; one that does not becomes the S3 endpoint under someone else's catalog (Chapter 33).

The rivals are not only storage vendors. Salesforce paid US$8 billion for Informatica's catalog and governance business (closed November 2025)3. The data-security posture management (DSPM) specialist Cyera raised US$600 million at a US$12 billion valuation in June 2026, up from US$6 billion a year earlier (reported)4. Those prices show where the value sits, and how costly it is to buy in.

docs.title: Metadata is the raw material
docs.text:
A storage system holds three kinds of metadata, and owns two of them by default (Chapter 21):

  1. System metadata: names, paths, sizes, owners, access-control lists (ACLs), timestamps, snapshots, replicas.
  2. Telemetry: who read or wrote what, when, from where. Control planes such as Pure1 log it (Chapter 22).
  3. Content-derived metadata: what the bytes are. This file holds a passport number; this table is EU customer data. Producing it means opening and classifying content, the job of discovery and DSPM tools and now Everpure Data Intelligence.

Semiconductor bridge: system metadata is the tag RAM of a cache: it tells you a line exists and where. Content metadata means reading the data array itself, which costs bandwidth. Telemetry is the on-die bus monitor: only something on the write path sees every transaction without sampling, the core of the storage-vendor argument (Chapter 28).

flowchart BT
    L1["Raw storage: blocks, files, objects, snapshots"]
    L2["Metadata and telemetry: names, owners, ACLs, access logs"]
    L3["Content classification and sensitive-data discovery"]
    L4["Catalog and semantic layer: what exists, what it means"]
    L5["Governance and policy: who may use it, for what, with what log"]
    L6["AI apps and agents via MCP, SQL and APIs"]
    L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> L4 --> L5 --> L6
    O1["Storage vendors own today"] -.- L2
    O2["Contested: DSPM, catalogs, storage newcomers"] -.- L3
    O2 -.- L4
    O3["Data platforms, security and identity vendors"] -.- L5

Figure 39.1 — Each layer is built from the one below; storage vendors own the bottom two, and the fight is over layers three and four, where meaning and sensitivity are attached to the bytes.

docs.title: Catalogs and semantic layers
docs.text:
A catalog records what datasets exist, their schemas, owners, classifications and lineage. A semantic layer records what business terms mean: one governed definition of "active customer" or "net revenue", with the joins and filters that compute it. Humans carry these definitions in their heads; agents do not. Ask an LLM for "Q3 churn" over 4,000 raw tables and it guesses a join, returning a confident wrong number.

The industry is standardising this layer. Snowflake's Open Semantic Interchange (OSI) published a first, Apache-2-licensed specification in January 2026 covering datasets, metrics, dimensions and relationships. Salesforce, dbt Labs, Collibra, Atlan, Alation and dozens of others were in the working group, and Databricks joined at the January update5. Snowflake calls v1 a starting point and plans foundation-led governance. An analyst noted Everpure is not a member6 [VERIFY: search-summary only]. Semiconductor bridge: the semantic layer is the instruction-set architecture between "software" (agents) and "hardware" (tables and files), and whoever writes the ISA shapes everything above it.

docs.title: MCP: the agent's I/O bus
docs.text:
MCP defines how an AI application (the host, with an MCP client) discovers and calls an MCP server that exposes tools (actions), resources (readable data) and prompts. Messages are JSON-RPC7. MCP replaces an M × N mesh of custom connectors8: a storage vendor writes one server and every compliant agent can use it.

MCP is a control and query plane, not a data plane: an agent asking for "contracts with change-of-control clauses" gets references and snippets; training-scale bytes still move over S3, NFS or GPUDirect (Chapter 11). It also pushes security onto the server. The 2025-11-25 specification treats MCP servers as OAuth resource servers, forbids passing the client's token through to upstream APIs, and warns of confused-deputy attacks, in which a server with broad privileges is tricked into acting for a caller who lacks them9. An MCP server in front of an array is a privileged deputy by design.

docs.title: Why agents create new access patterns
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as Agent
    participant M as MCP server
    participant C as Catalog and semantic layer
    participant P as Policy engine
    participant S as Storage or database
    participant L as Audit log
    U->>A: Ask question
    A->>M: Tool call with user identity
    M->>C: Resolve business terms to datasets
    C-->>M: 25 candidate objects with classifications
    M->>P: May this user via this agent read them
    P-->>M: Allow 18, deny 7 PII, mask 2 fields
    M->>S: Parallel small reads of allowed objects
    S-->>M: Chunks and rows
    M->>L: Log request, decision, object versions
    M-->>A: Results with source references
    A-->>U: Answer with citations

Figure 39.2 — The policy check and audit write sit on the critical path of every agent tool call.

An agent splits a task into parallel sub-queries, retries and chains tools. Four properties follow.

  • Many small reads. Metadata lookups and 4–64 KB chunk fetches dominate, favouring low-latency flash and fast metadata services over raw GB/s.
  • Fan-out. Like a GPU warp's scatter-gather loads, the slowest of hundreds of object touches sets completion time.
  • Fine-grained, delegated permissions. The agent acts on behalf of a user, so the effective right is the user's entitlements intersected with the agent's scope, often at row or field level, finer than array ACLs.
  • Lineage. Auditing or undoing an action requires knowing which object versions informed it; snapshots make that possible.

Worked example (illustrative). 5,000 employees each give an agent 10 tasks a day; each task makes 8 tool calls touching 25 objects. That is 5,000 × 10 × 8 × 25 = 10 million access decisions a day. Over a 10-hour workday that averages 10M ÷ 36,000 s ≈ 280 per second, with peaks several times higher. The same humans opening ~50 files each make 250,000, 40× fewer. At ~1 KB per log record, that is ~10 GB of audit log a day, or ~1.8 TB over six months. Databricks says agents created ~80% of databases on Neon (company-stated, 2025)10.

Semiconductor bridge: the policy engine is to agents what an IOMMU is to DMA-capable devices. Every access is translated and permission-checked, and the decision cache works like an IOTLB. Too slow and every I/O stalls; cache too long and a revoked permission stays live.

docs.title: Governance becomes a runtime requirement
docs.text:
The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) entered into force on 1 August 2024. Its prohibitions applied from 2 February 2025 and general-purpose AI model obligations from 2 August 202511. For high-risk systems, defined by use case (hiring, credit, critical infrastructure), not by whether an agent is involved, Article 10 requires governed, representative training data and Article 12 automatic event logging, with logs kept at least six months11. The Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation 2026/1744, published 24 July 2026, in force 27 July 2026) moved high-risk deadlines to 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (embedded in regulated products). It did not delay prohibitions, GPAI rules or the Article 50 transparency duties, which applied from 2 August 20261213. Fines reach €35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover for prohibited practices11.

Gartner predicted in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects would be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing cost, unclear value and weak risk controls14: governance decides whether agents reach production.

docs.title: Can storage vendors own this layer?
docs.text:
The storage-vendor case: the array holds the inventory and sits on the write path, so it can classify on ingest or from snapshots without weekly crawls. It can enforce policy where the bytes live, and immutable snapshots can undo what an agent did.

The data and security-vendor case: data sits on many vendors' storage, in SaaS and in cloud, so one vendor's governance is partial; the buyer (CDO or CISO) is not the storage buyer; and catalog and DSPM vendors are neutral and already wired to identity systems. Coverage of other people's data decides it, which is why NetApp's September 2026 move to index any NFS, SMB or S3 store15 and Dell's claim that its orchestration engine works beyond Dell storage16 matter more than their feature lists.

Figure 39.3 — Atlas judgment, not vendor data: storage vendors are climbing while data vendors are not descending, and VAST sits furthest up.

Trade-offs. VAST is the steelman for "storage becomes the AI data platform": database, runtime and policy in one system, but scoped to data on VAST. NetApp has the deepest metadata heritage and now indexes rival storage. Dell (Dataloop) and Everpure (1touch) each bought a ~US$120–125M startup to get here. Cohesity and Rubrik hold a full copy of most enterprise data and can undo agent actions. Everpure's asset is entity-level classification plus a Pure1-managed fleet (Chapter 28); its gap is proof on non-Everpure data.

Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information:

  1. Neutral metadata hub. Price Data Intelligence separately, lead with non-Everpure estates, connect to Unity Catalog, Polaris and Purview, and join OSI.
  2. Best substrate, partner above. Feed write-path events and snapshot-based scanning to DSPM and catalog vendors.
  3. Agent-safety primitives. Package SafeMode snapshots, per-agent QoS and audit export as "agent undo".
  4. Tuck-in M&A. Semantic-layer or lineage assets in the 1touch price range. DSPM leaders at Cyera-type valuations are out of reach.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Agentic data access, 2024 to 2026
    2024 : EU AI Act in force : Cohesity Gaia GA : Anthropic open-sources MCP
    2025 : VAST AI OS with AgentEngine : Rubrik Agent Rewind : NetApp AI Data Engine : Salesforce closes Informatica : MCP moves to Linux Foundation
    2026 : OSI spec v1 : Everpure closes 1touch : Dell Data Orchestration Engine : AI Omnibus in force : Everpure Data Intelligence adds MCP : NetApp indexes rival storage

Figure 39.4 — In two years the industry gained an agent protocol, a semantic-layer spec and a regulatory clock.

The arc runs from storage-resource reports (2000s) through GDPR-era classification tools (2010s) to AI data platforms. NVIDIA's AI Data Platform design (March 2025) gave vendors a template for GPUs and retrieval next to data (Chapter 34). The 2026 shift is from preparing data for RAG to governing agent access. Signals to watch over the next 12–18 months: separate disclosure of data-intelligence revenue; delegated-identity support in MCP; OSI moving to a foundation; and buying driven by the December 2027 deadline.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What share of Data Intelligence bookings cover data not on Everpure?" Strong: a number and named estates (Oracle, M365, rival NAS).
  2. "Who is the buyer: storage admin, CDO or CISO, and who carries the quota?" Strong: a named persona, separate SKU and quota credit for non-array deals.
  3. "How does Data Intelligence coexist with a customer's Purview, Collibra or Cyera?" Strong: it feeds them, no rip-out.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What does the MCP server do with a user's identity: pass it through, exchange it, or use a service account?" Strong: token exchange, per-agent scopes, no shared superuser.
  2. "How many policy decisions per second can you sustain, and how fast does a revocation take effect?" Strong: measured rates, cache lifetime in seconds, fan-out behaviour.
  3. "Is classification on the write path or off it?" Strong: off-path, snapshot- or event-triggered, bounded controller impact.

Don't say this:

  • "MCP moves the data." It moves requests and results; bulk bytes use S3, NFS or SQL.
  • "The EU AI Act regulates all agents as high-risk." Risk class depends on use case.
  • "Array ACLs are enough for agents." They work at file or share level; agents need delegated, field-level decisions.
  • "Storage vendors will displace Databricks or Snowflake." The realistic prize is the metadata and policy beneath them.
  • "Data intelligence is just RAG." RAG retrieves; data intelligence decides what may be retrieved.

docs.title: 40. Market structure and sizing
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: What storage does · Consumption models · Everpure's hyperscaler business and financials · Hyperscaler AI storage

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• The headline "storage market" is IDC's external enterprise storage systems tracker: US$33.0B in calendar 2025 and US$10.3B in 2Q26, up 33.6% year on year. It counts branded arrays sold to enterprises. Most hyperscaler storage spend is outside it.
  • The 2026 growth is mostly price. NAND contract prices more than doubled in the first half of 2026, and IDC says customers paid more for less capacity. Treat 30%+ revenue growth as pass-through inflation, not units.
  • Share is fragmented and stable. Dell holds 23.8%, Huawei 11.3%, NetApp 9.6%, Everpure 8.1% and HPE 6.8%, and about 40% sits with everyone else. Everpure gained the most in 2Q26 (+50% revenue growth), but a year's gain is under one share point.
  • No credible public "AI storage TAM" exists. The big-number reports come from market-research firms with loose definitions. IDC's AI infrastructure tracker puts storage at only 2.4% of AI infrastructure spend. A defensible triangulation gives roughly US$9–25B for 2026, and the independent-vendor slice of that is much smaller.
  • Growth is concentrated in all-flash, in the high end (systems above US$250K, +91%), and in AI-dedicated file/object platforms. Of those, only the first two appear cleanly in IDC's tracker.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Every market number in a board deck, sell-side model or acquisition memo starts from a definition. A US$33B market growing 3–4% a year supports a share-gain story. A US$10B quarter growing 34% looks like a boom, but much of it reverses when NAND prices normalise. An "AI storage market" of US$100B+ by 2030 would justify almost any acquisition multiple, yet it comes from firms that count any storage with "AI-powered" features.

Definitions matter for Everpure specifically. Its fastest-growing new lines, hyperscaler DirectFlash design wins and AI-factory storage for neoclouds, sit partly or wholly outside the tracker that ranks it fourth. Tracker share and tracker-based TAMs therefore understate its exposure to where storage dollars are growing.

docs.title: Four different "storage markets"
docs.text:
"The storage market" usually means one of four things.

  1. External enterprise storage systems (IDC's "External OEM ESS"). These are branded arrays sold by OEMs such as Dell, NetApp or Everpure into enterprise and public-sector datacentres, measured as vendor revenue. They were US$33.0B in 2025, +3.9%1. This is the number vendors quote share against.
  2. Total enterprise storage systems. This adds storage inside servers ("server-based") and ODM direct: systems that ODMs such as Quanta or Wiwynn build to a hyperscaler's design and sell to it directly. In the last public split we found, ODM direct was already US$3.9B a quarter and 27.7% of total enterprise storage spend in 3Q182. IDC no longer publicises the total; that share has almost certainly risen since.
  3. Cloud storage services. S3, Azure Blob and Google Cloud Storage are rented, not bought. They show up in cloud-provider revenue, and the hardware behind them shows up as ODM purchases and drive purchases.
  4. Media. These are the SSDs and HDDs themselves. In 2Q26 the top five enterprise SSD vendors alone booked about US$37.6B3. That is 3.6× the entire external array market in the same quarter, because most enterprise SSDs go into servers rather than arrays.
flowchart LR
    E["Enterprise and public-sector buyers"] --> OEM["Branded arrays<br/>Dell, NetApp, Everpure, Huawei, HPE"]
    E --> SB["Server-based and HCI/SDS storage"]
    H["Hyperscalers<br/>~US$725B capex in 2026"] --> ODM["ODM-built servers<br/>to hyperscaler design"]
    H --> DRV["SSDs and HDDs bought direct"]
    N["Neoclouds and AI factories"] --> AI["AI-dedicated platforms<br/>VAST, DDN, WEKA, EXA"]
    OEM --> IDC["IDC external storage<br/>US$33.0B in 2025"]
    AI -. "only partly counted" .-> IDC
    SB --> TOT["Total enterprise storage<br/>no longer published"]
    ODM --> TOT
    DRV --> MED["Media revenue<br/>eSSD top 5 ~US$37.6B in 2Q26"]

Figure 40.1 — The tracker vendors quote counts only branded arrays sold to enterprises; hyperscaler storage flows through ODMs and direct drive purchases, which is why it mostly isn't in any array vendor's TAM.

Why hyperscaler storage is (mostly) not in vendor TAMs. The four largest US hyperscalers were guiding to roughly US$725B of combined capex for 20264. Little of it buys branded arrays. Meta's Tectonic and Google's Colossus are in-house file systems running on commodity servers5 (see Chapter 36). The value chain looks like a captive fabless model: the hyperscaler does the design (software), the ODM is the foundry, and NAND makers sell the wafers. An array vendor captures margin only if it licenses something the hyperscaler can't build cheaply. That is why Everpure's second top-five hyperscaler win is structured as a master supply agreement for software and non-NAND parts, with the hyperscaler buying NAND itself and revenue starting in FY20286. Whether IDC counts such deals as external storage is unclear [VERIFY: IDC treatment of hyperscaler DirectFlash licence/component revenue].

docs.title: Reading the IDC number properly
docs.text:
Figure 40.2 — For seven years the external array market grew about 3% a year; 2026 broke the pattern, and the break coincides with the NAND price spike. Data: data/ch40_market_size.csv

Three cautions apply. First, IDC restates. Its 1Q26 growth rate was revised from 22.7% to 28.7% one quarter later7. It published 2024 at US$33.5B8, yet reported 2025's US$33.0B as 3.9% growth, which implies a lower 2024 base of about US$31.8B. Second, quarters are seasonal (Q4 budgets, a weak Chinese Q1). In 1Q26 Huawei's share was 6.7% and Dell's 31.2%9, against 12.6% and 23.7% the quarter before1. Use four-quarter totals. Third, trackers disagree on level: Omdia sized 2022 external storage at about US$38B [VERIFY: search-summary only]10. Never splice two sources.

docs.title: Price, not units: the 2026 NAND surge
docs.text:
TrendForce put NAND contract prices up 55–60% quarter on quarter in 1Q26 and a further 70–75% in 2Q26 (the 2Q26 figure comes from secondary aggregation)11. It expects enterprise SSD prices to rise another 23–28% in 4Q2612. Array vendors passed it on; Everpure raised prices on 9 February 202613. IDC's 2Q26 commentary says the component increase lifted system prices across all-flash, hybrid and HDD-only systems, that customers bought less capacity while paying more, and that some orders were pulled forward to beat further increases14.

The arithmetic: revenue growth = (1 + price per TB change) × (1 + capacity change) − 1. If revenue grew 33.6% while capacity shipped was flat to down, the price per TB of a system rose at least 33.6%.

Capacity shipped, YoY Implied price per TB, YoY Reading −10% +48% Rationing; consistent with IDC's "less capacity" comment 0% +34% Pure price pass-through +10% +21% Unlikely given supply constraints +25% (a normal pre-2026 year) +7% Would need a historic demand surge

Table 40.1 — Worked example: with capacity flat or falling, essentially all of 2Q26's 33.6% revenue growth is higher prices per terabyte.

For a semis reader this is the DRAM cycle seen from downstream: a component shortage inflates the system market's revenue line. Growth rates will compress mechanically once contract prices plateau; IDC expects component costs to stay high well into 202714. And share gains during a shortage partly reflect supply access: the vendor with secured NAND ships. Everpure's 2Q FY27 cash flow was negative partly because of strategic NAND prepayments15, which is effectively buying share with working capital. Chapter 48 covers the cycle itself.

docs.title: Where the growth is concentrated
docs.text:
In 2Q26, all-flash arrays were US$5.4B (+42.9%), or 52.1% of the market. Systems priced above US$250K grew 90.6% to US$2.7B14. Backing out the year-ago bases from those growth rates gives about US$7.74B total, US$3.78B all-flash and US$1.42B high-end. So hybrid and disk systems grew about 25%, and the high-end band alone contributed about US$1.3B of the market's US$2.6B increase, roughly half. Large configurations are where AI-adjacent buying and pull-forward show up first.

Figure 40.3 — Everpure (+50%) and Dell (+42.5%) took share in 2Q26; the long tail lost two points, but the market remains fragmented. Data: data/ch40_vendor_share.csv

The 2Q26 shares and growth rates come from IDC's release and trade-press tables1416; year-ago shares other than Dell's are derived from them, so treat half-point moves as approximate. Dell added about US$0.73B, Everpure US$0.28B. "Others" (IBM, Hitachi Vantara, Lenovo, IEIT Systems, Fujitsu and more) grew about 27%.

docs.text:
The tracker cuts revenue by vendor and price band, not by workload. Strategy needs a workload cut, where public share data is thin.

Figure 40.4 — Incumbents lead the measured segments; the fastest-growing segment, AI-dedicated storage, is led by private specialists and only partly visible in the trackers.

Evidence differs by box. In block, the IDC top five is a fair proxy. In backup, Veeam says IDC ranked it first with 13.6% of data-replication-and-protection software in 2H25 (vendor-reported)17. Cohesity, Commvault, Rubrik, Veeam, Dell and Druva were 2025 Gartner Leaders18. For file, object, HCI and AI-dedicated storage, no current public share data exists; the names are frequent shortlist entries, not a ranking. Company detail lives in Chapter 46 (incumbents), Chapter 47 (challengers and SDS) and Chapters 42–44 (VAST, WEKA, DDN).

docs.title: Sizing AI storage: what exists, and a triangulation
docs.text:
Estimate Source and access Year Definition Caveats US$33.0B (+3.9%) IDC, public press release1 CY2025 External OEM enterprise storage systems, vendor revenue Excludes ODM direct, server-based, cloud; restated periodically US$10.3B (+33.6%) IDC, public press release14 2Q26 Same Inflated by NAND pass-through and pull-forward US$2.2B, 2.4% of US$89.7B IDC AI Infrastructure Tracker, public blog19 1Q26 Storage systems deployed for AI workloads, as share of AI infrastructure Methodology and buyer mix in paid tracker; likely includes cloud builders US$497B AI infrastructure IDC, public blog19 2026 forecast Servers plus storage for AI Storage share not given for the forecast ~US$10.5B storage in 2029 (~1.4%) Next Platform, derived from IDC's US$758B 2029 forecast20 2029 Press derivation, not an IDC number [VERIFY: search-summary only] US$30.6B → US$118.4B, 25.9% CAGR Grand View Research, paid report (public summary)21 2024 → 2030 "AI-powered storage", which includes storage with AI features Definition sweeps in general-purpose storage; low confidence US$73.6B / US$162.5B Lucintel / Allied Market Research, paid reports (public summaries)22 2030 / 2031 "AI-powered storage" Ranges this wide signal definitional noise >US$23B → US$38B IDC file and object storage, public release23 2013 → 2017 File- plus object-based storage incl. hyperscale Stale; no current public file/object figure found [VERIFY]

Table 40.2 — Public market-size estimates: only IDC's tracker figures are measured spend; the "AI storage" reports differ by 2× because they measure different things.

No analyst firm publicly publishes a measured, vendor-addressable AI storage market, so a strategy team must triangulate. Worked example (assumptions in italics):

  • Top-down. IDC forecasts US$497B of 2026 AI infrastructure spend19. Applying IDC's measured 1Q26 storage share of 2.4% (our extrapolation; IDC gives no storage share for the forecast), AI storage is about US$12B. If dedicated shared storage is instead 5% of cluster spend, a plausible upper bound for data-heavy training clusters (see Chapter 31), it is about US$25B.
  • Run-rate. IDC's US$2.2B in 1Q26 × 4 is about US$9B annualised.
  • Bottom-up floor. VAST claims over US$0.5B of committed ARR exiting its fiscal year 2026 (company-stated)24. DDN told Forbes it expects about US$1B of 2026 revenue (reported by press)25. WEKA's ARR is estimated at US$0.10–0.15B (estimated, Globes)26. Together that is about US$1.6–1.7B for the three AI-native specialists. Treat it as an order of magnitude, not a sum: the three figures are different metrics (committed ARR, a revenue target, an ARR estimate), none is audited, and DDN's includes HPC and its Tintri enterprise business, not only AI.

The result is a 2026 AI storage spend range of roughly US$9–25B. The low end is anchored on IDC's measured share; the high end rests on our 5% assumption. Assume half of it is hyperscaler self-build that no vendor can address: the vendor-addressable pool is then about US$5–12B. There, 10 points of share is worth US$0.5–1.2B a year, which helps explain specialist valuations that price in share not yet won.

docs.text:
Vendor Measured position (IDC 2Q26) Where it is strong outside the tracker Market-structure bet Everpure #4, 8.1%, fastest-growing (+50%)14 Hyperscaler DirectFlash licensing (Meta plus a second top-five)6; neocloud AI Grow outside the array TAM via licensing and AI; Gartner Leader, top on both axes in 202627 Dell #1, 23.8%, +42.5%1 AI servers and storage bundled into AI-factory deals Breadth: sell storage attached to the server and GPU wallet Huawei #2, 11.3%16 China and markets closed to US vendors Geographic moat; limited exposure in the US NetApp #3, 9.6%16 Unified file, first-party cloud services on all three hyperscalers Storage OS that runs inside the hyperscalers HPE #5, 6.8%16 GreenLake consumption, AI servers Bundling with compute and services VAST / DDN / WEKA Not reported in top five; partly uncounted Neoclouds, sovereign AI, hyperscaler AI tenants AI-dedicated platforms; define the segment the trackers miss

Table 40.3 — Incumbents compete on share of a slow, measured market; Everpure and the AI specialists are betting on the unmeasured parts.

Steelman the incumbents. Dell's +42.5% on a base three times Everpure's added the most absolute dollars, and in AI factories the vendor selling GPU servers often controls the storage line too. NetApp attacks the hyperscaler problem from the other side by monetising storage software inside the clouds. Gartner's Magic Quadrant assesses vision and execution, not share. Its 2025 edition merged the separate primary-storage and file-and-object reports into one "Enterprise Storage Platforms" report28. In 2026 its Leaders were Everpure, Huawei, HPE, NetApp, IBM and Dell27. VAST, a Leader in the last standalone file-and-object MQ in 202429, was not included in the 2026 report, and DDN was dropped from it30. Gartner covers high-performance file and object vendors in separate research. Use the MQ as a buyer-perception signal, not a sizing input.

docs.text:
timeline
    title External storage market signals
    2018 : 2Q18 at US$6.1B : ODM direct reaches 27.7% of total storage spend
    2021 : 2Q21 at US$6.9B after the pandemic dip
    2024 : Gartner names VAST a file and object Leader
    2025 : Year at US$33.0B, up 3.9% : Gartner merges MQs into Enterprise Storage Platforms
    2026 : NAND contract prices surge : 2Q26 at US$10.3B, up 33.6% : Everpure second hyperscaler win

Figure 40.5 — Eight years of low-single-digit growth ended in 2026 because of component pricing, while the structurally important shift, storage moving to hyperscalers and AI specialists, ran underneath the tracker the whole time.

From 2Q18 (about US$6.1B) to 2Q25 (about US$7.7B) the external market grew roughly 3% a year31: falling flash prices offset capacity growth, and hyperscalers absorbed workloads that once bought arrays. Three signals point ahead. Gartner raised its 2026 data-centre systems forecast to US$822B (+62.5%)32, of which arrays are a small fraction. IDC's 2.4% AI storage share is the number to watch: if inference and KV-cache tiers (see Chapter 32) push it toward 4–5%, the AI storage pool doubles at the same compute spend. And NAND normalisation, not expected before 2027, will expose how much of 2026's growth was price.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "When we say we gained share, which tracker, which period, and is it four-quarter rolling?" Strong: names IDC external storage, says whether it is IDC's figure or Everpure's "modified" one, and separates price from units.
  2. "What share of our AI revenue would IDC count as external storage?" Strong: splits EXA sold to neoclouds, DirectFlash hyperscaler licensing and Evergreen//One, and knows how each is classified.
  3. "How much of this year's growth survives a 30% NAND price decline?" Strong: models price per TB and capacity separately and knows pull-forward exposure.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "In an AI factory bill of materials, what fraction is shared storage, and what moves it?" Strong: cites GB/s per GPU and PB per thousand GPUs and how checkpointing and KV-cache tiers change them.
  2. "What would a hyperscaler have to build itself to replace our licensed component?" Strong: names the hard parts (flash management, metadata, density) and the engineering years needed.
  3. "Which workloads are leaving arrays for server-based or cloud storage, and why?" Strong: specific about latency, data gravity and cost per TB.

Don't say this:

  • "The storage market grew 34%." Say that external array revenue grew 34%, mostly on price, and that capacity was flat to down.
  • "Everpure has 8% of the storage market." It has 8.1% of IDC external storage in one quarter; of total storage spend including hyperscalers and cloud, far less.
  • "AI storage is a US$100B+ market." Those are low-confidence, broadly defined figures; IDC measures 2.4% of AI infrastructure.
  • "Gartner ranks Everpure #1." It is highest on both MQ axes: an assessment, not share.
  • Comparing single-quarter shares across vendors. Seasonality (Q1 China, Q4 budgets) moves them several points.

  • IDC's Worldwide Quarterly AI Infrastructure Tracker methodology: how it assigns storage systems to AI workloads.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• External enterprise storage systems — branded arrays sold as standalone systems; IDC's headline tracker.
  • ODM direct — storage hardware built by ODMs to a hyperscaler's design and sold to it directly.
  • Server-based storage — drives inside servers, managed by software (HCI, SDS, hyperscaler file systems).
  • TAM / SAM — total / serviceable addressable market.
  • Price/volume decomposition — splitting revenue growth into price-per-unit change and unit (capacity) change.
  • Pull-forward demand — orders placed early to beat expected price rises.
  • See the glossary for the rest.
