docs.title: 41. Why AI-native storage vendors gained so much traction
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~12 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Disaggregated shared-everything · Parallel file systems · Metadata · NVIDIA's ecosystem · AI factories and neoclouds

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• The traction is real but concentrated. VAST, WEKA and DDN won the largest GPU clusters at neoclouds and AI labs. VAST's US$1.17B CoreWeave agreement1 and US$30B valuation2 are the headline signals. Enterprise AI storage, by revenue, still mostly goes to incumbents.
  • Three drivers did most of the work, and they compound. The first is architectures built for parallel, metadata-heavy GPU I/O. The second is early NVIDIA alignment: reference designs, certification and equity. The third is a new buyer class, the neoclouds, whose criteria matched those architectures.
  • Four drivers amplified them. Software on commodity servers, HPC talent, fast product cadence and incumbent blind spots: enterprise-feature roadmaps, controller-bound designs, channel incentives and scale-up habits.
  • The thesis is weakest where it is loudest. About US$37B of combined private valuation sits on roughly US$1.1B of revenue signals. Customers are concentrated, NVIDIA can make or unmake vendors, all three skipped MLPerf Storage v3.0, and the 2026 NAND shortage hits vendors that do not buy their own flash.
  • The window is closing, not closed. Everpure's FlashBlade//EXA, NetApp AFX, Dell Lightning and HPE X10000 (2024–2026) remove the architecture gap. They do not remove the challengers' installed base or their NVIDIA relationships.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Most board conversations about AI storage now start with the challengers' numbers. If the reader cannot separate the causes of their success from the noise around it, two errors follow. One is to over-copy: chasing valuation-driven narratives such as an "AI operating system". The other is to under-react: treating VAST, WEKA and DDN as niche HPC suppliers. This chapter breaks the thesis into drivers and asks of each one whether it is copyable, structural or fading.

For a strategy team, that framing sorts the options. Architecture gaps can be closed by engineering, and FlashBlade//EXA is that bet (Chapter 27). NVIDIA certification can be earned. A neocloud anchor account and NVIDIA equity cannot simply be built. They have to be won, partnered for or bought. The vendor-level detail is in Chapter 42 (VAST), Chapter 43 (WEKA) and Chapter 44 (DDN). This chapter is the cross-cutting explanation, and it is deliberately sceptical.

docs.title: What "traction" means here
docs.text:
The scoreboard has four kinds of evidence, and they should not be blended:

  • Contracts. VAST's US$1.17B multi-year CoreWeave agreement (reported by Reuters on 2025-11-06, confirmed by VAST)1. DDN says it supports more than 500,000 NVIDIA GPUs, including xAI's Colossus (company-stated)3. WEKA lists Nebius, Cohere, Midjourney and Stability AI as customers4.
  • Capital. VAST's valuation rose from US$1.2B in 20205 to US$30B in April 2026 (company-stated)2. Blackstone put US$300M into DDN at US$5B in January 2025, which Blackstone called DDN's first institutional investment6. (DDN did take about US$12M of venture money around 2002 and later bought those investors out; see Chapter 44.) WEKA reached US$1.6B in May 20247.
  • Revenue signals. All are self-reported. VAST cites more than US$500M of committed ARR (CARR)8. WEKA said it passed US$100M of ARR in 20249. DDN is reported to be targeting about US$1B of revenue in 2026 (reported by Forbes)10.
  • Analyst recognition. Gartner named VAST a Leader in its 2024 Magic Quadrant for File and Object Storage, the same edition that dropped DDN and NetApp from the report11.

The diagram below shows how the drivers connect. The point it makes is that they form a loop, not a list.

flowchart LR
  G["GPU clusters from 2023"] --> IO["Parallel, metadata-heavy I/O"]
  IO --> FIT["Driver 1: architecture fit"]
  HPC["Driver 5: HPC heritage and talent"] --> FIT
  IT["Driver 6: fast iteration"] --> FIT
  NV["Driver 2: NVIDIA certification and equity"] --> REF["On the reference design"]
  NEO["Driver 3: neoclouds as buyers"] --> CRIT["Criteria: tenancy, speed, NVIDIA fit"]
  SDS["Driver 4: software on commodity servers"] --> CRIT
  BS["Driver 7: incumbent blind spots"] --> GAP["Gap left open, 2019-2024"]
  FIT --> WIN["Wins at neoclouds and AI labs"]
  REF --> WIN
  CRIT --> WIN
  GAP --> WIN
  WIN --> CAP["Bookings, valuations, logos"]
  CAP -->|"funds R&D"| IT
  CAP -->|"signals safety"| NV

Figure 41.1 — The drivers form a flywheel: architecture fit and NVIDIA alignment won the first neocloud deals, and the capital and logos those deals produced paid for faster iteration and deeper NVIDIA ties.

docs.title: Driver 1: architecture fit for parallel GPU I/O and metadata
docs.text:
Mechanism. A training cluster makes thousands of clients read millions of small samples at once. It then has them write checkpoint shards in synchronized bursts. Two designs handle this well. A parallel file system stripes data across many servers (DDN EXAScaler, WEKA). A disaggregated shared-everything system lets every stateless node reach every SSD (VAST). Both spread metadata across many nodes instead of a controller pair. A dual-controller array tops out at whatever two controllers can serve.

Evidence. NVIDIA's own Eos supercomputer uses 48 DDN AI400X2 appliances for about 4 TB/s (company-stated)12. WEKA, running on HPE servers, topped all five SPECstorage Solution 2020 workloads in January 202513.

Rating: strong, but eroding. The architecture gap explained 2019–2024. By 2026 every major incumbent ships a disaggregated or parallel design (Table 41.3).

docs.title: Driver 2: NVIDIA alignment and certification
docs.text:
Mechanism. NVIDIA's reference architectures work as procurement shortlists (Chapter 34). Being early on the list, and being in NVIDIA's own data centres, de-risks the purchase for a buyer spending hundreds of millions on GPUs. Equity adds a signal of strategic intent.

Evidence. NVIDIA joined VAST's Series D in 202114 and WEKA's Series E in 20247. VAST, WEKA and DDN were early GPUDirect Storage partners15. DDN ran inside Selene and Eos12.

Rating: strong historically, now non-exclusive. By GTC 2025 at least seven vendors, including Pure Storage, Dell, NetApp and IBM, had SuperPOD certification or validation16. NVIDIA's 2026 STX storage architecture named 12 co-design partners17. Certification sets a floor. It no longer separates vendors.

docs.title: Driver 3: neoclouds as a new buyer class
docs.text:
Mechanism. A neocloud resells storage per GB-month to hundreds of tenants (Chapter 35). It values hard multi-tenancy, API provisioning, deployment speed and NVIDIA's blessing over $/TB, because storage is about 1% of its capex but can idle every GPU. Enterprise array vendors had built for the opposite buyer: one tenant, trusted administrators, procurement through a channel partner.

Evidence. CoreWeave's agreement with VAST is the largest disclosed storage deal1. WEKA powers Nebius's premium tier18. CoreWeave lists VAST, WEKA, DDN, IBM and Pure Storage as dedicated-storage partners19. That is a multi-vendor shelf, not a monopoly.

Rating: strong. This is the single best explanation of where the challengers won. It also explains why their revenue is concentrated.

docs.title: Driver 4: software-defined on commodity hardware
docs.text:
Mechanism. Selling software on partner servers keeps the vendor capital-light. Inventory and NAND risk sit with Supermicro, Cisco or the customer. It also lets a neocloud run storage on the same qualified servers, spares pool and automation as its compute. VAST left the hardware business in April 2021 for this model20.

Evidence. VAST reports positive free cash flow despite rapid growth (company-stated)8. WEKA runs natively on Nebius servers and in four public clouds (Chapter 43).

Rating: moderate. The counter-evidence is that hardware still sells. DDN, self-funded and profitable for about 25 years by its own account6, sells appliances. WEKA announced WEKApod 3, appliances on its own hardware design, in July 2026, with deliveries from fall 202621. In the 2026 NAND shortage, owning supply became an advantage (see below).

docs.title: Driver 5: HPC heritage and talent
docs.text:
Mechanism. Parallel I/O, RDMA and failure handling at thousands of clients are rare skills. They concentrate in a few teams: national-lab file-system engineers and Israel's enterprise-flash alumni.

Evidence. DDN bought Intel's Lustre engineering team in 2018 and revived it as the Whamcloud division22. WEKA's CEO led IBM's XIV platform team23. VAST's CEO came from XtremIO24.

Rating: moderate. Talent explains execution quality. It does not explain market choice. VAST's founders came from enterprise flash, not HPC, and won anyway.

docs.title: Driver 6: speed of product iteration
docs.text:
Mechanism. AI workloads changed every 12–18 months: training, then checkpointing, then RAG, then KV cache for inference. Single-product, venture-funded firms can ship a new tier faster than an incumbent juggling five product lines and a large installed base.

Evidence. WEKA shipped Augmented Memory Grid, a KV-cache tier, in November 2025, months before NVIDIA standardised that tier25. VAST announced GPU-equipped CNodes (CNode-X) and two new engines in February 202626. It also launched VAST Amplify in January 2026, a programme to reuse customers' installed SSDs, competitors' included, during the shortage27. DDN shipped Infinia 2.0, AI400X3 and DDN CORE within one year28.

Rating: moderate. Launches are not adoption, and most claims are vendor-tested.

docs.title: Driver 7: incumbents' blind spots
docs.text:
Mechanism. This is the classic innovator's dilemma. Incumbents' best customers asked for snapshots, replication, compliance and five-nines dual-controller uptime, and those features carried the margin. Early GPU clusters were small, odd and HPC-flavoured. Channel partners earned more selling familiar arrays. Scale-up engineering habits made "one controller pair, more shelves" the reflex answer.

flowchart TD
  A["Best customers: enterprise IT"] --> B["Roadmap: snapshots, replication, compliance"]
  B --> C["Controller-bound, channel-sold arrays"]
  C --> D{"AI cluster wants multi-TB/s, one namespace, tenancy"}
  D -->|"small and odd, 2019-2022"| E["Deprioritised as HPC"]
  E --> F["Challengers win neoclouds and labs"]
  F --> G["Segment explodes with GPU capex, 2023-2025"]
  G --> H["Incumbents respond: EXA, AFX, Lightning, X10000"]
  H --> I{"Can they win early adopters back?"}
  I -->|"enterprise AI: often"| J["Installed base and channel carry the deal"]
  I -->|"neoclouds: hard"| K["Challenger switching costs hold"]

Figure 41.2 — Incumbents did not misjudge the technology so much as the customer: the early AI buyer looked unprofitable until it became the fastest-growing segment, and by then challengers held the reference accounts.

Evidence. Most of it is indirect, so read this as inference from behaviour. The response launches all arrive in 2024–2026 (Table 41.3). The channel motive became visible when HPE told partners in November 2025 that it would stop reselling WEKA, Qumulo and Scality in favour of its own Alletra MP line, with orders no longer accepted from 3 March 202629. Partners can still sell those products on standard HPE servers.

Rating: moderate, and fading. The blind spot was real. It is now being closed.

docs.text:
Driver Best evidence (dated) Rating Counter-evidence 1. Architecture fit DDN in NVIDIA Eos at ~4 TB/s (2024)12; WEKA SPECstorage sweep (Jan 2025)13 Strong, eroding Everpure EXA topped MLPerf v3.0 checkpointing among entrants, a round VAST, WEKA and DDN skipped (Sep 2026)30, and SPECstorage AI_IMAGE (Mar 2026)31 2. Table 41.1 — The strongest drivers (fit, NVIDIA, neoclouds) explain where challengers won; the weaker ones explain how fast, and every row now has dated counter-evidence.

docs.title: The semiconductor bridge: fabless accelerators versus the CPU incumbent
docs.text:
The closest analogy is GPUs against x86 CPUs. Intel optimised for latency-bound, single-thread code and high-margin server CPUs. Throughput-parallel work, first graphics and then deep learning, looked like a niche until it became the growth market. NVIDIA, a fabless company, won with an architecture fitted to the workload and a software ecosystem (CUDA) that made it the default. Intel's response combined in-house projects and acquisitions. It bought Nervana in 2016, then paid about US$2B for Habana in December 2019 and shut down Nervana's training chip weeks later33. NetApp's 2026 purchases of DataPelago and PEAK:AIO follow the same catch-up-by-acquisition pattern34.

Dimension CPU incumbent vs GPU challengers Storage incumbents vs AI-native vendors Under-served workload Massively parallel math Parallel, metadata-heavy GPU I/O Incumbent's optimisation Single-thread latency, x86 margin Dual-controller uptime, enterprise data services Challenger's edge Throughput architecture plus CUDA ecosystem DASE or parallel FS plus NVIDIA reference status Supply model Fabless on TSMC Software on Supermicro, Cisco and partner servers Incumbent response Larrabee, Xeon Phi, Nervana, Habana EXA, AFX, Lightning, X10000; DataPelago, PEAK:AIO Where the analogy breaks CUDA lock-in is deep NFS/S3 clients are standard; switching is easier

Table 41.2 — The pattern rhymes with GPUs versus CPUs, but storage has no CUDA: standard protocols make challenger lock-in shallower than NVIDIA's.

The last row is the important caveat. VAST serves standard NFS and S3 clients. DDN and WEKA need their own clients but expose POSIX semantics. Nothing in storage is as sticky as a decade of CUDA kernels. The fabless analogy also has a supply-side lesson. In a foundry shortage, fabless firms queue behind those with prepaid capacity. In 2026 the "foundry" is NAND.

docs.title: Where the thesis is weak or overhyped
docs.text:
Valuations versus revenue. Combined last valuations are US$30B + US$5B + US$1.6B ≈ US$36.6B. Combined revenue signals are about US$0.5B of VAST CARR, at least US$0.1B of WEKA ARR9 and about US$0.5B of reported DDN 2025 revenue10 [VERIFY: search-summary only], roughly US$1.1B in total. For scale, IDC's external enterprise storage tracker recorded US$10.34B in the second quarter of 2026 alone, about US$41B annualised32. The challengers are about 3% of that by revenue. The definitions differ, and IDC's tracker of branded external systems may under-count software sold on partner servers, but not by an order of magnitude. VAST's 60x multiple on CARR, and about half of its Series F being secondary35, price in a winner-take-most outcome.

Figure 41.3 — The market has priced one winner: VAST's multiple is about four times WEKA's and five times DDN's, so "AI-native vendors" is really a VAST valuation story with two more modestly priced peers. Data: data/ch41_valuations.csv

Customer concentration. The CoreWeave agreement alone is about 29% of VAST's US$4B cumulative bookings (Chapter 42). DDN's 2026 growth is reportedly tied to xAI and sovereign supercomputers10. A pause in neocloud capex would hit all three at once.

NVIDIA is a kingmaker, and kingmakers change their minds. The equity and reference status that lifted VAST and WEKA now flow to everyone through STX17. NVIDIA's own software decides which tiers matter for KV cache. A vendor whose differentiation is "NVIDIA-aligned" holds a licence that NVIDIA can dilute.

Enterprise AI is buying from incumbents. IDC's 2Q26 tracker shows the external-storage market up 33.6%, Dell up 42.5% and Everpure up 50%32. Dell says more than 5,000 customers are deploying its AI Factory36. Enterprises mostly run inference and RAG next to existing data, so installed base and channel decide.

Incumbents caught up architecturally. See Table 41.3. Each launch removes a talking point the challengers had in 2023.

MLPerf absences. VAST, WEKA and DDN all skipped MLPerf Storage v3.0, the first round with a KV-cache test. Their histories differ: DDN entered v0.5, v1.0 and v2.0, WEKA entered v0.5 and v1.0, and VAST has never submitted (Chapters 42–44). Everpure entered for the first time and posted the top checkpoint result among entrants3730. Absence proves nothing about performance, but it leaves the challengers' inference claims vendor-tested (Chapter 37).

The NAND shortage cuts against software-only vendors. TrendForce forecast another 15–20% rise in NAND contract prices for 4Q2638. VAST passes hardware through at cost, so its customers and server partners carry the price spike and the allocation risk. Its response, Amplify, is about reusing flash, not securing it27. Everpure, by contrast, made strategic NAND and component purchases in Q2 FY27 that pushed free cash flow negative; analysts read a ~US$577M rise in prepaid expenses as advance NAND buying (third-party reading, not an Everpure disclosure)39 (Chapter 26). That is the IDM-with-capacity position in a foundry shortage, bought with working capital.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Everpure's answer to drivers 1, 2 and 7 is FlashBlade//EXA. Pure Storage launched it in March 202540. It splits a metadata core on FlashBlade from data nodes that clients reach directly over pNFS. The other incumbents took different routes to the same gap.

Vendor and product Date Design What it closes What it does not (yet) Everpure FlashBlade//EXA Mar 202540 Metadata core plus direct-path data nodes, standard pNFS Throughput and metadata scale; peer-reviewed MLPerf v3.0 lead among entrants30 NVIDIA-Certified Storage validation being extended to EXA (announced March 2026); no completed EXA certification, NCP or SuperPOD badge published by November 2026 (Chapter 27); no large neocloud anchor NetApp AFX Oct 202541 Disaggregated ONTAP, optional GPU data node ONTAP data services at scale-out Shipping by 2026 (ONTAP 9.18.1 onward, AFX 2K added)42, but no neocloud references found [VERIFY: AFX 1K GA date] Dell Lightning File System Mar 202643 Parallel file system inside Dell AI Data Platform A "Tier 0" parallel FS sold through Dell's channel New code with an unproven field record HPE Alletra MP X10000 Nov 2024; native file 202644 Object-first, 16 compute plus 16 storage nodes, 23 PB raw NVIDIA-certified object at Foundation level Scale ceiling well below multi-exabyte neocloud pools

Table 41.3 — By 2026 every major incumbent ships an AI-scale design; the challengers' remaining edge is installed base, NVIDIA intimacy and neocloud references, not architecture.

Steelmanning the challengers: incumbents' launches are 12–24 months old, and the hardest part of a 100,000-GPU deployment is operational history, not a datasheet. VAST's CoreWeave relationship and DDN's place inside NVIDIA's own clusters are referenceable in a way no 2025 launch is yet. Everpure's strengths are different: a public company's audited financials, NAND supply, Evergreen consumption models and the enterprise installed base where IDC shows it growing fastest. Chapter 45 runs the four-way comparison, and Chapter 46 profiles the incumbents.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In the last ten AI deals we lost to VAST or WEKA, which driver decided it?" A strong answer splits losses by buyer type (neocloud, AI lab, enterprise) and names the deciding factor: NVIDIA certification, tenancy, an existing relationship or price. Lumping them together as "AI deals" is a weak answer.
  2. "Which challenger advantage can we copy in 12 months, and which can't we?" Strong: certification and multi-tenancy are copyable. NVIDIA equity and a CoreWeave-scale reference are not, and need a partnership or a different segment.
  3. "How does the NAND shortage change our pitch against software-only vendors?" Strong: it quantifies delivery dates and price locks versus a customer sourcing servers through a partner, and it does not overclaim, since hyperscaler NAND is bought separately.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Where does EXA's metadata core saturate, compared with VAST's shared-SCM approach, at a million small-file creates per second?" Strong: a number, the limiting resource, and how it scales with added nodes.
  2. "What does a neocloud tenant-isolation audit look like on our system?" Strong: per-tenant keys, QoS floors, noisy-neighbour test results and API coverage.
  3. "Why would a customer pick our pNFS client over WEKA's or Lustre's agent?" Strong: it names the operational win (no kernel module to track) and the performance cost, with measurements.

Don't say this:

  • "AI-native vendors won the AI storage market." They won the largest neocloud and lab clusters. Enterprise AI spend mostly went to incumbents in 2026.
  • "VAST's valuation proves its technology is superior." It proves investors expect a dominant share. The audited test is still to come.
  • "NVIDIA picked VAST." NVIDIA invests in and certifies several vendors, and its own clusters run on DDN.
  • "Software-only is always the better model." In a NAND shortage, owning supply wins deals.
  • "They avoid MLPerf because they'd lose." Absence is not evidence either way. Say "their inference claims are not independently benchmarked."

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• AI-native storage vendor — a storage company whose growth and product roadmap centre on GPU-cluster workloads (VAST, WEKA, DDN), as opposed to general enterprise storage.
  • Neocloud — a GPU-specialist cloud that rents accelerator capacity and resells storage as a metered service.
  • Committed ARR (CARR) — annualised value of signed recurring contracts, including those not yet live; larger than ARR.
  • Innovator's dilemma — the pattern in which incumbents rationally serve their best customers and miss a new segment that later becomes the growth market.
  • Kingmaker risk — dependence on a platform owner (here NVIDIA) whose endorsements can be extended to rivals.
  • Reference-design status — being named in a platform vendor's validated architecture, which works as a procurement shortlist.
  • Catch-up launch — an incumbent product built to close an architectural gap opened by challengers.
  • Software-defined storage — storage sold as software that runs on partner or customer servers rather than vendor appliances.

docs.title: 42. VAST Data deep dive
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~20 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Disaggregated shared-everything architectures · Data reduction · Data protection and resilience · AI factories and neoclouds · Why AI-native storage vendors gained traction

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• VAST is a software company that built a hardware architecture, then climbed up the stack. Its base is DASE: stateless compute nodes sharing SCM plus QLC flash over NVMe-oF. On top sit the Element Store (one metadata structure for files, objects, tables and blocks), and then a growing set of "engines" sold together as the VAST AI Operating System.
  • The economics come from three mechanisms: very wide erasure codes, similarity-based data reduction, and cheap QLC. At large scale, protection overhead falls to about 3% and data reduction is cluster-wide. That makes all-flash credible for whole datasets, not just hot tiers.
  • The business numbers are company-stated and large. VAST cites more than US$500M in committed ARR, more than US$4B in cumulative bookings, positive operating margin and free cash flow, and a US$30B valuation in an April 2026 Series F of about US$1B, roughly half of it secondary (reported by Bloomberg).
  • The customer base leans heavily on neoclouds and frontier labs. CoreWeave signed a US$1.17B agreement, and VAST says it is the main data platform for xAI's Colossus, a claim DDN contests. Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure routes were announced in late 2025.
  • The risks mirror the strengths. VAST's valuation runs ahead of its disclosed revenue, it depends on partners for hardware during a NAND shortage, its customers are concentrated, NVIDIA is spreading the same architecture to every rival, and a database play takes it into Databricks and Snowflake territory.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
VAST is the competitor that defined the AI-native storage category in buyers' minds. At large GPU clusters it is often the incumbent that Everpure's FlashBlade//EXA must displace or sit beside. In April 2026 its company-stated valuation reached about 25 times that of its 2020 round12. Its pitch has moved from "cheaper all-flash" to "the operating system for AI data." Buyers now compare storage on more than GB/s and $/TB: they also ask whether it can host embeddings, event streams, SQL tables and agent runtimes.

For a strategy team, VAST is a benchmark three ways: technically, the reference design for shared-everything disaggregation (Chapter 16); commercially, proof that software on partner hardware can generate cash at scale, if the company-stated figures hold; strategically, a test of whether storage vendors can capture value above the storage layer. Everpure faces the same question with Fusion, its KV-cache work and its data-management roadmap (Chapter 28).

docs.title: DASE in one paragraph, and what VAST adds
docs.text:
Chapter 16 covers the architecture in depth, so here is the short version. VAST splits a cluster into CNodes, stateless servers that run every protocol and data service, and DBoxes, enclosures of SSDs behind redundant fabric endpoints called DNodes. An NVMe-over-RDMA fabric connects the two tiers, so every CNode can reach every SSD. All state, including metadata, lives on shared persistent media: a small storage-class-memory (SCM) tier and a large QLC tier3. A write is acknowledged once it is mirrored into SCM on two enclosures. Data reduction and wide-stripe erasure coding happen later, when the data migrates to QLC. Any CNode can serve any read.

Figure 42.1 — VAST's moat is no longer the DASE hardware pattern, which rivals now copy. It is the single Element Store underneath, which lets every new layer reuse the same data without copies.

Semiconductor bridge. The arc resembles a fabless chip company's path. VAST first sold a reference board (the appliance). It then licensed the design while partners handled manufacturing and inventory (Gemini and the OEMs). Most recently it has put its IP on the customer's own silicon (BlueField-4 inside the GPU server), much as an IP vendor ends up as a block inside someone else's SoC. Each step lowers capital intensity and cedes some control over the bill of materials.

docs.title: The Element Store: one metadata structure for every data type
docs.text:
Most storage systems keep separate metadata for each personality: a file-system inode tree, an object index, a LUN map. VAST's Element Store keeps one. Files, objects, block volumes and database tables are all "elements" in the same persistent metadata structure, which lives in SCM and which every CNode reads and writes directly over the fabric3. Three consequences follow.

  1. Multiprotocol is native, not gatewayed. An object written over S3 is the same element an NFS client sees as a file, with no translation copy. Snapshots, replication and quality-of-service apply to every protocol, so block volumes added in 2025 inherited them on day one14.
  2. Metadata is byte-granular. Data is stored at its exact byte length, not padded to a 4 KB or 32 KB block15. That matters for small files and for the reduction scheme below.
  3. Capacity and metadata scale together. Because metadata lives on shared SCM, not in the DRAM of a server that owns it, adding DBoxes adds metadata capacity, and adding CNodes adds metadata processing. The cost is a fabric round trip on every metadata lookup, as described in Chapter 16.

The persistent tier is tiny: in a DF-3060V2, SCM is 12 ÷ 1,364 ≈ 0.9% of raw capacity9. It acts as last-level cache plus page table, with QLC as bulk memory, except that this "cache" is persistent, so a power loss leaves nothing to flush.

docs.title: Similarity-based data reduction
docs.text:
Classic deduplication finds identical chunks by hash, and classic compression squeezes each chunk on its own. Both miss a common pattern in real data: chunks that are almost the same. Two checkpoint shards, two VM images or two versions of a genomics file can differ by a few bytes per block. A shifted timestamp then defeats deduplication, and per-block compression never sees the redundancy between blocks.

VAST's approach, described in its patent and engineering blog, works in three steps161715:

  1. Compute a similarity hash for each chunk. Unlike a cryptographic hash, a similarity hash gives nearby values for chunks that share most of their bytes.
  2. Group chunks with matching similarity hashes. Store one as a reference block.
  3. Compress every other chunk in the group against the reference (VAST cites Zstandard-class compression with the reference used as a dictionary), so each one is stored only as a small delta. Exact duplicates collapse to pointers as before.

Worked example (illustrative). Take 1,000 daily snapshots of a 1 TB dataset in which 2% of the bytes change each day, scattered across blocks. Deduplication at 32 KB granularity finds few identical blocks, because nearly every block has at least one changed byte. Similarity reduction keeps one reference copy (1 TB) and stores each day's changes as deltas. That is about 0.02 TB a day plus compression overhead, or roughly 1 + 1,000 × 0.02 = 21 TB, against 1,000 TB logical, close to 48:1. On unrelated, already-compressed data such as JPEGs or encrypted video, the same machinery finds little and the ratio approaches 1:1. In January 2026 VAST's co-founder put the average across roughly 1,000 customers at 3.4:1 but the median at 1.75:1 (company-stated)1819. A few highly reducible estates pull the average up, so the median is the better planning number.

Semiconductor bridge. This is base-plus-delta compression, the idea proposed for CPU caches: store a base value and small deltas for neighbouring words. VAST applies it across a whole namespace, which is only practical because the metadata that tracks the references sits in shared SCM.

The trade-off. Reading a delta-compressed chunk means fetching its reference too, and reduction burns CNode CPU during migration. VAST says locally decodable compression limits the extra fetch15, but reduction-heavy data still costs more CPU per GB/s, so CNode counts scale with workload as well as capacity.

docs.title: Locally decodable erasure codes: why wide stripes are safe
docs.text:
Wide stripes cut overhead but traditionally made rebuilds expensive. With Reed-Solomon k+m, rebuilding one lost strip means reading k surviving strips. VAST's locally decodable codes add structure so that a single lost strip can be rebuilt from about a quarter of the stripe20.

Worked numbers. A 146+4 stripe, which VAST uses on clusters of 75 or more DBoxes, has an overhead of 4 ÷ 150 = 2.7%21. Plain Reed-Solomon would read 146 strips to rebuild one. Reading about a quarter means roughly 37. Compare a classic 8+2 layout, at 20% overhead and 8 reads per rebuild. VAST gets 7× lower overhead for about 4.6× more rebuild reads per strip. The rebuild is spread across every CNode and SSD in the cluster, so wall-clock rebuild time stays short. On a 50 PB usable cluster the overhead gap is worth about 50 ÷ 0.8 − 50 ÷ 0.973 ≈ 11 PB of raw flash.

Bridge. This resembles cloud storage's local reconstruction codes, or HBM's split between cheap local on-die ECC and stronger system-level ECC: most repairs stay local, and only rare multi-failure cases fall back to the wide code.

docs.title: Protocols: NFS to Kafka on the same bytes
docs.text:
By late 2026 the access layer includes NFSv3/v4 (including NFS over RDMA, which VAST paired with GPUDirect Storage from 202122), SMB, S3, block over NVMe/TCP and a Kafka-compatible Event Broker. Block and Kafka arrived in early 20251423. VAST built the Kafka producer and consumer APIs as just another protocol module, so event topics land as tables that SQL can query. VAST claims its largest clusters handle 500 million messages per second (company-stated)23 [VERIFY: search-summary only]. Two choices matter:

  • Standard NFS clients, no proprietary driver. Lustre and WEKA each need a client module on every GPU node (Chapter 17). VAST asks for none, which matters to neoclouds that run locked-down images. FlashBlade//EXA makes the same choice with standard pNFS.
  • One namespace across protocols. A dataset ingested through S3 can be trained on through NFS and catalogued through SQL without an ETL copy.

docs.title: I/O walkthrough: one object, three personalities
docs.text:
The clearest way to see the Element Store's value is to follow one piece of data through the stack. Take a pharma company ingesting microscope images for a vision model:

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Instrument via S3
    participant C as Any CNode
    participant S as SCM mirror
    participant E as DataEngine trigger
    participant G as GPU on CNode-X or external
    participant D as DataBase table
    participant T as Training node via NFS
    participant Q as Analyst via SQL
    P->>C: PUT bucket/run42/img001.tif
    C->>S: write data and element metadata twice
    S-->>C: persisted
    C-->>P: 200 OK
    C->>E: new-object event fires
    E->>G: run embedding function on the image
    G->>D: insert row with path, labels, vector
    Note over C,S: later, migration reduces data and writes a wide QLC stripe
    T->>C: open /datasets/run42/img001.tif over NFS
    C-->>T: same bytes, no copy
    Q->>D: SELECT similar images WHERE label = tumor
    D-->>Q: rows with vector matches and file paths

Figure 42.3 — One write serves object ingest, file-based training and SQL plus vector search. The copies a conventional stack makes between object store, file system and vector database never happen.

Worked example (illustrative). Take a 10 PB image corpus. A conventional pipeline lands it in object storage, copies a working set into a parallel file system for training, and builds embeddings in a separate vector database. If the training copy is half the corpus, that is 5 PB of extra flash plus the pipelines to keep it fresh. The embeddings are small by comparison. For 2 billion images at 1,024 dimensions × 2 bytes (FP16), they come to about 2e9 × 2,048 bytes ≈ 4 TB. The win is not the vector bytes. It is eliminating the 5 PB copy and the staleness window between copies. The counter-argument is that a parallel file system or a specialised vector database may be faster at its single job, and that many enterprises already own a lakehouse (Chapter 33).

docs.title: Why put GPUs and DPUs into storage nodes
docs.text:
CNode-X and the BlueField-4 CNode push compute in opposite directions. CNode-X brings GPUs into the storage cluster, so vector search (NVIDIA cuVS), data clustering and SQL (VAST cites the open-source Sirius GPU SQL engine and claims 44% faster queries, company-stated) run next to the data instead of hauling it to a GPU farm12. The BlueField-4 CNode does the reverse. It puts the storage controller on the DPU inside each GPU server, which serves NVIDIA's inference context-memory tier for KV cache (Chapter 32). VAST claims 75% lower power for KV-cache operations than with separate controllers (company-stated)13. Both build on VAST Undivided Attention (VUA), a KV-cache agent for GPU servers that VAST open-sourced in April 2025; it keeps prefix chunks on shared NVMe reached over RDMA, and VAST says it performs best on VAST's own namespace33.

The bridge is near-memory compute: move the operation to the data when its output is far smaller than its input, as in a similarity search over billions of vectors. The strategic catch is that NVIDIA published BlueField-4 STX as a reference architecture with a dozen storage partners, Everpure among them34. The DPU placement is therefore not unique to VAST, and the differentiation has to come from the software.

docs.title: How VAST makes money
docs.text:
Since 2021 VAST has sold software, not hardware. Under Gemini, customers buy certified servers and enclosures at cost from a manufacturing partner and pay VAST a subscription priced on capacity, with support included. VAST says customers can renew at the same price for up to ten years (company-stated)535. VAST also sells through OEMs that bundle its software with their hardware (HPE, Cisco, Supermicro) and through cloud marketplaces. Per-TB prices are not public.

Two consequences matter. First, VAST's gross margin should look like a software company's, while the customer's total cost still carries full hardware cost, including NAND, which VAST neither marks up nor controls. Second, "bookings" and "CARR" capture multi-year commitments that GAAP revenue would spread over time, so they are not comparable with Everpure's revenue or subscription ARR.

docs.title: Revenue, profitability and the "Rule of X"
docs.text:
VAST is private and publishes no audited financials. All of the following is company-stated unless marked otherwise:

  • Committed ARR (CARR) above US$500M on exiting fiscal year 2026, cumulative bookings above US$4B, and positive operating margin and free cash flow424546. The release does not give the fiscal year-end month; coverage places it in January 2026 [VERIFY: VAST fiscal year-end month].
  • At the Series E in late 2023, VAST cited US$1B of cumulative software bookings, more than US$200M of ARR at the end of its fiscal third quarter, and 12 consecutive quarters of positive cash flow383947. Bookings therefore roughly quadrupled in about 2.3 years. ARR (live contracts) and CARR (signed contracts, including those not yet live) are different measures, so the two figures do not give a clean growth rate.
  • A "Rule of X" score of 228%42. Bessemer defines Rule of X as revenue growth × a multiplier (about 2× for private companies) + free-cash-flow margin48. VAST did not disclose the components. Worked inference: if the FCF margin is between 10% and 30%, 228 = 2g + FCF implies growth of about 99–109%. With a 3× multiplier, which some analysts use49, it implies about 66–73%. In other words, the score is consistent with revenue growing by roughly two-thirds to double. That is an inference, not a disclosure.
  • Press and analyst estimates vary widely. Sacra estimated about US$200M ARR in January 2025 (estimated)50, which matches VAST's own late-2023 figure and is probably stale. Blocks & Files speculated that run-rate "could even be topping $2 billion" after the CoreWeave deal (speculation, not a disclosure)51. The gap between CARR (>US$0.5B) and that speculation is a definitions problem: multi-year bookings booked up front versus annualised recurring value.
  • Headcount: about 1,200, roughly a third in Israel, as of March 2026 (reported)52 [VERIFY: headcount].

Worked valuation multiple. US$30B ÷ US$0.5B CARR = 60× trailing CARR. If CARR doubles in FY2027, which is consistent with the Rule of X inference, the forward multiple is about 30×. For scale, Everpure reported US$2.13B of subscription ARR in Q2 FY2753. That is about four times VAST's CARR, though the definitions differ and Everpure also books large product revenue.

docs.text: VAST's direct team chases the largest deals (neoclouds and labs), while OEMs extend reach into enterprise accounts. NVIDIA is a co-seller in all but name: an investor since 2021, it certified VAST for DGX SuperPOD and launched its AI Data Platform and STX designs with VAST as a partner6734. VAST has never submitted to MLPerf Storage, in any round from v0.5 (2023) to v3.0 (2026); it sells on reference customers rather than peer-reviewed benchmarks6869.

docs.title: Why it gained traction
docs.text:
Chapter 41 covers the category-level reasons. For VAST specifically, the steelman has six parts:

  1. It bet on the right media curve early. It designed for QLC, SCM and NVMe-oF in 2016, before all three matured, and incumbents could not retrofit that design onto dual-controller or shared-nothing code.
  2. It made flash cheap enough for "all the data." Wide codes at about 3% overhead plus global reduction let VAST pitch one flash tier instead of flash plus disk, which suits AI jobs that reread whole datasets each epoch.
  3. It fit neocloud operations. A neocloud needs standard NFS clients, multi-tenancy, a single namespace, and the ability to add throughput or capacity independently as tenants change. DASE gives all four.
  4. It chose the software model before AI demand arrived. Gemini (2021) meant that when GPU clusters exploded in 2023–2025, VAST could scale bookings without a manufacturing balance sheet.
  5. It stayed close to NVIDIA. NVIDIA invested from the Series D, early GPUDirect Storage work over NFS-RDMA followed, and NVIDIA launches have featured VAST since. In AI infrastructure, NVIDIA's reference designs are de facto procurement lists.
  6. It sold a story and then shipped against it. The "operating system" framing is ambitious, but VAST has shipped a database, event streaming, block and agent tooling at a cadence rivals have struggled to match.

docs.title: Strategic relevance to Everpure
docs.text:
Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information:

  1. Compete head-on at large AI scale with FlashBlade//EXA. EXA's case against VAST is a shorter data path (client to data node, no CNode hop), standard pNFS, Purity's metadata engine, and peer-reviewed MLPerf v3.0 results in a round VAST skipped (Chapter 27). The gaps are reference customers at 100k-GPU scale, DFM-based data nodes, and certification badges.
  2. Turn the NAND shortage into a wedge. Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) designs its own DirectFlash Modules and buys NAND as a large volume buyer (Chapter 26). VAST's customers buy servers at cost in a tight market. If supply stays constrained into 2027, a vendor that guarantees capacity and price may matter more than one with a lower software fee (Chapter 48).
  3. Match the platform story selectively, not wholesale. Everpure already has KV-cache work (KVA), Data Stream and Fusion. The open question is which of VAST's up-stack layers buyers actually pay for. The evidence so far points to the storage-native ones (multiprotocol, global namespace, event triggers) rather than agent runtimes.
  4. Coexist inside neoclouds. CoreWeave also lists Everpure among its dedicated-storage partners73. Neoclouds multi-source, so a second-source position is a realistic entry point.
  5. Watch the IPO. A VAST S-1 would give the first audited view of AI-native storage economics: gross margin, revenue recognition on bookings, and customer concentration. That would reset the benchmark for Everpure's own valuation conversation. Acquiring VAST at a US$30B private mark would be a transformational, likely stock-heavy deal for any storage incumbent, with OEM-channel conflicts attached. Smaller up-stack assets are the more common pattern, as NetApp's 2026 purchase of DataPelago shows74 [VERIFY: deal date and terms] (Chapter 46).

The steelman for VAST in this comparison is that breadth compounds. Every new engine runs on the same Element Store, so each one makes the platform harder to remove. docs.text:
timeline

Figure 42.6 — VAST added a major layer roughly every year. Since 2023 the additions have been software services more than hardware.

The trajectory has three phases: a storage architecture (2016–2020), a software business with a data platform (2021–2023), and since 2024 an AI infrastructure company that happens to store data. Signals for 2026–2027 are CNode-X and BlueField-4 shipments in 2H 2026, TuningEngine and PolicyEngine general availability by year-end30, a possible IPO43, and whether CARR growth broadens beyond neoclouds.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In the last ten EXA deals against VAST, what decided the outcome?" A strong answer separates neocloud from lab and enterprise deals. It names the deciding factor in each (reference customers, NFS versus pNFS client support, $/TB under NAND inflation, up-stack features), and admits where VAST's breadth won.
  2. "Which VAST AI OS features show up in RFPs as requirements, not nice-to-haves?" A strong answer distinguishes multiprotocol on one namespace and event triggers, which appear often, from AgentEngine-style features, which rarely gate deals. It says how Everpure covers the ones that do.
  3. "How does the NAND shortage change our competitive pitch against a software-only vendor?" A strong answer quantifies the hardware share of total cost of ownership for a 50 PB deal, explains Everpure's supply position versus at-cost white-box hardware, and avoids overclaiming price guarantees.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Walk me through a 1 GB/s write on VAST versus EXA: fabric crossings, persistence point, and where reduction happens." A strong answer gives roughly 4× back-end traffic for VAST's mirror-then-migrate path (Chapter 16) and the direct data-node write for EXA, and says where each spends CPU.
  2. "Is similarity reduction a real advantage on AI training data?" A strong answer says it helps on checkpoints, versions, logs and near-duplicate corpora. It helps little on compressed media and tokenised shards. It asks for measured ratios, not marketing medians.
  3. "What does BlueField-4 STX change for us?" A strong answer explains that the DPU-resident controller becomes a shared NVIDIA pattern. It identifies the software that still differentiates (metadata engine, reduction, multi-tenancy) and the timeline for EXA's STX alignment.

Don't say this:

  • "VAST is a hardware company." It has sold software on partner hardware since 2021.
  • "VAST has US$2B of ARR." That is press speculation. The company-stated figure is more than US$500M of CARR.
  • "VAST powers xAI." Both VAST and DDN claim a primary role at Colossus, and the split is unknown.
  • "VAST's data reduction is 3:1." That is close to its customer average (3.4:1); the company-stated median is 1.75:1, and the ratio depends entirely on the data.
  • "FlashBlade//EXA beat VAST in MLPerf." VAST did not enter.
  • "The AI OS is all shipping." Several engines and CNode-X were announced in 2026 with GA targeted for later in the year.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• VAST's US patent application 2019/0379394 on global similarity-based compression16, and its engineering blog series on locally decodable codes20.
  • Lockwood et al., PDSW'21, for an independent benchmark of a VAST system's read and write behaviour80.
  • VAST knowledge-base pages on DBox high availability, rack resiliency and data reduction, for stripe and failure-domain rules.
  • NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX and inference context-memory documentation, to see which parts of the KV-cache design are NVIDIA's and which are VAST's.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Element Store — VAST's single metadata and data structure underneath every protocol and service.
  • Similarity-based data reduction — compressing near-duplicate chunks as deltas against a shared reference block.
  • Locally decodable erasure code — a wide erasure code that rebuilds a lost strip from a fraction of the stripe.
  • VAST AI Operating System — VAST's 2025 umbrella brand for DataStore, DataBase, DataSpace and its compute engines.
  • CNode-X / EBox / Ceres — GPU-equipped compute node, converged server, and BlueField-based storage enclosure.
  • Gemini — VAST's model of hardware at cost plus a capacity-priced software subscription.
  • Committed ARR (CARR) — annualised value of signed recurring contracts, including those not yet live.
  • Rule of X — Bessemer's growth-weighted variant of the Rule of 40.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 43. WEKA deep dive
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~17 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Scale-out shared-nothing clusters · Parallel and distributed file systems · The GPU data path · Inference and KV cache

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• WEKA sells software, not boxes. Its product is a parallel, shared-nothing file system for NVMe flash. It was called WekaFS, became NeuralMesh in June 2025, and NeuralMesh 6 was announced in July 2026. It runs on commodity servers, inside GPU servers, or in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and OCI. Its technical signature is a kernel-bypass data path with metadata sharded across every node.
  • It was among the first vendors to make KV-cache offload a commercial product. Augmented Memory Grid (AMG) became commercially available on 2025-11-18, with OCI as launch partner. WEKA claims up to 20x faster time to first token (TTFT). That is physically plausible but has not been independently verified.
  • The business is smaller than the noise around it. WEKA passed US$100M ARR in 2024 (company-stated) and has raised about US$415M in total. Its last priced round valued it at US$1.6B in May 2024, and it has not raised since. VAST has repriced to US$30B in the meantime.
  • The risks are scale, channel and proof. WEKA turned over its executive team in 2024–25, and HPE stopped reselling its software in March 2026 (announced November 2025). It has no MLPerf Storage results since 2024. Demand is concentrated in NVIDIA-driven neocloud spending.
  • For Everpure, WEKA is the cleanest "software-anywhere" foil to FlashBlade//EXA. The contrasts are a proprietary client versus pNFS, any hardware versus DirectFlash, and a KV-cache head start versus PureKVA.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
WEKA sits on most GPU-cluster shortlists that Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) contests with FlashBlade//EXA, next to VAST and DDN. It wins differently from both. VAST sells shared-everything plus data reduction (Chapter 42), and DDN sells Lustre heritage and NVIDIA reference installs (Chapter 44). WEKA sells portability and latency: the same file system on a neocloud's GPU servers, a customer's own hardware or four public clouds.

WEKA is also a corporate-development reference point. It is a sub-scale, NVIDIA-aligned AI storage software company with a first-mover KV-cache product and a valuation unchanged for two and a half years. Chapter 45 has the four-way comparison, and Chapter 50 has the diligence checklist.

docs.title: What the product is, and what the names mean
docs.text:
Liran Zvibel (CEO), Maor Ben-Dayan and Omri Palmon founded WekaIO in Israel in 2013 to build a flash-native file system faster than local disk1. The company is now based in Campbell, California, and calls itself WEKA. Buyers use its product names interchangeably:

  • WekaFS / WEKA Data Platform (to mid-2025): a POSIX parallel file system with an S3 object tier. WEKA 4 (June 2022) ran it natively on AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and OCI2.
  • NeuralMesh (June 2025): a re-architecture into containerised microservices for data, metadata, auditing and observability, forming a self-healing mesh3. It shipped in limited release first, with GA planned for fall 20254.
  • NeuralMesh Axon (July 2025): the same software running inside GPU servers on their local NVMe. Cohere and CoreWeave were the launch references5.
  • NeuralMesh 6 (announced 2026-07-21): adds multi-tenancy, data reduction, native object and an enhanced AMG. GA is planned for 2H 2026 and is a free upgrade6.

Shared-nothing (Chapter 15) and parallel-file-system (Chapter 17) mechanics apply; this chapter covers only what WEKA does differently.

docs.title: The architecture in one picture
docs.text:
Figure 43.1 — WEKA runs the same user-space services on every backend server and spreads both metadata and data across all of them, so there is no metadata server to saturate.

Three design choices define WEKA:

1. Everything is a user-space process. WEKA defines four process roles. Frontend processes serve clients, compute processes run file-system logic, drive processes own NVMe devices and a management process handles control. NFS, SMB and S3 run as separate containers7.

2. Metadata is sharded, not centralised. Lustre-style systems keep the namespace on dedicated metadata servers, which choke on millions of small files (Chapter 21). WEKA splits metadata into thousands of "buckets", each run by a virtual metadata server inside the compute processes on every node. A hash of each operation, not just the inode, picks the owning bucket, so even block ranges of one hot file spread across owners. Buckets journal to WEKA's own protected storage8.

Semiconductor bridge: this is address interleaving across DRAM channels and banks. A hashed address map stops any one access pattern from hammering one bank. The cost is also the same: an operation spanning many buckets, such as a cross-directory rename, becomes a distributed transaction.

3. Protection is distributed erasure coding. Each stripe holds data strips plus 2 or 4 parity strips; older (4.1) docs give 3–16 data strips, current docs a total stripe width of 5–20. N+2 is the default. Stripes are spread any-to-any across servers, and the stripe shape is fixed when the cluster is formed9. A 16+4 stripe keeps 16/20 = 80% of raw capacity as data, while 5+2 keeps ≈ 71%. The full stripe must fit within the number of failure domains, with headroom for spare capacity, so 16+4 needs at least 20 servers (or racks, if racks are the failure domain); one docs example runs 16+2 on 20 servers. Small clusters therefore pay more for parity, the usual shared-nothing trade.

docs.title: The kernel-bypass data path
docs.text:
WEKA's latency comes from bypassing the operating system's I/O plumbing. Backend servers run DPDK, which maps the NIC into user space via SR-IOV. Clients use DPDK too, falling back to kernel UDP where it is unavailable, such as some AWS instance types. In performance mode, WEKA processes busy-poll on dedicated cores. A CPU-optimised mode, added in release 5.0, uses interrupts instead7. Drive processes reach NVMe from user space, in the style of SPDK.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as App on GPU server
    participant F as WEKA client frontend
    participant B as Bucket-owner compute process
    participant D as Drive processes on several servers
    participant N as NVMe SSDs
    A->>F: read 4 MB at offset X
    Note over A,F: driver passes the request via shared memory, no kernel network stack
    F->>F: hash file and offset to find the owning bucket
    F->>B: DPDK message to the owner
    B->>B: look up extent locations in bucket metadata
    B->>D: request strips from the servers that hold them
    D->>N: user-space NVMe reads, polled not interrupt-driven
    N-->>D: data
    D-->>F: strips returned over DPDK or RDMA
    F-->>A: copy into app buffer, or DMA into GPU memory with GDS
    Note over B,N: Writes reverse this - the owner cuts data into N plus 2 or 4 strips across failure domains and acks once they are durable

Figure 43.2 — A WEKA read never enters the kernel network or block stack; the price is CPU cores dedicated to polling. Simplified: WEKA does not publish the exact internal hop order.

Illustrative budget (orders of magnitude, not WEKA measurements): if a kernel path spends ~5 µs of CPU per small I/O on syscalls, interrupts and copies, and a polled user-space path spends ~1 µs, then 1M IOPS needs ~5 cores in the first case and ~1 in the second. Polling also removes scheduler jitter, so tail latency tightens. The catch is that a polling core stays busy even when there is no work. On a GPU server in converged mode, that is a core taken from the data loaders.

Semiconductor bridge: this is the trade between an interrupt-driven peripheral and a command engine spinning on a doorbell register. You spend silicon to make latency deterministic. NVMe made the same move on the SSD side (Chapter 7), and WEKA extends it across the network.

One consequence buyers notice: the fast path needs the WEKA client, a kernel module plus agent, on every compute node. Agentless access goes through NFS, SMB or S3 gateways at lower performance. EXA and VAST both use standard NFS or pNFS clients instead.

docs.title: Four ways to deploy the same software
docs.text:
Mode Where WEKA runs Who buys the hardware Best for Main cost or risk Dedicated (on-premises) Qualified servers from Supermicro, Dell, Lenovo, Hitachi and others10 Customer, via OEM or reseller Separate enterprise/HPC storage tier Customer integrates a multi-vendor stack WEKApod appliance WEKA-branded servers, now WEKApod 3 (Nitro, Prime, Prime Max)11 Customer, from WEKA One-vendor support, SuperPOD certification WEKA takes hardware margin and supply risk Converged / Axon Inside GPU servers, on local NVMe and spare cores5 Already bought with the GPUs Neoclouds, large training fleets Shares failure domains, CPU and NICs with compute Public cloud AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, OCI instances, plus marketplace listings2 Cloud provider Cloud-native AI, burst capacity Ephemeral instance NVMe; durability rests on EC and object tiering

Table 43.1 — One software stack, four packaging models: this flexibility is WEKA's moat and its support burden.

Worked example: converged economics. A DGX H100-class server carries eight 3.84 TB NVMe drives, about 30.7 TB that many clusters use only as scratch. Across 128 servers that is ≈ 3.9 PB raw, or ≈ 3.1 PB usable at 16+4, with no storage-server capex, rack space or power. Stability AI, WEKA's first converged reference, claimed a 95% storage-cost cut and 93% GPU utilisation (company-stated)12. At Axon's launch, CoreWeave reported more than 30 GB/s read, 12 GB/s write and 1M IOPS to a single GPU server (vendor-supplied)5.

The risks are equally concrete. A GPU server reboot becomes a storage-node failure. Rebuild traffic then shares NICs with the collectives that keep GPUs in lockstep. Axon answers with static per-workload allocation of cores, memory, NVMe and NIC bandwidth5. That is a partitioning fix, not a physics fix.

docs.title: NVIDIA plumbing: GPUDirect Storage, Spectrum-X, NIXL
docs.text: WEKA supported GPUDirect Storage (GDS) when NVIDIA finalised GDS 1.0 in 202113. GDS DMAs data straight into GPU memory, skipping the CPU bounce buffer (Chapter 11). NVIDIA's Spectrum-X storage tests included WEKA and claimed up to 48% faster reads14. WEKA also open-sourced a plugin for NIXL, NVIDIA's data-movement library, so Dynamo-based serving can use WEKA as a KV tier15. NVIDIA invested in WEKA's Series E16.

docs.title: Augmented Memory Grid: KV cache as a storage product
docs.text:
Chapter 32 explains why the attention key/value (KV) cache is the memory problem of long-context inference. AMG is WEKA's productised answer. KV blocks evicted from GPU memory go to a NeuralMesh "token warehouse" on pooled NVMe. When a later request shares the prefix, the blocks stream back over RDMA and GDS instead of being recomputed. WEKA unveiled AMG at GTC in March 202517 and made it commercially available on 2025-11-18, with OCI as exclusive launch partner via Oracle Cloud Marketplace15.

flowchart TB
    E["Inference engine - vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM under Dynamo"]
    subgraph SRV["Inside each GPU server - private tiers"]
        G1["G1 GPU HBM - active KV blocks"]
        G2["G2 host DRAM - warm KV blocks"]
        G3["G3 local NVMe - optional"]
    end
    subgraph SH["Shared context tier - AMG on NeuralMesh"]
        W["Token warehouse - KV blocks on pooled NVMe, visible to every GPU server"]
    end
    O["S3 object tier - cold contexts"]
    E --> G1
    G1 <-->|evict and reload| G2
    G2 <--> G3
    G1 <-->|"NIXL plugin over RDMA and GDS"| W
    W -.->|tiering| O

Figure 43.3 — AMG fills the shared-storage slot in NVIDIA Dynamo's tier model; its value is that a prefix computed on one GPU server can be reused by any other.

Dynamo's KV Block Manager labels the tiers G1 (HBM), G2 (host DRAM), G3 (local SSD) and G4 (remote storage)18. AMG is a G4 built to perform like a fast G3.

Worked example (illustrative, Llama-3-70B geometry, FP16 KV). Each token's KV state takes 2 × 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dims × 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes ≈ 320 KiB. A 128,000-token context is therefore ≈ 42 GB, more than half an 80 GB H100. Recomputing that prefill costs ≈ 2 × 70×10⁹ × 128,000 ≈ 1.8×10¹⁶ FLOPs, ignoring attention's quadratic term. Eight H100s at ~400 TFLOP/s each (≈40% of dense FP16 peak) need ~5.6 s for it. Reading the 42 GB from a tier delivering 100 GB/s per server takes ~0.4 s. That ≈ 13x gap is why "up to 20x faster TTFT" at 128K context is plausible. Short prompts gain little.

Claims and evidence. At launch WEKA claimed up to 20x faster TTFT at 128K tokens versus a standard vLLM baseline on OCI15. In June 2026, WEKA and Oracle reported results from a nine-node, 72-GPU H100 cluster with 100K-token contexts: about 2M tokens/s versus under 200K for DRAM-only, about 5,000 versus 600 concurrent users, and the cache grown from 8.64 TiB of DRAM to 287 TiB of NVMe (vendor-run joint test)19. At 100K tokens and the 70B geometry above (~33 GB per context; the test model's geometry may differ), 287 TiB holds ~9,600 contexts against ~290 in DRAM. The capacity grew ~33x but throughput only ~10x, which shows the bottleneck moved to decode or the network. And 5,000 ÷ 600 is ~8x, not the headline 10x. NAND Research noted that WEKA's 10x claims lack a reproducible methodology20. WEKA did not enter MLPerf Storage v3.0, the first round with a peer-reviewed KV-cache workload (September 2026)21.

docs.title: NeuralMesh 6 and WEKApod 3: closing feature gaps
docs.text:
NeuralMesh 6 reads as a catch-up list for neoclouds and enterprises6:

  • Multi-tenancy: hardware-isolated "composable clusters" plus virtual tenants with private VLANs, per-tenant keys and separate authentication. Coverage cites up to 50,000 logical tenants per cluster.
  • Data reduction: always-on dedupe, similarity hashing and compression. WEKA claims up to 6x on AI training data at under 5% write overhead and contractually guarantees both. This is the feature on which VAST built its business, and WEKA had lacked it.
  • Native object, replication, remote caching and Kubernetes-native operations.

WEKApod 3 is WEKA's first chassis designed from the ground up for its own software. It comes in three configurations, Nitro, Prime and Prime Max, with deliveries starting in fall 20266. Prime Max claims 1.1 EB effective per rack from 441.5 PB raw, using about 1,800 Micron 245.76 TB SSDs11. Checking the arithmetic: 1,800 × 245.76 TB ≈ 442 PB raw, so "1.1 EB" assumes ~2.5:1 reduction on raw capacity (coverage describes it as about 3:1 on usable capacity after protection)22. The rack is also quoted at 10.2 TB/s23 [VERIFY: 10.2 TB/s and 210M IOPS per rack from secondary coverage only]. The exabyte is therefore a reduction assumption, not a capacity spec.

docs.title: BlueField-4 and NVIDIA STX: storage moving onto the DPU
docs.text:
In October 2025 WEKA said its next NeuralMesh would run directly on NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs, which offer 800 Gb/s networking and ~6x BlueField-3's compute. It projected over 100x better tokens per watt than CPU-attached storage, an expectation rather than a measurement24. In March 2026 NVIDIA launched BlueField-4 STX, a storage reference architecture whose first rack-scale implementation is the CMX context-memory platform. WEKA, Everpure, VAST and DDN were among the named storage partners25. WEKA positioned AMG as STX's shared KV layer and claimed 4–10x higher context-memory throughput26 [VERIFY: whether validation used BlueField-3 or BlueField-4; sources conflict].

This cuts both ways for WEKA. Its poll-mode, user-space design already resembles DPU firmware, so porting is natural. But STX makes the KV tier a standard NVIDIA slot that every partner can fill, which erodes AMG's 2025 head start.

docs.title: Business model & financials
docs.text:
Model. WEKA sells capacity-based software subscriptions. The hardware comes from partners, from WEKApod or from the cloud provider. One reseller lists a Lenovo-branded edition at US$339 per TB per year in the 1–2.5 PB band27 [VERIFY: single reseller listing]. At that list price, 10 PB is about US$3.4M a year. US$100M of ARR at list would imply ~295 PB under subscription.

timeline
    title WEKA milestones 2013 to 2026
    2013 : Founded in Israel by Zvibel, Ben-Dayan and Palmon
    2019 : Series C of 31.7M dollars with NVIDIA, Mellanox and HPE investing
    2022 : 73M dollar round in January : WEKA 4 goes multicloud in June : Series D of 135M dollars in November
    2023 : Converged mode on AWS with Stability AI
    2024 : Series E of 140M dollars at 1.6B valuation : President, CFO and CRO depart in December
    2025 : Over 100M dollars ARR disclosed : AMG unveiled at GTC : NeuralMesh and Axon launched : AMG commercially available on OCI
    2026 : HPE resale ends in March : STX integration at GTC : NeuralMesh 6 and WEKApod 3 in July

Figure 43.4 — WEKA's product cadence accelerated in 2025–26, but it has raised no new money since May 2024.

Funding. WEKA said it had raised US$66.7M in total after a US$31.7M Series C in May 2019, a round that included NVIDIA, Mellanox, HPE, Seagate, Western Digital Capital and Qualcomm28. A US$73M round led by Hitachi Ventures followed in January 2022. Outlets disagree on whether it was a C extension or a Series D29. In November 2022 came a US$135M Series D led by Generation Investment Management, at ~US$750M (reported by Calcalist, not disclosed by WEKA)30. The May 2024 Series E raised US$140M at US$1.6B post-money, combining primary and secondary transactions31; the split often cited is US$100M primary and US$40M in secondary sales by long-serving employees [VERIFY: primary/secondary split not in WEKA's release]. Valor Equity Partners led, joined by NVIDIA, Atreides, Generation, Qualcomm Ventures and Hitachi Ventures16. The rounds sum to ≈ US$415M, which matches PitchBook's estimate32. No later priced round was found, and a 2026 Globes interview still treated the Series E as the latest33.

Figure 43.5 — WEKA has raised about US$415M, but its US$1.6B mark is now a third of DDN's and about 5% of VAST's. Data: data/ch43_funding.csv

Revenue and burn. In February 2025 Zvibel wrote that WEKA passed US$100M ARR in 2024, after more than doubling revenue for three straight years (company-stated)34. The same month, WEKA cut about 50 go-to-market roles while still planning about 120 hires35. Calcalist reported Zvibel expecting revenue to triple in 2025, with burn of about US$0.5M a month (reported by press)36 [VERIFY: date and context of tripling and burn figures]. Globes later cited estimates of US$100–150M ARR (estimated)33. No company-stated figure for 2025 or 2026 was found.

Valuation arithmetic. At the Series E, US$1.6B on about US$100M ARR was ≈ 16x ARR. VAST's April 2026 round priced it at US$30B on more than US$500M of committed ARR (company-stated), ≈ 60x37. If WEKA did triple in 2025, its 2024 mark would now be a single-digit multiple.

Leadership churn. In December 2024, WEKA parted with its president, CFO and CRO while describing itself as being in a pre-IPO growth phase38. The replacement CFO left after four months. April 2025 brought a new CRO (Brian Froehling) and CPO (Ajay Singh), and the previous CPO moved to strategy and corporate development39. A new CMO followed in July 2026 as messaging shifted to inference at scale40.

docs.title: Customers & go-to-market
docs.text:
WEKA sells direct and through partners. Hardware partners include Supermicro, Dell, Lenovo and Hitachi10, and Hitachi Vantara OEM'd WekaFS from 202041. The biggest channel change went against WEKA. HPE told partners in November 2025 that it would stop selling WEKA, Qumulo and Scality software, with quoting ending on 31 January and orders no longer accepted from 2026-03-03, in favour of its own Alletra MP42. HPE resellers can still sell WEKA on standard HPE servers, and WEKA said only the transaction route changed42. That came months after WEKA on HPE Alletra 4110 servers had topped all five SPECstorage Solution 2020 workloads43.

Customer or partner Relationship (as publicly described) Evidence label Oracle Cloud Infrastructure AMG launch partner; joint inference validation in 20261519 Company-stated, joint releases CoreWeave Lists WEKA NeuralMesh as a dedicated-storage option; Axon launch reference445 Company-stated by both Cohere Deployed Axon in public cloud, then on CoreWeave5 Company-stated Nebius WEKA chosen for premium AI Cloud storage tier, June 202545 Company-stated Stability AI Converged mode on AWS reference12 Company-stated Midjourney, Yotta (Shakti Cloud) Listed on WEKA customer page46 Company-stated, no detail Memorial Sloan Kettering IO500 submission on WEKA47 Company-stated [VERIFY: against io500.org list] Tesla Named as a customer in Globes coverage33 Reported by press "30% of the Fortune 50" WEKA marketing claim46 Company-stated, unverifiable

Table 43.2 — WEKA's visible references skew to AI labs, neoclouds and one hyperscaler partner (OCI); few are independently corroborated.

Since 2023, WEKA's growth has come from AI-native buyers: model builders, GPU clouds and OCI. Its older HPC, EDA and media base is stickier but slower-growing. Two things are missing: anything like VAST's reported US$1.17B CoreWeave deal48, and a flagship NVIDIA-internal reference like DDN's.

docs.title: Why it gained traction
docs.text:
1. It solved GPU starvation early. WEKA bet that flash plus kernel bypass could beat local NVMe for shared data. When GPU clusters arrived, that made it the default "fast file system that isn't Lustre".
  2. Software-only suits neocloud economics. Converged mode turns flash the neocloud already owns into a file system, and marketplace listings fit cloud billing.
  3. Portability is real. Few high-performance file systems run the same code on-premises and natively in four clouds. That matters to labs that train wherever GPUs are free.
  4. Sharded metadata handles small files. Datasets of images and checkpoint shards can run into a metadata-server ceiling, and WEKA's buckets avoid it. WEKA led SPECstorage in early 202543.
  5. It productised KV cache first. AMG gave WEKA an inference story as the market pivoted, months before NVIDIA standardised the tier.

docs.title: Risks & open questions
docs.text:
• Scale and capital asymmetry. VAST's company-stated committed ARR is several times WEKA's, and its valuation is ~19x37. That lets VAST outspend WEKA on R&D, field engineering and neocloud terms. A flat mark also complicates retention and any IPO.
  • One demand cycle. WEKA's customers cluster in GPU clouds and AI labs whose spend follows NVIDIA cycles and their own financing.
  • NVIDIA gives and takes. NVIDIA is an investor and certifier. But STX/CMX turns the KV tier into a slot any partner can fill, and Dynamo decides which tiers matter1825.
  • Hardware-agnostic support burden. Supporting many servers, NICs, kernels and four clouds is costly, and partners can defect, as HPE showed42. WEKApod 3 eases the burden by moving WEKA toward appliances.
  • Benchmark posture. WEKA entered MLPerf Storage v0.5 (2023)49 and v1.0 (2024)50, then skipped v2.0 (per StorageReview's submitter history51) and v3.0, including v3.0's KV-cache test21. FlashBlade//EXA displaced the HPE–WEKA configuration at the top of SPECstorage AI_IMAGE in 202652. Skipping rounds proves nothing about performance, but WEKA's inference claims now rest on vendor-run tests.
  • Open questions. Did NeuralMesh 6 reach GA on time? What share of revenue is now WEKApod hardware? Did revenue triple? Is there an unannounced financing or strategic process?

docs.title: Strategic relevance to Everpure
docs.text:
These are options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information:

  1. WEKA as an EXA competitor. WEKA's portability and converged mode attack where EXA is weakest: storage on hardware buyers already own, in a cloud, or inside GPU servers. EXA's counters are a standard pNFS client, Purity's metadata engine, DirectFlash on the metadata tier, appliance-grade support and peer-reviewed MLPerf v3.0 results in a round WEKA skipped21.
  2. WEKA as a signal about software-only storage. Pure software can win AI share but struggles to capture value at scale. WEKA has had to build appliances, add data reduction and absorb a partner exit. That is consistent with Everpure's integrated thesis, but VAST's company-stated cash generation on a software-only model points the other way, so it is a signal, not proof.
  3. WEKA as a corporate-development reference. WEKA brings a US$1.6B last mark, about US$415M raised, NVIDIA and Qualcomm Ventures on the cap table, a KV-cache product, cloud-native code and Israeli engineering. An acquirer would weigh overlap with its own stack, client-agent support liabilities, neocloud concentration and the preference stack at a flat valuation. For Everpure the overlap with Purity//FB and EXA is large. Lighter options include interoperability, such as Everpure object storage as a WEKA tier, or competing head-on with PureKVA.

docs.text:

Table 43.3 — WEKA leads on deployment flexibility and KV-cache maturity; EXA leads on standard clients and 2026 public benchmark results; VAST leads on scale and data reduction.

Steelman WEKA. WEKA is the only one of the three that follows a customer anywhere: into GPU servers, four clouds, customer-chosen hardware and, next, onto DPUs. Its kernel-bypass path and sharded metadata are serious engineering, not marketing. It unveiled a KV tier a year before NVIDIA's STX standardised one and had it commercially available months ahead.

Where EXA's trade is better. EXA needs no client agent, runs its metadata on Everpure's own hardware with mature Purity software, scales data nodes independently, and has peer-reviewed MLPerf v3.0 numbers in the very workloads WEKA skipped. It trails WEKA on cloud reach, converged deployment and KV-cache track record (Chapter 27).

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
WEKA's arc has three phases:

  • 2013–2019, the HPC file system that wasn't Lustre. About US$67M from VCs and strategics including NVIDIA, Mellanox and HPE funded the core technology28.
  • 2020–2024, cloud and AI scale-up. WEKA signed a Hitachi Vantara OEM deal41, went multicloud2 and won converged-mode AI labs12. It raised about US$348M in three rounds (January 2022, November 2022 and May 2024), reaching a US$1.6B valuation293016.
  • 2025–2026, the inference pivot under pressure. WEKA restructured35, rebuilt as NeuralMesh3 and shipped AMG15. It aligned with BlueField-4 and STX2426 and filled feature gaps with NeuralMesh 66. It also lost HPE as a reseller42.

Signals to watch through 2027:

  • NeuralMesh 6 GA and WEKApod 3 shipments.
  • Any financing event that reprices the US$1.6B mark.
  • MLPerf Storage participation, especially the KV-cache workload.
  • STX/CMX deployments that name WEKA as the shipped software.
  • Large neocloud wins, or losses to VAST.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Three questions for a PM

  1. "When we lose an EXA deal to WEKA, is it portability, converged mode or KV cache?" A strong answer separates the three:
  2. Cloud losses are structural, because EXA has no cloud SKU.
  3. Converged losses come down to capex optics, and a TCO that includes the CPU tax and failure-domain coupling can counter them.
  4. KV-cache losses may narrow once PureKVA ships and buyers weigh MLPerf KV results, but WEKA has a year of production references that Everpure does not yet have.
  5. "How do we answer NeuralMesh 6's guaranteed data reduction?" A strong answer treats the guarantee as a commercial instrument, since AI training data is often already compressed. It asks what the guarantee excludes and compares measured, workload-specific effective capacity.
  6. "Does HPE's exit from reselling WEKA help us?" A strong answer is cautious: HPE left to push Alletra MP, but resellers with WEKA practices may want another AI file platform.

Three questions for an engineer

  1. "What does WEKA's kernel bypass buy that EXA's pNFS-over-RDMA path doesn't?" A strong answer: both keep bulk data out of the kernel. WEKA's edge is polled handling of metadata and small I/O across a sharded namespace. EXA's edge is a standard client and metadata kept off the data path. The workload's metadata-to-data ratio decides it.
  2. "How does bucket-sharded metadata compare with Purity//FB's metadata core under a rename storm or a million-file listing?" A strong answer covers hash distribution versus a dedicated tier, the cost of cross-bucket transactions, and where tail latency comes from. It cites test data, not datasheets.
  3. "What does converged mode really cost?" A strong answer counts pinned cores, memory and NIC bandwidth per node, then covers rebuilds during GPU maintenance and the blast radius when a node fails.

Don't say this:

  • "WEKA is just another Lustre." It has no dedicated metadata server, runs in user space and deploys differently (Chapter 17).
  • "WEKA is a hardware company now." WEKApod exists, but WEKA's revenue is still mostly software subscriptions running on partner hardware.
  • "AMG gives 20x faster inference." The 20x is TTFT at very long context in vendor tests. Throughput gains in the OCI test were nearer 8–10x.
  • "WEKA is worth US$1.6B." That was the May 2024 mark, and today's price is unknown in either direction.
  • "WEKA avoids MLPerf because it would lose." It did submit in 2023 and 2024. It simply has no peer-reviewed results from 2025 or 2026.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• WEKA's internals: the "Architecture Key Concepts" paper (buckets and hashing)8, and the docs on networking and on redundancy79.
  • Where AMG plugs in: NVIDIA Dynamo's KVBM design doc, which covers the NIXL integration point18.
  • The OCI evidence: the June 2026 WEKA/OCI validation, read against MLPerf Storage v3.0's KV-cache rules1921.
  • The SPECstorage record: the HPE Alletra 4110 + WEKA results (January 2025) versus FlashBlade//EXA (2026)4352.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• NeuralMesh / NeuralMesh Axon — WEKA's platform since June 2025; Axon runs it inside GPU servers.
  • Augmented Memory Grid (AMG) — WEKA's KV-cache offload tier.
  • Converged mode — storage backends on the application or GPU servers.
  • DPDK / kernel bypass — user-space networking that skips the OS stack.
  • Metadata bucket — a WEKA namespace shard owned by one virtual metadata server.
  • WEKApod — WEKA's appliance line.
  • NVIDIA STX / CMX — NVIDIA's BlueField-4 storage reference architecture and its context-memory rack.

See the glossary.
