docs.title: 44. DDN deep dive
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~17 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Parallel and distributed file systems · Object storage architecture · Inference and KV cache · The NVIDIA ecosystem

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• DDN is the 28-year-old incumbent of AI storage. Founded in 1998 and still run by its two founders, it owns the commercial centre of gravity of Lustre and sold the storage inside NVIDIA's own Selene and Eos supercomputers12.
  • It now runs two engines. EXAScaler (Lustre in appliances) serves training and HPC bandwidth. Infinia, a key-value-store-based platform announced in 2023, targets inference, KV cache and multi-tenant object data3. DDN CORE (November 2025) is the control plane over both4.
  • The money is real but opaque. Blackstone paid $300M for a stake at a $5B valuation in January 2025, DDN's first institutional capital in about two decades5. Press reports put revenue near $500M in 2025 with a ~$1B target for 2026, but the base figures conflict67.
  • The moat is intimacy, not code. Lustre is open source; DDN's edge is the engineers who maintain it, reference designs inside NVIDIA, and a profitable, government-friendly supplier record.
  • The risks are structural. A kernel client on every GPU node, two platforms to fund, late enterprise features, hardware-heavy margins and founder succession. DDN, which entered every earlier MLPerf Storage round, sat out v3.0, as did VAST and WEKA8.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
In large AI and HPC deals, DDN is often already on the floor: the DGX SuperPOD reference architectures many GPU buyers copy were validated with DDN early9, and labs and governments have run Lustre for two decades. When Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) pitches FlashBlade//EXA into those accounts, it is usually trying to displace or sit beside an EXAScaler system. EXA uses the same metadata-plus-data-nodes architecture but swaps the Lustre kernel client for standard pNFS (Chapter 17).

DDN is also changing shape in ways that move it closer to Everpure's home ground. It hired a former Pure Storage executive as President and Chief Revenue Officer to push into the enterprise10, built a new platform (Infinia) aimed at inference and KV cache, and is reportedly seeking strategic investors11. Knowing where DDN is strong (bandwidth, NVIDIA reference status, sovereign HPC) and thin (enterprise operations, data reduction, simplicity) tells Everpure where to fight and where to coexist.

docs.title: The company in one paragraph
docs.text: DataDirect Networks was formed in 1998 by Alex Bouzari (CEO) and Paul Bloch, who had run a predecessor, MegaDrive Systems, since 198812. It took about $12M of venture money around 2002, fell out with the investors, and the founders bought them out13. Until 2025 it grew on its own cash flow, selling high-bandwidth storage to supercomputing sites, and by Forbes' account each founder still owns about 40%6. Hence DDN's character: engineering-led, lab-focused, frugal, profitable (company-stated), and run by two people who have made every major decision for 28 years.

docs.title: Two engines, one company
docs.text:
Figure 44.1 — DDN sells two different architectures: a mature Lustre engine tuned for bandwidth, and a young key-value engine tuned for tenancy and inference, joined only at the control plane.

The two engines share almost no code. EXAScaler descends from Lustre, a 1999 research project that DDN took over commercially in 201814. Infinia was written from scratch and announced in 2023 as "not a development of" EXAScaler3. DDN's Chief Product Officer said in January 2026 that EXAScaler remains central, with the two products as partners under one control plane15. In practice, training and simulation go to EXAScaler; data preparation, inference and multi-tenant service-provider work go to Infinia.

The semiconductor analogy is a foundry running a mature high-performance node and a new specialty node. The old node pays the bills and holds the reference customers; the new one is where demand is supposed to land, but it lacks yield history, and every engineer on it is one not working on the cash cow.

docs.title: EXAScaler: Lustre, productised
docs.text:
EXAScaler is DDN's distribution of Lustre plus management tooling, monitoring and DDN's own hardware16. The mechanism is exactly the Lustre design of Chapter 17. A metadata server (MDS) hands out a file's layout once. The client then moves data directly, in parallel, to and from many object storage servers (OSSs) over RDMA.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as GPU node with Lustre client
    participant M as MDS and MDT
    participant O1 as OSS 1
    participant O2 as OSS 2
    C->>M: open checkpoint file, request layout and lock
    M-->>C: layout - stripes on OST0 to OST3
    par stripes in parallel
        C->>O1: RDMA write stripes 0 and 2
    and
        C->>O2: RDMA write stripes 1 and 3
    end
    O1-->>C: ack
    O2-->>C: ack
    C->>M: close and release lock
    Note over C,O2: metadata touched twice, bulk data never passes the MDS

Figure 44.2 — On EXAScaler the metadata server is consulted at open and close; the bulk bytes flow client-to-OSS in parallel, which is why aggregate bandwidth scales with the number of appliances.

DDN adds packaging and people. Buying Intel's Lustre business in June 2018 brought the development team, support team and contracts, and revived the Whamcloud name14. Owning the main Lustre engineering team lets DDN fix a client bug or backport a feature faster than any rival distributor; for a national lab, that is the product. Rivals ship Lustre too, including HPE and Microsoft (Azure Managed Lustre posted 642.2 GiB/s of checkpoint writes in MLPerf Storage v3.08). The code is open; the moat is the team.

The costs are those of any parallel file system: a client module matched to every GPU server's kernel, hot directories that bottleneck one metadata target, RAID under each target and little data reduction. Lustre buyers accept them for bandwidth and coherent POSIX semantics on shared files.

docs.title: The appliances: A³I and the AI400X line
docs.text:
DDN sells EXAScaler mostly as A³I ("Accelerated, Any-scale AI") appliances: 2U all-NVMe building blocks sized to slot into NVIDIA reference architectures.

Product What it is Launched Headline figures (vendor-stated) Role in 2026 AI400X First A³I all-flash EXAScaler appliance c. 2019–2020 ~7 PB behind NVIDIA Selene1 Installed base AI400X2 / X2 Turbo Second generation; Turbo refresh 2022 / 2024-03 96 GB/s read, 65 GB/s write; Turbo up to 120 GB/s1718 NVIDIA Eos (48 units)2 AI400X3 Third-generation 2U EXAScaler appliance 2025-06 +55% read, +70% write vs prior gen19; reseller lists 140 GB/s read, 110 GB/s write20 MLPerf Storage v2.0 entry21 AI400X3M Refresh with KV-cache support 2026-06 190 GB/s read, 110 GB/s write, 8M IOPS in 2U22 Current flagship Infinia 2.0 → 2.4 Software-defined key-value data platform 2023; 2.0 2025-02; 2.4 2026-07 Sub-ms metadata; up to 10x data reduction (claims)2324 Inference, KV cache, tenancy DDN CORE Control plane and data fabric over both engines 2025-11 On-prem, Google Cloud, OCI, neoclouds4 Unifying brand Google Cloud Managed Lustre First-party Google service built on EXAScaler GA 2025-07 Up to 1 TB/s per namespace25 Cloud channel Tintri VMstore / IntelliFlash Enterprise virtualisation and primary storage Acquired 2018 / 2019 VMstore T7290 GA 2025-0926 Separate enterprise unit

Table 44.1 — DDN's portfolio is a bandwidth appliance line, a young software platform and an enterprise sidecar; the AI400X generations double bandwidth roughly every two to three years.

A worked check on Eos shows how DDN sells. Eos used 48 AI400X2 appliances for 576 DGX H100 systems, in under three racks and about 100 kW, delivering about 4 TB/s2; one trade outlet gives 4.3 TB/s read and 3.1 TB/s write18. At the 96 GB/s datasheet rate, 48 × 96 GB/s = 4.6 TB/s, so delivery was about 87–93% of the summed datasheets (4.0 or 4.3 TB/s): near-linear scaling. Density is 4 TB/s ÷ 100 kW ≈ 40 GB/s per kW, or 4.3 TB/s ÷ 576 ≈ 7.5 GB/s per DGX node.

Now size a checkpoint (Chapter 31). A 405B-parameter model with Adam state is about 6.5 TB. At the reseller's 110 GB/s write figure, eight AI400X3s (16U) give about 880 GB/s, so a synchronous checkpoint takes 6.5 ÷ 0.88 ≈ 7.4 seconds. That is the pitch: a few rack units keep a large cluster's checkpoint stall in single-digit seconds.

docs.title: Infinia: a key-value store wearing many protocols
docs.text:
Infinia's base layer is a distributed key-value store built on a Bε-tree (B-epsilon tree)3. A Bε-tree is a write-optimised B-tree: each internal node holds a buffer of pending updates, which are pushed down the tree in batches. Small random writes therefore become large sequential ones, much as a DRAM controller's write queue coalesces scattered writes into full bursts. Data and metadata both live there, and S3, SDK, block, KV-cache and (since 2.4) limited POSIX access sit on it as peer services, not layers stacked on a file system324.

Two design choices follow. First, tenancy is in the keyspace. Keys run realm, cluster, tenant, subtenant, dataset, and each tenant gets a fixed share of performance and capacity at creation, DDN's answer to noisy neighbours3. Infinia 2.4 (July 2026) made this the headline: isolation, quotas and provisioning in about ten seconds via REST, aimed at NVIDIA cloud partners and managed AI services24. Second, it is hardware-agnostic. Infinia runs on commodity NVMe servers and on Oracle Cloud, uses network erasure coding across nodes, and claims up to 10x always-on data reduction234.

The claims need care. The 2.0 launch claimed up to 100x faster metadata and 10x better cost efficiency without a published baseline23. POSIX in 2.4 is limited availability (RHEL and Ubuntu); GPUDirect Storage and POSIX ACLs remain roadmap items24. The public materials reviewed do not say whether isolation extends to per-tenant encryption keys, which is a fair diligence question [VERIFY: Infinia per-tenant encryption]. The flagship proof point is scale: DDN says xAI runs a single 350 PB Infinia cluster (company-stated)15.

sequenceDiagram
    participant G as Inference server with NIXL plugin
    participant A as Infinia access service
    participant K as Key-value store
    participant N as NVMe nodes
    G->>A: GET cached prefix blocks for tenant T
    A->>K: look up keys in tenant keyspace
    K-->>A: hit - fragment locations
    A->>N: read erasure-coded fragments
    N-->>A: fragments
    A-->>G: KV blocks over RDMA into GPU memory
    Note over G: prefill skipped for cached tokens
    G->>A: PUT new KV blocks after the turn
    A->>K: insert keys, apply quota and eviction policy

Figure 44.3 — Infinia's path is a key lookup, not a file open: a cached prompt prefix comes back as KV blocks, saving the GPU from recomputing it (simplified logical view).

docs.title: KV cache and GPU-initiated access: the inference bet
docs.text:
Why a second engine? Inference changes the I/O pattern (Chapter 32). Training wants a few huge streaming files; long-context inference wants billions of small KV-cache blocks keyed by prompt prefix, retrieved in milliseconds and shared across tenants. That is a key-value workload, and Lustre's MDS-centric design fits it poorly.

DDN's July 2025 benchmark is the reference claim. On Qwen3-32B with a 112K-token context, recomputing the prefill took 57 seconds; loading the cached KV from Infinia took 2.1 seconds, a 27x gain (vendor test on two A100 GPUs)27. A sanity check: Qwen3-32B has 64 layers and 8 KV heads of dimension 128 [VERIFY: model config from public model card], so each token's KV is 2 × 64 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 256 KiB in BF16. For 112K tokens that is about 29 GB, and loading it in 2.1 seconds implies roughly 14 GB/s to two GPUs, plausible for RDMA storage. But recompute is the weakest baseline; the more useful number is Nebul's, a European sovereign cloud reporting nearly 10x faster time to first token than its own CPU-memory cache (October 2026, joint release)28. The semiconductor analogy is spill-to-memory versus recompute: a storage tier pays when fetching a byte costs less GPU time than regenerating it.

DDN has also moved down the stack. In June 2026 both EXAScaler and Infinia gained KV-cache support through NVIDIA Dynamo and NIXL22. In August 2026 DDN and NVIDIA announced joint work, under NVIDIA's Storage-Next initiative, on GPU-initiated data access for Infinia, where GPU threads issue data operations without a CPU round-trip. No performance figures or availability dates were given29. If it ships, the storage client moves into the GPU, favouring vendors with deep NVIDIA ties.

docs.title: Inside NVIDIA's clusters, and the xAI question
docs.text:
DDN's best marketing asset is that NVIDIA bought it for itself. Selene, NVIDIA's DGX A100 SuperPOD ranked seventh in the world in 2020, used about 7 PB of DDN AI400X storage1. Eos used the 48 AI400X2s described above2. DDN also claimed to be the first storage validated with DGX SuperPOD at any scale (company-stated)9. When a GPU buyer copies NVIDIA's own design, DDN is in the bill of materials by default.

xAI is murkier. In November 2024 DDN announced that EXAScaler and Infinia support xAI's 100,000-GPU Colossus in Memphis30. VAST Data has also claimed Colossus, saying xAI trains, checkpoints and stores data on VAST, and in October 2025 Blocks & Files reported VAST in xAI's Colossus expansion while noting DDN's continuing role31. Both can be true at different tiers or phases; no public source settles the split. The honest statement: xAI references both, and Forbes credits xAI contracts as a driver of DDN's 2026 growth6.

docs.title: Benchmarks: present in v0.5 to v2.0, absent in v3.0
docs.text: DDN has been a regular MLPerf Storage entrant: it was one of five submitters in the first round, v0.5 (September 2023)32. In MLPerf Storage v2.0 (August 2025) a single AI400X3 sustained more than 110 GiB/s of reads, and DDN emphasised density (simulated GPUs fed per rack unit) over absolute cluster numbers21 [VERIFY: per-workload accelerator counts differ between DDN materials and secondary write-ups]. In v1.0 an AI400X2T posted 99,018 MiB/s on 3D U-Net with 36 simulated H100s33. DDN skipped v3.0 (September 2026), which moved to simulated B200s and added KV-cache tests; VAST and WEKA also stayed out, while Everpure entered8. On IO500 (June 2025) DDN claimed the top spot, but Argonne's DAOS systems held the first two places on the 10-node production list, with a Hudson River Trading EXAScaler system third34. The pattern: DDN shows up where its density story is strongest (Chapter 37).

docs.title: The enterprise sidecar: Tintri, Nexenta, IntelliFlash
docs.text: In 2018–2019 DDN bought three enterprise businesses: Tintri's assets out of bankruptcy for about $60M (September 2018)35, Nexenta, a software-defined storage vendor (May 2019, terms undisclosed)36, and Western Digital's IntelliFlash arrays (ex-Tegile, November 2019), with WD becoming a preferred drive supplier37. These cheap, distressed assets bought enterprise revenue and customers. Tintri still ships (VMstore T7290, September 2025)26, but the units run separately and play little part in the AI story. They show DDN's enterprise experience sits in virtualisation niches, not mainstream primary storage.

docs.title: Business model & financials
docs.text:
DDN's model is classic systems vendor: integrated appliances (hardware, software, support) sold per deal, increasingly complemented by software licences (Infinia, CORE) and cloud royalties (Google Cloud Managed Lustre). Because it is private, every figure below is company-stated or reported by press, and they do not reconcile.

Figure 44.4 — DDN's revenue history is a set of unaudited, partly contradictory data points; the only consistent message is a step-change from roughly US$0.4–0.5B toward a US$1B target in 2026. Data: data/ch44_milestones.csv

  • Revenue. The Register gave $25M (2003), $45M (2005) and $188M (2010)13; DDN said it reached $400M in 20207. In January 2025 Blocks & Files put 2023 at $500M and estimated 2024 at $750M7 [VERIFY: search-summary only]. Forbes' August 2026 profile, as syndicated, gives about $400M (2024) and $500M (2025), on track to double to about $1B in 2026, while the English original calls DDN historically a roughly $300M-a-year business6. Treat ~$0.5B (2025) and a ~$1B 2026 target as a working range, not facts.
  • Momentum. DDN's new President told an October 2026 press tour that bookings were growing about 3x year on year (company-stated)38.
  • Profitability. Blackstone's release cites a self-funded, profitable record (company-stated)5. No margins are public; appliance-heavy revenue usually means lower gross margin than software-only rivals.
  • Capital and valuation. Blackstone Tactical Opportunities invested $300M at a $5B valuation in January 2025 and took a board seat5. Coverage described it as a financial investment, with the founders keeping control39. At $5B against ~$400–500M revenue, the implied multiple is about 10–12x. VAST's $30B valuation on more than $500M of committed ARR is roughly 60x40, and WEKA's $1.6B on ~$100M ARR (2024) about 16x41. Investors valued DDN like a profitable hardware company, not an AI software platform. In June 2026 Bouzari told Bloomberg DDN wanted to raise again by year-end and bring in strategic investors. No size, valuation or close had been reported by 2026-11-0111.
  • Scale. An outside estimate puts 2025 headcount near 1,334 (estimated)42, which on ~$500M revenue is roughly $375k per employee.

docs.title: Customers & go-to-market
docs.text:
DDN's customers fall into five groups:

  • Supercomputing and government. National labs, defence and university HPC centres. Recent IO500 lists include SoftBank's CHIE-4, the University of Florida's HiPerGator and Hudson River Trading43.
  • NVIDIA itself. Selene, Eos and Cambridge-1, and the SuperPOD reference designs that follow from them129.
  • AI labs. xAI, plus an unnamed frontier lab where DDN says it runs Infinia as a managed service across roughly 200,000 GPUs (company-stated)38.
  • Sovereign and regional AI clouds. DDN cites Yotta's Shakti Cloud in India, Singtel, Nebul and SCX.ai, and launched "Sovereign AI Blueprints" at SC254428.
  • Hyperscalers and neoclouds. Google, through Managed Lustre (GA July 2025, up to 1 TB/s per namespace)25, plus CoreWeave, Nebius and Scaleway via CORE, and Oracle via Infinia on OCI4.

DDN says its platforms support more than 500,000 NVIDIA GPUs (company-stated, January 2025)45. Customer counts in DDN materials range from 5,000+ to 11,000+ [VERIFY: definitions differ]3812.

Go-to-market has three routes. NVIDIA-led: DDN rides SuperPOD and NVIDIA Cloud Partner designs into GPU purchases. Integrators and OEMs: national HPC procurements go through prime contractors, and SC25 added a Supermicro-built "Enterprise AI HyperPOD"4. Cloud: Google sells EXAScaler as a first-party service, giving DDN reach without a sales force. In 2026 DDN professionalised its leadership: Guido Torrini (ex-CFO of OneTrust and Celonis) became Chief Financial Operating Officer in February, a hire Bloomberg tied to a possible IPO46; Kevin Delane (ex-Salesforce, Pure Storage and Cohesity) became President and Chief Revenue Officer in April to drive enterprise adoption10; and a Vice Chair was named47.

docs.title: Why it gained traction
docs.text:
1. It was already in the reference design. NVIDIA ran its own clusters on DDN, so the "safe" choice for a SuperPOD buyer in 2020–2024 was DDN. Reference status works like a foundry's process design kit: switching costs appear before price is discussed.
  2. Bandwidth per rack when stalls were expensive. Every second a checkpoint blocks thousands of GPUs is paid at GPU rental rates (Chapter 11); appliances with known GB/s per 2U let architects size storage by arithmetic.
  3. Open source with a throat to choke. Sovereign and public buyers like Lustre because it is open (GPL); DDN employs most of its core developers, so buyers get open code plus a vendor that can fix it.
  4. A boring balance sheet. A profitable, founder-owned supplier with 25 years of lab references passes government procurement and multi-year support tests that venture-funded rivals sometimes do not.
  5. Speed into inference. Infinia, Dynamo/NIXL support and GPU-initiated access gave DDN a credible inference story quickly, so it was not trapped as a training-only vendor.

docs.title: Risks & open questions
docs.text:
• Lustre complexity and the client. The kernel client is both DDN's performance edge and its operational tax: it must be rebuilt and qualified for every kernel and GPU-server image. Standard-client designs (FlashBlade//EXA's pNFS, VAST's NFS) attack exactly this pain (Chapter 8).
  • Two platforms, one R&D budget. EXAScaler and Infinia share a control plane, not a data path. DDN funds a mature parallel file system and a young KV platform where VAST and WEKA each fund one, and customers must pick which engine holds their data. Infinia's POSIX GA, ACLs and GPUDirect support were still on the roadmap in mid-202624.
  • Enterprise feature gaps. Enterprise buyers expect always-on data reduction, snapshots, replication, non-disruptive upgrades and simple multi-tenancy. EXAScaler was built for scratch bandwidth; Infinia adds tenancy and reduction but is young.
  • Appliance margins and supply. Selling hardware means DDN carries NAND and server-cost swings that software-only vendors pass to OEMs (Chapter 48), and doubling revenue strains supply chains; Torrini's remit includes supply chain46.
  • Founder succession and governance. Bouzari and Bloch have run DDN since 1998 and control roughly 80% of it6. The 2026 hires look like institutionalisation ahead of an IPO or strategic round4610; no succession plan is public.
  • Concentration and disclosure. Growth leans on a few huge AI and sovereign contracts, xAI among them; revenue figures are unaudited and inconsistent; skipping MLPerf v3.0 leaves no like-for-like evidence against 2026 rivals.
  • Open questions. Who joins the strategic round, and on what terms? Does Infinia reach POSIX GA and win training workloads, or stay an inference sidecar? How much of the 2026 revenue is one-off cluster builds versus recurring?

docs.title: Strategic relevance to Everpure
docs.text:
DDN matters to Everpure in three ways. First, it is the incumbent EXA must displace in Lustre-heritage accounts: Everpure offers the same metadata/data split without a kernel module, plus Purity's data reduction, Evergreen ownership and enterprise operations (Chapter 27); DDN counters with exascale references, coherent shared-file writes and NVIDIA's own clusters. Second, DDN is moving toward Everpure's ground: Infinia's tenancy targets the neocloud buyers EXA's 2026 tenancy features target, its KV-cache tier competes with PureKVA, and an ex-Pure Storage executive runs its revenue organisation. Third, its capital event is a signal: a strategic investor such as NVIDIA, a hyperscaler or a sovereign fund would harden DDN's channel.

Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information:

  • Compete where Lustre hurts. Target accounts whose pain is client management, metadata hot spots or capacity cost, not raw bandwidth, and publish per-rack, per-kW and per-TB figures beside DDN's density claims.
  • Coexist where it does not. Where labs keep EXAScaler as scratch, position FlashBlade or EXA as the protected capacity and AI-data tier behind it.
  • Treat the round as intelligence. Watch who invests, at what valuation, and whether CORE or Infinia gains an OEM. A full acquisition would face founder control, a multi-billion price and heavy overlap with EXA; narrower moves (for example, Lustre-to-EXA migration tooling) look more plausible.

docs.text:
Dimension DDN EXAScaler / Infinia Everpure FlashBlade//EXA VAST Data WEKA Core architecture Lustre MDS/OSS appliances; separate KV-store platform Purity metadata core plus independent data nodes48 DASE: stateless CNodes, shared SCM and QLC DBoxes49 Shared-nothing NeuralMesh microservices50 Client Lustre kernel client; S3, SDK, NIXL for Infinia Standard pNFS client48 Standard NFS (incl. RDMA), S3, SMB49 Proprietary user-space client (DPDK); NFS, S351 Data reduction Minimal on EXAScaler; up to 10x claimed on Infinia23 Purity reduction on metadata core; data-node scheme maturing Similarity-based, global49 Added in NeuralMesh 6 (2026)50 Hardware model DDN appliances; Infinia on commodity or cloud DFM blades plus third-party data nodes48 Software on OEM hardware (Supermicro, Cisco, HPE)49 Software; WEKApod appliances KV-cache tier Infinia and EXAScaler via Dynamo/NIXL22 PureKVA on FlashBlade//EXA (availability announced for Oct 2026)52 VUA (open source, 2025)53; BlueField-4-hosted CNodes for NVIDIA's context-memory tier (announced 2026); GPU-equipped CNode-X for vector search54 Augmented Memory Grid55 Cloud Google Cloud Managed Lustre; Infinia on OCI254 No managed EXA service found in public sources Google Cloud hybrid namespace (2025)56 Native on AWS, GCP, Azure, OCI57 Capital Founder-owned; Blackstone $300M at $5B5 Public (NYSE: P) $30B valuation, Series F 202640 $1.6B valuation, Series E 202441 MLPerf Storage v3.0 Did not submit Submitted; top checkpoint write8 Did not submit Did not submit

Table 44.2 — DDN wins on bandwidth heritage and NVIDIA intimacy; Everpure, VAST and WEKA each attack it on a different axis: standard clients, shared-everything economics or a software-only mesh.

Steelman DDN. For a 10,000-GPU training cluster whose owners already run Lustre, DDN is the low-risk answer: known GB/s per 2U, references inside NVIDIA, coherent POSIX writes from thousands of ranks, and an owner-operated supplier whose engineers wrote the code. Profitability means it need not win every deal, and its government relationships take years to replicate. Where Everpure is stronger: no client to install, data reduction and enterprise data services, an ownership model built around non-disruptive upgrades, and public, audited financials. Where VAST and WEKA are stronger: each runs one architecture across training and inference, with deeper software monetisation, and VAST has higher valuation currency for M&A.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title DDN milestones, 1998 to 2026
    1998 : DDN formed by Alex Bouzari and Paul Bloch
    2002 : Founders buy out venture investors
    2018 : Buys Intel Lustre team and revives Whamcloud : Buys Tintri assets for about 60M USD
    2019 : Buys Nexenta : Buys IntelliFlash from Western Digital
    2020 : NVIDIA Selene runs on DDN AI400X
    2023 : Infinia key-value platform announced
    2024 : NVIDIA Eos on 48 AI400X2 : xAI Colossus announced
    2025 : Blackstone invests 300M USD at 5B USD : Infinia 2.0 and AI400X3 : Google Cloud Managed Lustre GA : DDN CORE
    2026 : New CFOO and President : AI400X3M with KV cache : Infinia 2.4 : GPU-initiated access work with NVIDIA

Figure 44.5 — DDN spent two decades as a self-funded HPC specialist, bought Lustre and enterprise assets in 2018–2019, then added outside capital, a second platform and a cloud channel in 2025–2026.

Three phases: 1998–2017, a bootstrapped bandwidth specialist growing from $25M (2003) to $188M (2010) revenue13; 2018–2023, consolidation around Lustre, cheap enterprise assets and NVIDIA's own clusters141; 2024–2026, the AI step-change with xAI, Blackstone, Infinia, Google Cloud and a reported revenue doubling6. Signals to watch: Infinia POSIX GA and GPUDirect support (roadmap after 2.4)24; productisation of GPU-initiated access29; the strategic round targeted for end-202611; and whether DDN returns to MLPerf Storage.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In accounts where DDN shipped the first SuperPOD, what wins the second phase?" Strong answer: names the trigger (a capacity tier, an inference build-out, a painful client upgrade), gives a win/loss pattern, and admits greenfield training pods often stay with DDN.
  2. "How do we answer DDN's 27x and 10x KV-cache numbers against PureKVA?" Strong answer: normalises the baseline (recompute versus a CPU-memory cache versus another storage tier), context length, cache hit rate and cost per token, then quotes Everpure's own MLPerf v3.0 KV-cache results with their configuration.
  3. "Does Google Cloud Managed Lustre show up in our pipeline?" Strong answer: knows which cloud-adjacent AI buyers are choosing a managed Lustre service over on-prem, and what Everpure offers them (data mobility, egress economics, subscription).

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What does a FlashBlade//EXA client give up against a Lustre client on shared-file writes and per-node bandwidth?" Strong answer: separates file-per-rank checkpoints (safe on pNFS) from N-to-1 shared writes, quantifies per-client GB/s, and explains recovery when a client hangs.
  2. "Size EXA against an eight-node AI400X3 rack: per U, per kW, per usable TB." Strong answer: uses datasheet and MLPerf figures, includes data reduction and protection overhead, and names the workload, not just peak reads.
  3. "Infinia keeps all metadata in a Bε-tree key-value store. How does the EXA metadata core compare, and where does each hit its limits?" Strong answer: covers write amplification, small-object rates, tenant isolation and how metadata scales across blades versus nodes.

Don't say this:

  • "DDN is just Lustre." Infinia is a separate, from-scratch platform, and CORE spans both.
  • "DDN is the storage behind xAI." DDN and VAST both claim Colossus; say xAI references both.
  • "DDN never took outside money." It had venture investors around 2002 and Blackstone in 2025.
  • "DDN topped MLPerf Storage." It entered v0.5 to v2.0 and emphasised density in v2.0, but did not enter v3.0.
  • "DDN does $1B in revenue." That is a reported 2026 target; 2025 figures conflict and are unaudited.
  • "Lustre is legacy." It runs most of the world's largest systems, and Google sells DDN's version as a service.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• EXAScaler — DDN's Lustre distribution plus management tooling, sold mostly in appliances.
  • A³I / AI400X series — DDN's 2U all-NVMe EXAScaler appliances for GPU clusters.
  • Infinia — DDN's software-defined data platform built on a distributed key-value store.
  • Bε-tree — a write-optimised B-tree that buffers updates in internal nodes.
  • DDN CORE — DDN's control plane and data fabric spanning EXAScaler and Infinia.
  • Whamcloud — the Lustre engineering unit, owned by DDN since 2018.
  • KV-cache offload — storing transformer key/value tensors outside GPU memory for reuse.
  • GPU-initiated data access — GPUs issuing storage operations without a CPU round-trip.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 45. Head-to-head: FlashBlade//EXA vs. VAST vs. WEKA vs. DDN
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~12 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Disaggregated shared-everything · Parallel file systems · FlashArray and FlashBlade · Reading benchmarks · VAST · WEKA · DDN

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• All four split metadata from data, but in different places. EXA runs metadata on a Purity core and sends bulk data straight to data nodes over pNFS. VAST keeps every byte and all metadata on shared SCM and QLC behind stateless CNodes. WEKA hashes metadata into buckets on every node. DDN puts Lustre metadata on an MDS and data on OSS appliances, and runs a second key-value engine, Infinia, beside it.
  • No vendor wins every deal. VAST leads where buyers want a multi-tenant, multiprotocol platform with references at 10,000+ GPUs. DDN leads where Lustre heritage, NVIDIA's own designs and sovereign procurement decide. WEKA leads where storage must follow the GPUs into clouds or into the GPU servers themselves. EXA leads on peer-reviewed throughput, standard clients and existing Everpure relationships.
  • EXA's evidence is strong but narrow. It posted the top MLPerf Storage v3.0 checkpoint-write and KV-cache-read results in September 2026, in a round VAST, WEKA and DDN all skipped.
  • EXA is behind on references, badges, cloud reach and data-node maturity. No public 10,000-GPU EXA reference exists. NVIDIA's SuperPOD and NCP badges belong to FlashBlade//S, not EXA. No public-cloud EXA exists, and data-node reduction and protection run on a young release train.
  • The features are converging, so the next fight is over proof and economics. Every vendor is an NVIDIA STX partner, every one sells or has announced a KV-cache tier, and WEKA and DDN are adding the data reduction VAST built its business on. What separates vendors in 2027 is reference scale, $/TB under NAND inflation, and operations.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
FlashBlade//EXA is Everpure's entry ticket to the GPU-cluster market that VAST, WEKA and DDN built (Chapter 41). The three rivals each won that market a different way, so a single "EXA vs. competitors" pitch fails. The architecture that beats Lustre on operations is not the one that beats VAST on platform breadth or WEKA on portability. A strategy team needs a map of which deals EXA should chase, which it should concede, and which gaps in product, certification or commercial terms change the odds.

This chapter is that map. It reuses the deep dives' facts (Chapters 27, 42, 43, 44) and adds a common frame: one diagram, one matrix, one scoring chart and a deal-by-deal verdict. Chapter 49 widens the lens to the whole field.

docs.title: Four architectures in one picture
docs.text:
Every scale-out file system has to answer three questions. Where does the namespace (the metadata) live? How many network hops does a byte take from flash to GPU? What has to be installed on the client? The four vendors answer them differently.

Figure 45.1 — EXA and DDN send bulk data one hop, straight to where it lives. VAST adds a CNode hop in exchange for shared, stateless compute. WEKA does away with the metadata server by spreading metadata across every node.

FlashBlade//EXA is a parallel file system built on a standard protocol. The metadata core is FlashBlade hardware running Purity//FB on DirectFlash blades. Launch materials described one to ten chassis of ten blades each1. Data nodes are third-party Linux servers with NVMe SSDs running Purity//DN. Clients fetch a file's layout over NFSv4.1 on TCP, then read and write data nodes directly over RDMA2. Chapter 16 explains why this is a metadata/data split rather than DASE.

VAST is the DASE reference design. Stateless CNodes run every protocol and data service. All state, metadata included, sits on DBoxes: about 1% SCM and about 99% QLC, reached over NVMe-oF34. Any CNode can serve any request.

WEKA NeuralMesh is shared-nothing. Every backend node runs the same user-space processes. Metadata is split into thousands of buckets spread across all nodes, and a hash of each operation picks the bucket that owns it5. The fast path needs WEKA's client driver and DPDK kernel bypass6.

DDN sells two engines. EXAScaler is Lustre: an MDS hands out layouts, and clients stream stripes to OSS appliances over RDMA. Infinia is a separate key-value platform built on a Bε-tree, serving S3, KV-cache and limited POSIX access78. The DDN CORE control plane spans both9.

Semiconductor bridge. Read the four as memory-system topologies. EXA and Lustre resemble a directory-based design: one lookup in a directory (the metadata server), then a direct transfer from the bank that holds the line. VAST is uniform memory access through a crossbar: every core is one hop from every bank, and the crossbar is always on the path. WEKA resembles address-interleaved channels with distributed tag ownership. There is no central directory, and the cost appears when one operation spans many owners.

docs.title: Five differences that decide deals
docs.text:
1. The data path and the client. EXA and Lustre move bulk data one hop. VAST takes two, and its write path multiplies back-end traffic. A 1 GB/s client write lands in SCM on two DBoxes (2 GB/s), is read back for migration (1 GB/s) and is written to QLC as a wide stripe (about 1.03 GB/s), so the fabric carries about 4 GB/s (Chapter 16). VAST pays that tax for stateless compute and global reduction. The client choice runs the other way. EXA and VAST use the stock NFS client, while WEKA and Lustre need a kernel module qualified against every GPU-server image. A neocloud that rebuilds images weekly counts that as an operating cost, not a footnote.

2. Where metadata lives. At thousands of GPUs, metadata is usually the bottleneck, not bandwidth (Chapter 21). EXA's bet is a dedicated, scale-out Purity metadata tier. VAST's is metadata in shared SCM, so it scales with DBoxes but costs a fabric round trip per lookup. WEKA's is hashing, which avoids hot spots but turns a cross-directory rename into a distributed transaction. Lustre's is an MDS that is sharded by hand (DNE) when one target saturates. No public benchmark compares the four on, say, a billion-file listing, so the strongest metadata claim belongs to whoever runs the buyer's proof of concept.

3. Capacity economics. Protection overhead compounds at scale. For 50 PB usable: VAST at 146+4 needs 50 ÷ 0.973 ≈ 51.4 PB raw; WEKA at 16+4 or a Lustre OST at 8+2 RAID needs 50 ÷ 0.8 = 62.5 PB. That is about 11 PB of raw flash between them before any data reduction. With NAND contract prices still rising (TrendForce forecast a further 15–20% for 4Q26)47, this is where VAST's design pays. EXA's data-node protection and reduction figures are not public. That is the single most important number for Everpure to publish.

4. KV cache. All four now sell, or have announced, a shared KV-cache tier (Chapter 32). WEKA shipped first: AMG became commercially available in November 202529, and in June 2026 a joint OCI test grew the cache from 8.64 TiB of DRAM to 287 TiB of NVMe (vendor-run)48. EXA has the only peer-reviewed number: 1,623.4 GiB/s of KV-cache read on 51 hosts21. To put that in tokens: a 70B model's 128K-token context is about 42 GB in FP16 (Chapter 43). 1,623.4 GiB/s ≈ 1,743 GB/s, so the system could reload about 41 such contexts per second (1,743 ÷ 42). But PureKVA itself was only announced on 30 September 2026, with availability slated for October26. NVIDIA's STX reference architecture now names all four as partners45, which turns the KV tier into a standard slot and shortens any lead.

5. Proof. Each vendor proves itself differently. DDN points to NVIDIA's own clusters (Eos used 48 AI400X2s for about 4 TB/s19). VAST points to CoreWeave's US$1.17B agreement (reported by Reuters)49. WEKA points to portability and SPECstorage. EXA points to peer-reviewed benchmarks. Chapter 37 explains why "absence is data" cuts both ways. Rivals skipping MLPerf v3.0 means EXA's first place came against a thin field, and a buyer running a 10,000-GPU proof of concept may trust a reference call over a leaderboard.

Worked example: one checkpoint, two kinds of number. Take a 405B-parameter model with Adam optimizer state, about 6.5 TB (Chapter 31). EXA's peer-reviewed 877.5 GiB/s is about 942 GB/s from 30 data nodes, so a synchronous save takes 6.5 ÷ 0.942 ≈ 6.9 seconds, or about 31 GB/s per data node. Eight DDN AI400X3 appliances at a reseller-listed 110 GB/s write each give about 880 GB/s, or 7.4 seconds (Chapter 44). The two times look equivalent, but they are different kinds of number. EXA's is a measured, peer-reviewed system result. DDN's is a sum of datasheet figures, though DDN's Eos install delivered about 93% of its summed datasheets. Neither tells a buyer the cost per usable TB or per kilowatt, which is the comparison that actually decides the purchase. A strategy team should insist that every competitive claim says which kind of number it is.

The radar below condenses the matrix into eight axes scored 1–5. These are the atlas's judgments, not measurements. Each score has a one-line rationale in the CSV.

Figure 45.3 — The atlas's judgment: EXA has the most lopsided profile of the four, excellent on proof and simplicity and thin on scale, flexibility and ecosystem. VAST has the broadest shape. Data: data/ch45_radar.csv

Two cautions. The axes are unweighted, so summing them is meaningless: a sovereign lab may weight NVIDIA standing at zero and procurement record at everything. The scores also date quickly. Two EXA scores (NVIDIA standing, capacity economics) depend on pending items: NCP-level certification, which Everpure has said it is working toward, and DFM data nodes. Either could move a full point in one quarter.

Table 45.2 — Everpure is the likely winner in one archetype of six, runner-up in two more and a credible challenger in a third. The pattern says EXA's growth depends on converting the enterprise base and on closing the neocloud reference gap.

The neocloud row deserves a closer look, because it is the largest pool of spend. Neoclouds rarely single-source. CoreWeave, VAST's largest customer, also lists WEKA and Everpure among its dedicated-storage options52, and Everpure holds an equity stake in it43. EXA's realistic entry is therefore a second-source tier, won on per-rack throughput, power and data-node sourcing. The aim is a named reference by 2027, not displacing VAST at CoreWeave.

The table is a base rate, not a forecast. Specific deals flip on price, supply and timing. In a NAND shortage, a vendor that can guarantee delivery of media it designs may beat a cheaper software licence on hardware the buyer cannot source (Chapter 48). That favours Everpure's DFM supply chain only once data nodes use DFMs.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Everpure's pitch is a parallel-file-system data path without the parallel-file-system client, backed by Purity metadata, Evergreen ownership and peer-reviewed numbers. Each rival has a credible counter.

Steelman VAST. Breadth compounds. One Element Store serves files, objects, tables, block and Kafka streams. Every new engine reuses the same data without copies, and the fleet of neoclouds running it is the largest in the category. VAST's company-stated committed ARR above US$500M and a US$30B valuation53 give it currency to outspend everyone on field engineering.

Steelman WEKA. It is the only one that follows the GPUs anywhere: on-premises, inside GPU servers, in four clouds, and next onto DPUs. Its KV-cache product, commercially available since November 2025, has the longest sales record of the four: about seven months ahead of DDN's Dynamo-integrated release and nearly a year ahead of PureKVA.

Steelman DDN. NVIDIA runs its own supercomputers on DDN. Lustre's coherent shared-file writes and open code suit labs and governments, and a profitable, founder-owned supplier passes procurement tests venture-backed rivals sometimes fail. Blackstone's US$300M at a US$5B valuation54 and a reported revenue doubling toward about US$1B in 2026 (reported by Forbes)55 show momentum.

Where FlashBlade//EXA is behind, stated plainly:

Gap Evidence Why it matters What would close it Scale references First enterprise EXA customer reported in Q4 FY2656; no public 10K-GPU EXA reference Buyers ask "who runs this at my scale?" before asking about speed A named neocloud or lab reference EXA-level NVIDIA badges NVCS validation extension announced Mar 2026, NCP reported for "later this year"; neither confirmed by 2026-11-01; badges sit on FlashBlade//S33 Gates NVIDIA-led deals NCP and SuperPOD certification for EXA Cloud reach No EXA cloud offering found Concedes cloud-native and burst buyers to WEKA, VAST, DDN Partner-hosted EXA or software on cloud instances Data-node maturity Third-party NVMe; Purity//DN on its own release train; DFM nodes not confirmed GA14 Weakens $/TB and Everpure's own-media story DFM data nodes and published EC and reduction ratios Protocol breadth pNFS only on EXA VAST wins multiprotocol consolidation S3 and object paths on EXA, or a clear FlashBlade//S hand-off Tenancy track record Multi-tenancy and QoS added June 202650 Neoclouds sell tenancy Production tenancy references

Table 45.3 — EXA's gaps are mostly maturity and proof, not architecture. That makes them closable, but only with time and reference wins.

Where EXA leads. The bulk-data path is one hop. Clients need no module. The metadata core runs mature Purity software on Everpure's own DirectFlash. Data nodes can be customer-sourced, and EXA's peer-reviewed MLPerf results scale about 89% per node from 10 to 30 data nodes (Chapter 27). Of the four, only Everpure is a public company (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) with audited financials, a point procurement teams weigh.

docs.text:
timeline

    2018 : DDN buys Intel's Lustre team
    2021 : VAST moves to software on partner hardware
    2022 : WEKA runs natively in four public clouds
    2023 : DDN announces Infinia key-value engine

Figure 45.4 — The four started far apart (appliance Lustre, shared-everything, software-anywhere, Purity) and are converging on the same feature list. Differentiation is moving to proof, economics and operations.

Three forces shape 2027. NVIDIA standardisation. STX and the Dynamo KV tiers make the inference storage slot a commodity interface45, and DDN's GPU-initiated access work could move the client into the GPU itself (Chapter 34). Capital events. A VAST IPO would give the first peer-reviewed view of AI-native storage economics, DDN is seeking strategic investors57, and WEKA's last priced round, US$1.6B, dates from May 202458. Media. NAND inflation rewards vendors with high reduction ratios (VAST) or their own module supply (Everpure, once DFM data nodes ship). Signals to watch: EXA NCP and SuperPOD badges; DFM data-node GA; NeuralMesh 6 GA; VAST's BlueField-4 CNode shipments; and whether VAST, WEKA or DDN enter MLPerf Storage v4.0.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Which of the six deal archetypes produced our last ten EXA wins and losses?" A strong answer maps wins and losses to archetypes, names the decisive factor in each, and admits where EXA should not compete. Consolidation deals, for example, belong to FlashBlade//S.
  2. "What is EXA's effective $/TB against VAST at 50 PB, including protection and reduction on the data nodes?" A strong answer gives measured ratios, the stripe geometry and the NAND cost assumption. It does not quote VAST's marketing median back at them.
  3. "When does EXA get its own NCP and SuperPOD badges, and which deals are we losing until then?" A strong answer gives a level, a GPU generation and a quarter, and names the deals.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Under a rename storm or a billion-file listing, how does the Purity metadata core compare with WEKA buckets and a DNE-sharded Lustre MDS?" A strong answer cites test data, separates throughput from tail latency, and explains where each design serialises.
  2. "What does EXA give up against a Lustre client on N-to-1 shared-file writes?" A strong answer separates file-per-rank checkpoints from shared files, covers pNFS layout recall, and quantifies the per-client GB/s.
  3. "With STX, what in our KV-cache path is still ours?" A strong answer separates NVIDIA's interfaces (Dynamo, NIXL, BlueField-4) from Everpure's own software: metadata scale, tenancy and placement.

Don't say this:

  • "EXA beat VAST, WEKA and DDN in MLPerf." They did not enter v3.0.
  • "FlashBlade//EXA is SuperPOD-certified." The public record shows FlashBlade//S, not EXA.
  • "VAST is a hardware company" or "WEKA is an appliance vendor." Both earn mostly software revenue on partner hardware, even though WEKA now sells WEKApod appliances.
  • "DDN is legacy Lustre." It runs NVIDIA's clusters, sells Lustre as a Google service and ships a second, newer engine.
  • "Everyone has KV cache, so it's a wash." Maturity, evidence and Dynamo integration differ by up to a year.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Metadata/data split — a design that keeps the namespace on a dedicated tier and moves bulk data directly between clients and data servers.
  • Bulk-data hop — one network traversal a data byte makes between flash and the client.
  • Purity//DN — the software running on FlashBlade//EXA data nodes.
  • Deal archetype — a recurring buyer profile whose binding constraint decides the vendor choice.
  • Binding constraint — the single requirement that eliminates most options in a deal.
  • Evergreen//One for AI — Everpure's storage-as-a-service offering for AI, extended to FlashBlade//EXA in 2026.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 46. Incumbents
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~15 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Market structure · Scale-up dual-controller arrays · Disaggregated shared-everything · Parallel file systems · The NVIDIA ecosystem

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Six incumbents still hold most of the external storage market. In IDC's 2Q26 count, Dell (23.8%), Huawei (11.3%), NetApp (9.6%) and HPE (6.8%) together held about 51%, with Everpure fourth at 8.1%1. IBM and Hitachi Vantara are outside the top five.
  • Every incumbent is retrofitting AI onto an enterprise-era core. Dell, NetApp and HPE built new systems (Lightning FS, AFX, X10000). HPE and Hitachi lean on partners (VAST, Hammerspace). NetApp bought software (DataPelago, PEAK:AIO). Huawei built an NVIDIA-free stack.
  • Their real weapons are commercial, not architectural: installed base, channel, bundling with servers and networking, captive financing and, for Huawei, sovereign demand. Dell and HPE (now with Juniper) can fold storage into an AI-factory purchase order.
  • Their weaknesses are specific. Dell runs five-plus storage operating systems. NetApp's WAFL core dates from the early 1990s and AFX is first-generation. HPE's AI file depends on VAST. IBM's AI strength rests on one product. Hitachi is block-heavy. Huawei is shut out of the US.
  • Against Everpure, the threat ranking is roughly Dell > NetApp > HPE > Huawei (outside the US) > IBM > Hitachi. This is the atlas's judgment: Dell wins on bundling, NetApp on unified file and installed base, the rest in niches.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
The AI-storage debate centres on VAST, WEKA and DDN (Chapter 42–Chapter 44), but most of Everpure's revenue is won from or lost to incumbents, whose arrays Pure Storage displaced for a decade. In the quarter to June 2026 it was the fastest grower in IDC's top five, at about +50% year on year1. The next leg depends on enterprise AI bought by the CIOs who own today's arrays. There the incumbent is already in the room, often holding the server order too.

Strategy teams should treat each incumbent as a bundle of three assets. The first is an installed base, which sets refresh timing and switching costs. The second is a route to market: direct sales, channel, OEM, or a server attach. The third is an AI architecture, which decides whether the incumbent can keep the AI workload or must cede it to a specialist. Each profile below uses the same sub-structure so they compare line by line.

docs.title: The incumbent playbook and the AI problem
docs.text:
An incumbent's moat is mostly commercial. Customers standardise on a vendor's tools, replication and support contracts, and resellers earn margin on the full stack. When the vendor also sells servers, it can price storage as an attachment rather than a standalone purchase. Captive finance arms (Dell Financial Services, HPE Financial Services, IBM Financing) turn capex into monthly payments. That competes directly with Everpure's Evergreen//One subscription (Chapter 23).

The AI problem is architectural. Incumbent flagships were designed in the 1990s–2010s for transactional block I/O and enterprise NAS. They are usually dual-controller, scale-up arrays or shared-nothing scale-out NAS. AI training and inference need terabytes per second of parallel throughput, metadata at billions of files, GPU-direct data paths and, now, a KV-cache tier. Incumbents can respond in four ways, and most use more than one:

  1. Build a new disaggregated or parallel system beside the legacy core.
  2. Partner with an AI-native specialist and resell or embed its software.
  3. Acquire a start-up for a capability.
  4. Certify, using NVIDIA's DGX SuperPOD, NVIDIA-Certified Storage and STX programmes as a credibility shortcut (Chapter 34).

All except Huawei were named NVIDIA STX co-design partners in March 20262.

Semiconductor bridge. Incumbents resemble integrated device makers when fabless-plus-foundry took off: their fabs (installed base, field sales) stay valuable, but their process (architecture) trails the specialist, so they license IP or partner while protecting legacy margin.

docs.title: Dell Technologies
docs.text:
Architecture. Dell has the broadest portfolio, much of it inherited from EMC. PowerStore and PowerMax are scale-up block arrays. PowerFlex is software-defined block. PowerScale (OneFS, ex-Isilon) is a shared-nothing scale-out NAS. ObjectScale is object storage. The new piece is the Lightning File System, previewed as Project Lightning: a parallel file system built on OneFS foundations, with a client that stripes I/O across nodes34.

AI strategy. In 2024 Dell said PowerScale was the first Ethernet storage certified for DGX SuperPOD5. At GTC 2026 it recast the Dell AI Data Platform as three storage engines on common hardware: PowerScale for file, Lightning for parallel "Tier 0" file and ObjectScale for object. Dell claims Lightning delivers 2x the throughput of competing parallel file systems and up to 150 GB/s per rack unit (vendor claim)6. Exascale Storage for Dell PowerRack is slated for 2H 2026, with a PowerFlex-inclusive version in 1H 20274.

Business model. Storage is a line inside the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG). In FY26 (ended 2026-01-30), storage revenue was $16.63B, up 1%, while ISG grew 40% to $60.8B on AI servers7. Storage therefore fell to about 27% of ISG (16.63 ÷ 60.8), from roughly 38% a year earlier (16.46 ÷ 43.4, with prior-year ISG derived from the 40% growth). In Q2 FY27 (May–July 2026) storage was $4.85B, up 26%, and Dell guided full-year storage up mid-teens. Dell-IP products are a rising share of the mix8.

Strengths. Dell has the largest share (23.8% in 2Q261), an enormous channel, and AI servers it can attach storage to. Its Future-Proof Program bundles guarantees and upgrade options positioned against Evergreen9.

Weaknesses. Dell runs five or more storage operating systems with separate management and replication. Flat FY26 storage, while Everpure grew 16%, shows the franchise underperformed before AI demand and NAND-driven price rises arrived. Lightning's scale and customer base are not yet public.

Against Everpure. Dell is the most frequent opponent in block (PowerStore against FlashArray) and file/AI (PowerScale and Lightning against FlashBlade), and can quote GPUs, networking, storage and services on one purchase order. The rivalry has history: Pure Storage settled EMC's patent litigation in 201610.

docs.title: NetApp
docs.text:
Architecture. NetApp is a storage pure-play built on one OS, ONTAP, which rests on the WAFL file system, first published in 199411, and runs as HA pairs (Chapter 14) clustered into a scale-out namespace. AFF and ASA serve file and block, StorageGRID object, and E-Series with BeeGFS parallel HPC. In October 2025 NetApp launched AFX, a disaggregated ONTAP system in which AFX 1K controllers share NVMe enclosures over a fabric, so performance and capacity scale independently. An optional DX50 data-compute node hosts GPU work (Chapter 16)12.

AI strategy. First, the AI Data Engine (AIDE) adds metadata indexing, vectorisation and guardrail services to ONTAP, integrated with NVIDIA's AI Data Platform; launch coverage expected GA in calendar 1Q2613. Second, acquisitions: NetApp bought DataPelago (a GPU-accelerated data-processing engine, price undisclosed) on 2026-07-1614, and in September 2026 announced its intent to buy PEAK:AIO, a maker of high-performance AI storage software15. The AFF A90 was validated for DGX SuperPOD and NVIDIA Cloud Partner designs in March 202516.

Business model. FY26 (ended April 2026) revenue was $6.93B (+5%), with all-flash arrays at $4.2B (+11%) and free cash flow of $1.87B17. Q1 FY27 (to 2026-07-31) revenue was $2.03B (+30%, a 14-week quarter), with all-flash about $1.31B (+47%) and public cloud $206M. Full-year FY27 guidance is $7.975–8.225B18.

Strengths. NetApp's unique asset is ONTAP running as a first-party service inside all three hyperscalers, which gives true hybrid file. Add a huge NAS installed base and mature data-management features.

Weaknesses. ONTAP's write path and HA-pair design date from a pre-flash era. AFX is a first-generation product with little public field evidence. Two AI acquisitions in three months suggest NetApp is buying capability it did not build.

Against Everpure. NetApp is Everpure's closest like-for-like rival: a storage pure-play selling unified block/file, subscriptions (Keystone against Evergreen//One) and AI data services. AFX against FlashBlade//EXA is the cleanest head-to-head in disaggregated AI storage.

docs.title: Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE)
docs.text:
Architecture. HPE has consolidated onto Alletra Storage MP, a common hardware platform with two personalities. The B10000 runs block (3PAR/Primera lineage) and now scales out to six nodes19. The X10000 is a disaggregated object store with native NFS, scaling to 16 compute and 16 storage nodes and 23 PB raw20. File for enterprise AI came first from GreenLake for File Storage, VAST Data software on Alletra MP hardware (2023)21. Cray ClusterStor serves Lustre; Nimble arrived by acquisition in 201722.

AI strategy. HPE describes the X10000 as the first object platform to earn NVIDIA-Certified Storage (Foundation level)23. A sponsored validation of X10000 KV-cache offload on H200 GPUs reported up to 20x faster time-to-first-token than no offload (partner content, not independent)24. HPE closed its ~$14B Juniper acquisition on 2025-07-02, which adds data-centre and AI networking to the bundle25.

Business model. In FY25 (ended October 2025) the Hybrid Cloud segment, which held storage and GreenLake private cloud, had revenue of $5.75B (+4.9%). Its gross profit fell 2.5% as HPE moved to the software-defined Alletra platform26. From FY26 storage is reported within Cloud & AI: Q3 FY26 storage was about $1.3B (+10.2%) against servers up 35%, with Alletra MP orders up strong double digits27. HPE was named a Leader in Gartner's 2026 Magic Quadrant for Enterprise Storage Platforms28.

Strengths. Compute, networking and storage on one GreenLake contract with financing; a credible disaggregated platform; Cray/HPC heritage and public-sector reach.

Weaknesses. HPE depends on a partner for high-end AI file, and that partner competes with it in neoclouds. X10000 native file now overlaps GreenLake for File [VERIFY: whether GreenLake for File (VAST) is still actively sold in 2026]. Storage growth lags HPE's server growth by roughly 25 points, and HPE's share (6.8%) trails Everpure's1.

Against Everpure. HPE shows up in mid-range block refreshes, especially where GreenLake or HPE servers are already standard, and in sovereign and HPC AI deals.

docs.title: IBM
docs.text:
Architecture. IBM's AI weight sits on Storage Scale (ex-GPFS), a shared-disk parallel file system sold as software or as Storage Scale System appliances. Beside it are FlashSystem scale-up block arrays, which use IBM's own FlashCore Modules. A 2026 generation added 105 TB modules29, making these the closest analogue to Everpure's DirectFlash. IBM Storage Ceph provides software-defined object and block, after Red Hat's Ceph team moved to IBM in 202230. IBM Fusion packages storage for OpenShift.

AI strategy. The Storage Scale System 6000 was certified for DGX SuperPOD in 202431. Storage Scale 6.0.1 and Storage Scale System 7.0.1 (GA June 2026) fold in content-aware storage, which embeds and indexes data inside the file system, as the "Storage Scale AI Data Platform". IBM says it is certified for BasePOD, SuperPOD and NVIDIA Cloud Partner reference architectures32. IBM added S3 over RDMA33 and demonstrated a 100-billion-vector database34.

Business model. IBM does not disclose storage revenue. Storage sits in Distributed Infrastructure within the Infrastructure segment. Infrastructure grew 12% in 2025 on the z17 mainframe cycle, but Distributed Infrastructure was only +3% in Q435.

Strengths. Storage Scale has a long record at exabyte HPC scale. IBM has deep financial-services and mainframe accounts, custom flash modules, and Red Hat/OpenShift integration.

Weaknesses. IBM's AI strength is narrow: one parallel file system with an HPC-grade operational burden. Mid-market and channel reach are limited, and storage is an opaque line in a software-and-consulting company.

Against Everpure. IBM meets Everpure with FlashSystem in regulated enterprises and Storage Scale in large training and research clusters, rarely across the portfolio.

docs.title: Hitachi Vantara
docs.text:
Architecture. Hitachi's core is high-end and mid-range scale-up block under the VSP One brand, plus VSP One File and VSP One Object. VSP One Block High End launched in late 2025 for mission-critical and AI workloads36.

AI strategy. Hitachi's AI offer is Hitachi iQ, a full-stack NVIDIA-based AI platform. VSP One earned DGX BasePOD certification in 202437. In March 2026 Hitachi expanded iQ with agent blueprints and said it will support NVIDIA STX. Scale-out AI file comes partly through Hammerspace, which orchestrates data that VSP One holds38.

Business model. Hitachi Vantara is a subsidiary of Hitachi Ltd. and does not publish storage revenue. It reported revenue up 12% and storage revenue up 45% (block +49%) in Q1 FY2026 (April–June 2026)39.

Strengths. High-end block reliability, mainframe connectivity and a strong Japanese and Asia-Pacific base.

Weaknesses. It has no home-grown scale-out file system at AI scale and relies on partners for the AI data layer. Share outside Japan is low, and Hitachi is absent from IDC's top five.

Against Everpure. Hitachi meets Everpure mainly in high-end block consolidation and mainframe-adjacent estates. It is rarely in AI-factory file deals.

docs.title: Huawei
docs.text:
Architecture. Huawei sells a complete, vertically integrated range. OceanStor Dorado is all-flash block/unified scale-up. The OceanStor A-series is AI storage: the A800 scales to 512 controllers and more than 1 EB, with a claimed 500 GB/s per controller enclosure40. OceanStor Pacific is distributed scale-out file and object. The A800 has replaced the retiring A600 as flagship41. In September 2026 Huawei added the OceanStor M900 context-memory system, which it says provides up to 64 PB of shared KV cache and 40 TB/s per SuperPod cluster (vendor claims)42.

AI strategy. Huawei pairs its storage with its own Ascend accelerators. It released Unified Cache Manager (UCM), KV-cache tiering software intended to reduce dependence on scarce HBM, in August 2025 and said it would open-source it43. Huawei is outside NVIDIA's STX programme2.

Business model. Huawei is privately held. Revenue in 2025 was CNY 880.9B (+2.2%)44, with storage inside ICT infrastructure, which reported CNY 375.0B [VERIFY: search-summary only]45. IDC ranks Huawei #2 in external storage (11.3% in 2Q26)1.

Strengths. A home market where US vendors are excluded from many accounts, plus sovereign-AI buyers in the Middle East, Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa. Its stack is vertically integrated, from SSDs to accelerators, and its pricing is aggressive.

Weaknesses. Huawei has been on the US Entity List since May 201946. That restricts its access to US technology and makes it unsellable to many Western regulated buyers. It has no NVIDIA certification path, and its claims are rarely independently benchmarked.

Against Everpure. Huawei rarely meets Everpure in the US. It matters in EMEA, APJ and sovereign deals, and as proof that a full AI-storage stack can be built without NVIDIA.

docs.title: What the revenue numbers do and don't say
docs.text:
Only four companies disclose a storage-relevant line, each defined differently. The chart aligns them on the fiscal quarter ending July or early August 2026.

Figure 46.4 — In the quarter to mid-2026 every disclosing vendor grew, but HPE's storage grew at a third of the others' pace; company-reported lines are roughly 1.5–2x what IDC's external-storage shares imply. Data: data/ch46_storage_revenue.csv

Work the IDC arithmetic to see the definitional gap. IDC sized 2Q26 external storage at $10.3B1:

  • Dell: 23.8% × $10.3B ≈ $2.45B, against $4.85B reported for a quarter offset by one month.
  • HPE: 6.8% ≈ $0.70B against $1.29B.
  • Everpure: 8.1% ≈ $0.83B against $1.19B. Everpure's total includes about $0.5B of subscription services47.

Company lines include maintenance, services, software and (for Dell) data-protection appliances; IDC counts external systems. The same method gives Huawei about $1.16B a quarter, or roughly $4.6B annualised (estimate, ×4). In external systems that is larger than NetApp's $0.99B (9.6%). Use IDC for share and filings for growth and margin; never mix them in one ratio.

The x-axis scores the range of block, file, object, data-protection, compute and networking products sold under one contract. docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Everpure's pitch has been stable since the Pure Storage era: one OS (Purity) across FlashArray and FlashBlade, its own DirectFlash modules, Evergreen non-disruptive upgrades, and Fusion/Pure1 management (Chapter 28). The table sets it against each incumbent's best argument.

Incumbent Typical deal where it meets Everpure Incumbent's best argument (steelman) Everpure's counter Where Everpure is exposed Dell Enterprise block refresh; AI factory with Dell servers One vendor for GPUs, network, storage, services and financing; installed base One OS vs five-plus; Evergreen upgrades; DirectFlash density and power Cannot bundle servers; smaller field force NetApp Unified NAS consolidation; hybrid cloud file ONTAP everywhere, including native in AWS, Azure and Google Cloud Simpler operations; FlashBlade//EXA vs first-generation AFX Cloud-native file presence weaker than ONTAP's HPE Mid-range block; GreenLake-standardised accounts; sovereign Compute + Juniper networking + GreenLake, one contract Mature subscription (Evergreen//One); own AI file system, not a partner's Sovereign and HPC relationships IBM Regulated-industry block; research clusters Storage Scale scale record; mainframe and Red Hat integration Broader enterprise AI portfolio; simpler operations Large-scale parallel FS heritage Hitachi Vantara High-end block consolidation Reliability guarantees; mainframe; Japan relationships Density, power and upgrade model High-end mainframe-attached block Huawei EMEA, APJ, sovereign tenders Price, full-stack China supply chain, financing Trust, compliance, NVIDIA ecosystem Price-led and sovereign deals

Figure 46.6 — Where each incumbent meets Everpure: incumbents mostly win on the commercial bundle, and Everpure mostly wins on architecture and operating model.

Two implications follow. Server-attached bundling (Dell, HPE) is the hardest weapon to copy; Everpure's options are server and network partnerships, such as its NVIDIA and Cisco reference designs (Chapter 34), or making storage a separate consumption purchase. And incumbents' reliance on partners and acquisitions shows what AI-native IP is worth, which bears on Everpure's own build/buy/partner map (Chapter 54).

Figure 46.7 — Incumbents moved from certifying existing arrays (2024) to shipping new disaggregated and parallel architectures and buying AI software (2025–26).

NVIDIA's 2025 AI Data Platform launch named Dell, HPE, Hitachi Vantara, IBM and NetApp alongside Pure Storage, VAST and WEKA48. Within a year three incumbents shipped new architectures (Lightning, AFX, X10000). Three trends to watch:

  1. KV-cache tiers. Huawei's M900 and HPE's X10000 offload work show incumbents now competing in inference context memory, not only training throughput.
  2. Consolidation. Expect more incumbent purchases of AI data software, following NetApp's two deals.
  3. The pricing cycle. Memory and NAND contract prices kept rising through 202649. Part of the growth in Figure 46.4 is likely price, not share (Chapter 48).

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In AI-factory deals where Dell supplies the GPU servers, what is our win rate, and what changes it?" A strong answer segments by who controls the purchase order (CIO, AI team, neocloud), names levers (NVIDIA reference designs, Evergreen//One pricing, power per petabyte) and says where Everpure walks away.
  2. "How do we position FlashBlade//EXA against NetApp AFX?" A strong answer contrasts metadata/data separation with shared-media ONTAP, cites MLPerf or customer evidence, and concedes ONTAP's hybrid-cloud advantage rather than denying it.
  3. "Where does HPE's dependence on VAST help or hurt us?" A strong answer grants that HPE+VAST is formidable in sovereign and HPC accounts, but notes the X10000/GreenLake for File overlap can confuse HPE's sales motion.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What would it take for Dell Lightning FS to match FlashBlade//EXA's metadata scale?" A strong answer asks whether Lightning's metadata is distributed or centralised, what OneFS heritage implies for small files, and separates vendor-claimed GB/s per rack unit from audited results.
  2. "How does IBM FlashCore compare with DirectFlash?" A strong answer notes both are custom modules, then compares where compression and flash translation run (in the module for FlashCore, in Purity for DirectFlash) and the capacity roadmaps.
  3. "Is a KV-cache tier on X10000 or M900 the same product category as PureKVA?" A strong answer compares data paths (NIXL, GDS, RDMA), shared namespace versus separate appliance, and flags that both rivals' claims are vendor or sponsored.

Don't say this:

  • "Incumbents can't do AI." All six have AI-certified or AI-specific systems, and Dell, NetApp and HPE shipped new architectures in 2025–26.
  • "Dell's storage business is shrinking." It was flat in FY26 and grew 26% in Q2 FY27.
  • "HPE sells VAST." It sells GreenLake for File on VAST software, and its own X10000 with native file.
  • "Huawei isn't a competitor." It is #2 worldwide by IDC's count, just absent from US deals.
  • Comparing IDC share percentages directly with company-reported storage revenue.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• ISG (Infrastructure Solutions Group) — Dell's segment containing servers, networking and storage.
  • Lightning File System — Dell's parallel file system, formerly Project Lightning.
  • AFX — NetApp's disaggregated ONTAP all-flash system.
  • GreenLake for File Storage — HPE's file service built on VAST Data software.
  • FlashCore Module — IBM's custom flash module with in-module compression.
  • OceanStor A-series — Huawei's AI-oriented scale-out storage line.
  • Unified Cache Manager (UCM) — Huawei's KV-cache tiering software.
  • Server attach — selling storage as part of a server-led purchase.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 47. Other challengers and software-defined players
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: File protocols · Object storage and S3 · Software-defined storage and HCI · Incumbents

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• The biggest challenger is the hyperscalers' own storage. S3 alone holds over 500 trillion objects; cloud-born data rarely goes out to bid.
  • Hammerspace is the most strategic of the smaller players. Its pNFS global namespace sits above everyone's arrays, and "Tier 0" turns idle GPU-server NVMe into shared storage. If it wins, arrays become interchangeable.
  • Open-source object broke in 2025–2026. MinIO gutted its free edition and archived the repository in April 2026, pushing users to paid AIStor, Ceph, forks or supported S3 from other vendors.
  • Software-defined and platform vendors win on control and cost, not peak speed. Ceph, Lightbits and Nutanix suit buyers who want to own hardware or leave VMware; Nutanix is also an Everpure partner.
  • Qumulo, Cloudian, VDURA and Lenovo-owned Infinidat are niche threats. Each has a defensible base and caps Everpure's share in one segment.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text: VAST, WEKA and DDN (Chapters 42–45) and the incumbents (Chapter 46) get the attention, but much of the pressure on Everpure's (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) margin comes from layers it does not control. Hammerspace and the hyperscalers compete for the namespace and control plane above the array. Ceph, MinIO and Lightbits put software on commodity servers, which caps what buyers will pay for an integrated system. Nutanix competes for the platform that VMware-exit budgets fund. Each tests Everpure's claim that integrated hardware plus Purity and Evergreen beats assembling parts. Most are also private, sub-scale or newly acquired: possible targets, partners or channels (Chapter 54).

docs.text:
Sort them by the layer they compete for.
