Figure 47.1 — Challengers grouped by the layer they attack: Hammerspace sits above the array, software-defined object and block compete on commodity hardware, and the hyperscalers substitute for the whole stack.

docs.title: Hammerspace: a namespace over everyone's storage
docs.text:
Hammerspace separates where a file appears from where its bytes live. Metadata servers (Anvil) hold one global namespace. Data-services nodes (DSX) and existing NFS, object or cloud storage hold the bytes1. Clients run the stock Linux NFSv4.2 client with the pNFS Flex Files layout: they get a layout from the metadata server, then do I/O directly against storage nodes (Chapter 8). Policies ("objectives") move open files between tiers and sites; only the layout changes.

Semiconductor bridge. This is virtual memory for files. The namespace is the page table; moving data is migrating a page from DRAM to CXL memory while the application keeps its address. The moat is that the "MMU" lives in the Linux kernel: CTO Trond Myklebust maintains the upstream Linux NFS client2.

Tier 0. Launched in November 2024, Tier 0 pools the local NVMe inside GPU servers into a shared, protected tier of the same namespace3. Protection is client-side mirroring across availability zones; client-side erasure coding is roadmap4. Version 5.2 added "affinitization", which writes a client's data to its own local Tier 0 volume5.

flowchart TB
    subgraph SITE["AI cluster, site A"]
        G1["GPU server 1: local NVMe, Tier 0"]
        G2["GPU server 2: local NVMe, Tier 0"]
        T1["Existing NAS or flash array, Tier 1"]
    end
    MD["Anvil metadata: one global namespace"]
    PO["Policy objectives: placement, protection, cost"]
    DX["DSX data movers"]
    OBJ["On-prem object store, Tier 2"]
    CLD["Cloud region or site B"]
    G1 -- "pNFS layout request" --> MD
    G1 == "direct data I/O" ==> G2
    G2 == "direct data I/O" ==> T1
    PO --> MD
    MD --> DX
    DX -- "live migration" --> T1
    DX -- "tier down" --> OBJ
    DX -- "replicate" --> CLD

Figure 47.2 — Hammerspace keeps file identity in one metadata layer and moves bytes freely across GPU-local NVMe, existing arrays, object and cloud, so the array becomes one tier among several.

Worked example (illustrative). Take 1,000 GPU servers with eight 3.84 TB NVMe drives each, a common DGX-class configuration: 1,000 × 8 × 3.84 TB ≈ 30.7 PB raw, already paid for, or about 15 PB mirrored. At about 6 GB/s per Gen4 drive, aggregate local bandwidth is 1,000 × 8 × 6 ≈ 48 TB/s, far more than any shared array. The catches: reboots take drives offline, mirror traffic shares the GPU network, and capacity follows the server refresh cycle. So Tier 0 suits checkpoints and scratch, later drained to a shared tier (Chapter 31).

Why it has customers. Meta is the flagship. Its two 24,576-GPU GenAI clusters used parallel NFS co-developed with Hammerspace, alongside Tectonic6. In April 2025 Hammerspace raised a US$100M Series B led by Altimeter, at a valuation above US$500M (reported by press), and talked of an IPO within about two years7. Weak spots: no NVIDIA SuperPOD or NVIDIA-Certified Storage designation8, and performance bounded by the storage underneath.

docs.title: Qumulo and VDURA: file specialists that changed their business model
docs.text:
Qumulo sells a scale-out NAS with real-time capacity and activity analytics, popular in media, life sciences and research. Under CEO Doug Gourlay (from July 2024) it moved from its own hardware to software for cloud, on-premises and edge9. Its distinctive asset is Azure Native Qumulo, a file service sold and billed inside Azure. In June 2026 it added tooling to migrate legacy NAS data into it10. Its last priced round was a US$125M Series E at US$1.2B in July 2020 (company-stated)11 [VERIFY: Qumulo funding since 2020]. Customers buy simplicity and file analytics, not peak GPU throughput.

VDURA is Panasas, rebranded in May 2024 as a software-first company12. In 2025 it relaunched PanFS as an AI/HPC platform aimed at VAST, WEKA and DDN, with a V5000 all-flash appliance and, from March 2026, hybrid flash-plus-disk options13. It claims one of the largest defense GPU installations (company-stated)14. It offers lab-proven PanFS and disk economics while flash is dear; its risk is scale [VERIFY: VDURA funding].

docs.title: MinIO: the open-source object store that closed itself
docs.text:
MinIO, a single fast, free binary, became the default S3-compatible store for developers, Kubernetes and many neoclouds. It raised US$103M at a US$1B valuation in January 2022, led by Intel Capital15. Then it withdrew the community edition in stages:

  1. June 2025: the admin console was removed, leaving a basic object browser; administration moved to the CLI or paid AIStor16.
  2. Late 2025: official binaries and images stopped updating, reportedly in October 2025; the README now says the community edition ships as source code only. On 3 December 2025 the project entered maintenance mode, with security fixes only case by case17.
  3. 2026: the README was changed to say the repository is no longer maintained (12 February, per a fork maintainer's account19). GitHub shows minio/minio archived on 25 April 2026. The AGPLv3 source remains readable, and the README points to AIStor Free and AIStor Enterprise18.

Semiconductor bridge: a licensor changing terms after an ecosystem standardized on its architecture. Licensees pay, fork19 or port, here to Ceph RGW or commercial S3.

AIStor itself is serious: it shipped S3 over RDMA in November 202420, and MinIO is an NVIDIA STX partner21. Worked example: a neocloud migrating 50 PB off community MinIO at a sustained 100 GB/s needs 50 × 10¹⁵ ÷ 10¹¹ = 500,000 s ≈ 5.8 days of saturated copying. With verification and cut-over it takes weeks, so many will simply pay MinIO.

docs.title: Cloudian and Ceph: object for people who want control
docs.text:
Cloudian HyperStore is S3-native object storage, sold as software, appliances or via HPE GreenLake, strong with regulated on-premises buyers. In June 2024 it raised US$23M of growth financing from Morgan Stanley Expansion Capital, citing 30% ARR growth, breakeven and about US$256M raised in total (company-stated)22. It was early to GPUDirect for object (200+ GB/s claimed, November 2024)23. Its HyperScale AI Data Platform adds in-storage vector search24; HyperStore 8.2.6 became NVIDIA-Certified (Foundation) in March 202625.

Ceph is the Linux of storage: one open-source system for block (RBD), file (CephFS) and object (RGW), free as code and costly to run well. Clyso tuned a 68-node NVMe cluster past 1 TiB/s26, showing both the ceiling and the skill required. It is commercialized three ways:

  • IBM Storage Ceph, inherited from Red Hat, with release 9.0 in January 202627.
  • Software and support specialists, Croit (management software and support)28 and Clyso (engineering and consulting)26.
  • Hardware integrators such as 45Drives, which ships servers with its Houston management UI for Ceph deployment29.

Think RISC-V: the ISA is free; value goes to whoever makes it reliable for telcos, universities, sovereign clouds and neoclouds.

docs.title: Block and platform: Lightbits, Infinidat, Nutanix
docs.text:
Lightbits sells software-defined block storage over NVMe/TCP, a standard it helped create (Chapter 7). Crusoe's AI-cloud block service runs on it at multi-petabyte scale3031. Last disclosed funding was US$42M in 2022 (US$105.3M total)32. Neoclouds use it to build EBS-like services.

Infinidat builds InfiniBox, a high-end block array serving most reads from DRAM in front of large HDD or flash pools. Lenovo announced the purchase in January 2025 and closed it in April 2026; Infinidat is now a unit of Lenovo's Infrastructure Solutions Group33. Calcalist estimated the undisclosed price at over US$500M (estimated)34. The gain is Lenovo's distribution.

Nutanix sells a platform: Nutanix Unified Storage (Files, Objects, Volumes) alongside the AHV hypervisor and NKP, its Kubernetes platform built from the D2iQ acquisition (2024)35. Broadcom's VMware licensing changes are the tailwind. Nutanix reported more than 1,000 new logos in fiscal Q2 2026, its best in eight years, mostly ex-VMware [VERIFY: search-summary only]36, and fiscal 2026 ARR of US$2.55B, up 16%37. AHV now also accepts external arrays: Dell PowerFlex, Pure Storage FlashArray over NVMe/TCP (May 2025), then NetApp ONTAP and Dell PowerStore3839. NUS also became NVIDIA-Certified in 202640.

docs.title: The biggest challenger: hyperscaler-native storage
docs.text:
Each hyperscaler sells a full menu: AWS S3, EBS and FSx (Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS, Windows); Azure Blob, Azure NetApp Files and Azure Managed Lustre; Google Cloud Storage and Managed Lustre. S3 alone holds more than 500 trillion objects and serves more than 200 million requests per second across hundreds of exabytes41. S3 Vectors (GA December 2025) shows them moving up the stack42.

The parallel is custom silicon: Graviton, Trainium and TPU did not beat merchant chips everywhere, but took the workloads already in the cloud. Clouds also rent partner technology as first-party services when that is faster than building. Google Cloud Managed Lustre runs on DDN EXAScaler and went GA in July 202543, and NetApp's first-party and marketplace cloud storage revenue grew 27% in fiscal Q3 202644. And they compete on AI performance: Azure Managed Lustre was the first hyperscale cloud service in MLPerf Storage, at 642.2 GiB/s checkpoint write in v3.045. Google's DAOS-based Parallelstore is reportedly being phased out for Managed Lustre [VERIFY: partner source only]46.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Company Architecture Model Funding / ownership Notable customers / proof points Threat to Everpure (judgment) Hyperscaler-native (AWS, Azure, Google) Proprietary object, block, file; partner-built file services Cloud service Public parents S3: 500T+ objects41; Azure Managed Lustre in MLPerf v3.045 High. Substitutes for the whole stack for cloud-born data. Everpure can only partner (Azure Native) or win repatriation. Hammerspace pNFS Flex Files global namespace; Tier 0 on GPU-local NVMe Software Private; US$100M Series B 2025, >US$500M valuation (reported)7 Meta GenAI clusters6 Medium-high. Sits above arrays and commoditizes them, but can also run on FlashBlade. Nutanix HCI plus external arrays; NUS file and object Software platform Public (NASDAQ: NTNX); ARR US$2.55B37 VMware-exit mid-market Medium. Wins platform budgets, yet also a FlashArray channel. MinIO AIStor Hash-placed erasure-coded object Software (commercial) Private; US$103M at US$1B, 2022 (company-stated)15 Developer and neocloud S3 Medium-low. Licensing fallout creates openings for FlashBlade S3. Ceph (IBM, Croit, Clyso, 45Drives) Open-source unified block, file, object Open source plus support/hardware IBM (public); others private Telcos, academia, sovereign clouds Medium on price. Sets the floor for commodity object. Lenovo Infinidat DRAM-cached high-end block Appliance Lenovo-owned, closed April 202633 Large enterprises, service providers Medium in high-end block, through Lenovo's reach. Cloudian S3-native object Software / appliance Private; ~US$256M raised (company-stated)22 Regulated industries, HPE GreenLake Low-medium. Strong on-premises S3 niche. Qumulo Scale-out NAS; Azure Native Qumulo Software / cloud Private; last round 2020, US$1.2B (company-stated)11 Media, life sciences Low-medium. Competes with FlashBlade file in mid-range. Lightbits NVMe/TCP software block Software Private; US$105.3M total by 202232 Crusoe30 Low-medium. Neocloud block, where FlashArray rarely plays. VDURA PanFS parallel file, hybrid flash/HDD Appliance / software Private; funding unclear HPC labs, defense (company-stated)14 Low. Sub-scale, but credible in HPC deals.

Table 47.1 — The threat ranking follows layer, not size: whoever owns the namespace or the cloud account matters more than another box vendor.

Against hyperscalers, Everpure puts Purity in the cloud: Pure Storage Cloud Azure Native is a jointly developed managed Azure service47. Its second top-five-hyperscaler DirectFlash design win (August 2026) makes a hyperscaler a customer48. The steelman is NetApp, whose ONTAP is first-party on all three clouds; Everpure has no AWS or Google equivalent. Against Hammerspace, FlashBlade//EXA uses the same pNFS idea with Everpure's own metadata engine. Is Hammerspace a partner over FlashBlade, or a layer that commoditizes it? Against Ceph, MinIO and Lightbits, it sells simplicity and Evergreen against "free plus engineers", winning where staff are scarce. With Nutanix, Everpure wins when VMware exits land on AHV with FlashArray.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Selected challenger funding, M&A and licensing events, 2024-2026
    2024 : May - Panasas rebrands as VDURA : Jun - Cloudian raises USD 23M growth financing : Jul - Qumulo appoints Doug Gourlay CEO : Oct - Lightbits expands Crusoe deal : Nov - Hammerspace launches Tier 0 : Nov - MinIO AIStor and Cloudian ship S3 over RDMA
    2025 : Jan - Lenovo agrees to buy Infinidat : Apr - Hammerspace raises USD 100M Series B : May - Nutanix adds FlashArray for AHV : Jun - MinIO strips community console : Jul - Google Managed Lustre GA on DDN : Dec - MinIO community enters maintenance mode
    2026 : Jan - IBM Storage Ceph 9.0 : Mar - Cloudian earns NVIDIA certification : Apr - Lenovo closes Infinidat : Apr - MinIO repository archived : Jun - Qumulo expands Azure Native work : Aug - Nutanix FY26 ARR reaches USD 2.55B

Figure 47.3 — Funding was small and sporadic. The defining events were a strategic acquisition, a licence retreat and the cloud and platform vendors moving in.

Three signals stand out. Capital went elsewhere. Hammerspace's US$100M is the largest disclosed primary raise here, while VAST raised about US$1B in 2026 alone (Chapter 42). CB Insights also lists a Hammerspace "Series B-II" in February 2026 with no amount [VERIFY: single aggregator]49. Open source is being monetized harder, which strengthens Ceph as the neutral default. Platform owners are absorbing storage: Lenovo bought Infinidat, Nutanix bundles storage with AHV, and the clouds rent Lustre and ONTAP as their own services. Expect more platform acquisitions of sub-scale storage software; an analyst quoted at Hammerspace's Series B thought a sale likelier than an IPO7.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "When a customer runs Hammerspace over FlashBlade, who owns the account?" Strong: separates namespace from capacity and says what EXA adds.
  2. "How many MinIO community users have we converted since December 2025, and with what?" Strong: FlashBlade or FlashArray S3, typical size, the rival Ceph or AIStor quote.
  3. "What share of Nutanix AHV migrations attach FlashArray rather than Nutanix storage?" Strong: an attach rate and how Nutanix sellers are paid.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What does Tier 0 lose if a GPU server reboots mid-checkpoint, and how does EXA handle that failure?" Strong: mirror placement, rebuild traffic on the GPU fabric, draining.
  2. "Where is our S3 slower than Ceph RGW or AIStor on small objects, and why?" Strong: a measured objects-per-second figure and the metadata-path reason (Chapter 18).
  3. "Could Purity run as a first-party service on AWS, as ONTAP does in FSx?" Strong: separates the engineering gap (control plane, multi-tenancy, billing) from the commercial one.

Don't say this:

  • "MinIO is dead." The community repository is archived; AIStor is sold and NVIDIA-partnered.
  • "Hammerspace is an array competitor." It is a namespace layer that can sit on top of Everpure.
  • "Ceph is free." The code is; running it at scale costs engineers, which is what Everpure sells against.
  • "Nutanix is just a competitor." Since May 2025 it is also a FlashArray route to market.
  • "The cloud is just another competitor." It is the default home for new data.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Global namespace — one file tree spanning many systems and sites.
  • Tier 0 — Hammerspace's shared tier built from GPU servers' local NVMe.
  • pNFS Flex Files — NFSv4.2 layout for direct client I/O to data servers.
  • AIStor — MinIO's commercial object store.
  • Open-core relicensing — shrinking a free edition to push users to paid ones.
  • Ceph RGW / RBD / CephFS — Ceph's object, block and file interfaces.
  • NVMe/TCP — NVMe over ordinary TCP/IP Ethernet.
  • First-party cloud storage service — partner storage sold and billed by the cloud as its own.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 48. Media suppliers and the NAND cycle
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Media physics · Inside an SSD · Purity and DirectFlash · Hyperscaler ecosystem and financials · Consumption models

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Five companies take about 88% of NAND revenue. Top-five revenue hit $68.87B in 2Q26, up 77% in a quarter1. YMTC ships as many bits as Kioxia but earns less per bit2.
  • 2026 is a supply-side super-cycle. Enterprise SSDs took ~48% of NAND bits2, wafer additions stayed thin and the HDD shortage pushed cloud buyers to QLC3. Compounded TrendForce forecasts put contract prices ~4.7× their mid-2025 level by 4Q26.
  • Array vendors feel the cycle as a lag. Costs reprice quarterly; price lists and contracts reprice slower. Product gross margin dips then recovers, revenue inflates, and cash goes into inventory and prepayments.
  • Everpure's exposure is split three ways. Arrays carry NAND on its books, Evergreen//One carries it at fixed contracted prices, and hyperscale DirectFlash carries none because the customer buys the NAND4.
  • HDD vs QLC is now about allocation as much as price. Flash's $/TB premium widened to ~19–23× [VERIFY: single-vendor index]5, far above the ~3× cloud buyers need3, but nearline HDD lead times passed 52 weeks.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
NAND is the largest single input in an all-flash array. Everpure buys raw NAND rather than finished SSDs, which makes it one of the few array vendors with a direct relationship to the fabs (see Chapter 26). In April 2026 the CEO wrote that input costs for many high-volume semiconductor components had risen 300–900% since mid-2025, and that Everpure's prices were up about 70% on average since January6. A shock that size moves revenue, gross margin, free cash flow and competitive pricing at once.

The strategy questions follow. How long until an upcycle hits product gross margin, and how fast does it reverse? Is negative free cash flow from strategic buying a hedge or an inventory bet? Does a fixed-price Evergreen//One book become a liability when NAND quadruples? Does the HDD shortage widen Everpure's QLC-versus-disk opening, or close it?

docs.title: The supply base: five oligopolists and a fast-rising sixth
docs.text:
Figure 48.1 — Samsung leads on both measures, but YMTC ships as many bits as Kioxia while earning less per bit, because its mix is still mostly consumer. All makers outside the top five together took 12.4% of revenue, so YMTC's revenue share is at most that, against Kioxia's 13.6%. Data: data/ch48_nand_share.csv

Revenue share rewards mix, because enterprise SSD bits sell at a large premium. Micron grew 99% in a quarter and passed Kioxia for third1. Counterpoint puts YMTC fifth by revenue (TrendForce's brand ranking, which leaves YMTC out of its top five, puts Sandisk fifth) because data-centre SSDs are a small part of its mix, and calls 15% share the level at which a NAND maker can self-fund capex2; YMTC is close.

Semiconductor bridge. This is the DRAM playbook: a handful of IDMs, each node a capex cliff (more decks, hybrid bonding), so wafer starts are the swing factor. Kioxia and Sandisk share fabs through Japanese joint ventures: two brands on one manufacturing base.

CXMT is DRAM-only and matters indirectly: AI has tightened DRAM too, which arrays need for controllers and caches.

docs.title: Why 2025–26 became a super-cycle
docs.text:
Four forces lined up:

  1. AI pulled enterprise SSD bits. Server SSDs reached ~48% of NAND bit shipments in 2Q262, and enterprise SSD is the one category TrendForce still sees accelerating in 4Q26 (+23–28% versus +15–20% blended)28.
  2. Supply discipline after the 2022–23 bust. In 1Q23 industry revenue fell to about $8.6B on a ~15% ASP drop29; three years later the top five took $68.87B in a quarter. Scarred suppliers add wafers slowly. Kioxia's FY26–28 capex averages ~¥470B a year, mostly at Kitakami20; SK hynix is building M17 but will stage ramps against demand visibility12. Meaningful new capacity is not expected before late 2027–28.
  3. The HDD shortage spilled into QLC. In September 2025 TrendForce reported nearline HDD lead times beyond 52 weeks and North American cloud providers evaluating QLC for cold data3. It named that spillover when it turned its 4Q25 outlook from flat to +5–10%30, so the HDD-to-QLC link is a stated driver, not hindsight.
  4. Supply became a contract. Sandisk had over a third of FY27 bits under long-term agreements (LTAs) of up to five years by May 202623, and reportedly over half later [VERIFY: secondary source]31, with prepayments and price floors and ceilings23. Micron's Crucial exit freed bits for strategic customers13.

Figure 48.2 — Two quarters of 55–75% increases did more than the whole 2023–24 recovery; even the "slowing" 3Q26 and 4Q26 forecasts still compound on a much higher base. Data: data/ch48_nand_price.csv

These are forecasts, revised upward repeatedly; the 1Q26 and 2Q26 figures come from secondary coverage [VERIFY: confirm against TrendForce releases]3233. The index is our arithmetic: 1.075 × 1.225 × 1.575 × 1.725 × 1.125 × 1.175 ≈ 4.7× from 2Q25 to 4Q26, the same order as Everpure's "300–900%" component-cost statement6.

docs.title: How the cycle reaches an array vendor's P&L
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["NAND contract price up"] --> B["BOM cost per raw TB up"]
    B --> C["Price list and quote validity reset"]
    C -->|"lag one to three quarters"| D["Product gross margin dips then recovers"]
    C --> E["Revenue per system inflates"]
    E --> F["Mix shifts to product so blended GM falls"]
    B --> G["Strategic buys and supplier prepayments"]
    G --> H["Operating cash flow and FCF fall now"]
    G -.->|"cheaper bits flow through COGS later"| D
    B --> I["Evergreen One capacity bought at new prices"]
    I --> J["Subscription GM squeezed at fixed price per TB"]

Figure 48.3 — One input-cost shock hits four lines at different speeds: cash immediately, margin with a lag, revenue upward, and the subscription book over the life of its contracts.

Worked example (illustrative). An array sells for $100 with a $35 bill of materials (BOM), $20 of it NAND: 65% gross margin (GM). NAND doubles; the BOM becomes $55. Three choices:

  • Hold price: GM falls to 45%.
  • Pass through dollars only: price $120 keeps gross profit at $65, but GM falls to 54%.
  • Hold GM at 65%: price must rise to $55 ÷ 0.35 ≈ $157, and gross profit dollars rise 57%: the "revenue inflation" in 2026 prints.

The evidence fits. Everpure raised prices on 9 February 2026 and guided product GM to the low end of its 65–70% range34; product GM went from 67.3% in Q4 FY2635 to 65.5% in Q1 FY2736 and 66.2% in Q237. Product revenue grew 54% in Q237 on fewer systems shipped; price, mix and capacity per system made up the difference38. NetApp, which buys finished SSDs, shows the lag more starkly: product GM fell 4.2 points to 55.3% in its January 2026 quarter39 and to 54.6% in its July quarter, and the FY27 GM guide slipped from 68.5–69.5%40 to 68.1–69.1%41. Products rose to 49% of revenue from 42%, dragging the blended margin down even if product GM holds41. One call summary describes a roughly three-quarter pass-through lag [VERIFY: secondary summary]42. Dell repriced ISG on 10 December 2025 and shortened quote validity43.

Cash. Everpure's Q2 FY27 operating cash flow was −$136M and free cash flow −$238M on strategic NAND and component purchases; a third party reads ~$577M as prepaid expenses [VERIFY: confirm in 10-Q]44. Management said supply coverage was sufficient "for the foreseeable future" and pricing had roughly caught up with costs45. In derivatives terms this is a long forward on NAND: it pays if 4Q26's +15–20% arrives, and becomes write-down risk if the cycle breaks as in 4Q24.

Evergreen exposure. Under Evergreen//One, Everpure owns the hardware and bills per TB used, so capacity added mid-contract is bought at today's NAND price but billed at yesterday's rate: a short position on NAND that pays in downcycles. Evergreen//One prices rose far less than product prices38; one partner reports ~+5% against 30%+ on Evergreen//Forever quotes [VERIFY: partner blog]46. Subscription GM slipped only from 75.6% to 74.9% between Q1 and Q2 FY273637. Hyperscale sits outside all this: Everpure does not procure that NAND4.

docs.title: HDD vs QLC economics in 2026
docs.text:
Enterprise SSDs cost about 10× nearline disk per TB in 202047 (Chapter 2 has the curve). In 2026 one index put the premium at 22.6× in Q1 and 18.6× in Q3 (a 30 TB TLC SSD at ~$22,600 against $1,216 for a 30 TB HDD) [VERIFY: single-vendor index]5. TrendForce says cloud buyers need QLC within ~3× of HDD $/TB3.

Worked example: does power close the gap? Store 10 PB raw. Micron's comparison gives ~8.2 TB/W for its 245 TB SSD and 4.4 TB/W for a 44 TB HDD48: about 1.2 kW versus 2.3 kW, a 1.05 kW gap. Over five years at PUE 1.4 and $0.10/kWh that saves 1.05 × 43,800 h × 1.4 × $0.10 ≈ $6.4k. HDD media at ~$40/TB cost $0.4M; a 3× premium adds $0.8M, an 18× premium about $7M. Power never closes the gap; rack space, performance per TB, data reduction and failure handling must. Hence array vendors sell effective $/TB and total cost of ownership (Chapter 4).

Disk makers have their own upcycle: Seagate and Western Digital both posted ~58% non-GAAP gross margins in the September quarter2725, adding exabytes through areal density, not factories. Neither medium is cheap and both are rationed, so delivery capacity decides as much as $/TB.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Vendor model What it buys Who carries NAND price risk Pass-through tools 2026 evidence Everpure enterprise arrays Raw NAND (Micron, Kioxia) → own DFMs Everpure List-price rises, 30-day quotes, strategic buys ~70% average price rise; product GM 65.5–66.2%; Q2 FCF −$238M63744 Everpure Evergreen//One Same NAND, owned by Everpure Everpure, at fixed $/TB Smaller price changes on new contracts Subscription GM 74.9% in Q2 FY2737 Everpure hyperscale licence Nothing: the customer buys NAND Hyperscaler Not needed No NAND procured4 NetApp, Dell, HPE arrays Finished SSDs from NAND makers Vendor; the SSD maker takes its own margin first Price increases, shorter quote validity NetApp product GM 54.6%; Dell ISG repricing4143 Software-only (VAST, WEKA) No media; hardware partners or the customer buy Customer or hardware partner Not on vendor P&L Deal sizes and timing exposed instead

Table 48.2 — Everpure is unusual in holding all three exposures at once: direct NAND buyer, fixed-price subscription owner and royalty-only licensor.

Steelman the alternatives. Buying finished SSDs lets NetApp or Dell switch among four or five suppliers without qualifying dies, and pushes yield and firmware risk onto the drive maker. Everpure's raw-NAND model removes the SSD maker's margin and controller, but each new die needs characterisation, slowing supplier additions (Chapter 26). Software-only vendors keep NAND off their P&L, though customers still pay it. VDURA's CEO accused Everpure of padding margins in the shortage; Everpure rejected the claim49.

Options a strategy team might evaluate (public information only):

  • Supply agreements with collars. Suppliers now offer multi-year LTAs with prepayments, floors and ceilings2312. A collar caps cost but locks a floor that becomes overpayment in the next bust.
  • A third NAND source. Adding SK hynix/Solidigm, Samsung or Sandisk to Micron and Kioxia buys allocation leverage at the cost of qualification effort. YMTC is ruled out by the Entity List.
  • Pricing mechanics. Index-linked pricing on large deals, short quote validity (adopted) or an Evergreen//One reset clause, each traded against the price predictability Evergreen sells.
  • Shift the exposure. Extend the hyperscale pattern, where the customer procures NAND, to sovereign or neocloud deals.
  • Use the cycle commercially. Evergreen//One price stability is a weapon while flash rises, if the balance sheet can carry the short position.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title NAND cycle and supplier events, 2022 to 2028
    2022 to 2023 : Demand bust and inventory glut : Production cuts : YMTC added to Entity List
    2024 : Recovery led by enterprise SSD : Kioxia lists in Tokyo in December
    2025 : Sandisk spins out from Western Digital : 4Q24 to 1Q25 correction : HDD shortage pushes QLC
    2026 : Contract prices up about 55 to 75 percent per quarter in 1H : LTAs with prepayments spread
    2027 to 2028 : New fabs from SK hynix and YMTC : HAMR scales at Seagate and WD

Figure 48.4 — Each bust taught suppliers capex discipline, and 2026 is the first upcycle where much of the supply was sold forward under multi-year contracts.

Kioxia listed in Tokyo on 18 December 202416 and Sandisk on Nasdaq on 24 February 202521, leaving Western Digital a pure HDD company and creating two NAND pure-plays with every reason to keep supply tight. YMTC is planning new fabs despite export controls24. Signals to watch: 1Q27 contract forecasts turning flat; LTA coverage at Sandisk and Kioxia (smoother for contracted buyers, choppier spot for everyone else); YMTC's eSSD mix; Everpure's cash flow normalising as guided; and product GM returning toward mid-range.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "How much of this year's product growth is price versus units?" Strong: splits price, mix (capacity per system, QLC share) and units, admits units fell in Q238, and says how comparisons look when NAND deflates.
  2. "What happens to Evergreen//One margins if NAND stays here two more years?" Strong: names the exposure (capacity added at today's cost against contracted $/TB) and the offsets: renewal repricing, data-reduction guarantees, DFM density.
  3. "Where does QLC beat disk in a 2026 deal, at a ~20× media premium?" Strong: effective $/TB after data reduction, plus space, power and performance; and an admission that pure cold archive still goes to disk.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What does qualifying a new NAND die for DFMs cost in time and testing?" Strong: names the steps (read thresholds, retention, program timing, endurance under Purity's write patterns) and a realistic timeline.
  2. "How does a layer jump change DFM cost per TB versus a commodity SSD?" Strong: separates NAND $/bit, the same for everyone, from controller, DRAM and over-provisioning savings, which are DirectFlash's own.
  3. "If one supplier's next node slips, how fast can volume shift?" Strong: dual-qualified module SKUs and Purity handling mixed NAND generations in one array.

Don't say this:

  • "DirectFlash protects Everpure from NAND prices." It removes SSD controllers and margins, not the NAND cost.
  • "Higher prices mean higher margins." GM% usually falls first, even as gross profit dollars rise.
  • "NAND makers are just gouging." Contract prices follow wafer supply: post-2023 capex restraint, AI demand and the HDD shortage.
  • "QLC has killed the hard drive." Disk makers posted record margins in 2026.
  • "YMTC is a cheap second source." Not for a US vendor under export controls.

docs.text:
• TrendForce quarterly NAND and enterprise SSD contract-price releases: read the segment tables, not the headlines.
  • Sandisk and Kioxia earnings materials on LTA structure (prepayments, collars, duration).
  • Everpure's Q2 FY27 10-Q (prepaids, inventory, purchase commitments) to size the forward NAND position; NetApp's purchase-obligation notes for comparison.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Contract price — the negotiated quarterly or monthly price large buyers pay NAND makers, as distinct from the volatile spot market.
  • Long-term agreement (LTA) — a multi-year supply contract, now often with prepayments and price floors and ceilings.
  • Pass-through lag — the delay between a component-cost change and the matching change in a vendor's selling prices.
  • Revenue inflation — revenue growth driven by higher prices rather than more units.
  • Strategic purchase — buying components ahead of need to secure supply and lock in cost, at the expense of near-term cash flow.
  • Nearline HDD — high-capacity 7,200 rpm drives used for warm and cold data in data centres.
  • HAMR — heat-assisted magnetic recording, which raises HDD platter density.
  • Bit share vs revenue share — share of NAND capacity shipped versus share of NAND sales dollars; the gap reflects product mix.

docs.title: 49. Competitive landscape matrices
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Architecture decision matrix · Market structure · VAST Data · WEKA · DDN · Incumbents · Other challengers

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• These matrices are the atlas's judgment, synthesising Chapters 24 and 40–47. Use them to structure a conversation, not as a ranking.
  • No vendor is top-right on all three quadrant charts. VAST leads on AI depth and momentum but is thin on enterprise data services; Dell and NetApp lead on breadth and scale with retrofitted AI; hyperscalers serve mostly data already in their cloud.
  • Everpure's distinctive position is media economics. It pairs vertical integration with differentiated flash management (DirectFlash) and is the only array vendor publicly known to license that IP into hyperscalers. Its weakest cells are cloud availability, sovereign presence and data intelligence (offered only since 2026).
  • 2025–26 moved the whole field upward. WEKA made KV-cache offload a commercial product in November 2025; by late 2026 nearly every serious vendor had one. NVIDIA's STX gave twelve partners one reference design, so certification differentiates less.
  • The matrices point to options a strategy team might evaluate: convert benchmark leadership into neocloud share, widen cloud reach beyond Azure, make data intelligence a full-strength capability, and decide whether the namespace layer above arrays is a partner or a threat.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text: A strategy team is asked "where do we sit against X?" in many forms. Chapters 42–47 answer vendor by vendor; these matrices give the overview. Each chart reduces the field to two dimensions that decide a class of deals, and the heatmaps show which capability or buyer segment drives each placement. They are also a discipline: a claim such as "Everpure is AI-native" or "Dell can't do AI" has to survive placement next to fifteen rivals, with stated reasons.

docs.title: How the matrices are built
docs.text: Every coordinate is an ordinal score from 0 to 1, assigned by the atlas from sourced facts in earlier chapters: 0.8 against 0.6 means "clearly ahead", not "33% better". Where an axis overlaps Figure 46.5 in Chapter 46, the same y-values are reused. Read the quadrant, not the decimal; everything is dated November 2026. "Hyperscaler" is one point for the native storage of AWS, Azure and Google, whose scale is not comparable with any vendor's: S3 alone holds more than 500 trillion objects1.

Figure 49.1 — The top-right is crowded but shallow; the AI-native specialists are deeper but narrower.

The y-axis, shared with Figure 46.5, measures how much of the AI data path runs on architecture the vendor owns and designed for AI: parallel or disaggregated data paths, GPU-direct I/O, KV-cache tiers, in-storage data services. Partner-sourced capability is discounted. The x-axis differs. Figure 46.5 scored total portfolio breadth, including servers and networking; here it scores the data services a buyer gets on the storage itself: protocols, snapshots and replication, ransomware recovery, cloud editions, consumption contracts and cataloguing.

So Everpure moves from 0.46 to 0.78: it sells no servers, but Purity carries one data-services stack across FlashArray and FlashBlade (Chapter 28). NetApp ranks highest because ONTAP runs first-party in all three hyperscalers.

Three placements are contestable:

  • VAST at 0.52 breadth. VAST would argue DataBase, DataSpace and DataEngine out-range any incumbent catalogue2; the atlas discounts this because block arrived only in 20253 and its replication and ransomware tooling have a shorter record.
  • DDN at 0.78 depth, despite Lustre being more than 20 years old. "AI-native" here means designed for the GPU data path, not new.
  • Hyperscalers at 0.94 breadth. It applies only to data already in their cloud.

    VAST: [0.74, 0.80]
    WEKA: [0.90, 0.46]
    Nutanix: [0.78, 0.36]

    Qumulo: [0.84, 0.22]
    MinIO: [0.92, 0.32]
    Hammerspace: [0.96, 0.10]

Figure 49.2 — Two routes to media economics: integrate flash management (Everpure, IBM, Huawei) or extract it in software from QLC (VAST); most vendors take neither.

The x-axis measures how much of the hardware a vendor designs and supplies. The y-axis asks whether the vendor turns NAND into a cost or density advantage through its own flash modules, raw-NAND management, very wide erasure codes on QLC or global reduction. Everpure is the extreme top-left point. Purity managing raw NAND on DirectFlash modules is why two top-five hyperscalers licensed the design4 (Chapter 36); hyperscalers sit left because they build their own systems.

The semiconductor bridge is IDM versus fabless. Everpure, like an integrated device maker, controls the bill of materials but carries supply risk in a NAND shortage (Chapter 48). VAST is fabless: hardware passes through at cost, so customers absorb the spike5.

Three placements are contestable:

  • Everpure at x = 0.20. Portworx, Cloud Dedicated and EXA's third-party data nodes would pull it right.
  • WEKA at y = 0.46. It rests on NeuralMesh 6's unproven claim of up to 6x reduction6.
  • VAST drifts left as it ships CNode-X with Supermicro and Cisco.

The main threat to the top-left corner is a standard, not a rival: Flexible Data Placement (FDP) SSDs could let hyperscalers rebuild DirectFlash-like economics.

Figure 49.3 — Outside the hyperscalers, momentum and scale are inversely related; Everpure is the mid-scale vendor furthest above the midline.

The x-axis is a roughly logarithmic ordering by storage revenue or installed base:

Vendor Storage scale Dell Storage revenue US$16.6B in FY267 NetApp Revenue US$6.9B8 Everpure FY27 revenue guided above US$5B9 HPE Storage about US$1.3B a quarter10 VAST More than US$500M committed ARR (company-stated)11 DDN About US$500M revenue (reported by Forbes)12 WEKA More than US$100M ARR (company-stated)13

Huawei is placed by its 11.3% IDC share, above NetApp's 9.6%14.

The y-axis aggregates 2025–26 evidence: growth, bookings, valuation, design wins, benchmarks and shipping KV-cache products. VAST tripled its valuation to US$30B11 and signed a US$1.17B CoreWeave deal15. DDN said bookings were heading past 3x16. Everpure grew revenue 38% in Q2 FY279, won a second hyperscaler4 and posted the top checkpoint result in MLPerf Storage v3.017. WEKA's valuation is unchanged since 2024, and HPE stopped reselling it in March 202618.

Caution: IDC's 2Q26 market grew 33.6%, mostly from NAND price pass-through (Chapter 40), so revenue growth overstates everyone's momentum. Two placements are contestable:

  • Hitachi at y = 0.46. Storage grew 45%, but block-led19, so it is not counted as AI momentum.
  • Dell at y = 0.60. Dell's storage grew 26% in Q2 FY27 after only 1% for all of FY267.

Steelman the rivals. VAST's Element Store, spanning files, tables and vectors, already occupies the data-intelligence cell Everpure is entering. NetApp can call Everpure's cloud ◐ structural: ONTAP is first-party on three clouds, Purity on one. Dell can argue that the server purchase order decides segment fit, a column no storage-only vendor fills (Chapter 46).

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
What moved in 2025–26:

  • KV-cache tiers. The column filled from one commercial product in late 2025 to most serious vendors by October 2026 (Chapter 32).
  • Certification. NVIDIA's March 2026 STX programme named twelve storage co-design partners, including Everpure, VAST, WEKA and DDN, and excluded Huawei44. Certification separates vendors less than in 2024.
  • Incumbents moved up Matrix 1 with NetApp AFX, Dell Lightning and HPE X10000; NetApp also bought AI software42.
  • Open-source object. MinIO's archived repository (April 2026)45 moved it down Matrix 3.
  • Everpure moved up Matrix 3 on MLPerf, a second hyperscaler win and PureKVA.

Four signals to watch in 2027:

  1. Whether VAST's database engines win public reference customers.
  2. Whether WEKA raises a new priced round or is acquired.
  3. Whether FDP adoption erodes DirectFlash's top-left position.
  4. Whether NAND normalisation exposes how much 2026 "momentum" was price.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Which ◐ cell in our row costs the most deals?" A strong answer names one (cloud availability or neocloud fit), with lost deals and a plan, not a feature roadmap.
  2. "Why aren't we higher than VAST on AI-native depth?" A strong answer concedes EXA's shorter field record, then cites peer-reviewed MLPerf results VAST has not entered.
  3. "Is Hammerspace a partner or a threat?" A strong answer separates accounts where it runs over FlashBlade from those where Tier 0 replaces shared storage.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Is our data-reduction ● a lead on AI data?" A strong answer cites DeepReduce's expected median 2:1 on FlashBlade20 and why compressed AI data reduces less.
  2. "Does DirectFlash still pay once FDP SSDs exist?" A strong answer quantifies what host-side NAND management does that placement hints cannot: global garbage collection, module density.
  3. "What makes a KV-cache tier ● rather than ◐?" Dynamo, vLLM and LMCache integration, RDMA into GPU memory, an independent benchmark and named production users.

Don't say this:

  • "We're top-right on every chart." No vendor is, including Everpure.
  • "Huawei doesn't matter." It is #2 by IDC share and a Gartner Leader47.
  • "NVIDIA certification is our moat." Most rivals hold the same badges, EXA does not yet, and twelve vendors share the STX reference design.
  • "Hyperscalers are customers, not competitors." Both statements are true at once.

docs.title: 50. Technical diligence framework for storage/AI-data targets
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Architecture decision matrix · Reading benchmarks · Distributed systems fundamentals · WEKA deep dive

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Storage diligence asks one question: will this code keep other people's data safe, fast and supportable at ten times today's scale? The process is standard software M&A. The critical risks (durability bugs, metadata walls, support load) do not appear in a data room by default.
  • Treat every performance number as a claim until you reproduce it. Normalise it per node, per rack unit, per kW and per usable TB. Then run your own proof of concept (PoC) on your own workload shape (Chapter 37).
  • Field data beats models. Annualised failure rates, rebuild-time distributions, data-loss incident logs and phone-home telemetry tell you more than any "eleven nines" durability figure.
  • Integration fit with Everpure has four seams: control plane, data path, licensing and channel. The data path is the expensive one. Purity and DirectFlash assume a single operating system managing raw NAND, so a second file system is a second product line, not a feature.
  • Public data can score a target, but only roughly. In the WEKA worked example, 38% of the weight rests on low-confidence scores, four of them placeholders; the score is 2.8 of 5, with a plausible range of 2.1 to 3.7.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
The AI storage cycle has produced private companies with large valuations and immature evidence. WEKA was last priced at US$1.6B in May 20241 and VAST at a reported US$30B in April 20262. Any build/buy/partner discussion at Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) about AI data infrastructure (Chapter 54) ends in questions a financial model cannot answer. Does it scale past the customer's next cluster? Has it ever lost data? Could it run under Fusion and on DirectFlash? Everpure's record is small and mid-sized software deals, such as Portworx at US$352.9M plus US$32.2M of retention payments3 and 1touch at US$125.0M in 20264. A frontier-AI target would be a different order of risk.

An ex-semis dealmaker already knows the analogous discipline. You would not buy a chip company on its datasheet. You would ask for characterisation across process corners, the errata list, RMA history, the tape-out record and third-party IP licences. Storage diligence maps onto each. Benchmarks are the datasheet. Data-loss incidents are the errata, except that they destroy customer data. Field failure rates are the RMA history, and open-source dependencies are the third-party IP.

docs.title: The diligence flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S["1 Screen - public signals"] --> T["2 Public-info teardown"]
    T --> G1{"Proceed?"}
    G1 -->|yes, NDA| M["3 Management technical sessions"]
    M --> P["4 Hands-on PoC and benchmark"]
    P --> G2{"Claims hold?"}
    G2 -->|yes| R["5 Reference calls"]
    R --> C["6 Code and architecture review - clean team"]
    C --> G3{"Integrable?"}
    G3 -->|yes| I["7 Integration plan"]
    G1 -->|no| X["Stop or monitor"]
    G2 -->|no| X
    G3 -->|no| X

Figure 50.1 — Technical diligence is a funnel with three kill gates; the cheap public teardown should kill most targets before anyone signs an NDA.

Access gets more expensive at each stage. The public-info teardown reads documentation, patents, benchmark submissions, GitHub repositories, job postings and certification lists; vendor documentation is far more candid about limits than marketing. Management technical sessions under NDA should be run by your own architects, not the corp-dev team. The PoC is where most deals should die if they are going to: the acquirer's workload shape, ideally its hardware, and its engineers at the keyboard. Reference calls should include a churned customer and the largest deployment, not just the three the target offers. Code review comes last, under a clean-team protocol, because it exposes trade secrets and, if the deal fails, contaminates the acquirer's engineers.

docs.title: The dimensions that matter
docs.text:
Architecture and its walls. Every architecture class has a known first wall (Chapter 24). Shared-nothing clusters hit rebalancing and east-west traffic (Chapter 15). Disaggregated shared-everything designs hit fabric and enclosure failure domains (Chapter 16). Parallel file systems hit the metadata server (Chapter 17). Good teams name their own wall in the first session.

Performance claims. Normalise before comparing. Suppose a vendor claims 1 TB/s from 40 nodes. That is 25 GB/s per node. If each node has 2×400 GbE (100 GB/s of line rate), the system runs at 25% of wire speed. That is either honest headroom or a software ceiling, and only a PoC tells you which. Chapter 37 lists the gaming techniques.

Scalability and metadata. Capacity, performance and metadata are three separate curves, and vendors usually quote only the flattering one (Chapter 21). The semiconductor bridge is tag RAM. A centralised metadata server is a single tag array that every access must consult, so it saturates. Sharded metadata spreads the load, but operations spanning shards, such as renames and snapshots, become distributed transactions.

Durability and data integrity. This is the dimension most likely to destroy deal value, and the one data rooms least often cover. Durability in "nines" is a model output, a mean time to data loss (MTTDL) estimate (Chapter 20), not a field fact. Field evidence is what counts. As a public baseline, Backblaze reported a 1.36% annualised failure rate (AFR) across about 344,000 hard drives in 20255. Worked example: a target with 500 clusters averaging 200 drives has 100,000 drives in the field. At 1% AFR that is 1,000 failures a year, about three rebuilds a day somewhere in the fleet. The question is how many rebuilds overlapped a second fault, and what happened then. Telemetry is also how the industry measured silent corruption: a FAST '08 study used NetApp call-home data from 1.53 million drives over 41 months6. A target without equivalent telemetry cannot answer at all.

Security and roadmap. Ransomware resilience means snapshots that an administrator credential cannot delete (Everpure's equivalent is SafeMode) and multi-party approval for destructive operations. Treat the roadmap as a tape-out record: dated announcements against dated general availability (GA). Slips are normal; re-announcements are not.

Code base and team. Map who wrote the data path and metadata engine, and whether they will stay. Run software composition analysis for open-source licences, because copyleft travels. Lustre is GPLv27, so distributed modifications to its kernel modules carry source obligations. MinIO moved its server to AGPLv3 in 20218, whose obligations can be triggered by network use. Disputes happen. In March 2023 MinIO said it had revoked WEKA's licences, and WEKA replied that its fork derived only from Apache 2.0 code9. No public resolution was found.

Support burden. Supporting many servers, NICs, kernels and clouds means a large qualification matrix, a cost hidden in operating expenses rather than gross margin. Telemetry is itself an asset. HPE bought Nimble in 2017 largely for InfoSight10, and Pure1 META has run on phone-home data since 201711.

Hardware and supply chain. An appliance vendor carries NAND exposure directly; Everpure raised prices in February 2026 as NAND costs surged12 (Chapter 48). A software-only vendor pushes that exposure to customers but depends on partners' goodwill.

Customer concentration. AI-native storage revenue clusters in a few neoclouds and model builders whose spend follows GPU deliveries (Chapter 35).

Unit economics. Gross margin depends on what is sold. Illustratively, software at 85% gross margin and pass-through hardware at 20% blend to 0.6 × 85% + 0.4 × 20% = 59% when hardware is 40% of revenue. Margin can move with packaging mix, independent of pricing power. For reference, Everpure's non-GAAP Q2 FY27 gross margin was 66.2% on product and 74.9% on subscription13 (Chapter 29).

Dimension Key questions Evidence to request Red flags Architecture and walls Which wall does this class hit, and at what scale? Architecture docs; largest-cluster topology; failure-domain map Team cannot name its wall; largest customer already near it Performance claims Do the numbers survive normalisation and our workload? Raw benchmark configs; peer-reviewed or audited submissions; PoC on our hardware Vendor-run only; withdrawal from audited rounds; reduction assumed in headline Scalability How do capacity, throughput and metadata scale separately? Node, file and metadata-op counts for the top five clusters Only capacity quoted; sub-linear curve beyond tens of nodes Metadata design How is the namespace partitioned, and how are cross-shard operations kept atomic? Design docs; small-file and rename benchmarks Single metadata server; small-file collapse; no crash-consistency testing Durability and integrity Has it lost or corrupted customer data, and how do you know? Data-loss incident log; field AFR; rebuild-time distribution; checksum design No end-to-end checksums; no incident log; "nines" offered instead of field data Security and ransomware Can an admin credential destroy the data? Immutability design; pen-test reports; CVE response times Deletable snapshots; no external testing; weak tenant isolation Roadmap credibility Did announced features ship when promised? Three years of dated announcements vs GA dates Re-announced features; GA slips over a year Code and team Who wrote the core, and will they stay? Are licences clean? Commit history by author; tenure and vesting; SBOM and licence scan Core authors gone; copyleft in proprietary paths; open licence disputes Support and telemetry What does each installed system cost to support? Tickets per system; severity mix; share detected by phone-home Large qualification matrix; customers find most issues first Hardware and supply chain What breaks if a partner or component goes away? Bill of materials; sole-source list; partner agreements Single-sourced parts; partner with a competing product Customer concentration How much revenue sits in the top five? Revenue by customer; contract terms; committed vs consumed capacity One customer above 30%; exclusivity or most-favoured terms Unit economics What does margin look like by packaging mix? Gross margin by software, appliance and cloud; burn; cohort expansion Margin falling with mix; growth bought with hardware at cost Integration fit Which of the four seams must close, and how fast? Target's APIs, drive assumptions, licence meters, channel contracts Full Purity overlap; OEM channel conflict; change-of-control clauses

Table 50.1 — The reusable checklist: each row pairs the question with the evidence that answers it and the signal that should stop the deal.

docs.title: Integration fit: the four seams
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph TGT["Target"]
        TC["Control plane and telemetry"]
        TD["Data path and client"]
        TL["Licence and price meter"]
        TS["Channel and OEM partners"]
    end
    subgraph EP["Everpure"]
        F["Fusion and Pure1"]
        PU["Purity on DirectFlash"]
        EG["Evergreen subscriptions"]
        CH["Everpure channel"]
    end
    TC -->|"API federation"| F
    TD -->|"parallel stack or port"| PU
    TL -->|"map meters and SLAs"| EG
    TS -->|"conflict check"| CH

Figure 50.2 — Control-plane federation takes months and data-path convergence years (illustrative), because Purity manages raw NAND that the target's software has never seen.

Control plane. Fusion is the fleet control plane at the core of the Enterprise Data Cloud14 (Chapter 22); exposing a target's clusters to it through APIs is the cheapest integration. Data path. Purity runs the flash translation layer (FTL) across DirectFlash modules itself (Chapter 26). A target built for commodity SSDs runs as a parallel stack or is ported, a multi-year job. Licensing. Evergreen//One SLAs commit Everpure to performance and durability guarantees (Chapter 28); anything sold under them inherits that bar. Channel. A target's OEM partners may be Everpure's competitors.

docs.title: The scorecard
docs.text:
Dimension Weight 1 = red flag 3 = acceptable 5 = best in class Architecture and walls 10 Wall within the next customer's scale; team cannot name it Known wall beyond the current largest deployment Wall well beyond roadmap scale, with a published mitigation Performance claims 8 Vendor-run only; not reproducible Some peer-reviewed results; PoC within 20% of claims Peer-reviewed results in current rounds; PoC matches claims Scalability (capacity, perf) 7 Sub-linear beyond a few dozen nodes Near-linear to the largest customer Proven linear at multiples of the largest customer Metadata design 6 Single metadata server; small-file collapse Scale-out metadata with known hot spots Sharded, with atomic cross-shard operations at scale Durability and integrity 10 Unexplained data-loss incidents; no end-to-end checksums End-to-end checksums; incidents disclosed and fixed Fleet telemetry, scrubbing, clean multi-year incident log Security and ransomware 6 Snapshots deletable by an admin credential Immutable snapshots; encryption at rest Multi-party authorisation, tenant isolation, external pen tests Roadmap credibility 6 Re-announced features; GA slips over a year Slips of a quarter or two Ships on announced dates Code base and team 10 Key authors gone; copyleft contamination Core authors retained; licences clean Deep bench, low attrition, clean SBOM Support burden 6 Huge qualification matrix; vendor rarely detects first Manageable matrix; partial telemetry Narrow matrix, call-home on most systems Hardware and supply chain 6 Single-sourced critical parts; partner can defect Multiple qualified sources Hardware-portable, or sourced at scale Customer concentration 7 One customer above 30% of revenue Top 10 below 50% Broad base across segments Unit economics 8 Gross margin falling with mix; heavy burn Stable margin; burn funded Software-like margin; self-funding Integration fit with Everpure 10 Full overlap with Purity; channel conflict Partial overlap; Fusion federation feasible Complementary layer; clean channel fit

Table 50.2 — A reusable 13-dimension scorecard, weighted toward the dimensions where a mistake costs the most after close (architecture, durability, team, integration).

docs.title: Worked example: WEKA, public data only
docs.text:
WEKA is the chosen case because its public record (Chapter 43) is unusually documented for a private company. It is a software-only target, which exercises every dimension. This is a method illustration, not a recommendation, and it implies nothing about non-public Everpure plans. Where public data is silent, the dimension gets a placeholder 3 with low confidence. Customer concentration is the one low-confidence dimension scored below 3, because the visible references lean on a few neoclouds and labs.

Figure 50.3 — WEKA scores well on engineering and poorly on team stability, support load and Everpure fit; "?" marks low-confidence scores (four placeholder 3s and the customer score of 2).

Reading the result. The weighted score is 283 ÷ 100 = 2.83. The five low-confidence dimensions (scalability, durability, security, customers, economics) carry 38 points of weight. Scoring them all 1 gives 2.14, and scoring them all 5 gives 3.66. Public data cannot tell a mediocre target from a good one, but it does set the agenda: field durability data, customer concentration and margin mix come first.

Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information. The score favours lighter-touch options over a full acquisition. These include interoperability (Everpure object storage as a WEKA tier), competing head-on with PureKVA31 against AMG, or monitoring signals such as financing events and MLPerf participation (Chapter 43). The integration score of 2 reflects data-path overlap, the costliest seam. The same template applied to VAST (Chapter 42) or DDN (Chapter 44) would raise other questions: valuation and data-reduction IP for VAST, Lustre GPL obligations and appliance margin for DDN.

Table 50.4 — Storage acquirers have mostly kept acquired data paths as separate product lines rather than merging them, which is the pattern a diligence plan should price in.

Dell and HPE run several data paths side by side. Everpure's moat is one OS (Purity) on one hardware architecture (DirectFlash) under one subscription model (Evergreen), so the data-path seam costs Everpure more than it costs Dell: a second file system weakens the one-platform story. The steelman for the portfolio approach is speed, since a portfolio vendor owns a segment the day a deal closes. Everpure's approach, building EXA in-house and buying software around the edges (Portworx, 1touch), keeps the platform coherent at the cost of time to market.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text: The focus of storage diligence has shifted with each wave. When EMC bought XtremIO before it had product revenue36, the bet was almost entirely architecture and team. HPE's Nimble deal made installed-base telemetry an asset in its own right10. Portworx moved the focus to cloud-native software and engineer retention3. AI targets add three layers: GPU-path claims such as KV-cache offload, which are rarely audited; NVIDIA certification status, which partners do not control (Chapter 34); and neocloud concentration. Valuations have outrun evidence. Audited KV-cache benchmarks began only with MLPerf Storage v3.0 in September 202618, so expect the PoC and reference-call stages to carry more weight through 2027.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "If we sold this under Evergreen//One, which SLAs could we sign on day one?" A strong answer names the metrics (performance per TB, durability, uptime), the telemetry needed to measure them, and the gap.
  2. "Which of the target's top customers are in our pipeline, and who resells it today?" A strong answer identifies overlap and flags OEM partners that compete with Everpure.
  3. "What does the target ship that our roadmap won't have within 18 months?" A strong answer names one dated capability and compares build time against deal time.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Where does this architecture hit its first wall, and how close is the largest customer?" A strong answer names the wall by architecture class and gives the largest deployment's metadata operation rate, not only its capacity.
  2. "Walk me through the worst data-integrity bug they shipped." A strong answer covers how it was found, how many systems it affected, and whether a fleet-wide scan confirmed the fix.
  3. "What would it take to run their data path on DirectFlash and under Fusion?" A strong answer separates API federation (months) from FTL assumptions (years) and names the modules to rewrite.

Don't say this:

  • "Their benchmark proves it scales." One hero configuration proves only that configuration.
  • "Software-only means no hardware risk." The risk moves into the qualification matrix, partner defection and support cost.
  • "Eleven nines is their field record." Nines come from an MTTDL model; field data is incident logs.
  • "Open source means free." GPL and AGPL obligations are diligence items, and licence disputes happen.
  • "We'll plug it into Fusion." That covers the control plane only, the cheapest of the four seams.

docs.text:
• Bairavasundaram et al., FAST '08, the field study of checksum mismatches across a vendor fleet6.
  • Backblaze Drive Stats datasets, a model for what field-failure data requests should look like5.
  • Chapter 56 covers architecture-review questions, and Chapter 49 has cross-vendor matrices.
  • SPDX-format software bills of materials (SBOMs).

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Technical due diligence — verifying a target's technology claims, risks and integration cost before a deal (see the glossary).
  • Proof of concept (PoC) — a hands-on test of the target's system on the buyer's workloads.
  • Clean team — a ring-fenced group allowed to see competitively sensitive material such as source code.
  • Software composition analysis — automated scanning of code for open-source components and their licences.
  • Copyleft — licence terms (GPL, AGPL) requiring derived works to be shared under the same terms.
  • Data-loss incident log — a vendor's record of every case of lost or corrupted customer data.
  • Key-person risk — dependence on a few engineers whose departure would stall the product.
  • Integration seam — one of the four places a target must join Everpure: control plane, data path, licensing, channel.
  • Placeholder score — a neutral score assigned where public data is silent, flagged for diligence.

docs.title: 51. History of storage, 1956–2026
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~12 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: The storage stack · Scale-up dual-controller arrays · Disaggregated shared-everything · Everpure company history

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Seventy years, six eras: captive disk, arrays and networks, scale-out and cloud, flash, software-defined, and AI. Each was organized around the most expensive resource of its time: the disk itself, then administrators and stranded capacity, then scale, then latency, now GPU time.
  • Cost fell by nearly nine orders of magnitude. Disk went from about US$10,000 per MB (1956) to US$0.014 per GB (2022), about 26% a year. Flash fell faster. In 2026 both curves are rising.
  • New media creates new vendors, but only when software captures the media's economics. Pure Storage (now Everpure) survived independently by selling data reduction and a business model, not speed. Violin sold speed and filed for Chapter 11.
  • Incumbents rarely die. They get acquired, usually after buying their way into the new wave. EMC bought Isilon and XtremIO, then was itself bought by Dell for about US$67B in 2016.
  • Architecture swings like a pendulum between centralized and distributed designs, and software-defined waves recur whenever commodity CPUs and networks catch up with proprietary controllers. AI-era disaggregation is the latest swing, not the last.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Storage has run the same plot several times. A media or interconnect shift opens a gap, start-ups pour in, one or two independents survive, incumbents buy the rest, and the survivors become the next incumbents. Pure Storage was the flash wave's surviving independent. Everpure is now an incumbent being attacked by AI-native vendors (VAST, WEKA, a re-energized DDN) that were founded on the next shift. Product-only responses lose. Acquisitions buy time. Business-model and platform responses last longest.

"Disaggregation", "software-defined" and "data platform" all have precedents, and so do the ways earlier waves ended. Chapter 52 covers flash cost curves in depth, Chapter 53 looks forward, and Chapter 46 profiles today's incumbents.

Figure 51.1 — Each era starts with a technology shift and ends with acquisitions; the eras overlap because a new wave begins before the previous one has finished consolidating.

Sources for Figure 51.1: 12345678910111213141516171819202122.

docs.title: Era 1, 1956–1987: the disk as a captive, costly peripheral
docs.text:
IBM's 350 disk unit shipped with the 305 RAMAC in 1956. It held about 3.75 MB on fifty 24-inch platters1, and its cost worked out to roughly US$10,000 per MB23. Disk was the scarce resource, so systems were designed to waste no byte. In June 1980 IBM's 3380 became the first gigabyte-class drive. It held 2.52 GB, was the size of a refrigerator, and listed at US$81,000–142,4002, or about US$32,000 per GB at the low end (81,000 ÷ 2.52).

The business model was the IDM model in semiconductors. IBM designed the heads and media, built the drives, owned the channel interface and sold the whole system. Margins were set by the system, not by the disk.

docs.title: Era 2, 1988–2005: arrays, cache and networks
docs.text:
The break came from below. In 1988 Patterson, Gibson and Katz argued that many small PC disks, protected by parity, could beat one "single large expensive disk" on cost, performance and reliability3. Their Table I is the thesis in two numbers. An IBM 3380 cost US$18–10 per MB including controller, and a small Conners CP3100 cost US$10–73. Semiconductor bridge: this is the "killer micros" argument applied to storage, and it rests on the same economics that make chiplets attractive. Many small, cheap, high-volume units plus clever redundancy beat one large, expensive, low-volume unit.

RAID turned the disk into a component and moved value into the controller: cache, parity, mirroring and later snapshots and replication. EMC's Symmetrix, launched in 1990, put a large cache in front of commodity disks and attached it to IBM mainframes4. It is the storage equivalent of putting SRAM in front of DRAM: most reads hit the cache, so cheap disks behind it look fast. By 1995, by one account, Symmetrix held 41% of mainframe disk terabytes against IBM's 35%24. A start-up selling software and cache beat the company that invented the disk.

Networking then made arrays shareable. NetApp was founded in 1992 to build file-serving "appliances" that did nothing but serve NFS, and it shipped its first systems in 19935. Fibre Channel's physical standard was approved in 19946, which let many servers share one block array over a SAN. The economic driver was utilization and administration. Disks scattered across hundreds of servers strand capacity and need hundreds of backup jobs. Consolidating them behind two controllers fixes both problems. That is the dual-controller array of Chapter 14.

docs.title: Era 3, 2001–2012: scale-out and the cloud
docs.text:
The next limit was the controller pair itself. Unstructured data outgrew any two-controller box. Isilon, founded in 2001, clustered x86 nodes behind a single file namespace. EMC bought it in 2010 for about US$2.25B7. Google published GFS in 200325, and Amazon launched S3 on 14 March 20068. By 2023 it held more than 280 trillion objects26. Nutanix shipped hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) in 2011, which put the storage software on the same x86 servers as the virtual machines9 (Chapter 19).

The shared enabler was cheap x86 cores and Ethernet. Once commodity servers could run erasure coding and metadata services in software, the proprietary controller stopped being necessary for scale. This was the first software-defined wave, and its biggest winner (AWS) was not a storage vendor at all.

docs.title: Era 4, 2007–2017: flash makes new vendors
docs.text:
Flash attacked the remaining scarce resource, which was latency. A 15K RPM disk delivers a few hundred random IOPS. A single SSD delivers tens of thousands or more. Fusion-io unveiled its ioDrive PCIe card in 200711. A wave of array start-ups followed: Violin, Nimble, XtremIO and Pure Storage (incorporated October 2009, FlashArray shipped May 2012)12. The NVMe 1.0 specification, published in March 2011, replaced a disk-era command interface with one designed for parallel flash10.

The cohort's outcomes are the most useful dataset in this chapter:

  • Fusion-io (server flash) was sold to SanDisk in 2014 for about US$1.1B27. A NAND maker integrated forward.
  • XtremIO was bought by EMC in May 2012, before it had any product revenue, for a reported US$430M13.
  • Nimble was bought by HPE in 2017 for US$1.09B15.
  • Violin, the early speed leader, IPO'd in 2013 and filed for Chapter 11 in December 201614.
  • Pure Storage stayed independent, IPO'd in 2015 and settled EMC's litigation for US$30M in 201628 (Chapter 25).

The difference was not raw performance, because flash made every array fast. Pure used inline deduplication and compression to bring low-cost MLC flash close to the effective price of performance disk. It wrapped that in a non-disruptive upgrade subscription (Evergreen) that attacked incumbents' forklift-refresh revenue. Speed is a property of the media and gets commoditized. Economics and business model are properties of the software and the contract, and they compound. Chapter 52 explains why flash won primary storage.

docs.title: Era 5, 2014–2020: software-defined again, and the incumbent exits
docs.text: While flash start-ups fought for arrays, the buying centre moved. Developers on public cloud and Kubernetes wanted storage that came from an API, not a ticket. Pure bought Portworx, a Kubernetes data-services company, in September 2020 for about US$370M18. EMC, the defining array company of the 1990s and 2000s, had bought into each new wave (Isilon for scale-out, XtremIO for flash). Dell nonetheless agreed to buy it in October 2015 for about US$67B and closed the deal on 7 September 201616. Its products live on: Dell led the external storage market in 2Q26 with 23.8% share29. What disappeared was EMC's independence and its ability to set the agenda.

docs.title: Era 6, 2019–2026: AI and the return of throughput
docs.text: GPUs made a new resource the most expensive one in the data centre, so storage is now judged by how fully it keeps accelerators busy (Chapter 31). That favoured designs born for parallel throughput. VAST Data (founded 2016, out of stealth 2019) built disaggregated shared-everything17. WEKA (founded 2013) built a parallel file system in software30. DDN, founded in 1998 and long an HPC niche player, became an AI supplier. Blackstone invested US$300M at a US$5B valuation in January 202520, and DDN told Forbes it expected about US$1B of revenue in 2026 (reported by press)31. MLCommons published the first MLPerf Storage round in September 202319. VAST raised capital at a US$30B valuation in April 202622. In February 2026 Pure Storage renamed itself Everpure to signal a shift from flash arrays to data management21.

docs.title: The cost curve underneath every era
docs.text:
Figure 51.2 — Nearly nine orders of magnitude of cost decline drove every architectural shift; 2026 is the first time both curves have turned up together. Data: data/ch51_cost_per_gb.csv

Worked numbers. Disk went from about US$10,000,000 per GB in 1956 to US$0.0144 per GB in November 20222332. That is a factor of about 6.9 × 10⁸ over 66 years, so the annual factor is (6.9 × 10⁸)^(1/66) ≈ 1.36. Prices fell about 26% a year, in nominal dollars, before any inflation adjustment. Flash fell from about US$50,000 per GB (a 20 MB SunDisk drive at about US$1,000 in 1991)33 to US$0.185 per GB for enterprise SSD in Q2 202034. That works out to about 35% a year. The faster slope is what let flash overtake disk for primary storage. In 2026 the curves turned up: a single-vendor index put a 30 TB TLC SSD at US$753 per TB, 18.6× the per-TB price of a 30 TB nearline HDD35. The bases differ, so read the chart for direction and orders of magnitude, not decimals.

Semiconductor bridge. The disk curve is storage's Moore's law. Like Moore's law, it changed architecture more than it changed products. Cheap capacity removed the need to economize on bytes, so designs shifted to economizing on whatever cost more: people (consolidation), scale (scale-out), latency (flash) and now accelerator time (AI).

docs.title: The architectural pendulum
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Centralized<br/>1956-1980s<br/>mainframe DASD"] -->|"cheap PC and mini disks"| B["Distributed<br/>1980s<br/>server-attached DAS"]
    B -->|"stranded capacity, admin cost, SANs"| C["Centralized arrays<br/>1990s-2000s<br/>SAN and NAS"]
    C -->|"x86 clusters, Ethernet, web scale"| D["Distributed<br/>2000s-2010s<br/>scale-out, HCI, cloud"]
    D -->|"flash, NVMe-oF, GPU throughput"| E["Disaggregated<br/>2016-2026<br/>shared media over a fabric"]
    E -.->|"next swing?"| F["CXL memory pools,<br/>DPUs, KV-cache tier"]

Figure 51.3 — Storage swings between consolidating media for efficiency and spreading it for scale; each swing is triggered by whichever component (media, network or CPU) just got cheap.

The swing has a mechanism. Centralize when the media is expensive and the network is cheap enough, because pooling raises utilization. Distribute when commodity compute is cheaper than the controller and the network becomes the bottleneck, because locality avoids the network. Disaggregate when the network becomes nearly as fast as local media. NVMe-oF adds roughly 5–15 µs to a ~100 µs flash read (Chapter 16), so it gives you pooling without giving up scale. The next swing is visible one level down, where CXL applies the same logic to memory (Chapter 12).
