docs.text:
Era Enabling tech Winners Losers Lesson for strategy today Captive disk, 1956–87 Magnetic recording; mainframe channels IBM Anyone without a system to attach to Owning media plus system holds margin until a cheaper media class arrives from below Arrays and networks, 1988–2005 RAID, large caches, Fibre Channel, NFS appliances EMC, NetApp IBM's mainframe disk share Controller software on commodity disks beat better hardware; the attach point moved value Scale-out and cloud, 2001–12 x86 clusters, Ethernet, erasure coding, HTTP APIs Isilon (exited to EMC), AWS S3, Nutanix Monolithic NAS for big unstructured data When the unit of scale changes from shelf to node, the buyer and the business model change too Flash, 2007–17 NAND, PCIe, NVMe Pure Storage; exits for Fusion-io, XtremIO, Nimble Violin; disk-centric arrays New media creates vendors only if software converts media cost into customer economics Software-defined, 2014–20 Containers, Kubernetes, public cloud AWS, Portworx (exited to Pure), Dell as consolidator EMC's independence SDS waves recur and are mostly absorbed by platforms; consolidation follows slowing growth AI, 2019–26 GPUs, RDMA, NVMe-oF, QLC, NVIDIA certification VAST, WEKA, DDN; Everpure via EXA (contested) Dual-controller designs in GPU-scale deals The scarce resource (GPU time) sets requirements, and the ecosystem gatekeeper matters as much as the box

Table 51.1 — Every era rewarded whoever turned the newly cheap component into a lower cost for the newly scarce one.

docs.title: Three recurring patterns, and the semiconductor parallel
docs.text:
1. How incumbents lose: slowly, then by acquisition. No storage leader collapsed. Each lost its agenda first. IBM lost mainframe disk share to EMC's cache-and-software design. EMC bought into each new wave, but buying products did not change a business built on large, refresh-driven hardware sales. The end was a sale, not a failure. Media went the other way, to three survivors each. Micron paid US$615M for bankrupt Elpida's equity in 201336, and Samsung, SK hynix and Micron held about 90% of DRAM revenue in 4Q25 (36.0 + 32.1 + 22.4)37. Hard-disk makers narrowed to Seagate, Western Digital and Toshiba38.

2. Why storage systems never consolidated like media. The capital intensity sits in the media: fabs and head/disk plants. Array vendors resemble fabless chip companies. They buy NAND or drives, add controller software and sell a system. Entry costs are venture rounds, not a multi-billion-dollar fab, so every technology shift produces a new crop of entrants. Everpure's DirectFlash strategy, which buys raw NAND and manages it in its own software, is like a fabless company designing its own memory controller. It captures media economics without owning the fab.

3. Why software-defined waves recur. Whenever commodity CPUs and networks catch up with the proprietary controller, someone runs storage as software on standard servers: scale-out in the 2000s, HCI and cloud in the 2010s, Kubernetes-native storage and VAST's 2021 exit from hardware39 in the 2020s. These waves rarely displace arrays. Arrays absorb the model (subscriptions, cloud editions, container integration), while hyperscalers keep the pure-software prize. Implication for the AI era: expect the current AI-native leaders to face the same cycle. They will be validated, imitated by incumbents (NetApp AFX, HPE X10000 and Everpure EXA already ship disaggregated designs), and then consolidated or forced into platforms. The open question is who does the consolidating.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Every major vendor still carries the architecture of the era it was born in.

Vendor Born in era Architectural inheritance AI-era response Steelman Dell (EMC lineage) Arrays (Symmetrix, 1990) Symmetrix lineage (PowerMax), Isilon (PowerScale) Parallel NFS on PowerScale40; broad portfolio Largest installed base and channel; #1 share29 NetApp Arrays, 1992 ONTAP unified file/block OS AFX disaggregated ONTAP (2025)41 Decades of enterprise data-management features HPE Arrays, via 3PAR/Nimble buys Alletra (3PAR, Nimble lineage) X10000 shared-everything; GreenLake for File runs VAST software42 Server plus storage plus GreenLake bundle Everpure Flash, 2009 Purity, DirectFlash, Evergreen subscription FlashBlade//EXA metadata/data split One OS and one upgrade model; raw-NAND economics DDN HPC, 1998 Lustre-based EXAScaler Infinia object platform; AI400X3 Large GPU-cluster deployments, e.g. xAI Colossus (company-stated)43; HPC know-how VAST Data AI/disaggregated, 2016 DASE on shared QLC and SCM Positions itself as an "AI operating system"44 Built for this era from the start WEKA Software-defined, 2013 Parallel file system as software NeuralMesh (2025)45; cloud and neocloud deals Hardware-agnostic; strong in public cloud

Table 51.2 — Founding era predicts architecture; in the AI era the founding-era advantage belongs to VAST and WEKA, not Everpure.

The honest read: Everpure sits where EMC sat around 2012, a successful incumbent of the previous wave with the cash and installed base to respond to the next one. EMC's responses were acquisitions on top of a hardware-refresh business. Everpure's are built in-house (EXA), subscription-led (Evergreen) and extended into hyperscale data centres by licensing DirectFlash (Meta in 2024, a second top-five hyperscaler in August 2026)46. That is closer to the business-model defence that let Pure itself survive in 2012–2016. The steelman for the challengers: VAST and WEKA did not retrofit anything, and the history of storage says architectural fit for the scarce resource usually beats installed base within one refresh cycle. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information, include where EXA wins outright, which capabilities to buy rather than build (Portworx is the template), and how to avoid an EMC-style end state (Chapter 54).

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
Three dated signals frame the next chapter of this history:

  • Costs reversed. Enterprise SSD went from US$185/TB (Q2 2020) to an index price of US$753/TB in Q3 2026, and nearline HDD from US$19/TB to about US$40/TB3435. Every earlier era assumed falling media prices; tight NAND supply rewards the data reduction Pure Storage built its first decade on (Chapter 48).
  • The market grew with the cycle. In 2Q26 external storage revenue reached US$10.3B (+33.6% YoY), and all-flash arrays were 52.1% of it. Everpure was #4 at 8.1% share and, at +50.0% YoY, the fastest grower among the top five vendors29.
  • Benchmarks and ecosystems became the gatekeepers. MLPerf Storage v3.0 had 19 submitters, 11 of them first-time, including Everpure47. As in the Fibre Channel and VMware eras, certification by the dominant platform (now NVIDIA) decides who gets considered (Chapter 34).

Where it goes next, with CXL, KV-cache tiers and PLC NAND, is covered in Chapter 53.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Which part of our value proposition is media speed, and which is economics or business model?" A strong answer separates them, admits speed claims erode within a generation, and names the durable parts: reduction ratios, Evergreen renewal economics, power per TB.
  2. "What could make an AI-native architecture irrelevant, as flash commoditized Violin's speed lead?" A strong answer names a concrete shift (KV-cache moving to CXL memory, storage services on DPUs) and how the product would ride it.
  3. "Which past deal is our template, Portworx or EMC's XtremIO?" A strong answer judges integration, not price: did the technology join the platform or stay a separate product line?

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Where does today's bottleneck sit: media, network, CPU or metadata?" A strong answer gives numbers (fabric µs versus flash µs, metadata operations per second) and which way that pushes the pendulum.
  2. "Which design decisions assume falling NAND prices?" Strong: over-provisioning, erasure-coding width, reduction assumptions, and what changes if $/TB rises for two years.
  3. "What from Purity's 2012 design would a 2026 clean-sheet design keep?" Strong: log-structured writes, global reduction, non-disruptive upgrades, plus what it would discard.

Don't say this:

  • "Flash killed disk." Disk still stores most bytes; flash took primary storage (Chapter 52).
  • "EMC failed." It was sold for about US$67B, and its products still lead the market inside Dell.
  • "Disaggregation is new." SANs pooled storage decades ago; what is new is NVMe-oF making remote flash nearly local.
  • "Storage prices always fall." 2026 is a counter-example on both curves.
  • "Software-defined storage will replace arrays." Three waves have tried; arrays absorbed each one.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• DASD — direct-access storage device, IBM's term for mainframe disk.
  • SLED — single large expensive disk, the RAID paper's foil.
  • Cached disk array — an array that fronts disks with a large RAM cache (EMC Symmetrix).
  • Filer / NAS appliance — a dedicated file server (NetApp).
  • SAN — storage area network, a block network such as Fibre Channel.
  • Architectural pendulum — the recurring swing between centralized, distributed and disaggregated storage.
  • Software-defined wave — a period when storage software moves onto commodity servers.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 52. History of flash and NAND economics
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Media physics for a semis person · Data reduction · History of storage, 1956–2026

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Consumers paid for flash's learning curve. Music players and phones funded NAND's scale from the mid-2000s; enterprise arrays inherited the curve. NAND fell from roughly $45/GB in 2005 to about 2¢/GB at the 2023 trough, around 35% a year.
  • The cost levers ran out one after another. Lithography carried the 2000s. Bits per cell (SLC→MLC→TLC→QLC) gave 50%, then 33%, then 25% cuts in cost per bit. 3D layers took over after Samsung's 24-layer V-NAND in 2013, and each new layer step now adds fewer bits per wafer and costs more capex.
  • Flash never beat nearline disk on raw $/TB. It beat performance disk (15K/10K RPM) on effective $/GB between about 2011 and 2015, because inline data reduction is cheap on flash and costly on disk. Latency, power and simpler operations did the rest.
  • NAND consolidated by changing owners, not by exits. Intel's fabs went to SK hynix (Solidigm), Toshiba's went to a Bain group (Kioxia), and SanDisk went to WD and was spun out again in 2025. DRAM consolidated through bankruptcies, to three players with ~88% of revenue. NAND still has five large suppliers, which partly explains its harsher cycles.
  • The cycle is a bit-growth-versus-wafer story. Booms bring capex, then supply overshoots and prices fall below cash cost (2008, 2012, 2018–19, 2022–23). The 2025–26 AI surge took spot NAND prices up roughly 13–15× from the 2023 trough. Suppliers are adding layers, not wafers.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Everpure's whole history sits on this curve. Pure Storage was incorporated in 20091, when NAND was still about $1/GB2. It sold all-flash arrays priced per usable gigabyte after data reduction, against 15K disk, and won the effective-$/GB argument before the raw one was close. The company's DirectFlash strategy is a bet on capturing more of each NAND generation's cost decline than SSD vendors pass through (Chapter 26). Its gross margin and pricing power still move with the NAND cycle (Chapter 48).

The history informs three live questions. Will the 2026 spike end in overbuild, as earlier ones did? How far can "flash replaces disk" go at an ~18× raw premium over nearline disk? And how much are supplier relationships worth when fab owners have changed at least four times in a decade?

docs.title: Five inflections in one picture
docs.text:
timeline
    title NAND flash inflection points
    1984-1987 : Masuoka team presents NOR flash at IEDM 1984 : NAND flash follows in 1987
    2005-2008 : iPod nano and Apple flash prepayments : IMFT formed : 2008 price crash and 30 percent output cut
    2011-2015 : All-flash arrays priced per usable GB : TLC reaches SSDs : Samsung 24-layer V-NAND : Flash arrays claim parity with 15K disk
    2016-2021 : WD buys SanDisk : First QLC SSD : Toshiba Memory sold and renamed Kioxia : Intel NAND becomes Solidigm
    2022-2026 : Deep downturn and wafer cuts : Kioxia IPO and Sandisk spin : AI-driven price surge : All-flash passes half of array revenue

Figure 52.1 — Flash went from invention to consumer scale in two decades, then won enterprise primary storage in about five years once data reduction made usable $/GB competitive.

docs.title: Invention, and why Toshiba did not own the economics (1984–2000)
docs.text:
Fujio Masuoka's team at Toshiba presented a flash EEPROM, the NOR type, at IEDM in December 19843. The NAND cell followed in a paper by Masuoka, Momodomi, Iwata and Shirota at IEDM in December 1987, and Kioxia, Toshiba's former memory unit, uses 1987 as the invention date4. The Semiconductor History Museum of Japan's exhibit gives 1988 for Toshiba's NAND announcement3, which appears to refer to a later device announcement. The peer-reviewed 1987 conference paper is the defensible date. NAND traded NOR's fast random reads for density: cells in series share contacts. That trade pays only when a controller handles errors and mapping, the origin of the FTL.

Masuoka later sued Toshiba over compensation for the invention, and the case settled in 20065. Kioxia's own retrospective puts 1990s NAND at about $10,000 per gigabyte (company-stated)6. Another industry recollection suggests nearer $1,250/GB in the mid-1990s7. Either way, flash was then a niche product.

docs.title: Consumers paid for the learning curve (2005–2012)
docs.text:
Apple's iPod nano launched on 7 September 2005 at 2 GB for $199 and 4 GB for $2498. Analysts estimated the 2 GB model held about $90 of flash, or roughly $45/GB, at a time when 1 GB sold for about $45 in the volume market9. Ten weeks later Apple signed supply agreements running to 2010 with Hynix, Intel, Micron, Samsung and Toshiba. It prepaid $1.25 billion10. Intel and Micron formed IM Flash Technologies (IMFT), 51% owned by Micron, with Apple expected as its first customer11.

This was a customer-funded capacity build: the buyer's balance sheet de-risked the suppliers' fab ramps. Music players, then smartphones, supplied the volume that drove the learning curve. Analyst data shows the result: about $45/GB in 2005, ~$0.90/GB for consumer NAND by Q4 20082, ~$1 in January 2011, ~$0.30 by July 2012 and ~$0.25 in early 201512.

Figure 52.2 — NAND fell roughly 35% a year on average from 2005 to the 2023 trough; the 2025–26 surge took spot prices back to roughly 2016–17 levels within months. Data: data/ch52_flash_cost.csv

The bases differ: retrospective claims, a retail card in 200313, analyst market prices1415 and TrendForce 512Gb TLC wafer spot quotes divided by 64 GB16171819. Read the slope, not the decimals. Worked trend: $45 ÷ $0.0219 ≈ 2,050× over 17.9 years, so ln(2,050)/17.9 ≈ 0.43 per year, which is about a 35% annual decline.

docs.title: The four cost levers, and how each ran out
docs.text:
Cost per bit = wafer cost ÷ (good dies per wafer × bits per die). Every era of NAND history leans on one term.

Lithography (to ~2013). Planar NAND shrank faster than logic because the array is regular. At around 15 nm, cells held so few electrons that cell-to-cell interference and endurance became limiting (Chapter 2 covers the physics).

Bits per cell. Storing more bits per cell multiplies bits per die at almost the same area, but the first step gives the most:

Transition Landmark product Bits per cell Cost-per-bit cut (worked, ideal) What it cost SLC → MLC Toshiba/SanDisk 1 Gb MLC NAND, announced November 2001 (first MLC NAND chip)20 1 → 2 50% 4 voltage states; slower program, lower endurance MLC → TLC Samsung SSD 840, 2012 (first TLC consumer SSD)20 2 → 3 33% 8 states; Samsung put TLC ~50% slower than its MLC TLC → QLC Micron 5210 ION, May 2018 (first QLC SSD)21 3 → 4 25% 16 states; launched as an HDD replacement for read-heavy work QLC → PLC Research only (SK hynix split-cell, IEDM 2025)22 4 → 5 20% 32 states; needs new cell tricks to be usable

Table 52.1 — Each extra bit per cell buys a smaller cost cut (1 − n/(n+1)) and costs more in speed and endurance, so bits per cell is a diminishing lever. Ideal figures ignore extra ECC and spare area.

Layers (2013 onward). Toshiba announced its BiCS 3D concept in June 200723, but Samsung reached mass production first, with 24-layer, 128 Gb V-NAND on 6 August 201324. Leading counts reached 321 (SK hynix, 2024)25 and 400+ (Samsung V10, 2026)26. Layers are no free lunch. Going from 32 to 64 layers roughly doubled bits per wafer, but 96 to 128 layers added only ~33%. Meanwhile the greenfield cost per 3D NAND wafer start rose from ~1.5× planar to ~2.2× by 202127. Layer steps also need far more deposition and etch time per wafer.

Wafers. Whatever the layers do not deliver, new fabs must. That makes the fourth lever the cyclical one.

docs.title: Bit growth versus wafer capacity: the engine of the cycle
docs.text:
Bit supply growth ≈ (1 + wafer-start growth) × (1 + bits-per-wafer growth) − 1. For years the industry's bit demand grew about 30% a year27. While a node or layer step delivered +30–40% bits per wafer, suppliers could meet demand with flat wafer starts. As migrations yield less, keeping up with 30% demand means adding wafers. That is expensive, lumpy capex that arrives with a multi-year lag, so it overshoots.

flowchart LR
    A["Demand shock: new device class or AI servers"] --> B["Prices and margins spike"]
    B --> C["Capex: new wafers plus layer migration"]
    C --> D["Bit supply jumps after a fab lag"]
    D --> E["Supply overshoots demand"]
    E --> F["Prices fall toward or below cash cost"]
    F --> G["Wafer-input cuts, capex freeze, deals"]
    G --> A

Figure 52.3 — The NAND cycle is a capacity-lag loop: margins fund wafers, wafers arrive late, and each bust ends with output cuts and ownership changes.

Semiconductor bridge: NAND versus DRAM. Both run the same loop, but DRAM consolidated through exits. Qimonda filed for insolvency in January 200928, and Elpida filed for bankruptcy in February 2012 with 15.4% share29; Micron completed its takeover of Elpida on 31 July 201330. In 2Q26, Samsung, SK hynix and Micron held 39.4%, 24.9% and 23.3% of DRAM revenue, about 88% together31. NAND kept five large suppliers. In 2008, TrendForce put Samsung at 40.4%, Toshiba 28.1%, Hynix 15.1%, Micron 7.9% and Intel 5.8%32. In 2Q26 the top five were Samsung (29.3%), SK hynix Group including Solidigm (18.2%), Micron (15.1%), Kioxia (13.6%) and Sandisk (11.4%), with $68.87B of revenue and 87.6% of the market between them33. Summing the squared market shares of the top five gives a Herfindahl index of about 2,750 for 2008 and about 1,730 for 2Q26 (worked: 29.3² + 18.2² + 15.1² + 13.6² + 11.4²). DRAM's top three alone score about 2,715. The 2008 shares are search-summary figures, so treat the gap as directional. NAND has become less concentrated, and its pricing less disciplined, although Kioxia and Sandisk share fabs, so there are fewer capacity decisions than brands.

docs.title: Boom and bust, 2008–2026
docs.text:
• 2008: Toshiba agreed in October to pay $1 billion for 30% of SanDisk's output. In December the two cut joint-venture output by 30%3435.
  • 2012: Toshiba cut Yokkaichi NAND output by ~30% in July after card and USB prices fell more than 20%36. In DRAM, the same year's bust killed Elpida.
  • 2018–19: Prices that had held near 25¢/GB in 2016–17 collapsed to about 5¢ spot14. A 13-minute power cut at Yokkaichi in June 2019 cost about 6 EB of wafer supply but did not reverse the slide37.
  • 2022–23: SK hynix posted its first loss in a decade in Q4 202238. In April 2023 Samsung joined SK hynix, Micron and Kioxia in cutting output39. The 512Gb TLC wafer spot price bottomed at about $1.40 (≈2.2¢/GB) in mid-202316.
  • 2025–26: AI servers absorbed enterprise SSD bits. TrendForce reported top-five NAND revenue up 77% QoQ to $68.87B in 2Q2633. It forecast 4Q26 contract prices up another 15–20%, with most new supply already committed40. Suppliers reportedly added almost no wafer capacity in 202641, and TrendForce expects them to put DRAM and HBM capex ahead of new NAND capacity33.

For a deal team, the pattern is that most busts were followed by transactions.

docs.title: Consolidation: the same fabs, new owners
docs.text:
Deal Year Value Consequence Apple prepays five NAND suppliers 2005 $1.25B10 Consumer demand underwrites capacity; IMFT's first anchor WD acquires SanDisk Signed 2015, closed May 2016 ~$19B at signing4243 HDD leader buys a seat in the Toshiba fab JV Intel–Micron end joint NAND development Jan 2018 n/a44 Intel's NAND strategy drifts; IMFT left making 3D XPoint Toshiba Memory sold to Bain-led consortium Closed Jun 2018 ~¥2tn (~$18B)45 Distressed-parent carve-out; SK hynix becomes an indirect investor46; renamed Kioxia Oct 2019 Micron buys Intel's IMFT stake Closed Oct 2019 ~$1.5B cash4748 IMFT unwound; Lehi fab sold to TI in 2021 for $900M49 SK hynix buys Intel NAND/SSD (Solidigm) Signed 2020; closings Dec 2021 and Mar 2025 $7B + ~$1.9B net5051 Intel exits; SK hynix gets enterprise QLC SSD share WD–Kioxia merger talks end Oct 2023 n/a46 SK hynix, a Kioxia investor, did not consent; the JV stays a JV Kioxia IPO Dec 2024 ~¥784B at pricing52 Bain gets a partial exit Sandisk spun from WD Feb 2025 Nasdaq: SNDK53 Pure-play NAND again; WD back to HDD only Kioxia–Sandisk JV extended to 2034 Jan 2026 n/a54 Shared Yokkaichi/Kitakami fabs locked in for another cycle

Table 52.2 — In twenty years almost every NAND fab outside Samsung changed owner or ownership structure, but the number of fab bases barely moved. Consolidation redistributed capacity rather than removing it.

Intel left with good technology because cyclical NAND was non-core inside a logic company. Toshiba sold because its parent needed cash after losses at its US nuclear unit45. The SanDisk round trip suggests public markets preferred a NAND pure play to an HDD/NAND conglomerate.

docs.title: The enterprise inflection: raw versus effective $/GB
docs.text:
The real contest was flash versus performance disk: 10K and 15K RPM drives, short-stroked and over-provisioned for IOPS.

Year Flash claim or market price Disk comparator Raw or effective? Source type 2011–12 Pure Storage FA-300: $5–10 per usable GB after ~5:1 reduction Performance disk ~$5/GB (vendor claim) Effective (flash) vs raw (disk) Trade press55 2014 HP 3PAR 7450: <$2 per usable GB at 4:1 "compaction"; ~$15/GB without 15K disk arrays ~$2 per usable GB, no reduction Effective vs raw Vendor claim56; Pure quoted at $3–457 2015 All-flash array: $16,500 per usable TB raw, $1,875 effective Tier-1 disk + flash tier: $8,000 per usable TB Both shown Analyst (Wikibon)58 Q2 2020 Enterprise SSD $185/TB Nearline HDD $19/TB Raw media: 9.7× TrendForce via Wells Fargo59 Q3 2026 30 TB TLC SSD ~$753/TB 30 TB HDD ~$41/TB Raw media: 18.6× Single-vendor index60

Table 52.3 — Flash crossed performance disk on an effective basis around 2012–2015. Against nearline disk it never crossed on raw $/TB, and at 4:1 reduction the 2026 premium is still about 4.6× (worked: 18.6 ÷ 4).

Data reduction was the decisive asymmetry. Deduplication turns sequential reads into random ones, and fingerprint lookups need fast metadata. On flash that is nearly free. On disk it costs seeks that performance arrays could not afford. So flash arrays could quote effective capacity and disk arrays largely could not (Chapter 5). Both 2014 and 2015 claims are vendor or analyst constructions with assumed reduction ratios. The robust conclusion is the direction, not the parity date.

docs.title: Why all-flash won primary storage, and disk kept the bulk tier
docs.text:
An illustrative worked example: delivering 100,000 random IOPS from 15K drives at ~200 IOPS each takes ~500 spindles. At 600 GB each that is ~300 TB raw to serve perhaps 20–30 TB of hot data, plus the power, rack space and failure rate of 500 motors. A single shelf of SSDs does the same with headroom. The other advantages compound:

  • Latency and consistency. ~100 µs reads instead of 5–8 ms seeks. Tail latency stopped depending on head position, so database and VDI performance became predictable.
  • Power and density. Fewer, denser devices. Today's 245 TB QLC drive rates at ~8.2 TB/W against ~4.4 TB/W for a 44 TB HDD (vendor comparison)61.
  • Operational simplicity. No short-stroking, tiering policies or hot-spot tuning.
  • Reduction economics. Inline dedupe and compression became safe to run.

The 15K drive died first; around 2017 ServeTheHome called Seagate's last Enterprise Performance 15K drives the likely final 15K series62. By 1Q26 all-flash arrays were 52.6% of IDC's external enterprise storage revenue, the first time above half63.

Nearline disk survived because it competes on raw $/TB at exabyte scale, not latency. Backup, archive and hyperscale bulk data reduce less or are already deduplicated upstream. At a 10–20× raw premium, power and density savings rarely close the gap. Coughlin estimates over 85% of data-centre data still sits on HDD [VERIFY: sponsored source]64. Chapter 2 has the media-level curves.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
Model Who How NAND cost reaches them Cycle exposure Strength Weakness Raw NAND in proprietary modules Everpure (DirectFlash) Buys NAND from qualified fabs (Micron, Kioxia)65 Direct on arrays; hyperscaler licences avoid NAND procurement66 Captures more of each generation's cost cut; 300 TB modules67 Carries qualification and inventory risk itself Commodity SSD arrays Dell, NetApp, HPE, VAST, WEKA, DDN Buys finished SSDs Pass-through with lag; SSD vendor margin stacked on NAND Multi-source, quick to adopt 245 TB drives Paying for drive-level FTL and spare area Vertically integrated NAND+SSD Samsung, SK hynix/Solidigm, Micron, Kioxia, Sandisk Owns fabs Full cycle: windfall in 2026, losses in 2023 Cost leadership and supply priority Commodity volatility; array vendors are customers, not partners Disk-heavy capacity tiers Seagate, WD, hyperscaler bulk tiers n/a Benefit when the flash premium widens Lowest raw $/TB IOPS per TB keep falling as drives grow

Table 52.4 — Where a company sits in this stack decides whether a NAND spike is a windfall, a pass-through or a margin squeeze.

The steelman for commodity-SSD vendors: in a shortage, allocation and multi-sourcing matter more than FTL efficiency. Options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information: long-term supply agreements or prepayments of the kind Apple used in 2005; whether the hyperscaler licensing model (customer buys the NAND) should extend to more segments while prices are high; and how much a structurally wider flash premium slows HDD-replacement deals.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text: NAND cost declines have resumed after every spike, but not on a fixed schedule. The signal to watch is whether suppliers turn 2026 profits into new wafer starts, the classic precursor to a bust. Kioxia/Sandisk's 332-layer BiCS10 out-densities Samsung's 400+-layer part, so density beats layer count68. PLC remains research22. Standard SSDs have reached 245 TB61, and Sandisk has shown a 512 TB roadmap for 202769. Consolidation is not over: Kioxia and WD's flash unit (now Sandisk) failed to merge in 202346. Chapter 53 takes up the 2026–2032 outlook.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "In past NAND spikes, how long did it take for array pricing to catch up, and what is different with Evergreen subscriptions?" Strong: separates list prices from contracted subscriptions, gives a lag in quarters, and names which lines absorb cost.
  2. "Against nearline disk at an 18× raw premium, which workloads still convert, and on what effective ratio?" Strong: names reduction ratios by data type (AI data reduces poorly) and a power or space constraint that makes the TCO case, not "flash is cheaper".
  3. "If NAND suppliers overbuild in 2027–28 as they did after 2017, how do we turn cheaper bits into share?" Strong: capacity-tier products, bigger DFMs and per-effective-TB pricing, plus how fast rivals' SSD costs follow.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "What does each bits-per-cell step cost you in write path design, and is PLC worth it for 25% more bits per cell (20% lower ideal cost per bit)?" Strong: weighs endurance and program-time penalties against that gain and explains how the system FTL hides them.
  2. "How do you compare suppliers' generations: layers, Gb/mm² or $/GB at module level?" Strong: density, yield and module-level cost, with layer count dismissed as a proxy.
  3. "How much raw NAND per effective TB do you save versus a commodity-SSD array, and where does it come from?" Strong: splits the gain into over-provisioning, write amplification and reduction, per workload.

Don't say this:

  • "Flash got cheaper than disk." Not on raw $/TB against nearline disk, ever. It beat 15K/10K performance disk on effective $/GB.
  • "NAND is like DRAM, a three-player market." DRAM has three; NAND has five large suppliers plus China's YMTC, and the structure has become less concentrated since 2008.
  • "More layers means cheaper bits." Each layer step adds fewer bits per wafer and more capex per wafer; density and yield decide.
  • "The 2026 shortage is a technology problem." It is supply discipline plus AI demand meeting a wafer-capacity freeze.
  • "Toshiba invented flash in 1987." NOR flash came first, at IEDM 1984; the NAND cell followed at IEDM 1987 (one museum source says 1988).

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• IEDM proceedings 1984 and 1987 for the original NOR and NAND cell papers.
  • Applied Materials' 3D NAND wafer-fab-equipment intensity analysis27.
  • TrendForce quarterly NAND and DRAM revenue rankings, for share and HHI tracking.
  • Intel 8-K filings on the SK hynix closings and the Kioxia IPO prospectus for JV terms.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• NOR / NAND flash — two flash array architectures: parallel cells (fast random reads) versus series strings (dense, cheap).
  • Bits per cell (SLC/MLC/TLC/QLC/PLC) — 1 to 5 bits stored per cell by distinguishing 2 to 32 voltage states.
  • V-NAND / 3D NAND — NAND built as vertical strings through stacked layers.
  • Wafer spot price — open-market price for unpackaged NAND wafers, quoted per die-equivalent.
  • Effective $/GB — price divided by logical capacity after data reduction.
  • Short-stroking — using only a disk's outer tracks to cut seek time, wasting capacity.
  • HHI — Herfindahl–Hirschman Index of market concentration.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 53. Future trends, 2026–2032
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~14 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Media physics · Interfaces and emerging tech · Inference and KV cache · Power and density · History of flash

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Capacity per device is the most certain trend, and Everpure's main lever. DirectFlash Modules (DFMs) are at 300 TB, standard SSDs at 245.76 TB, and 512 TB drives are on 2027 roadmaps. The scarce resources are rebuild time, NAND supply and watts, not slots.
  • Disk is not dying this decade. Vendor HAMR roadmaps take nearline drives from 44 TB toward 100 TB by about 2029, and Seagate says its output is largely sold out through 2028. Flash takes performance and power-constrained AI capacity; disk keeps cold bulk.
  • AI inference creates a new tier between HBM and shared storage. NVIDIA's KV cache hierarchy (Dynamo KVBM, BlueField-4 STX/CMX) makes context memory a purchasable category from 2H 2026. Every storage vendor, Everpure included, is fighting to be its backend.
  • The value is moving up into data services and down into the fabric. Catalogs, governance and vector search are converging with storage. DPUs, Ultra Ethernet and S3 over RDMA are commoditizing the data path.
  • Be calibrated. CXL pooling, co-packaged optics in storage and PLC flash are real but later and smaller than vendor decks imply. DNA and glass archives are pre-commercial. Several of today's "certainties" are vendor roadmaps that have slipped before.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) has built its strategy on three bets that run through this window: flash replaces disk at hyperscale, its own flash modules stay ahead of commodity SSDs, and it can move up from storage into data management (the 1touch acquisition, Data Intelligence, the Everpure rename itself). Each bet depends on the trends below. A NAND cost curve that stalls, a HAMR ramp that holds, or a commodity 512 TB SSD that arrives on time each change the economics of the hyperscaler licensing model. KV cache tiers and sovereign AI decide which new buyers exist.

This chapter gives each of twelve trends a likelihood, a timing call, winners and losers, and options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information. It separates vendor roadmaps (what a supplier says it will ship) from independent forecasts (analysts, standards bodies and observed adoption). The strategic responses are developed in Chapter 54.

docs.title: How to read the calls
docs.text:
Each trend gets three calls. Likelihood is the probability that the trend is material by 2032, meaning it changes a meaningful share of storage buying decisions. High means 70% or more, Medium 40–70%, Low under 40%. Timing is when it becomes material, which is usually two to four years after the first product ships. Evidence is labelled as vendor roadmap or independent signal. Vendor roadmaps slip, but unevenly. Seagate's 50 TB HAMR drive was once planned for 2026 and now enters qualification in late 20271, and the LTO tape consortium cut its future capacities in 20252. Roadmaps a vendor controls more fully can fare better: Pure Storage set a 300 TB DFM target for 2026 in March 20233 and met it, though that is one data point, not a rule.

Figure 53.1 — Most of what matters to Everpure lands in 2027–28; the exotic technologies cluster in the outer rings.

docs.title: Media
docs.text:
1. Larger flash modules: 300 TB, then 600 TB, then 1 PB. Everpure's DFMs are at 300 TB per module4. The largest standard SSD, Micron's 6600 ION, shipped at 245.76 TB in May 20265. A co-founder has described 600 TB and then 1 PB-plus modules, without dates6 [VERIFY: search-summary only]. The commodity side is closing in: Sandisk's roadmap shows 512 TB in 20277, and Meta has said it plans QLC drives up to 512 TB8 [VERIFY: source reused from Ch 26; confirm Meta statement]. Vendor roadmap on both sides. The independent signal is TrendForce's report that hyperscalers are buying QLC for AI workloads in 4Q269.

The constraint shifts from slots to failure physics. Take 24 modules per enclosure. At 300 TB that is 7.2 PB raw; at 1 PB it is 24 PB. Rebuilding one failed module at 1 GB/s takes 300,000 s (about 83 hours) at 300 TB and 1,000,000 s (about 11.6 days) at 1 PB. Spread across many modules at an aggregate 20 GB/s, the same rebuilds take about 4.2 and 13.9 hours. So bigger modules reward vendors who own the FTL and the rebuild path, which is the DirectFlash argument (Chapter 26). Call: High likelihood; 600 TB-class in 2027–28; 1 PB-class by 2029–30. The timing is an extrapolation of the 2023–26 doubling pace (75 → 150 → 300 TB), not a dated Everpure roadmap; none has been published for 600 TB or 1 PB.

2. PLC and 400–1,000-layer NAND. Samsung's V10 passes 400 layers using hybrid bonding10, while Kioxia/Sandisk's 332-layer BiCS10 claims higher density per mm²11. Bit density, not layer count, is the metric. Kioxia has described a technical path to 1,000 layers by 202712, and Samsung was reported to target 1,000 layers by 203013. Vendor roadmaps, and they conflict. PLC (5 bits per cell) adds only 25% more bits than QLC, against 33% for TLC to QLC, and halves the voltage margin again (32 states versus 16). SK hynix's split-cell PLC is research presented at IEDM in December 202514. No product is announced. Call: layer scaling High and continuous; PLC Medium at best, 2029–32, and probably first in read-mostly archive flash. The semis frame: layer count is the new node name. It is a marketing number that diverges from cost per bit once string stacking and bonding add process steps.

3. HDD's future: HAMR, nearline and archive. Seagate says its Mozaic 5 platform (more than 5 TB per platter, so 50 TB-plus drives) enters customer qualification in late 2027, with nearline output largely committed through 20281. Western Digital targets HAMR ramping in 2027, 60 TB ePMR and 100 TB HAMR by 202915. Vendor roadmaps, but the sold-out order books are an independent-ish demand signal. In 2026 enterprise SSDs cost roughly 18.6× HDD per TB16, far above the ~10× of 2020. The weakness is access density. A 50 TB drive at roughly 250–300 MB/s takes about 50 hours to read end to end, so IOPS and bandwidth per TB fall with every generation. Call: High that disk keeps the nearline bulk tier through 2032; flash takes the performance and power-constrained share. The winners are the two HAMR suppliers and the object and tiering vendors that blend disk with flash. The loser is any flash vendor whose case rests on purchase price rather than watts, density and operations (Chapter 38).

11. DNA, glass and ceramic archival. Microsoft says Project Silica's research phase finished in 2025, with lifetime claims beyond 10,000 years, but has announced no product17. Cerabyte targets 100 PB-plus ceramic archive racks by 2030. Its strategic investors include Western Digital (2025) and Pure Storage itself (July 2024, with co-founder John Colgrove joining Cerabyte's board), so Everpure is not a neutral observer of this trend18. Atlas Data Storage spun out of Twist Bioscience in May 2025 with US$155 million to commercialize DNA storage19. Write throughput is the gating problem: DNA synthesis needs orders-of-magnitude gains. Call: Low likelihood of material impact by 2032. Watch for hyperscaler production use, not lab capacity records.

docs.title: Interconnect and architecture
docs.text:
4. CXL memory pooling and tiers. CXL 4.0 (November 2025) runs at 128 GT/s on the PCIe 7.0 PHY20, and PCIe 8.0 targets a 2028 final spec21. Direct-attached CXL memory expanders ship, while switched pooling is only starting (Chapter 12). The independent evidence is sobering. Microsoft's Pond study found pooling across 16 sockets cut DRAM needs by about 7%22. Forecasts for the CXL market in 2028 range from about US$3.5 billion to more than US$15 billion23. The new use case is KV cache: Samsung and AMD showed CXL pooling cutting time to first token by 38% at OCP 2026 (vendor demo)24. CXL memory is still DRAM priced like DRAM, so it is a faster tier, not a cheaper one. Call: Medium; 2029–32 for storage relevance; it competes with flash for KV cache only at the hot edge.

5. Disaggregation everywhere, including DPUs. Disaggregated designs are now mainstream. VAST built the category, NetApp's AFX scales controllers and capacity independently25, and Everpure's FlashBlade//EXA splits metadata from data (Chapter 16). The next step moves storage software onto DPUs. NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX reference architecture launched in March 2026 with twelve storage co-design partners, Everpure among them2627. VAST runs its controller software on BlueField-4 inside GPU servers, with hardware due in 2H 202628. The semis analogy is the chiplet I/O die. Control moves into a standard part whose roadmap the platform owner, NVIDIA, sets. Call: High; adopt now. Disaggregation itself becomes table stakes. The open question is who owns the DPU software slot.

6. Photonic interconnects and co-packaged optics (CPO). CPO puts the optical engine next to the switch ASIC, cutting pluggable-module power and lasers. NVIDIA said in May 2026 that Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics switches were in production, with "4x fewer lasers" (vendor claim)29. TrendForce reported shipments to some partners by July 2026; broad availability is not yet confirmed. Its Kyber racks for Rubin Ultra (2027) will scale up over copper and CPO30. Broadcom ships 102.4 Tb/s Tomahawk 6 silicon31. Vendor roadmaps throughout. Storage rides on the same switches but rarely drives them, and storage NICs and arrays stay pluggable for serviceability. Call: Medium; CPO in AI scale-out switches by 2027–28; storage-side optics changes 2029–32. Few direct consequences for array vendors beyond rack power budgets.

7. KV cache as a new tier ("context memory"). Inference keeps each session's attention keys and values. A Llama 3.1 70B-class model needs 320 KiB per token, so a 128K-token session is about 43 GB (Chapter 32). Keeping 10,000 such sessions warm takes about 430 TB, or one to two 300 TB modules. NVIDIA's Dynamo KV Block Manager defines tiers G1 (HBM) to G4 (networked storage)32, and BlueField-4 context memory storage (CMX) adds a pod-level tier, with availability in 2H 202633. The independent signals are MLPerf Storage v3.0 adding a KV cache workload in September 202634 and TrendForce linking QLC demand to KV cache9. Everpure (PureKVA)35, WEKA (Augmented Memory Grid)36, DDN, VAST and HPE all ship offerings. The semis bridge is a victim cache. Blocks evicted from HBM drop into host DRAM, then into pod flash, then into shared storage, and a hit at any level saves recomputing the prefill. As with an L3 cache, value depends on hit rate and fill bandwidth, not capacity alone. Call: High; material in 2027–28. The risk is that NVIDIA's reference design turns the tier into a commodity flash box.

docs.title: Data services
docs.text:
8. Data-management convergence: storage, catalog, governance and vector. Storage vendors are absorbing the layers above them. Everpure bought 1touch for US$125.0 million37 and shipped Data Stream on NVIDIA's AI Data Platform design38. VAST sells a database and agent engine, and AWS put vector indexes (S3 Vectors, generally available December 2025) inside object storage39. The nearest independent forecast is narrower. Gartner predicts that by 2029 more than 80% of on-premises unstructured data will sit on consolidated file-and-object platforms, up from 50% in 202540. Its 2023 version predicted 70% by 202841, so the forecast has been raised, not delayed. But it measures file-and-object consolidation, not storage vendors absorbing catalogs and governance, so it supports the platform half of this trend only. The steelman against: Databricks, Snowflake and the security vendors own the buyer and see every vendor's storage (Chapter 39). Call: High that storage vendors ship these features; Medium that they capture the economics; 2027–28.

10. Object as the primary AI interface; S3 over RDMA. S3 over RDMA keeps HTTP for authentication and moves bulk bytes over RDMA into GPU memory. MinIO shipped it in November 202442, NVIDIA productized the pattern for Cloudian, Dell and HPE in 202543, and Pure Storage announced it for FlashBlade44. About one-sixth of MLPerf Storage v3.0 submissions used S334 (Chapter 9). A 400 GbE port moves 50 GB/s, which classic S3 over TCP and TLS cannot fill per client without heavy CPU. RDMA removes the reason to buy a parallel file system for many AI reads. Call: High; 2027–28. It erodes the file-system moat of AI-native vendors and commoditizes object.

docs.title: Deployment and operating models
docs.text:
9. Sovereign and edge AI storage. Gartner forecasts sovereign cloud IaaS spending of about US$80 billion in 2026, up 35.6%, with Europe overtaking North America in 202745. IDC reports the fastest AI infrastructure growth in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, driven by sovereign programs46. These are independent forecasts. DDN launched sovereign AI blueprints at SC2547, and Portworx added an edge SKU in 202648. Sovereign buyers want on-premises control, local support, air-gap options and no dependence on a US hyperscaler control plane. That favors appliance vendors and open, portable software. Call: High; adopt now. Volumes are lumpy national deals; edge AI storage stays small per site.

12. AI-driven operations. Storage AIOps is two decades old. What is new is agents that act. Everpure made Pure1 "agentic" through read-only MCP servers, with Copilot moving toward guided triage49. Gartner reportedly predicts that fewer than 1% of storage leaders run agentic storage management today, rising to 20% by 202850 [VERIFY: search-summary only]. Trust, not capability, is the bottleneck: agents that change production state need audit, rollback and blast-radius limits. Call: Medium; assistive agents now, write-capable autonomy for routine tasks in 2027–28.

Table 53.2 — Trend scorecard: Everpure is well placed on module capacity, early but unproven on convergence, and most exposed where NVIDIA's reference designs set the terms.

The steelman for competitors cuts several ways. VAST is most aligned with disaggregation, DPUs and convergence. It already runs on BlueField-4 and sells a database layer, so trends 5, 7 and 8 play to its strengths. WEKA and DDN hold the strongest KV cache and HPC positions. Dell, NetApp and HPE have the reach for sovereign deals and full-stack bundles. Hyperscalers pull convergence into S3 itself. Everpure's distinct asset is trend 1. No competitor ships a proprietary flash module at 300 TB (IBM's FlashCore Module is the nearest analogue), and the hyperscaler design wins monetize it without NAND exposure51. The steelman against: commodity 512 TB SSDs and FDP could narrow that lead within one product cycle. Its main exposure is that NVIDIA's STX turns trends 5 and 7 into reference designs where storage software is a feature on someone else's hardware.

The options sort into two groups. No-regret moves pay off under almost any scenario: dated module roadmaps, default integration with Dynamo and NIXL, RDMA-capable S3 everywhere, and publishing cost-per-token rather than TTFT multipliers. Real options are cheap to hold now and valuable only if a trend breaks favorably: early PLC qualification for archive flash, running Purity services on DPUs, and sovereign reference designs with local partners. CXL, co-packaged optics and DNA or glass archives need monitoring, not investment. A strategy team might rank build, buy or partner choices for each group in Chapter 54.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
Storage forecasts have a poor record, and in a consistent direction. Every new tier was predicted to arrive faster than it did. Intel's Optane was meant to be the persistent-memory tier; Intel wound it down in 2022 with a US$559 million charge52. ZNS SSDs were meant to remake flash management; the gentler Flexible Data Placement (FDP), driven by Meta and Google, has drawn more hyperscaler support53. "Flash kills disk by 2026" missed because NAND prices rose: enterprise SSD premiums over disk widened in 2026 instead of narrowing16. Forecasts based on supply-side physics (density, layers, PCIe doubling) have held up better than those based on demand-side adoption (new tiers, new interfaces).

The demand backdrop is not in question. IDC raised its 2026 AI infrastructure forecast to US$497 billion and expects spending to pass US$1 trillion in 202946. Storage is a small share of that, so the issue is not whether storage demand grows. It is which tiers and which business models capture it.

That history sets the calibration here. Capacity trends get High. New tiers get High only where a dominant platform owner (NVIDIA with Dynamo and STX) is standardizing them. Tiers that need a whole ecosystem to move (CXL pooling, PLC, DNA) get Medium or Low. The 2026 NAND shortage is a reminder that the cycle can override the roadmap for two years at a time (Chapter 48).

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What has to be true for a 600 TB DFM to ship before commodity 512 TB SSDs?" Strong: names the NAND generation and die capacity, the rebuild design and the qualification lead time. It says whether the gap to commodity drives is widening or narrowing.
  2. "In a sovereign AI deal, what do we lose on today?" Strong: names specifics such as local support, air-gap, certification or a domestic partner, and which competitor wins (often Dell, Huawei or DDN).
  3. "How does PureKVA make money if NVIDIA's CMX becomes the default context tier?" Strong: positions PureKVA as the G4 shared tier behind CMX, or as a CMX-compatible software layer, and gives a cost-per-token comparison, not a TTFT multiplier.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "At 1 PB per module, what is the rebuild time and the exposure window to a second failure?" Strong: gives aggregate rebuild GB/s, the erasure-code geometry and the probability of data loss during rebuild.
  2. "Which parts of Purity could run on a BlueField-4 DPU, and what breaks?" Strong: separates data path from metadata and global deduplication, and names memory and core limits.
  3. "What does PLC do to our write path and endurance budget?" Strong: quantifies P/E cycles, read-retry latency and how much log structuring and wear leveling absorb.

Don't say this:

  • "Disk is dead." HAMR order books run through 2028 and flash costs about 18× more per TB in 2026.
  • "CXL will replace storage tiers." CXL memory is DRAM at DRAM prices; it is a memory tier.
  • "DNA storage is coming soon." No production system exists, and write throughput needs orders-of-magnitude gains.
  • "1,000-layer NAND means 3× cheaper flash." Cost per bit depends on bonding and process steps, not layer count.
  • "Our KV cache gives 20× faster TTFT." Without the baseline and cost per token, that number persuades no one.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Context memory — storage tier holding inference KV cache between GPU memory and shared storage.
  • CMX / STX — NVIDIA's BlueField-4 context memory storage platform and storage reference architecture.
  • Co-packaged optics (CPO) — optical engines packaged next to a switch or processor die instead of pluggable modules.
  • HAMR — heat-assisted magnetic recording, which lets disks write smaller bits.
  • PLC — penta-level cell, 5 bits per NAND cell.
  • Sovereign AI — AI infrastructure built to keep data, control and operations within a jurisdiction.
  • Technology radar — chart placing trends by maturity ring and category.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 54. Strategic option map
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: The storage stack · Company history and strategy · Platform and software · Hyperscaler business and financials · Technical diligence framework

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Read the industry as an eight-layer value stack, from NAND media to AI data platforms and agents. Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) owns the middle (flash modules, flash management and array software), competes in file, object and fleet management, and entered KV cache, data management and AI data platforms (layers 5, 7 and 8) only in 2026.
  • Each layer has a natural mode. Media is hedged, modules and array software are built, and buy and partner options cluster in the AI-data layers, where the scarce assets and neutral buyers sit.
  • Prices rise steeply up the stack. Everpure's largest deal was Portworx, at about $370M. Recent data-management and AI-data deals ran from $28M to $11B. A Securiti-sized deal ($1.725B) would cost almost three years of Everpure's FY26 free cash flow.
  • A good option clears five gates, not one: strategic fit, fit with Purity and Fusion, valuation against ARR and margin, integration risk (above all, a second operating system), and antitrust or foreign-investment review. Most options fail the second or fourth gate, not the first.
  • "Do nothing new" is a serious option. Revenue guidance implies ~38% growth, NAND is consuming cash, and Everpure's record favours small tuck-ins. The case against it is neutrality: whoever owns the catalog above the array owns the customer.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
This chapter puts the atlas's layers, architectures and competitors on one page. Strategists ask "where do we play, how do we get there, and what does it cost?", and those questions differ by layer. The answer for NAND (hedge supply, never buy a fab) is the opposite of the answer for data intelligence (Everpure bought 1touch for $125.0M in cash in 20261). The 2026 rebrand to Everpure and the "Data Primacy" pitch (Chapter 28) have moved strategy discussion toward the upper layers, which are also the most expensive and contested.

This chapter is a synthesis. It contains options a strategy team might evaluate, based on public information, and nothing about non-public Everpure plans. Company names in the matrices illustrate a category of target or partner, or a past public transaction; no deal, approach or partnership is implied.

docs.title: From the I/O stack to a value stack
docs.text:
Chapter 13 traced a write through eight technical layers. The strategy stack below regroups them by who captures value. The bottom three hold Pure Storage's founding insight: consumer-grade NAND managed by Purity's global FTL inside DirectFlash Modules (DFMs). The middle three layers are where storage systems compete. The top two are where storage meets data management and AI software, the claim the Everpure name makes.

Semiconductor bridge. Media is the fab: capital-intensive, cyclical and owned by IDMs. DirectFlash is the integrated memory controller, IP that makes commodity silicon behave better than a standard part. Purity is the firmware stack customers standardise on. The top layers resemble EDA plus cloud software, with higher multiples, more vendors and buyers who value neutrality. As in semis, value migrates toward whichever layer is scarce. Today that is trusted context about data, and GPU-adjacent memory capacity.

Figure 54.1 — Everpure owns the middle of the stack. Its 2026 launches put it early in KV cache, data management and AI data platforms, the layers where public deal prices are highest and partner neutrality matters most.

docs.title: Where Everpure stands, zone by zone
docs.text:
The owned core (layers 1–3). Everpure does not make NAND. It buys raw flash, with qualified parts from Micron and Kioxia23, and turns it into DFMs reaching 300 TB per module in 20264. The middle layers are also licensable on their own: Meta and, from August 2026, a second top-five hyperscaler license DirectFlash technology while buying their own NAND5. Everpure was fourth in IDC's 2Q26 external-storage tracker with 8.1% share, the fastest grower in the top five6. Nobody is likely to sell Everpure a better FTL, so the open question for layers 2–3 is how far to license them. Layer 1 is a supply-chain question: strategic NAND buying turned Q2 FY27 free cash flow to –$238M7.

The contested middle (layers 4–6). FlashBlade//EXA is Everpure's entry into GPU-cluster file storage. It posted the top results among MLPerf Storage v3.0 entrants8, but VAST, WEKA and DDN sat that round out, and EXA still lacks DFM-based data nodes, NCP certification and very-large-cluster references (Chapter 27). For KV cache, PureKVA (September 2026)9 and a named role in NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX architecture10 put Everpure in a tier that NVIDIA itself defines (Chapter 32). In the control plane, Pure1 and Fusion manage the fleet; Fusion users passed 1,200 in Q1 FY27, still under a tenth of the base11. Portworx, bought in 2020, carries Everpure into Kubernetes and VMware-exit projects.

The frontier (layers 7–8). Data Intelligence (ex-1touch) classifies content and entities. Data Stream, generally available in June 2026, feeds GPU pipelines on NVIDIA's AI Data Platform design12. Both are early, mostly sold with arrays, and face much larger catalog, data-security and lakehouse vendors (Chapter 39).

docs.text:

Table 54.1 — Build dominates the owned core; buy and partner options cluster at the top, where targets are expensive and partners own the buyer.

Three patterns stand out. First, the natural mode changes with the layer. Below layer 4, Everpure's advantage is integration, so buying rarely adds anything that building cannot. Above layer 6, the scarce asset is reach into data Everpure does not store, which building cannot easily supply. Second, prices rise up the stack (Table 54.2). Third, partnering is cheapest but least defensible at the top. A catalog vendor that reads Everpure metadata also reads everyone else's.

docs.title: Five gates for evaluating any option
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Option: build, buy or partner at layer N"] --> B{"Strategic fit: does it move a layer the customer pays for?"}
    B -- no --> X["Pass or monitor"]
    B -- yes --> C{"Technical fit with Purity and Fusion: one OS, one control plane?"}
    C -- "needs second OS" --> P["Prefer partner or interoperability"]
    C -- fits --> D{"Financial: price vs ARR, gross margin, payback from FCF"}
    D -- "fails" --> P
    D -- passes --> E{"Integration risk: team, code, channel conflict"}
    E -- high --> F["Prefer build or minority stake"]
    E -- manageable --> G{"Antitrust, CFIUS, foreign-investment review"}
    G -- "remedies needed" --> H["Re-scope or price in delay"]
    G -- clear --> I["Decision memo: build, buy or partner"]
    P --> I
    F --> I
    H --> I

Figure 54.2 — Most options clear the strategic-fit gate; the real filters are Purity fit, price against ARR and integration risk.

Gate 1, strategic fit. Does the option strengthen a layer customers pay for separately, or one that protects a layer they do pay for? KV cache passes if it is paid from the GPU budget (Chapter 32); a feature only sold inside array deals passes only as defence.

Gate 2, fit with Purity and Fusion. Everpure's distinctive claim is one OS and one subscription model across products (Chapter 28). An asset that brings a second data path or OS breaks that claim; Dell's five-plus storage operating systems are the cautionary example (Chapter 46). Ask whether the asset can run on Purity, beside it under Fusion, or only instead of it.

Gate 3, financial. FY26 free cash flow was $616M24, year-end cash and marketable securities $1.5B25, and management guides FY27 free cash flow to $600–800M after the NAND build7. Worked example (illustrative): a target with $50M ARR at 15× costs $750M. For a five-year payback from gross profit alone, it must add $150M of gross profit a year; at the ~75% subscription gross margin Everpure reports26, that is about $200M of revenue a year, roughly 9% of Q2 FY27 subscription ARR of $2.13B26. The bar is high because private AI-data marks are high: WEKA's last round valued it at ~16× ARR, and VAST's at ~60× committed ARR, both on company-stated figures (Chapter 43).

Gate 4, integration risk. Everpure's record is mixed. Compuverde became FlashArray file services within about a year. StorReduce's ObjectEngine was quietly withdrawn (Chapter 25). Risk rises with channel conflict (a target selling through rivals) and with client software on every GPU node.

Gate 5, antitrust and regulatory. Small software tuck-ins rarely draw review. Larger deals do. The DOJ sued to block HPE's ~$14B Juniper deal in January 2025. It closed in July 2025 after a settlement that required HPE to divest its Instant On WLAN business and auction licences to Juniper's Mist AI source code27; IBM–HashiCorp waited about ten months for US and UK clearance28. Intel's NAND sale to SK hynix closed in two steps between 2021 and 202523. Cross-border targets add foreign-investment screening.

Table 54.2 — The money has moved up the stack: 2024–2026 deals in data management and AI data dwarf the array and file deals of the same period.

Four lessons follow. Storage incumbents are buying small and specific: NetApp's two 2026 deals and Dell's Dataloop are undisclosed or around $120M, the same scale as 1touch. Data and security companies pay platform prices for governance and DSPM: $1.7B to $8B. That is an order of magnitude above Everpure's deal history, and it makes those buyers likelier partners, or competitors for the same assets. Arrays consolidate through installed bases, as with Lenovo–Infinidat. Memory-tier software is attracting chip companies, as AMD–MEXT shows, which hints that the KV-cache tier could be captured from the silicon side.

docs.title: Steelmanning "do nothing new"
docs.text:
The strongest option may be to stay focused. Growth is already high. FY27 guidance of $5.03–5.07B implies ~38% growth26. Cash is committed: strategic NAND purchases pushed Q2 FY27 free cash flow negative7, and that hedge is a bigger bet than any tuck-in. The record favours restraint. Four deals in 17 years cost about $594M in total291, and the smallest one failed (Chapter 25). Neutrality is an asset. A storage vendor that partners with every catalog, backup and lakehouse vendor gets carried into deals by all of them. One that buys into those layers becomes their competitor. Single-OS discipline is the moat, and most targets would dilute it.

The counter-argument is the one Chapter 39 makes. In an agentic enterprise, whoever answers "what is this data, and who may use it?" owns the customer relationship. If that is a catalog vendor, Everpure risks becoming a fast S3 endpoint under someone else's control plane. "Do nothing new" is defensible only if Data Intelligence and Fusion can reach non-Everpure data organically, quickly enough to matter.

docs.title: How to use this map in conversation
docs.text:
• Start from the layer, not the deal. Ask "how strong are we on layer 7 without new spending?" rather than "should we buy X?". People can answer the first without discussing non-public plans.
  • Use category language. Say "a DSPM-type asset" or "a parallel-metadata team", never a named private company as a target. Named companies are for precedents and competitive benchmarks.
  • Bring the five gates. PMs engage on gates 1–2, engineers on gate 2 and gate 4, finance on gate 3.
  • Treat partnering as a real option, not a consolation. At layers 5–8, being the best backend for NVIDIA, catalog or backup ecosystems may beat owning a layer outright.
  • Name the do-nothing case first. It signals respect for the core business.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:

Table 54.3 — Peers have chosen different modes: NetApp buys, VAST builds, HPE partners and IBM buys at platform prices; Everpure's record is build-centric with small tuck-ins.

The steelmen differ. NetApp's two 2026 deals are the strongest argument for speed. Two AI-software deals in about ten weeks (DataPelago in July, PEAK:AIO announced in September 2026) put GPU data processing and parallel metadata beside ONTAP while Everpure builds EXA's equivalents. VAST is the strongest argument for building. One codebase that reaches from DASE to agent runtimes avoids every gate-2 problem. HPE shows that partnering can carry a vendor into AI deals while it builds, but HPE's AI file still depends on a partner that also competes with it. Everpure sits between them: more integration discipline than NetApp, far less capital than VAST, so tuck-ins plus deep partnering is its revealed preference to date.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
timeline
    title Storage and data-infrastructure deals move up the stack
    2019 : Pure Storage buys Compuverde for file services
    2020 : Pure Storage buys Portworx : SK hynix agrees to buy Intel NAND
    2024 : Databricks buys Tabular : Cohesity combines with Veritas
    2025 : IBM closes HashiCorp : Databricks buys Neon : HPE closes Juniper : Salesforce closes Informatica : Veeam closes Securiti AI
    2026 : IBM closes Confluent : Lenovo closes Infinidat : Everpure closes 1touch : NetApp buys DataPelago and agrees to buy PEAK AIO

Figure 54.3 — Between 2019 and 2026 the centre of gravity of deal activity moved from storage plumbing (file systems, NAND) to data management and AI data platforms.

In 2019–2020 Pure Storage bought capabilities (file, then Kubernetes) to widen what Purity could serve. From 2024 the largest deals moved to table formats, databases, streaming and governance, bought by data-platform and security companies, not storage vendors. Storage vendors responded with small AI-data buys in 2025–2026. The signals to watch next: a VAST S-1, which would give audited AI-native storage economics (Chapter 42); the outcome of DDN's reported search for strategic investors (Chapter 44); whether NVIDIA's STX turns the KV-cache tier into a commodity shelf; and whether Data Intelligence wins standalone, non-Everpure deployments.

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Which layer above the array do customers pay for separately today?" Strong answer: names standalone deals (Fusion or Data Intelligence on non-Everpure storage) and admits where attach is mostly inside array deals.
  2. "Where would a partner get you to market faster than building?" Strong answer: names an ecosystem (NVIDIA Dynamo, a catalog, a backup vendor), the integration needed and a success metric.
  3. "What would make Data Intelligence credible on data that is not on Everpure?" Strong answer: connectors, a separate price, reference customers with mixed estates, and a timeline.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "If you had to absorb outside code, where in Purity or Fusion could it live without a second data path?" Strong answer: separates control-plane plug-ins, sidecar services and the data path, and says which are off-limits.
  2. "What would it take for PureKVA to be the default backend in NVIDIA's KV stack?" Strong answer: upstream NIXL and LMCache work, STX conformance, published latency and hit-rate figures.
  3. "Which DirectFlash capabilities could a hyperscaler replicate with FDP SSDs, and how fast?" Strong answer: separates global scheduling and density, which are hard to copy, from features FDP already covers (Chapter 26).

Don't say this:

  • "Everpure should buy VAST" (or any named private company). Speculative, ignores a ~$30B mark, and breaks the public-information rule.
  • "Partnering is what you do when you can't afford to buy." At layers 5–8, neutrality is often worth more than ownership.
  • "Storage vendors can't climb the stack." NetApp, Dell and Everpure are all trying; the open question is reach beyond their own arrays, not permission.
  • "M&A is how Everpure grows." Four deals in 17 years says otherwise; organic product and the Evergreen model built the business.
  • "A bigger array share is the obvious next deal." It buys an installed base on a second OS, which Everpure's model is built to avoid.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• Purchase-price allocation notes for Portworx (FY2021 10-K) and 1touch (Q1 FY27 10-Q): goodwill share, retention and earn-out structures.
  • DOJ and HPE filings on the Juniper settlement, a recent model of behavioural and divestiture remedies in IT infrastructure.
  • NVIDIA Dynamo/KVBM and NIXL plug-in interfaces: where a storage backend integrates, and how much is open source.
  • Chapter 50's scorecard, applied to any category in Table 54.1.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Value stack — industry layers ranked by where profit is captured, not by the I/O path.
  • Build / buy / partner — develop a capability in-house, acquire it, or contract for it.
  • Tuck-in acquisition — a small purchase of a team or product absorbed into an existing platform.
  • Strategic fit — whether an option strengthens a layer customers pay for, or protects one.
  • Technical fit — whether an asset runs on or beside the existing OS without a second data path.
  • Second-OS problem — the cost and confusion of running two storage operating systems after a deal.
  • Neutrality — a vendor's ability to serve data stored on rivals' systems.
  • ARR multiple — purchase price or valuation divided by annual recurring revenue.
  • Antitrust remedy — a divestiture or behavioural commitment required by regulators to clear a deal.
  • Foreign-investment review — government screening of cross-border deals, such as CFIUS in the US.
  • DSPM — data security posture management: software that finds sensitive data and checks who can access it.
  • Do-nothing option — the current plan with no new deals or major partnerships, judged as a real alternative.
