docs.title: 55. Talking with product managers
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Product portfolio: FlashArray and FlashBlade · Platform and software · Hyperscaler business, ecosystem and financials · Consumption models

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A storage PM is the general manager of a trade-off, not of a feature list. Every roadmap item is a bet on one persona and one workload, made with a known cost in engineering capacity, margin or partner dependence.
  • Know what they are measured on. Public Everpure metrics include subscription ARR, net dollar retention, product versus subscription gross margin, and adoption counts such as Fusion customers.
  • Ask about losses, not wins. A PM who can name the last three lost deals, the competitor and the deciding attribute is worth the meeting. One who answers with logos is not.
  • Bring a hypothesis with a number. "If DeepReduce yields 1.5:1 on checkpoints, EXA's $/usable TB beats X; what do you actually see?" gets a real answer. "Tell me about EXA" gets the pitch deck.
  • Each product line has a different scorecard. FlashArray PMs defend share and margin, FlashBlade//EXA PMs race certification and benchmarks, Portworx and Data Intelligence PMs fight for a buyer outside storage, and the hyperscale PM sells IP, not boxes.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Corporate development work at Everpure runs through product managers. They own the gap analyses that justify a build, partner or buy decision. They have the win/loss data that tells you whether a target's product would close a real hole. They will also run the integration roadmap after a deal closes. 1touch, closed in May 2026 for $125.0M1, is now a PM-owned product line, Everpure Data Intelligence. Whether it was a good acquisition will be judged on metrics that a PM sets and reports.

PMs are also the fastest route to ground truth that is not in filings. The earnings release says subscription ARR was $2.13B, up 20%2. A PM can tell you which SKU, persona and competitive motion produced the growth, and which one is stalling. That conversation works only if you speak their language. You need to understand the workload, respect the trade-offs, and ask questions they cannot answer with a slide. This chapter is the method; Chapter 57 is the full question bank, and Chapter 56 covers engineers and the Office of the CTO.

docs.title: How a storage PM thinks
docs.text:
A storage PM's mental model runs from persona to scorecard. The persona is who buys and who operates: a VMware admin, an AI platform team, a neocloud's infrastructure lead, a CISO. The persona's workload fixes the I/O shape: small random block writes, multi-GB/s sequential checkpoint bursts, billions of small objects, KV-cache reads on every inference request (Chapter 24). The workload produces requirements, the PM compares them with the product, and the gaps compete for engineering capacity. Every gap ends in one of three answers: build it, get it from a partner, or defer it and accept the losses.

Four inputs constantly reshape the model. Win/loss reviews show which gaps actually cost deals. Pure1 telemetry shows how the installed base really behaves, for example reduction ratios, fill rates and protocol mix. Partner calendars decide when a feature matters: an NVIDIA GPU generation, a VMware licensing change, a Nutanix integration. Component costs, above all NAND, feed straight into pricing and packaging (Chapter 48).

flowchart LR
    P["Persona: who buys, who operates"] --> W["Workload: I/O shape, scale, protocol"]
    W --> R["Requirements and gaps"]
    R --> T{"Build, partner or defer?"}
    T --> K["Packaging and pricing"]
    K --> S["Scorecard: ARR, attach, win rate, margin"]
    S -. "next cycle" .-> P
    WL["Win/loss reviews"] --> R
    TL["Pure1 telemetry"] --> R
    PC["Partner and certification calendar"] --> T
    NC["NAND and component cost"] --> K

Figure 55.1 — A PM's world runs from persona to scorecard; your questions land best when they target one arrow, such as why a gap was deferred or how NAND cost reached a price.

Semiconductor bridge. This is the same discipline as a chip product line. The persona is the design-win target, the workload is the benchmark suite, "build, partner or defer" is the tape-out feature freeze, and certification cycles play the role of a hyperscaler's qualification calendar. Miss the window and you wait a generation.

docs.title: What they are measured on
docs.text:
Everpure does not publish PM scorecards, but its disclosures show what the company rewards. Subscription ARR ($2.13B) and remaining performance obligations ($4.1B, up 44%) measure recurring commitment2. Net dollar retention among subscribers was 113% in FY26, down from 117%3. That moves PMs who own Evergreen//One and Portworx expansion. Gross margin differs by line: in Q2 FY27, non-GAAP product margin was 66.2% and subscription margin 74.9%4. A PM who shifts a customer from capex to subscription changes the margin mix, not just the revenue timing.

Attach is the metric for platform products. Fusion passed 1,200 customers5. Worked, illustrative: against a base of roughly 15,000 customers [VERIFY: current Everpure customer count], that is about 8% attach. A good question is not "how many customers?" but "how many run Fusion presets in production via API?" (Chapter 28).

PM phrase What it usually means Follow-up that earns respect "Attach" Share of array deals that also buy the software line Attached at signature, or deployed and renewed? "Effective capacity" Usable TB × an assumed data-reduction ratio Which ratio, measured on which workload class? "Design win" A customer chose the technology; revenue may be years out When does revenue start, and what could stop it? "Certified" Passed a partner's floor test at one tier and GPU generation Which program, which level, which GPU generation? "GA" Orderable and supported, not necessarily feature-complete What is still in preview or on a support exception? "On the roadmap" Anything from funded to a slide Is it staffed, and is it dated externally? "Platform" Shared OS, control plane or contract across SKUs Which deal did the platform win that a point product would have lost? "We don't lose on architecture" Losses are blamed on price or relationship Name the last loss where price was not the reason.

Table 55.1 — PM vocabulary often hides the qualifier; the follow-up question restores it.

docs.title: Partner and certification cycles
docs.text: AI product lines run on NVIDIA's calendar. NVIDIA-Certified Storage launched at GTC in March 2025, with Foundation, Enterprise and NCP levels6. SuperPOD certification is tied to a GPU generation; its B200 "enhanced" storage tier works out to roughly 0.5 GB/s of read per GPU7. FlashBlade//S500 gained SuperPOD certification in November 20248, and FlashBlade added NCP high-performance-storage certification in March 2025 (Chapter 27). For FlashBlade//EXA, Everpure said in March 2026 that NVIDIA-Certified Storage validation extended to EXA; NCP and SuperPOD certification for EXA were not on the public record as of this writing (Chapter 34). For an EXA PM, the certification date is a pipeline gate. For you it is a diligence question: in which deals is the gap used against us, and when does it close?

docs.title: Question sets by product line
docs.text:
Each line below has a different scorecard, so the questions differ. The second column is the PM's likely optimisation target, inferred from public positioning.

Product line What the PM is optimising Questions to ask A strong answer sounds like FlashArray (//X, //XL, //C, //E, //ST) Share in VMware-exit and database refreshes; margin under NAND inflation Where does //ST win that //XL190 with Purity Turbo loses? How much NAND inflation was passed through versus absorbed? Separates latency-bound from IOPS-bound buyers; gives pass-through on new sales versus absorption in fixed-price contracts FlashBlade (//S, //E) Unstructured-data share against PowerScale, ONTAP and HDD object On what metric do we lose to HDD object, and at what capacity and term does TCO flip? A $/TB gap, plus power, rack and refresh numbers at a stated capacity FlashBlade//EXA AI training and neocloud wins; benchmark leadership; certification What share of pipeline is gated on DFM data nodes or NCP certification? Which deal profiles do we lose to VAST, and why? Splits enterprise from neocloud, names the gate and a quarter; names an architectural loss, not only price Portworx Container and KubeVirt attach, including on non-Everpure storage Where did Portworx win: cloud-native, VM migration, or both? What do customers lose on third-party disks? Customer counts per motion; candid about reduction and replication gaps off FlashArray Fusion / Pure1 Fleet automation that raises retention and lowers support cost How many customers automate presets via API or Terraform, and do they renew or expand faster? "Enabled" separated from "in production", tied to NDR Evergreen//Forever, //One Recurring revenue and margin under SLAs What does the 25% buffer cost in deployed capacity? How does margin behave when reduction falls short? Quantified buffer and reduction risk; the contract lever that recovers it Everpure Cloud (Dedicated, Azure Native) Hybrid footprint; marketplace consumption Which workloads run there in production, and is it a land motion or a disaster-recovery add-on? Named workloads, consumption trend, and the AWS gap versus FSx for ONTAP Data Intelligence (ex-1touch) A new buyer (CDO, CISO) and separate ARR What share of bookings cover data not on Everpure? Who carries the quota? A number, named estates (Oracle, M365, rival NAS), and how it feeds Purview or Collibra KV cache (PureKVA on FlashBlade, EXA) Inference attach to existing FlashBlade; a recurring workload What baseline, hit rate and context length sit behind "up to 20×" TTFT? How would we price a KV tier? Baseline and model stated; price anchored to the customer's recompute cost Hyperscale / DirectFlash licensing Exabytes deployed, licence economics, the next design win What keeps a licensee from in-sourcing the FTL? How does pricing behave as module capacity doubles? Software updates and NAND qualification as the dependency; per-TB versus per-module economics

Table 55.2 — Ten product lines, ten scorecards; the strong answers share a pattern: a number, a named loss, and a date.

A few lines deserve extra care. Data Intelligence went GA in June 20269, so its PMs are still defining the persona. Questions about who signs and who is paid will be welcome. KV cache is new: PureKVA and its "up to 20×" time-to-first-token claim were announced on 2026-09-30 for October availability, and GA had not been confirmed publicly at this writing10, so the useful question is the baseline, not the multiple (Chapter 32). Hyperscale PMs sell a licence. The first customer, Meta, passed 2 EB in FY2611, and a second, unnamed top-five hyperscaler signed in August 202612, so their scorecard is exabytes and design wins, not arrays.

docs.title: Preparing for a PM meeting
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Identify product line and PM role"] --> B["Read latest earnings remarks and launch coverage"]
    B --> C["Pull the chapter playbook and staged ASK lines"]
    C --> D["Write one hypothesis per lens, with a number"]
    D --> E{"Answerable from public sources?"}
    E -- "Yes" --> F["State it yourself, then ask the next layer"]
    E -- "No" --> G["Frame as a trade-off question"]
    F --> H["In the meeting: listen for mechanism, number, date, loss"]
    G --> H
    H --> I["Within a day: log answers, update open questions"]

Figure 55.2 — Do the public homework first, so meeting time goes to what only the PM knows.

Three habits make the flow work. First, never spend meeting time on a question the 10-Q answers; state the fact and ask what it hides. Second, frame questions as trade-offs ("if you had one more team, would it go to DFM data nodes or to NCP features?"), because a trade-off forces a priority. Third, ask for the loss; PMs rehearse wins.

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
PMs and executives across the industry frame their products publicly in ways that shape what they will push on in a meeting, including a target's PMs during a formal diligence process. Use the counter-questions with Everpure colleagues, in public forums or under a diligence agreement; never to draw non-public information out of a competitor's staff.

Vendor Public framing What their PMs will push Your counter-question Everpure One OS (Purity) across arrays and cloud; Evergreen ownership; "Data Primacy" Simplicity, non-disruptive upgrades, subscription economics Where does one-OS consistency cost you a feature a specialist has? VAST Data "AI Operating System" since May 202513 One system for files, objects, tables and agents Which layers are production-proven, and which are new? WEKA NeuralMesh microservices (June 2025)14; KV-cache memory grid Software on any hardware or cloud; GPU-server convergence What does the customer own operationally when hardware is theirs? DDN EXAScaler for HPC; Infinia for inference and object (2023)15 Largest-scale AI references, NVIDIA's own clusters How much code do the two platforms share? NetApp ONTAP unified, plus AFX and the AI Data Engine16 Installed base, data services, hybrid cloud reach Is AI Data Engine GA in production, and on which hardware?

Table 55.3 — Each vendor's public story predicts its PMs' talking points; counter-questions target the edge of the story.

The steelman for competitors' PMs is real. VAST's PMs can argue that one system for every data type removes integration work Everpure leaves to partners. WEKA's can argue that customers who own their hardware or run in public cloud are a market Everpure's appliance model under-serves. Everpure's PMs answer with operational simplicity and Evergreen economics. Your job is to test where each story stops being true, not to pick a side (Chapter 45).

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text:
Storage product management has moved through three scorecards. In the disk era, PMs competed on IOPS, capacity and price per GB, sold in three-to-five-year forklift cycles. Pure Storage changed the commercial axis: Forever Flash (2014) and Evergreen Storage (2015) turned controller refresh into a subscription entitlement17, and the 2022 relaunch as //Forever, //Flex and //One made consumption terms a PM-owned product18. Since 2023 the AI cycle has added a third axis, partner certification and benchmark position. EXA's MLPerf Storage v3.0 checkpoint write, 877.52 GiB/s on 30 data nodes (vendor-submitted, peer-reviewed, in a round VAST, WEKA and DDN did not enter), is now part of the sales motion19.

The next shift is already visible. Data Intelligence, MCP servers and KV cache all sell to buyers outside the storage team. That requires PMs who can price software separately from arrays and defend a non-storage persona. Watch whether Everpure starts disclosing per-line software metrics (Chapter 25).

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "What were the last three deals you lost, to whom, and on which attribute?" Strong: names competitor, workload and the deciding attribute (certification, per-node throughput, price per usable TB). It also says whether the fix is roadmap, partner or walk away.
  2. "If you got one more engineering team next quarter, where would it go, and what would you stop?" Strong: a ranked choice with the deals or ARR at stake on each side. "Everything is a priority" is a weak answer.
  3. "Which number on your scorecard would you most like to see disclosed, and why isn't it?" Strong: candid about maturity, for example an attach rate not yet stable enough to report.

Questions for an engineer (to test what the PM said)

  1. "Which PM requirement was hardest to build, and what did it cost elsewhere?" Strong: names the displaced feature and the architectural constraint behind it.
  2. "Is the roadmap item the PM mentioned staffed today?" Strong: team size, dependency (NAND die, NIC, NVIDIA software), and the first date that slips.
  3. "Where does telemetry disagree with what sales hears?" Strong: a concrete gap, such as reduction ratios on AI data versus the quoted ratio.

Don't say this:

  • "Which features are on the roadmap?" PMs will not share non-public dates. Ask about trade-offs and gating dependencies instead.
  • "Everpure is NVIDIA-certified, so that's solved." Name the program, level and GPU generation.
  • "Evergreen means free upgrades." Entitlements depend on subscription terms.
  • "Data Intelligence is a storage feature." It targets a different buyer and data beyond Everpure arrays.
  • Quoting "up to 20×" or "10 TB/s" without the baseline. The PM will know you have read only the headline.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• Everpure earnings prepared remarks and 10-K segment discussion: the closest public view of what management rewards.
  • Evergreen//One product guide and SLA briefs: the contractual terms PMs price against.
  • NVIDIA-Certified Storage and SuperPOD storage reference architectures: the gates AI PMs plan around.
  • Chapter 57 for 150 tagged questions, and Chapter 50 for turning answers into a diligence scorecard.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Persona — the buyer or operator a product is designed for.
  • Attach rate — share of customers or deals that also buy a given add-on product.
  • Net dollar retention (NDR) — this year's recurring revenue from last year's customers, divided by last year's.
  • Win/loss review — structured analysis of why deals were won or lost.
  • Design win — a customer's commitment to adopt a technology, with revenue possibly years away.
  • Gating requirement — the one capability without which a deal cannot close.
  • Packaging — how features are bundled into SKUs, tiers and contracts.
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 56. Talking with engineering leaders and the CTO office
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: The storage stack, layer by layer · Distributed-systems fundamentals · Metadata · Purity and DirectFlash · Reading benchmarks critically

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• An architecture review is seven questions in a fixed order: data path, metadata, failure domains, upgrades, scale limits, performance claims, roadmap dependencies. Each answer should carry a mechanism and a number.
  • Good answers are specific and admit limits. They name the bottleneck, the tested (not theoretical) maximum, and the failure that hurts most. Red flags are the reverse: "it scales linearly", "no single point of failure", benchmarks without configurations.
  • Your credibility comes from L2, not from faking L3. Whiteboard the path, do the arithmetic, then ask the engineer to correct you. Engineers forgive "I don't know the on-disk format"; they never forgive a bluff.
  • Your own reasoning has red flags too: GiB read as GB, certification read as ranking, a launch claim read as a published result, and architecture assumed to beat execution.
  • Engage the Office of the CTO with falsifiable 3–5-year theses, each with a signpost and a date, not with "what's next?".

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
Every build, partner or buy decision ends with an engineering judgment: is the target's architecture sound, and could its code meet Purity's quality bar? Engineering leaders give that verdict candidly only to people they respect. If you can trace a write, estimate a rebuild window and spot a cherry-picked benchmark, you get the candid view; otherwise you get the polite one.

The Office of the CTO matters for a different reason: it frames the long bets. Everpure's CTO, Rob Lee, has an official bio that gives a combined technology-and-growth title1 [VERIFY: current title and remit], which suggests technical and commercial strategy sit close together. That is where questions such as "does DirectFlash licensing survive FDP on commodity SSDs?" get argued. Chapter 55 covers PMs; Chapter 50 turns these conversations into a diligence scorecard.

docs.title: The architecture review in seven questions
docs.text:
The order matters: jump to performance before you understand the data path and the slides steer the review.

flowchart TD
    S["Pick one workload and one claim"] --> DP["1. Data path: hops, copies, ack point"]
    DP --> MD["2. Metadata: where it lives, how it scales"]
    MD --> FD["3. Failure domains: blast radius, rebuild time"]
    FD --> UP["4. Upgrades: NDU, mixed versions, rollback"]
    UP --> SL["5. Scale limits: tested vs architectural"]
    SL --> PC["6. Performance claims: config, units, baseline"]
    PC --> RD["7. Roadmap dependencies: NAND, PCIe, CXL, NVIDIA"]
    RD --> V{"Mechanism and number for each?"}
    V -- "Yes" --> OK["Record as L2-verified"]
    V -- "No" --> FU["Follow up, or flag for L3 review"]

Figure 56.1 — Anchor the review in one workload and walk the stack in order; a missing number at any step is the follow-up list.

1. Data path. Ask the engineer to trace one write and one read: how many network hops, how many copies before acknowledgement, and where the acknowledgement happens. In a dual-controller array, a write is acknowledged once it sits in mirrored or shared NVRAM; FlashArray uses chassis NVRAM that both controllers reach (Chapter 14). In FlashBlade//EXA, clients get a layout from the metadata core and then talk to data nodes directly2. In a DASE design, every I/O crosses a back-end fabric, and NVMe over RDMA adds roughly 5–15 µs per access3. Hops set the latency floor; copies set the bandwidth tax.

2. Metadata. Where does it live (DRAM, NVRAM, SCM, flash)? How is it partitioned, and what happens with a single hot directory? AI checkpointing makes this concrete. If 16,384 ranks each write one shard file into one directory, that is 16,384 creates in a burst. A design that serialises them on one directory lock turns a bandwidth problem into a metadata stall (Chapter 21).

3. Failure domains. What is the largest unit that can fail together: a drive, a node, an enclosure, a rack? How long until full redundancy returns? Worked example: a 300 TB DirectFlash Module at 80% full holds 240 TB. At a 2 GB/s rebuild rate, restoring it takes 240,000 GB ÷ 2 GB/s = 120,000 s ≈ 33 hours. Declustered across the array at 10 GB/s, it takes about 6.7 hours. Ask which of the two the system achieves under production load.

4. Upgrades and NDU. Non-disruptive upgrade is a Purity signature. Pure Storage reported more than 7,000 non-disruptive controller upgrades for over 2,700 customers between 2015 and mid-20214. The questions that matter for a target are how long mixed-version clusters are supported, what can be rolled back, and what an upgrade costs in performance while one controller or node is out.

5. Scale limits. Separate the architectural maximum from the tested and supported one. NetApp's AFX is a clean example: a design maximum of 128 controllers5, with 32 supported in an early ONTAP release, per WWT6. Neither number is wrong, but only the second belongs in a deal model.

6. Performance claims. Ask for configuration, units and baseline. EXA's MLPerf Storage v3.0 checkpoint write of 877.52 GiB/s on 30 data nodes7 is about 942 GB/s, or roughly 31 GB/s per node. That is a vendor-submitted, peer-reviewed result with a published configuration. The ">10 TB/s" figure at launch came from preliminary testing, not a published configuration8. Both came from the same vendor, but they carry very different weight (Chapter 37).

7. Roadmap dependencies. Which outside roadmaps does the plan assume? NAND density sets module capacity: DFMs reached 300 TB, released in 2025 according to the FY26 10-K as read via search summary9, while the steps to 600 TB and 1 PB are undated. PCIe 6.0 doubles drive-link bandwidth to about 29.5 GB/s per x4 direction (64 GT/s × 4 lanes ÷ 8, less flit overhead), but front-end networking usually binds first (Chapter 12). CXL matters for controller memory, not for flash. NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX, launched in March 2026, could move storage services onto a DPU10. The sharp question is which dependency is single-sourced, and what happens if it slips a year.

Semiconductor bridge. This is a chip design review: dataflow, tag and directory structures, redundancy, field-upgradable firmware, characterised versus simulated corners, datasheet versus silicon, and process and IP dependencies.

docs.title: Good answers and red flags
docs.text:
Topic A good answer sounds like Red flag in the target Red flag in your own reasoning Data path "Two hops, two NVRAM copies, ack after both persist" "It's all RDMA, so latency isn't an issue" Treating fewer hops as always better, ignoring copy and reduction cost Metadata "Hash-partitioned; one hot directory caps at N creates/s, here's why" "Metadata is distributed, so it scales" Assuming metadata scales with data nodes Failure domains "Enclosure loss is survivable; rebuild is about 6 h at 80% fill under load" "No single point of failure" with no rebuild time Counting nines without correlated failures Upgrades "Mixed versions supported for N releases; rollback within one" "Upgrades are seamless" with no rollback story Assuming NDU on arrays carries over to an acquired codebase Scale limits "Tested to 30 nodes; architecture allows more; we'd re-test past 60" "Linear scaling" with no tested ceiling Using the design maximum in a deal model Performance "Config, client count, units and baseline are in the report" Multipliers ("20×") without baseline Reading GiB/s as GB/s, or certification as a ranking Roadmap "If PCIe 6.0 NICs slip, we lose X but ship Y" Every dependency described as "on track" Assuming architecture beats execution Team "Three people know the allocator; here's the succession plan" Key-person risk denied Rating code you have not seen

Table 56.1 — Good answers carry a number and a limit; the last column is the mistake you make, not the target.

The last column matters most in diligence, where self-inflicted errors are usually arithmetic. GiB is about 7% larger than GB. NVIDIA certification sets a throughput floor, roughly 0.5 GB/s of read per GPU at the SuperPOD B200 enhanced tier, not a ranking11.

docs.title: The credibility ladder
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    L1["L1 Vocabulary"] --> L2["L2 Mechanism"] --> L3["L3 Implementation"]
    L1 --- B1["Uses terms correctly; asks what a term means in their system"]
    L2 --- B2["Whiteboards the path, does the arithmetic, invites correction"]
    L3 --- B3["Ask about it; never assert it"]
    L3 -.- X["Bluff zone: claiming code-level knowledge"]
    classDef target fill:#56B4E9,stroke:#0072B2,color:#222222
    classDef danger fill:#F0E442,stroke:#D55E00,color:#222222
    class L2,B2 target
    class X danger

Figure 56.2 — Operate at L2 and treat L3 as territory you ask about; credibility collapses the moment you assert an implementation detail you cannot defend.

L2 behaviour has a recognisable script. Draw your understanding, put a number on it, and hand over the marker: "My mental model is a log-structured layout with a global FTL, so write amplification should sit well below a standard SSD's. Where is that wrong for your system?" At L3, the move is a precise question: "Is the dedup index in controller DRAM or paged from flash?" Never offer an opinion on code paths. Engineers spot bluffs by vague adjectives and borrowed numbers.

docs.title: Ten whiteboard prompts
docs.text:
# Prompt Expected sketch What it tests 1 Trace a 4 KB write on a dual-controller array Host → primary controller → mirrored or shared NVRAM → ack → later flush and reduction to flash Ack point, mirroring 2 Trace a read on FlashBlade//EXA Client gets layout from metadata core, then RDMA reads directly from data nodes Metadata/data split 3 Compare DASE, shared-nothing and EXA Three boxes-and-arrows: shared media, owner nodes, direct-to-data-node Who owns data, hop counts 4 Show where the FTL lives: SSD vs DFM Per-drive FTL and DRAM vs one global FTL in Purity over raw NAND DirectFlash thesis 5 Rebuild a failed module Stripe layout, survivors read in parallel, rebuild time = data ÷ aggregate rate Failure-domain arithmetic 6 Size a checkpoint write Model state ÷ target stall window = GB/s; then GB/s per node Burst sizing 7 Draw the KV-cache hierarchy HBM → host DRAM → local NVMe → shared flash tier, with capacity and bandwidth per tier Inference tiering 8 Walk a non-disruptive controller swap Fail over to partner, replace, resync, fail back; performance during the window NDU mechanics 9 Show a checkpoint create storm Thousands of ranks → one directory → lock or partition → creates/s Metadata scaling 10 Draw the GPU-direct path Storage → NIC → GPU memory via RDMA, bypassing CPU bounce buffers GDS, PCIe topology

Table 56.2 — If you can draw these ten in under two minutes each, you can hold an L2 conversation with any Everpure engineering team.

docs.title: Engaging the Office of the CTO
docs.text:
The CTO office thinks in three-to-five-year bets, so bring theses, not questions about next quarter. A useful thesis has four parts: a claim, a mechanism, a signpost and a date. For example: "FDP on standard QLC SSDs narrows DirectFlash's write-amplification lead by 2028, so the remaining moat is density and watts per TB. The signpost is FDP adoption in hyperscaler procurement specs." Then ask what would prove it wrong.

Good bets to bring, all grounded in public signals:

  • HDD displacement. In 2023 a Pure executive predicted no new hard drives would be sold after 202812. Analysts disputed it13. Ask what share of hyperscaler nearline capacity DirectFlash can realistically displace, and at what HDD capacity point the argument fails (Chapter 53).
  • DPU-resident storage. If BlueField-4 STX makes the controller a commodity, which Purity services move to the DPU, and which stay on x86?
  • Memory tiers. Does CXL-attached memory belong inside controllers for dedup and metadata, or as a KV-cache tier?
  • Benchmarks as strategy. VAST, WEKA and DDN did not submit to MLPerf Storage v3.014, although DDN and WEKA entered earlier rounds and VAST never has (Chapter 37). Does public, peer-reviewed benchmarking stay a differentiator, or do POCs decide?

docs.title: How Everpure approaches it vs. competitors
docs.text:
What an engineering organisation publishes determines what you can verify before a meeting.

Vendor How engineering speaks publicly Evidence you can check What to test (from public evidence or in formal diligence) Everpure Peer-reviewed design paper (Purity, SIGMOD 2015)15; peer-reviewed MLPerf v3.0 submissions7 Paper, MLPerf configurations, technical briefs Data-node protection on EXA; FDP response VAST Data Architecture white papers; independent HPC benchmarking (PDSW'21)16 White papers, third-party lab studies Fabric and enclosure blast radius WEKA Microservices re-architecture as NeuralMesh (2025)17 Cloud marketplace deployments Operational burden on customer-owned hardware DDN Lustre stewardship since acquiring it from Intel in 201818 Open-source Lustre code, HPC site reports Code sharing between EXAScaler and Infinia

Table 56.3 — Public engineering evidence varies by vendor; in diligence, weight what you can verify above what you are told.

Steelman the alternatives. VAST's engineers can argue that shared media makes global data reduction and wide erasure codes natural, which EXA's split design must work harder to match. Everpure's strongest engineering argument is maturity: one OS hardened across a large installed base, with a published design rationale.

docs.title: History and trajectory
docs.text: Review questions have shifted with each media era: RAID rebuild windows and seek-bound IOPS for disk; write amplification and endurance for flash, which Purity's log-structured design addressed15; software and network latency for NVMe-oF; GPU-direct paths, metadata storms and incast for AI. The next shift is already under way: storage services moving onto DPUs, as with BlueField-4 STX in March 202610, and memory tiers spanning HBM to shared flash for KV cache (Chapter 32).

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Questions for a PM

  1. "Which engineering constraint most often forces you to defer a requirement?" Strong: names it (controller memory, metadata core count, certification cycle) and a deal it cost.
  2. "Which competitor claims do your engineers dispute most, and with what evidence?" Strong: a specific claim plus an internal or third-party test.
  3. "Which roadmap item depends on an outside vendor's schedule?" Strong: the dependency (NAND die, NIC, NVIDIA software) and the fallback.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Trace the write path for me, and tell me where I've drawn it wrong." Strong: corrects specifics such as ack point and copy count, then volunteers the bottleneck.
  2. "What failure took longest to diagnose in the field last year?" Strong: a real incident, its root cause and the fix that went into the code or the process.
  3. "What is the tested limit, and what breaks first past it?" Strong: a number plus the first resource to saturate (metadata, fabric ports, controller memory).

Don't say this:

  • "It scales linearly." Ask for the tested ceiling and efficiency; EXA's 10-to-30-node scaling worked out to about 89%, not 100% (Chapter 27).
  • "No single point of failure, so it's safe." Ask about correlated failures: firmware batches, enclosures, power domains.
  • "877 GB/s." It is 877 GiB/s, about 942 GB/s.
  • "CXL will replace flash for this." CXL is memory at DRAM economics.
  • Any claim about code you have not read.

docs.title: Going deeper (optional, L3 pointers)
docs.text:
• Colgrove et al., SIGMOD 2015, on Purity's log-structured, highly available design15.
  • MLPerf Storage v3.0 submission configurations, to practise reading performance claims14.
  • Chapter 20 on consensus and failure models; Chapter 57 for the full question bank.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Architecture review — a structured walk through a system's data path, metadata, failure domains, upgrades, limits, claims and dependencies.
  • Acknowledgement point — the moment a storage system tells the host a write is durable.
  • Blast radius — the data or service affected when one component fails.
  • Tested limit — the largest configuration a vendor has validated and supports, as opposed to the architectural maximum.
  • Credibility ladder — the progression from vocabulary (L1) through mechanism (L2) to implementation (L3).
  • See the glossary for the rest.

docs.title: 57. Question bank: 150 questions
docs.text: Depth: L2 · Reading time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: Talking with product managers · Talking with engineering leaders and the CTO office

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• 150 questions in 14 topics, each tagged by audience, distilled from every chapter's playbook and the staged ASK lines.
  • Bring five to seven to a meeting: one audience, one goal (Figure 57.4).
  • Strong answers carry a number, its conditions and its baseline. Forty-one "Listen for" notes show what to expect.
  • Differentiating questions sit on DirectFlash versus FDP, EXA versus shared media, and NVIDIA's context tier.
  • These are for colleagues. Many ask for internal telemetry; never use them to fish for competitors' non-public data.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text: A new strategy hire is judged by the questions they ask. "How fast is rebuild?" marks a tourist; "time to full redundancy at 80% fill, under load?" earns an engineer's respect and a number for the model. Most questions also transfer to diligence on a target (Chapter 50).

docs.title: 1. Media and NAND
docs.text:
1. [PM] At today's flash premium, which workloads still convert from disk? ↳ Listen for: binding constraint per segment, break-even premium (Ch 52).
  2. [PM] How much NAND inflation is passed through versus absorbed?
  3. [CTO] Does owning raw NAND management let us adopt PLC first?
  4. [Eng] How do you manage read disturb on read-mostly AI data?
  5. [Eng] What does PLC cost the write path and endurance budget?
  6. [Eng] How long does qualifying a new NAND die take?
  7. [CTO] Which components are single-sourced, and what did Optane teach?
  8. [PM] How many quarters does the strategic NAND buy cover? ↳ Listen for: prepaid-versus-inventory split, contract-price assumption (Ch 48).
  9. [SE] Where disk was unavailable, did QLC win on availability?
  10. [Eng] What does a layer jump do to DFM cost per TB?

docs.title: 2. SSD and DirectFlash
docs.text:
1. [Eng] What field write amplification does Purity see on QLC? ↳ Listen for: measured ranges by workload, converted to DWPD headroom (Ch 3).
  2. [CTO] If FDP goes mainstream, which DirectFlash advantages survive? ↳ Listen for: concedes the WAF gap; quantifies DRAM avoided and W/TB (Ch 26).
  3. [Eng] Without module DRAM, where does the map live, per PB?
  4. [PM] When 512 TB standard SSDs ship, what keeps DFMs ahead?
  5. [Eng] How are LDPC read retries kept off the latency tail?
  6. [Eng] What is the blast radius of a DFM firmware bug?
  7. [PM] Why does FlashArray//ST use commercial SSDs?
  8. [SE] How do we explain usable-per-raw-TB against SSD-based arrays? ↳ Listen for: over-provisioning, reserve, parity and reduction separated (Ch 3).
  9. [Eng] How much raw NAND per effective TB do we save?
  10. [CTO] Could a hyperscaler licensee internalise the global FTL? ↳ Listen for: what keeps it dependent, and the AWS Nitro precedent (Ch 13).
  11. [PM] What limits 600 TB modules: dies, packaging, power or rebuild?

docs.title: 3. Protocols and networking
docs.text:
1. [PM] What is the host-attach mix, and how fast is NVMe/TCP growing?
  2. [Eng] What is the NVMe/TCP versus RoCE gap at QD1 and saturation?
  3. [Eng] What are NVMe-oF connection limits with thousands of Kubernetes hosts?
  4. [PM] Why pNFS for EXA, and what does it cost us? ↳ Listen for: no kernel module; candour on shared-file writes (Ch 8).
  5. [SE] Which distros and kernels does the EXA client support?
  6. [Eng] A data node fails mid-write: what happens to in-flight I/O?
  7. [PM] Is S3 over RDMA generally available, and cuObject-compatible?
  8. [Eng] In S3 over RDMA, how are tokens scoped without TLS?
  9. [SE] What happens to RoCE on a lossy fabric without PFC?
  10. [Eng] How do our storage ports absorb synchronized checkpoint incast?
  11. [PM] How often does an InfiniBand compute fabric cost us deals?
  12. [CTO] How would our RDMA protocols map onto Ultra Ethernet?

docs.title: 4. Architecture
docs.text:
1. [Eng] Walk a 4 KB write: persistence point and per-layer p99? ↳ Listen for: NVRAM persistence point (mirrored or shared), per-layer microseconds (Ch 13).
  2. [PM] What does a customer lose during an Evergreen controller swap?
  3. [Eng] Under Purity Turbo, how does the secondary's read cache stay coherent?
  4. [PM] When a block customer outgrows one //XL, what do we sell?
  5. [Eng] Is the next FlashArray ceiling CPU, memory, PCIe or NVRAM?
  6. [PM] Where does EXA beat shared-media designs, and where not? ↳ Listen for: throughput, GPU-count and namespace thresholds; credit to VAST (Ch 16).
  7. [Eng] How many fabric crossings precede an EXA write acknowledgement?
  8. [Eng] An EXA data node dies mid-checkpoint: what do clients see? ↳ Listen for: protection scheme, degraded-throughput percentage, rebuild time (Ch 27).
  9. [Eng] 16,384 ranks create files in one directory: what happens? ↳ Listen for: directory hashing, lock granularity, creates/s at p99 (Ch 21).
  10. [CTO] Is the metadata/data split permanent, or could shared media return?
  11. [Eng] Which services run consensus, and what stalls without quorum?
  12. [SE] A neocloud says "we'll run Ceph": what's our TCO counter? ↳ Listen for: staff, rebuild windows, free-space reserve, watts per usable TB (Ch 15).

docs.title: 5. Data services and protection
docs.text:
1. [PM] What are fleet median reduction ratios by workload? ↳ Listen for: distributions excluding thin provisioning; candour on AI data (Ch 5).
  2. [Eng] How big is the dedupe index per PB, and where?
  3. [Eng] When does inline reduction defer, and for how long?
  4. [Eng] What read amplification does similarity encoding add?
  5. [SE] How does the Right-Size Guarantee treat irreducible data?
  6. [Eng] A large DFM dies at 80% fill: time to full redundancy? ↳ Listen for: hours under load, host impact, declustered or not (Ch 6).
  7. [Eng] What if ActiveCluster's mediator and link fail together?
  8. [Eng] What stops stolen credentials shortening SafeMode retention? ↳ Listen for: out-of-band authentication, multiple approvers, audit trail (Ch 6).
  9. [PM] In ransomware recovery, how much of the RTO is storage?
  10. [CTO] What is in the denominator of our six nines?

docs.title: 6. Everpure products
docs.text:
1. [PM] Where does //ST win deals that //XL190 would lose?
  2. [PM] What share of EXA pipeline awaits DFM nodes or certification? ↳ Listen for: enterprise and neocloud gates, each with a date (Ch 27).
  3. [Eng] How are EXA data nodes protected today?
  4. [SE] Who beats FlashBlade//E, and on what metric?
  5. [PM] For VMs moving to KubeVirt, where does Portworx win?
  6. [Eng] What does Portworx lose on non-Everpure disks?
  7. [PM] Is Fusion adoption "enabled" or "presets in production"? ↳ Listen for: turned-on versus automating, tied to renewal (Ch 28).
  8. [Eng] How does Fusion pick an array for a workload?
  9. [SE] If Pure1 and Fusion are unreachable, what still works?
  10. [CTO] What may an agent do via MCP without human approval? ↳ Listen for: read-only defaults, scoped credentials, approval gates (Ch 22).
  11. [PM] What share of Sev-1 cases does Pure1 open first?
  12. [CTO] Which Purity code came from acquisitions, and how much was rewritten?

docs.title: 7. Platform, Evergreen and consumption
docs.text:
1. [PM] What is Evergreen//One gross margin by contract year? ↳ Listen for: early hardware drag, later payback, utilization assumption (Ch 23).
  2. [PM] How much deployed headroom sits idle, at whose cost?
  3. [CTO] What happens to //One margin when reduction underdelivers?
  4. [PM] How is //One capacity growth priced after NAND inflation? ↳ Listen for: exposure first, then repricing and density offsets (Ch 48).
  5. [PM] Why do customers pick Evergreen//Forever over //One?
  6. [Eng] What breaks non-disruptive upgrades at generation boundaries?
  7. [Eng] Is consumption metered on provisioned, written or effective capacity?
  8. [SE] Which //One SLAs fail at dark sites?
  9. [Eng] Is the watts-per-TiB guarantee measured or modelled?
  10. [CTO] Does subscription reweight the roadmap toward density and watts?

docs.title: 8. AI training and checkpointing
docs.text:
1. [PM] In lost training deals, how was checkpointing specified? ↳ Listen for: framework, checkpoint size, burst versus time-to-resume (Ch 31).
  2. [Eng] For a ~6 TB checkpoint, how long are GPUs blocked?
  3. [Eng] Cold 16K-rank restore: opens/s, GB/s, time to first step? ↳ Listen for: metadata and data separated; slowest-client tail (Ch 31).
  4. [Eng] Why was EXA's MLPerf v3.0 checkpoint read below write?1 ↳ Listen for: cache-clear rule, client DRAM, bottleneck named (Ch 37).
  5. [SE] Which tool turns model size and GPU count into EXA nodes?
  6. [SE] How do we size for async checkpointing to local NVMe? ↳ Listen for: drain rate, restore bandwidth, retention, not peak write (Ch 31).
  7. [CTO] As async checkpointing spreads, where does differentiation move?
  8. [Eng] What happens when billions of small files reshuffle each epoch?
  9. [PM] Why enter MLPerf checkpointing and KV cache, but not training?

docs.title: 9. Inference and KV cache
docs.text:
1. [PM] What baseline sits behind PureKVA's 20× TTFT claim?2 ↳ Listen for: model, context, concurrency; recompute or local NVMe (Ch 32).
  2. [Eng] What GB/s per GPU and p99 per block at 1,000 sessions?
  3. [Eng] Is our NIXL backend upstream, and which plugin path?
  4. [Eng] What happens to cached KV when weights change?
  5. [CTO] Versus NVIDIA CMX: supplier, tier behind it, or rival?3 ↳ Listen for: a position per deal type, value beyond flash (Ch 34).
  6. [PM] Price a KV tier per TB, per GB-hour or per token?
  7. [Eng] Does DeepReduce shrink fp8 KV tensors at all?
  8. [SE] How do we answer DDN's and WEKA's KV-cache multiples? ↳ Listen for: baseline, context and concurrency normalised first (Ch 44).
  9. [PM] Does PureKVA ride existing FlashBlade deals?
  10. [Eng] Where does a KV fetch's latency budget break first?

docs.title: 10. RAG and data intelligence
docs.text:
1. [PM] In RAG on FlashBlade, where does the vector index live?
  2. [Eng] How does a billion-vector DiskANN index perform on FlashBlade?
  3. [PM] Which engines run Iceberg on FlashBlade in production?
  4. [Eng] Can random Lance reads and Parquet scans share a bucket?
  5. [PM] What share of Data Intelligence covers non-Everpure data?4 ↳ Listen for: a number, named estates, separate pricing (Ch 39).
  6. [PM] Who buys Data Intelligence, and who carries quota?
  7. [CTO] Catalog of record, or neutral feeder to Unity Catalog? ↳ Listen for: an explicit choice; coexistence without rip-out (Ch 33).
  8. [Eng] How does the MCP server handle identity and revocation?
  9. [Eng] Is classification on the write path or off it?
  10. [CTO] Is agent memory a storage workload beyond KV cache?

docs.title: 11. NVIDIA and ecosystem
docs.text:
1. [PM] Beyond NVCS validation, what gates EXA's NCP and SuperPOD certification? ↳ Listen for: level, GPU generation, gating tests, waiting deals (Ch 34).
  2. [SE] What headroom over SuperPOD storage sizing, and what limits it?
  3. [Eng] What did certification skip that production hits?
  4. [CTO] Which Purity services fit on a BlueField-4 DPU? ↳ Listen for: data path versus metadata and dedupe; memory limits (Ch 53).

docs.text:
Questions for a PM (follow-ups to any answer)

  1. "What's the denominator?" Strong: population, period, exclusions.
  2. "Against what baseline?" Strong: recompute, disk, or a named rival.
  3. "Which deals did it decide?" Strong: counts, not anecdotes.

Questions for an engineer

  1. "Under what conditions?" Strong: fill, load, failure state.
  2. "What saturates first?" Strong: one resource, one number.
  3. "What if it fails halfway?" Strong: recovery path and client view.

Don't say this:

  • Reading questions verbatim from a list.
  • Accepting a number without its conditions.
  • Treating "we don't measure that" as evasion; it may be the finding.

docs.title: 58. Explain it in 30 seconds
docs.text: Depth: L1 · Reading time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: None; each line links to its source chapter.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Use these 66 one-liners when a CFO or director asks "what is X, and why care?"
  • Four beats: what it is, why it matters, one number, what it means for us.
  • Quote only sourced, dated numbers; flag private-vendor figures as company-stated.
  • Keep the trade-off. "Flash costs ~18× more per terabyte yet wins on density" beats "flash is better."
  • Memorise the eight numbers at the end.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text: Corporate development carries the technology story to people who approve capital, and they give each concept half a minute. Everpure (NYSE: P, formerly PSTG) is hard to explain: its value sits in software (Purity), its own flash module (DirectFlash), a business model (Evergreen) and hyperscaler licensing, none visible from the hardware.

docs.title: Media and economics
docs.text:
1. Flash vs disk. Chips versus spinning platters. Flash wins speed, power and space; disk wins cold-data price (Ch 2).
  2. Flash price premium. Enterprise SSDs cost ~18.6× disk per terabyte in Q3 2026, up from ~10× in 20201, so flash sells on density (Ch 53).
  3. NAND. The chip inside every SSD. Five suppliers earned $68.87B in 2Q262, and also sell competing drives (Ch 48).
  4. NAND cycle. Forecasts compound to ~4.7× mid-2025 contract prices by 4Q263. Revenue inflates first; margins recover later (Ch 48).
  5. QLC. Four bits per cell: cheapest flash, but less durable. Purity makes it work by writing large sequential chunks (Ch 2).
  6. Data reduction. Deduplication and compression multiply usable capacity. Purity averages ~5:14; AI data barely shrinks (Ch 5).
  7. Raw, usable, effective. Three prices: before protection, after it, and after assumed reduction. Compare like with like (Ch 4).
  8. Watts. AI sites are power-capped, so storage watts displace GPUs. A rack of the largest SSDs holds ~5× the petabytes of a disk rack, at 2–3× the power (Ch 38).

docs.title: How storage systems work
docs.text:
1. Block, file, object. Blocks for databases, folders for people, keys for cloud and AI; each has its own buyer (Ch 1).
  2. Array. A computer that pools, protects and serves drives over a network; customers really pay for its software (Ch 13).
  3. Dual controller. Two servers share drives, so either can fail without downtime, as in FlashArray (Ch 14).
  4. Scale-out. Add boxes rather than enlarge one. It reaches petabytes but loads the network (Ch 15).
  5. Disaggregation. Buy engines and fuel tanks separately. VAST pioneered it; rivals now ship versions (Ch 16).
  6. Parallel file system. One lookup, then clients read from many servers at once. Lustre runs over 60% of the Top5005 (Ch 17).
  7. Metadata. The card catalogue: names, folders, permissions. AI's millions of small files make it the usual bottleneck (Ch 21).
  8. Erasure coding. Parity math that survives drive failures: eight-plus-two costs 25% extra capacity, a mirror 100% (Ch 6).
  9. Immutable snapshots. Copies even an administrator cannot delete, so ransomware victims restore instead of paying (Ch 6).
  10. Synchronous replication. Every write lands at two sites first, so a site loss loses nothing; distance limits it to metros (Ch 6).
  11. "Eleven nines." A modelled durability figure, not a measurement. Correlated failures are what actually lose data (Ch 20).
  12. Non-disruptive upgrade. Swapping controllers while data keeps flowing: the engineering behind Evergreen (Ch 14).
  13. Control plane. Fleet-management software. More systems reporting telemetry predict more failures, so the moat compounds (Ch 22).

docs.title: Protocols and networks
docs.text:
1. Protocol. The language servers and storage speak; it decides which buyers a product reaches (Ch 7).
  2. NVMe. The protocol built for flash, with thousands of parallel queues. It replaced SCSI as the speed standard (Ch 7).
  3. NVMe over Fabrics. NVMe across a network, so shared flash feels local; the TCP version is becoming the default (Ch 7).
  4. NFS and pNFS. NFS is Linux's file language; pNFS reads many servers in parallel. FlashBlade//EXA uses it to avoid special clients (Ch 8).
  5. S3. Amazon's object interface, now the standard. AWS S3 holds over 500 trillion objects6 (Ch 9).
  6. RDMA. Network cards copying memory between machines, skipping the CPU, to keep GPUs fed (Ch 10).
  7. Ethernet vs InfiniBand. Ethernet took over two-thirds of AI back-end switch sales in 20257, favouring vendors built on standard networks (Ch 10).
  8. DPU. A network card that runs storage software. NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX named 12 storage partners, Everpure included8 (Ch 34).

docs.title: AI and storage
docs.text:
1. Storage for AI. Keeping GPUs busy. At about $2–6 per GPU-hour910, an idle 1,024-GPU cluster burns ~$0.6–1.7 a second (Ch 11).
  2. "AI storage." At least eight workloads, from bulk ingest to inference. Ask vendors which stage they actually win (Ch 30).
  3. Checkpoint. Saving the game. A 405B-parameter model's state is ~6.5 TB; saving it in a minute needs ~108 GB/s (Ch 31).
  4. Failure rate. Meta's Llama 3 run had 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days11, so fast restores protect GPU spend (Ch 31).
  5. GPUDirect Storage. Data straight into GPU memory; nearly every vendor claims it, so it no longer differentiates (Ch 11).
  6. KV cache. The AI's short-term memory: ~43 GB per long session on a 70B model12, so fleets reach petabytes (Ch 32).
  7. Context memory. NVIDIA's new flash tier between GPU memory and shared storage; every vendor wants to supply it (Ch 53).
  8. RAG. AI looking up company documents before answering, turning storage into search and governance (Ch 33).
  9. Agents and MCP. Agents need findable, permitted data. MCP passed 10,000 servers13, turning metadata into a product (Ch 39).
  10. NVIDIA certification. NVIDIA's approved-vendor list: absence usually means no deal, but it proves a floor, not a ranking (Ch 34).
  11. Neocloud. A GPU-specialist cloud; CoreWeave guides 2026 capex to $35–39B14. The largest disclosed storage contract is about 1% a year of a neocloud's capex, yet storage can idle every GPU (Ch 35).
  12. MLPerf Storage. A peer-reviewed benchmark with simulated GPUs. EXA led v3.0 checkpoint writes at 877.5 GiB/s15 (read was 588 GiB/s); VAST, WEKA and DDN skipped the round16 (Ch 37).

docs.title: Everpure's model
docs.text:
1. FlashArray and FlashBlade. Block for databases and VMs; file and object at scale. Both run Purity (Ch 27).
  2. Purity. Everpure's storage operating system. It writes like a database log, which makes cheap flash last (Ch 26).
  3. DirectFlash. Raw flash modules run by Purity, without SSD controllers. Modules reach 300 TB17 versus 245.76 TB for standard SSDs18 (Ch 26).
  4. Evergreen. Hardware refreshes in place, without migration; over 10,000 such upgrades by 202219 anchor retention (Ch 23).
  5. Evergreen//One. Storage on a utility bill; Everpure owns the hardware. It lowers reported growth while raising contracted revenue (Ch 23).
  6. ARR and RPO. Subscription ARR $2.13B (+20%) and RPO $4.1B (+44%) at Q2 FY2720: the recurring base under the hardware (Ch 29).
  7. Hyperscaler licensing. Hyperscalers license DirectFlash and buy their own NAND. Meta passed 2 EB in FY2621; a second signed August 202617 (Ch 29).
  8. FlashBlade//EXA. Purity runs metadata, third-party servers hold data, clients use standard pNFS: Everpure's AI-scale answer to VAST and WEKA (Ch 27).
  9. Pure1 and Fusion. Fleet analytics and policy control. Fusion passed 1,200 customers22, moving switching costs into software (Ch 28).
  10. Portworx and 1touch. Kubernetes storage, and data classification bought for $125.0M23. Both bet on selling software above the array (Ch 28).
  11. Margin squeeze. Q2 FY27 non-GAAP product margin was 66.2% versus 74.9% for subscription24; strategic NAND and component purchases made Q2 free cash flow −$238M25 (Ch 29).
  12. The rename. A bid for a data-platform valuation while revenue is still mostly arrays (Ch 25).

docs.title: Competition
docs.text:
1. Market share. In 2Q26: Dell 23.8%, Huawei 11.3%, NetApp 9.6%, Everpure 8.1%, HPE 6.8%26. One share point is a big year (Ch 40).
  2. Incumbents. Dell, NetApp and HPE win on installed base, channel and server bundles. Their weakness is pre-AI software estates (Ch 46).
  3. VAST. The AI-native leader, valued at $30B27 on over $500M committed ARR (company-stated)28. Its $1.17B CoreWeave deal29 anchors the segment (Ch 42).
  4. WEKA. Software-only parallel file system, last valued at $1.6B in 202430. Early in KV cache, smaller than its profile (Ch 43).
  5. DDN. The Lustre incumbent inside NVIDIA's own supercomputers; Blackstone invested at a $5B valuation31 (Ch 44).
  6. Hyperscaler self-build. At their volume, building beats buying arrays; they buy parts and IP, Everpure's licensing seam (Ch 36).
  7. Hammerspace. A namespace layer above everyone's arrays. If it wins, arrays look interchangeable (Ch 47).

docs.title: Market and financial dynamics
docs.text:
1. Market size. IDC's external storage market was $33.0B in 202532, branded arrays only; hyperscaler self-builds sit outside (Ch 40).
  2. Price-led growth. The market grew 33.6% in 2Q2633, mostly flash costs passing through, not more capacity (Ch 40).
  3. AI storage TAM. No credible figure. Storage is 2.4% of IDC's AI infrastructure spend34; the atlas estimates ~$9–25B for 2026 (Ch 40).

docs.title: Future
docs.text:
1. Bigger drives. 512 TB SSDs are on 2027 roadmaps35. Rebuild time and watts become the limits (Ch 53).
  2. Disk's future. Not dying: Western Digital targets 100 TB drives by 202936. Disk keeps cold bulk (Ch 53).
  3. Where value moves. Up into data services and down into the network; the box matters less (Ch 53).

docs.title: Conversation playbook
docs.text:
Three questions for a PM

  1. "Explain your product to our CFO in one sentence." Strong: buyer, problem and one dated number, with no adjectives.
  2. "Which board question worries you most?" Strong: names a real gap, such as EXA's pending NCP certification, and the plan.
  3. "Which number belongs on one slide?" Strong: a customer outcome, not a peak benchmark.

Three questions for an engineer

  1. "What do skeptics get wrong about DirectFlash?" Strong: system-level, not datasheet, gains.
  2. "Where does my disaggregation one-liner break?" Strong: fabric and minimum size.
  3. "Is the KV-cache opportunity storage or memory?" Strong: only cache not being decoded can leave GPU memory, so it is a bandwidth tier.

Don't say this:

  • "Flash is cheaper than disk." Not per raw terabyte in 2026.
  • "We're #1 in MLPerf." Say first among those who entered.
  • "AI storage is a $50B market." Nothing credible supports that.
  • "Evergreen means free upgrades." It is a paid subscription.

docs.title: 59. Self-test: 279 flashcards
docs.text: Depth: L1–L2 · Reading time: ~54 min · Last verified: 2026-11-01 Prerequisites: None to start, but the deck pays off most after a first pass through Parts 1–7. Begin with What storage does; pair it with the Question bank and Explain it in 30 seconds.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• This chapter is a deck, not a reading. 279 cards (Q1–Q279), one per <details> block, grouped by Part plus a mixed strategy set. Read the question, say the answer out loud, then click to check.
  • Two depths. 111 untagged L1 cards test vocabulary ("can you define it?"); 168 cards tagged "(L2)" test mechanism and trade-off ("can you say why?"). Credibility with engineers comes from the L2 cards.
  • Use spaced repetition, not rereading. Sort cards into three boxes: missed (review daily), shaky (every three days), solid (weekly). A card moves up a box when you get it right and back to box 1 when you miss it.
  • Two weeks gets you conversation-ready. The schedule below covers every card in the first five days, then spends nine days on misses, interleaved Parts and a timed 50-card mixed test.
  • Misses are a map. Every answer ends with the chapter it came from. Three misses from one chapter mean reread that chapter, not drill the cards.

docs.title: Why this matters for Everpure strategy
docs.text:
A strategy hire is judged in the first few meetings by whether they can follow a PM or an engineer without stopping them for definitions. Product managers talk in Evergreen tiers, R-generations, Fusion presets and STaaS TCV. Engineers talk in write amplification, ANA paths, erasure-code geometry and KV-cache tiers. The Office of the CTO talks in trade-offs: why DirectFlash beats FDP SSDs, why EXA uses pNFS instead of a proprietary client, why a 300 TB module changes rebuild risk. Recognising a term is not the same as being able to use it under time pressure, and these cards train recall, which is the skill a meeting tests.

The deck also guards against the most expensive mistake an outsider can make: repeating a vendor claim as fact. Many L2 cards end with a qualifier, such as "company-stated", "against a no-cache baseline" or "in a round the strongest rivals skipped". The point is to remember the claim and its caveat together, which is how Everpure's own engineers will talk about VAST, WEKA and DDN, and how they expect a strategy colleague to talk about Everpure.

docs.title: How the deck is built
docs.text:
Every card was written from the chapter it links to: its TL;DR, its core-concept explanations and its "Numbers that matter" table. No card adds a fact the atlas does not already contain. Where a chapter labels a figure company-stated, worked example or illustrative, the card keeps the label. Numbers are therefore only as current as the atlas's last-verified date (2026-11-01). Financial, market-share and benchmark cards go stale fastest (see History and trajectory).

The split is roughly 40% L1 and 60% L2. An L1 card has one right answer, usually a definition or a list. An L2 card asks why or what follows, and a good answer names a mechanism, a number and a consequence. Score yourself strictly on L2: an answer that gets the mechanism right but not the consequence counts as a miss.

docs.title: Scoring an L2 answer
docs.text:
L1 cards are right or wrong. L2 cards need a rubric, because a half-right answer is the kind that sounds fine in a meeting and fails under one follow-up question.

Element Full credit Partial credit Example Mechanism Names the cause, e.g. "decode rereads the whole cache per token" Names the topic only, e.g. "KV is big" Q170 Number Gives the chapter's figure with its unit and basis Right order of magnitude, wrong basis Q163 Consequence Says what it means for a buyer or for Everpure Stops at the mechanism Q134 Qualifier Keeps "company-stated", "illustrative" or "among entrants" Drops the caveat Q143

Figure 59.5 — An L2 card counts as correct only with all four elements; without the consequence or the qualifier, score it as a miss and move it back to box 1.

docs.title: A two-week review schedule
docs.text:
The schedule front-loads breadth (every card seen once by day 5) and then shifts to retrieval of what you missed. Interleaving, mixing cards from different Parts in one sitting, feels harder than drilling one Part, and that difficulty is the point: in a meeting, questions arrive in no particular order.

flowchart TD
    A["Day 1: Parts 1-2 first pass"] --> B["Day 2: Part 3 first pass"]
    B --> C["Day 3: Box 1 misses + Part 4"]
    C --> D["Day 4: Part 5 first pass"]
    D --> E["Day 5: Parts 6-7 + strategy set"]
    E --> F["Day 6: Box 1 misses, all Parts"]
    F --> G["Days 7-8: Box 2 shaky cards, shuffled"]
    G --> H["Day 9: reread chapters from the weak-area table"]
    H --> I["Days 10-12: Box 1 daily, Box 2 on day 11"]
    I --> J["Day 13: Box 3 solid cards, shuffled"]
    J --> K{"Day 14: 50 random cards, 20 min: 90% or better?"}
    K -->|Yes| L["Maintenance: Box 3 monthly, refresh after earnings"]
    K -->|No| M["Repeat days 9-14 on missed Parts"]

Figure 59.6 — A suggested 14-day plan: five days of first passes, nine days of spaced, interleaved retrieval, ending in a timed mixed test.

The box rules are simple enough to run with a pen and the card numbers:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Box1: first miss
    [*] --> Box2: first hit
    Box1 --> Box2: correct
    Box2 --> Box3: correct
    Box2 --> Box1: missed
    Box3 --> Box1: missed
    Box3 --> Retired: correct twice in a row

Figure 59.7 — Leitner-style boxes: a miss always sends a card back to daily review, so effort concentrates where recall is weakest.

docs.title: Diagnosing weak areas
docs.text:
Score by Part, not just in total. A miss cluster usually points to one missing mental model, and rereading the chapter that builds it is faster than drilling the cards that depend on it.

docs.title: Part 1 — Storage fundamentals
docs.text:
The Part 1 cards cover the physics and arithmetic that every later argument reuses: the memory–storage wall, NAND wear, FTL overheads, tail latency, data-reduction ratios and rebuild time.

Chapter Cards (L1 / L2) Card numbers Ch 1 6 (3 / 3) Q1–Q6 Ch 2 6 (2 / 4) Q7–Q12 Ch 3 6 (3 / 3) Q13–Q18 Ch 4 6 (3 / 3) Q19–Q24 Ch 5 6 (2 / 4) Q25–Q30 Ch 6 7 (4 / 3) Q31–Q37

Figure 59.9 — Part 1 — Storage fundamentals: 37 cards over 6 chapters (17 L1, 20 L2), numbered Q1–Q37; use the card numbers to log misses by chapter.

Q1. What are the three jobs of any storage system? Keep bytes safely, find them again, and serve them fast enough. Every product trades those three jobs against cost per terabyte. ([Ch 1](../01-storage-fundamentals/01-what-storage-does.md)) Q2. Name the three ways to address stored bytes, and say who owns the meaning in each. Block uses numbered blocks and the host owns the meaning. File uses paths in a tree and the storage system owns the file system. Object uses flat keys plus metadata over HTTP (S3). ([Ch 1](../01-storage-fundamentals/01-what-storage-does.md)) Q3. (L2) Why do storage buyers split by workload rather than by technology? DBAs and VM admins buy block, research and HPC groups buy file, and cloud-native, data and AI teams increasingly buy object. Each group has its own criteria and budget, so the abstraction decides who buys. ([Ch 1](../01-storage-fundamentals/01-what-storage-does.md)) Q4. What distinguishes primary, secondary and archive tiers? The job a copy does. Primary serves live applications, secondary holds backup and recovery copies, and archive keeps data for years at the lowest cost. ([Ch 1](../01-storage-fundamentals/01-what-storage-does.md)) Q5. (L2) Why is AI blurring the old block/file/object map? Training data needs file-like speed at object-like scale, and cold archives are being reheated as training sets. That opens room for flash vendors and AI-native challengers. ([Ch 1](../01-storage-fundamentals/01-what-storage-does.md)) Q6. (L2) How wide is the hot-to-cold cloud price gap? S3 Standard at US$0.023 per GB-month against Glacier Deep Archive at US$0.00099 is about 23×. A petabyte for a month costs roughly US$23,000 hot and US$990 cold. ([Ch 1](../01-storage-fundamentals/01-what-storage-does.md)) Q7. What is the memory–storage wall? The ~1,000× latency step between memory tiers (~100–400 ns; HBM is ~350 ns from the GPU, a bandwidth tier rather than a latency one) and NAND (~50–150 µs). Most storage-system design is about hiding it. ([Ch 2](../01-storage-fundamentals/02-media-physics.md)) Q8. (L2) Why does NAND need a flash translation layer at all? NAND programs pages but erases only whole blocks, and every cell wears out after a finite number of P/E cycles. Something must remap writes, reclaim space and level wear. ([Ch 2](../01-storage-fundamentals/02-media-physics.md)) Q9. (L2) Why is QLC harder to use than SLC? Each extra bit per cell roughly halves the voltage margin. QLC's 16 states make it cheaper per bit but slower, less durable and more fragile, so it works in enterprise only when software turns small random writes into large sequential ones. ([Ch 2](../01-storage-fundamentals/02-media-physics.md)) Q10. Define a P/E cycle and DWPD. A P/E cycle is one program/erase of a NAND block, the unit of flash wear. DWPD is the number of full drive writes per day the drive can sustain over its warranty. ([Ch 2](../01-storage-fundamentals/02-media-physics.md)) Q11. (L2) What should you ask for instead of a NAND layer count? Bit density per mm². Leading 3D NAND went from 24 layers in 2013 to 400+ in 2026, and scaling has moved from lithography to layers and now to bonding. ([Ch 2](../01-storage-fundamentals/02-media-physics.md)) Q12. (L2) How did the 2026 shortage change the flash-versus-disk argument? Enterprise flash cost about 18–23× disk per TB in 2026, up from ~6–10×. "Flash replaces disk" now rests on power, density and operations, not purchase price. ([Ch 2](../01-storage-fundamentals/02-media-physics.md)) Q13. What is an SSD, architecturally? A small computer wrapped around NAND. A controller SoC with Arm cores, ECC engines and 8–16 flash channels runs firmware that makes erase-before-write NAND look like a simple disk. ([Ch 3](../01-storage-fundamentals/03-inside-an-ssd.md)) Q14. (L2) Why do the largest QLC drives map 16 KB indirection units? At 4 KB granularity the FTL map needs about 1 GB of DRAM per TB. A 16 KB unit shrinks the map on a 245.76 TB drive from ~240 GB to ~60 GB, but a 4 KB write then costs 4× NAND writes before GC. ([Ch 3](../01-storage-fundamentals/03-inside-an-ssd.md)) Q15. What is write amplification (WAF)? NAND writes per host write. Garbage collection copies live pages to reclaim stale ones, and those extra writes are the amplification. ([Ch 3](../01-storage-fundamentals/03-inside-an-ssd.md)) Q16. What is over-provisioning (OP)? Spare flash the host never sees. It gives garbage collection room to work and is the main lever against write amplification. ([Ch 3](../01-storage-fundamentals/03-inside-an-ssd.md)) Q17. (L2) How does over-provisioning buy endurance? In the chapter's illustrative random-write model, WAF falls from ~7.8 at 7% OP to ~2.1 at 37% OP. That is most of the gap between read-intensive and mixed-use drives built from the same NAND. ([Ch 3](../01-storage-fundamentals/03-inside-an-ssd.md)) Q18. (L2) What is "log-on-log", and why does it matter to Everpure? A log-structured array on top of SSDs duplicates the drive's FTL: a second map, a second spare area and a second, unscheduled garbage collector. ZNS, FDP and DirectFlash are three answers to that waste. ([Ch 3](../01-storage-fundamentals/03-inside-an-ssd.md)) Q19. How are IOPS, throughput and latency related? Throughput = IOPS × I/O size, and Little's law ties IOPS to latency through queue depth. A datasheet number means nothing without its I/O size, mix and queue depth. ([Ch 4](../01-storage-fundamentals/04-performance-and-economics-metrics.md)) Q20. What is tail latency (p99, p99.9)? The latency that the slowest 1% (or 0.1%) of requests exceed. ([Ch 4](../01-storage-fundamentals/04-performance-and-economics-metrics.md)) Q21. (L2) Why does latency hockey-stick? Past roughly 70% utilisation of the bottleneck, queueing dominates. The p99 and p99.9 blow up long before the average looks bad. ([Ch 4](../01-storage-fundamentals/04-performance-and-economics-metrics.md)) Q22. (L2) Why does the tail, not the mean, set application speed? Databases chain I/Os and GPU clusters synchronise thousands of workers, so the slowest request governs. If a request fans out to 100 servers that are each slow 1% of the time, 63% of requests hit a slow one. ([Ch 4](../01-storage-fundamentals/04-performance-and-economics-metrics.md)) Q23. Define raw, usable and effective capacity. Raw is the drive total. Usable is what remains after protection and reserves, typically 20–30% less. Effective is usable multiplied by an assumed data-reduction ratio. ([Ch 4](../01-storage-fundamentals/04-performance-and-economics-metrics.md)) Q24. (L2) In the chapter's TCO example, does flash beat disk for 10 PB of cold data? No. At 2026 prices all-flash costs ~3.2× hybrid disk over five years (~$429 vs ~$133 per effective TB; ~2.7× once disk's own 2026 price rise is included), reaching parity only with cheap NAND and ~4:1 reduction. Power and space are under 10% of TCO. ([Ch 4](../01-storage-fundamentals/04-performance-and-economics-metrics.md)) Q25. Name the four stacking data-reduction techniques. Pattern removal (zeros and fills), deduplication, similarity reduction (near-duplicates stored as deltas) and compression. DRR is logical data written ÷ physical capacity consumed. ([Ch 5](../01-storage-fundamentals/05-data-reduction.md)) Q26. What is content-defined chunking? Deduplication that sets chunk boundaries with a rolling hash over the content, so an insertion does not shift every later chunk. ([Ch 5](../01-storage-fundamentals/05-data-reduction.md)) Q27. (L2) Why does "the ratio belong to the data, not the array"? VDI reaches 12–20:1 and SQL Server 2–3:1, while JPEGs, encrypted volumes and most AI data sit near 1:1. The least reducible slice dominates a blend. ([Ch 5](../01-storage-fundamentals/05-data-reduction.md)) Q28. (L2) What separates DRR from "total efficiency"? Total efficiency adds thin provisioning and snapshots, inflating the headline with no change to the data. Pure Storage's datasheet separates ~5:1 average reduction from ~10:1 total efficiency. ([Ch 5](../01-storage-fundamentals/05-data-reduction.md)) Q29. (L2) What should you check in a data-reduction guarantee? The fine print. Dell (6:1), NetApp (4:1 SAN), HPE (4:1) and Everpure's workload-based Right-Size Guarantee mostly cover reducible data only and pay out in capacity. ([Ch 5](../01-storage-fundamentals/05-data-reduction.md)) Q30. (L2) Why is AI data the hard case for reduction? Images, tokens and BF16 checkpoints barely shrink with generic tools; format-aware BF16 compression saves about 33%. Similarity reduction (VAST, Purity DeepReduce) and format-aware compression are the attempted fixes. ([Ch 5](../01-storage-fundamentals/05-data-reduction.md)) Q31. What does a k+m erasure code survive, and what does 8+2 cost? Any m simultaneous failures. 8+2 costs 25% extra raw capacity; a very wide 146+4 stripe costs under 3%. ([Ch 6](../01-storage-fundamentals/06-data-protection-and-resilience.md)) Q32. What is declustered RAID? A layout that spreads stripes and spare space across all drives, so a rebuild reads from and writes to many drives at once. ([Ch 6](../01-storage-fundamentals/06-data-protection-and-resilience.md)) Q33. (L2) Why do 245 TB SSDs make rebuild time a strategic issue? Rebuilt onto a single spare at 1 GB/s, one takes about 68 hours, longer than a 30 TB hard drive did. Declustering over 100 drives, each reading ~4 GB/s for 8+2 stripes, delivers ~50 GB/s of rebuild output and cuts that to ~1.4 hours; dual parity covers the window. ([Ch 6](../01-storage-fundamentals/06-data-protection-and-resilience.md)) Q34. (L2) Why is synchronous replication confined to metro distances? It buys RPO = 0 by adding a round trip to every write, about 1 ms per 100 km of fibre. ([Ch 6](../01-storage-fundamentals/06-data-protection-and-resilience.md)) Q35. Define RPO and RTO. RPO is how much data you can afford to lose; RTO is how long you can afford to be down. ([Ch 6](../01-storage-fundamentals/06-data-protection-and-resilience.md)) Q36. What does 3-2-1-1-0 mean? Three copies, on two media, one off-site, one immutable, and zero errors on restore tests. ([Ch 6](../01-storage-fundamentals/06-data-protection-and-resilience.md)) Q37. (L2) How did ransomware turn storage into a security product? Recovery now depends on snapshots even an administrator cannot delete early, such as Everpure SafeMode (24-hour default eradication delay, up to 30 days on FlashArray), plus contractual recovery SLAs from Everpure, NetApp and Dell. ([Ch 6](../01-storage-fundamentals/06-data-protection-and-resilience.md))

docs.title: Part 2 — Protocols and networking
docs.text:
Part 2 cards test how bytes travel: block, file and object protocols, RDMA fabrics, the GPU data path and the interfaces underneath.

Chapter Cards (L1 / L2) Card numbers Ch 7 7 (3 / 4) Q38–Q44 Ch 8 7 (3 / 4) Q45–Q51 Ch 9 6 (3 / 3) Q52–Q57 Ch 10 6 (3 / 3) Q58–Q63 Ch 11 5 (2 / 3) Q64–Q68 Ch 12 6 (3 / 3) Q69–Q74

Figure 59.10 — Part 2 — Protocols and networking: 37 cards over 6 chapters (17 L1, 20 L2), numbered Q38–Q74; use the card numbers to log misses by chapter.

Q38. What two layers does every block protocol have? A command set (SCSI, then NVMe) and a transport (parallel cable, Fibre Channel, TCP/IP or RDMA), plus fabric services such as discovery. NVMe-oF carries NVMe over FC, RDMA or TCP. ([Ch 7](../02-protocols-and-networking/07-block-protocols.md)) Q39. What are NVMe's SQ, CQ and doorbell? The submission queue holds commands, the completion queue holds results, and a doorbell is the device register the host writes to announce new queue entries. ([Ch 7](../02-protocols-and-networking/07-block-protocols.md)) Q40. (L2) What is NVMe's real advantage over SCSI and AHCI? Its queue model: up to 65,535 I/O queues of up to 64K entries, one or more per core, with no shared lock. SATA AHCI tops out near 320K IOPS at 100 µs; NVMe concurrency reaches ~20M in the worked example. ([Ch 7](../02-protocols-and-networking/07-block-protocols.md)) Q41. (L2) Why is NVMe/TCP the enterprise default trajectory? It runs on any Ethernet NIC and every major OS and array, and adds only ~20–35 µs, small next to a flash read. ([Ch 7](../02-protocols-and-networking/07-block-protocols.md)) Q42. (L2) Why does NVMe over RoCE win AI back-ends? GPU servers already carry 400G RDMA NICs, and copy-free data movement (an RDMA adder of ~5–15 µs) keeps GPUs fed. ([Ch 7](../02-protocols-and-networking/07-block-protocols.md)) Q43. (L2) Is Fibre Channel dying? No. FC sales grew 6% in 2025 and 128G (Gen 8) launched in November 2025; most FC estates will move to NVMe/FC on the same hardware. ([Ch 7](../02-protocols-and-networking/07-block-protocols.md)) Q44. What is ANA? Asymmetric Namespace Access, NVMe's multipath mechanism for telling hosts the state of each path to a namespace. ([Ch 7](../02-protocols-and-networking/07-block-protocols.md)) Q45. How do file protocols differ from block protocols? They carry operations on names, not blocks; the server owns the namespace, locks and byte placement. NFS rules Linux and AI clusters, SMB rules Windows. ([Ch 8](../02-protocols-and-networking/08-file-protocols.md)) Q46. Contrast NFSv3 and NFSv4.x. NFSv3 is stateless. NFSv4.x is stateful, with leases, delegations and integrated locks; v4.1 added sessions and pNFS, v4.2 server-side copy and sparse files. ([Ch 8](../02-protocols-and-networking/08-file-protocols.md)) Q47. What is close-to-open consistency? NFS's rule that a client's writes become visible to others only after it closes the file and they reopen it. ([Ch 8](../02-protocols-and-networking/08-file-protocols.md)) Q48. (L2) What is classic NAS's "single head" problem? Each mount goes to one server, so every byte crosses one controller. A single NFS/TCP mount on 100 GbE gives ~2–2.5 GB/s, so feeding a 100 GB/s GPU server would take ~44 flows. ([Ch 8](../02-protocols-and-networking/08-file-protocols.md)) Q49. (L2) How does pNFS separate the control path from the data path? The client gets a layout from a metadata server, then does I/O directly and in parallel to the data servers. The Flex Files layout (2018) lets those data servers be plain NFSv3 servers. ([Ch 8](../02-protocols-and-networking/08-file-protocols.md)) Q50. (L2) Rank the fixes for single-head NAS from least to most disruptive. nconnect (up to 16 TCP connections per mount), RDMA, client multipath, pNFS, then a proprietary parallel client. ([Ch 8](../02-protocols-and-networking/08-file-protocols.md)) Q51. (L2) Which vendors bet on which parallel-file approach? Hammerspace, Everpure FlashBlade//EXA, Dell and NetApp bet on pNFS with the stock Linux client. VAST bets on its multipath NFS client; Lustre, GPFS and WEKA on proprietary clients. ([Ch 8](../02-protocols-and-networking/08-file-protocols.md)) Q52. What is S3, mechanically? A REST API over HTTP. Whole objects are PUT into a bucket under a key and fetched with GET; every request is signed (SigV4) and priced, and there are no directories, in-place edits or locks. ([Ch 9](../02-protocols-and-networking/09-object-storage-and-s3.md)) Q53. (L2) Why are LIST and small objects S3's weak spots? Folders are only key prefixes, and LIST pages through an index 1,000 keys at a time. Per-request fees can exceed the storage bill: storing 1 PB as 4 KB objects costs ~$1.25M in PUTs alone. ([Ch 9](../02-protocols-and-networking/09-object-storage-and-s3.md)) Q54. Since when has AWS S3 been strongly consistent? Since December 2020, for GET, PUT, LIST and DELETE. Other S3-compatible systems vary, especially across sites. ([Ch 9](../02-protocols-and-networking/09-object-storage-and-s3.md)) Q55. What are S3's multipart upload limits?
